stories.title: Historian Carl Berger offered a dramatic new understanding of Canada’s past
stories.summary: The University of Toronto professor wrote a groundbreaking pair of books considered key to the study of this country’s political mechanics and intellectual imagery
stories.author: Michael Valpy
stories.content:
Sometimes a nation’s story gets shaken in such a way as to make its teeth rattle. University of Toronto historian Carl Clinton Berger did just that in 1970. He turned the study of Canada’s past topsy-turvy with his book The Sense of Power: Studies in the Ideas of Canadian Imperialism, 1867-1914 . His book, as ordinary Canadians and academics came to see, was not really about Canadians’ attachment to imperialism. It was a masterful introduction to Canadian intellectual history, to the history of ideas and how they develop, spread and transform across time.

The book brought Prof. Berger to the finding that what he was really looking at was not an English-Canadian notion of imperialism but an English-Canadian notion of nationalism. And as historians Douglas Owram and Gerald Friesen wrote in the introduction to Thinkers and Dreamers , their 2011 collection of essays honouring Prof. Berger’s work, The Sense of Power had a huge impact on how Canadian history was thought about, put into words and taught.

The principles of intellectual history, Prof. Berger declared, did not exist in a vacuum; they needed to be understood within the context of their specific political, social, cultural and material environments. And as he laid bare these layers of intellectual history, Prof. Berger revealed that what he was looking at was not really imperialist thought with a maple sugar coating – it was Canadian nationalism.

His approach combined a narrative presentation of history – stories about what people said and thought about their country – with the body of literature dealing with technical historical matters, including techniques, theories and principles of historical research as well as the critical examination of material from primary and secondary sources subject to scholarly criteria.

The dust jacket of Prof. Berger’s book showed a two-cent Canadian stamp from Christmas 1898 (Prof. Berger was a serious stamp-collector), bearing a map of the globe with countries belonging to the then-British Empire coloured red. A big, red blob of Canada was shown at the map’s centre, with the inference that Canada would be a dominant partner in a reorganized British Empire. But really, what the story of the stamp reveals was Prof. Berger’s argument that allusions to imperialism were a form of Canadian nationalism taking place in the country’s intellectual discourse between the seminal dates of Confederation in 1867 and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914.

Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote in their introduction to Thinkers and Dreamers that whereas earlier work on political history in Canada was primarily limited to depictions of the ideas of politicians, the opinions of journalists and sometimes references to historiography (the study of how history is written and recorded by historians over time), Prof. Berger probed the thinking and utterances of a much broader swath of Canadians. He examined and recorded myths and legends that Canadians had about their country and looked into their origins. He used textual analysis and archival research to figure out what past writers and speakers actually meant to do with their words rather than judging them in the context of modern settings.

In his revisionist interpretation of what was largely considered to be a Canada glued to imperialist thinking, he assembled his findings into what Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote of as a lucidly constructed, carefully documented and stylishly written argument to the contrary.

It was the groundbreaking academic path he took for the rest of his career – nearly 40 years at University of Toronto – and on which he led others.

He followed The Sense of Power with his 1976 book The Writing of Canadian History: Aspects of English-Canadian Historical Writing, 1900-1970 , the first in-depth study of Canadian historiography, which garnered critical praise and won the Governor-General’s Award for non-fiction. He was also elected a Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada.

The two books together were unified by a similar preoccupation – the identity of Canada as revealed by its history – and together they examined the pronounced shift of thinking in Canada from British North American to North American, from one century to the next, and were described by academic historians as all that students of history needed to know about the political mechanics and intellectual imagery of how Canada worked.

Prof. Berger died in Toronto on Oct. 1 at the age of 87.

He was born on Feb. 25, 1939, in The Pas, Man., the son of a millworker. He did his undergraduate degree at the University of Manitoba where he proved to be a brilliant student, graduating with the university’s gold medal. He then went to University of Toronto to do a master’s degree in 1961 on a Woodrow Wilson Fellowship and, after obtaining his master’s degree, began a doctorate under the supervision of J.M.S. Careless, one of English Canada’s leading historians.

Carl Berger’s appearance at U of T as a graduate student and his appointment to its history department coincided with the rapid expansion of advanced Canadian historical studies – a heretofore neglected academic discipline – centred in Canada on work being done at U of T. And Prof. Berger’s chosen specialty, the Victorian period in Canada, alongside the framework for study he had built for his early writings, were among the major factors drawing students to the U of T’s program.

Prof. Berger had a tremendous ability to use the study of very specific, often quiet, elite organizations to paint a larger picture of what was being said and thought about in the country. This was not an easy task, as Prof. Owram and Prof. Friesen wrote.

Much intellectual history work foundered like snuffed candles because the chosen groups or organizations for academics to study did not illuminate larger responses. Prof. Berger’s work did not founder; it wasn’t snuffed. Both The Sense of Power and The Writing of Canadian History wrestle successfully with the way in which private groups tried to understand Canada.

“All written history is in a sense a form of autobiography and an essay of self-knowledge,” Prof. Berger once wrote.

Prof. Berger was a modest, private man who could also be wickedly funny. His approach to historical writing was founded on a deep sense of irony. (His close friend, the celebrated late York University historian Ramsay Cook, titled his essay on Prof. Berger for the Owram-Friesen book, Carl Berger: Ironic Man as Historian , and noted that in much of Prof. Berger’s written work, irony dripped from every page.)

Prof. Berger’s essay “The True North Strong and Free” in political scientist Peter Russell’s 1966 collection Nationalism in Canada begins with some truly outrageous purple poetry (“Hail! Rugged monarch, Northern Winter, hail!”) by William Henry Taylor.

The essay illustrates some of the appalling beliefs that many leaders of Anglo-Saxon Canadian society once held, weaving together racism and nationalism. The following passage, for example, looks at the writing of Upper Canada College headmaster George Parkin (1846-1922).

“[Parkin] asserted, we May attribute to the Anglo-Saxon race a unique aptitude for self-government. The special importance of the Canadian climate, therefore, was not merely that it sustained the hardy character of the stronger races, but that it also constituted, in Darwinian terms, ‘a persistent process of natural selection.’”

The essay, it needs to be pointed out, was referring to Canadian attitudes of the previous century and not to Prof. Berger’s own views (a perfect example of the mechanics of intellectual history referring to attitudes of the past often being starkly different from beliefs of the present).

“If Canadian nationalism is to be understood,” Prof. Berger wrote, “its meaning must be sought and appreciated in myths, legend and symbols.” And setting down his thoughts on the differences between French-Canadian and English-Canadian intellectuals, he wrote: “For both the French-Canadian nationalists and the English-Canadian imperialists, history had ordained a special avocation and nationalism was consecrated by the hand of God.”

Prof. Berger leaves his wife, Laurel Sefton MacDowell; his younger sister, Eileen; his daughters, Rachel Berger and Clare Barnett; stepchildren, Jen MacDowell and Lawrence MacDowell; five grandchildren and two stepgrandchildren.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

content_blocks.text: The essay illustrates some of the appalling beliefs that many leaders of Anglo-Saxon Canadian society once held, weaving together racism and nationalism. The following passage, for example, looks at the writing of Upper Canada College headmaster George Parkin (1846-1922).

“[Parkin] asserted, we May attribute to the Anglo-Saxon race a unique aptitude for self-government. The special importance of the Canadian climate, therefore, was not merely that it sustained the hardy character of the stronger races, but that it also constituted, in Darwinian terms, ‘a persistent process of natural selection.’”

The essay, it needs to be pointed out, was referring to Canadian attitudes of the previous century and not to Prof. Berger’s own views (a perfect example of the mechanics of intellectual history referring to attitudes of the past often being starkly different from beliefs of the present).

“If Canadian nationalism is to be understood,” Prof. Berger wrote, “its meaning must be sought and appreciated in myths, legend and symbols.” And setting down his thoughts on the differences between French-Canadian and English-Canadian intellectuals, he wrote: “For both the French-Canadian nationalists and the English-Canadian imperialists, history had ordained a special avocation and nationalism was consecrated by the hand of God.”

Prof. Berger leaves his wife, Laurel Sefton MacDowell; his younger sister, Eileen; his daughters, Rachel Berger and Clare Barnett; stepchildren, Jen MacDowell and Lawrence MacDowell; five grandchildren and two stepgrandchildren.

stories.title: Landmark Amazon union contract imposed in B.C.
stories.summary: About 800 workers in Delta, B.C. now covered by the first binding collective agreement for the retailing giant’s workers in North America, Unifor says
stories.author: Canadian Press Staff
stories.content:
A union representing about 800 Amazon workers in Delta, B.C., says they are now covered by the first binding collective agreement for the retailing giant’s workers in North America.

Unifor and Amazon both say an independent arbitrator imposed the terms of the three-year deal on Friday.

While the union hails the agreement, and workers who it says “stood up to one of the most powerful companies on Earth,” Amazon says it was imposed without giving workers a chance to vote on it.

Amazon vice-president J. Ofori Agboka says in an online posting that the process was “improper, unfair and defies common sense,” and the company would take its concerns to court if necessary.

Unifor says the agreement includes wage increases that bring hourly rates to $29 by its conclusion, enhanced severance protections and an additional week of vacation for workers with 10 years of service.

British Columbia’s Labour Relations Board ruled in August in favour of using binding arbitration to settle the labour dispute despite the e-commerce giant fighting the idea.

“Amazon told everyone a union contract would never happen, but workers proved them wrong,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said in a statement, praising the “courage” of workers.

Payne said Amazon “tried to convince workers that they were too big to organize and used their power and money to deter workers while making billions in profits.”

“They have fought every decision and tried to rewrite reality at every step but they have failed,” Payne said.

But Agboka said union dues meant the workers “could actually take home less money than they did before.”

“Our associates weren’t allowed to vote on whether to accept it, which has become an unfortunate pattern with the British Columbia Labour Relations Board,” he said.

He added that Amazon believed the best workplace was “one where associates have direct input and we work together to make progress quickly, and where nobody should have to pay dues or go through a third party to be heard.”

stories.title: Brother of man set on fire testifies at murder trial about alarming phone call with the accused
stories.summary: The brother of 29-year-old Jonathan Graham told a London Courtroom what went down in the moments before his sibling was set on fire on July 12, 2022.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The brother of 29-year-old Jonathan Graham told a London Courtroom what went down in the moments before his sibling was set on fire on July 12, 2022.

Shane Irwin called the accused in the early morning hours because they had all been friends.

He said there had been a number of disturbing text messages from 36-year-old Bradley Jourdrey.

It was shortly after Graham and Joudrey got into a physical altercation.

Irwin says the accused was upset after being punched saying that Joudrey told him, “I’m going to throw a fireball at Jon’s Jeep.”

Irwin says he was concerned, “I worried about my brother Jon.”

The Crown’s theory is that both the victim and the accused would eventually meet minutes after the confrontation at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street in east London.

Gasoline would be found on the from seat of the white Jeep which was owned by the victim.

Graham would be set on fire and die from the thermal injuries that he suffered.

The court has heard that Joudrey would race away from the scene and crash his Dodge vehicle.

He would be arrested within hours and has pled not guilty to first degree murder.

Later under cross-examination from defence Alexandra Mamo, the witness was questioned about the intentions of the accused.

Mamo asked, “He didn’t say anything about wanting to hurt Jonathan or kill Jonathan? And Irwin replied, “No, he did not.”

The Crown’s case resumes next week.

stories.title: Ottawa, Ontario working on package to persuade Stellantis to cancel sale of Brampton plant
stories.summary: Ministers say they will present new scenarios, worked out with Unifor, to company’s global CEO Antonio Filosa
stories.author: Jason Kirby
stories.content:
The federal and Ontario governments are offering new funding and production options to Stellantis NV Stla-N to persuade the company not to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant, just a day after Industry Minister Mélanie Joly threatened to sue the automaker to recover hundreds of millions of dollars in subsidies.

Ms. Joly said Friday the governments, along with the union representing workers at the plant, have put “an aggressive package” in front of Stellantis, adding the parties remain “in solution mode to prevent the sale” of the idled factory to defence contractor Roshel Inc.

That sale was announced Monday and is expected to close by the end of the year.

Ms. Joly and Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli spoke at an auto-sector funding announcement in Vaughan, Ont. They said they will present new scenarios, worked out with Unifor, to Stellantis global chief executive officer Antonio Filosa. That plan came out of a meeting on Thursday between the two governments, the union and Stellantis Canada CEO Trevor Longley.

No date has been set for the meeting with Mr. Filosa.

Mr. Fedeli said a $2.5-billion federal-provincial auto fund would be “part of the solution, not all of it.” The fund, announced last month as part of an $8.7-billion plan to help tariff-hit industries, is meant to pay for automotive capital projects over two years.

In return, he said, the governments want Stellantis to “buy some time” for the idled plant.

“When you sell an auto plant, it’s gone, it’s not going to come back,” Mr. Fedeli said. “We have new funds that we can help keep a warm plant until we look for something that we can put in there.”

He pointed to General Motors’ plant in Oshawa, Ont., which stopped building vehicles in 2019. At the time, Unifor pressed GM to keep the facility running rather than sell it. The company later brought in Chevrolet Silverado production, and Mr. Fedeli said about 1,800 people now build the pickups there.

Along with the offer, Ottawa is still threatening to sue. On Thursday, it served Stellantis with a notice of default on a 2022 agreement. Under that deal, Ottawa committed up to $529-million to help retool the Brampton and Windsor, Ont., plants to build electric vehicles.

Ms. Joly’s letter to Stellantis gave the company 30 days to fix the breaches, which include halting Jeep Compass production in Brampton, and failing to name a replacement vehicle. If the company continues with the assembly plant sale, Ms. Joly warned, it could face penalties, including repaying all or part of the funding it received, plus interest.

Stellantis said Thursday it intends to repay only $24-million it said it received for the Brampton retooling. Ms. Joly rejected that offer.

“Documents are clear, contracts also are clear,” she said. “The Brampton facility of Stellantis is linked to the Windsor plant and the battery investment, and that’s why I continue to say Stellantis is on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars.”

Ottawa has leverage because Stellantis asked for public money to support its investment in Brampton, Windsor and the battery plant, she said, adding the government also wants to protect the roughly 10,000 jobs in Windsor.

Ontario’s share of the 2022 deal with Stellantis was roughly $500-million, including $132-million earmarked for Brampton. However, ON Friday Mr. Fedeli said the province’s investment in Brampton was “zero. We’ve not advanced any funds to Brampton, period.”

He said the province has so far advanced $55-million in Windsor, where Stellantis “built the plant they said they’d build.”

Unifor national president Lana Payne sounded less hopeful after Thursday’s meeting with federal and provincial officials and the company’s local head. She said she did not hear the governments commit to using their levers to reverse the sale.

“The sale has occurred, so we would have to reverse it, which is doubly difficult, obviously,” she told reporters.

Retooling at Brampton began in early 2024. Stellantis paused its plan to build the Compass there in February 2025, weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office and threatened to impose tariffs on Canadian goods. The company later moved Compass production to Illinois, and more than 2,000 Brampton workers were laid off.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Feds tout programs helping London manufacturers build resilience to U.S. tariffs
stories.summary: A London manufacturer is investing in new technology and expanding into new markets after U.S. tariffs slashed its business by 10 per cent.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
A London manufacturer is investing in new technology and expanding into new markets after U.S. tariffs slashed its business by 10 per cent.

Attica Manufacturing employs more than 70 people at its London CNC machine shop, where increasingly sophisticated equipment is helping the locally-owned family business compete for contracts in Canada and around the world.

Rather than retreat during challenging economic times, the company reinvested with an eye on diversifying its customer base.

“The introduction of new technology and new equipment has opened up markets in aerospace space, satellite componentry. It enhances our defense sector and certainly opens up mining (and) energy,” explained owner Andy Mavrokefalos.

During a tour, Canada’s Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Innovation Evan Solomon was shown how a federal investment of $750,000 supported the acquisition of state-of-the-art equipment.

“The kinds of machines that you’re seeing around us are the most innovative machines. So a company like Atticus can compete, stay innovative, win contracts around the world and keep this workforce building,” said Solomon.

A tax policy change called the productivity mega-deduction will also allow businesses to deduct certain equipment costs immediately, rather than spreading the deduction over many years.

“It’ll not just stabilize, but allow businesses like Attica to be able to pivot and see extra growth beyond the tariff attack,” said London West MP Arielle Kayabaga.

Defence manufacturing is expected to account for a growing share of Attica’s business.

London Centre MP Peter Fragiskatos explained, “About 30 per cent of the business here is comprised of making products for the defense sector. And you’re going to see that increased to 50 per cent in coming years, all of which tells a story about changes that are happening in the Canadian economy. Manufacturing continues to thrive. It’s just looking different.”

The federal government’s recent purchase of an additional 190 armoured vehicles from London-based General Dynamics Land Systems (Gdls) has generated more work for Attica and other businesses in sectors hit hard by U.S. tariffs.

“Investment in our defense, in a company like Gdls, that creates the demand signal, that creates more customers, more resilience and more sovereign control. So it’s all connected,” said Solomon.

Kayabaga added, “Businesses like Gdls have been able to begin to work with Canadian steel, we want to see that in mass production, and that’s what we’re working towards.”

For Fragiskatos, the response to the latest economic challenges reflects London’s manufacturing history.

“Particularly from the 1980s through the 1990s and through the 2008 financial crisis, what’s defined our community is resilience,” said Fragiskatos.

After 50 years as a family business, Attica Manufacturing sees a promising future making complex parts for customers in Canada-- and around the world.

“My next generation is also involved in the business, and that gives them hope that this will continue into their future,” said Mavrokefalos.

stories.title: Danielle Smith says she’ll call up UCP officials not signing anti-separatism pledge
stories.summary: Danielle Smith said it's not an issue of free speech and she wants the United Conservative Party to work as a team to win next year's provincial election.
stories.author: Jack Farrell
stories.content:
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says she plans to call officials in her United Conservative Party who are refusing to sign a pledge to stop advocating for Alberta separatism .

Smith says it’s not an issue of free speech and that she wants the UCP to work as a team to win next year’s provincial election.

Some party officials have refused to sign an agreement to publicly respect the results of last month’s referendum, when Albertans voted against holding a binding separation vote.

The CBC reported that all 87 UCP constituency association presidents have been asked by the party’s executive director to sign the new code of conduct by the end of Friday.

But 15 say in a letter that they won’t be signing the pledge and argue the requirement amounts to the party punishing them for free speech.

Smith says she’ll be speaking with those who refuse but didn’t say whether they would be removed from their roles.

stories.title: Ottawa’s Rideau Canal Skateway could get artificial freezing
stories.summary: National Capital Commission is looking into using cooling pipes to help freeze 900-metre stretch of rink
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler
stories.content:
The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in the coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city’s Winterlude festival.

A feasibility study investigating the option of using refrigeration pipes to help freeze a 900-metre stretch of the canal in Ottawa’s downtown is currently under consideration by the National Capital Commission.

The project would cover just over 10 per cent of the skateway. The rest would still rely on the co-operation of nature.

The NCC is the capital’s public lands planner and manages the cultural character of the area. It manages the Rideau Canal Skateway as a part of a parliamentary mandate.

Tobi Nussbaum, NCC chief operating executive officer, told CBC Radio’s Ottawa Morning show this week the study recommends using refrigeration pipes embedded in concrete – a system similar to the ones used to freeze many outdoor rinks.

Bruce Devine, the Ncc’s senior manager of facilities and programs, told The Canadian Press that if the project proceeds, it would be costly.

“It’s significant. It will be in the millions. We will be looking for funding from a federal program. Other sources of funding will be researched,” he said.

He said the number of days the canal is open could triple if the plan goes ahead, but it wouldn’t happen until after 2030.

Devine said an emphasis would be placed on reducing the project’s carbon footprint.

“If such a system is feasible, the project would be aiming for carbon neutrality. And this is true by identifying opportunities to recover and reuse the heat. So that’s a principle that we have with this project,” he said.

The Skateway first opened in 1971 when the NCC cleared a small portion of ice on the canal for skating. It has since expanded to become the world’s largest skating rink, offering 7.8 kilometres of ice for people to enjoy.

The NCC says it sees 19,000 visitors daily during the winter months.

The Skateway is also a popular feature of Ottawa’s Winterlude festival, which hosts an average of 500,000 visitors over about two-and-a-half weeks every February.

In 2023, one of the warmest winters on record kept the Skateway from opening at all for the first time in its history. In 2024, another warmer-than-usual winter meant it could open for just 10 days.

Devine says a plan to ensure at least some of the Skateway can open each year could drive tourism at the Unesco World Heritage site.

“I think people will be able to make a clear decision as to which day they would like to come and plan around their visits. That will be known information, ‘Definitely, I can skate and it’s not weather-permitted.’ So no, I think it’s going to sustain and help tourism,” he said.

The Weather Network says this winter is expected to be warmer than the average.

stories.title: CFL players invited to Canadian flag football camp
stories.summary: Tyrell Ford and Tyson Philpot won't have much down time after playing in the Grey Cup game Sunday.
stories.author: Dan Ralph
stories.content:
Calgary – Tyrell Ford and Tyson Philpot won’t have much down time after playing in the Grey Cup game Sunday.

Ford will be looking to give the Edmonton Elks their first CFL title since 2015 while Philpot and the Montreal Alouettes will chase their second championship since 2023.

But both were among 20 CFL players invited to Football Canada’s first-ever professional national flag team camp in Chula Vista, Calif., from Nov. 29 to Dec. 5. The gathering is to educate the pro players on the rules and nuances of flag football.

Canada’s men’s and women’s flag teams both qualified for 2028 Los Angeles Games last year. The women punched their ticket by winning the world championship in Germany while the men were third in their event.

The Canadian men’s team is coached by Paul LaPolice, a longtime CFL coach. Flag Football will make its Olympic debut in Los Angeles. Both the CFL and NFL will allow their players to participate in the Games.

“Our goal was simple _ give CFL players the opportunity to pursue their dreams of representing their country,” CFL commissioner Stewart Johnston said. “Thanks to the collaboration of our clubs and the Cflpa, that opportunity now exists.

“This is a meaningful step for our players and for the growth of the game in Canada.”

Ford and Philpot both have twin brothers playing in the CFL _ Jalen Philpot is a receiver with the Calgary Stampeders while Tre Ford is a quarterback with the Hamilton Tiger-Cats. Both Fords and Philpots were selected to the camp.

Ford, who had a CFL-high seven interceptions this season, was one of nine defensive backs selected. The others were: Alonzo Addae (Ottawa); Cristophe Beaulieu (B.C.); Malcolm Bell (Hamilton); Tevaughn Campbell (Saskatchewan); Jackson Findlay (B.C.); Adrian Greene (Calgary); Ashton Miller-Melancon (Calgary); and Stavros Katsantonis (Hamilton).

Joining the Philpots at receiver are: Nic Demski (Winnipeg); Samuel Emilus (Saskatchewan); Justin McInnis (B.C.); Kevin Mital (Toronto); Kian Schaffer-Baker (Saskatchewan); and Keelan White (Ottawa).

Tyson Philpot led the CFL in catches (124), yards (1,809) and was tied with teammate Tyler Snead for most TDs (13). Philpot set single-season records for receptions and yards by a Canuck in being named the league’s top Canadian.

Nathan Rourke of the B.C. Lions and Taylor Elgersma of the Winnipeg Blue Bombers were the other quarterbacks selected.

David Mackie, executive director of the CFL Players’ Association, said the union fully supports its players taking to the flag game.

“I think it’s a fantastic opportunity for our membership,” he said. “But the key word is opportunity, they still have to earn their spot on the roster.

“It’s going to provide tremendous visibility for those members, the stars of the game, but the league as well. To have CFL players on the world stage at the Olympics would just be amazing for both the players and league.”

The CFL and its nine member teams have agreed on the players being available for national team participation. They’ve also come to terms with the Cflpa regarding insurance coverage and health benefits for all participating players while attending camp.

“Those players will be protected,” Mackie said. “If they were to get hurt they’ll be taken care of as if it was a CFL injury.

“The clubs are willing to take that risk.”

The Los Angeles Games will be held during the CFL regular season but Johnston doesn’t believe the league will halt play during the Olympics.

“Right now, there is no plan to pause our season,” he said. “We think our league and our teams are strong enough to play through the Olympics.

“The Olympic teams, let’s face it, they’re not large teams (10 total players) so this won’t be a huge portion of our players. We think with creative scheduling of our bye weeks we can mitigate the impact of some of our stars potentially missing some games.”

Union president Solomon Elimimian said CFL players participating in the L.A. Games will continue to be paid by their pro clubs.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

ByJoshua Smith Staff Reporter

U.S. flights going to and from Toronto Pearson International Airport have been halted amid a nationwide grounding of planes south of the border.

“There are currently no scheduled U.S.-bound departures or arrivals at this time,” due to the U.S.-based Federal Aviation Administration’s halting of American flights,Pearson airport’s social media account posted just before 5 p.m. Friday.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them. — Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 13, 2026

The FAA grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centres. The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

stories.summary: Vancouver - The judge in the trial of author Steven Galloway’s defamation lawsuit has cautioned that testimony from a University of British Columbia official can’t refer to “rumours and innuendo” about Galloway.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - The judge in the trial of author Steven Galloway’s defamation lawsuit has cautioned that testimony from a University of British Columbia official can’t refer to “rumours and innuendo” about Galloway.

Nov. 13, 2026

By Darryl Greer The Canadian Press

Justice Neena Sharma says potentially inadmissible and prejudicial evidence could come out in the testimony of Gage Averill, dean of arts at the time Galloway was suspended from the university in 2015 amid unproven allegations of sexual assault from a former student.

Galloway accuses the former student, with whom he had an affair, and others of spreading defamatory allegations.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Averill, now a provost of the university, was set to testify in the afternoon.

Galloway says the allegations by the ex-student known as A.B. are false and ended up ruining his writing career, and the court heard that Averill had to be legally compelled by a subpoena to testify at the trial.

Sydney Gomez, a lawyer for A.B., told the court that factors that caused the university to publish a statement about Galloway’s suspension were of “fundamental importance” to her defence.

A.B., whose name is under a publication ban, is not testifying at the trial and is not defending her allegations against Galloway as true.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: AI could escape human grasp within 6 months, Canadian Nobel winner warns European leaders
stories.summary: Future fears about AI agents could include developing killer robots, taking control of critical infrastructure and engineering pandemics
stories.author: Stewart Lewis
stories.content:
Artificial intelligence could soon grow beyond the controlling grasp of humans.

That’s the dire warning that professor Geoffrey Hinton, Nobel Prize winner and professor emeritus in the University of Toronto computer science department, is set to deliver to European leaders at an AI summit in Dublin, reports the Daily Mail.

Hinton didn’t believe that would be possible for a few years. However, after sitting through this year’s AI Safety Foundation’s “Hinton Lectures” at U of T this week, he changed his tune. The conclusion of Hinton lecturer and AI researcher Paul Christinao is that this frightening benchmark May occur within three years, even six months.

“That’s terrifying,” Hinton said during a discussion after one of the lectures. “I’m going to actually tell a bunch of government leaders that on Friday, and we’ll see how they react,” he said during a discussion at the conclusion of one of the lectures.

Christiano, an American AI researcher, is the founder of the Alignment Research Centre. Previously, he worked at OpenAI and has been heavily involved in AI safety standards.

His set of three lectures presented at U of T this year looked at AI risk, its behaviour, maintaining control of “self-improving AI,” as well as how scientific oversight, shared safety standards and international cooperation could help manage the risks.

Not long ago, AI was simply attempting to write fluid sentences, Christiano remarked during one of his lectures, but, he added, more recently it has solved some of the world’s most complex math problems.

As its development becomes more rapid, future fears about AI agents, Christiano said, include developing new weapons like killer robots, taking control of critical infrastructure and engineering biological threats, such as pandemics.

He thinks there “is a high risk of an AI takeover within the next three years. What I mean by an AI takeover is a system situation where there are AI systems pursuing goals, and those systems call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots in what happens on Earth, and where if, say you or me or Donald Trump, wanted to stop them, they would be as ineffective as if you or me (were) trying to stop the U.S. military.

Christiano suggests alarmingly that “many people would die during that transition, or that many people would die shortly thereafter, if we were unable to maintain a habitable environment.” Alternatively, he says a takeover would be the end of human self-determination, “something we should be working incredibly hard to avoid.”

Christiano spoke about the prospect of billions of superhuman AI systems, with “much, much more capacity than any state cyber program” and about opportunities to undermine human control.

A common suggestion for halting AI is to simply turn it off, but Christiano says that’s not so simple. He says it will be hard to know if it’s ours or the the other guy’s AI that has has gone awry. Shutting down could be dangerous, or at least costly, if there is a lot of infrastructure that is running on AI, he adds.

The response to AI’s rapid development has to be a public one, he says. “So I think a goal of transparency is both to understand what is happening, and then for hard scientific questions to understand that the relevant evidence is available publicly for independent review.”

He argues that existing law May provide governments with some power to intervene to control AI development and there’s the prospect of passing new laws. “You should think of them as taking steps like empowering a regulator to actually turn what are industry best practices into binding requirements.”

However, he understands that there is a certain amount of fear involved in applying the brakes and getting entrenched in regulating.

If you are “looking at how you’re going to regulate this technology, you naturally fear falling behind if you slow down. (There is a) concern that if we were to impose safety requirements, it would cause us to fall second place. I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”

As a result, he affirms the idea that AI development needs to slow down. “My view is now we should probably slow down immediately until we actually have the infrastructure to slow down later, right? Until we have a high enough degree of security, governance, risk management that we are able to detect and react to future risks as they emerge.”

“If it’s super intelligent, it’s not going to be you controlling it,” he said during a conversation at the conclusion of the lecture series. “It’s going to be smarter than us. People haven’t really absorbed that. Once you absorb that, my own feeling is that our best hope is to make it like us.

“One thing that seems clear to me is that no government wants AI to take over, so their interests are actually aligned on preventing AI from taking over.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

If you are “looking at how you’re going to regulate this technology, you naturally fear falling behind if you slow down. (There is a) concern that if we were to impose safety requirements, it would cause us to fall second place. I think that is one of the most likely ways that we end up in an extremely bad situation.”

As a result, he affirms the idea that AI development needs to slow down. “My view is now we should probably slow down immediately until we actually have the infrastructure to slow down later, right? Until we have a high enough degree of security, governance, risk management that we are able to detect and react to future risks as they emerge.”

“If it’s super intelligent, it’s not going to be you controlling it,” he said during a conversation at the conclusion of the lecture series. “It’s going to be smarter than us. People haven’t really absorbed that. Once you absorb that, my own feeling is that our best hope is to make it like us.
“One thing that seems clear to me is that no government wants AI to take over, so their interests are actually aligned on preventing AI from taking over.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Expert insight: We found rare dinosaur tracks from the Coniacian age in British Columbia
stories.summary: The Coniacian dinosaur tracks were first found in Canada in 1988 but the remote nature of the site delayed further investigation until 2022.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Imagine the Western Plains of North America, from Texas to Alaska, submerged under a broad, shallow seaway. To the west lay the ancestral Rocky Mountains. To the east were low-lying plains traversed by large, sluggish rivers.

This was the landscape of North America in the mid-Cretaceous period – a geological age with a time span of 105 to 75 million years ago – when the global sea level was around 100 metres higher than it is now.

A high concentration of atmospheric carbon dioxide, due to massive volcanism, created a “greenhouse” climate such that Earth lacked significant polar ice caps. Alaska and Antarctica enjoyed temperate climates.

The record of dinosaur bones and tracks from this time in North America is sparse, especially from the Coniacian age – a sub-stage of this Cretacious period, spanning 89.75 to 86.5 million years ago.

We have discovered the first Canadian dinosaur tracks from this Coniacian age, in the Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern British Columbia.

One of us, Guy Plint, first noticed these tracks in 1988. However, the remote nature of the site, best accessed by helicopter, delayed further investigation until 2022 when, together, we were able to begin a more comprehensive study. The findings were recently published in Historical Biology.

The authors explore the Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern B.C., searching for dinosaur tracks. (Guy Plint)

North America has yielded an abundant record of dinosaurs, both skeletal material and tracks. Because dinosaur tracks can only be made and preserved in non-marine, terrestrial sediments, most North American tracks are found in sedimentary rocks laid down by rivers that drained the Rocky Mountains.

Their sediment load gradually built deltas and coastal plains along the Western margin of the Interior Seaway.

Over millions of years, the sea level slowly rose and fell, alternately narrowing and widening the coastal plain.

The late Cenomanian, Turonian, Coniacian and Santonian stages of the Cretaceous period – between about 95 and 84 million years ago – were times of exceptionally high net sea level when shorelines were pushed to the west, lapping against the foothills of the Rocky Mountains.

In Western Canada, Coniacian rocks are entirely marine with the exception of the small Tumbler Ridge area of northeastern British Columbia.

Ornithopods, or duck-billed dinosaurs, could stand on their hind legs. Here, the skeleton of a Hadrosaur duck-billed dinosaur is displayed in the Royal Ontario Museum in Toronto. (Wikimedia Commons/Thomas Quine)

Here, a river system built a delta that protruded eastward into the seaway. The deposits of that ancient delta are called the Marshybank formation, which, critically, includes some terrestrial strata that preserve the tracks we found.

In addition to these rocks of Coniacian age, the Tumbler Ridge area includes terrestrial deposits spanning much of the Cretaceous period. These have yielded an abundant and diverse record of other fossil vertebrate tracks.

These include traces of giant crocodiles, birds and pterosaurs, as well as abundant dinosaur tracks.

The Tumbler Ridge Museum is a repository and exhibition area for many examples of such tracks. The area was designated the Tumbler Ridge Unesco Global Geopark in 2014.

The Marshybank delta was very low-lying with shallow lakes, mires and floodplains traversed by sluggish, sinuous rivers. Abundant fossil roots attest to dense vegetation, and preserved tree stumps indicate stands of large trees, probably conifers like the dawn redwood.

River floods washed sand beyond the river banks to form thin sand sheets called crevasse splays.

The bottom surfaces of these splays preserve, as natural casts, a variety of dinosaur tracks, originally impressed in soft mud. The sandy banks of ancient river channels were also pervasively trampled by dinosaurs.

The most common tracks we found have three broad blunt toes and are typically 30 to 50 centimetres wide. These are ornithopod, or “duck-billed dinosaur” tracks. These large herbivores could walk on their hind legs, or shift to a quadrupedal gait.

The second most common track type has three, narrower and more elongated toes, tipped with claw impressions; we believe these to be carnivorous theropod dinosaur tracks.

We also found some rare rounded tracks with four or five indistinct digits, which might belong to ankylosaurian (“armoured”) dinosaurs.

The dinosaur tracks from the Marshybank Formation near Tumbler Ridge, which are mostly ornithopods, resemble a similar discovery from the contemporaneous Frontier Formation in southwestern Montana. They also have many elements in common with dinosaur fauna from the overlying Wapiti Formation (from 84 to 66 million years ago).

However, the ornithopod-dominated tracks of the Marshybank Formation differ markedly from those of the underlying Dunvegan Formation (97-95 million years ago) and Gates Formation (109-107 million years ago), which are dominated by ankylosaur tracks.

Fossil plants in the Marshybank strata include gymnosperms (for example conifers, cycads and ginkgos), ferns and horsetails. Most of the flora, however, are angiosperms (flowering plants) that May be distantly related to modern plane, poplar and willow trees, plus laurel, buckthorn, soapberry and low-growing shrubs and herbs.

Angiosperms evolved in tropical latitudes about 130 million years ago and spread rapidly to high latitudes, appearing in Alaska about 30 million years later.

Flowering plants provided a more nutritious and easily digested source of food than conifers, cycads and ferns. They were also faster-growing and better able to recover from cropping by dinosaurs.

The proliferation of the Coniacian herbivorous dinosaurs, particularly ornithopods, and the sustenance of the carnivores that preyed on them, is therefore related to the diversification and dispersal of flowering plants.Image 3: The Conversation

Guy Plint, Professor Emeritus, Earth Sciences, Western University and Charles Helm, Research Associate, African Centre for Coastal Palaeoscience, Nelson Mandela University

stories.title: Politics Insider: Stelco recalling 175 workers
stories.summary: Also, thoughts on why Eby lost and an update on the Darlington nuclear station
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Stelco Inc. is recalling 175 laid-off steel workers effective Dec 1., seemingly ending a faceoff that started in early fall between Ottawa and the company’s parent, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc.

Niall McGee reports that Hamilton-based Stelco announced in a statement today that sufficient demand from customers for its steel made the recall possible.

The restart of operations will take several weeks. All affected employees will be compensated retroactively for any pay missed while off the job, the company said.

Stelco announced on Sept. 28 that it was laying off up to 500 workers at its plants in Hamilton and Nanticoke, Ont., because of its inability to make money in its galvanized-steel business. Ottawa almost immediately alleged that Cliffs had violated a legally binding commitment to maintain employment levels in Canada after it acquired the Canadian steelmaker in 2024.

Eby seemed inauthentic during failed election campaign, former minister says: Brenda Bailey, who served as finance and jobs minister under David Eby, called last month’s crushing defeat of the NDP government in British Columbia a “harsh judgment” on the outgoing Premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.

Ottawa to invest $200-million in Woodfibre LNG project, source says: Owners Enbridge and Singapore-based Pacific Energy designed Woodfibre to produce 2.1 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas a year, all of which is contracted to BP.

Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?: Ontario Power Generation and Ontario’s government promised the refurbishment would position Darlington for 30 years of reliable service. It’s too early to know whether its recent unplanned outages amount to teething pains or indicate deeper reliability challenges of the sort that have plagued other refurbished stations featuring Candus, the country’s homegrown reactors.

Parliamentary break: Both the House of Commons and the Senate are on a break this week.

Prime Minister’s Day: Mark Carney was scheduled to arrive in Manila on Saturday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit, which he is attending as a guest of the chair. He is to meet with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., and hold a news conference. Carney is on a trip that began Wednesday and also includes stops in Dublin, Phnom Penh and the Chinese city of Shenzhen (for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Economic Leaders’ meeting). His trip concludes Thursday.

Party Leaders: In Ottawa, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May is scheduled to attend Saturday’s announcement of the results of the party’s contest to pick a new leader. No schedules released for other party leaders. On Saturday, NDP Leader Avi Lewis will be in Winnipeg to address a convention of the Manitoba NDP.

Ministers on the Road: With the House of Commons on a break, ministers continue to travel Canada, talking about the federal budget.

In the St. John’s-area municipality of Mount Pearl, Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson visited Solace Power . In the rural Nova Scotia community of Gaspereau, Justice Minister Sean Fraser talked about budget support for the Canadian wine sector.

In Thunder Bay, Public Safety Minister Gary Anandasangaree talked about budget measures to advance reconciliation with Indigenous Peoples. Northern Affairs Minister Rebecca Chartrand did the same in Winnipeg.

In Woodbridge, Ont., Industry Minister Mélanie Joly, accompanied by Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli, talked about the budget during an event. In Toronto, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne participated in a armchair discussion hosted by the Empire Club of Canada.

Two ministers were out in Calgary. Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty attended an event at the Mini Thni Subdivision at the Bearspaw First Nation and Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski talked about the operation of the Productivity Mega deduction .

And in Vancouver, Energy Minister Tim Hodgson and B.C. premier-designate Lorne Doerkson made a funding announcement for a liquefied natural gas project.

New job for Merrifield: Katy Merrifield, the campaign director for the B.C. Conservatives, is joining GT & Company as a partner for the public affairs consultancy. An announcement on LinkedIn said Merrifield will lead GT’s practice across British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan while advising clients on federal matters.

“You look at how the world sees Canada today, and I would say the most sought-after currency today is trust. Who can you trust in this world today where you have extreme volatility?” – Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne , in Toronto today.

The Green Party of Canada is set to name a new leader this weekend, succeeding Elizabeth May. How many leaders has the party had since it was founded in 1983?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Ottawa should adopt B.C.’s orphan port

For more than a century, private players have seen the advantages offered by the port of Prince Rupert. It is time Ottawa does the same. — The Globe and Mail Editorial Board

For an Anishinaabe jurist, the Canadian Museum for Human Rights’ Nakba exhibit gets a failing grade

The Canadian Museum for Human Rights has received piles of feedback about its small exhibition “Palestine Uprooted: Nakba, Past and Present” – both positive and negative. Perhaps the most surprising critique has not yet made it to its inbox. It’s a report by Anishinaabe scholar and retired justice Harry LaForme and his wife Janice LaForme, a lawyer, written for the Network of Engaged Canadian Academics (Neca), a non-partisan group of university and college faculty concerned about campus antisemitism. — Marsha Lederman, Columnist

Ottawa’s plan to sharpen oversight of banks’ anti-money-laundering efforts might work

Ottawa’s plan to designate Osfi as the primary supervisor of major banks’ anti-money laundering and anti-terrorist financing obligations could stem the rising tide of dirty money – but only if it does it the right way. — Rita Trichur, Columnist

Follow along for our stories on Canada-U.S. relations as news develops

Got a news tip that you’d like us to look into? E-mail us at tips@globeandmail.com . Need to share documents securely? Reach out via SecureDrop .

The answer to today’s question: The party has had 14 permanent and interim leaders, starting with Trevor Hancock.

stories.title: Shaping Saskatchewan: Naomi Lendvay
stories.summary: At just six years old, Naomi Lendvay was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma and was told she had just 12 months to live. Unexpectedly, a testing drug ended up killing her cancer.
stories.author: Chris Carr
stories.content:
At just six years old, she was in a battle for her life. Naomi Lendvay was diagnosed with Rhabdomyosarcoma and was told she had just 12 months to live.

Doctors started her on a ‘testing drug’ they hoped would extend her life. Unexpectedly, it ended up killing her cancer.

“Still to this day, we don’t know why, but I am very grateful it did, because I am still here to share my story,” said Lendvay.

Today, spends part of her time raising awareness and money for childhood cancer research. “Now I get to use my voice and inspire others to and help give others hope and make it, so others know what to fight for,” added Lendvay.

Lendvay recently shared her story with hundreds of people at the Synergy 8 Community Builders Drive for Kids Golf Tournament and Banquet. She said a mom reached out to her following the event to share her story about her child getting sick.

“When they went to the doctor, they were dismissive and not really taking in… the mother’s intuition. They knew something was wrong with their child. And that they were really sick,” said Lendvay. “She said she wouldn’t have fought as hard if she hadn’t have heard our story,” said Lendvay.

So, what does Lendvay think about the positive impact she’s having on others?

“I’m just glad we decided to take action and get the word out that kids get cancer too because it has probably really changed people’s lives, probably more than we know.”

Lendvay has since help raise more than $350,000 for cancer research.

stories.title: ‘How does space smell?’ Halifax students connect with Canadian astronaut aboard ISS
stories.summary: High school students in Halifax enjoyed the rare opportunity to chat with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk, direct from the International Space Station.
stories.author: David Murdock and Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
High school students in Halifax enjoyed the rare opportunity to chat with Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk , direct from the International Space Station.

Kutryk, a former CF-18 fighter pilot, is serving as a mission specialist during a six-month mission , as part of Nasa’s four-person Crew 13.

On Friday, students at École Secondaire du Sommet had the chance to quickly connect with the crew.

“I thought it was amazing to have an opportunity like this to talk to an astronaut. It’s not something I thought I’d ever see in my lifetime,” said student Marie Gooding.

The school had a small window of time to chat: just 10 minutes as the station whizzed overhead at 25 times the speed of sound.

“I think the most interesting answer would be the reply to how does space smell and from what I remember, he said it smelled like iron or metal, which is very interesting, I hadn’t expected that,” said Gooding.

“It has pushed me really to go into the sciences and now it makes me want to be like a doctor. So while I might not be going into the space domain, it does make me want to learn a lot more about how space works and the planets that surround us in our universe.”

The Ariss, or Amateur Radio on the International Space Station, program is run internationally by volunteers and lets students speak directly with astronauts in orbit using ham radio.

The program aims to inspire students to explore science, technology, engineering and math through hands-on radio projects.

“Science is not just in their classroom, it’s not just what they learn out of a textbook, it’s really bigger than that. So to see if they can start making connections between what they learned and what they see outside in the real world,” said science teacher, Karen Scarcella.

For students, the chance to connect with a real-life astronaut was eye-opening.

“This inspires me to enter in like a space agency of some kind but not actually going into space, maybe working like a scientist at Nasa or something similar,” said student Christopher Succar.

stories.title: Nova Scotia gives family doctors a dedicated billing code for menopause care
stories.summary: Move recognizes the time proper consultations require, advocates say
stories.author: Kristy Kirkup
stories.content:
Family physicians in Nova Scotia who have recognized expertise in women’s health can now apply a dedicated code for compensation when they offer reproductive and sexual health services, including perimenopause care.

After Manitoba, Nova Scotia is the second province in the country to create a distinct billing code for specialized women’s health services, a change some health experts say is necessary to recognize the added time and expertise required to support patients navigating hormonal transitions.

Doctors do not require a certificate of added competence in family medicine to bill the code.

“Previously it wasn’t feasible, I think, financially to do the care, which is a huge problem in and of itself,” said Sarah Fraser, a family doctor based in Halifax. “Now it’s actually possible, and I think it’s encouraging.”

Doctors across Canada have traditionally used general assessment and consultation codes for perimenopause and menopause care, rather than a specific billing code.

But advocates say dedicated codes recognize that this kind of care often requires longer appointments to allow doctors to review patient history, address a wide range of symptoms and discuss a treatment plan.

“When we have a billing code, it allows us as physicians to be appropriately compensated but, more importantly, to be able to give women the time to ask their questions, and for us to be able to provide enough time to make them feel validated and heard,” said Shafeena Premji, a Calgary-based menopause specialist and medical advisory board member of the Menopause Foundation of Canada.

In Alberta, more than 300 physicians and menopause practitioners signed a petition last December calling for a menopause-specific billing code under the province’s public insurance plan. The petition described the absence of the code as a “major barrier” preventing equitable care access.

“This is a dire issue,” Dr. Premji said. “The sooner we do it, the sooner we’re going to be able to support half of our population.”

Women typically reach perimenopause and menopause in their 40s and 50s. While these hormonal changes are considered a natural part of the aging process, some women struggle with debilitating symptoms – including hot flashes, mood disturbances and trouble sleeping – and face barriers when trying to obtain care.

The new code in Nova Scotia took effect in July. Previously, family physicians could apply a consult code for providing menopause care, but many felt the fee was not clearly defined, creating confusion about when it could be used.

In October 2023, Manitoba became the first Canadian jurisdiction to create a billing code to compensate doctors specifically for menopause visits. Since then, Doctors Manitoba says, tens of thousands of such appointments have been covered.

Physicians in Manitoba can claim $93.66 for each assessment and additional tests; follow-up care is also covered.

Doctors Manitoba says this coverage stands in contrast with the hundreds of dollars patients are often charged for assessments when they turn to health care providers outside the public system.

Omolayo Famuyide, a certified menopause practitioner who founded the Layo Clinic in Winnipeg, which offers women’s reproductive health care, described Manitoba’s menopause billing code as “groundbreaking,” saying it’s been beneficial for both doctors and patients.

Manitoba is also one of only two Canadian provinces, along with British Columbia, that publicly fund menopause hormone therapy.

In Ontario, Sheila Wijayasinghe is among the family physicians who support creating a dedicated code.

“We can do comprehensive care in the public system. It’s just that we are often stretched for time,” said Dr. Wijayasinghe, who practices in Toronto.

“If you give us a designated code that allows us and acknowledges that it takes extra time, this could be very helpful.”

This sentiment was echoed by Aimee Debow, a Toronto-based menopause coach whose company, Menovate, works with corporations supporting employees through menopause.

She believes a dedicated menopause billing code could have been “life-changing” and spared her several years of suffering.

In her early 40s, she experienced perimenopause symptoms, including sleep challenges and brain fog, but felt dismissed by doctors. After countless medical appointments, she turned to the private system, which she knows many women cannot afford.

“It’s not just a code. It’s a code that actually gives the doctor enough time to help the person,” Ms. Debow said.

“When we have a billing code, it allows us as physicians to be appropriately compensated but, more importantly, to be able to give women the time to ask their questions, and for us to be able to provide enough time to make them feel validated and heard,” said Shafeena Premji, a Calgary-based menopause specialist and medical advisory board member of the Menopause Foundation of Canada.

In Alberta, more than 300 physicians and menopause practitioners signed a petition last December calling for a menopause-specific billing code under the province’s public insurance plan. The petition described the absence of the code as a “major barrier” preventing equitable care access.
“This is a dire issue,” Dr. Premji said. “The sooner we do it, the sooner we’re going to be able to support half of our population.”

Women typically reach perimenopause and menopause in their 40s and 50s. While these hormonal changes are considered a natural part of the aging process, some women struggle with debilitating symptoms – including hot flashes, mood disturbances and trouble sleeping – and face barriers when trying to obtain care.

The new code in Nova Scotia took effect in July. Previously, family physicians could apply a consult code for providing menopause care, but many felt the fee was not clearly defined, creating confusion about when it could be used.

In October 2023, Manitoba became the first Canadian jurisdiction to create a billing code to compensate doctors specifically for menopause visits. Since then, Doctors Manitoba says, tens of thousands of such appointments have been covered.
Physicians in Manitoba can claim $93.66 for each assessment and additional tests; follow-up care is also covered.
Doctors Manitoba says this coverage stands in contrast with the hundreds of dollars patients are often charged for assessments when they turn to health care providers outside the public system.

Omolayo Famuyide, a certified menopause practitioner who founded the Layo Clinic in Winnipeg, which offers women’s reproductive health care, described Manitoba’s menopause billing code as “groundbreaking,” saying it’s been beneficial for both doctors and patients.
Manitoba is also one of only two Canadian provinces, along with British Columbia, that publicly fund menopause hormone therapy.
In Ontario, Sheila Wijayasinghe is among the family physicians who support creating a dedicated code.
“We can do comprehensive care in the public system. It’s just that we are often stretched for time,” said Dr. Wijayasinghe, who practices in Toronto.
“If you give us a designated code that allows us and acknowledges that it takes extra time, this could be very helpful.”
This sentiment was echoed by Aimee Debow, a Toronto-based menopause coach whose company, Menovate, works with corporations supporting employees through menopause.
She believes a dedicated menopause billing code could have been “life-changing” and spared her several years of suffering.

In her early 40s, she experienced perimenopause symptoms, including sleep challenges and brain fog, but felt dismissed by doctors. After countless medical appointments, she turned to the private system, which she knows many women cannot afford.
“It’s not just a code. It’s a code that actually gives the doctor enough time to help the person,” Ms. Debow said.

stories.title: Manitoba May need to spend far less on new power generation: Kinew
stories.summary: Winnipeg - Manitoba's premier says the province May need to spend far less than previously thought on new power plants.
stories.author: Ian Bickis The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wab Kinew says the Manitoba Public Utilities Board has concluded that one natural gas-fired turbine is needed for now, at a cost of about $1 billion.

The Crown corporation Manitoba Hydro has maintained that three turbines, costing $3 billion, are needed to meet peak demands within a few years.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The utilities board submitted its findings in a report to the government earlier this week, following lengthy hearings over the summer.

Kinew says Manitoba Hydro hasn’t seen the report yet, and he didn’t say when the government would make it public.

He says the news is good for both the province’s finances and the environment.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: U.S. grounds flights nationwide after air traffic control communication outage
stories.summary: The ​US Federal Aviation ‌Administration on Friday issued a national ground stop "due to ​extraordinary circumstance and ​reasons for safety."
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all departing flights nationwide after a communications failure hit air traffic control centres across the country, resulting in thousands of disrupted flights.

“The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centres,” the FAA told Global News in a statement.

It said technicians are investigating the issue and it will provide updates as they become available.

The ground stop order is affecting flights between the U.S. and Canada’s major airports.

In a statement posted to social media, Toronto Pearson International Airport said flights were “impacted” and “there are currently no scheduled U.S.-bound departures or arrivals at this time.”

Vancouver International Airport told Global News it was aware of a “nationwide technology issue” that forced the ground stop.

“As a result, YVR is seeing delays for U.S. bound departures as well as some international flights that would fly over the U.S. Domestic flights within Canada are not impacted,” it said.

Edmonton International Airport told Global News in a statement that it has seven flights bound for the U.S. set to depart by the end of the day. It said these flights could be impacted.

“As this is an evolving situation, passengers travelling to the United States today should check directly with their airline for the latest information on their flight before coming to the airport,” a spokesperson said.

Montreal-Trudeau International Airport said on social media that “all flights to and from the U.S. are suspended until further notice.”

A spokesperson for Calgary International Airport told Global News all U.S. bound flights are being held.

Spokespeople for Saskatoon International Airport and Regina International Airport told Global News they have no scheduled direct flights to the U.S. for the rest of the day Friday.

A spokesperson for Air Canada told Global News that flights to and from the Caribbean and South America May also be impacted.

“Any flights currently airborne have been advised they are permitted to continue,” they said in an email.

The disruption ​is the latest sign of strain on the US air traffic ​control system, which has been beset by equipment failures, communications problems and shortages of ‌controllers ⁠while the FAA tries to replace aging infrastructure.

Congress approved $12.5 billion for the overhaul last year, and the FAA and White House asked lawmakers on Friday for another $30.1 billion.

Shortly before the announcement, the FAA halted traffic ​in Chicago due to ​air traffic ⁠control communications issues. The agency said, “All departing traffic should remain groundstopped until further notice.” The FAA said it ​would manage international flights on a case-by-case basis.

Friday’s halt ​was the ⁠second nationwide ground stop of all departures since the September 11, 2001, attacks. The other happened in January 2023, when the FAA paused all domestic ⁠departures ​for less than two hours.

With files from Reuters

stories.title: With no age requirement, Sobey Award recognizes well-established artists
stories.summary: The work of the six regional finalists is displayed at the National Gallery of Canada
stories.author: Kate Taylor
stories.content:
It has been five years since the Sobey Art Award eliminated its 40-and-under age requirement, a bold move then followed by an eventual suppression of the word emerging in its criteria. You can see the results at the National Gallery of Canada in this year’s exhibition of work by the six regional finalists, five of whom are in their 40s and 50s. It’s a tight show, smaller than in some years, including several works produced by what are clearly long-standing careers.

Although the marketing now sometimes talks about artists at “a critical juncture in their careers,” this is not an exhibition that gives the viewer any new clues as to what the 24-year-old Sobey Award is actually recognizing. Is it a prize for mid-career artists? Or underrecognized artists? On the positive side, the show in Ottawa is full of convincing work.

First up, as you enter, is Caroline Monnet, representing Quebec. The child of a French father and Anishinaabe mother who made their living renovating houses in Gatineau, Monnet is already well known for her work using construction materials to create patterns inspired by her Indigenous heritage. There is a strong selection here of her wall pieces created by embroidering or marking on various housing membranes – one provocative work uses mould to create a pattern on gypsum board – as well as a ceramic sculpture, a striking black and white geometric shape, technically an icosahedron, or an object with 20 triangular faces.

Monnet works intelligently with issues of Indigeneity and modernity – she enjoyed a large retrospective at the Canadian Museum of History this summer – and should have been on the Sobey short list before she hit her 40s, so this is something of a catch-up. There she is getting well-deserved recognition; better late than never.

Right across from her work is a large piece by Audie Murray, the candidate for the Prairies and the only artist here still in her 30s. So, she’s less well known and the tight show weighs against her because she is only represented by one piece. (Thankfully, the Sobey judges assess the whole career, not the exhibited works alone.)

For the show, Murray has marked the wall with ashes from a smudging, as though a fire had smoked it. Pleasingly minimalist, it’s a powerful gesture at the intersection of Indigenous spiritualism and Western art practice, where charcoal is a traditional drawing tool. However, it’s also a work that could use some space so that viewers could stand back and let its ideas breathe. Instead, it’s shoehorned into the gallery.

The New Brunswick artist Shane Perley-Dutcher, a member of the Tobique First Nation representing the Atlantic region, also mixes Western and Indigenous artistry to reflect on distinctions between art and craft in different traditions. He uses the materials of a metalsmith – copper, brass and silver – to produce sculptural versions of the ash-splint baskets of the Wolastoqey (Maliseet).

He is well-established in his practice. So too is Samuel Roy-Bois, a Quebecker who teaches at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan and represents the Pacific region. His highly intellectual art considers our relationship in space with both sculpture and architecture. He is represented here by two photographs featuring red aluminum ladders against a snowy landscape and an installation that reproduces, as fragile skeletons balanced on plastic pails, sections of the balloon framing used in domestic architecture.

Lotus L. Kang of Ontario is also no neophyte. She showed at the Venice Biennale this year, filling the pavilion of corporate sponsor Bulgari with her evocative installations of celluloid and light. Perhaps the most intriguing thing about her use of film is that it does not project any image; it only reminds you that it contains images. In Ottawa, she is showing Azaleas II , a giant spinning drum of a kind once used to dry developed photographic film where the strips mounted on it project faint moving patterns yet always decline to become a video. Fragile sculptural pieces – coloured glass bottles, an open notebook – are scattered on the ground beside it.

Meanwhile, Melaw Nakehk’o, a Dene/Denesuliné artist from Fort Simpson, NWT, who is representing the circumpolar region, is still at a stage in her career where she seems to be shopping around for the right medium and right motif. Her works here include semi-abstract paintings showing patterns created by strings of sinew, figurative paintings of a young woman and of a two-headed reindeer, and, more interestingly, a soft sculpture of caribou hide in which four tattooed hands fan out from a single wrist. The title is Mostly Human and suggests the artist’s most promising theme is metamorphosis.

Her work is like that of the Sobey nominees of old – emerging but not yet there. On Saturday, the Sobey judges will reveal whether they are choosing achievement or potential.

The 2026 Sobey Art Award Exhibition continues at the National Gallery of Canada in Ottawa to Jan. 3.

He is represented here by two photographs featuring red aluminum ladders against a snowy landscape and an installation that reproduces, as fragile skeletons balanced on plastic pails, sections of the balloon framing used in domestic architecture.

content_blocks.text: Lotus L. Kang of Ontario is also no neophyte. She showed at the Venice Biennale this year, filling the pavilion of corporate sponsor Bulgari with her evocative installations of celluloid and light. Perhaps the most intriguing thing about her use of film is that it does not project any image; it only reminds you that it contains images. In Ottawa, she is showing Azaleas II , a giant spinning drum of a kind once used to dry developed photographic film where the strips mounted on it project faint moving patterns yet always decline to become a video. Fragile sculptural pieces – coloured glass bottles, an open notebook – are scattered on the ground beside it.

Her works here include semi-abstract paintings showing patterns created by strings of sinew, figurative paintings of a young woman and of a two-headed reindeer, and, more interestingly, a soft sculpture of caribou hide in which four tattooed hands fan out from a single wrist. The title is Mostly Human and suggests the artist’s most promising theme is metamorphosis.

By Lisa Johnson The Canadian Press

Premier Danielle Smith won leadership of the United Conservative Party with the sovereignty act as her signature proposal in 2022, and it became her flagship first law.

Smith said the Alberta Sovereignty within a United Canada Act was needed to push back against federal encroachment into provincial jurisdiction.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

When she invoked it for the first time, Smith conceded she didn’t need the law to implement new measures to fight against Ottawa’s energy regulations and that the act’s use was symbolic.

Onion Lake Cree Nation argues the act is unconstitutional because it goes against the Treaty 6 relationship with the Crown and should be declared unenforceable.

The province argues the act doesn’t authorize anything that would go against the Constitution or federal law and that Onion Lake’s claim doesn’t show the act has impacted any treaty rights.
