stories.title: Organized crime suspected in rash of high-end car thefts in Sarnia
stories.summary: Sarnia Police believe organized crime is behind a recent rash of high-end Toyota and Lexus thefts in the city.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
Sarnia Police believe organized crime is behind a recent rash of high-end Toyota and Lexus thefts in the city.

Police say there were five thefts or attempted thefts in two days. Car thieves targeted Toyota Highlanders, Toyota Tundras, and various Lexus models – each typically valued at between $60,000 and $100,000.

Acting Inspector Kent Jamieson says they’re stolen from driveways or taken off the street from in front of homes.

“So, anybody who is scouting in the area can see that they’re there. Can see how readily available they are. How vulnerable they are to being stolen,” said Jamieson.

He also says the thefts are connected to organized crime involving suspected culprits from outside the area. Once a vehicle is taken it can be difficult to trace.

“There’s various ways that they can be sold. They can be re-identified. They can be shipped to other countries where any type of theft that happened over here, there’s no real accountability measures over there,” he explained.

Western University tech expert Apurva Narayan says thieves are becoming more technologically sophisticated, and can now use artificial intelligence to their advantage. He says they can enter and start a car without leaving a mark on it.

“When you unlock your car you send a signal to the car. That’s basically your security unlocking signal that goes to the car and they can actually monitor that. That allows them to replicate and do some type of signal attack. Then once that hits, they know what the vulnerability is and now they can unlock all these cars,” he explained.

In the meantime, police say prevention is the best protection. The Sarnia Police Service officers a security consult at no charge. You can have officers come to your home and do a full security check. It’s called Crime Prevention through Environmental Design.

“We have trained officers here. You can schedule an appointment and they will come visit you at your home, and actually go around the property with you and provide their suggestions based on their experience and training,” explained Jamieson.

Sarnia Police Service shared the following list.

Theft Prevention Tips

Residents can reduce their risk of vehicle theft by:

Parking vehicles inside a locked garage whenever possible.

Using a visible steering wheel lock, such as a “Club” style device. Physical anti-theft devices remain one of the most effective deterrents, as they require additional time and effort to defeat.

Installing an aftermarket immobilizer approved by insurers or vehicle manufacturers.

Parking another vehicle behind the targeted vehicle when parked at home.

Parking in well-lit areas and ensuring residential security cameras are operational.

Keeping keys and key fobs secured inside the home. While the current thefts do not appear to involve relay attacks, protecting keys remains an important theft prevention measure.

stories.title: ‘Intent is to try to appeal’ encampment cleanup order, Saskatoon organization says
stories.summary: Station 20 West says it received a notice to remove the encampment in front of its 20th Street facility from the City of Saskatoon but will not comply until the two parties meet.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A Saskatoon organization said it will not follow an order to remove an encampment on its property until it can discuss the implications of that move with the city.

In the order to remedy the contravention, which is dated Oct. 30, the City of Saskatoon instructed Station 20 West to clean the encampment by Nov. 30. The notice states that more than 15 tents and structures are in front of the 20th Street facility, which is creating a nuisance for people in the neighbourhood.

The site is also in “an unsightly condition” and May provide a home for wildlife, according to the city’s notice.

Wanda Martin, the director of Station 20 West’s board, said that the city delivered that notice without any prior consultation on Sunday, when the building was closed. The community enterprise works to improve the wellbeing of those living in the city’s core and helps connect people with services – including those that can help find housing or employment.

“Our intent is to try to appeal the bylaw contravention, and to really support people as well as we can,” Martin said, speaking with Global News at the encampment site Friday.

In a news release shared earlier that day, the organization said it would not voluntarily dismantle the encampment without a conversation with the city about the expected consequences of that move on its residents.

Those discussions with the city would involve safety concerns and ensuring that appropriate, permanent solutions will be available for displaced encampment residents. If not, the problems that residents are facing would be shifted, not solved, the board director said.

Martin acknowledged the various safety concerns associated with encampments but said that removing the site does not provide a long-term solution for the people who live in it.

“While we don’t believe this is a great idea, for people to live like this, we do believe that just simply displacing them back to homelessness in another area only just moves the problem around,” she continued, adding that the people who live at the site have developed relationships with one another and Station 20 West staff.

In response to a request for an interview, the City of Saskatoon provided the following statement to Global News on behalf of Deputy Chief of the Saskatoon Fire Department (SFD) Yvonne Raymer.

“Station 20 West is privately owned and responsible (for) complying with The Property Maintenance and Nuisance Abatement Bylaw. The SFD does not publicly discuss operational plans when bylaw enforcement May be involved,” the emailed statement reads.

The bylaw cited by the city says that properties in Saskatoon must not negatively affect the safety, health, or wellbeing of those around them. It also bars nuisances on properties. The city’s definition of “nuisance” included “untidy or unsightly property.” The bylaw puts the onus of managing issues on private property on the land’s owner.

Mavis Daniels, 49, has lived at the encampment site at Station 20 West for a few weeks after another encampment, across 20th Street, was dismantled . She said the organization has helped provide her and other residents with food, clothing and washrooms.

“I tried finding homes everywhere; I’ve been on all of the housing sites,” she said. “I put my name down everywhere just to apply, but with my budget so low, it’s really, really difficult.”

“Winter is coming and I don’t know where we’re going to go if we get kicked out of here. Where is everybody going to go? We’re going to have to just post up anywhere and it’s just not going to work.”

Daniels said she hopes that the City of Saskatoon will work with the advocates to allow the encampment residents to stay at their homes.

stories.title: London art teacher recognized nationally for lasting impact on students
stories.summary: A longtime art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary is one of five educators across the country to win a prestigious...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
A longtime art teacher at H.B. Beal Secondary is one of five educators across the country to win a prestigious art award.

Kim Davy, is the only teacher in Ontario to win the Rita L. Irwin Art Teacher Dissemination of Knowledge Award , through the Canadian Society for Education through Art.

Kim Davy (Credit: Thames Valley District School Board)

The nomination came from a former student, who is now enrolled at the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design.

“It’s so lovely,” said Davy, who has taught at Beal for 17 years.” I think because it comes from a student, it’s very heartwarming,” she said. “That a kiddo would think of me … because I had an impact on how they’re living their lives now or helping them find a direction that’s well suited, and they’re happy, healthy humans. That’s just perfect. It’s beautiful. It’s very affirming, right? It tells me that I’m doing the right thing, which I love.”

As Davy walked around Beal’s art department Tuesday, she took pride in her school and how much freedom and unique projects those that enroll have access to.

Students said Davy leaves a positive impact on everyone she has the opportunity of educating, “I love Mrs. Davy. She’s taught me a lot about how to explore my own style, and how to actually protrude the voice of the artist that I am,” said Kade Campbell, one of Davy’s post-secondary students.

Davy is a fixture in the Beal Art Program, which is a specialized program designed to help students move toward a career in fine arts. While it starts in Grade 9, the program offers students two years beyond Grade 12.

Ace Clements said Davy is always there for her students beyond the classroom.

“If there’s something that you need, she’ll be there,” said Clements. “If you have personal things going on, she will relate and help you through those.”

The Rita L. Irwin award is named for a University of British Columbia art professor who is deeply committed to the arts. It is meant to recognize art educators who foster “ meaningful learning through the visual arts ,” according to the Thames Valley District School Board news portal .

Davy’s students recalled inspiring sentiments the passionate educator has shared with them. “(Davy would say) ‘You really don’t have to be scared about talking about your art, because you’re a really great person, and I think that people should be happy to talk about you,'” said Campbell. “That made me feel really happy, because I’m not very great at talking about myself, and I’ve always struggled with that,” said Campbell.

Davy took great pride in boasting about the art around her.

Beal Art classroom (Credit: Sam Luis/ XFM News)

Amber Wallace said Davy’s encouragement “sparked (her) interest more in ceramics and being able to make forms freely.”

Davy was once a Beal Art post-secondary student herself. She then went to the Nova Scotia College of Art and Design, and 11 years later got her Bachelor of Education from Western University.

After finding out about her award, Davy was especially excited to her mom, who encouraged her to go into education as a past educator herself. “She’s very proud that I’m a teacher. She was very proud and very supportive that I would be recognized in this way and at a national level, which is so lovely,” Davy said

While students say they’ve learned so much from Davy, she said she’s also learned from them.

“I can honestly say that who I am as a teacher has been greatly impacted by the Beal art program,” said Davy. “We have this wonderful cycle of young people. They’re sensitive, they’re emotional, they’re figuring life out. I learn as much from them as I think they do from me.”

stories.title: Halifax council backs long-term strategy for fire services as population grows
stories.summary: The Halifax Professional Fire Fighters Union is praising Halifax council for taking steps to develop a long-term service and resource strategy.
stories.author: Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
The Halifax Professional Fire Fighters Union is praising Halifax council for taking steps to develop a long-term service and resource strategy.

The union says the service has been underfunded since amalgamation, and that it needs to keep up with significant population growth.

“I say the mountain continues to grow if we don’t continue to climb,” said Brendan Meagher, the union’s president.

“And so the deficits that we’re looking at now in our capabilities are due to the first 20 years after amalgamation of contracting our service. So it’s time to build.”

Coun. Janet Steele brought two motions to council on Tuesday to ask staff to develop a long-term strategy for Halifax Regional Fire & Emergency, noting that since she’s been on council, the department has come to budget meetings asking for more staffing and resources every year.

She hopes her motion will help with future planning.

“This is about more predictability for council, more transparency, a little more planning ahead, and I think it gives residents a better idea of what’s coming up as well as firefighters who serve all of us,” she said.

Coun. Tony Mancini says insufficient resourcing is part of the broader issue of rapid growth in the municipality.

“We have to add to that concern of infrastructure, in my opinion, our emergency services, both police and fire,” he said.

“Do we have enough as it is right now? And fire (and) emergency (services are) a very expensive business.”

Meagher says this work is a long time coming and hopes to see a significant increase in staffing as part of the strategy, as well as improvements to firefighting training for high-rise fires.

But he warns this can’t be a one-time endeavour and will require years of work that could be potentially expensive.

“I would suggest that if a good objective look is taken at the fire service, that the economic impact of not investing properly in emergency response is potentially catastrophic,” he said.

The motion passed at council unanimously.

stories.title: How Microsoft outage shows risk of tech monopolies: ‘We were just helpless’
stories.summary: Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Many businesses and consumers were unable to communicate through digital channels as a global outage of some Microsoft services left people scrambling, and experts say this event further highlights the need for Canada to adopt more sovereign digital tech.

“The fact that Canada basically closed for business because one U.S. company had a glitch on some servers shows how dependent we are, how vulnerable we are,” says Joshua Pearce, who holds the Thompson Chair of Innovation at Western University.

On Thursday, the outage hit a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services.

Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down. As of publication, Microsoft said most services had been restored but fixes were still ongoing and there was no timeline for full restoration as of 3:00 p.m. Friday.

The full extent of the fallout from the outage is unclear, but regions spanning North America to the Asia Pacific were included in Microsoft’s updates, and the company reported its 365 suite of services had nearly half a billion paid subscriptions as of January.

“I was just shocked how much white collar work depends on the single Microsoft product, and when it’s down, really lots of people weren’t able to do their jobs,” says Emily Osborne, a policy research associate at the Canadian Shield Institute.

“There was nothing we could do to sort of address the outage as it was happening — we were just helpless to Microsoft’s control,” she added.

“We depend on so few providers, and when the services of one of them stops working that has a huge impact on our economy.”

Even the federal government said they were impacted by the outage, according to a statement in response to a Global News request Friday.

“The Government of Canada experienced impacts from the Microsoft service outage. Ensuring government digital services are secure, reliable and resilient is a priority, and we continually assess our systems and dependencies with that objective in mind,” said AI and Digital Innovation Minister Evan Solomon in a statement.

Diversifying reliance on different providers and expanding beyond some of the big American names can give businesses and consumers more options when a problem arises, experts say.

Osborne says having more sovereign digital providers is something that Canada could work on.

“There’s also certainly a role for the government to play. We’ve seen lots of governments in the EU making the very active and strategic choice to move away from products delivered by American firms. So that’s certainly something that Canada could consider doing to increase our resilience,” says Osborne.

“It would be hard to switch everything all at once, but there’s certainly an argument to be made for starting somewhere small with some sort of government communication platform that is a sovereign alternative — a privacy-preserving alternative to Microsoft products.”

Global News sent a request for comment to Shared Services Canada (SSC), the federal government’s IT provider, asking if a form of sovereign digital communications software is being developed or considered for use. A SSC spokesperson acknowledged the request, but did not provide a response by publication.

In the EU, a service known as Euro-Office is a suite of cloud-based digital sovereignty initiatives launched this year to serve as an alternative to American platforms like Microsoft 365.

“This is the actual data sovereignty or digital sovereignty we need to talk about is the physical infrastructure and the software that we use,” says Evan Light, associate professor at the faculty of information at the University of Toronto.

“It’s an open source office suite that does everything Microsoft Office does, but it’s developed by the European Union. It’s open source, it’s free, and it’s meant to be a project to sort of decouple the European Union from these tight, vulnerable things to American software.”

Light says these systems can be tailored and scaled to individual organizations, which can help limit the impact of an outage.

“So I could run a server here at U of T for my faculty, and if we need to reboot that thing, we’d reboot that thing and it affects a hundred people rather than millions.”

Experts says businesses and consumers should also have backup plans for technology failures, including maintaining alternative communications services to help limit disruptions.

“Thinking in terms of multi-homing and then having sort of multimodal forms of communication at your disposal rather than just getting into the habit of using one service all the time over and over and over again,” says Brett Caraway, associate professor of media economics at the University of Toronto.

“Institutions, I think, need to think more carefully about what they would do if they lost something. You’ve got to game that out.”

“There’s a lot of convenience and a lot efficiency that comes out of having a centralized coordination system, but it also exposes you to a great deal of risk.”

– with files from Global News’ Uday Rana

“It would be hard to switch everything all at once, but there’s certainly an argument to be made for starting somewhere small with some sort of government communication platform that is a sovereign alternative — a privacy-preserving alternative to Microsoft products.”

Global News sent a request for comment to Shared Services Canada (SSC), the federal government’s IT provider, asking if a form of sovereign digital communications software is being developed or considered for use. A SSC spokesperson acknowledged the request, but did not provide a response by publication.
In the EU, a service known as Euro-Office is a suite of cloud-based digital sovereignty initiatives launched this year to serve as an alternative to American platforms like Microsoft 365.

“This is the actual data sovereignty or digital sovereignty we need to talk about is the physical infrastructure and the software that we use,” says Evan Light, associate professor at the faculty of information at the University of Toronto.

“It’s an open source office suite that does everything Microsoft Office does, but it’s developed by the European Union. It’s open source, it’s free, and it’s meant to be a project to sort of decouple the European Union from these tight, vulnerable things to American software.”
Light says these systems can be tailored and scaled to individual organizations, which can help limit the impact of an outage.
“So I could run a server here at U of T for my faculty, and if we need to reboot that thing, we’d reboot that thing and it affects a hundred people rather than millions.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Cloudflare outage disrupts major websites'

content_blocks.text: What can be done next?
Experts says businesses and consumers should also have backup plans for technology failures, including maintaining alternative communications services to help limit disruptions.

“Thinking in terms of multi-homing and then having sort of multimodal forms of communication at your disposal rather than just getting into the habit of using one service all the time over and over and over again,” says Brett Caraway, associate professor of media economics at the University of Toronto.
“Institutions, I think, need to think more carefully about what they would do if they lost something. You’ve got to game that out.”
“There’s a lot of convenience and a lot efficiency that comes out of having a centralized coordination system, but it also exposes you to a great deal of risk.”

stories.title: Vancouver police investigating after local mosque vandalized with graffiti
stories.summary: Vancouver - Police in Vancouver are investigating after graffiti was discovered on the front doors of a local mosque.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver police say the case was reported by a maintenance worker, who flagged down patrolling officers in the area of West 8th Avenue on Friday morning.

The worker from the Al Masjid Al Jamia Mosque told police that graffiti that read “UK blood is on your hand” was spray-painted across the mosque’s front doors.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

No suspect has been identified or arrested.

Police say they have increased patrols in the area of the mosque and are asking anyone with information to come forward.

Investigators are also actively collecting evidence, and say police would like to assure Vancouver’s Muslim community that the crime will not be tolerated and May be pursued as a hate crime if evidence supports it.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Alberta implementing new oil royalty payment system to encourage production
stories.summary: Calgary - Alberta's government is introducing a new royalty payment program that it says is aimed at incentivizing development in the oil industry.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The framework would give companies a guaranteed 10-year royalty schedule for new projects or expansions.

They would pay two per cent of revenues for the first five years, then see one per cent annual hikes until reaching a maximum six per cent.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Premier Danielle Smith says it will stimulate investment and boost oil production in the long-term to fill the Pacific Link pipeline, which the province is trying to build to the West Coast.

The government says that after the 10-year period expires, each project would fall back under the existing royalty payment system.

Oil companies currently pay rates on a sliding scale, depending on the benchmark price of oil and whether a company has recouped the capital it puts into building each project.

If a company is still in what’s called the pre-payout phase, it pays rates between one per cent and nine per cent of gross revenue depending on the price of West Texas Intermediate, with the maximum taking affect when oil hits US$120 per barrel.

As of Friday afternoon, West Texas Intermediate was trading at about US$88 per barrel.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

— By Jack Farrell in Edmonton

stories.title: Students showcase their artistry at 25th Annual Juried Exhibition
stories.summary: Visual arts students showcased their creations Thursday at Western University. The visual arts department's 25...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Visual arts students showcased their creations Thursday at Western University.

The visual arts department’s 25th annual Juried Exhibition included paintings, sculptures, videos and printmaking created by students in all levels.

“It’s my passion. It’s something I can’t live without,” said student Prinda Sudhikam, who won two awards at the exhibition.

Sudhikam’s work titled “Thai sweet mung bean rice-skin dumpling that looks like a zebra,” won the People’s Choice Award.

At the end of the event, which was held at Western’s John Labatt Visual Arts Centre, a jury of art professionals judged the works. Students could win up to $300 in cash prizes, subscriptions and gift cards.

“This is the first time I’ve ever won anything, this is a huge honour for me.” Sudhikam said.

Sudhikam said she used “pointillism” in her work inspired by her experiences scuba diving

Prinda Sudhikam photographed with her artwork at the Annual Juried Exhibition at the John Labatt Visual Arts Centre on Nov. 12 Callum Contursi/XFM News

For other students, having their art included was an achievement in itself.

“As soon as I got chosen, I felt very grateful and happy. It made me feel very valued and appreciated,” said Maya Dugas, a student whose work was featured in the exhibition as well.

“I would like to become a high school art teacher,” Dugas said when asked why she began studying art.

“That is my dream as of right now because my favorite teacher growing up was my high school art teacher.”

The exhibition will continue showcasing the students’ artwork from Nov. 12 to Dec. 3.

Maya Dugas photographed with her artwork titled “& we still met” at the 25th Annual Juried Exhibition at the John Labatt Visual Arts Centre on Nov 12. _mayadugas/Instagram

stories.title: Three plead guilty in connection with 2025 Best Defence Conference protests
stories.summary: Four people charged with mischief in connection with protests at a defence conference in London last year appeared in court Friday.
stories.author: Bailey Shakyaver
stories.content:
Four people charged with mischief in connection with protests at a defence conference in London last year appeared in court Friday.

The group was charged following demonstrations at RBC Place in October 2025. Police alleged that paint was thrown at staff, protesters barricaded the parking garage, and one person used a hammer to break locks on the building.

One defendant pleaded guilty to mischief and obstructing a peace officer and was sentenced to three years of house arrest, followed by a three-month curfew.

Two others pleaded guilty to mischief and received conditional discharges, while charges against the fourth defendant were withdrawn.

ByJacques Gallant Courts and Justice Reporter

A lawsuit brought by Canadian news organizations against OpenAI can move forward in Ontario, the province’s top court ruled Friday, dismissing the tech giant’s argument that its lack of a physical presence in Ontario means the lawsuit should be heard in the United States.

The copyright lawsuit, filed by a coalition of media organizations including the Toronto Star, alleges the tech giant illegally used news articles to train its generative AI software ChatGPT and is now profiting unjustly.

California-based OpenAI had been looking to overturn a decision made last year by Superior Court Justice Jessica Kimmel, who concluded that the case was “sufficiently connected to Ontario” with three OpenAI-affiliated companies named in the lawsuit — OpenAI OpCo, LLC, OpenAI, LLC, and OpenAI, Inc. — being identified as doing business in the province.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Writing for a unanimous three-judge appeal panel, Justice Bradley Miller said Kimmel did not err in her findings, including that at least some of the affiliated companies “either made contractual arrangements in Ontario, advertised to users including in Ontario, or licensed their tools to customers either directly or through third parties.”

In other words, Miller wrote, the lower-court judge had found multiple instances of the companies carrying on business in Ontario.

The companies relied “heavily” on the argument that they didn’t have a physical presence in Ontario, Miller noted, but he said the case law cited by the appellants didn’t support their argument. He said Kimmel was not wrong to find that “there was a good arguable case that the appellants carried on business in Ontario for the context of assumed jurisdiction, even without a physical presence.”

“This decision matters well beyond the news media industry,” said lawyer Sana Halwani of the firm of Lenczner Slaght LLP, which represented the news media organizations. “Digital businesses earn money from Canadian content and users, and their activity reaches into Canada. When disputes arise, they must answer to Canadian law in Canadian courts.”

The media companies welcome technological innovations; however, all participants must follow the law, Lenczner Slaght LLP said in a written statement.

“Canadian journalism is created by Canadians, for Canadians, at significant cost. We look forward to having our clients’ claims decided on their merits by a Canadian court,” the firm said.

United States

NEW YORK (AP) — A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence…

OpenAI can still choose to ask the Supreme Court of Canada for permission to hear its appeal, although the country’s top court only agrees to hear a small number of cases from the Ontario Court of Appeal.

The court ordered OpenAI to pay $100,000 in legal costs.

ChatGPT and other popular AI models have become the subject of litigation on a number of fronts.

Similar copyright infringement lawsuits are ongoing against OpenAI in the U.S., including one filed by the New York Times in 2023. According to the Times, eleven other publishers have joined the suit, which remains before a U.S. court in New York.

In a California court on Thursday, a coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups sued a group of leading AI firms, including OpenAI, to halt development, alleging the giants are unable to prevent the risk of “catastrophic” harm caused by their advancing AI models.

With files from the Associated Press

The companies relied “heavily” on the argument that they didn’t have a physical presence in Ontario, Miller noted, but he said the case law cited by the appellants didn’t support their argument. He said Kimmel was not wrong to find that “there was a good arguable case that the appellants carried on business in Ontario for the context of assumed jurisdiction, even without a physical presence.”

“This decision matters well beyond the news media industry,” said lawyer Sana Halwani of the firm of Lenczner Slaght LLP, which represented the news media organizations. “Digital businesses earn money from Canadian content and users, and their activity reaches into Canada. When disputes arise, they must answer to Canadian law in Canadian courts.”
The media companies welcome technological innovations; however, all participants must follow the law, Lenczner Slaght LLP said in a written statement.
“Canadian journalism is created by Canadians, for Canadians, at significant cost. We look forward to having our clients’ claims decided on their merits by a Canadian court,” the firm said.
United States
Advocacy groups sue AI giants to freeze new models, warning of ‘catastrophic’ risks
NEW YORK (AP) — A coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups on Thursday sued five of the world’s leading artificial intelligence…

OpenAI can still choose to ask the Supreme Court of Canada for permission to hear its appeal, although the country’s top court only agrees to hear a small number of cases from the Ontario Court of Appeal.
The court ordered OpenAI to pay $100,000 in legal costs.
ChatGPT and other popular AI models have become the subject of litigation on a number of fronts.

Similar copyright infringement lawsuits are ongoing against OpenAI in the U.S., including one filed by the New York Times in 2023. According to the Times, eleven other publishers have joined the suit, which remains before a U.S. court in New York.

In a California court on Thursday, a coalition of online safety and consumer advocacy groups sued a group of leading AI firms, including OpenAI, to halt development, alleging the giants are unable to prevent the risk of “catastrophic” harm caused by their advancing AI models.

stories.title: Flu activity 'high' in several provinces including B.C., Alberta and P.E.I.
stories.summary: Toronto - Health Canada says flu activity is on the rise and expected to continue trending upward in the coming weeks.
stories.author: Hannah Alberga The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The federal health agency says several regions are seeing a ‘high’ percentage of cases testing positive including British Columbia, Alberta, Prince Edward Island and the Yukon.

The latest national data released Friday shows more than 4,200 influenza cases detected in the first week of November.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The highest levels are reported in P.E.I., where between 26.1 and 39.5 per cent of those tested for influenza tested positive.

The national positivity rate is 13.7 per cent, which is considered ‘moderate.’

The spread of COVID-19 is also gradually increasing, but remains “low” and “stable,” while RSV activity is still “very low.”

People 65 years and older are the most affected age group.

stories.title: Ottawa won’t clarify stance on possibility of future streamer payments for CanCon
stories.summary: Ottawa — Days after Prime Minister Mark Carney said it isn't necessary to impose a tax on big tech companies, his office won’t clarify if that means financial contributions from streamers are off the table entirely.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Shortcut buttons for streaming services Netflix and Amazon's Prime Video are seen on a television remote control in Ottawa, ON Monday, Aug. 24, 2026. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

Posted November 13, 2026 2:52 pm.

Last Updated November 13, 2026 3:18 pm.

Ottawa — Days after Prime Minister Mark Carney said it isn’t necessary to impose a tax on big tech companies, his office won’t clarify if that means financial contributions from streamers are off the table entirely.

Carney made the comments at a press conference in Montreal Tuesday, in response to a question about a Crtc-mandated requirement for streamers to pay a percentage of their revenues toward Canadian content.

The Liberals said in June they wanted the regulator to back down on that contribution policy and would instead provide $600 million in annual funding directly.

But the federal budget only allocated $600 million for this fiscal year, and a government spokesperson confirmed the amount could vary in future because the Crtc could still impose some level of financial contribution on streamers.

Culture Minister Marc Miller also told CTV this week that streamers will need to invest in Canadian content.

Spokespeople for the Prime Minister’s Office did not answer questions from The Canadian Press about where the government stands on imposing financial contributions on streamers in future years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

November 13, 2026 at 2:14 p.m.

Ottawa – The parent company of steelmaker Stelco, Cleveland Cliffs Inc., announced on Friday that it will recall 175 laid off workers to its plant in Hamilton, following a pressure campaign from the federal government.

“On September 28 th Stelco announced that, in response to unsustainable market conditions for its cold rolled and coated products, Stelco temporarily idled our Hamilton finishing operations — a measure that impacted 175 of our employees,” the statement said.

“We are pleased to announce that we have reached agreement with a sufficient volume of our customers to restart our Hamilton finishing operations and recall all 175 workers on December 1,” it added.

The company cited better customer demand for its products as the reason for the recall. But the announcement also follows a dispute that has played out through several letters back and forth between Industry Minister Mélanie Joly and Stelco Canada president Paul Simon.

Joly has contended that the layoffs announced by Cliffs were in contravention of its employment undertakings that it signed when its acquisition of Stelco was approved by the Government of Canada under the Investment Canada Act in 2024.

Cliffs has denied it was in contravention of the terms and argued lack of demand in the domestic market and the U.S. trade war made the “temporary” layoffs necessary. Originally, the company announced its intention to lay off 500 workers, but only laid off 175.

In her letters to the company, the industry minister had threatened court action against Cliffs, which could lead to Cliffs’ forced divestiture from Stelco. On Friday morning, Joly followed through on that threat, telling reporters if she did not hear from the company by the end of the day, she would ask a court to order Cliffs to sell Stelco.

Cliffs’ standing in the dispute was further complicated by comments made by its CEO Lourenco Goncalves to CBC News. Goncalves said he had bought Stelco to stop the steelmaker from undercutting his U.S. business. Last Friday, Joly asked Canada’s competition competition bureau to look into the CEO’s statements.

“I would like to thank our valued customers for the faith they have placed in us, and our workers for the patience and resilience they have continued to demonstrate during this challenging period,” said Simon, in the statement.

Joly joined United Steelworkers Local 1005, in Hamilton, Ont. on Friday evening, where she said the fight with Cliffs was “absolutely worth it.”

“I’m very proud and touched that 500 workers will be able to have their job just before Christmas, and I know and I can feel that you will have the peace of mind necessary to to be able to celebrate with your family and friends, and also start 2027 with a strong footing,” she said, during a press conference.

Joly added that Canada will continue to be a place for companies to invest, but those same companies must respect their contracts.

Jordan Gowling joined National Post's parliamentary bureau in 2026 after two years as Financial Post's economics reporter on Parliament Hill. She previously worked as a producer at CTV News in Ottawa.

stories.title: London parents worried after accused child-exploitation suspect released on conditions
stories.summary: The end of the school day has become a source of of palpable anxiety for London mother Eilan.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
The end of the school day has become a source of of palpable anxiety for London mother Eilan. Waiting for her daughter’s school bus just steps from where a man accused of numerous online sex offences lives, Eilan voiced a concern shared by other parents in her neighbourhood.

“I don’t want to feel unsafe in my community. Right now, I just don’t feel safe for my child at the moment,” she said.

The concern follows the arrest of 47-year-old Timothy Ryan Shirk, who faces 11 charges related to online interactions involving children . The London Police Service (LPS) Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit made the arrest as part of a broader international investigation into child sex trafficking organizations.

Eilan, who asked that her last name not be published, said she believes in the principle of innocent until proven guilty, but stressed the importance of protecting children. The situation has prompted serious conversations with her daughter about safety, including reminders not to talk to or go anywhere with strangers.

“She’s an empathetic child. She wants to help people, right? You can’t always trust that,” Eilan said.

To provide some immediate peace of mind, the school bus operator agreed to move the evening drop-off point for children one block farther from the suspect’s residence. However, Eilan remains concerned about other young children in the area who walk nearby.

“There are children who walk alone in this community, right past this area. When my daughter’s bus stop is moved I’m not going to be watching those children, and I don’t know if their parents are aware of what’s going on. How do we help keep those kids safe too?” she said.

The investigation, launched by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) between January and October 2025, focused on organizations facilitating livestream child sexual abuse (Lcsa). The investigation involved extensive international collaboration, including the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation, the RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (Ncecc) and the LPS ICE Unit.

During an operation in October 2025, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation rescued five children. Information from the operation was later shared with Canadian and international partners. In Ottawa, an RCMP Ncecc-led operation, in partnership with HSI, identified a London man allegedly sending money to a facilitator in the Philippines.

On Nov. 5, 2026, members of the LPS ICE Unit executed a search warrant at a residence in the area of Grosvenor Street and Gammage Street. Timothy Ryan Shirk was arrested and electronic devices were seized, leading to the discovery of child sexual abuse and exploitation material (Csaem).

Three counts of communicating electronically to make an agreement to commit a specific criminal offence with a person under, or believed to be under, the age of 16.

Printing, publishing or possessing child sexual abuse material for the purpose of publication.

Possession of child sexual abuse and exploitation material.

Sexual assault as a party to an offence with another person.

Sexual interference involving a person under the age of 16.

Obtaining sexual services for consideration from a person under the age of 18.

Detective Sgt. Jason Eddy of the London Police Service’s Technological Crimes Section said issuing a public warning under the Community Safety and Policing Act does not necessarily indicate an imminent threat to the public or that additional victims are being solicited.

“We’re doing so under the authority of the Community Safety and Policing Act. And we’re not suggesting there’s a danger to the public or soliciting more victims in this case,” Eddy said.

The accused appeared in a London court on Nov. 5 and has since been released on strict court-imposed conditions. Those conditions prohibit him from being within 20 metres of any public park, public swimming area, daycare centre, school grounds, playground or community centre, and from being alone with anyone under the age of 18. He is also prohibited from possessing weapons.

“That’s for the public to be aware and if they believe they see breaches of those conditions, we welcome them to contact the London police,” Eddy said.

Shirk is scheduled to reappear in London court on Jan. 28, 2027.

stories.title: Pitching in: Hitting the lake in the fight against breast cancer
stories.summary: Laura Hughes’s annual kayaking fundraiser is held in Muskoka on the same day as Cibc Run for the Cure
stories.author: Paul Waldie
stories.content:
The organizer: Laura Hughes

The pitch: Founding Kayak For The Cure

The reason: To fund breast cancer care and research

For years, Laura Hughes regularly participated in the annual Cibc Run for the Cure, which raises money for Canadians impacted by breast cancer. And then she received her own cancer diagnosis.

Doctors told her in April 2023 that she had lobular breast cancer, a common form of the disease that can be harder to detect.

“I was actually just finishing up four months of chemotherapy when the Run was to be held, and I was in a really low spot. I’d lost my hair, and I just was kind of in a shell, pulling back from the world,” Ms. Hughes recalled from her home in Toronto, where she’s a kindergarten teacher.

She retreated to her family’s cottage on Go Home Lake near Muskoka, Ont., where she often finds solace paddling in her kayak. A friend suggested they hit the water on the day of the Run for the Cure in early October.

“Why don’t we just get out our kayaks and paddle. We’ll still try to raise some money but we’ll just paddle instead,” the friend said. As they headed out across the lake, they were joined by a couple of dozen more paddlers. “It was a really powerful moment, and I realized that there was something here,” Ms. Hughes said.

They raised $2,500 for cancer care that day and decided to make it an annual event. They called it Kayak For The Cure and held it at the same time as the Run.

In 2024, they raised $5,000. They more than doubled that the following year to $12,000. This year’s Kayak For The Cure attracted 53 paddlers, who covered five kilometres and raised $30,000.

The event now includes a social gathering as well as a decorated boat that follows the kayakers, allowing those who can’t paddle to participate.

The money raised helps fund a variety of research and care programs through the Canadian Cancer Society, and participants can direct their donations to five different areas. Planning is under way for the 2027 paddle and the hope is to expand Kayak For The Cure to other lakes.

Ms. Hughes, 57, is feeling much better physically and she finds working on the event helps her heal on the inside. “It gives me a little bit of control, sort of accepting the diagnosis and using it for good. And it gives me hope.”

'Listen, everybody thinks their children are angels' — Winnipeg restaurant owner on why she doesn't want kids at her tables

Navigate

Const. Jeff Smith was hospitalized following the attack. Const. Michael McCurdy aided him but was not physically injured

A sign thanking Belleville police officers stands in front of Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont. (Postmedia)

November 13, 2026 at 1:35 p.m.

Donations continue to arrive for Const. Jeff Smith and Const. Michael McCurdy, the two Belleville police officers who foiled a would-be massacre at a synagogue in the Ontario city in September.

The fundraiser for Smith, who was injured, had a stated goal of raising $1 million. It has surpassed that, and more. And even though McCurdy was not physically injured, a fundraiser was launched for him as well, saying that the emotional toll of the incident was significant.

On Thursday, Derek Kreindler, the organizer of the GoFundMe campaign for Smith, wrote that the effort was just $12,898 shy of the million-dollar mark. Two hours later, he reported that it was now over the top. As of Friday morning, the total was $1,000,527 and still growing.

“To everyone who responded to the final appeal today, thank you,” Kreindler wrote on the page.

“Raising $12,898 in two hours was an extraordinary display of generosity,” he continued. “To every person who donated at any point, shared the campaign, contacted a prospective supporter, covered the story, offered advice or encouraged me to continue: this achievement belongs to you.”

Bullet holes can still be seen in the windows of Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont. Postmedia

Kreindler added: “Our gratitude also remains equal for Constable Mike McCurdy, who confronted the same danger, came immediately to his colleague’s aid and displayed the same courage. We remain profoundly thankful that he was not physically injured. Please consider donating to the GoFundMe set up in his name.”

The page in McCurdy’s name has a goal of $65,000 and, as of Friday, was less than $3,300 away from meeting that amount.

“We are profoundly thankful that McCurdy did not sustain life threatening physical injuries,” Devorah Fogel, the page’s organizer, wrote. “However, the emotional toll of this experience is significant, and mental recovery is just as vital as physical healing. Our goal is to ensure he feels the full support and appreciation of our community.”

Smith, a 13-year veteran of the Belleville police force, was stationed outside Sons of Jacob Synagogue Sept. 20 during a Yom Kippur service. There were about 25 people inside.

He was ambushed by 29-year-old Sean Ward and gravely injured when he was shot in the head and body. The attacker yelled “You are going to die for the Jews” as he opened fire.

Smith was joined less than three minutes later by McCurdy, a seven-year veteran of the force. Ward was struck when the officers returned fire, and died in hospital the next day. Neither McCurdy nor anyone inside the synagogue was injured.

“We cannot imagine the stress of Const. Mike McCurdy arriving on scene to an active shooter and to his fellow officer, Const. Smith, who was suffering from multiple gun shot wounds,” Fogel wrote on the GoFundMe page.

She added that McCurdy “fulfilled the most righteous possible deed. In Judaism, we refer to this as Pikuach Nefesh, the preservation of human life. Const. McCurdy’s actions were selfless and nothing short of heroic.”

Smith has since been released from hospital and is “recovering well at home,” the Belleville Police Service said late last month.

“Constable Smith and his family remain incredibly grateful for the overwhelming support shown by the community and beyond over the past several weeks,” police said in a press release. “Every well wish and message of encouragement has been sincerely appreciated.”

National Post has reached out to Belleville Police Services for more information about both officers.

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: National Capital Commission considering artificial freezing for Rideau Canal Skateway
stories.summary: Ottawa — The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city's Winterlude festival.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
People are seen through a span of the Bank Street Canal Bridge as they skate along the Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa, ON Monday, March 2, 2026. The Rideau Canal is a Unesco World Heritage Site. THE Canadian Press/Justin Tang

By Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

Posted November 13, 2026 1:26 pm.

Last Updated November 13, 2026 5:04 pm.

Ottawa — The operators of the iconic Rideau Canal Skateway in Ottawa May turn to artificial cooling to keep it frozen in coming years, as climate change wreaks havoc with the centrepiece of the city’s Winterlude festival.

A feasibility study investigating the option of using refrigeration pipes to help freeze a 900-metre stretch of the canal in Ottawa’s downtown is currently under consideration by the National Capital Commission.

The project would cover just over 10 per cent of the Skateway. The rest would still rely on the co-operation of nature.

The commission, known as the NCC, is the capital’s public lands planner and manages the cultural character of the area. It manages the Rideau Canal Skateway as a part of a parliamentary mandate.

Tobi Nussbaum, NCC chief operating executive officer, told CBC Radio’s Ottawa Morning show this week the study recommends using refrigeration pipes embedded in concrete — a system similar to the ones used to freeze many outdoor rinks.

Bruce Devine, the Ncc’s senior manager of facilities and programs, told The Canadian Press that if the project proceeds, it would be costly.

“It’s significant. It will be in the millions. We will be looking for funding from a federal program. Other sources of funding will be researched,” he said.

He said the number of days the canal is open could triple if the plan goes ahead, but it wouldn’t happen until after 2030.

Devine said an emphasis would be placed on reducing the project’s carbon footprint.

“If such a system is feasible, the project would be aiming for carbon neutrality. And this is true by identifying opportunities to recover and reuse the heat. So that’s a principle that we have with this project,” he said.

The Skateway first opened in 1971 when the NCC cleared a small portion of ice on the canal for skating. It has since expanded to become the world’s largest skating rink, offering 7.8 kilometres of ice for people to enjoy.

The National Capital Commission says it sees 19,000 visitors daily during the winter months.

The Skateway is also a popular feature of Ottawa’s Winterlude festival, which hosts an average of 500,000 visitors over about 2.5 weeks every February.

In 2023, one of the warmest winters on record kept the Skateway from opening at all for the first time in its history. In 2024, another warmer-than-usual winter meant it could open for just 10 days.

Devine says a plan to ensure at least some of the Skateway can open each year could drive tourism at the Unesco World Heritage site.

“I think people will be able to make a clear decision as to which day they would like to come and plan around their visits. That will be known information, ‘Definitely, I can skate and it’s not weather-permitted.’ So no, I think it’s going to sustain and help tourism,” he said.

The Weather Network says this winter is expected to be warmer than the average.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alyssa Wheeler, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stelco to recall 175 laid-off workers in Hamilton, Ont. on Dec. 1
stories.summary: Stelco is recalling 175 temporarily laid off workers as it plans to restart its Hamilton, Ont., finishing operations on Dec. 1.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Stelco is recalling 175 temporarily laid off workers as it plans to restart its Hamilton, Ont., finishing operations on Dec. 1.

The company says the move is due to increased customer demand.

Stelco parent company Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. raised the ire of Ottawa when it announced the layoffs in September.

The federal government said the cuts went against conditions it set when it approved the American company’s purchase of the steelmaker.

Cleveland-Cliffs cited US tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as reasons for the cuts.

However, it says it has now reached agreement with a sufficient volume of its customers to restart the operations and recall all of the laid off workers.

The company noted that it will take several weeks to restart the operations, but that all affected employees will be made whole retroactively for the standard wages they would have received during the period in which they were temporarily laid off.

stories.title: Feds investing $200M in B.C.'s Woodfibre LNG over three years
stories.summary: Vancouver - The federal government says it is investing $200 million in the Woodfibre LNG project in British Columbia.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Energy Minister Tim Hodgson says the investment in the project in Squamish, north of Vancouver, will take place over three years.

He says it’s a project that’s being advanced in collaboration with the Squamish Nation that should make Canadians proud.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Speaking at a news conference in Vancouver, Hodgson says the investment will support a near-25-per-cent increase in the project’s capacity from 2.1 million tonnes to 2.6 million tonnes of LNG per year.

Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson says the federal investment is welcome news for the region and for British Columbia’s economy.

He says the project, which the operators say will be substantially completed next year, demonstrates what is possible “when governments, First Nations and industry work together.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: More electric vehicles exempt from luxury tax, Ottawa says
stories.summary: Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne announced that starting Friday, all electric vehicles that cost less than $150,000 would be exempt from the 10 per cent tax.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
More electric vehicles will now be exempt from Canada’s luxury tax , Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said.

In a press release on Friday, the minister said all electric vehicles that cost less than $150,000 would be exempt from the 10 per cent tax.

The price threshold for luxury vehicles subject to the tax was originally set at $100,000 and included electric vehicles over that threshold.

Canada’s luxury tax was originally proposed in the 2021 budget and covers luxury cars , planes and boats bought for personal use and leisure. The tax was rolled out in September 2022 and would amount to either 10 per cent of the taxable amount of the item, or 20 per cent of the amount over the price threshold – whichever is less.

Champagne said by increasing the price threshold for electric vehicles to $150,000, the government “recognizes the higher upfront cost of zero-emission vehicles and supports the global shift to electric vehicles (EVs).”

All other vehicles remain subject to the $100,000 price threshold.

According to the Canadian Automobile Association, the average price of a new electric vehicle in Canada sits around $50,000, but some models from BMW, Mercedes-Benz, Audi, Cadillac and Tesla cost well over $100,000.

According to Statistics Canada data released in September, zero-emission vehicles made up 3.5 per cent of Canada’s 25.3 million registered light-duty vehicles in 2025. That same year, there were more than 58,000 new registrations of zero-emission vehicles across the country.

The Department of Finance said EVs are projected to account for nearly 40 per cent of global car sales within five years.

Budget 2026 committed $587 million over five years to install more than 55,000 EV chargers which will more than double the availability of federally supported chargers.

“With Budget 2026, we are expanding our electricity system, cutting emissions, and unlocking new investment in clean technologies,” Champagne said in a news release. “By updating this measure to reflect today’s vehicle market, we are supporting the transition to a cleaner, more competitive economy.”

This is not the first time the luxury tax has been amended.

In Nov. 2025, the federal government scaled back the tax on aircraft and boats after budget numbers showed tax revenues for those items did not yield initial government projections.

stories.title: Stelco recalling laid-off Hamilton workers, citing sufficient demand for its steel
stories.summary: Parent Cleveland-Cliffs laid off 175 workers in September, igniting a fight with Ottawa
stories.author: Niall McGee
stories.content:
Stelco Inc. is recalling 175 laid-off steel workers.

The layoffs were announced in September and caused a political firestorm in Canada with Ottawa alleging that Stelco parent Cleveland-Cliffs had violated a legally binding commitment to maintain employment levels in Canada after it acquired the steelmaker in 2024.

Hamilton-based Stelco announced on Friday that owing to sufficient demand from customers for its steel it is in a position to recall all of the laid-off workers.

stories.title: Avril Lavigne gets her happy ending, welcomes first child
stories.summary: Canada's pop-punk princess is now a pop-punk parent.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The 42-year-old “Sk8er Boi” singer announced the arrival of her first child, a daughter, in an Instagram post on Friday, featuring a series of black-and-white photos.

The images show Lavigne and her partner holding the newborn’s tiny hand, while another captures the singer-songwriter cradling the baby against her chest.

A final photo features three pairs of checkered Vans sneakers — two adult-sized pairs and a miniature set — laid out on a skateboard.

Lavigne has not publicly identified the child’s father.

“Our Mini F–king Princess has arrived,” she wrote in her caption.

Lavigne, who shot to fame with her 2002 debut album “Let Go,” has had several high-profile relationships, though she has kept her current romance under wraps.

She was married to Sum 41 frontman Deryck Whibley from 2006 to 2010 and Nickelback singer Chad Kroeger from 2013 to 2015. She was also engaged to musician Mod Sun before the pair split in 2023, and was later romantically linked to rapper Tyga.

Earlier this year, the 10-time Juno winner recorded a cover of Alanis Morissette’s “Ironic” for the Canadian rom-com “Mile End Kicks.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Alberta landowners urge farmers, ranchers to resist oil development
stories.summary: Group says province is failing to deal with issues like orphan wells and unpaid municipal taxes by oil and gas companies
stories.author: Amanda Stephenson
stories.content:
An Alberta landowner advocacy organization is urging farmers and ranchers to “actively resist” new oil and gas development on their land, an unprecedented move highlighting growing tensions between industry and rural residents in Canada’s main energy-producing province.

Growing opposition to oil and gas development in a province that has long supported the oil industry could challenge Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to boost oil output, build new pipelines and attract new markets for Canadian energy.

The Alberta Surface Rights Federation, in a letter sent to Premier Danielle Smith on Thursday, said landowners must push back against energy development given what it calls government’s failure to deal with issues like orphan and abandoned wells, delayed reclamation of oil and gas sites, and unpaid municipal taxes owed by oil and gas companies.

Both the federal and Alberta governments are keen to expand domestic oil production in the face of an escalating trade war with the U.S. But the move by Alberta landowners is evidence of pushback by some who believe economic growth is being prioritized over environmental rules and regulatory obligations.

“Some of these politicians clearly don’t have long-term thinking on their minds,” said Bill Heidecker, president of the Alberta Surface Rights Federation, in an interview.

A spokesman for Alberta’s Energy Minister Brian Jean said the province is committed to working with landowners. He said the government will be bringing forward legislation that addresses liabilities and orphan wells, and is working on a framework to assess a company’s financial viability which will ensure landowners, municipal taxes and creditors are paid by companies.

“We recognize there are frustrations that need to be addressed,” the spokesman said in an e-mail.

The federal government declined to comment.

Heidecker, who describes himself as a conservative rancher not opposed to responsible energy development, said there has been a “stunning erosion of support” for the oil and gas industry in rural Alberta in part due to the province’s struggle to cope with thousands of so-called “orphan” wells that dot Alberta’s rural landscape.

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, remains popular there and his efforts to appeal to the oil industry likely helped quell a non-binding referendum on separatism last month.

In September, however, a group of landowners launched legal action to argue that the province’s energy regulator has chronically and knowingly underfunded a program meant to protect the public from the cost of cleaning up these abandoned oil and gas wells.

Studies have shown that abandoned oil and gas wells pose many risks, including potential methane leakage, soil and ground contamination, as well as the financial cost associated with cleanup.

Rural residents are also concerned about the impacts of newer forms of energy development including lithium mining and electricity generation for AI data centres and bitcoin mining, Heidecker said.

In Alberta, landowners possess surface rights – giving them the right to farm the land or exploit surface resources like trees, gravel or water – but mineral rights are for the most part owned by the province, which leases them to energy companies.

Those companies then have the right to enter a landowner’s land to extract the resources.

Heidecker said his organization is not recommending that landowners physically bar energy companies from their property, but that they verbally withhold consent and refuse to sign any new surface leases.

Without consent, oil and gas companies then must seek a legal right-of-entry order to access the property.

Heidecker said Alberta must address issues of energy infrastructure liability and environmental regulation before pushing ahead with its proposed one million-barrel-per-day Pacific Link pipeline project, which would increase Canada’s west coast oil export capabilities and potentially pave the way for oil and gas production expansion in the province.

stories.title: ‘It’s heartbreaking’: Defibrillator donation honours fallen OPP officer
stories.summary: Twenty years ago, a beloved Huron County OPP officer died from injuries sustained in a crash while responding to a call for help.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Twenty years ago today, a beloved Huron County OPP officer died from injuries sustained in a crash while responding to a call for help.

“It’s heartbreaking. But I think he’s watching from above,” said Brenda Orr.

Dave Mounsey’s memory lives on through one of the police officers he trained many years ago. Patrick Armstrong is donating defibrillators to community organizations across Ontario in the names of fallen police officers, firefighters and soldiers. Mounsey and Orr were fundraising for a defibrillator for the Blyth Fire Department shortly before he died.

“In a way, I’m carrying on Dave and Brenda’s work. I’m not going to take the credit and say 275. They did the first one, but I think it’s important to recognize that they did do the first one, and they started what became the Memorial Fund without even knowing it,” said Armstrong.

The first defibrillator from the Dave Mounsey Memorial Fund was installed at the Blyth Festival in 2009. To replace that unit, which simply wore out over time, defibrillator No. 274 was donated to the festival on Thursday.

“The mission of the festival, really, we’re here to inspire and to fill people’s hearts, and to know that now we have this instrument here in this building that is here to protect their hearts and save lives, it just means so much,” said Gil Garratt, artistic director of the Blyth Festival.

“It warms my heart because Dave, obviously, being a police officer, he wanted to serve and protect, save lives. And he was a volunteer firefighter too, same sort of mission. And the fact that there’s a defibrillator in his name that could save a life, and he can continue to do the stuff he was doing when he was alive, just makes me very happy,” said Orr, Mounsey’s partner.

Armstrong said eight lives have been saved by defibrillators donated through the Dave Mounsey Memorial Fund. It is a powerful legacy for a man who touched so many lives in Huron County and beyond.

stories.title: Two dead, one missing after flood-related boating incident in Squamish, B.C.
stories.summary: Police say all others involved have been accounted for and search is challenging due to elevated water levels and weather conditions
stories.author: Brenna Owen
stories.content:
RCMP say two people are dead and one person is missing after a boating tragedy in the Squamish Valley north of Vancouver, where a river is swollen by floodwaters and days of heavy rain.

Police said in a statement Friday that all others involved in the incident that happened on Thursday around 2 p.m. have been accounted for.

Cpl. Ashley MacKay with Squamish RCMP said search, rescue and recovery operations were continuing in the “time-sensitive and complex response.”

“The weather and river conditions have played a significant role in the response efforts,” MacKay said in a statement.

“This is a very dynamic and evolving incident, and the safety of responders and the public remains paramount.”

MacKay said the search, about 90 kilometres north of Vancouver, had been challenging due to elevated water levels and weather conditions.

Squamish RCMP said the search involved Squamish Search and Rescue, RCMP Air Services, the Lower Mainland District Integrated Emergency Response Team, the RCMP Underwater Recovery Team, and West Coast Marine Services.

“Weather patterns, water levels, and river conditions can change rapidly, and those factors are being continuously assessed as search and recovery efforts continue,” MacKay said.

“We are asking the public to stay off the water at this time due to dangerous flow rates and debris throughout the river systems.”

Some residents about 16 kilometres north of Squamish have been sheltering in place after flooding triggered by a parade of drenching storms that has brought more than 300 millimetres of rain to parts of southwest B.C. this week

The village of Pemberton, about 90 kilometres north of Squamish, is still under an evacuation alert, with parts of the community under evacuation order.

Evacuation orders were also imposed by the Lil’wat First Nation and in Zeballos this week.

Search and rescue teams gathered at the local airport in Squamish on Friday.

A white pickup truck pulled an RCMP boat around the parking lot as members gathered inside, and a rescue team member could be heard discussing the deployment of drones in the search.

BC Emergency Health Services said it received a call at 2:48 p.m. about the incident near the 15900 block of Squamish Valley Road. It said no one was taken to hospital.

Legislator Jeremy Valeriote, who represents West Vancouver-Sea to Sky, said he was “devastated” and his thoughts were with the families of the victims.

Valeriote, who was re-elected as the community’s Green legislator last month, said the Sea to Sky region “is a strong and resilient community, but no one should have to navigate this alone.”

“My team and I are here to support residents however we can as the community begins the difficult process of recovery,” he said.

Deluged residents of coastal areas of southwest B.C. were meanwhile facing a new flooding risk, even as rains eased, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.

Environment Canada said the surge could hit low-lying and exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.

It said elevated water levels surpassing tidal predictions were being driven by high winds and “enhanced wave activity,” and were expected to peak from 10 a.m. to noon Friday.

Most of the rainfall warnings that had blanketed the region were lifted on Thursday, though three yellow warnings remained in place for Western, north and inland Vancouver Island.

Those warnings said heavy rain was expected into late Friday afternoon, with the highest rainfall expected near Zeballos and Tahsis in northwest Vancouver Island.

stories.title: Fundraiser for officer injured in Belleville synagogue shooting surpasses $1-million goal
stories.summary: Organized as an expression of gratitude from the Canadian Jewish community, the fundraiser met its target on Thursday.
stories.author: Gabriel Hilty
stories.content:
A police officer walks past the Sons of Jacob Synagogue where a man armed with a shotgun exchanged gunfire with a police officer stationed outside the building in September.

Nick Lachance/Toronto Star file photo [](https://www.thestar.com/news/ontario/fundraiser-for-officer-injured-in-belleville-synagogue-shooting-surpasses-1-million-goal/article_fc630325-23dc-45b4-b726-ca0ff69dd4ad.html)

ByGabriel Hilty Staff Reporter

A fundraiser for Const. Jeff Smith, the officer injured in theshootout outside the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, has reached and surpassed its goal of raising $1 million.

With congregants gathered insideon the eve of Yom Kippur, shots pierced the air and riddled the place of worship on Sept. 20 amid a shootout between a lone gunman, Sean Ward, and police. Ward died the next day in hospital while Smith was admitted into the ICU.

Organized by members of the Canadian Jewish community, the GoFundMe fundraiser was set up as an expression of “profound gratitude” to Smith, who was stationed outside the synagogue as part of routine duty, and to support Smith and his family during his recovery, according to organizer Derek Kreindler.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Sons of Jacob congregants returned to the building for the first time since bullets pierced its

Around two dozen members were inside Belleville’s Sons of Jacob synagogue when police say Ward arrived with a stockpile of ammunition and gasoline. Police and the suspect exchanged gunfire, between 20 and 30 shots according to some witnesses, and Smith was hit multiple times.

In Judaism, “pikuach nefesh” is the principle of preserving a life, Kreindler wrote, adding that Smith exemplified this in September.

“Const. Smith fulfilled that obligation not through words, but through courage and action. When members of a vulnerable community needed protection, he put himself in harm’s way,” Kreindler said on the GoFundMe.

In an update posted Friday morning,Kreindler said the fundraiser has stopped accepting donations after reaching its target at the request of Smith’s family, and that the money raised will be administered to the family’s designated beneficiary through GoFundMe.

According to an update in late October, Belleville police informed the fundraiser that Smith was released from the hospital and continuing to recover at home.

In a video released by police, Ward was heard saying “you are going to die for the Jews,” as he started his attack, with investigators classifying it as a hate-motivated crime and describing it as a thwarted attempt at a mass killing of Jewish worshippers.

Sham Vigodda, vice-president of the synagogue, says that costly enhanced security measures are necessary to protect congregants.

Speaking at a press conference in Ottawa on Nov. 2, Vigodda said priorities include replacing windows and installing burglar alarms.

He said it has become clear that more expensive measures are also necessary, including bullet-resistant glass, building a safe room and having security personnel or armed police on site.

“These measures are necessary not only to ensure our physical safety, but to deter would-be attackers,” Vigodda said. “For many in our congregation who were there on Yom Kippur, it is also a necessity for them to feel comfortable to return.”

He indicated that money from a federal program to help places of worship improve security would not fully cover the more extensive measures.

With files from The Canadian Press

Gabriel Hilty is a staff reporter with the Toronto Star. He can be reached atghilty@thestar.ca.

stories.title: Alberta changes graduation requirements for high school students
stories.summary: Students will soon be allowed to graduate with fewer math, science and humanities courses under their belts
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
High school students in Alberta will soon be allowed to graduate with fewer math, science and humanities courses under their belts.

Alberta’s government says that starting with students entering high school in 2028, only 47 credits in core classes will be required, down from the current 56.

The government’s new requirements mean that students will only need to complete one senior level course in either English or social studies, while senior level math and science classes will still not be mandatory.

Education Minister Demetrios Nicolaides says the new system will allow students to spend more time developing interests or learning hands-on skills for jobs after graduation by taking more optional classes.

While the government is reducing the need for core subjects, it is making physical education classes mandatory throughout high school instead of just Grade 10.

Nicolaides says the government also plans to mandate a new wellness and financial literacy course for all three years of high school.

“These changes will give students more choice to find their passions, prepare for further schooling or rewarding job opportunities,” Nicolaides told reporters in Calgary on Friday.

“More flexibility does not mean lower expectations. Students will continue to build strong basics in core classes and will have to write at least one diploma [exam] to graduate.”

“More flexibility does not mean lower expectations. Students will continue to build strong basics in core classes and will have to write at least one diploma [exam] to graduate.”

stories.title: E-mail services restored to Toronto hospitals after Microsoft outage caused some disruptions
stories.summary: The City of Toronto has said some services May be temporarily unavailable or delayed as a result of the outage
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Hospitals and other health institutions in Toronto say their e-mail services are returning to normal after a global Microsoft 365 outage caused some delays and disruptions.

Unity Health Toronto, which includes St. Michael’s Hospital and St. Joseph’s Health Centre, says staff experienced difficulties sending and receiving e-mails on Thursday but people could reach a clinic or department by calling the main hospital phone line.

The health-care network says patient and resident care is not affected by the outage and its hospitals continue to operate.

University Health Network, which includes Toronto General Hospital, Princess Margaret Cancer Centre and others, also says the e-mail outage didn’t impact patient care.

Sunnybrook Hospital, the largest trauma centre, says it remains open for care as staff experience difficulties sending and receiving e-mails, but people can still reach clinics about upcoming appointments by calling the main hospital phone line.

The outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot.

Microsoft said Outlook e-mail service was up and running again for many users in North America as of Friday morning, but warned that some users May still encounter “intermittent access issues or delayed e-mail delivery.”

The City of Toronto has said some services May be temporarily unavailable or delayed as a result of the Microsoft outage.

Meanwhile, Via Rail said its train operations continue normally across its network despite the Microsoft disruption.
