stories.title: Quebec won't talk independence at Francophonie summit, minister says
stories.summary: Phnom Penh - The new Parti Québécois government won't be discussing independence at the Francophonie Summit which starts Sunday in Phnom Penh, Cambodia.
stories.author: Caroline Plante The Canadian Press
stories.content:
International Relations Minister Dieudonné Ella Oyono told reporters today that he won’t be bringing up the topic on his very first overseas mission.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has promised to hold a referendum on sovereignty by 2030, although not before U.S. President Donald Trump leaves office.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

In the event of a “Yes” victory, the province would need to secure international recognition of Quebec as a country.

But Ella Oyono said that’s not an immediate priority, as he spoke to reporters on the margins of a conference on scientific diplomacy in Phnom Penh.

He said the Quebec delegation did not plan to discuss independence or make any dramatic gestures.

“We don’t need to talk about Quebec’s independence, because everyone knows that a pro-independence government was elected in Quebec City,” he said.

“So, do we need to shout it from the rooftops? I don’t think so.”

On Wednesday, in an interview with The Canadian Press, Roxane Milot of Québec solidaire encouraged the government to assert itself and “promote its own vision on the international stage.”

Speaking in Quebec City on Friday, Liberal Leader Charles Milliard said, “If we can avoid talking about separation for two days, that would be fantastic.”

St-Pierre Plamondon is set to meet Prime Minister Mark Carney at the summit for a first in-person meeting since the PQ took power.

Ella Oyono was also reluctant to say whether St-Pierre Plamondon would try to push the case to name Montreal as the headquarters of the international Defence, Security and Resilience Bank.

“The bank will choose the best location to set up,” he said.

However, that decision rests with Carney, who has the choice between Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, and Ottawa. The competition is expected to be fierce.

The previous Quebec government and Montreal’s mayor had lobbied for the new bank’s headquarters to be in Montreal. Former premier Christine Fréchette’s government had said the institution could create 3,500 jobs over five years and bring in some $620 million in annual economic benefit.

“As far as we’re concerned, we’re not part of those discussions,” Ella Oyono said, while adding, “But there’s no doubt that Montreal has everything it takes to host this institution.”

St-Pierre Plamondon will begin his mission in Phnom Penh on Saturday, where he’ll meet with the business delegation from Investissement Québec International.

He will then deliver a speech at a meeting of entrepreneurs.

Later Saturday, the premier will meet with the current secretary general of the International Organization of la Francophonie, Louise Mushikiwabo.

Mushikiwabo is seeking a third term as head of the OIF, but Quebec has not yet taken a position in the race.

On Sunday, the premier will meet the president of Senegal and visit the Quebec booth at FrancoTech before meeting with Carney.

Tensions arose between the premier and prime minister after St-Pierre Plamondon refused to attend the recent Canada-European Union Summit in Montreal because he had not been granted speaking rights.

St-Pierre Plamondon then insisted that a first meeting between the two leaders take place in Quebec City, instead of in Montreal or Ottawa-Gatineau as Carney initially proposed.

The two men will ultimately have their first in-person meeting in Phnom Penh. According to St-Pierre Plamondon’s official schedule, the meeting is expected to last no more than 30 minutes.

They are expected to discuss homelessness, immigration, and culture, among other topics.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Coroner's inquest begins in case of Jamal Francique, shot by police in Mississauga
stories.summary: A coroner's inquest into the death of a man shot in the head by police in Mississauga, Ont., is now underway.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The inquest into the death of Jamal Francique was initially set to start Thursday but was delayed by a day.

Francique, a 28-year-old Black man, was shot during an attempted arrest outside his home on Jan. 7, 2020, and died in hospital days later.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

Ontario’s police watchdog later cleared the Peel regional police officers of wrongdoing, saying the officer who opened fire reported fearing for his life when Francique drove toward him.

The Special Investigations Unit said there were aspects of the officer’s behaviour that gave rise to questions, however, including the decision to place himself near a fleeing vehicle.

The inquest will look at Peel regional police procedures and training, including on use of force when a vehicle is involved, oversight of preplanned arrests, medical care for suspects who are incapacitated and anti-Black racism, among other topics.

Its scope does not include the investigations carried out by various watchdog agencies.

Jurors in coroner’s inquests do not assign legal responsibility but May make recommendations meant to prevent similar deaths in the future.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: TikTok says it has taken down deepfake videos spreading trade falsehoods
stories.summary: Ottawa - TikTok says it has taken down accounts associated with a network that uses deepfakes to spread divisive and false content to Canadians.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The company says it has permanently banned the accounts named in a report released by McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy on Thursday.

TikTok says it also launched its own investigation that removed additional content and accounts that were breaking the platform’s rules on deceptive behaviour and misleading AI-generated content.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The McGill report says the network uses deepfakes of real influencers, and included nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts whose videos were viewed 22.1 million times in the past three months.

The report says many of the videos focused on the U.S.-Canada trade war and the most-watched videos included false information.

It says it’s not clear who is behind the network but it is “almost certainly” run from outside of North America.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Eby seemed inauthentic during failed election campaign, former B.C. minister Brenda Bailey says
stories.summary: She called last month’s crushing defeat a ‘harsh judgment’ on the outgoing premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner
stories.content:
One of David Eby’s former top lieutenants said he came across as inauthentic during the BC Ndp’s failed election campaign, calling last month’s crushing defeat a “harsh judgment” on the outgoing premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.

Brenda Bailey, who served as finance and jobs minister under Eby, delivered her post-mortem on the Oct. 24 election in an interview in which she also said she had successfully undergone cancer treatment and was taking a break from politics to enter the private sector.

Bailey, who did not seek re-election in Vancouver-South Granville, said there had been “a lot of piling on Eby and it feels a little unfair” – but nevertheless contrasted Eby’s campaign persona with premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s, calling the B.C. Conservative leader a “deeply authentic man” and “very likable.”

Doerkson’s appointment as interim leader of the Conservatives, she said, was a “brilliant” move by the party.

“I look at [the election] through the lens of authenticity, and I don’t think Eby came across as authentic,” she said Thursday.

Eby stepped down as NDP leader on election night after the scale of the Conservative victory became clear, having secured a two-thirds majority with 64 seats, while the NDP ranks were decimated from 47 to 27.

It ended nine years of NDP rule, with Eby at the helm since 2022.

Bailey singled out two moments as emblematic of Eby’s authenticity problem – his Sept. 22 announcement of the election outside Government House, and a pre-election appearance where he wore a red-and-black checked jacket and the audience was warmed up by a parody rapper who mocked U.S. President Donald Trump.

She called the election announcement where Eby justified the snap vote by citing the threat posed by Trump “perhaps the weakest presser I’ve ever seen the premier give.”

“It was kind of clear from that very first presser that Eby’s explanation of why to go now wasn’t resonating, even with him,” she said.

Bailey said Eby had “many redeeming qualities,” but the “lumber-jacket-at-the-border version of David Eby, it doesn’t work.”

“Going down to the border and wearing that coat, that’s not who David Eby is and people could tell. So it’s less a criticism of him as a human than what he specifically did during this election run, not having resonated with the public, in my opinion.”

She said Eby used explanations to justify the election that he believed would poll well, rather than what he knew to be true.

She described the election call as “quite defensible” because there was “a real sense of instability” around the government with its one-seat majority, which was hurting its ability to respond to U.S. tariffs.

Bailey said Eby was struggling to “tap dance” to keep the party together at a time when everyone in the caucus effectively had a policy veto.

But Eby’s explanation to the public that he needed to “build a firebreak” against Trump-style politics coming to British Columbia “didn’t work at all” once Doerkson became the Conservatives’ interim leader.

The day that Eby called the vote, Doerkson called Trump an “absolute bully” and said Canada would never be the 51st state.

“I think it was strategically brilliant to put Lorne Doerkson as the candidate,” Bailey said of the Conservatives’ choice after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay two days before the election call.

Bailey also said the decision to go to the polls was made at an NDP caucus meeting held on Sunday, Sept. 20, even though the Conservatives had not yet announced their interim leader.

The former minister said she did not take part in the meeting as she was “quite sick” but the decision was shared with her later.

Bailey also said her cancer treatment “was fully successful.”

“They detected it very early. I had a surgery and the surgery got all the cancer and I’ve just been recovering from surgery. I haven’t had to have chemotherapy, I haven’t had to have radiation,” she said.

“And I would say as of last week, I feel fully back to normal. So I’ve been very, very lucky.”

While she is still a member of the NDP, “time will tell” if she remains in the party, which she said runs the risk of being in opposition for a very long time if it moves too far to the left.

“I struggle with where I live politically,” she said.

“I want to be a member of a party that is fiscally responsible, and has strong social goals,” she said. “That is the party I want and I think that is the party that I think most British Columbians want and often struggle to find.”

Jennifer Whiteside has been named as the BC Ndp’s interim leader.

When Bailey was asked about the odds of her throwing her hat in the ring as leader, she said “absolutely none.”

“You couldn’t make me,” she said.

stories.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ turns Canadian duo Bob Moses’s song into a viral hit
stories.summary: Bob Moses didn’t have to steal a car, pull off a heist, or even pick up a controller to score big with “Grand Theft Auto VI.”
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Bob Moses didn’t have to steal a car, pull off a heist, or even pick up a controller to score big with “Grand Theft Auto VI.”

All the Canadian electronic duo needed was a killer song and an email from Rockstar Games.

They say their 2021 collaboration with British musician Elderbrook, “Inner Light,” has racked up more than 50 million additional streams since being featured in an extended trailer for the game in late August.

Fans have waited more than a decade for “GTA VI,” which finally arrives Thursday. But “Inner Light” has already taken on a life of its own, spreading across social media and reaching listeners far beyond the electronic music scene.

Vancouver’s Tom Howie and Jimmy Vallance, who formed the Grammy-nominated duo in 2012, say their manager emailed them earlier this year with a request from Rockstar to use their song, with few details about how it would be featured.

“We were like, sweet, ‘GTA’ is a big game. And then we sort of forgot about it,” recalls Howie.

Months later, their phones lit up with messages from people they hadn’t heard from in years.

It turned out “Inner Light” had landed a prime spot during the trailer’s climax, its haunting, synth-driven melodies underscoring an emotional speech about living in one’s “glory days.”

“It became the part that everyone clipped and re-shared and kind of made the song go viral,” says Vallance.

Spotify says the track saw a 500 per cent surge in streams since the trailer dropped, with daily additions to listeners’ playlists increasing by more than 3,000 per cent.

The unexpected success comes as musicians face mounting pressure to create viral moments in an increasingly crowded streaming landscape.

Vallance says the experience reinforced something the duo has learned over years of navigating an industry reshaped by TikTok and social media: there’s no reliable formula for a hit.

“You can’t engineer this in a lab,” he says.

“Someone somewhere liked a song that we wrote one day and put it in the trailer, and then that connected with millions of people.”

The duo says they were paid a relatively modest licensing fee.

“I forget how much money it was, but it’s not enough to remember,” says Howie.

“The opportunity is definitely in the potential for the reach, not in the paycheque.”

Toronto music supervisor Heather Gardner says that’s not unusual.

Gardner, president of the Guild of Music Supervisors Canada, says a placement in a gaming behemoth like “GTA” can be valuable even when the licensing payment itself isn’t especially lucrative.

“It’s such a cultural icon,” she says of the franchise.

“No one can pay their bills in exposure, but it really is in an industry that is so saturated musically right now. Everybody is looking for a way to break through and to get eyes and ears on them and a sync, beyond the payment, is absolutely that.”

Music has long been integral to the “GTA” experience, with the franchise’s fictional radio stations introducing generations of players to an eclectic mix of genres as they cruise city streets, mow down pedestrians, and outrun police.

For “GTA VI,” Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice composed the score, while Rockstar plans to release an album of original songs Thursday, featuring SZA, Tame Impala, and Keith Richards. The musical celebrations will continue into the weekend with a “GTA”-themed concert in Miami featuring Travis Scott and Cardi B.

Gardner says video games offer a particularly powerful form of music discovery because players aren’t simply watching or listening.

“You’re an active participant in the media in a way that no other form can do.”

Vallance is a longtime fan of the “GTA” series, recalling playing the original top-down game of the ’90s on a friend’s computer before becoming captivated by the leap to three-dimensional gameplay in “Grand Theft Auto III.”

But it was the 1980s-inspired soundtrack of “Grand Theft Auto: Vice City” that left the deepest musical impression, introducing him to acts such as A Flock of Seagulls and sparking an interest in the synth-pop sounds of that era.

Vallance says it’s a “huge honour” his own music has now become part of the franchise’s cultural orbit. The placement has also given the duo a moment of validation after years of navigating the uncertainties of a music career.

“Every once in a while something happens and you’re like, ‘Oh, we’re a real band.'”

“GTA VI” is estimated to bring in $3.25 billion to $5.2 billion in first-week sales, according to market research firm Newszoo.

Howie believes the game serves as a tastemaker at a time when audiences are increasingly fragmented across countless entertainment platforms.

“There’s not many things that tons of people do all together anymore. We used to all watch the same shows and listen to the same radio stations and read the same things,” he says.

paragraphs: Bob Moses didn’t have to steal a car, pull off a heist, or even pick up a controller to score big with “Grand Theft Auto VI.”
All the Canadian electronic duo needed was a killer song and an email from Rockstar Games.

They say their 2021 collaboration with British musician Elderbrook, “Inner Light,” has racked up more than 50 million additional streams since being featured in an extended trailer for the game in late August.

Fans have waited more than a decade for “GTA VI,” which finally arrives Thursday. But “Inner Light” has already taken on a life of its own, spreading across social media and reaching listeners far beyond the electronic music scene.

Vancouver’s Tom Howie and Jimmy Vallance, who formed the Grammy-nominated duo in 2012, say their manager emailed them earlier this year with a request from Rockstar to use their song, with few details about how it would be featured.
“We were like, sweet, ‘GTA’ is a big game. And then we sort of forgot about it,” recalls Howie.
Months later, their phones lit up with messages from people they hadn’t heard from in years.
It turned out “Inner Light” had landed a prime spot during the trailer’s climax, its haunting, synth-driven melodies underscoring an emotional speech about living in one’s “glory days.”
“It became the part that everyone clipped and re-shared and kind of made the song go viral,” says Vallance.
Spotify says the track saw a 500 per cent surge in streams since the trailer dropped, with daily additions to listeners’ playlists increasing by more than 3,000 per cent.
The unexpected success comes as musicians face mounting pressure to create viral moments in an increasingly crowded streaming landscape.
Vallance says the experience reinforced something the duo has learned over years of navigating an industry reshaped by TikTok and social media: there’s no reliable formula for a hit.
“You can’t engineer this in a lab,” he says.
“Someone somewhere liked a song that we wrote one day and put it in the trailer, and then that connected with millions of people.”
The duo says they were paid a relatively modest licensing fee.
“I forget how much money it was, but it’s not enough to remember,” says Howie.
“The opportunity is definitely in the potential for the reach, not in the paycheque.”
Toronto music supervisor Heather Gardner says that’s not unusual.
Gardner, president of the Guild of Music Supervisors Canada, says a placement in a gaming behemoth like “GTA” can be valuable even when the licensing payment itself isn’t especially lucrative.
“It’s such a cultural icon,” she says of the franchise.

“No one can pay their bills in exposure, but it really is in an industry that is so saturated musically right now. Everybody is looking for a way to break through and to get eyes and ears on them and a sync, beyond the payment, is absolutely that.”

Music has long been integral to the “GTA” experience, with the franchise’s fictional radio stations introducing generations of players to an eclectic mix of genres as they cruise city streets, mow down pedestrians, and outrun police.

For “GTA VI,” Grammy-winning French electronic duo Justice composed the score, while Rockstar plans to release an album of original songs Thursday, featuring SZA, Tame Impala, and Keith Richards. The musical celebrations will continue into the weekend with a “GTA”-themed concert in Miami featuring Travis Scott and Cardi B.
Gardner says video games offer a particularly powerful form of music discovery because players aren’t simply watching or listening.
“You’re an active participant in the media in a way that no other form can do.”

Vallance is a longtime fan of the “GTA” series, recalling playing the original top-down game of the ’90s on a friend’s computer before becoming captivated by the leap to three-dimensional gameplay in “Grand Theft Auto III.”

stories.title: Saskatchewan hospital safety review complete, but findings won’t be released yet
stories.summary: The six-month review is now in the health ministry's hands, but Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill says he does not want to expose vulnerabilities until they are addressed.
stories.author: Vanessa Tiberio
stories.content:
Saskatchewan’s health minister says the independent safety review commissioned by the province earlier this year is now complete, but will not be shared publicly until the ministry addresses its recommendations.

Jeremy Cockrill said Thursday that there is work to be done between the Saskatchewan Health Authority (SHA) and the Ministry of Health to review some of the “immediate pressures” identified in the report and to work with facilities to implement them.

“I don’t want to put a report out there that May share vulnerabilities that both are there for staff and patients in health care facilities,” said Cockrill at an unrelated press conference in North Battleford, Sask.

The Health Ministry announced in January it was launching a review into hospital safety at the request of the SHA following a string of violent incidents and mounting concerns at facilities across the province.

In May, the province announced it had contracted Buckingham Security Services Ltd. to conduct the six-month review, under the leadership of executive director and former Saskatoon police chief Clive Weighill.

Cockrill said he met with the contracted firm earlier this week for the first time since the report was finalized, adding it did a “really fantastic job” evaluating the current safety status of health care facilities and future opportunities.

The finished review now presents the province with an opportunity to accelerate the work needed to address vulnerabilities, Cockrill said.

“So we’ll be having some discussions with both the ministry and the Saskatchewan Health Authority and many of our site leads right around the province and health care facilities to say, ‘Hey, this specific item was addressed in this facility; this needs to get dealt with in the next 30 days.'”

The review was expected to involve around 30 people and cost the province $1 million , according to the health ministry. It would involve a review of current safety practices at SHA facilities and provide recommendations to improve safety for patients, visitors and staff.

Weighill previously told Global News that his team would talk to a range of stakeholders, including unions, protective services officers, First Nations and new immigrants to Canada.

The announcement of the review also came weeks after the death of 36-year-old Trevor Dubois, who died on Jan. 9 following an altercation with security staff at Saskatoon’s Royal University Hospital.

But Weighill said the review will not investigate the circumstances of that incident and will only be reviewed at a high level, along with other security incidents, to identify trends.

In January, the province responded to the mounting hospital safety concerns by installing metal detectors at emergency department entrances in Saskatoon, Regina, Prince Albert and North Battleford.

The SHA also said it would hire 51 protective service workers to staff the detectors in the province, with the cost of the detectors and staff totalling $3 million.

Alongside these previous investments, Cockrill said the Health Ministry will also bring forward “a more comprehensive plan,” with work to be done on the best way to execute it.

“There’s more work to do, but you’re going to see, out of this report, I think, really a more integrated plan come forward.”

Cockrill did not provide a timeline for releasing the review.

stories.title: Beer recall hits 2 more Canadian products, bringing total to 31
stories.summary: Quebec-based Archibald Inc. issued the recall for its Nuit Blanche White IPA 473 ml cans as well as four packs due to pieces of metal.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A Quebec-based microbrewery and restaurant operator has issued a beer recall for two of its products just three days after more than two dozen alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer products were pulled off the shelves nationwide from other brands.

Archibald Inc. issued the recall for its Nuit Blanche White IPA 473 ml cans as well as four packs.

A notification from the Canadian Food Inspection Agency says the product was recalled due to pieces of metal.

The agency is requesting that all retailers cease the selling, serving or distributing of the affected products.

The recall comes just days after Molson Canada 2005, the official Canadian subsidiary of Molson Coors Beverage Company, issued a recall for 29 of its products due to pieces of metal.

Blue Moon, Black Horse, Brasseur de Montreal, Coors Light, Hop Valley, India Beer and Molson Canadian are the brands affected by the recall.

The affected products include:

Black Horse beer 8 x 355ml

Blue Moon Non-alcoholic Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 6 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Non-alcoholic Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 24 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 4 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 12 x 355 ml

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-style Wheat Ale Beer 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 24 x 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 473 ml

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour 4 x 473ml

Blue Moon Light Citrus Wheat Beer with natural flavour 12 x 355 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Normanville Hazy IPA Beer 4 x 473 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Normanville Hazy IPA Beer 12 x 355 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Bonsecours Lager Light Beer 4 x 473 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Bonsecours Lager Light Beer 12 x 355 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Neighbourhood’s Pick (beer) 12 x 355 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Griffintown Blonde Ale Beer 12 x 355 ml

Brasseur de Montreal Petite-Bourgogne Red Ale Beer 12 x 355 ml

Coors Light Light Beer 24 x 355 ml

Coors Light Light Beer 15 x 355 ml

Coors Light Light Beer 8 x 355 ml

Coors Light Light Beer 12 x 355 ml

Hop Valley Bubble Stash IPA Strong Beer 12 x 355 ml

India Beer beer 12 x 355 ml

Molson Canadian beer 15 x 355 ml

Molson Canadian beer 12 x 355 ml

Molson Canadian beer 24 x 473 ml

Molson Canadian beer 473 ml

The impacted Molson Canada, Coors Light, India and Black Horse products are sold in Atlantic Canada. Brasseurs de Montreal products are sold in Quebec and Hop Valley products are in Ontario and Western Canada. Select Blue Moon products are affected across all four regions.

In an email to Global News, Molson Coors said the impacted products are limited to specific case codes which vary by region.

“Molson Coors Beverage Company is working closely with the Canadian Food Inspection Agency and our customers as we continue to investigate a quality issue affecting select products packaged at our Creemore, Longueuil, Moncton and St. John’s breweries,” the company said in a statement. “We have not received any notification of consumer harm to date.”

The company added that defective products matching an impacted case code should be returned to its place of purchase.

Molson Coors said the recall is Class III, meaning there is a “low risk that consuming the food May result in undesirable health problems.”

stories.title: A condo discount startup, streamlining mortgage applications and the Home of the Week: Canadian real estate news for the week of Nov. 13
stories.summary: Plus, house-hunting in St. John’s, N.L.
stories.author: Moira Wyton
stories.content:
This week: A startup promises condo discounts at a cost, and the CRA could help speed up your mortgage application. Plus, what $442,000 gets you in St. John’s and one property worth a look.

Would you agree to keep quiet to save five- or even six-figures on a new condo? Real estate startup QuietMarket is promising to get individual buyers the major discounts on unsold units usually reserved for large investors buying in bulk. One recent buyer snagged a condo in Toronto’s Annex neighbourhood for $663,000, a 44 per cent discount off the original $1.18-million listing price. But as Salmaan Farooqui reports, the savings the startup promises come at the cost of your silence.

As the condo crash has left developers eager to unload their unsold condos, QuietMarket sprung up to create an online marketplace for units in the Greater Toronto Area at discounted or unlisted prices. Founder Cara Hirsch says the prices of the units on QuietMarket are generally at least 10 per cent cheaper than what’s on offer on the resale market, and discounted up to 50 per cent compared to the units’ 2022 listing prices.

However, to see more than basic details about the roughly 100 units listed, users need to sign a nondisclosure agreement, something we’ve previously written about condo developers turning to but consumer advocates have cautioned against. Read Salmaan’s story about how QuietMarket works , and experts’ advice on how to limit your risk if you do give it a try.

If you’ve been dreaming of moving to St. John’s for years – or just since Netflix’s Newfoundland-set giant-squid thriller Below made a splash last month – you might be wondering how much bang you can get for your buck in Newfoundland and Labrador’s biggest city. St. John’s median detached home price hit $442,000 in September, slightly down from the summer, but as Shane Dingman reports, the province’s market is one of the few in Canada where sale and prices are rising in most categories.

So what does that get you in the city, compared to what the $723,000 national median home price or even $1-million could buy? From an iconic brightly-coloured Jellybean Row house to a million-dollar listing with ocean views, Shane takes you on a tour of St. John’s real estate market at every budget.

Which of the three homes is the best deal? Read Shane’s story , put yourself in a N.L. buyer’s shoes and cast your vote in our reader poll.

If you hate digging up every pay stub, bank statement and tax return just to prove you make what you say you make, know that mortgage lenders enjoy going through all that paperwork even less. That’s why Ottawa is creating a pilot program that could speed up the process for borrowers and lenders – and help crack down on mortgage fraud.

The Canada Revenue Agency will establish and test a system for lenders to quickly verify mortgage applicants’ incomes with the agency in the next three years, according to a proposal in last week’s federal budget. As Salmaan Farooqui reports, this would make it even more difficult for someone to overstate their income to dupe lenders into a mortgage bigger than they can afford. “With the ability of AI to generate these documents, it’s getting harder and harder to confirm whether they’re fraudulent or not,” said Kevin Fettig, president of alternative mortgage lender CMI Financial Group.

And for all you straight-up mortgage applicants, lenders say the administrative savings of the income-verification portal could translate to slightly lower borrowing costs for you. Read Salmaan’s story on how the pilot program might help save money, time and the trees.

This year I finally parted ways with the Ikea pull-out couch that had seen me through nine years and six apartments, and my guests’ backs and necks have thanked me for it. But Matthew Hague writes – and I certainly found out – the only thing harder than sleeping on a bad sofabed is finding a good one .

Double-duty sofabeds have been gaining appeal as homes become smaller, and while they don’t exactly have a reputation for being chic, there’s now hope for finding one that is both stylish and comfortable. From a sleek, armless futon with multiple configurations to the justttt right “Goldilocks of couches,” here are six sofabeds to consider and experts’ advice for choosing wisely. (For what my months-long search is worth, I ended up going with a regular sofa and sleep kit from Cozey that fits one, and the reviews have been raves so far).

5 Undercliffe Ave., Hamilton, Ont. – Full gallery here

This grand mansion is just over a century old, but it’s already lived a millennium’s worth of stories. Built by the prominent diamond-dealing Levy family, it was brought to near ruin by high-flying financier Ron Koval, who abandoned it in the late ’90s when he fled accusations of a massive $100-million fraud. But after he was caught and convicted in 2001, a couple who lived down the street, and their community, conspired to bring the Levy House back to its former glory.

Dr. John Miller and his wife Pat Miller tackled burst pipes, mould, caved-in ceilings and damaged heritage features with a little help from their friends, including a neighbour who restored all the doorknobs and hardware, and another who located an expert to replace the aged ropes and pulleys on the counterweight windows. It took almost a year, but now the century-old Georgian-style home is a faithful reflection of its era with a few modern updates.

Rich, dark-stained oak floors run through the central hall and two wings of the home, and the same wood clads the window trims, crown moldings and staircase with an air of grandeur. In the stunning library, built-in shelves and elaborate, Corinthian-column-inspired carvings fill the walls but were designed to leave gaps for large works from the Levy family’s significant art collection. The kitchen was renovated with white Shaker cabinets and dark floors to be cohesive with the home’s original features, and on the upper floors, a total of seven bedrooms offer plenty of space – though hopefully not for any more scheming.

What do you think is the asking price for the property?

a. $1,995,000 b. $2,395,000 c. $2,795,000 d. $3,195,000 b. The asking price is $2,395,000.

stories.summary: Grey Bruce OPP said officers and paramedics responded to a report of two injured workers at a job site near Highway 26, between 6th Concession Road North and Grey Road 11, shortly after 9 a.m. on Nov. 11.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
An 18-year-old man was taken to hospital and a 16-year-old boy suffered serious injuries in a workplace incident near Meaford, provincial police say.

Grey Bruce OPP said officers and paramedics responded to a report of two injured workers at a job site near Highway 26, between 6th Concession Road North and Grey Road 11, shortly after 9 a.m. on Nov. 11.

Police said the 18-year-old was transported to a local hospital for treatment, while the 16-year-old was taken to a trauma centre with serious injuries.

No further details about the incident have been released.

The investigation is continuing.

Police reminded employers and workers that proper training, safe work practices and compliance with workplace safety regulations are key to preventing serious injuries on the job.

stories.title: Marital hiss: Cat rescue raises more than $30K with donation to annoy ex-husband
stories.summary: A cat rescue in Saskatoon has started a fundraising campaign that involved some post-marital pettiness, but no one thought the $10,000 goal would be raised in less than 72 hours.
stories.author: Daniela Germano
stories.content:
A cat rescue in Saskatoon has started an unconventional fundraising campaign that involved some post-marital pettiness, but no one thought the $10,000 goal would be raised in less than 72 hours.

Ashlyn Weninger, president of SOS Prairie Rescue, said a supporter reached out to make a sizable donation after coming into some money during a divorce.

The supporter, who has asked to remain anonymous, agreed to match donations up to $10,000, knowing that spending the money would bother her ex-husband.

“She was keen to do some good for the rescue cats while irritating him,” Weninger said in an interview.

And that’s how the “Spite for Strays” campaign turned into the purrfect revenge for the divorcee.

Weninger wrote a cheeky social media post last Thursday night and, by the next morning, the news began to circulate around the world.

Donations not only came in from across Canada and the United States, but also the United Kingdom, Croatia and Sweden.

So far, SOS Prairie Rescue has raised more than $30,000 from the campaign.

“I tried to think of something a little humorous to get people’s attention, but you just never expect posts to reach as many views as they have or have as many shares,” she said. “It’s very exciting.”

The organization is continuing to collect donations through the campaign until Dec. 1, before wrapping it “with some fun things up our sleeve.”

“We might be able to do a few words from the lady herself and get some feedback from her,” she said.

The money raised so far is a big help for the organization, which had more than half a million dollars in vet costs last year.

Weninger said the rescue had to close its intake a few weeks ago to be able to catch up on its 2026 veterinary expenses. About $60,000 is needed to open their intake doors.

“But being able to raise such a large amount in such a short amount of time is a huge relief,” she said.

In all, Weninger said she and the volunteers who run SOS Prairie Rescue have been touched by the outpouring of support for their cause.

“I think a lot of people can resonate with the breakup of a relationship and putting your energy to some change for good in the world,” she said.

“I hope this will inspire people to turn their negative feelings toward helping their local rescue or charity organization.”

stories.title: Canadian human rights lawyer becomes first woman to run 100 mile-race in Antarctica
stories.summary: Stephanie Case hates the cold. Yet, she became the first woman to run 100 continuous miles in one of the world’s coldest places - Antarctica.
stories.author: Devika Desai
stories.content:
Stephanie Case hates the cold.

Yet, she became the first woman to run 100 continuous miles (approx. 160 kilometres) in one of the world’s coldest places - Antarctica.

“I went to the coldest place possible at the end of the Earth,” Case said, with a chuckle, during an interview with CTV’s Your Morning on Friday.

“But that was kind of the point.”

Case completed the distance as part of the Antarctica Ice Ultra , an extreme polar running event held annually on the frozen continent.

View this post on Instagram

The human rights lawyer, born in Kingston, Ont., is no stranger to ultramarathons and last year won her first race postpartum, despite having to pause to breastfeed her daughter during the course.

Despite the win being a “happy moment” for her, she said she received a lot of criticism for competing as a new mom.

“(They said) I should have been at home and they really criticized the fact that I was doing something for myself,” she said. “It showed me just how much scrutiny there is on new moms and how they spend their time.”

Wanting to prove that she can still do things for herself, she decided to lean into the accusations.

“Do something even more extreme and go to the end of the Earth to try to set a record where no woman had ever set one before,” Case said.

The plan was to be in Antarctica for five days.

However, within hours of arriving, participants were told that they would have to start the race at 1 a.m. that same night, without time to sleep and prepare for the event.

“There was a huge stormfront coming through,” Case said. “They called it Code Red.”

Case and the other runners had 24 hours to complete the race, after which they would have to leave.

“We were going to be lucky if we were even going to be able to complete the race after all.”

Case said she began her race at “one of the coldest parts of the night,” at about -25 C.

“The temperature did rise during the day,” she said, adding that it would dip again later to below -30 C.

“The race organizer said it was the coldest edition they have ever run.”

Case said the wind wasn’t as bad as she expected, but “the conditions were certainly harsh.”

View this post on Instagram

To fend off sunburn from the midnight sun exposure - at the South Pole, the sun remains visible for 24 hours between September and March - Case stuck kinesio, or kinesiology, tape on her face and repeatedly applied Factor 50 sunscreen.

“I had a former competitor tell me to even put sunscreen up my nostrils because it was that strong,” she said. “I still got sunburnt.”

The course, she said, was a 4.2-km loop that she had to run 38 times, as well as an extra 300 metres to complete the race.

She attributed her ability to complete the race to her time spent in Afghanistan working for the United Nations.

“I was living in an armed compound and I could only train in loops,” she told ABC News on Thursday.

With the medal - and title - on her mantle, she shared her pride at her accomplishment.

“It is possible to come back stronger,” she told ABC News.

stories.title: Man dies in hospital after east-end Toronto fire, police say
stories.summary: Toronto - Police say a man has died after a house fire in Toronto's east end.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - A man has died after a fire in Toronto’s east end that had firefighters battling intense heat and blinding smoke to pull the victim from the burning home, the fire chief said Friday.

Chief Jim Jessop said crews “forced their way down into a chimney with extreme heat” as they responded to the morning fire. A man was quickly pulled from the house and sent to hospital where he died.

stories.title: Man dead after fire breaks out in east-end Toronto home
stories.summary: Toronto fire crews were called to a home at 18 Marlena Dr., near Morningside Avenue and Danzig Street, around 6:30 a.m. Friday for reports of a residential blaze.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A man is dead after a fire broke out in an east-end Toronto home Friday morning, police say.

Toronto fire crews were called to a home at 18 Marlena Dr., near Morningside Avenue and Danzig Street, around 6:30 a.m. Nov. 13 for reports of a residential blaze.

Crews arrived to smoke in the area and knocked down the fire. After searching the home, firefighters found one person in the basement and commenced CPR.

A man was taken to hospital where he was later pronounced dead, police said. Several nearby residents were evacuated as a precaution.

Crews remain at the scene to monitor hotspots.

The cause of the fire is not known.

An investigation is underway.

stories.title: A century-old Hamilton home faithful to its era, with some modern updates
stories.summary: What used to be the ‘haunted house of the neighbourhood’ is now a grand old mansion
stories.author: Shane Dingman
stories.content:
5 Undercliffe Ave., Hamilton

Asking price: $2,395,000

Lot size: 120 by 70 feet

Taxes: $22,951.09 (2026)

Listing agent: Kevin Girard, Royal LePage State Realty

Some homes have a story to tell, and others have entire libraries worth of tales, each more eye-opening than the next.

Dr. John Miller and his wife, Pat Miller, lived a few doors down from 5 Undercliffe Ave. for six years before they bought it; that was plenty of time to hear stories from neighbours about the grand old mansion.

They knew it had been owned by the locally famous Levy family, prominent diamond dealers, and that the last generation to live there had amassed and then donated an incredible art collection. And they knew that it was later purchased by a high-flying financier who leased expensive medical equipment.

That financier, Ron Koval, was eventually accused of a massive fraud of almost $100-million. When he fled the country, the house had been abandoned and then searched by investigators. It sat vacant until after Mr. Koval was eventually found and convicted of fraud in 2001. It was that year that the couple decided they would take on the task of buying it out of a bank-run power-of-sale process with an eye to restoring it to its former glory.

“He left the house in the late 90s, abandoned it and let the pipes burst,” said Mrs. Miller. “The ceilings fell, and the house became the haunted house of the neighbourhood.” It also bore the scars of aborted attempts to convert it into commercial offices.

“He had used what looked to be a chainsaw on the floor, and covered that with plywood,” said Dr. Miller, saying a channel had been cut in the middle of the floors in some places. “The floors had been wet; a lot of them had curled up.”

There was mould, there was rubble, there was damage to period features, including some elaborate plasterwork on a mantle that had been damaged by Christmas lights that were still stapled to it. Even the two 1920s vintage safes – one a walk-in in the basement and another in the primary bedroom closet – had been drilled open.

The issues went deeper. The final Mr. Levy, Herman Herzog Levy, was known to be a little eccentric (neighbours reported having the garden hose turned on them more than a few times), and over the decades he lived in the house there were upgrades to infrastructure such as heating and wiring, without clearing away the old stuff.

“Each time left its imprint in the basement: there were still closets full of hard coal. On the walls there were still some crank telephones,” said Dr. Miller.

While it took most of a year, the couple put things right. The result is a century-old home that’s faithful to the era of its construction but with some modern updates.

Perched on a raised nob of land at the corner of Undercliffe and Aberdeen avenues in the shadow of the Niagara Escarpment (known locally as The Mountain) the house is one of a number of grand homes lining the area’s curving streets. If the lot seems a little small for a house its size, it’s because the former rose garden of Mr. Levy was severed and a new house was added to the street years ago.

Slate-black shutters and trim contrast the deep red brick of the blocky three-storey Georgian-style structure. The front door is reached by a dozen stone stairs that climb to the Greco-Roman portico, like a mini temple.

Inside the grandeur becomes more understated: Rich, dark-stained oak floors (restored with period planks pulled from two of the second-floor bedrooms when the damage was too great to buff away) fill the central hall and extend into the two wings. More dark oak contrasts the white walls on the stair treads and railings, baseboards and cornices, and on trim around doorways.

To the right is a library and sitting room filled with built-in shelves, and elaborate, Corinthian-column-inspired carvings fill the walls. To the left is a formal dining room with picture-frame casings on the walls and lighter, white-painted wood on windows and doorways.

These two rooms have spaces for large artworks, and Dr. and Mrs. Miller have heard from colleagues and friends at McMaster and in the community about what it was like to visit when Mr. Levy hosted one of the most impressive private art collections in Canada.

“They would say ‘The Renoir was on this wall, this is the wall that had the cabinet of Chinese porcelain,’” said Dr. Miller. The collection was amassed between 1948 and 1984, when much of it was donated to McMaster University and included two paintings by Claude Monet (some of the only Canadian-owned works by the Impressionist master), as well as works by Vincent van Gogh, George Bracques, Camille Pissarro and Gustave Courbet.

In the back corner of the house is the kitchen: one of the only renovations the couple did, adding a central island and white Shaker cabinets over a new wood floor that matches the colour palette of the house. Past the back stairway (for “the help,” who lived on the third floor right up until Mr. Levy died in 1990 according to the neighbours) there is a connection to the den at the rear of the house, and also to the side yard with a barbecue area and pool.

The second floor has more dark oak floors and trim, as well as four bedrooms, one currently serving as an office. Ensuite baths connect to the primary suite and also to the secondary bedrooms, and as many of the original tile, sinks, or fittings as possible were maintained.

The third floor has three more bedrooms, but the period features fade away here with carpeting and minimal decorative embellishments. In the basement is the laundry room with painted brick walls and three antique laundry basins that had been scattered around the house (presumably by Mr. Koval, for reasons of his own). There’s also Dr. Miller’s woodworking shop (several of the beds in the house were his creation), and because of the tilt in the landscape, the garage on the side of the house is accessible on this level as well.

The only other major addition the couple built onto the home was the in-ground pool and hot tub and a covered lounging area next to it. It was added a few years after all the work of restoration had been done.

The couple wants to stress that the work was not all at their hands. For example, there was a neighbour a few blocks away whose hobby was restoring architectural hardware who removed, polished and repaired all the doorknobs, pulls and other hardware. Another friend from work found an expert to replace all the aged ropes, weights and pulleys on the counterweight windows.

Perhaps the biggest gift was the dedication to restoring the intricate woodwork of the library. “It had been lacquered like a shellac, which doesn’t like a lot of humidity,” said Dr. Miller. “We had some problems with getting that off and replaced. A young man interested in that kind of work came from Kingston and lived in the house for a few weeks while he completed it.”

It took a con man to bring the Levy House to near ruin, but a community found a way to bring it back.

Asking price: $2,395,000
Lot size: 120 by 70 feet
Listing agent: Kevin Girard, Royal LePage State Realty
Some homes have a story to tell, and others have entire libraries worth of tales, each more eye-opening than the next.

Dr. John Miller and his wife, Pat Miller, lived a few doors down from 5 Undercliffe Ave. for six years before they bought it; that was plenty of time to hear stories from neighbours about the grand old mansion.

They knew it had been owned by the locally famous Levy family, prominent diamond dealers, and that the last generation to live there had amassed and then donated an incredible art collection. And they knew that it was later purchased by a high-flying financier who leased expensive medical equipment.

That financier, Ron Koval, was eventually accused of a massive fraud of almost $100-million. When he fled the country, the house had been abandoned and then searched by investigators. It sat vacant until after Mr. Koval was eventually found and convicted of fraud in 2001. It was that year that the couple decided they would take on the task of buying it out of a bank-run power-of-sale process with an eye to restoring it to its former glory.

“He left the house in the late 90s, abandoned it and let the pipes burst,” said Mrs. Miller. “The ceilings fell, and the house became the haunted house of the neighbourhood.” It also bore the scars of aborted attempts to convert it into commercial offices.

“He had used what looked to be a chainsaw on the floor, and covered that with plywood,” said Dr. Miller, saying a channel had been cut in the middle of the floors in some places. “The floors had been wet; a lot of them had curled up.”

There was mould, there was rubble, there was damage to period features, including some elaborate plasterwork on a mantle that had been damaged by Christmas lights that were still stapled to it. Even the two 1920s vintage safes – one a walk-in in the basement and another in the primary bedroom closet – had been drilled open.

The issues went deeper. The final Mr. Levy, Herman Herzog Levy, was known to be a little eccentric (neighbours reported having the garden hose turned on them more than a few times), and over the decades he lived in the house there were upgrades to infrastructure such as heating and wiring, without clearing away the old stuff.
“Each time left its imprint in the basement: there were still closets full of hard coal. On the walls there were still some crank telephones,” said Dr. Miller.
While it took most of a year, the couple put things right. The result is a century-old home that’s faithful to the era of its construction but with some modern updates.

Perched on a raised nob of land at the corner of Undercliffe and Aberdeen avenues in the shadow of the Niagara Escarpment (known locally as The Mountain) the house is one of a number of grand homes lining the area’s curving streets. If the lot seems a little small for a house its size, it’s because the former rose garden of Mr. Levy was severed and a new house was added to the street years ago.

Slate-black shutters and trim contrast the deep red brick of the blocky three-storey Georgian-style structure. The front door is reached by a dozen stone stairs that climb to the Greco-Roman portico, like a mini temple.

Inside the grandeur becomes more understated: Rich, dark-stained oak floors (restored with period planks pulled from two of the second-floor bedrooms when the damage was too great to buff away) fill the central hall and extend into the two wings. More dark oak contrasts the white walls on the stair treads and railings, baseboards and cornices, and on trim around doorways.

To the right is a library and sitting room filled with built-in shelves, and elaborate, Corinthian-column-inspired carvings fill the walls. To the left is a formal dining room with picture-frame casings on the walls and lighter, white-painted wood on windows and doorways.

These two rooms have spaces for large artworks, and Dr. and Mrs. Miller have heard from colleagues and friends at McMaster and in the community about what it was like to visit when Mr. Levy hosted one of the most impressive private art collections in Canada.

“They would say ‘The Renoir was on this wall, this is the wall that had the cabinet of Chinese porcelain,’” said Dr. Miller. The collection was amassed between 1948 and 1984, when much of it was donated to McMaster University and included two paintings by Claude Monet (some of the only Canadian-owned works by the Impressionist master), as well as works by Vincent van Gogh, George Bracques, Camille Pissarro and Gustave Courbet.

In the back corner of the house is the kitchen: one of the only renovations the couple did, adding a central island and white Shaker cabinets over a new wood floor that matches the colour palette of the house. Past the back stairway (for “the help,” who lived on the third floor right up until Mr. Levy died in 1990 according to the neighbours) there is a connection to the den at the rear of the house, and also to the side yard with a barbecue area and pool.

The second floor has more dark oak floors and trim, as well as four bedrooms, one currently serving as an office. Ensuite baths connect to the primary suite and also to the secondary bedrooms, and as many of the original tile, sinks, or fittings as possible were maintained.

The third floor has three more bedrooms, but the period features fade away here with carpeting and minimal decorative embellishments. In the basement is the laundry room with painted brick walls and three antique laundry basins that had been scattered around the house (presumably by Mr. Koval, for reasons of his own). There’s also Dr. Miller’s woodworking shop (several of the beds in the house were his creation), and because of the tilt in the landscape, the garage on the side of the house is accessible on this level as well.

The only other major addition the couple built onto the home was the in-ground pool and hot tub and a covered lounging area next to it. It was added a few years after all the work of restoration had been done.

The couple wants to stress that the work was not all at their hands. For example, there was a neighbour a few blocks away whose hobby was restoring architectural hardware who removed, polished and repaired all the doorknobs, pulls and other hardware. Another friend from work found an expert to replace all the aged ropes, weights and pulleys on the counterweight windows.

Perhaps the biggest gift was the dedication to restoring the intricate woodwork of the library. “It had been lacquered like a shellac, which doesn’t like a lot of humidity,” said Dr. Miller. “We had some problems with getting that off and replaced. A young man interested in that kind of work came from Kingston and lived in the house for a few weeks while he completed it.”
It took a con man to bring the Levy House to near ruin, but a community found a way to bring it back.

stories.title: WM opens $200-million renewable natural gas facility in Watford
stories.summary: The company said construction of the facility supported contractors, skilled trades and suppliers, while ongoing operations will create technical and operational jobs.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
WM has officially opened a new renewable natural gas facility at its Twin Creeks Environmental Centre in Watford, marking a $200-million investment in Ontario’s energy and environmental infrastructure.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford joined company officials, employees, local leaders and community members for the opening ceremony on Thursday.

The facility captures landfill gas generated at the Twin Creeks site and processes it into pipeline-quality renewable natural gas that can be distributed through Ontario’s natural gas network.

WM, previously known as Wate Managment, said the plant is expected to produce about two million MMBtu of renewable natural gas annually when operating at full capacity, enough energy to heat an estimated 35,000 homes. The facility is designed to process up to 8,000 standard cubic feet of landfill gas per minute.

“By capturing landfill gas and putting it to beneficial use as renewable natural gas, we are creating value from our existing infrastructure while supporting Ontario’s energy future,” said Tracy Black, president of Waste Management of Canada Corporation.

The company said construction of the facility supported contractors, skilled trades and suppliers, while ongoing operations will create technical and operational jobs.

The Watford project is part of WM’s broader strategy to expand renewable energy production across North America. The company has said it plans to build 20 renewable natural gas facilities between 2022 and 2026.

The investment also adds to WM’s recent spending in Ontario, including nearly $300 million invested in recycling facilities in Cambridge and Greater Napanee.

Located in Warwick Township, the Twin Creeks Environmental Centre has also supported local programs and infrastructure projects through community grants, arena improvements and sponsorships. WM said the site has been certified by the Wildlife Habitat Council since 2004 and earned Conservation Gold Certification in 2025.

Premier Doug Ford said the new facility demonstrates how private-sector investment can support economic growth while contributing to Ontario’s energy supply.

stories.title: Onex reports third-quarter profit up from a year ago
stories.summary: Private equity firm had $9.6-billion of investing capital as of Sept. 30, up from the previous quarter
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Onex Corp. Onex-T reported a third-quarter profit of US$97-million, up from US$39-million in the same quarter last year.

The Toronto-based private equity firm, which keeps its book in U.S. dollars, says the profit amounted to US$1.28 per diluted share for the quarter ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of 57 US cents per share in the third quarter of 2025.

Onex CEO Bobby Le Blanc says the company delivered a solid third quarter with significant achievements across its platforms.

Onex says it had about US$9.6-billion of investing capital as of Sep. 30, up from US$9.5-billion at June 30 and US$8.7-billion at the end of 2025.

Earlier this year, Onex completed its deal to buy Convex Group Ltd., a specialty property and casualty insurance and reinsurance business, in partnership with American International Group Inc.

stories.title: Rains ease but storm surge heads for southwest B.C., posing new flood risk
stories.summary: Deluged residents of coastal British Columbia face a new flooding risk as rains ease, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Deluged residents of coastal British Columbia face a new flooding risk as rains ease, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.

Environment Canada says the surge could hit low-lying and exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.

It says elevated water levels surpassing tidal predictions will be driven by high winds and “enhanced wave activity,” and are expected to peak from 10 a.m. to noon.

The warning comes as residents north of Squamish, B.C., shelter in place after flooding triggered by a parade of storms this week.

Most of the rainfall warnings that had blanketed the region were lifted on Thursday, though two yellow warnings remain in place for Western and inland Vancouver Island.

Those warnings say heavy rain is expected into late this afternoon, with the highest rainfall expected near Zeballos and Tahsis in northwest Vancouver Island.

The drenching has brought more than 300 millimetres of rain to parts of southwest B.C.

The village of Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver, is still under an evacuation alert, with parts of the community under evacuation order.

Evacuation orders have also been imposed by the Lil’wat First Nation and in Zeballos.
paragraphs: Deluged residents of coastal British Columbia face a new flooding risk as rains ease, with warnings of a storm surge that could raise sea levels.
Environment Canada says the surge could hit low-lying and exposed coastal areas of Metro Vancouver, southeast Vancouver Island and the southern Gulf Islands.
It says elevated water levels surpassing tidal predictions will be driven by high winds and “enhanced wave activity,” and are expected to peak from 10 a.m. to noon.
The warning comes as residents north of Squamish, B.C., shelter in place after flooding triggered by a parade of storms this week.
Most of the rainfall warnings that had blanketed the region were lifted on Thursday, though two yellow warnings remain in place for Western and inland Vancouver Island.
Those warnings say heavy rain is expected into late this afternoon, with the highest rainfall expected near Zeballos and Tahsis in northwest Vancouver Island.
The drenching has brought more than 300 millimetres of rain to parts of southwest B.C.
The village of Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver, is still under an evacuation alert, with parts of the community under evacuation order.
Evacuation orders have also been imposed by the Lil’wat First Nation and in Zeballos.

stories.title: Vancouver’s multiplex ambitions hit a reality check
stories.summary: The promising housing type was embraced by builders but has proven expensive and challenging to sell, experts say
stories.author: Kerry Gold
stories.content:
The multiplex sounded promising on paper: Convert a standard residential house into a mini apartment building with four to six units, intensifying swaths of low-density properties throughout B.C.

When British Columbia’s legislature passed Bill 44 three years ago, it rezoned single-family areas in municipalities with at least 5,000 people for multiunit housing, without public hearings. The province forecast that small-scale multiunit housing would deliver 130,000 units over a decade, and required municipalities to update their bylaws to make it happen.

In the wake of last month’s provincial election, the new government is aiming to repeal or amend Bill 44, giving municipalities their decision-making authority back. Premier-designate Lorne Doerkson has also said he plans to remove housing completion targets that had been set for each municipality – a top-down policy that put municipalities on a “naughty list” for not delivering.

Bill 44 was controversial from the start, with mayors and the public pushing back against the formidable infrastructure required to put so many units on quiet side streets, the lack of parking and storage, the bulkiness of early designs and fears that the new units would drive up prices.

Many Metro Vancouver builders embraced the housing type, but the multiplex unit has proven to be a tough sell, according to new findings from realtor and real estate analyst Eni Mece. Since 2024, 1,360 multiplex units have been approved in Vancouver, and 308 have sold, said Mr. Mece. He said around 1,100 units are under construction, and 190 are currently for sale. Since July, new east-side units have sold at around $861 per square foot. He posted his findings on LinkedIn and said that a builder needs about $990 per square foot to break even on a fourplex built on a standard 33-foot east-side lot purchased for about $1.7-million. According to his numbers, a fourplex built on land bought at today’s prices will lose money in the current market – and it’s not affordable housing for average income earners.

“At today’s prices, a fourplex only earns a normal margin if the lot costs under about $600,000,” he wrote. “Over the next 12 to 24 months, expect stalled sites, price cuts and units quietly turned into rentals. About 110 multiplex homes have already been taken off the market without selling.”

In an interview, Mr. Mece said government policies should be able to adjust to market conditions.

“All I know is that whatever they’ve done in the past, in terms of just layering and piling regulation and legislation on, trying to control and move markets, it has not worked,” said Mr. Mece. “There’s red tape everywhere. They just keep adding costs.”

His numbers only include MLS listings, not private sales, he said. Units built by families who intend to live in them, for example, don’t show up in his analysis. But the message is clear: multiplex supply is greater than demand.

The multiplex might have played a part in the election results. Bill 44 was hotly debated in Saanich, B.C., the largest municipality in southern Vancouver Island. Saanich South flipped from an NDP stronghold to a Conservative riding.

Newly re-elected Port Coquitlam Mayor Brad West recently told an online webinar how the legislation likely played a role in the provincial election. Bill 44 prompted 16 mayors to sign an open letter to Premier David Eby in opposition almost a year ago. Mayors from Burnaby, Richmond, Delta, White Rock, Port Moody, North Vancouver, Surrey, West Vancouver, Port Coquitlam, Coquitlam, Langley Township, Belcarra, Anmore, Lions Bay, Maple Ridge and Pitt Meadows signed the letter, arguing against a “one-size-fits-all” approach, the interference with municipal governance, and the impact on local services, including no parking rules.

Mr. West said the legislation “united mayors of various partisan political inclinations across the province.”

“Through a number of discussions with provincial officials, [we said] at some point: ‘Can you just dull the edges here a bit, take some of the feedback and even make slight adjustments?’ It was just a flat: ‘No, this is happening, we are not going to back up from this one iota.’ Then you get into a provincial and municipal election at the same time, and I can guarantee you, municipal candidates were not out there saying positive things about the NDP and about Premier Eby, even if they felt that was their natural political home,” he told the public webinar, held by Laidler Capital, which specializes in pre-zoned multifamily projects.

Developer and consultant Michael Geller agreed that Bill 44 should be repealed “since it’s absurd to direct that multiplex projects can be built on every single-family lot throughout the province in communities of more than 5,000 people.”

As is, a multiplex is too expensive to build to make it an affordable option, he added. He’s built two multiplex projects himself, which did not prove profitable.

Under the control of local government, however, he said they have a role to play. The housing type does work on bigger lots, he said, and municipalities should consider the height of the buildings, which are higher than houses because they don’t have basements.

“If you go down to Seattle, there are a lot of successful small-scale infill projects. And with some adjustments, I think there can be more projects here,” said Mr. Geller. “While they will not be as affordable as people were led to believe, they can offer greater housing choices in established single-family neighbourhoods.”

David Eger, vice-president, valuation and advisory for Newmark Canada, said that multiplex projects “likely do not pencil out” in the current market. He said the assembly of three to five lots to build low- to mid-rise buildings is an even better use of land for a developer. He also questioned turning homeowners into developers, which was one of the ideas behind the plan, so that downsizers, for example, could redevelop the family house and offer units to their grown children.

“Instead of creating zoning which allows for fourplexes or sixplexes permitted on single-family lots, I think it is better to find a way to make it faster, easier, cheaper, for developers to assemble three to five old homes and build a low- to mid-rise multifamily rental or strata condo buildings with proper parking, that are very well constructed, and offer various unit sizes from smaller bachelor units to larger family units,” Mr. Eger said in an e-mail.

“Development is not easy. Construction is not easy. It is really easy, however, to make costly mistakes that May be too expensive to correct. My advice would be that development should be done by those people and those firms with extensive knowledge, extensive experience, and financial capability versus the first-time citizen developers.”

stories.title: Microsoft struggles to restore email and other services in a global outage
stories.summary: Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted users, companies and some government operations.
stories.author: Chan Ho-him
stories.content:
From Asia to the U.S., Microsoft’s outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on for hours and impacted users, companies and some government operations as the technology giant struggled to fix the issue.

Microsoft said the outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

The extent of the outage wasn’t clear but the company said in January that it had more than 450 million paid Microsoft 365 commercial subscriptions.

The company indicated that its recovery efforts were making progress Friday, saying it was “seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements,” and that there was “incremental improvement in several workloads.” But problems appeared to persist, according to an outage tracking site, status reports from organizations that depend on the company’s services and anecdotal reports on social media.

Microsoft scrambles to recover services

The Redmond, Washington-based company said it was trying different ways to identify the cause of the problem and get its servers back online, using “a measured approach to identify and repair affected infrastructure.”

The company said it did not have any indication that the outage was caused by malicious activity and would treat the incident “with urgency and priority until full resolution.”

A series of posts by the company on X suggested its engineers were struggling to get the problem fully under control.

Hours after saying it managed to successfully restore service health and functionality, the company said it had updated its list of impacted services and was continuing to address the issue.

An earlier post offered little hope for users expecting a quick resolution.

“We’ve monitored the status of the changes applied to improve serviceability and confirmed they’re not taking as expected,” the company wrote.

In a pair of more recent updates on Friday, Microsoft said “we’re seeing early stabilization and capacity improvements as recovery actions continue.”

“Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.”

Governments, businesses from Japan to Australia affected

The British government said it is “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” are in place to minimize disruption.

British police forces said they’re unable to receive crime reports online and are urging people to call emergency responders to make any urgent reports.

The National Pharmacy Association said people could face delays getting their prescriptions because the outage is affecting the email systems of the state-run National Health Service. Hospitals urged patients to attend appointments as usual.

U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.

Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

“They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company could not receive updates from its U.S. customers throughout Outlook. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.

Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.

The Philippines’ Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that officials were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.
