“Recovery actions are ongoing across affected Microsoft 365 infrastructure and progressing in phases,” the company said in a second post. “We’re seeing incremental improvement in several workloads, but service health remains variable and capacity has not yet fully returned to baseline.”
Governments, businesses from Japan to Australia affected
The British government said it is “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” are in place to minimize disruption.
British police forces said they’re unable to receive crime reports online and are urging people to call emergency responders to make any urgent reports.

The National Pharmacy Association said people could face delays getting their prescriptions because the outage is affecting the email systems of the state-run National Health Service. Hospitals urged patients to attend appointments as usual.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call for its quarterly earnings because of the outage.

In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread disruption to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft’s top executive in Australia and the government’s national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

“They (Microsoft) don’t believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry,” Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company could not receive updates from its U.S. customers throughout Outlook. If the situation dragged on further, this could “impact the production timeline,” he said. Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw part of their operations disrupted.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the global Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore’s Government Technology Agency said that government emails were down and that the agency is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines’ Supreme Court said in a statement on X that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.

In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government’s IT infrastructure and that officials were “keeping a close eye on the developments.” Japanese authorities had taken steps including securing alternative communication tools such as telephones, the government said.

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported that they were facing problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

stories.title: Fatality reported after October collision in Morris-Turnberry
stories.summary: The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 68-year-old Huron-Kinloss Township man has died from injuries sustained in a two-vehicle collision last month in Morris-Turnberry, provincial police say.

Huron County OPP, Huron County Paramedic Services and the North Huron Fire Department responded to the crash on Amberley Road between Currie Line and Helena Street on Oct. 14.

Police said the collision involved a passenger vehicle and a van.

The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.

OPP said the 68-year-old driver died on Nov. 10 as a result of injuries sustained in the collision.

No further details were released.

stories.title: Toys ‘R’ Us Canada’s new owner drops trademark fight with Calgary swingers club
stories.summary: Next Century will await decisions in two other trademark battles launched by the retail chain’s previous owner
stories.author: Tara Deschamps
stories.content:
The new owner of Toys “R” Us Canada appears to have abandoned the retailer’s fight to keep a Calgary swingers club from using the phrase “Club R.”

In filings made with the country’s intellectual property office this year, the toy chain’s previous owner argued letting Club Rendezvous Inc. use “Club R” would cause confusion. In some markets, Toys “R” Us has called its loyalty program R Club.

Toys “R” Us Canada had until Sept. 30 to file a statement of opposition in the case, but the intellectual property office’s database shows Next Century – which picked up the some of retailer’s assets after it entered creditor protection – failed to meet the deadline and didn’t ask for an extension.

With no one actively fighting the use of “Club R,” the case was closed a month later by the trademark opposition board, which handles intellectual property disputes.

The closure gave Club Rendezvous the go-ahead it needed to use “Club R.”

The owners of the swingers organization, who The Canadian Press agreed not to name because their families are unaware of their involvement in the business, are pleased with the outcome.

They said the whole dispute seemed “unusual,” given the club operates in an entirely different industry from children’s toys, and that they were happy with the outcome.

Neither Next Century, whose parent company Ad Populum also owns Party City and manages the Chia Pet brand, nor its lawyer responded to requests for comment on the case.

Next Century plans to open the first of about 300 Toys “R” Us Canada shops within Staples Canada stores on Saturday in Richmond Hill, Ont.

The company acquired the rights to the Toys “R” Us Canada name and about 150 of the retailer’s trademarks earlier this year, when the toy chain was in creditor protection and selling off its assets to cover off its debts.

When Toys “R” Us Canada sought creditor protection, it had already launched trademark battles with the swingers club and two other brands.

The intellectual property office’s database shows that Next Century appears to be continuing with the two other cases .

In the first, the retailer is trying to stop Russian firm Biomicrogeli from using the phrase Wonderlab, the name Toys “R” Us Canada gave to its indoor jungle gym and craft centres. That segment of business was eventually renamed Playlab.

In the second case, Toys “R” Us Canada is trying to keep tech giant Acer from using a backwards R, saying the retailer has trademarks preventing others from applying the reversed letter to electronic devices and other products.

Erin McEwen, a trademark agent at Nelligan Law in Ottawa who is not involved in any of the cases, wasn’t surprised Next Century is adopting both fights.

Companies usually prefer to stop any use of names and logos similar to their own for fear that they could confuse consumers, dilute their brand and harm their business’s reputation.

Next Century likely also realized that considerable resources have probably already been spent on the cases.

Trademark opposition cases can take three to four years to conclude and Toys “R” Us Canada’s fight with Acer is either at the evidence stage – the halfway point or tail end, depending on whether cross-examination and hearings are required. The Wonderlab fight is awaiting a decision.

“If I were in their shoes, I wouldn’t jump ship just yet,” McEwen said of Next Century. “Toys ‘R’ Us already put in all that time and money, why waste it? They might as well just ride it out and wait for the decision.”

McEwen thinks it’s possible Next Century backed away from the battle with Club Rendezvous because the Calgary business dates back to 1983. The longer they’ve had a name, the harder it is fight a trademark dispute, she said.

stories.title: Ottawa to invest $200-million in Woodfibre LNG project, source says
stories.summary: Funds intended to boost capacity at Squamish, B.C., site as owners explore possibility of a second phase
stories.author: Amanda Stephenson
stories.content:
The federal government will invest $200-million in the Woodfibre LNG project under construction near Squamish, B.C., said a person familiar with the matter, an investment that will increase announced capacity by up to 24 per cent.

Owners Enbridge ENB-T and Singapore-based Pacific Energy designed Woodfibre to produce 2.1 million metric tons of liquefied natural gas a year, all of which is contracted to BP BP-N .

The new funding will raise capacity to between 2.5 million and 2.6 million tons via upgrades to cooling systems and the commissioning and mooring of floating storage tanks, the person said on condition of anonymity.

The owners are also exploring a second phase for the project, the person said.

The owners aim to begin operations in late 2027.

stories.title: Soviet-era spy story sheds new light on hunt for Canadian mole
stories.summary: There is new evidence that a Soviet spy who defected to Britain in the early 1980s played a key role in helping Canada unravel the mystery of a mole who passed secrets to Russian intelligence.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — There is new evidence that a Soviet spy who defected to Britain in the early 1980s played a key role in helping Canada unravel the mystery of a mole who passed secrets to Russian intelligence.

The recently published book Redwood, by journalist and author Ben Macintyre, tells the story of Vladimir Kuzichkin, who agreed to defect in the hope that he would receive medical treatment to cure his impotence.

It also fleshes out previous claims that Kuzichkin alerted Canadian intelligence officials to a high-ranking traitor within the ranks of the RCMP — a tip that led molehunters to zero in on former Mountie Gilles Brunet.

The Moscow-born Kuzichkin served in the Soviet army before being recruited in the 1970s into the KGB, the country’s main security agency at the time.

Macintyre’s book says Kuzichkin was stationed in Tehran in 1981 when he nervously approached the British about working for them.

During a clandestine meeting with a British intelligence officer, Kuzichkin revealed his disillusionment with the Soviet Union and the KGB, the book says. He also spoke of his desperation to solve the difficulties he was experiencing in the bedroom.

“Kuzichkin’s impotence was his overriding, overwhelming burden, the driving psychological impetus behind his decision to swap sides,” Macintyre writes.

The tall Soviet spy, who was given the code name Redwood, helped the British in Iran before fleeing to England via Turkey. He died in 2009.

Kuzichkin’s defection prompted a flood of queries from allied intelligence services, Macintyre writes.

In August 1982, the British informed the RCMP that “a top-level defector” had pointed to a KGB mole, code-named Nikon, in the Canadian police force, the book says.

“The British could supply no additional details: no name, and no certainty about whether this spy was still in the Canadian service,” Macintyre writes. “But the source was unimpeachable. The revelation sent a shudder through Canada’s intelligence establishment.”

The ensuing RCMP review of operational case files involving the Soviets from 1967 to 1973 did not yield anything that might identify the agent, according to records obtained by The Canadian Press in 2021 through the Access to Information Act.

An examination of hundreds of personnel files and interviews with members also turned up no firm leads.

Brunet spent much of the 1960s in Ottawa with the RCMP Security Service, the wing of the national police force responsible at the time for protecting Canada from foreign spies and extremists. His father had led the RCMP’s security branch for a time in the 1950s.

Brunet excelled in a Russian language course. But he had marital problems and ran up debt. In 1968 he transferred to Montreal, where he continued to work on security files.

Brunet was dismissed from the force in 1973 for refusing to cut ties with a person alleged to have underworld connections. He went into the private security business and later sold prearranged funeral packages.

Brunet was seen as intelligent, aggressive and ambitious but also “avaricious, vindictive and devoid of morals,” the internal records reviewed by The Canadian Press say.

“When it suited his purposes, he was extremely outgoing and gregarious. He played ‘hard’ and was a heavy drinker.”

In December 1983, a security investigator probing Brunet’s past believed the Mounties had found their mole.

The research showed that no Soviet-linked case of which Brunet was aware ever came to a successful conclusion, even though there were operational successes in other areas of the country during the same period.

In each case molehunters were able to document, “operations died immediately upon Brunet learning of them,” says the investigator’s memo. “It appears that not only was Brunet compromised, but that he was so committed that he gave his Soviet handlers everything he got his hands on.”

Investigators believed that the well-connected Brunet continued to feed information to the KGB even after leaving the RCMP.

The RCMP secretly followed Brunet for several days in early April 1984, surveilling his visits to the dry cleaners, a grocery store and — on the day before his sudden death from an apparent heart attack — a pizzeria.

There would be no chance to interrogate the suspect.

“The Mounties never did get their man, but at least, thanks to Kuzichkin, they knew who he was,” Macintyre writes.

Brunet’s grave marker at a Montreal cemetery depicts a beach scene in Acapulco, Mexico — a favourite destination — and a martini glass. It remembers him as a “bon vivant” and a “very special man.”

The newly created Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which took over responsibility for counter-intelligence work, continued to investigate, drawing on additional information received through a tip in 1985 or early 1986. Although details were stripped from the Access to Information release, this tip is believed to have come from another Soviet defector.

A 1987 Csis report said the spy service “is satisfied” that Brunet was the agent recruited by Soviet intelligence. Csis concluded that money, ego and career frustrations were the likely reasons for his betrayal.

Macintyre, who cites the Canadian Access to Information records in recounting the Brunet episode, is not the first to highlight Kuzichkin’s role in helping the Canadians.

A 2016 book, At Her Majesty’s Secret Service by Nigel West, also identifies Kuzichkin as the source of the tipoff about a spy for Moscow in the RCMP.

Kuzichkin’s valuable disclosure is also mentioned in unpublished research on the Brunet case carried out in the 1990s by Peter Marwitz, a former member of the RCMP Security Service and Csis.

Marwitz suggested Brunet’s misdeeds included revealing the location of listening devices planted at the Soviet Embassy in Ottawa and betraying the activities of a Canadian military attaché stationed in Moscow. He said Brunet was paid more than $700,000 by the KGB.

Macintyre writes that Brunet “was able to expose double agents within KGB ranks” and that he gave the Soviets a British debriefing report on Oleg Lyalin, who defected from the KGB in 1971.

Macintyre interviewed former American, British and Russian security officials, as well as friends and family members of those involved in the Kuzichkin saga. He teases out some intriguing new details about the Canadian elements.

Macintyre says Brunet’s KGB handlers taught him Soviet tradecraft, such as the use of cigarette packs to carry film and how to signal for a meeting by placing a piece of tape on a pole — horizontal for Ottawa, vertical for Montreal.

Brunet ignored it all, preferring to meet at a favourite pub, “exchange intelligence for bundles of cash, and then get blind drunk,” the book says.

“Brunet’s espionage is said to fill 20 KGB files of 250 pages each.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

“Kuzichkin’s impotence was his overriding, overwhelming burden, the driving psychological impetus behind his decision to swap sides,” Macintyre writes.
The tall Soviet spy, who was given the code name Redwood, helped the British in Iran before fleeing to England via Turkey. He died in 2009.
Kuzichkin’s defection prompted a flood of queries from allied intelligence services, Macintyre writes.
In August 1982, the British informed the RCMP that “a top-level defector” had pointed to a KGB mole, code-named Nikon, in the Canadian police force, the book says.

“The British could supply no additional details: no name, and no certainty about whether this spy was still in the Canadian service,” Macintyre writes. “But the source was unimpeachable. The revelation sent a shudder through Canada’s intelligence establishment.”

The ensuing RCMP review of operational case files involving the Soviets from 1967 to 1973 did not yield anything that might identify the agent, according to records obtained by The Canadian Press in 2021 through the Access to Information Act.
An examination of hundreds of personnel files and interviews with members also turned up no firm leads.

Brunet spent much of the 1960s in Ottawa with the RCMP Security Service, the wing of the national police force responsible at the time for protecting Canada from foreign spies and extremists. His father had led the RCMP’s security branch for a time in the 1950s.
Brunet excelled in a Russian language course. But he had marital problems and ran up debt. In 1968 he transferred to Montreal, where he continued to work on security files.

Brunet was dismissed from the force in 1973 for refusing to cut ties with a person alleged to have underworld connections. He went into the private security business and later sold prearranged funeral packages.
Brunet was seen as intelligent, aggressive and ambitious but also “avaricious, vindictive and devoid of morals,” the internal records reviewed by The Canadian Press say.
“When it suited his purposes, he was extremely outgoing and gregarious. He played ‘hard’ and was a heavy drinker.”
In December 1983, a security investigator probing Brunet’s past believed the Mounties had found their mole.

The research showed that no Soviet-linked case of which Brunet was aware ever came to a successful conclusion, even though there were operational successes in other areas of the country during the same period.

In each case molehunters were able to document, “operations died immediately upon Brunet learning of them,” says the investigator’s memo. “It appears that not only was Brunet compromised, but that he was so committed that he gave his Soviet handlers everything he got his hands on.”
Investigators believed that the well-connected Brunet continued to feed information to the KGB even after leaving the RCMP.

The RCMP secretly followed Brunet for several days in early April 1984, surveilling his visits to the dry cleaners, a grocery store and — on the day before his sudden death from an apparent heart attack — a pizzeria.
There would be no chance to interrogate the suspect.
“The Mounties never did get their man, but at least, thanks to Kuzichkin, they knew who he was,” Macintyre writes.
Brunet’s grave marker at a Montreal cemetery depicts a beach scene in Acapulco, Mexico — a favourite destination — and a martini glass. It remembers him as a “bon vivant” and a “very special man.”

The newly created Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which took over responsibility for counter-intelligence work, continued to investigate, drawing on additional information received through a tip in 1985 or early 1986. Although details were stripped from the Access to Information release, this tip is believed to have come from another Soviet defector.

A 1987 Csis report said the spy service “is satisfied” that Brunet was the agent recruited by Soviet intelligence. Csis concluded that money, ego and career frustrations were the likely reasons for his betrayal.
Macintyre, who cites the Canadian Access to Information records in recounting the Brunet episode, is not the first to highlight Kuzichkin’s role in helping the Canadians.
A 2016 book, At Her Majesty’s Secret Service by Nigel West, also identifies Kuzichkin as the source of the tipoff about a spy for Moscow in the RCMP.
Kuzichkin’s valuable disclosure is also mentioned in unpublished research on the Brunet case carried out in the 1990s by Peter Marwitz, a former member of the RCMP Security Service and Csis.

Marwitz suggested Brunet’s misdeeds included revealing the location of listening devices planted at the Soviet Embassy in Ottawa and betraying the activities of a Canadian military attaché stationed in Moscow. He said Brunet was paid more than $700,000 by the KGB.
Macintyre writes that Brunet “was able to expose double agents within KGB ranks” and that he gave the Soviets a British debriefing report on Oleg Lyalin, who defected from the KGB in 1971.

Macintyre interviewed former American, British and Russian security officials, as well as friends and family members of those involved in the Kuzichkin saga. He teases out some intriguing new details about the Canadian elements.

Macintyre says Brunet’s KGB handlers taught him Soviet tradecraft, such as the use of cigarette packs to carry film and how to signal for a meeting by placing a piece of tape on a pole — horizontal for Ottawa, vertical for Montreal.
Brunet ignored it all, preferring to meet at a favourite pub, “exchange intelligence for bundles of cash, and then get blind drunk,” the book says.
“Brunet’s espionage is said to fill 20 KGB files of 250 pages each.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.
Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ottawa should adopt B.C.’s orphan port
stories.summary: Prince Rupert cannot be overlooked any longer in the Liberals’ export push
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
When one of the Titanic’s most industrious passengers – railroad baron Charles Melville Hays – perished in icy Atlantic waters, he left behind a northern B.C. town that would come to be known as “Hays’ Orphan.”

Mr. Hays was a champion of Prince Rupert. He had arrived on the rain-swept shores of Kaien Island in Northern B.C. nine years before meeting his fate, where he had identified what he considered the perfect conditions for the terminus of his intercontinental railroad – a port with deep waters located closer to Asia than any other along the west coast of North America. Mr. Hays’ passion for Prince Rupert contributed to his death. He was on board the Titanic on the return leg of a business trip to London, where he had solicited financing for the railroad project.

Today this small community of just 14,000 people has, somewhat, delivered on its promise to Mr. Hays. The port of Prince Rupert is the third largest port in the country. Over $8-billion of Canadian exports are shipped out of six terminals that export everything from bulk grain, coal and pellets to containers to propane.

And yet, orphan remains a fitting descriptor for the port of Prince Rupert.

Ottawa is in the midst of an ambitious trade diversification strategy to double non-U.S. exports within a decade. Trade infrastructure is essential to accomplishing this goal. The federal government categorized the container expansion project at the Port of Vancouver a “project of national interest.” The Port of Vancouver and its sweeping growth strategy was added to the Major Projects Office alongside Montreal’s Contrecoeur Container Terminal Project, Grays Bay Road and Port in Nunavut and Manitoba’s Port of Churchill (a 146-year-old dream that has largely failed to turn a profit, soured investors from a host of industries, and cost governments millions of dollars to keep in operation).

Prince Rupert has received no such special treatment. The port has not been referred to the major projects office or deemed a project of national interest.

The private sector is willing to invest, keen to capitalize on the same natural advantages Mr. Hays identified over a century ago. Prince Rupert is 36 hours closer to Shanghai than the Port of Vancouver, and 68 hours closer than the port of Los Angeles. The port’s 14-mile harbour is also the third deepest natural ice-free harbour in the world, and the main rail line to the port (purchased by Canadian National after Mr. Hays’ railroad went bankrupt in 1919) travels on the flattest grade through the Rocky Mountains.

The port is in the midst of a $3-billion expansion that would double its trade volumes past 50 million tonnes in the next decade. In August it unveiled a $750-million facility designed to make it easy to move exports into containers, and an additional berth owned by Trigon Terminals is set to come online soon, hopefully.

But unlocking the true potential of the port will require the federal government to adopt this port into a broad trade strategy by addressing some of the challenges it faces.

For example, the port is only serviced by one railroad, which May have hurt its chances of securing an up to $1-billion investment in a new export terminal from Saskatchewan’s fertilizer giant Nutrien. (The company selected the Port of Longview, Washington as its new Pacific terminus late last year). Policies that would allow competing railroads to use these tracks would reduce CN’s dominance along this route.

The new Trigon Terminals berth is also looking for a shipper, and liquid propane gas is a promising commodity. Yet a 2015 exclusivity deal between the port authority, AltaGas Ltd. and Royal Vopak is standing in the way. Transport Canada could apply pressure to at least disclose the details of this agreement, such as when it is set to expire.

The 2019 federal ban on oil tankers stopping, loading or unloading in Northern B.C. also reduces opportunity. Prime Minister Mark Carney is increasingly facing pressure to address this ban. Calgary-based Strathcona Resources has proposed to move up to 250,000 barrels of crude a day by rail to the port. This week the company announced an up to $3.5-billion partnership with CN rail to make this plan a reality within two years.

For more than a century, private players have seen the advantages offered by the port of Prince Rupert. It is time Ottawa does the same.

stories.title: Metis man who played high-speed chicken with police has reduced ‘moral blameworthiness,’ says judge
stories.summary: One officer 'believed a head-on collision would kill her'
stories.author: Chris Lambie
stories.content:
A Metis man who used a stolen car to play a high-speed game of chicken with police in High Prairie, Alta., has been sentenced to 30 months behind bars by a judge who noted the driver’s Indigenous background “meaningfully reduces his moral blameworthiness.”

Daniel Tanner Bigcharles was convicted this past May in Alberta’s Court of King’s Bench on two counts of assaulting a peace officer with a weapon, fleeing from police, dangerous driving and resisting a peace officer.

“All convictions arose from events on May 10, 2025, when Mr. Bigcharles fled a lawful traffic stop in a stolen Kia Seltos. He led police through High Prairie and surrounding communities, driving at very high speeds before deliberately directing the vehicle at marked police vehicles occupied by Constables Monique Doré and Tristin Dow,” Justice Anna Loparco wrote in a Nov. 9 decision out of Peace River.

The court heard that the chase began when another officer, Const. Cody Kube, stopped the Kia just after 9 p.m.

“A plate search showed the vehicle was stolen. Before Constable Kube could leave his marked vehicle, the Kia accelerated away through a back alley,” said the judge.

Doré joined the pursuit and Dow “positioned himself near Range Road 143 and observed the Kia pass at high speed,” the decision said.

Police continued pursuing the Kia on Highway 2.

“The Kia then manoeuvred into the oncoming lane and travelled directly toward Constable Doré’s marked vehicle at a speed initially approaching 160 km/h. She slowed and pulled into the ditch because she believed a head-on collision would kill her,” said the decision.

“The conduct was not confined to one pass. The Kia returned toward Constable Doré in her lane at approximately 70 to 80 km/h while swerving back and forth in what she described as a taunting or chicken-like motion. She again feared for her life. The Kia also drove head-on toward Constable Dow’s marked vehicle at approximately 80 km/h, requiring him to take evasive action.”

The Kia eventually went off the road and got caught on a barbed-wire fence.

“Mr. Bigcharles exited the driver’s side, ran into a field, ignored Constable Dow’s direction to stop, and resisted arrest by fleeing on foot,” said the decision.

An Indigenous Background Report on Bigcharles “describes his Métis identity, the colonial and intergenerational experiences of his family, childhood neglect and abuse, early and chronic substance use, mental-health struggles, repeated bereavements, criminal-justice involvement, and proposed supports,” said the decision.

The 31-year-old is registered with East Prairie Métis Settlement.

“His maternal grandparents attended St. Bernard’s Indian Residential School, and the report states that his mother May have attended Indian Day School,” said the decision.

“The report identifies intergenerational trauma, parental addiction, cultural disconnection, and normalized substance use within the home.”

Bigcharles experienced “poverty, bullying, cultural isolation at school, and an inappropriate relationship with a teacher,” said the decision.

He reported “using alcohol at age six or seven, marijuana at age seven, and later cocaine, crack cocaine, methamphetamine, Mdma, fentanyl, and other substances.”

He has previous convictions for assault with a weapon, obstructing a peace officer, theft, possession of stolen property, aggravated assault, possession of a firearm and mischief.

His Indigenous Background Report “provides a persuasive broad nexus between colonial dislocation, childhood trauma, substance dependence, gang involvement, and his recurring presence in the criminal-justice system,” said the judge.

“Mr. Bigcharles grew up amidst the intergenerational effects of residential schooling, parental addiction, unstable caregiving, poverty, violence, sexual abuse, cultural disconnection, and profound grief. Substance use began at an extraordinarily young age and developed into chronic methamphetamine dependence. These factors help explain impaired coping mechanisms, addiction, gang attachment, criminalization, and repeated institutional involvement,” she said.

“I accept that these circumstances attenuate moral culpability to a meaningful degree. They do not reduce it to a low level.”

Loparco said that “gang culture and his institutional experiences informed his hostility toward police.”

paragraphs: A Metis man who used a stolen car to play a high-speed game of chicken with police in High Prairie, Alta., has been sentenced to 30 months behind bars by a judge who noted the driver’s Indigenous background “meaningfully reduces his moral blameworthiness.”

Daniel Tanner Bigcharles was convicted this past May in Alberta’s Court of King’s Bench on two counts of assaulting a peace officer with a weapon, fleeing from police, dangerous driving and resisting a peace officer.

“All convictions arose from events on May 10, 2025, when Mr. Bigcharles fled a lawful traffic stop in a stolen Kia Seltos. He led police through High Prairie and surrounding communities, driving at very high speeds before deliberately directing the vehicle at marked police vehicles occupied by Constables Monique Doré and Tristin Dow,” Justice Anna Loparco wrote in a Nov. 9 decision out of Peace River.
The court heard that the chase began when another officer, Const. Cody Kube, stopped the Kia just after 9 p.m.
“A plate search showed the vehicle was stolen. Before Constable Kube could leave his marked vehicle, the Kia accelerated away through a back alley,” said the judge.
Doré joined the pursuit and Dow “positioned himself near Range Road 143 and observed the Kia pass at high speed,” the decision said.
Police continued pursuing the Kia on Highway 2.

“The Kia then manoeuvred into the oncoming lane and travelled directly toward Constable Doré’s marked vehicle at a speed initially approaching 160 km/h. She slowed and pulled into the ditch because she believed a head-on collision would kill her,” said the decision.

“The conduct was not confined to one pass. The Kia returned toward Constable Doré in her lane at approximately 70 to 80 km/h while swerving back and forth in what she described as a taunting or chicken-like motion. She again feared for her life. The Kia also drove head-on toward Constable Dow’s marked vehicle at approximately 80 km/h, requiring him to take evasive action.”
The Kia eventually went off the road and got caught on a barbed-wire fence.
“Mr. Bigcharles exited the driver’s side, ran into a field, ignored Constable Dow’s direction to stop, and resisted arrest by fleeing on foot,” said the decision.

The 31-year-old is registered with East Prairie Métis Settlement.
“His maternal grandparents attended St. Bernard’s Indian Residential School, and the report states that his mother May have attended Indian Day School,” said the decision.
“The report identifies intergenerational trauma, parental addiction, cultural disconnection, and normalized substance use within the home.”
Bigcharles experienced “poverty, bullying, cultural isolation at school, and an inappropriate relationship with a teacher,” said the decision.
He reported “using alcohol at age six or seven, marijuana at age seven, and later cocaine, crack cocaine, methamphetamine, Mdma, fentanyl, and other substances.”
He has previous convictions for assault with a weapon, obstructing a peace officer, theft, possession of stolen property, aggravated assault, possession of a firearm and mischief.

His Indigenous Background Report “provides a persuasive broad nexus between colonial dislocation, childhood trauma, substance dependence, gang involvement, and his recurring presence in the criminal-justice system,” said the judge.

“Mr. Bigcharles grew up amidst the intergenerational effects of residential schooling, parental addiction, unstable caregiving, poverty, violence, sexual abuse, cultural disconnection, and profound grief. Substance use began at an extraordinarily young age and developed into chronic methamphetamine dependence. These factors help explain impaired coping mechanisms, addiction, gang attachment, criminalization, and repeated institutional involvement,” she said.
“I accept that these circumstances attenuate moral culpability to a meaningful degree. They do not reduce it to a low level.”

There’s a “meaningful but indirect” connection between his Indigenous background factors and his crimes, said the judge.
“Mr. Bigcharles’ background helps explain his addiction, gang attachment, distrust of authority, and recurrent criminalization,” Loparco said.

“Those circumstances attenuate moral blameworthiness and require restraint. They do not explain away the repeated, conscious decisions to continue the flight, turn the vehicle back toward Constable Doré, threaten her a second time, and then direct the vehicle toward Constable Dow. His moral culpability remains high, though lower than it would be if the same conduct had been committed by an offender without these systemic and background circumstances.”

His defence lawyer proposed two years in jail and a two-year driving ban.
His moral culpability is high, said the judge.

“At the same time, his Métis background, intergenerational trauma, childhood sexual abuse and neglect, cultural disconnection, extremely early substance exposure, methamphetamine addiction, gang vulnerability, cumulative grief, institutionalization, and alienation from the justice system are connected to the pathway into offending and reduce his moral blameworthiness to a meaningful, though not determinative, degree,” said the judge.

stories.title: Federal government moves to overhaul airport security after CTV News investigation
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is making sweeping changes after a W5 investigation revealed how corrupt airport workers are trafficking drugs using innocent passengers’ luggage tags.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part three of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government is making sweeping changes after a W5 investigation revealed how corrupt airport workers are trafficking drugs using innocent passengers’ luggage tags.

“When we saw your report, we once again went back to the drawing board,” Transportation Minister Steven MacKinnon said in a recent interview from his office on Parliament Hill.

New laws will tighten access to security clearances and restricted areas, he said.

A bag tag switching scheme describes a scenario where a corrupt airport employee takes the tag off an unsuspecting passenger’s luggage and attaches it to a suitcase filled with drugs headed to that traveller’s destination.

A courier on the other end waits to pick it up. But if the bag is intercepted by security, the innocent passenger is left to face the consequences.

W5 has identified more than two dozen cases where Canadians have been caught up in this scheme, almost all of them flying out of Toronto’s Pearson International Airport. Several have been detained overseas, in countries where police aren’t interested in hearing, “That’s not my bag.”

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA.

System can’t prevent criminals getting into ‘trusted positions’: government

Sixteen Pearson workers have been arrested over the past five years, most in relation to drugs, and at least five in connection with tag switching schemes, the RCMP said in an email to W5.

In the previous W5 documentary, Trafficked: The Airport Conspiracy , a former RCMP investigator revealed that corrupt airport insiders routinely keep their security clearances despite being flagged for potential links to organized crime.

Months later, the government now admits in an online discussion paper that it’s not fully equipped to prevent organized criminals from getting into “trusted positions within the transportation system.”

That’s because the system that decides who gets security clearances isn’t working properly, according to the government’s discussion paper.

Right now, the system focuses on filtering out people who could put planes in danger — but “limits our ability to consider … links to organized crime or patterns of suspicious activity,” Transport Canada wrote, adding that organized crime is a growing threat inside Canadian airports.

‘Higher thresholds for security clearances’ coming: minister

Now, the man in charge says he’s taking action.

Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said he plans to use expanded powers in Bill C-39, the government’s omnibus “Building Canada Strong Act,” to institute “higher thresholds for security clearances” and more restrictions on who has access to secure areas in airports.

“Whether you’re working in a restaurant at the airport or working as part of ground crews or baggage handlers, we are watching ever more closely,” he said.

The bill, which is currently before Parliament, would give the minister expanded powers to change the security clearance application process, grant or revoke individual clearances and expand the list of workers who require clearance.

Transport Canada said the new system could more comprehensively screen for factors like “links to organized crime networks,” “involvement in suspicious activities” and “signs of coercion, corruption, or vulnerability to exploitation.”

Bill C-39 would also allow for more information sharing about security clearances with foreign governments and law enforcement.

The bill is currently in committee and could pass before the end of the year.

Not just baggage staff

Aviation management expert John Gradek said airport employees need to be physically screened as they’re entering secure areas, so drug bags are stopped before they have a chance to take flight.

“We have to make sure we watch cargo, food services, commissary,” he said. “All of that stuff has to be screened to make sure you’re not bringing contraband along with the 50 or 60 packs of toilet paper that you’re bringing into the airport.”

Minister MacKinnon said he’s on it — the government has increased how often employees are screened on their way into work, he said, adding that he plans to boost the practice further.

But the screening that happens now won’t necessarily stop drugs from getting in the back door.

Part 1: Pearson luggage tag switch leaves Toronto man facing 15 years in Albania

Part 2: Who’s responsible? Pearson tag-switching victims sue across the system

That’s because the body responsible for that screening only looks for things “that could pose a threat to aviation security,” Transport Canada spokesperson Hicham Ayoun said in a statement.

“Searching for drugs is outside Catsa’s screening mandate. Suspected illegal items identified during screening are reported to the police of jurisdiction,” Ayoun said.

Bill not a silver bullet: transport critic

Conservative transport critic Dan Albas said the changes the government is proposing are welcome, but they won’t solve the problem.

Organized criminals often try to work with people with clean records — people who wouldn’t be screened out by increased scrutiny on background checks, he said.

Airports could be required to take photos of travellers’ baggage, he noted. And a review of the secure areas where employees handle baggage is needed to root out the blind spots where tag switching takes place, he said.

These changes wouldn’t require the minister to introduce another bill, Albas said.

“He can do these things unilaterally. And I’m quite disappointed to see we have not seen more action on this,” he said.

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Sunday at 10 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave following the Grey Cup.

stories.title: Snow, rain mix expected in southwestern Ontario
stories.summary: The coldest air of the season has arrived in southwestern Ontario, bringing lake-effect snow and a chance of mixed precipitation Friday, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
The coldest air of the season has arrived in southwestern Ontario, bringing lake-effect snow and a chance of mixed precipitation Friday, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

A stream of precipitation downwind of Lake Huron is bringing snow to parts of Lambton County, including along Highway 402.

Atchison says the snow and rain mix will move east through Lambton County and Chatham-Kent, with some snowflakes possible in London and Strathroy during the afternoon.

London has a 40 per cent chance of mixed precipitation. Sarnia could see another couple of centimetres of snow.

Temperatures will remain cold throughout the day, with a high of just 5 C.

Showers are expected Saturday before conditions improve Sunday, with sunshine returning Monday through Wednesday.

Temperatures are also expected to climb back into double digits by midweek, with highs between 10 C and 12 C.

stories.title: An Ontario dairy daughter faces a rite of passage at the winter fair
stories.summary: For Carina Jones and Amaryllis the calf, the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair was a chance to step out as the ‘moo’ kids in town
stories.author: Laura Proctor
stories.content:
Carina Jones, 16, isn’t afraid of hard work. The daughter of a fourth-generation dairy farmer, she stays busy with chores on the family farm in Midland, Ont., as well as with school, hockey and friends.

Since the spring, Carina has been preparing to show a calf for the first time at the Royal Agricultural Winter Fair in Toronto.

In the Canadian 4-H Dairy Classic competition, exhibitors are judged on the calf’s physical characteristics and appearance, but also on their own showmanship – their poise in the ring.

Carina’s father, Steve Jones, has previously accompanied his three sons to the competition, but this is his first time bringing his daughter.

Mr. Jones is hopeful that his dairy farm will be handed down the family line, but he and his wife, Yvonne, won’t push their kids in a direction they don’t want to go. So far, two of his sons have gone into engineering rather than joining the family business, which Mr. Jones co-owns with his brother.

One thing that’s certain is Carina’s love of agriculture. For as long as she can remember, she’s wanted to go to the University of Guelph’s renowned agriculture program, which her brother Luke is enrolled in too.

But Carina says her parents are supportive of whatever path she and Luke May choose. “That takes a lot of the pressure off,” she says.

stories.title: Wealth One raises $50-million as new owners push to partner with Canadian fintechs
stories.summary: Next goal is to find investors in U.S. and U.K. to raise an additional $150-million
stories.author: Alexandra Posadzki
stories.content:
Toronto-based Wealth One Bank of Canada has raised $50-million of new capital to fuel its growth as it looks to position itself as a partner to Canadian fintechs.

Fintechs use technology to deliver financial services more cheaply and efficiently than traditional banks, but most don’t have banking licenses. Instead, they partner with licensed financial institutions that provide underlying banking services, such as accepting deposits from customers.

Wealth One’s new owners see a chance to be that provider. A consortium assembled by Toronto-based investment firm Globalive Corp. acquired the bank last year .

“We think there’s a really great opportunity to empower the Canadian fintechs,” Globalive chairman Anthony Lacavera said in an interview.

“They are just chronically underserved by the major banks.”

Ottawa promised in last week’s federal budget to make legislative changes aimed at bolstering competition in the banking sector by making it easier for new financial institutions to enter the market and grow larger.

Canada’s banking industry is dominated by six big players – Royal Bank of Canada, Toronto-Dominion Bank, Bank of Nova Scotia, Bank of Montreal, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce and National Bank of Canada – which together hold more than 90-per-cent market share.

Most of the members of the consortium that acquired Wealth One have doubled down on their investment in the recent financing round, Mr. Lacavera said.

That includes Globalive; Western Canadian property developer Ryan Beedie and his direct-investment platform Beedie Capital; Chris Kayat and Gary Mauris, co-founders of mortgage company Dominion Lending Centres Inc.; wealth-management firm Optimize Financial Group; and John Webster, a long-time financial services executive and the bank’s chief executive officer.

Calgary-based insurance financing company Grasslands Finance Corp. did not invest additional capital, although it remains a shareholder, Mr. Lacavera said. There are also six additional investors who Mr. Lacavera declined to name, citing pending regulatory approvals. The financing round closed on Aug. 31.

Mr. Lacavera has high hopes for the challenger bank. He plans to start looking abroad to the U.S. and Britain for investors with the aim of raising another $150-million.

“We have really big ambitions to get it to $10-billion in assets and then list the bank in Canada,” he said.

Wealth One, which has a Schedule I bank licence, has been growing rapidly since last year’s acquisition. On April 30, 2025, before the deal had closed, it had $516-million in assets, primarily uninsured mortgages on residential real estate.

By July 31, 2026, its balance sheet had grown to over $800-million of assets, according to a report by Wowa Data Labs, which provides data and intelligence on the Canadian lending market.

Mr. Webster, Wealth One’s CEO, said he expects that the bank will be profitable by the middle of next year.

Wealth One is engaged in discussions with “all of the major fintechs,” not only about taking deposits but also about other services the bank might be able to offer them, Mr. Webster said.

Serving as a correspondent bank for U.S.-based financial institutions is another potential opportunity, he noted.

Correspondent banking is a financial arrangement where one bank, known as the correspondent bank, provides services such as wire transfers and currency exchange on behalf of another bank, which is called the respondent bank.

Mr. Webster called Wealth One the “fastest-growing bank in both deposits and mortgages in Canada.” However, achieving that growth was not without challenges, particularly when it came to expanding its wholesale deposits, he said.

Wealth One was founded in 2016 with a $50-million investment and a focus on catering to Chinese-Canadian clients. In April 2023, then-finance minister Chrystia Freeland ordered three of its original shareholders to divest their stakes because of concerns about their alleged ties to the Chinese government.

“We had to overcome some of the reputational damage that was done by the founding group and the previous management and board,” Mr. Webster said.

“The risk guys Google it and they read the story of the named parties. ... We’ve had to invest a lot of effort into telling people the story of the new Wealth One.”

stories.title: This company wants to connect buyers with discounted condos – if they sign an NDA
stories.summary: QuietMarket gives buyers a way to shop for unsold condo inventory at prices that aren’t publicly listed
stories.author: Salmaan Farooqui
stories.content:
A small upstart operating in the Greater Toronto Area promises to connect individual buyers with deeply discounted, unsold condos – provided they sign a non-disclosure agreement, or NDA.

The company, called QuietMarket, sprung up as the condo-market crash has left developers with a large amount of unsold inventory in cities like Toronto and Vancouver. In some cases, large purchasers, ranging from provincial and federal governments to investment funds, have been buying up swaths of units at discounts of roughly 40 per cent from their original selling price.

QuietMarket’s co-founder, Cara Hirsch, who has worked in Toronto’s real estate sector for more than 15 years, says she wants to leverage her industry connections to bring similar deals to the average consumer. The company has created an online marketplace for unsold Toronto-area condos at discounted prices that are not publicly listed.

But to access the deals, prospective buyers need to sign an NDA, something that consumer advocates say carries risks.

QuietMarket users fill out quick surveys about their budget and the location and size of the condo they’re looking for. They are then shown limited details about available units, including square footage and the neighbourhood, before they are prompted to sign an NDA, according to a trial of the platform by The Globe and Mail. The agreements prohibit users from disclosing the details of the deal in perpetuity.

The site had roughly 100 units available across the GTA as of October, ranging from studios to multibedroom apartments priced at levels that the company said were up to 50 per cent below their 2022 listing prices.

The units are screened for quality and the prices are generally at least 10 per cent cheaper than what’s on offer in the resale market, Ms. Hirsch said. She estimated that only 8 per cent of condo inventory that is brought to her company makes it onto the platform.

QuietMarket has facilitated almost 20 condo sales so far, Ms. Hirsch said. Realtors aren’t necessary for a transaction, but buyers are welcome to use them. QuietMarket doesn’t charge a fee directly to consumers and is instead paid out by the developer, she added.

The NDAs are key to facilitating the deals, she said.

Condo developers have been turning to non-disclosure clauses to grant big discounts on certain units without causing drops in the estimated value of other units in the same project or that of properties already sold. But critics say the practice creates a marketplace where listing prices don’t reflect actual home values and consumers don’t always understand what they’re signing.

Barbara Captijn, a real estate consumer advocate, reviewed a sample agreement provided by QuietMarket and noted that the language in the document is more limiting than other NDAs she’s seen in the pre-construction market.

QuietMarket’s agreement requires buyers to keep the details of a sale secret in perpetuity, something that could complicate a buyer’s ability to discuss issues with the property in a dispute with the developer, Ms. Captijn said. She added that NDAs she has seen in the past have allowed consumers to talk about their deal after three years.

She cautioned that the NDA might leave a purchaser liable if their agent or real estate lawyer was to accidentally divulge details of the sale.

Ms. Hirsch at Quietmarket said the company’s NDAs use all-encompassing language because they have to be applicable to a wide array of developers and units, ranging from unsold new homes to projects that are still being built.

She added that QuietMarket would support customers through any disputes in a purchase and that any realtors representing a buyer would need to sign an NDA as well.

Julie Macfarlane, distinguished professor emerita specializing in law at the University of Windsor and the co-founder of advocacy group Can’t Buy My Silence, cast doubt over whether much of the document would be legally enforceable. She added that developers would be unlikely to sue because of the reputational damage they’d face.

However, Prof. Macfarlane, who also reviewed a sample NDA, said the average condo buyer is generally not informed enough to understand the repercussions or the enforceability of what they’re signing.

Recent buyer Dayan Henson, 53, said he was happy with the purchase process and unconcerned with the NDA. He bought a brand new apartment with two bedrooms and two bathrooms in the Annex, a desirable neighbourhood in downtown Toronto. The 750-square-foot condo was originally listed at $1.18-million, but Mr. Henson purchased it for $663,000 – a 44-per-cent discount.

“The savings relative to what prices were two years ago were insane,” Mr. Henson said.

Toronto realtor Sundeep Bahl encouraged prospective buyers to compare QuietMarket’s listings with the resale market. In some cases, he said, better deals are available for relatively new condos – especially for “power of sale” deals in which a financial institution is selling a condo that it has seized from a financially distressed owner.

“There are a lot of power of sale listings going on, and they offer much more of an opportunity to buyers,” Mr. Bahl said.

But critics say the practice creates a marketplace where listing prices don’t reflect actual home values and consumers don’t always understand what they’re signing.

Barbara Captijn, a real estate consumer advocate, reviewed a sample agreement provided by QuietMarket and noted that the language in the document is more limiting than other NDAs she’s seen in the pre-construction market.

QuietMarket’s agreement requires buyers to keep the details of a sale secret in perpetuity, something that could complicate a buyer’s ability to discuss issues with the property in a dispute with the developer, Ms. Captijn said. She added that NDAs she has seen in the past have allowed consumers to talk about their deal after three years.
She cautioned that the NDA might leave a purchaser liable if their agent or real estate lawyer was to accidentally divulge details of the sale.

She added that QuietMarket would support customers through any disputes in a purchase and that any realtors representing a buyer would need to sign an NDA as well.

She added that developers would be unlikely to sue because of the reputational damage they’d face.
However, Prof. Macfarlane, who also reviewed a sample NDA, said the average condo buyer is generally not informed enough to understand the repercussions or the enforceability of what they’re signing.

Recent buyer Dayan Henson, 53, said he was happy with the purchase process and unconcerned with the NDA. He bought a brand new apartment with two bedrooms and two bathrooms in the Annex, a desirable neighbourhood in downtown Toronto. The 750-square-foot condo was originally listed at $1.18-million, but Mr. Henson purchased it for $663,000 – a 44-per-cent discount.

In some cases, he said, better deals are available for relatively new condos – especially for “power of sale” deals in which a financial institution is selling a condo that it has seized from a financially distressed owner.
“There are a lot of power of sale listings going on, and they offer much more of an opportunity to buyers,” Mr. Bahl said.

stories.title: Ontario spent nearly $13-billion and 20 years refurbishing the Darlington nuclear station. Why has it struggled?
stories.summary: Some experts question the wisdom of more overhauls in the province
stories.author: Matthew McClearn
stories.content:
The cavernous turbine hall at the Darlington Nuclear Generating Station is more than half a kilometre long. In late October, the plant’s Unit 3 was nearing the end of a prolonged outage. Green covers had been placed back on its turbines and workers were already laying down materials near Unit 2’s yellow turbines in preparation for an outage next year.

Freshly emerged from an extensive overhaul that took 20 years and cost $12.8-billion, the nuclear station in Clarington, about 70 kilometres east of Toronto, is not yet purring like a kitten. Unit 3’s outage is merely the first in a series the station’s owner, Ontario Power Generation, has planned over the next several years. In addition, the station suffered several unexpected outages this year caused by leaking pipework, faulty pumps and other problems. During August, when Ontario’s electricity demand typically nears its annual peak, just one of Darlington’s four units was operating.

OPG and Ontario’s government promised the refurbishment would position Darlington for 30 years of reliable service. It’s too early to know whether its recent unplanned outages amount to teething pains, or indicate deeper reliability challenges of the sort that have plagued other refurbished stations featuring Candus, the country’s homegrown reactors. But OPG plans additional, lengthy outages over the next few years to replace equipment that was not addressed during the refurbishment – work Ontarians will pay for through their utility bills.

Nuclear stations are enormously complex machines; it would be unreasonable to expect one to continue operating for years on end with little more than occasional oil changes. But the billions of additional spending planned at Darlington are worth keeping in mind as OPG embarks on a $26.8-billion overhaul in Pickering, about 40 kilometres east of Toronto. It’s the most expensive refurbishment of a Candu station ever contemplated.

To venture inside Darlington is to be confronted with a dizzying puzzle of wires, pipes, ducts tanks and stairwells. Crews attend to daily tasks in the stationʼs hot, noisy bowels, co-ordinated from an office adjacent to the control room. Theyʼre monitoring wear-and-tear and plotting when and how to intervene, often years in advance.

Developed during the 1950s and 60s, the Candu’s unique design allowed it to consume natural uranium, and had the added benefit that Canadian manufacturers could build almost every part of it.

But the Candu’s design had significant maintenance consequences. Most of the world’s reactors feature a robust, thick-walled cylindrical structure called a pressure vessel. A Candu core, in contrast, contains thousands of much thinner pressure tubes, each with its own fittings on either end, and pipes conveying water in and out known as feeders – the stuff of plumbers’ nightmares.

Pressure tubes deteriorate and weaken over time, eventually reaching the point when they’re unsafe to continue operating. David Keith, a physicist and professor of geophysical sciences at the University of Chicago, said the Candu’s elaborate piping and numerous connections make it inherently more costly and challenging to maintain than other reactors.

OPG has asserted that Darlington’s cables, laid end-to-end, could stretch to the moon and back. A single unit can have well over 100,000 components. Using inspections, experience and intuition, utilities must decide what to replace, rebuild or leave be.

Steam generators, which faintly resemble giant light bulbs and use the reactor’s heat to produce steam, are among the big-ticket items of Candu plants. Replacing them requires massive cranes to lift them out through holes cut in the powerhouse roof.

Nuclear units each have their own generator and set of turbines, which harness steam to produce power. These complex machines, too, wear down over decades of use.

Even a limited nuclear overhaul can be more expensive than building brand new conventional power plants. On the other hand, the plant will be offline for years and much of it will already be disassembled, allowing workers to reach normally inaccessible components. Misjudgments about equipment longevity can lead to lengthy, expensive outages.

Sunil Nijhawan, a reactor safety expert who once performed consulting work for OPG and foreign Candu owners, said the term “refurbishment” can be misleading because so much of the plant is left untouched.

“Refurbishment is a misnomer because you have replaced only a small part of the total system, whose original cost was only a small fraction of your whole reactor’s cost. There are 20 other systems which are obsolete and old.”

New Brunswick’s Point Lepreau was among the first Candu stations to undergo refurbishment, completed in 2012 following massive cost overruns and delays. Just like OPG, NB Power expected it would be rewarded with 30 years of reliable service.

There’s no longer any doubt that refurbishment was botched . NB Power officials have acknowledged that it focused mainly on restoring the reactor. Less attention was given to turbines and other components in the plant’s “conventional” side. Point Lepreau consequently suffered a series of lengthy outages, rendering the utility incapable of paying down its sizeable debts, which it had been ordered to do by the provincial government.

OPG studied previous refurbishments before attempting Darlington. It nonetheless faced difficult calls. For example, Darlington’s steam generators are far larger than those at other Candu stations, so replacing them would be even more daunting.

Instead, OPG opted to inspect and clean them using a process called “water lancing.” In a 2018 video, Michael Allen, OPG’s on-site leader at Darlington, declared that Unit 2’s “are in excellent condition. They’ve been cleaned and prepared for 30 more years of service.”

A different picture emerged after OPG began refurbishing Unit 3. Each steam generator contains more than 100 components known as primary moisture separators, located in the bulbous section at its top. They’re crucial for supplying dry steam to the turbines, but Unit 3’s had deteriorated. OPG decided to replace them in all of four units, costing hundreds of millions of dollars.

Further surprises awaited once OPG had turbines and generators apart for inspection. Components inside the generators of Units 1 and 2, known as stators, had suffered damage; those repairs are expected to cost $300-million.

Most consequentially, OPG determined turbine rotors in all four units must be replaced. The first, Unit 3, is scheduled to begin in 2029. The tab for the first three units: $2-billion. (There’s a silver lining: OPG expects this work will increase each unit’s output by a minimum of 21 megawatts, which combined would be enough to power roughly 80,000 homes.)

Some of this additional work was completed during the refurbishment, and some was pushed into future outages. But none of it was added to the refurbishment budget; rather, it was paid for from OPG’s budget for sustaining capital.

This allowed officials, including Ontario’s Energy Minister Stephen Lecce, to present the refurbishment as an unqualified success. “Darlington refurbishment was nearly 5 months ahead of schedule and $150M below budget,” he declared in a social media post in September.

But OPG estimates it will spend $3.5-billion over the next few years on the additional maintenance at Darlington. That spending has already begun: For the nine months ended Sept. 30, OPG reported that capital spending had increased by $386-million over the same period last year, largely reflecting additional work at the station. OPG seeks to recover that from consumers through increased rates.

The Association of Major Power Users in Ontario represents industrial consumers. Its president, Brad Duguid, says there’s “no question” OPG’s capital investments will significantly raise rates over the long term. That spending is necessary to preserve reliability, he added, so his organization doesn’t oppose it. But he called on the provincial and federal governments to direct taxpayer support to help mitigate rate increases.

Ibrahim Attieh, a reactor physicist who once worked on designing Candu reactors, describes the additional work at Darlington as “refurbishment by stealth.”

“‘Ahead of schedule and under budget’ is a bogus claim,” Dr. Attieh said.

Moving through questions about Darlington’s unplanned outages during a Sept. 2 hearing, Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission president Pierre Tremblay (who once served as OPG’s chief nuclear operating officer and was responsible for the operation and maintenance of its nuclear plants) observed: “You know, the expectation is a unit coming out of refurbishment would have pretty high reliability.”

Not necessarily.

David Novog, a professor of engineering at McMaster University who specializes in nuclear safety and maintenance, said failure rates of complex systems such as nuclear plants often follow a “bathtub-type curve.” There can be an initial period during which new equipment fails at a higher rate. It can be followed by a “random mode” during which the probability of failure is constant (and hopefully low.) This can be followed by a “wearout” mode in which failures increase again.

Students are taught the “bathtub” concept to illustrate broad trends in reliability, but patterns in individual systems vary, Dr. Novog wrote in an e-mail.

“I don’t think there is enough data to draw any conclusions from the [Darlington] events as yet.”

OPG expected initial hiccups. Its business plan anticipated “reliability outages” following Darlington’s refurbishment, with the station reverting to historical performance by 2028. If achieved, this year’s mishaps might soon be forgotten.

Allan Grace, OPG’s senior vice president for Darlington, said Unit 4 suffered more problems than expected after returning to service. But he pointed out Darlington’s other units have so far performed much better.

One hallway inside Darlington is lined with plaques from the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations recognizing “excellence in nuclear power plant performance.” Those are awarded bi-annually after intrusive inspections from a couple dozen foreign experts, he said.

“It’s effectively 15 years we’ve been at the top echelon of power plant operations for North America,” he said, adding that utilities from other countries regularly seek out OPG’s experience before overhauling their own stations.

“People want to come and see how we’ve done it, because not many other utilities have come even close.”

Bruce Power, an independent power producer which is in the middle of an extensive overhaul at its Candu station along Lake Huron’s eastern shore, reports that the first refurbished unit (Unit 6) has shown “excellent performance” since its restart in 2023. Such is the company’s confidence that it’s expecting overhauled Bruce units will run for up to 35 more years.

The four Pickering B units east of Toronto shut down in late September for their own overhaul. The budget for that, $26.8-billion, was approved by the province in November 2025. That is as much as the combined budgets for refurbishing 10 larger units at Bruce and Darlington. The Pickering units are expected to return to service by the mid-2030s.

OPG previously decided against refurbishing Pickering B because its board of directors warned the units were at significant risk of performing poorly once returned to service, with high operating costs.

In its latest rate application, OPG reported that “very limited sustaining work” had been done at Pickering in the run-up to what was long expected to be its permanent retirement in 2024. (That year, it spent just $6.7-million on station maintenance.)

OPG now plans a lot of additional work at Pickering to renew infrastructure “that is not required for refurbishment but nevertheless needed to support reliable, safe operations during Pickering’s second life.” This work is expected to cost more than $900-million over the next few years.

Dr. Nijhawan said refurbishing Pickering will be tremendously lucrative for the companies involved. But if the station lasts as long as OPG hopes, he added, “it’ll be 90 years old. No concrete structure is designed to last that long, nor any wiring, nor any of these other vessels.

“These reactors were fine when they were designed in the 1960s. Their time is gone. No reason to refurbish them … we should junk these things."

“I don’t think there is enough data to draw any conclusions from the [Darlington] events as yet.”

OPG expected initial hiccups. Its business plan anticipated “reliability outages” following Darlington’s refurbishment, with the station reverting to historical performance by 2028. If achieved, this year’s mishaps might soon be forgotten.

Allan Grace, OPG’s senior vice president for Darlington, said Unit 4 suffered more problems than expected after returning to service. But he pointed out Darlington’s other units have so far performed much better.

One hallway inside Darlington is lined with plaques from the Institute of Nuclear Power Operations recognizing “excellence in nuclear power plant performance.” Those are awarded bi-annually after intrusive inspections from a couple dozen foreign experts, he said.

“It’s effectively 15 years we’ve been at the top echelon of power plant operations for North America,” he said, adding that utilities from other countries regularly seek out OPG’s experience before overhauling their own stations.
“People want to come and see how we’ve done it, because not many other utilities have come even close.”

Bruce Power, an independent power producer which is in the middle of an extensive overhaul at its Candu station along Lake Huron’s eastern shore, reports that the first refurbished unit (Unit 6) has shown “excellent performance” since its restart in 2023. Such is the company’s confidence that it’s expecting overhauled Bruce units will run for up to 35 more years.

The four Pickering B units east of Toronto shut down in late September for their own overhaul. The budget for that, $26.8-billion, was approved by the province in November 2025. That is as much as the combined budgets for refurbishing 10 larger units at Bruce and Darlington. The Pickering units are expected to return to service by the mid-2030s.

OPG previously decided against refurbishing Pickering B because its board of directors warned the units were at significant risk of performing poorly once returned to service, with high operating costs.

In its latest rate application, OPG reported that “very limited sustaining work” had been done at Pickering in the run-up to what was long expected to be its permanent retirement in 2024. (That year, it spent just $6.7-million on station maintenance.)

OPG now plans a lot of additional work at Pickering to renew infrastructure “that is not required for refurbishment but nevertheless needed to support reliable, safe operations during Pickering’s second life.” This work is expected to cost more than $900-million over the next few years.

Dr. Nijhawan said refurbishing Pickering will be tremendously lucrative for the companies involved. But if the station lasts as long as OPG hopes, he added, “it’ll be 90 years old. No concrete structure is designed to last that long, nor any wiring, nor any of these other vessels.
“These reactors were fine when they were designed in the 1960s. Their time is gone. No reason to refurbish them … we should junk these things."

In late October, the plant’s Unit 3 was nearing the end of a prolonged outage. Green covers had been placed back on its turbines and workers were already laying down materials near Unit 2’s yellow turbines in preparation for an outage next year.

Unit 3’s outage is merely the first in a series the station’s owner, Ontario Power Generation, has planned over the next several years. In addition, the station suffered several unexpected outages this year caused by leaking pipework, faulty pumps and other problems. During August, when Ontario’s electricity demand typically nears its annual peak, just one of Darlington’s four units was operating.

stories.title: My brother’s not sick enough to be detained, but not well enough to be free
stories.summary: He’s served by a mental health system that budgets for catastrophe, but offers little in prevention
stories.author: Sara Bourque
stories.content:
Sara Bourque is a former journalist and a PhD student in communication.

I left the meeting about my brother and drove toward a wildfire.

It was September, and the smoke had risen into enormous columns over the hills outside Sooke, a small town west of Victoria, in B.C. People pulled onto the shoulder to take photographs. It struck me that I was not particularly frightened of it. Fire had a perimeter. It had incident commanders and evacuation zones and maps that changed colour as the danger moved. If it came close enough, someone would tell us where to go.

What frightened me more was the hospital room I had just left.

My brother is in his 40s. For about 20 years he has lived with mental illness, and addictions to alcohol and gambling. He has tried to kill himself twice. His life narrowed in increments, slowly enough that each loss could be absorbed before the next arrived: a relationship, work, friends. Then came the conspiracy theories, drinking, encounters with police. For long stretches he lived with our parents, now in their mid-70s, who became, without ever agreeing to it, the entire mental-health infrastructure surrounding one adult man.

That afternoon, as the fire burned in the distance, we sat down with his clinical team. We had asked for the meeting to tell them his history, in the hope that it would get him properly assessed. He was not going anywhere that day. He had overdosed and he was still not stable. We asked whether British Columbia’s Mental Health Act could force him to stay in hospital, which is what we hoped for.

The answer was careful and legally sound. Involuntary admission requires a specific set of criteria to be met, and the threshold is deliberately high, because taking away someone’s liberty is a serious thing for the state to do. The message, as I heard it, was that he was an adult, and adults are allowed to make mistakes, even years of them. I understood that. I understood why the law was cautious.

Then I asked the question the answer left open: Where does someone go if they don’t have a place?

A shelter, someone said.

Nobody in the room was cruel. Cruelty would make this easier. There would be someone to blame, a decision to reverse. Instead, there were competent people describing the available options accurately. The answer was administratively correct.

It was also absurd. The system had concluded that my brother was too capable to be kept in hospital and not capable enough to survive without help. Somewhere between those two findings, responsibility for what happened next disappeared.

Not being detained is not the same as being free. My brother is free to walk out of any door, but nothing is built to catch him on the other side.

Between obvious need and legal detention should lie a whole landscape of care: assessment, residential treatment, supportive housing, crisis stabilization, somewhere to sleep that is more therapeutic than a shelter and less restrictive than a locked ward.

In theory much of it exists. In practice every part of it has a gate, and every gate asks something of the person trying to enter. A referral. Sobriety. An appointment kept. A phone answered. A form completed. Enough stability to prove you deserve help becoming stable.

Perversely, the healthier you are, the easier it is to navigate the services designed for sick people.

For years, my mother asked his family doctor for a psychiatric assessment. He never got one. What he got was a prescription for benzodiazepines, a class of drug that carries serious warnings about addiction, and no diagnosis to go with it. It was legal. I have never known whether it helped. Addiction counselling was also offered, voluntarily, to a man whose illness told him nothing was wrong. He did not go. His illness became the reason he needed help and the reason he could not get it. Eventually the doctor retired. There was no dramatic moment of abandonment. The file simply stopped moving.

Families hide institutional failure by filling the space it leaves. A parent provides the bedroom that supportive housing did not. Someone drives to the appointment, replaces a lost phone, calls everyone who might help, searches for the missing person. There is no billing code for a 75-year-old mother lying awake because she does not know whether her son is alive.

People will ask why he does not simply come home. We did that. We took him in, over and over, for the better part of a decade. Our homes became his hospital, his treatment centre and his supportive housing. He overdosed in my parents’ basement. We cannot keep him alive with love and a spare room, and we should never have been asked to try. Eventually families run out of their ability to be substitutes.

Earlier this year, my brother drove an uninsured car, ON a suspended licence, into a rock wall at high speed and broke his neck in seven places. He was not paralyzed. After about a week he went home to our parents. Then the Insurance Corporation of British Columbia sent him a cheque for roughly $40,000.
