No one asking whether a lump sum in the hands of a man with an active gambling addiction would improve his life or accelerate its destruction. Icbc wrote the cheque. What happened next was not its problem.

We have come to suspect the cheque was not generosity but the cheaper door. Rehabilitation for a man who broke his neck in seven places, carrying 20 years of untreated illness, would have been long and expensive. A lump sum is fast, and it ends the conversation. I cannot prove that is what happened. But Icbc should have to explain, in public, why a man with an active gambling addiction got cash instead of care.

We believe he gambled it away.

Then he overdosed in our parents’ basement.

He spent days in intensive care and then in a high-acuity unit, delirious and difficult but alive. He did not know where he was. He thought he was in Australia, where he had once visited me. He was discharged that day.

He left in a cab wearing a hospital gown. No shirt, no shoes, no phone, no money. The cab took him to the CVI Restaurant and Lounge, a local hotel and pub in Duncan.

This is how systems do things that people would not.

Not long after, we found a residential treatment program in Nanaimo. Five weeks of structured care. Private cost: about $40,000. His social worker did the paperwork. An Island Health psychologist assessed him and, as far as we know, sent in the referral. The program never got back to my mother.

By then I had noticed a number that kept recurring.

Forty thousand dollars.

It arrived as an insurance cheque, paid for by every driver in the province, in the hands of a man with a gambling addiction. It came up again as hospital care: twelve days in intensive care this year, at a published, decade-old Canadian average of roughly $3,600 a day, comes to about $43,000 before a single ambulance or emergency visit is counted. That is not irony. Irony suggests accident. This is an accounting system organized around different moments in one person’s collapse. Insurance is one ledger, acute care another, housing and treatment another. Each makes a rational decision within its own walls, but the total becomes irrational. No single budget contains the life being budgeted.

The catastrophe has a budget. Prevention has to apply for one.

Even leadership pay tells you what an institution considers necessary. Island Health reports about $2.35-million in combined compensation for six senior executives in 2025/26. Halve it and you free up roughly $1.17-million, about 29 stays at the private rate of the program my brother never entered.

But an institution that finds nearly a half-million dollars a year for its chief executive, and no capacity at all for the sustained work of keeping a profoundly vulnerable man alive, is telling you something. “There is no money” is rarely a description of a budget. It is a description of where the money has already been pointed.

My brother now receives about $1,500 a month in disability assistance, which in much of this province cannot pay for housing. Supportive housing exists, but demand outstrips supply, so a person May have to become homeless enough to qualify for the housing that would have prevented his homelessness. He must deteriorate into eligibility. When every adjacent system works this way, the thresholds form a staircase going down. At each step, getting worse opens a door that was closed one step above.

The final threshold is catastrophe.

British Columbia has just elected a new government, and mental illness and addiction were all over the campaign. More beds. More treatment. More housing. Different rules for involuntary care. Some of it May help many people. I hope it does.

But I listened through the whole campaign for the promise that would have changed what happened to my brother, and I never heard it.

At various moments, every program he needed existed: counselling, psychiatry, addiction treatment, disability assistance, hospitals, a residential treatment bed. What did not exist was anyone responsible for the whole person moving among them. We keep trying to solve fragmentation by adding fragments.

What if the unit of care stopped being the episode or the momentary need and became the person?

After a second suicide attempt, an overdose, a pattern of serious hospitalizations, the question would no longer be which program he qualifies for. It would be: Who is responsible for making sure this person does not disappear?

Not responsible for detaining him. Responsible for staying.

One team. One accountable lead. One record that does not close when the hospital door does. Someone empowered to arrange the next appointment rather than hand over a phone number, to notice when he does not arrive, to find another route when a program says no. Discharge plans for high-risk patients that name not just an address but a person or service accepting the hand-off. Navigators with the money to buy an available bed when waiting for one is itself the danger. Crisis places that are neither a locked ward nor a shelter. And a review mechanism for the other side of the Mental Health Act, asking not only whether the state was justified in keeping someone, but whether it was justified in letting him go with nothing to keep him safe.

We already understand this in emergency management. When a wildfire crosses municipal boundaries, we do not let the fire decide which jurisdiction responds. Responsibility follows the threat. Why does a human being become nobody’s responsibility every time he crosses an institutional line?

The Mental Health Act asks who May take responsibility for my brother once he is sick enough to lose his liberty. Our new government should have to answer a harder question: Who takes responsibility while he is still free?

The votes have been counted. The question has not been answered. Not how many beds. Not how much money.

Tell me who owns the gap. Because right now, nobody does.

There is an old photograph of my brother, grinning from inside a dog crate. I can no longer remember why he climbed in. We called him Fisher Boy because he would come out on the boat and fall asleep while everyone else fished. He liked snacks. He liked the water. He was funny. These are remarkably ordinary facts, which is exactly why I want them recorded. Illness colonizes biography. Eventually every story starts with the diagnosis, the attempt, the hospital.

But he existed before the file. He still exists outside it. That is why I have left his name off this essay. He has been observed by enough institutions.

And I am afraid. Of the phone call.

Families who live beside serious mental illness long enough develop a peculiar relationship with the telephone. My parents know it better than I do. Nobody ever tells them to wait until it gets worse. The language is more professional than that. He does not meet the criteria. There is no bed. The referral has been submitted. The program is voluntary. Call back if his condition changes. But under every one of those sentences is the same instruction.

Come back when the emergency is undeniable.

My brother has complied. He has come back in an ambulance, after an overdose, to intensive care, delirious. And each time, for a little while, the doors open. The cruelty is not that British Columbia refuses to spend money on him. It spends enormous amounts. The cruelty is the timing.

We have confused crisis response with care.

The night after one of his hospitalizations, I sang my youngest You Are My Sunshine . Somewhere in the middle I stopped thinking about her. I was thinking about the boy asleep in the fishing boat. The man in the hospital gown. My mother’s son.

Love is useful for many things. It is a terrible substitute for mental-health infrastructure.

The province can map a wildfire across a mountain range and move a town out of its path on a Tuesday afternoon. It has the apparatus. It understands that waiting for the flames to arrive is not prudence. It is a choice. Somewhere in British Columbia tonight there are families who already know what that choice looks like, lying awake beside a telephone, waiting to be told.

stories.title: British spy tale about Cold War defection sheds new light on Canadian mole hunt
stories.summary: There is new evidence that a Soviet spy who defected to Britain in the early 1980s played a key role in helping Canada unravel the mystery of a mole who passed secrets to Russian intelligence.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — There is new evidence that a Soviet spy who defected to Britain in the early 1980s played a key role in helping Canada unravel the mystery of a mole who passed secrets to Russian intelligence.

The recently published book Redwood, by journalist and author Ben Macintyre, tells the story of Vladimir Kuzichkin, who agreed to defect in the hope that he would receive medical treatment to cure his impotence.

It also fleshes out previous claims that Kuzichkin alerted Canadian intelligence officials to a high-ranking traitor within the ranks of the RCMP — a tip that led molehunters to zero in on former Mountie Gilles Brunet.

The Moscow-born Kuzichkin served in the Soviet army before being recruited in the 1970s into the KGB, the country’s main security agency at the time.

Macintyre’s book says Kuzichkin was stationed in Tehran in 1981 when he nervously approached the British about working for them.

During a clandestine meeting with a British intelligence officer, Kuzichkin revealed his disillusionment with the Soviet Union and the KGB, the book says. He also spoke of his desperation to solve the difficulties he was experiencing in the bedroom.

“Kuzichkin’s impotence was his overriding, overwhelming burden, the driving psychological impetus behind his decision to swap sides,” Macintyre writes.

The tall Soviet spy, who was given the code name Redwood, helped the British in Iran before fleeing to England via Turkey. He died in 2009.

Kuzichkin’s defection prompted a flood of queries from allied intelligence services, Macintyre writes.

In August 1982, the British informed the RCMP that “a top-level defector” had pointed to a KGB mole, code-named Nikon, in the Canadian police force, the book says.

“The British could supply no additional details: no name, and no certainty about whether this spy was still in the Canadian service,” Macintyre writes. “But the source was unimpeachable. The revelation sent a shudder through Canada’s intelligence establishment.”

The ensuing RCMP review of operational case files involving the Soviets from 1967 to 1973 did not yield anything that might identify the agent, according to records obtained by The Canadian Press in 2021 through the Access to Information Act.

An examination of hundreds of personnel files and interviews with members also turned up no firm leads.

Brunet spent much of the 1960s in Ottawa with the RCMP Security Service, the wing of the national police force responsible at the time for protecting Canada from foreign spies and extremists. His father had led the RCMP’s security branch for a time in the 1950s.

Brunet excelled in a Russian language course. But he had marital problems and ran up debt. In 1968 he transferred to Montreal, where he continued to work on security files.

Brunet was dismissed from the force in 1973 for refusing to cut ties with a person alleged to have underworld connections. He went into the private security business and later sold prearranged funeral packages.

Brunet was seen as intelligent, aggressive and ambitious but also “avaricious, vindictive and devoid of morals,” the internal records reviewed by The Canadian Press say.

“When it suited his purposes, he was extremely outgoing and gregarious. He played ‘hard’ and was a heavy drinker.”

In December 1983, a security investigator probing Brunet’s past believed the Mounties had found their mole.

The research showed that no Soviet-linked case of which Brunet was aware ever came to a successful conclusion, even though there were operational successes in other areas of the country during the same period.

In each case molehunters were able to document, “operations died immediately upon Brunet learning of them,” says the investigator’s memo. “It appears that not only was Brunet compromised, but that he was so committed that he gave his Soviet handlers everything he got his hands on.”

Investigators believed that the well-connected Brunet continued to feed information to the KGB even after leaving the RCMP.

The RCMP secretly followed Brunet for several days in early April 1984, surveilling his visits to the dry cleaners, a grocery store and — on the day before his sudden death from an apparent heart attack — a pizzeria.

There would be no chance to interrogate the suspect.

“The Mounties never did get their man, but at least, thanks to Kuzichkin, they knew who he was,” Macintyre writes.

Brunet’s grave marker at a Montreal cemetery depicts a beach scene in Acapulco, Mexico — a favourite destination — and a martini glass. It remembers him as a “bon vivant” and a “very special man.”

The newly created Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which took over responsibility for counter-intelligence work, continued to investigate, drawing on additional information received through a tip in 1985 or early 1986. Although details were stripped from the Access to Information release, this tip is believed to have come from another Soviet defector.

A 1987 Csis report said the spy service “is satisfied” that Brunet was the agent recruited by Soviet intelligence. Csis concluded that money, ego and career frustrations were the likely reasons for his betrayal.

Macintyre, who cites the Canadian Access to Information records in recounting the Brunet episode, is not the first to highlight Kuzichkin’s role in helping the Canadians.

A 2016 book, At Her Majesty’s Secret Service by Nigel West, also identifies Kuzichkin as the source of the tipoff about a spy for Moscow in the RCMP.

Kuzichkin’s valuable disclosure is also mentioned in unpublished research on the Brunet case carried out in the 1990s by Peter Marwitz, a former member of the RCMP Security Service and Csis.

Marwitz suggested Brunet’s misdeeds included revealing the location of listening devices planted at the Soviet Embassy in Ottawa and betraying the activities of a Canadian military attaché stationed in Moscow. He said Brunet was paid more than $700,000 by the KGB.

Macintyre writes that Brunet “was able to expose double agents within KGB ranks” and that he gave the Soviets a British debriefing report on Oleg Lyalin, who defected from the KGB in 1971.

Macintyre interviewed former American, British and Russian security officials, as well as friends and family members of those involved in the Kuzichkin saga. He teases out some intriguing new details about the Canadian elements.

Macintyre says Brunet’s KGB handlers taught him Soviet tradecraft, such as the use of cigarette packs to carry film and how to signal for a meeting by placing a piece of tape on a pole — horizontal for Ottawa, vertical for Montreal.

Brunet ignored it all, preferring to meet at a favourite pub, “exchange intelligence for bundles of cash, and then get blind drunk,” the book says.

“Brunet’s espionage is said to fill 20 KGB files of 250 pages each.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Ottawa — There is new evidence that a Soviet spy who defected to Britain in the early 1980s played a key role in helping Canada unravel the mystery of a mole who passed secrets to Russian intelligence.

The recently published book Redwood, by journalist and author Ben Macintyre, tells the story of Vladimir Kuzichkin, who agreed to defect in the hope that he would receive medical treatment to cure his impotence.

It also fleshes out previous claims that Kuzichkin alerted Canadian intelligence officials to a high-ranking traitor within the ranks of the RCMP — a tip that led molehunters to zero in on former Mountie Gilles Brunet.
The Moscow-born Kuzichkin served in the Soviet army before being recruited in the 1970s into the KGB, the country’s main security agency at the time.
Macintyre’s book says Kuzichkin was stationed in Tehran in 1981 when he nervously approached the British about working for them.

During a clandestine meeting with a British intelligence officer, Kuzichkin revealed his disillusionment with the Soviet Union and the KGB, the book says. He also spoke of his desperation to solve the difficulties he was experiencing in the bedroom.
“Kuzichkin’s impotence was his overriding, overwhelming burden, the driving psychological impetus behind his decision to swap sides,” Macintyre writes.
The tall Soviet spy, who was given the code name Redwood, helped the British in Iran before fleeing to England via Turkey. He died in 2009.
Kuzichkin’s defection prompted a flood of queries from allied intelligence services, Macintyre writes.
In August 1982, the British informed the RCMP that “a top-level defector” had pointed to a KGB mole, code-named Nikon, in the Canadian police force, the book says.

“The British could supply no additional details: no name, and no certainty about whether this spy was still in the Canadian service,” Macintyre writes. “But the source was unimpeachable. The revelation sent a shudder through Canada’s intelligence establishment.”

The ensuing RCMP review of operational case files involving the Soviets from 1967 to 1973 did not yield anything that might identify the agent, according to records obtained by The Canadian Press in 2021 through the Access to Information Act.
An examination of hundreds of personnel files and interviews with members also turned up no firm leads.

Brunet spent much of the 1960s in Ottawa with the RCMP Security Service, the wing of the national police force responsible at the time for protecting Canada from foreign spies and extremists. His father had led the RCMP’s security branch for a time in the 1950s.
Brunet excelled in a Russian language course. But he had marital problems and ran up debt. In 1968 he transferred to Montreal, where he continued to work on security files.

Brunet was dismissed from the force in 1973 for refusing to cut ties with a person alleged to have underworld connections. He went into the private security business and later sold prearranged funeral packages.
Brunet was seen as intelligent, aggressive and ambitious but also “avaricious, vindictive and devoid of morals,” the internal records reviewed by The Canadian Press say.
“When it suited his purposes, he was extremely outgoing and gregarious. He played ‘hard’ and was a heavy drinker.”
In December 1983, a security investigator probing Brunet’s past believed the Mounties had found their mole.

The research showed that no Soviet-linked case of which Brunet was aware ever came to a successful conclusion, even though there were operational successes in other areas of the country during the same period.

In each case molehunters were able to document, “operations died immediately upon Brunet learning of them,” says the investigator’s memo. “It appears that not only was Brunet compromised, but that he was so committed that he gave his Soviet handlers everything he got his hands on.”
Investigators believed that the well-connected Brunet continued to feed information to the KGB even after leaving the RCMP.

The RCMP secretly followed Brunet for several days in early April 1984, surveilling his visits to the dry cleaners, a grocery store and — on the day before his sudden death from an apparent heart attack — a pizzeria.
There would be no chance to interrogate the suspect.
“The Mounties never did get their man, but at least, thanks to Kuzichkin, they knew who he was,” Macintyre writes.
Brunet’s grave marker at a Montreal cemetery depicts a beach scene in Acapulco, Mexico — a favourite destination — and a martini glass. It remembers him as a “bon vivant” and a “very special man.”

The newly created Canadian Security Intelligence Service, which took over responsibility for counter-intelligence work, continued to investigate, drawing on additional information received through a tip in 1985 or early 1986. Although details were stripped from the Access to Information release, this tip is believed to have come from another Soviet defector.

A 1987 Csis report said the spy service “is satisfied” that Brunet was the agent recruited by Soviet intelligence. Csis concluded that money, ego and career frustrations were the likely reasons for his betrayal.
Macintyre, who cites the Canadian Access to Information records in recounting the Brunet episode, is not the first to highlight Kuzichkin’s role in helping the Canadians.
A 2016 book, At Her Majesty’s Secret Service by Nigel West, also identifies Kuzichkin as the source of the tipoff about a spy for Moscow in the RCMP.
Kuzichkin’s valuable disclosure is also mentioned in unpublished research on the Brunet case carried out in the 1990s by Peter Marwitz, a former member of the RCMP Security Service and Csis.

Marwitz suggested Brunet’s misdeeds included revealing the location of listening devices planted at the Soviet Embassy in Ottawa and betraying the activities of a Canadian military attaché stationed in Moscow. He said Brunet was paid more than $700,000 by the KGB.
Macintyre writes that Brunet “was able to expose double agents within KGB ranks” and that he gave the Soviets a British debriefing report on Oleg Lyalin, who defected from the KGB in 1971.

Macintyre says Brunet’s KGB handlers taught him Soviet tradecraft, such as the use of cigarette packs to carry film and how to signal for a meeting by placing a piece of tape on a pole — horizontal for Ottawa, vertical for Montreal.

stories.title: Akwesasne elder makes history as first graduate of McGill’s Indigenous languages PhD program
stories.summary: At 73, Mary Onwá Tekahawáhkwen Macdonald is the first graduate of McGill’s Indigenous language revitalization PhD program.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Phil Carpenter
stories.content:
A woman from the Mohawk community of Akwesasne is making history at McGill University , becoming the first graduate of its Indigenous language revitalization PhD program.

Mary Onwá Tekahawáhkwen Macdonald, 73, completed the program in three years, two years ahead of its usual five-year timeline.

Macdonald has spent decades teaching Kanyen’kéha, the traditional name for the Mohawk language — her First Nations language.

Her academic achievement is also helping inspire a new generation of students working to preserve Indigenous languages at risk of disappearing.

Macdonald retired at age 70 after 45 years of teaching Indigenous languages in Akwesasne to pursue her doctorate at McGill.

At first, she worried about returning to school alongside younger students. “How does a 70-year-old woman compete with 20-year-olds?” she told Global News.

But the fear soon disappeared, and Macdonald became a mentor to other students pursuing their master’s degrees.

The program, created in 2023, is designed for students who already speak an Indigenous language and live in communities in the Americas where their languages are threatened.

Jessica Coon, a linguistics professor at McGill, said the program aims to equip students with the skills to advance language preservation.

“To provide them with the tools and concepts that they need to further advance language documentation, revitalization, reclamation work in their home communities,” Coon said.

Macdonald hopes to continue that work as an elder in residence at McGill, mentoring other students.

Among them is Jasmine Jimerson, an Oneida PhD student from Wisconsin who is following in the footsteps of her great-grandmother, Maria Hinton, who produced an Oneida dictionary.

Jimerson said Hinton was the last speaker in their community, and she is proud of the work her great-grandmother did.

“So it’s my goal to continue that work and make sure that we’re still using her work,” Jimerson told Global.

With Macdonald now among those helping guide students, the effort to preserve Indigenous languages is being carried forward by a new generation.

stories.title: CFL commissioner says Quebec City has emerged as leading contender for expansion
stories.summary: Calgary - CFL commissioner Stewart Johnston took the cautious approach Friday regarding the league expanding into Quebec City.
stories.author: Dan Ralph The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Johnston admitted he’s been to Quebec City, had discussions with a potential ownership group there and toured where a football team might play. But all he would say during his second state of the league address was that Quebec City had emerged as a leading candidate for an expansion franchise.

“We have been engaged with very productive conversations with a local ownership group in Quebec City,” Johnston told reporters. “We are encouraged by those, and we can say that Quebec City has emerged as the leading contender for the 10th franchise in the CFL.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

“There is still a lot of work to do, and when there’s something more to report, we’ll hand it over to you (media). I think we need to do our due diligence; this is a step-by-step process. I want to make sure the sequence of events is correct.”

Johnston declined to identify the head of the ownership group, although real estate developer William Trudel has spoken to Quebec media about his interest in a CFL expansion club. And Quebec City Mayor Bruno Marchand has voiced his support of the project.

Johnston wouldn’t say if, or when, a Quebec City franchise might be up and running.

“I’ll just remind you we’ve not announced a 10th team, so no target dates,” Johnston said. “Having said that, what makes that market so attractive is the culture of football is incredibly strong, the population growth is positive, and the economic industry in that region is positive.

“And certainly we’ve seen that the mayor is all in support. These are very good signs of momentum, but we’re not there yet.”

However, Johnston gushed about the merits of Quebec City becoming a CFL city.

“That is such an incredible market,” he said. “When we think of the regional rivalry that a team there could develop with the (Montreal) Alouettes, that would be spectacular.

“We know that Quebec City can handle big events. It’s an outstanding market; it’s an outstanding football market.”

A new stadium would need to be built for a Quebec franchise. But Johnston was open to Telus Stadium — home of the Laval Rouge et Or — or other university venues serving as temporary sites while a permanent facility was being constructed.

“In general, there are some university stadiums that could be available for an expansion franchise to play in,” he said. “I don’t think any one of them, including at Laval, could be a permanent option.

“Maybe an introductory option, whether it’s Laval or anywhere else across the country, while a better facility or appropriate facility is built. Perhaps.”

The CFL has long sought a 10th franchise, but Johnston said the league is also talking to other Canadian markets. Johnston initially declined to comment when asked about Halifax — a city long championed as the league’s 10th franchise by former commissioner Randy Ambrosie — but said it remains on the league’s radar.

“We’ve seen with Touchdown Atlantic the success we can have there,” Johnston said. “So certainly our interest in that region has not waned simply because we’re discussing other markets.”

MOVING THE GOALPOSTS IN 2027

The Grey Cup game Sunday between the Montreal Alouettes and Edmonton Elks will signify the end of an era for the CFL. It will mark the last CFL game played on a 150-yard field (110-yard playing surface, 20-yard end zones) with goalposts on the goal line.

Starting next season, CFL fields will be reduced to 100 yards between the goal lines, with 15-yard end zones. And the goalposts will move to the back of the reconfigured end zones.

“We have full expectation that all nine clubs are going to have fields that reflect the guidelines of our expectations for 2027,” Johnston said. “We’re in discussions with all of those clubs and progress is being made.”

What’s more, the 2027 regular season will open on the Victoria Day weekend — this year’s schedule began June 4 — meaning rookie and training camps will begin in late April and the CFL draft will be held roughly two weeks earlier than normal.

The Grey Cup will be played Nov. 7 — the earliest in league history — in Regina.

And the path to the Grey Cup will be different as eight of the league’s nine teams will qualify for post-season play. This year, just the top six clubs made the playoffs.

Johnston faced stiff fan backlash when he unveiled the changes early in his first year on the job. He was severely criticized by many for trying to Americanize the Canadian game, although Johnston said the reason for moving the goalposts back was to allow for more touchdowns to be scored.

“This is, absolutely, at its core, a Canadian game,” he said. “This three downs, 12 players, a wide field, unlimited motion, it’s all of those things.

“I’ll also say 90 per cent of feedback I get when I get recognized on the street, at the airport, is enthusiastic; it’s positive. They love the direction we’re going. They can see we aren’t going to be changing what makes the Canadian game so special. We’re modernizing it so we can grow into the future.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: A classic failure: Two automotive outsiders are rewriting car culture
stories.summary: Rejected by traditional groups, a pair of Ontario enthusiasts built thriving global communities for misunderstood DeLoreans and high-performance Hyundais
stories.author: Kunal D’souza
stories.content:
In the world of car enthusiasts, Justin Sookraj and Billy Chan are poles apart. Sookraj owns and operates Wells Auto in Milton, Ont., a shop specializing in the restoration of DeLoreans – the iconic gull-wing car from the early 1980s made famous in Back to the Future .

Chan, by contrast, is into much newer vehicles. He is the founder of N-SHFTRZ (pronounced shifters), one of Canada’s largest online communities for Hyundai N enthusiasts.

Yet they share a common thread: the cars they are passionate about never fit neatly into established car clubs, so they created their own.

Out of Oblivion

The DeLorean was built from 1981 to 1983 and failed to meet classic-car requirements when Sookraj tried to enter one into a local Milton car show in 2016 and 2017. He was turned down both times.

“But the car was old,” Sookraj says. “We were going grey and it was always this boomer anthem that if it’s not before 1979, it’s not old and meanwhile time has moved on.”

Although there is no single defining rule, it’s generally agreed that anything older than 25 years is considered a classic car. In Canada, a vehicle can be imported as a classic once it’s 15 years old, and the earliest DeLoreans are now pushing 45.

Look around and it is easy to find car clubs dedicated to Chevrolet Corvettes, mid-1950s General Motors cars and trucks, and pre-war classic Ford Model Ts, BMWs or Jeeps. However, there were no such established spaces for the vehicles Sookraj and Chan were passionate about.

The DeLorean was a misunderstood vehicle from a short-lived company, sitting in a grey area between a modern American classic, an exotic Italian-designed, Irish-built sports car, and a movie prop. It didn’t have a place in traditional automotive groups and neither did the Korean-made Hyundai, which wasn’t considered part of the Japanese domestic market (JDM) movement that dominated the Canadian car scene in the 1990s, especially among millennials.

Today, non-traditional car shows are becoming more common, with events like Euro Klassik, formerly Berlin Klassik, in Grand Bend, Ont., which celebrates vintage to modern European cars, and the Concours d’Lemons, which features forgotten and unloved vehicles that were just bad from the start.

Driven by frustration, Sookraj and two other DeLorean owners decided to launch a show dedicated to modern classics – 30- to 40-year-old cars that didn’t fit in with Baby Boomers’ 1967 Ford Mustangs and 1970 Chevrolet Chevelles.

The inaugural 80s and 90s Oblivion Car and Culture Show was held in 2018 in the parking lot of the Milton Memorial Arena, featuring vehicles from 1980 to 1999. Sookraj describes them as “plastic fantastic cars meant to be banished into oblivion,” because they were considered disposable at the time.

Oblivion has continued to evolve, transforming into the ultimate millennial nostalgia fest, attracting fans of music, movies and toys from the 1980s and ’90s. Past shows have featured a cast reunion of the hit Canadian TV show Degrassi High , retro arcade games and even a full Jurassic Park theme. Oblivion has also brought its nostalgia-fuelled flair to the Canadian International AutoShow in Toronto, showcasing many of the same vehicles and memorabilia.

“Oblivion might have started out of frustration but it’s kept alive by my team who are passionate about the vehicles and the history and, more importantly, what this era was like in Canada,” Sookraj says. “Much of what we feature is Canadiana, and only found here.”

Shifting gears with Hyundai

Passion is the glue that binds car enthusiast communities together. For Chan, it began watching YouTube videos of the Hyundai i30 N and Veloster N, the first two N models Hyundai produced.

“What other brand besides Hyundai offered that level of customization, performance, and sound at that price point?” Chan says.

The i30 N, which debuted in 2017, wasn’t sold in North America, but the sister-platform Veloster N arrived here a year later. Packing a 275-horsepower, turbocharged four-cylinder engine, a manual transmission and plenty of exhaust-popping shenanigans, the Veloster N was a legitimately fun drive that threatened the status quo long established by the Honda Civic Type R and other Japanese performance cars. It was deemed so good that it won Road & Track magazine’s 2020 Performance Car of the Year, beating out heavyweights like the Porsche 911 Carrera S, BMW M2 and Toyota Supra.

Despite that accolade, Hyundai still carries a somewhat negative reputation among car enthusiasts, often perceived as a lower-quality brand compared to Honda and Toyota.

“This isn’t the Hyundai of 40 years ago,” Chan says. “Look at what the N division is doing today, from their [gas-powered] models all the way to pushing the boundaries of EV performance.”

Chan, who is based in Toronto and owns a 2020 Veloster N, envisions N-SHFTRZ as more than just an online community. The primary mission, he says, is to drive the culture forward through local meetups, autocross days and track events – like the Ontario N track day the club hosted in June 2025 at Canadian Tire Motorsport Park.

Hyundai Canada has also been supportive, Chan says, hosting meets at its headquarters in Markham, Ont., inviting members to N product launches, and providing vehicles from its media fleet for content creation.

Chan has channelled this energy into expanding the brand internationally by organizing global N meetups. Volunteers host meets on the exact same day in different corners of the world, with the largest event in September 2025 linking 13 cities across seven countries.

“I just want people to understand these cars, learn what they are truly capable of and, hopefully, love them as much as I do,” Chan says. “I want the broader automotive world to finally realize that Hyundai N is a force that simply can’t be ignored.”

stories.title: Many Ontario pain patients swear by these controversial treatments. Now, they’re ‘terrified’ of possible Ohip cuts
stories.summary: Nadia Lopez says weekly nerve block injections let her manage chronic pain. Her doctor has told her changes May be on way.
stories.author: Kerry Gillespie
stories.content:
Every week for the past two years, Nadia Lopez has sat on an examination table, as a doctor has stuck 10 needles into her back and shoulders.

The shots are injections of lidocaine, a treatment that Lopez says has allowed her to overcome chronic pain enough to attend university, where she’s working toward her dream of becoming a high school teacher.

“Before I started this, I was unemployed, I was suffering a lot, I was not doing great mental health-wise,” said Lopez, 26. “I had some days where I was almost completely bedridden, and being able to get this treatment has really turned things around.”

She was devastated when her doctor told her the Ontario government is considering cuts to Ohip coverage that could sharply limit how often she can get injections, and force some pain care clinics to close. When she looked for details, she found only a campaign launched by clinics like hers to rally patients to “ save pain clinics .”

Lopez is caught in a fraught corner of health care, where the easiest treatments to get for chronic pain — a complex physical and psychological condition — are not necessarily the ones backed by evidence.

Physicians working in community pain clinics say they’ve been told by their representative to a joint Ontario Medical Association and Health Ministry committee that discussions are underway to reduce public funding for the nerve blocks that many patients have come to rely on and they maintain helps them.

Toronto studies see some success in treating pain, depression. But ketamine’s potential is still poorly understood.

The province hasn’t said anything publicly, but this wouldn’t be the first time it has tried to rein in a practice that experts in pain medicine and research say has become common in Ontario without any real evidence to show it works.

Neither the OMA nor the ministry responded to specific questions about whether limits on Ohip coverage for nerve blocks are being proposed. The OMA said it “recognizes the importance of access to care for patients living with chronic pain” but such matters are dealt with in a process with the province. The ministry said only that Ohip coverage remains unchanged.

One in five Canadians lives with chronic pain, which is defined as pain that persists for more than three months, often with no identifiable cause or long after the body has healed from an injury.

The gold-standard, multidisciplinary approach — combining physical therapy, psychological support and, in some cases, medication or limited interventional procedures like injections — targets the body and brain’s pain pathways together, experts say.

Chronic pain is one of the most expensive untreated health conditions, and patients often wait years for ministry-funded multidisciplinary services, according to Pain Ontario , a community-based non-profit. Trying to cobble together that level of care privately leaves patients paying out of pocket.

What’s easy to find, and publicly funded, are nerve block injections.

Nadia Lopez says nerve block injections for managing her chronic pain are making a big difference in her life.

Dr. Anuj Bhatia, division head of pain medicine at the University Health Network, is the lead author on the first Canadian evidence-based guidelines for spinal procedures for chronic pain.

Published last month, the guidelines were five years in the making and involved over 50 contributors. He hopes they will help educate physicians and guide policymakers toward care “that follows the evidence.”

Right now, there is no evidence that shows regular, repeat nerve block injections are an effective way to treat chronic pain, Bhatia said.

Nerve blocks can be used as a diagnostic tool to locate the source of a problem or to deliver a numbing local anesthetic or anti-inflammatory steroid to provide short-term pain relief.

“There’s certainly a billing code for these injections and enterprising people are using the code but, outside of that, I don’t understand what the clinical rationale is for doing this repeatedly,” he said.

“Outside Ontario, no one is really doing this kind of practice. When I tell colleagues in Europe, or I go to conferences in America, they can’t really understand what the problem is. They say: ‘Why would somebody do this in the first place?’”

A 2020 Star investigation found that Ontario’s top-billing pain doctors , working in privately owned clinics, gave patients weekly injections under loose limits on publicly funded nerve blocks, despite the lack of evidence they work. Ontario has previously proposed reining in billings, as part of its effort to reduce “inappropriate” medical services but not followed through in the face of pushback from the OMA and patients rallying around clinics that they believe provide necessary care.

“Many of the physicians who are doing it are not doing it just to generate the billing. Many of them actually believe that this is the best care they can provide the patient who is standing up in their clinic,” Bhatia said, adding that’s why more education for physicians in evidence-based pain care is needed.

Jason Busse, scientific director of the Michael G. DeGroote Institute for Pain Research and Care at McMaster University, said that chronic pain is vastly underresearched and the roughly three million Ontarians who live with it suffer enormously.

“They’re desperate. They’re looking for solutions,” he said. “You can get lots and lots of treatment that doesn’t have much evidence for effectiveness, and it can be very hard to get therapy that does have evidence.”

He said more needs to be done to sell patients on physical and psychological therapies rather than “dramatic” sounding nerve blocks and that is challenging work because it can be perceived by patients as diminishing their suffering.

Adding to that complication: observational data on nerve blocks looks great. “Patients are happy, (they say) they’re doing great, it’s a quick procedure to do, the reimbursement is excellent. What’s the problem?” he said.

“When we look at the randomized controlled trials where patients don’t know if they’re getting a real nerve block or a sham (procedure), the current evidence is not showing us that there is much difference between the two.”

He was involved in a study, published in 2023, of the perceptions of 562 chronic pain patients receiving nerve blocks in Ontario’s community clinics. They reported pain relief and functional improvement. Most attended clinics weekly for more than three years and the majority who were not retired were still unable to work, he said.

“That’s a lot of nerve blocks that people are getting … I think it’s reasonable to ask what it is accomplishing.”

Still, he understands why the prospect of losing this treatment is terrifying for patients. “If you’re going to move people away from something that they have become reliant on, what are you going to provide in its place?”

If the province is concerned that practice is not following evidence, it should fund a strong trial to end the debate, he said, “instead of arbitrary policies being made in some kind of black box manner where no one understands them.”

The ministry didn’t answer the Star’s questions about the challenges for patients and systemic issues involved in limiting nerve blocks.

Dr. Christine Giordani has treated chronic pain with nerve blocks for a decade and said pain care doctors were told change is coming through their representative to the Appropriateness Working Group, but specific details are being kept under wraps. That’s a joint OMA-Health Ministry effort to curb medically unnecessary services and improve patient care.

“We know that it’s happening,” she said. “At least give us some transparency … so we can all be part of the conversation.”

Giordani, who says there is “sufficient evidence” to continue treating patients with nerve blocks, worries changes to Ohip coverage, service rules or referral pathways would centralize pain care in major cities and leave many patients without easy access.

“One of the things that we pride ourselves on as chronic pain doctors, because it’s not an easy job … is that we at least take a lot of the burden off family doctors and ERs,” said Giordani, who works in Welland, Niagara Falls and St. Catharines.

Lopez, who pays $500 a month for physiotherapy and other treatments to manage her pain, has never gone longer than two weeks without a visit to her Pain Care Clinic for nerve blocks. She was particularly concerned when her doctor told her changes could require a three-month wait between Ohip-covered visits.

“Just going to school in person is something that would have been impossible for me before,” she said. “I’m terrified that I’m going to lose the functionality and the progress I’ve made in getting my life back.”
paragraphs: Every week for the past two years, Nadia Lopez has sat on an examination table, as a doctor has stuck 10 needles into her back and shoulders.

The shots are injections of lidocaine, a treatment that Lopez says has allowed her to overcome chronic pain enough to attend university, where she’s working toward her dream of becoming a high school teacher.

“Before I started this, I was unemployed, I was suffering a lot, I was not doing great mental health-wise,” said Lopez, 26. “I had some days where I was almost completely bedridden, and being able to get this treatment has really turned things around.”

She was devastated when her doctor told her the Ontario government is considering cuts to Ohip coverage that could sharply limit how often she can get injections, and force some pain care clinics to close. When she looked for details, she found only a campaign launched by clinics like hers to rally patients to “ save pain clinics .”

Lopez is caught in a fraught corner of health care, where the easiest treatments to get for chronic pain — a complex physical and psychological condition — are not necessarily the ones backed by evidence.

Physicians working in community pain clinics say they’ve been told by their representative to a joint Ontario Medical Association and Health Ministry committee that discussions are underway to reduce public funding for the nerve blocks that many patients have come to rely on and they maintain helps them.
Toronto studies see some success in treating pain, depression. But ketamine’s potential is still poorly understood.

The province hasn’t said anything publicly, but this wouldn’t be the first time it has tried to rein in a practice that experts in pain medicine and research say has become common in Ontario without any real evidence to show it works.

Neither the OMA nor the ministry responded to specific questions about whether limits on Ohip coverage for nerve blocks are being proposed. The OMA said it “recognizes the importance of access to care for patients living with chronic pain” but such matters are dealt with in a process with the province. The ministry said only that Ohip coverage remains unchanged.
One in five Canadians lives with chronic pain, which is defined as pain that persists for more than three months, often with no identifiable cause or long after the body has healed from an injury.

The gold-standard, multidisciplinary approach — combining physical therapy, psychological support and, in some cases, medication or limited interventional procedures like injections — targets the body and brain’s pain pathways together, experts say.

Chronic pain is one of the most expensive untreated health conditions, and patients often wait years for ministry-funded multidisciplinary services, according to Pain Ontario , a community-based non-profit. Trying to cobble together that level of care privately leaves patients paying out of pocket.
What’s easy to find, and publicly funded, are nerve block injections.
Nadia Lopez says nerve block injections for managing her chronic pain are making a big difference in her life.
Dr. Anuj Bhatia, division head of pain medicine at the University Health Network, is the lead author on the first Canadian evidence-based guidelines for spinal procedures for chronic pain.

Published last month, the guidelines were five years in the making and involved over 50 contributors. He hopes they will help educate physicians and guide policymakers toward care “that follows the evidence.”
Right now, there is no evidence that shows regular, repeat nerve block injections are an effective way to treat chronic pain, Bhatia said.
Nerve blocks can be used as a diagnostic tool to locate the source of a problem or to deliver a numbing local anesthetic or anti-inflammatory steroid to provide short-term pain relief.

“There’s certainly a billing code for these injections and enterprising people are using the code but, outside of that, I don’t understand what the clinical rationale is for doing this repeatedly,” he said.

“Outside Ontario, no one is really doing this kind of practice. When I tell colleagues in Europe, or I go to conferences in America, they can’t really understand what the problem is. They say: ‘Why would somebody do this in the first place?’”

A 2020 Star investigation found that Ontario’s top-billing pain doctors , working in privately owned clinics, gave patients weekly injections under loose limits on publicly funded nerve blocks, despite the lack of evidence they work. Ontario has previously proposed reining in billings, as part of its effort to reduce “inappropriate” medical services but not followed through in the face of pushback from the OMA and patients rallying around clinics that they believe provide necessary care.

“Many of the physicians who are doing it are not doing it just to generate the billing. Many of them actually believe that this is the best care they can provide the patient who is standing up in their clinic,” Bhatia said, adding that’s why more education for physicians in evidence-based pain care is needed.

Jason Busse, scientific director of the Michael G. DeGroote Institute for Pain Research and Care at McMaster University, said that chronic pain is vastly underresearched and the roughly three million Ontarians who live with it suffer enormously.

“They’re desperate. They’re looking for solutions,” he said. “You can get lots and lots of treatment that doesn’t have much evidence for effectiveness, and it can be very hard to get therapy that does have evidence.”

He said more needs to be done to sell patients on physical and psychological therapies rather than “dramatic” sounding nerve blocks and that is challenging work because it can be perceived by patients as diminishing their suffering.

Adding to that complication: observational data on nerve blocks looks great. “Patients are happy, (they say) they’re doing great, it’s a quick procedure to do, the reimbursement is excellent. What’s the problem?” he said.

“When we look at the randomized controlled trials where patients don’t know if they’re getting a real nerve block or a sham (procedure), the current evidence is not showing us that there is much difference between the two.”

He was involved in a study, published in 2023, of the perceptions of 562 chronic pain patients receiving nerve blocks in Ontario’s community clinics. They reported pain relief and functional improvement. Most attended clinics weekly for more than three years and the majority who were not retired were still unable to work, he said.
“That’s a lot of nerve blocks that people are getting … I think it’s reasonable to ask what it is accomplishing.”

Still, he understands why the prospect of losing this treatment is terrifying for patients. “If you’re going to move people away from something that they have become reliant on, what are you going to provide in its place?”

If the province is concerned that practice is not following evidence, it should fund a strong trial to end the debate, he said, “instead of arbitrary policies being made in some kind of black box manner where no one understands them.”

stories.title: Meet the five Canadian authors vying for the $100K Giller Prize
stories.summary: Toronto - Five Canadian writers are first-time finalists for the prestigious Giller Prize, which awards $100,000 to the author of the best Canadian novel, graphic novel or short story collection published in English this year.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Five Canadian writers are first-time finalists for the prestigious Giller Prize, which awards $100,000 to the author of the best Canadian novel, graphic novel or short story collection published in English this year.

For the first time, the prize will be decided by a jury of nine independent booksellers from across Canada. The winner is scheduled to be announced at a glitzy gala hosted by Rick Mercer on Nov. 16 at the Ritz-Carlton in Toronto.

Here is a closer look at the authors and their books.

Michelle good balances truth with fiction in ‘eliza sunshine’

“Eliza Sunshine” follows three generations of Cree women connected by their family’s tradition of storytelling. Good has said the novel is “very personal” as it’s based off her mother and great-grandmother’s life.

While it’s a work of fiction, Good said there are aspects that are “actually factual.”

“I often say something need not be factual in order to be true,” she said.

“More and more, I’m beginning to think that there really is no such thing as fiction,” she said. “Because whether we’re conscious of it or not, we’re drawing from our own points of view, our own experiences in life, our own observations. And so I think there’s a level of truth to all fiction, really.”

Good has previously been longlisted for the Giller for her 2020 novel “Five Little Indians.”

Nicholas herring examines fear, love in ‘your breath in charcoal’

“Your Breath in Charcoal” is about a directionless young Islander who picks up an acquaintance’s brother from a mental health hospital in New Brunswick, and the pair decide to travel further west to Toronto.

The novel is Herring’s second, following 2022’s ‘Some Hellish,” which won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. Herring, who works as a carpenter in his native Prince Edward Island, described his writing voice as “working-class” and “philosophical.”

Herring said fellow P.E.I. writer Keir Lowther summed up his Giller-nominated novel best: “He said I wrote a fearless book about fear.”

“That’s a pretty good summation; I should give him credit,” Herring said. “I was just trying to tackle big issues — big sort of philosophical things like fear and love.”

Nazanine hozar returns to iran in ‘the small ones’

“The Small Ones” tells the story of children caught up in a military insurgence along the Iran-Iraq border in the early 1980s and is based on real conflict from the time.

The novel is Hozar’s second, following her 2019 national bestselling debut “Aria.”

Both novels take place in Iran, where Hozar was born and lived until she was seven years old and moved to Canada with her family in 1985. She said she returns to Iran through her writing because growing up amid the aggression of the revolution and the Iran-Iraq War “really marked me.”

“You can never, as an Iranian, get away from it, you’re always met with it. And so sometimes I feel that I don’t know if it’s my duty to write about it, but it’s my will to write about it,” she said. “And even in the future, if I might not specifically write about Iran itself, I think I’ll be quite inspired by the events there and what people there have to go through on a daily basis.”

Patmeena sabit builds off thesis in ‘good people’

“Good People” follows a wealthy Afghan-American family thrust into the court of public opinion after a tragedy, forcing them to navigate as the media and members of their community examine every aspect of their lives.

Born in Afghanistan, Sabit’s family fled to Pakistan following the Soviet invasion and later moved to Virginia, where the novel is set. She moved to Canada in 2000 for university.

It was at Montreal’s McGill University, studying international development, that Sabit wrote a thesis about honour-based violence and crimes in Jordan. That academic research laid the groundwork to later explore the topic in her first novel.

“I was coming at it from a developmental human rights (and) women’s advocacy point of view,” Sabit said of her thesis. “I never dreamed that years and years later, I would sit down and write a book about the issue.”

Sabit said she wrote the book over a period of 10 years, balancing contract work and later a nine-to-five job that meant she spent her mornings, evening and weekends writing, “which I think is such a common experience for so many people who want to write.”

Tara gereaux inspired by métis heritage in ‘wild people quiet’

“Wild People Quiet” explores the repercussions of a woman’s decision to hide her Métis identity while living in a prairie town in the 1940s.

Gereaux said the theme of her third book was inspired by a question she had about her own family, including her grandfather, who did not publicly discuss their Métis identity when she was growing up.

“My family never talked about us being Métis aside from saying that we were, but not really identifying as such outside the home. We always identified as French,” she said.

While the book is historical-fiction, Gereaux said she set it in the 1940s “because I really wanted to understand the time period that my grandfather was living in when he was a young man,” she said.

While touring with this book, Gereaux noted she has met other people across the country who have shared with her similar experiences of their families not talking openly about their Métis heritage.

“I was just shocked at how many people feel so personally connected to it,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.
paragraphs: Toronto - Five Canadian writers are first-time finalists for the prestigious Giller Prize, which awards $100,000 to the author of the best Canadian novel, graphic novel or short story collection published in English this year.

For the first time, the prize will be decided by a jury of nine independent booksellers from across Canada. The winner is scheduled to be announced at a glitzy gala hosted by Rick Mercer on Nov. 16 at the Ritz-Carlton in Toronto.
Here is a closer look at the authors and their books.
Michelle good balances truth with fiction in ‘eliza sunshine’

“Eliza Sunshine” follows three generations of Cree women connected by their family’s tradition of storytelling. Good has said the novel is “very personal” as it’s based off her mother and great-grandmother’s life.
While it’s a work of fiction, Good said there are aspects that are “actually factual.”
“I often say something need not be factual in order to be true,” she said.

“More and more, I’m beginning to think that there really is no such thing as fiction,” she said. “Because whether we’re conscious of it or not, we’re drawing from our own points of view, our own experiences in life, our own observations. And so I think there’s a level of truth to all fiction, really.”
Good has previously been longlisted for the Giller for her 2020 novel “Five Little Indians.”
Nicholas herring examines fear, love in ‘your breath in charcoal’

“Your Breath in Charcoal” is about a directionless young Islander who picks up an acquaintance’s brother from a mental health hospital in New Brunswick, and the pair decide to travel further west to Toronto.

The novel is Herring’s second, following 2022’s ‘Some Hellish,” which won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize. Herring, who works as a carpenter in his native Prince Edward Island, described his writing voice as “working-class” and “philosophical.”
Herring said fellow P.E.I. writer Keir Lowther summed up his Giller-nominated novel best: “He said I wrote a fearless book about fear.”
“That’s a pretty good summation; I should give him credit,” Herring said. “I was just trying to tackle big issues — big sort of philosophical things like fear and love.”
Nazanine hozar returns to iran in ‘the small ones’
“The Small Ones” tells the story of children caught up in a military insurgence along the Iran-Iraq border in the early 1980s and is based on real conflict from the time.
The novel is Hozar’s second, following her 2019 national bestselling debut “Aria.”

Both novels take place in Iran, where Hozar was born and lived until she was seven years old and moved to Canada with her family in 1985. She said she returns to Iran through her writing because growing up amid the aggression of the revolution and the Iran-Iraq War “really marked me.”

“You can never, as an Iranian, get away from it, you’re always met with it. And so sometimes I feel that I don’t know if it’s my duty to write about it, but it’s my will to write about it,” she said. “And even in the future, if I might not specifically write about Iran itself, I think I’ll be quite inspired by the events there and what people there have to go through on a daily basis.”
Patmeena sabit builds off thesis in ‘good people’

“Good People” follows a wealthy Afghan-American family thrust into the court of public opinion after a tragedy, forcing them to navigate as the media and members of their community examine every aspect of their lives.
Born in Afghanistan, Sabit’s family fled to Pakistan following the Soviet invasion and later moved to Virginia, where the novel is set. She moved to Canada in 2000 for university.

It was at Montreal’s McGill University, studying international development, that Sabit wrote a thesis about honour-based violence and crimes in Jordan. That academic research laid the groundwork to later explore the topic in her first novel.

“I was coming at it from a developmental human rights (and) women’s advocacy point of view,” Sabit said of her thesis. “I never dreamed that years and years later, I would sit down and write a book about the issue.”

Sabit said she wrote the book over a period of 10 years, balancing contract work and later a nine-to-five job that meant she spent her mornings, evening and weekends writing, “which I think is such a common experience for so many people who want to write.”
Tara gereaux inspired by métis heritage in ‘wild people quiet’
“Wild People Quiet” explores the repercussions of a woman’s decision to hide her Métis identity while living in a prairie town in the 1940s.
Gereaux said the theme of her third book was inspired by a question she had about her own family, including her grandfather, who did not publicly discuss their Métis identity when she was growing up.
“My family never talked about us being Métis aside from saying that we were, but not really identifying as such outside the home. We always identified as French,” she said.
While the book is historical-fiction, Gereaux said she set it in the 1940s “because I really wanted to understand the time period that my grandfather was living in when he was a young man,” she said.
While touring with this book, Gereaux noted she has met other people across the country who have shared with her similar experiences of their families not talking openly about their Métis heritage.
“I was just shocked at how many people feel so personally connected to it,” she said.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Career college saw Osap usage rise 6,000 per cent, but wasn't cut off this spring
stories.summary: Toronto - An Ontario career college with four campuses saw the amount of students receiving financial aid explode over a few years, including an increase of nearly 6,000 per cent at one campus, but it was not one of the schools the government cut off this spring.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - An Ontario career college with four campuses saw the amount of students receiving financial aid explode over a few years, including an increase of nearly 6,000 per cent at one campus, but it was not one of the schools the government cut off this spring.

The Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology, with campuses in the Greater Toronto Area, had 562 students accessing the Ontario Student Assistance Program in 2021-22, and three years later that number was 17,157, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

That is an increase of nearly 3,000 per cent.

One campus went from 74 students on Osap in 2021-22 to 4,481 in 2024-25, an increase of 5,955 per cent. The amount of provincial grants for students at that one campus rose by more than 8,000 per cent in that timeframe, to $39 million.

The students at four campuses in total in that latter year accounted for about $151 million in provincial grants.

The vast majority of the growth in Osap usage was driven by students enrolled in online programs, the data shows. More than 97 per cent of the students accessing Osap at the school in 2024-25 were online, a stark difference from 2021-22, when six per cent of the students were studying online.

Critics question why the college was not among the six schools that Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn denied Osap eligibility to this May.

Quinn at the time cut off four Academy of Learning locations and two campuses of Citi College of Canadian Careers, citing concerns about admissions practices. They are fighting the decision in court and deny any wrongdoing. Allegations made by the government have not been proven in court.

In early October, Quinn announced a pause on Osap payments to all career colleges and other private post-secondary institutions while Kpmg conducts an audit of the sector, with the minister saying there is now evidence of systemic concerns. He has not flagged specific schools as being under suspicion.

Quinn has come under fire in the legislature over his handling of Osap as opposition parties accuse him of not acting quickly enough, given that Career Colleges Ontario was raising concerns as early as January 2023.

He has defended his ministry’s actions by saying repeatedly that the ministry heard increasing concerns in late 2024, did targeted inspections in the summer of 2025, prevented all career colleges from qualifying for grants — only allowing loans — earlier this year, and made six schools ineligible for Osap this May.

“I’m not sure how we’re said to be turning a blind eye when, this year, we eliminated the eligibility of six of those institutions prior to pausing Osap across the whole sector,” Quinn said in the legislature on Nov. 3.

The increases at two of the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology campuses in particular far outstrip the percentages seen at those six schools.

NDP colleges and universities critic Peggy Sattler said if the ministry did not notice a 6,000 per cent increase, that suggests “total incompetence and mismanagement.”

“It just gets worse and worse for this government, which is what we suspected all along from this complete failure to provide any oversight of what was going on with the Osap program,” she said.

“Why was the government allowing this money to continue to go out the door when clearly there were some questions that needed to be asked?”

Neither the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology nor its president have responded to multiple requests for comment.

Citi College has said its growth was in part due to aligning its programs with the job market, and that a more accurate calculation would use a pre-pandemic figure and rely on a compound annual growth rate, in which case it would have been at about 38 per cent per year.

The Academy of Learning has said its campuses often serve newcomers and adults retraining for a second career, and as those populations grew, enrolment grew with it.

Career Colleges Ontario said that it conducted an “extensive membership review” and as of Sept. 1, the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology is no longer a member of its association, but it did not say why.

A spokesperson for Quinn would not say if the Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was on the government’s radar or if the minister finds its growth percentages concerning.

“As of this year, private career colleges are no longer eligible for Osap grants,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in response.

“As we have already done in some cases, when serious concerns are identified, we will not hesitate to cut an institution off from Osap entirely.”

Quinn announced Thursday that legislation being tabled next week will seek to put a cap on Osap-funded enrolment growth at career colleges and ban online-only programs from Osap eligibility, among other measures he says will strengthen accountability.

The federal government last year flagged the schools Ontario ultimately made ineligible for Osap, but would not say why Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not among them.

“While Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology was not one of the institutions that was identified for potential suspension in September 2025, the Government of Canada continues to work closely with provinces and territories to monitor program activity, ensure compliance, and investigate potential risks to the integrity of student financial assistance,” Employment and Social Development Canada spokesperson Natalie Huneault wrote in a statement.

“As potential risks and issues of concern are identified, further reviews and investigations May be triggered.”

The six schools Quinn made ineligible for Osap saw the number of students receiving Osap increase between about 650 per cent and 1,375 per cent from 2021-22 to 2024-25.

Increases at the four Canadian College of Business, Science and Technology campuses, meanwhile, were about 1,663 per cent at one campus, 2,230 at another, with the other two seeing increases of 5,282 per cent and 5,955 per cent.

Liberal critic Tyler Watt said numbers like that should have been impossible to miss.

”(The Ontario government) only cut off the campuses the federal government warned them about, which raises the question of whether they would have ever caught any bad actors on their own, and how many more they missed,” he wrote in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Carney heads to Southeast Asia summit as Rohingya refugee crisis grows worse
stories.summary: Dublin - Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to a major summit of southeast Asian leaders as the ongoing Rohingya refugee crisis shows no sign of easing.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Dublin - Prime Minister Mark Carney is heading to a major summit of southeast Asian leaders as the ongoing Rohingya refugee crisis shows no sign of easing.

Randeep Sarai, Canada’s secretary of state for international development, said the federal government is not abandoning the nearly one million Rohingya people expelled from Myanmar into Bangladesh.

“They know that Canada is there for them,” said Sarai, who visited the world’s largest refugee camp in Bangladesh last month. He said he met Rohingya children there who were born in the camp nearly a decade ago.

“They’ve only seen one life, which is at a refugee camp.”

The Council on Foreign Relations says almost a decade ago, the government of Myanmar launched a military campaign that forced roughly 700,000 Rohingya to flee the country.

Rights groups suspect the government has committed genocide against the Rohingya, but officials deny the accusations.

Human rights groups say the country’s military killed and raped Rohingya civilians and burned down entire villages.

The crisis forced families to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh, where they still languish in an overcrowded camp in the town of Cox’s Bazar.

In 2021, a military junta overthrew Myanmar’s civilian government and intensified ethnic violence, often through airstrikes. Amnesty International reported in October that 150 to 700 new Rohingya refugees had been arriving weekly in Bangladesh.

The International Court of Justice is set to rule later this month on whether Myanmar has committed an act of genocide.

The instability is a major issue for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, a bloc of 11 countries that includes Myanmar, previously known as Burma. Carney arrives Saturday in Manila for the Asean leaders’ summit, where he’s expected to pursue new trade arrangements with the region.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau appointed Bob Rae as a special envoy to Myanmar to advocate for Rohingya people, a role he retained after Trudeau named him Canada’s ambassador to the United Nations.

Rae said the crisis is worse since then, as the world has shifted its attention to crises in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran and as Canada works to rebalance its trading relationships.

“It remains a challenge for the Canadian government to put it at a high enough level of priority, when the country’s facing a whole bunch of other crises,” he told The Canadian Press.

The instability has caused Rohingya and others to flee Myanmar to countries across Southeast Asia such as Malaysia, where 126,000 people live as undocumented migrants.

Meanwhile, scam centres in Myanmar have engaged in human trafficking by luring people from multiple countries into forced labour.

Rae said the spillover beyond Bangladesh is a source of deep concern for the entire region.

The Asean bloc agreed in 2021 to a five-point plan involving a ceasefire — which never happened — to be followed by negotiations, mediation, an influx of aid and a delegation to Myanmar.

“A lot of pressure is also on the Asean countries,” Sarai said. “We feel that they have a duty to work and put pressure, to make Myanmar bring [Rohingya refugees] back and give them a safe place.”

Rae argued pressure from Asean countries will only work if Canada and others put up enough aid money to help with the refugee crisis, and convince India and China to help more. Russia has helped to arm Myanmar, he noted.

Rae oversaw two plans for Canada’s response to the crisis; the last plan expired in early 2024. Ottawa folded its Rohingya programming into general aid programming that year.

“Our level of funding has gone down since the beginning of the crisis in 2017,” Rae said, arguing Canada needs to be vocal on the issue if it wants to be seen as a credible security partner for the region.

“The continuing issue is to make sure that it’s enough of a priority, that it’s seen as enough of priority for Canada, that we can continue to have strong credibility in our relationships with Asean.”

Rae said he regularly receives messages from desperate Rohingya pleading for funding for education initiatives.

The UN’s humanitarian head Tom Fletcher told The Canadian Press on a visit to Ottawa last month that he raises the Rohingya issue regularly with foreign ministers from Asean countries.

“It’s a really sustained, expensive, prolonged crisis,” he said.

Fletcher said the ultimate goal must be the voluntary return of Rohingya refugees to Myanmar under safe conditions.

“There has to be a horizon where we can see a pathway to that,” he said, adding that refugees “clearly don’t feel that it’s safe enough.”

Queen’s University professor Stéphanie Martel said the Rohingya issue is part of a broader Myanmar crisis that will be a “top priority” at this weekend’s summit, though she does not expect progress.

“I don’t think a lot of people actually have leverage when it comes to managing this awful, tragic situation,” she said, adding that lack of leverage is due in part to Asean’s format.

“This is an organization with a diverse set of regimes and that was built around this notion of non-interference in domestic affairs, and that everybody gets to do basically what they deem is right for their own regime and country,” she said.

Canada also has limited leverage, Martel added.

“I don’t think there’s a whole lot that Canada can do differently than what it’s already doing,” she said.

Sarai said Canada is committed to helping Rohingya gain skills they can use to support themselves within the camp and, ideally, after they return to Myanmar.

“Canada is one of the leading supporters of the Rohingyas. And when you talk to them, they’re ... still very strong in their dream to go back home,” he said.

“It’s foolish for the Myanmar regime to not have them back, as I think as soon as they get back, they will be adding to their economy, they’ll be contributing.”

The refugee camp is not connected to Bangladesh’s power grid. Sarai said Rohingya refugees have taught themselves how to wire up the camp with solar power and to engage in commercial activities, such as making shoes and repairing motorcycle engines and bicycles.

Sarai said he also saw the effects in the camp of Canadian-funded programs that train women to start daycares and help teenagers learn how to preserve their language and culture.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.
