'Listen, everybody thinks their children are angels' — Winnipeg restaurant owner on why she doesn't want kids at her tables

Navigate

In the past month, Brigitte Legault, the Caq’s director general and main organizer, has spared no efforts to overhaul the party she built from the ground up

Quebec Premier Christine Fréchette addresses her crowd of supporters after announcing that she has called and congratulated Paul St-Pierre Plamondon for his election victory in Trois-Rivières on Oct. 5, 2026. (Tim Snow / Montreal Gazette)

Catherine Lévesque

November 13, 2026 at 4:00 a.m.

Ottawa — Brigitte Legault has no family relation to François Legault.

Yet, she has been in the shadows since the beginning of the Coalition Avenir Québec on Nov. 14, 2011, building the coalition of federalists and sovereigntists to offer Quebecers a political force that would go on to form two majority governments.

On Oct. 5, all that hard work came crashing down.

The CAQ went from having an astonishing 90 seats four years ago to being completely wiped off the electoral map. Quebec’s outgoing premier, Christine Fréchette, stepped down as leader the next day and said she took full ownership of her party’s defeat.

“I haven’t had much time since the defeat to go for my walk in the snow,” she said with a chuckle during an interview with National Post.

The CAQ can rest easy — Legault has no intention of going anywhere.

“Personally, I feel somewhat responsible for not leaving, given my very high level of loyalty toward the party and toward what we have built,” she said.

The first task of the reconstruction, she said, was to find an interim leader.

“That position had to be filled quickly — by someone with energy, who represents the CAQ, and who has been around for a long time,” she said.

The party appointed Mathieu Lévesque, a former minister from Gatineau who has been involved in the CAQ since its creation 15 years ago.

The party has also already held nine post-mortems with candidates and their teams across the province to understand what went wrong and what needs to change.

Legault said the Caq’s former ministers, MNAs and former candidates are already hard at work to address those findings, whether that means improving communication with voters, and reviewing, redefining, or renewing the party’s identity and platform.

“I believe our members are particularly interested in being able to roll up their sleeves and get involved in this process,” she said.

The party reconstruction should culminate with a leadership race ending in the fall of 2027, she said, the details of which should be announced in the coming days.

“We certainly didn’t slack off. We managed to put together a one-year schedule.”

Legault describes herself as “someone who bounces back quite quickly” and “who doesn’t spend a lot of time overanalyzing things.”

But there were still many factors that explain why the CAQ won zero seats.

Legault said there was not one mistake, but an accumulation of things that went wrong during the campaign but also well before it had even started.

She pointed to the series of events that brought them to this point — including the François Legault’s decision to resign as leader in January, which led to a leadership race and left his successor, Fréchette, only a few months to get her ducks in a row.

“We had to work at an accelerated pace on many fronts. In that respect, things were perhaps more difficult,” the party’s director general said.

She noted that one of the broader observations from the campaign is that voters had difficulty following the Caq’s message with four other main political parties at play.

It was a common criticism from voters, who felt overwhelmed by the barrage of daily promises coming from a total of five political parties with different messages.

“This was one of the most highly regionalized provincial campaigns,” she said.

Legault brushed off suggestions that it was a mistake for Fréchette to focus too much on the trade war with U.S. President Donald Trump at the start of the campaign.

At the time, Canada had just decided to walk away from the negotiating table.

“We were in the midst of a crisis,” she said. “That was, after all, a very pressing, current issue.”

But there was also a deliberate political calculation in the mix.

“In general, this was part of a strategy to ensure that the economy remained the Caq’s primary offering,” she said.

Legault also would not zoom in on particular elements of the campaign, such as the Caq’s odd accusation near the end of the campaign that an obscure website constituted U.S. foreign interference to help the Parti Québécois get elected.

Legault simply said there were “some missteps here and there regarding specific elements.”

Overall, the CAQ was affected by the wear and tear of power after eight years.

Fréchette was able to bring the CAQ back up in the polls when the trade war was top of mind, but the party lost its steam after the debates.

Legault admitted it was “definitely a drag” when polling aggregators showed the CAQ winning zero seats before the election had happened.

Despite all its troubles, Legault noted nearly 600,000 people still voted for the CAQ.

“So, I believe that, as a national party, we have a responsibility to roll up our sleeves and put forward something that truly reflects what we are capable of doing,” she said.

Their interim leader is already hard at work convincing the different parties to let him hold media availabilities in the provincial legislature.

“We cannot leave the chair empty for a year. We are very aware of that,” Legault said.

The party’s path back to relevance won’t be easy. New numbers from Pallas Datashow that the CAQ is continuing its nosedive in public opinion in the polls.

If there is any glimmer of hope for the CAQ, it’s that those numbers also show that Quebecers aren’t all that crazy about their new PQ government either.

Catherine Lévesque covers federal-Quebec relations for National Post. She joined the parliamentary bureau in Ottawa in 2022, after a decade spent in French media in Montreal, Quebec City and Ottawa.

stories.title: Meet the MP and father of six pushing to make it easier for Canadians to have kids
stories.summary: Garnett Genuis is well-positioned to understand the modern realities of parenting: he recently announced that he and his wife are expecting their seventh child
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — It all started with a cancelled flight.

After 11 years of flying between Edmonton and Ottawa, that’s nothing new to Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan MP Garnett Genuis, but rebooking five seats at once proved extra complicated.

Which explains how Genuis ended up cruising down the Qeii to Calgary last Monday in a Toyota Yaris, with four of his six children filling out the seats.

They finally arrived at their destination around 2:30 a.m. Ottawa time, settling in to the apartment Genuis calls home during sittings of the House of Commons.

By 11 a.m., all five filed into a committee room on Parliament Hill where Genuis and his fellow Conservatives are pushing to improve Canada’s parental leave benefits.

As employment critic he is the lead on a suite of policies aimed at giving parents more flexibility and work-life balance.

Genuis is well-positioned to understand the modern realities of parenting: he recently announced that he and his wife Rebecca will welcome their seventh child in the spring.

“Maybe we’ll get to official party status at some point,” he quips. (For those counting, that would be 12.)

So far it’s been about 13 years of continuous diaper changes.

“We’re at a stage where the kids can help with the diapers sometimes too, so that takes the edge off a little bit,” he says.

He insists there isn’t a direct link between his own family and the policies he’s championing, though.

“We’re not really the applicable case,” he says.

For one thing, MPs earn a salary of $217,700 a year, plus expenses, and (since the pandemic) have built-in flexibility to participate in Parliament virtually from anywhere in Canada.

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis and four of his children, from left, Gianna, 13, Augustine, 4, Phineas, 7, and Lilly, 8, attend a House of Commons committee meeting on Nov. 3, 2026. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia

Genuis usually flies back to Edmonton on Thursday evening or Friday during House sittings, returning to Ottawa on a red-eye Sunday night to maximize the time at home.

Rebecca is a physician with a virtual practice who typically sees patients on weekends. Her practice, as it happens, is dedicated to helping couples conceive.

The family also has hired help at home.

And the kids have always been involved in Genuis’s work: Lilly helped knock on doors on the day of the Alberta referendum in October. They attend community events, or tag along as their dad takes French immersion courses in Quebec during the summers.

On this Tuesday morning, the quintet is getting ready for a two-hour committee meeting — something that can leave even seasoned journalists and staffers restless.

“They will behave very well in committee,” Genuis says confidently, then repeats himself as he looks down the table to where 13-year-old Gianna is sitting with Lilly, 8, Phineas, 7, and four-year-old Gus (short for Augustine, Gianna notes).

This week, eleven-year-old Judah and two-year-old Isidore are home with their mom. The other four are thrilled to be walking the halls of Parliament despite their late night.

Genuis brings the kids to Ottawa once or twice a year, in various combinations, though he’s mindful that the older ones can’t miss out on too much school. They do have a chance to catch up on missed classwork during meetings like this.

As the committee gets underway, all four settle in to a row of seats near the back.

About 20 minutes in, Gus crawls into his big sister’s lap and she rocks him gently. Soon, though, he’s squirmed away and is barely holding back tears. Gianna motions to her dad, who comes back to carry Gus out into a hallway.

They return a few moments later, tears dried, and Genuis explains that he’d been poked by the pin of a poppy. (Really, who can blame him?)

The younger three noticeably perk up when it’s Genuis’s turn to ask questions of a panel of witnesses.

One proposed policy change discussed at committee would allow a family to continue collecting EI benefits if the parent on leave dies. Presently, those payments will stop in a family’s time of grief. “This is crazy to me,” Genuis says to the committee, noting that the parliamentary budget officer estimates the remedy would cost less than $1 million a year.

The Conservatives are advocating for parents on leave to be able to pursue their education, and to earn money from childcare without facing benefit clawbacks. Another proposal would allow both parents to take parental leave at the same time without penalties to their Canada Pension Plan benefits.

They’re also trying to change the rules so parents can pause their leave and return as needed — think of an accountant, for instance, who May wish to work through income tax filing season.

“The goal of the policy we’ve been championing in this area is to try to maximize flexibility and not have the government get in the way of the kinds of creative arrangements that people try to develop,” Genuis said.

Many of the ideas come from other parents, including the many parents of young children in the Conservative caucus.

At a recent press conference, Genuis introduced his colleagues Michael Barrett, Sandra Cobena and Colin Reynolds, noting the four are collectively the parents of 19 kids, while Reynolds is also a grandfather of four. Cobena welcomed her fourth baby this past summer.

Genuis hasn’t yet sorted out what he will do when the latest addition joins the family in April. The House of Commons is set to sit until late June, so he expects to be voting virtually for a little while. And he has a series of small helpers to make things run smoothly.

“Everybody does have to pitch in; that’s a natural part of a larger family, and I really appreciate how helpful they are, especially when I’m away,” he said.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

content_blocks.text: Ottawa — It all started with a cancelled flight.
After 11 years of flying between Edmonton and Ottawa, that’s nothing new to Sherwood Park—Fort Saskatchewan MP Garnett Genuis, but rebooking five seats at once proved extra complicated.
Which explains how Genuis ended up cruising down the Qeii to Calgary last Monday in a Toyota Yaris, with four of his six children filling out the seats.
They finally arrived at their destination around 2:30 a.m. Ottawa time, settling in to the apartment Genuis calls home during sittings of the House of Commons.
By 11 a.m., all five filed into a committee room on Parliament Hill where Genuis and his fellow Conservatives are pushing to improve Canada’s parental leave benefits.
As employment critic he is the lead on a suite of policies aimed at giving parents more flexibility and work-life balance.
Genuis is well-positioned to understand the modern realities of parenting: he recently announced that he and his wife Rebecca will welcome their seventh child in the spring.
“Maybe we’ll get to official party status at some point,” he quips. (For those counting, that would be 12.)
So far it’s been about 13 years of continuous diaper changes.
“We’re at a stage where the kids can help with the diapers sometimes too, so that takes the edge off a little bit,” he says.
He insists there isn’t a direct link between his own family and the policies he’s championing, though.
“We’re not really the applicable case,” he says.
For one thing, MPs earn a salary of $217,700 a year, plus expenses, and (since the pandemic) have built-in flexibility to participate in Parliament virtually from anywhere in Canada.

Conservative MP Garnett Genuis and four of his children, from left, Gianna, 13, Augustine, 4, Phineas, 7, and Lilly, 8, attend a House of Commons committee meeting on Nov. 3, 2026. Hyungcheol Park / Postmedia
Genuis usually flies back to Edmonton on Thursday evening or Friday during House sittings, returning to Ottawa on a red-eye Sunday night to maximize the time at home.
Rebecca is a physician with a virtual practice who typically sees patients on weekends. Her practice, as it happens, is dedicated to helping couples conceive.
The family also has hired help at home.

And the kids have always been involved in Genuis’s work: Lilly helped knock on doors on the day of the Alberta referendum in October. They attend community events, or tag along as their dad takes French immersion courses in Quebec during the summers.
On this Tuesday morning, the quintet is getting ready for a two-hour committee meeting — something that can leave even seasoned journalists and staffers restless.

“They will behave very well in committee,” Genuis says confidently, then repeats himself as he looks down the table to where 13-year-old Gianna is sitting with Lilly, 8, Phineas, 7, and four-year-old Gus (short for Augustine, Gianna notes).
This week, eleven-year-old Judah and two-year-old Isidore are home with their mom. The other four are thrilled to be walking the halls of Parliament despite their late night.

Genuis brings the kids to Ottawa once or twice a year, in various combinations, though he’s mindful that the older ones can’t miss out on too much school. They do have a chance to catch up on missed classwork during meetings like this.

stories.title: Calgary water rules not expected to hamper Grey Cup, pubs promise plenty of beer
stories.summary: Calgary - Calgary residents and businesses are being asked to restrict their water use for the month, but local pubs are telling football fans not to worry.
stories.author: Dayne Patterson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - Calgary residents and businesses are being asked to restrict their water use for the month, but local pubs are telling football fans not to worry.

There will be enough beer to go around for Grey Cup.

“We’re trending so that we shouldn’t be running out of our own product,” said Geoff Allan, general manager and co-owner of Bottlescrew Bill’s Pub.

“If we do, we do know lots of other guys here we can buy similar stuff from.

“So, not all is lost there.”

The city is hosting festival events this week in the lead-up to the Canadian Football League’s championship game Sunday, when the Edmonton Elks take on the Montreal Alouettes.

Calgary is expected to host up to 350,000 fans, with about 35,000 out-of-towners from across Canada, said organizers. Another 6,000 hotel room nights have been booked.

At the same time, the city is in the final repair stage of a problematic water main that has twice had major ruptures in the last two years.

The city has put water restrictions in place until around the end of the month.

People are being asked to take shorter showers, make fewer toilet flushes and run only full loads in the washing machine and dishwasher. Businesses are being asked to limit their use too.

Melissa Pawlak, Bottlescrew Bill’s head brewer, said brewing happens weeks ahead of time, so it won’t have an impact on the quantity or quality of Grey Cup beers.

Its brewing process usually takes about 2,000 litres of water, but the team cut that in half by halting a system that isn’t as water efficient.

Previous breaks of the Bearspaw South Feeder Main threw the city into water restrictions before the Calgary Stampede in 2024, with most rules lifting after the event kicked off. The rules were also in place over New Year’s Eve in 2025.

This go-round, there were months to prepare for the restrictions.

Kampus Brewing, just a short drive from McMahon Stadium, is expecting a busy weekend. General manager Chris Schneider said they’re well stocked.

“We have a lot of regulars here that love CFL and love the Grey Cup,” said Schneider.

Since imposing this round of restrictions on Nov. 4, the city has stayed below its set threshold of 500 million litres of water used per day.

City officials said Thursday that they don’t expect any challenges with staying under that limit over Grey Cup.

John O’Connell, general manager of the downtown Hyatt Regency Calgary, said one of the most common comments from visitors is that they don’t know about the water restrictions.

“But once we inform them, it seems like everyone’s happy to do their part,” said O’Connell.

It’s the fifth time Calgary has been under water restrictions because of the pipe problems, and O’Connell said the hotel is well versed in how to manage.

There are posters around the hotel telling guests about the rules, and guests are only served water at the attached restaurant when requested.

O’Connell said he expects all hotels will likely be filled to the brim, but with the right measures, the city can stay on track.

“We anticipate that they’re going to have a great time and the water restriction is going to have little effect to their fun of visiting and seeing the game.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 13, 2026.

stories.title: Why the U.S. asylum system was in the spotlight this week in Canada's Federal Court
stories.summary: Litigants suing Ottawa argue the Safe Third Country Agreement disproportionately harms women, children, Lgbtq refugees.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
America’s asylum system and treatment of refugees were on trial in a Canadian court this week.

The Federal Court heard the claim by lawyers for litigants suing Ottawa that the Canada-U.S. Safe Third Country Agreement disproportionately harms women fleeing gender-based persecution, children and Lgbtq refugee claimants by denying them access to protection and returning them to the U.S., thus subjecting them to the “deficient” U.S. asylum and detention systems. They argue it’s a breach of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

The risks faced by these groups, they allege, have intensified since January 2025 with the mass detention and deportation effort under “Trump 2.0.”

“The system is stacked against certain groups more than others,” lawyer Kate Webster told the court. She represents the three organizations leading the lawsuit — the Canadian Council for Refugees, Amnesty International and the Canadian Council of Churches.

The court has been asked to declare the designation of the U.S. as a safe third country be “invalid and of no force or effect.” A ruling in the advocate’s favour would effectively reopen Canada’s land border to asylum seekers crossing from the U.S., allowing them to make a claim and enter Canada.

The border pact, effective since 2004, requires refugee claimants to seek protection in the first country they arrive in — either Canada or the United States. Those who cross into the other country are turned back unless they meet one of a few narrow exemptions, such as having an immediate family member there or being an unaccompanied minor.

Although the rules are meant to apply to everyone equally, the lawsuit claims that some groups face discriminatory impacts based on their gender, age and sexual orientation , when compared to other returnees to the U.S. and those who benefit from being able to pursue asylum claims in Canada, which only uses detention as a last resort and recognizes gender-based persecution and the rights of sexual minorities.

The suit alleges that the border agreement violates section 15 of the Canadian Charter of Rights, which guarantees equality rights.

At the core is the question of whether the Canadian Charter can apply to American law and practice, and whether the legal action should continue in what the government calls “a factual void,” given that both the Salvadoran and Syrian families who initiated the lawsuit ultimately made it to Canada and acquired permanent residence.

“There is no direct non-hearsay evidence before the court of a person who was returned under the Stca and who did not have a fair asylum adjudication process,” argued counsel David Knapp, who represents the federal government.

“Their entire argument was about American law and asking you to find that it violates section 15” of the Canadian Charter.

The border agreement was the subject of two failed attempts to strike it down in court, in 2007 and 2020. In a ruling in 2023, the Supreme Court of Canada upheld the pact, saying it did not violate the Charter’s section 7 guarantees of liberty and security of the person . However, it sent the issue of whether it violated equality rights back to the Federal Court, noting the “profound seriousness of the matter.”

Jared Will, lawyer for the Syrian family, said because the top court has sent the equality rights claim back for reconsideration, the case is not moot. Citing case law, he argued that a stand-in applicant is not required.

There wouldn’t be one person whose experience embodies all the issues involved, he said, hence the litigation relies on individuals “knowledgeable” about the U.S. asylum and detention systems.

While the court must examine what happens to returnees to the U.S. and the conditions they face, Will said: “There is absolutely no infringement on U.S. sovereignty by ruling on the constitutional issues in this case.”

Webster said women fleeing gender-based persecution are often denied protection due to restrictive interpretations of the refugee definition in U.S. law. The lawsuit cited a documented case involving a Mexican schoolgirl who was kidnapped and repeatedly raped but was denied asylum because she couldn’t prove her perpetrator raped her “on account of her gender.”

Children are held in “deplorable conditions” in detention, causing “profound and lasting” harms, Webster added.

Lgbtq individuals also face particular risks in immigration detention of sexual abuse, discrimination and harassment, and are often denied medical and mental health treatment, she noted. Things have gotten worse especially for transgender women after the Trump administration issued an executive order that male and female are the only two recognized sexes, she noted.

The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement “closed transgender dedicated pods,” Webster told court. “Transgender women are housed with men or put in solitary confinement.”

Lawyers for the government argued that returnees from Canada are not automatically detained by American officials, noting millions of migrants are in the U.S. without status but only 70,000 of them were held at any given time.

There is no uniform practice imposed on states under the U.N. Refugee Convention, which only provides a framework for member countries to run their asylum systems. The U.S. asylum system and practice, they argued, fall within “the margin of appreciation.”

It allows countries to “find a balance between the needs of refugees on the one hand and the wish of sovereign states to maintain control over those seeking entry to their territory,” Knapp told Judge Mandy Aylen.

Meanwhile, he said there are safeguards available for exemptions to the Safe Third Country Agreement, allowing Canadian border authorities to use discretion to defer immediate removal to the U.S. and let the person enter on a special temporary permit, humanitarian grounds or public policy.

In fact, said Knapp, the Salvadoran and Syrian families in this case benefited from these measures to circumvent their initial inadmissibility.

“The record in this case cannot sustain the conclusion that the applicable curative mechanisms are illusory,” Knapp argued.

Will, the counsel for the Syrian litigant, underscored that the families only received relief from the Canada Border Services Agency because of the court’s intervention through their lawyers.

Asylum seekers arriving at the Canadian land border are not asked about their fears if returned to the U.S. or provided with publicly available information on these mechanisms, how to access it and the bar to meet to succeed, he stressed.

“Claimants are left in a void,” Will told the court. “They have no idea what they need to prove to access the safety valves.”

The hearing continues on Dec. 16.

Lawyers for the government argued that returnees from Canada are not automatically detained by American officials, noting millions of migrants are in the U.S. without status but only 70,000 of them were held at any given time.

There is no uniform practice imposed on states under the U.N. Refugee Convention, which only provides a framework for member countries to run their asylum systems. The U.S. asylum system and practice, they argued, fall within “the margin of appreciation.”

It allows countries to “find a balance between the needs of refugees on the one hand and the wish of sovereign states to maintain control over those seeking entry to their territory,” Knapp told Judge Mandy Aylen.

Meanwhile, he said there are safeguards available for exemptions to the Safe Third Country Agreement, allowing Canadian border authorities to use discretion to defer immediate removal to the U.S. and let the person enter on a special temporary permit, humanitarian grounds or public policy.
In fact, said Knapp, the Salvadoran and Syrian families in this case benefited from these measures to circumvent their initial inadmissibility.
“The record in this case cannot sustain the conclusion that the applicable curative mechanisms are illusory,” Knapp argued.
Will, the counsel for the Syrian litigant, underscored that the families only received relief from the Canada Border Services Agency because of the court’s intervention through their lawyers.

Asylum seekers arriving at the Canadian land border are not asked about their fears if returned to the U.S. or provided with publicly available information on these mechanisms, how to access it and the bar to meet to succeed, he stressed.
“Claimants are left in a void,” Will told the court. “They have no idea what they need to prove to access the safety valves.”
The hearing continues on Dec. 16.

They argue it’s a breach of Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

content_blocks.text: The court has been asked to declare the designation of the U.S. as a safe third country be “invalid and of no force or effect.” A ruling in the advocate’s favour would effectively reopen Canada’s land border to asylum seekers crossing from the U.S., allowing them to make a claim and enter Canada.

General News

All Notices and Updates

Wednesday, November 2026 | 4:00 – 7:00 p.m. Thames Valley District School Board (1250 Dundas St., London)

TVDSB, LDCSB and Tvcc are hosting an information fair for students in Grades 7-8 and High School with disabilities/special education needs, their parents/caregivers, educators and community partners residing within the Elgin, London, Middlesex, Oxford regions, with representation from both school boards and multiple community partners.

The focus of the event is supporting students with special needs through secondary transitions to a variety of post-secondary pathways including school to work, college, university or community.

Youth and families will receive information about supports and services they can access in pursuit of their dreams and goals.

Cost: None

Parking: Free

Registration: This is a drop-in information fair with no online registration required.

Contact: Gordana Rojas, g.rojas@TVDSB.CA Naomi Powers, n.powers@TVDSB.CA

stories.title: Dangerous offender designation sought for man convicted in brutal fatal stabbing
stories.summary: It’s been a long five years for the daughter’s of Kenneth Wallis after he was brutally stabbed to death in December 2021 while at a rooming house on Wharncliffe Road South in London.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
It’s been a long five years for the daughter’s of Kenneth Wallis after he was brutally stabbed to death in December 2021 while at a rooming house on Wharncliffe Road South in London.

“I’m just glad it’s finally over,” said Ashley Johnston.

In her victim impact statement she told the court, “This loss has affected more than my emotional well being, it has affected my ability to feel secure.”

“I miss my father in ways that are difficult to express,” she added.

At the sentencing hearing for the man convicted of manslaughter in the stabbing death, the court heard an unusual joint submission from the Crown and the defence.

With both sides asking Justice Helen Rady to designate 43 year old Robert Charnock as a dangerous offender along with giving him a 10 year sentence followed by a 10 year supervision order.

It’s unusual because normally a dangerous offender designation comes with an indeterminate sentence. Justice Rady will hand down her decision next Wednesday.

Meanwhile, Wallis’ other daughter Sherry Wallis says she is still reeling from his death, “I have a three-year-old son that my father will never be able to spent time with.”

stories.title: Flooding worsens along B.C.’s South Coast as heavy rains continue
stories.summary: Swollen rivers have cut off roads and threatened communities, with residents facing evacuation orders, flood warnings and landslide risks
stories.author: Mike Hager, Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Kris Latham is used to seeing the rescue horses she cares for traversing her riverside ranch in Squamish, B.C. – not coho salmon.

But after heavy rain rocked British Columbia’s South Coast, her ranch staff on Thursday morning noticed fins flapping in a flooded field at her acreage, which offers glamping and a wedding venue in addition to its equine services.

For a week, a succession of powerful storms have battered B.C., swelling rivers, obstructing some roadways and raising the threat of landslides. By Thursday, communities on Vancouver Island and along the Sea-to-Sky corridor were facing evacuation orders, alerts and warnings to shelter in place.

The District of Squamish warned Thursday morning that water being discharged from BC Hydro’s Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake could lead to localized flooding of roads and properties. The district said the decision to release the water would create room in the reservoir for more rain.

Cheakamus Dam, a landmark beside Highway 99 to Whistler, is upriver from Ms. Latham’s ranch. She said at around 8:30 a.m. the nearby river swelled; frigid water overcame the metre-high berm and poured into the low-lying part of the horse sanctuary.

Luckily, she said, an equipment operator was able to jump into the excavator stored on-site and quickly begin rebuilding the dyke. That’s when they noticed the salmon.

“We got some fishing nets, and we got them up and put them back in the river,” she said.

There was no lasting damage to the fish or her property, and Ms. Latham said she doesn’t begrudge BC Hydro for releasing the water from the dam.

Still, her local district told residents of Paradise Valley to shelter in place after the dam discharge swamped nearby roads.

Peter Spitzer is one of the nearby residents staying home after being cut off by the swollen river waters.

He has been at his property near the confluence of the Cheakamus River and Culliton Creek for nearly 40 years, and has seen floodwaters break their banks before.

Mr. Spitzer and his neighbours in the flood zone about 16 kilometres from Squamish know the drill.

“We all stay put and help the neighbours out if somebody needs anything. We usually have food and water for quite a few days before we run out,” he said Thursday.

To the north, past Whistler, the entire Village of Pemberton is under an evacuation alert.

Pemberton issued an evacuation order on Wednesday for a stretch of Airport Road in the community’s southeast, due to “immediate danger to life safety caused by flooding.”

Residents elsewhere in the village, put under evacuation alert one day earlier, were advised to shelter in place as extremely high river flows and significant rain threatened to cut off road access and trigger landslides.

The Lil’wat Nation upgraded an evacuation alert to an order early Thursday morning, citing “exceptionally high flows” on the Green River near Pemberton.

Floodwater had rushed over a section of Highway 99, and sections of Lillooet Lake Road were covered with up to a foot of water, the Lil’wat Nation chief and council said in an update.

The province’s River Forecast Centre issued a flood watch for the entire Central Coast, along with flood warnings for Kingcome, Howe Sound and Pemberton Valley regions.

Environment Canada had lowered most rainfall warnings by Thursday, although yellow warnings were still active for west and inland Vancouver Island, where heavy rains were forecast to last into Friday afternoon.

The weather agency reported rainfall levels of 307 millimetres in Port Mellon from Tuesday morning to Thursday at noon, the highest in the province, followed by Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island, with 261 mm.

Last Friday, the Village of Zeballos, ON the northwest coast of Vancouver Island, ordered the evacuation of 10 properties and evacuation alerts for 13 others, because of landslide risks that posed a threat to life and safety. Those directives remained in place on Thursday.

The storm has been linked to two deaths in Metro Vancouver. On Nov. 6, the driver of a sedan struck a 78-year-old woman who was attempting to cross the street during heavy rain in Vancouver’s Dunbar neighbourhood, according to police. The day after, a driver was killed when a falling tree struck two vehicles in Surrey.

Meanwhile, the search for a canoeist who has been missing off northern Vancouver Island since Nov. 6 was called off three days later because of challenging weather conditions, RCMP said.

With a report from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Italian couple who hid Jewish family during Second World War awarded rare title in Canadian ceremony
stories.summary: Donatello and Zelmira De Luigi entered the rarefied echelons of Righteous Among the Nations in a Toronto-area ceremony
stories.author: Ron Csillag, Special to National Post
stories.content:
Rome, September 1943: The Nazis had just arrived in the Italian capital, and Donatello and Zelmira De Luigi made their choice. They would shield their Jewish physician, Dr. Alfred Strom, and his family.

“What I did had to be done,” Donatello said later.

This week, the De Luigis entered the rarefied echelons of Righteous Among the Nations, a title bestowed by Yad Vashem in Israel, the world’s foremost Holocaust memorial, museum and research centre, ON only 28,707 non-Jews from 51 countries who risked their lives to rescue Jews from the Nazis.

The couple were honoured posthumously Tuesday night at a moving ceremony in Vaughan, Ont., that was attended by members of the De Luigi family, elected officials, the ambassadors to Canada of Israel and Italy, and 300 leaders of Toronto’s Jewish and Italian communities. The event was hosted by the Canadian Society for Yad Vashem.

The De Luigis’ nephew, 95-year-old Emilio De Luigi, a resident of St. Catharines, Ont., was presented with a specially struck medal and certificate proclaiming Donatello and Zelmira among the 810 Italian Righteous recognized by Yad Vashem.

Dani Dayan, chairman of Yad Vashem, awarded De Luigi the citation, the highest civilian honour bestowed by the State of Israel. Dayan recalled Toronto’s riot at Christie Pits park in 1933, when a brawl broke out between Jews and supporters of the local Swastika Club. Italians, he noted, came to the support of the Jewish participants that night.

“Tonight our communities gather in solidarity once again in a shared commitment to preserve the truth of the Holocaust,” he said.

Italy’s ambassador to Canada, Alessandro Cattaneo, noted recent full-page advertisements in Canadian newspapers, signed by the Italian-Canadian community, launching a national campaign against antisemitism. It demonstrates “that it is possible to stand up to hatred, even in difficult times.”

Iddo Moed, Israel’s ambassador to Canada, recalled how he owes his own existence to a Belgian Catholic family that sheltered his father and other relatives in 1943, and were declared Righteous in 1980. The De Luigis and others like them, he said, shows that “courage is contagious.”

Jewish physician Dr. Alfred Strom, his wife Perla, also a doctor, and their two young children were sheltered by Donatello and Zelmira De Luigi during the Second World War. Courtesy the De Luigi family

For nearly nine months, from the Nazi occupation of Rome in September 1943 to its liberation in June 1944, Donatello and Zelmira De Luigi hid Dr. Strom, his wife Perla, also a doctor, and their two young children in the De Luigis’ rented villa in Monteverde, then on the outskirts of Rome.

Strom asked Donatello to hide only his children, Roberto, 4, and Liliana, who was just nine months old, according to a book Emilio De Luigi wrote about his aunt and uncle’s heroism, aptly titled It Had to Be Done. Donatello “found this unacceptable and extended the invitation to the entire family.”

Added to the hidden, wrote Emilio, were Strom’s brother, Davide, also a doctor, his wife, and their two daughters. The clan came to live with the De Luigis and their two children, Luciano and Rossana.

Yad Vashem’s citation is for “help rendered to Jewish persons during the period of the Holocaust at the risk of their lives.” Plans call for the names of all Righteous to be inscribed on the Wall of Honor in the Garden of the Righteous at Yad Vashem.

Alfred Strom and Perla Strom-Rosenzweig were Polish-born Jews who had come to Italy in 1930 to study medicine at the University of Padova, and settled in Rome after graduating. But in 1938, the government of fascist dictator Benito Mussolini enacted anti-Jewish “Racial Laws” that stripped the couple of their citizenship and right to practise medicine. They were forced into underground medical work and were interned for two years at a camp for foreign-born Jews in Perugia, north of Rome.

An Axis partner, Italy surrendered to the Allies on Sept. 3, 1943, but German forces entered and seized control of Rome on Sept. 10. Roberto Strom, frightened and sweating, fled to his patient’s office to evade a Nazi patrol and asked to stay awhile. Donatello De Luigi, a well-off book publisher, took Strom’s family to the cellar of his villa that very day.

“You are safe here,” he assured the Stroms on arrival, according to his nephew’s book, “and we have left no traces. Apart from us here, no one knows that you are in my house.”

Donatello and Zelmira De Luigi were honoured as Righteous Among the Nations for shielding their Jewish physician, Dr. Alfred Strom, his wife Perla, and their two children during the Second World War in a ceremony in Vaughan, Ont., ON Nov. 10, 2026. The De Luigis’ nephew, 95-year-old Emilio De Luigi, centre, received the medal and certificate on their behalf from Israel’s Ambassador to Canada Iddo Moed, left, and Dani Dayan, chairman of Yad Vashem. Ron Csillag

Perla Strom was distraught. “We are human beings and we have done nothing wrong. We are doctors, we treat people. Our children are children like yours. And here we are, hunted like animals!”

On Oct. 10, a small Waffen SS unit, with army reinforcements, seized about 1,200 Jews in Rome, about one-tenth of the city’s pre-war Jewish population, and confined them to a military college. Two days later, roughly 1,000 of them, including 200 children under the age of 10, were shipped to Auschwitz to be murdered. “The children were crying,” historian Martin Gilbert quoted an eyewitness in his history of the Holocaust. “Everywhere you could hear pleas for help and cries of distress.” Only 15 of the deportees survived the war.

The De Luigis provided food and forged Aryan identity papers for Alfred. Little Roberto’s identity was masked so he could attend a local kindergarten run by Catholic nuns, while the toddler Liliana was called “Marisa” (she kept the new name for life). Perla was rechristened “Maria.”

On occasion, Perla boldly went out with Zelmira to buy food and supplies.

Emilio wrote of one close call in which a group of German soldiers came to the villa and announced they would confiscate it if they found it suitable for a high-ranking officer. But they decided the rooms were too small and left. The Stroms emerged from hiding inside a second-storey wardrobe, shaking.

Via video from Rome, Roberto Strom, now 87, paid tribute at the ceremony to the De Luigis, recalling, in Italian, the silence the clan had to maintain in the cellar of the villa. They could not even turn on a light.

Emilio, then 12, visited the villa regularly, chiefly for food.

“I went practically every week a couple of times to visit, mainly because it was the worst period of the war and difficult to find food,” he told the Post in an interview. “If you didn’t have enough money, the black market was flourishing (and) my uncle was very well off. So I had an extra reason to go there, ON every possible occasion. Sometimes I slept there with my cousins.”

He grew especially close to Perla Strom. “She was a very human, very affectionate person. I called her ‘Aunt Maria.’”

Emilio was sworn to secrecy, “never to tell anyone, for any reason, that they had Jews in the house,” he wrote. To the Canadian Jewish News’ “North Star” podcast, he put an exclamation point to the directive: “Never, never, never!”

After the war, the Stroms returned to their medical practices. Donatello died in 1969 at the age of 71, Zelmira in 1985.

Emilio, who lived in Ethiopia and Eritrea, one-time Italian possessions, for 35 years except for four years of university in Rome, came to Canada in 1983 and started advocating for Righteous status for his aunt and uncle in 2010. He spoke to Roberto Strom for the first time in 2019.

Unlike many other Righteous Among the Nations, the De Luigis were not motivated to act by any religious sentiment. The family, though Catholic, was left-wing and “traditionally secular,” Emilio said.

“Believe me, what I did was not an impulsive and distracted act,” Donatello asserts in Emilio’s book.

Donatello “was a good person.” If people needed help, he helped, Emilio recalled, his voice cracking. “He knew what would have happened (to the Stroms) if he had abandoned them.”

stories.title: Witnesses at murder trial testify about fight prior to man being set on fire
stories.summary: The former girlfriend of Jonathan Graham testified about being at the same after hours hangout on Noel Avenue in east London before he was set on fire in the early morning of July 12, 2022.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
The former girlfriend of Jonathan Graham testified about being at the same after hours hangout on Noel Avenue in east London before he was set on fire in the early morning of July 12, 2022.

Madison Abrams said she was there with friends when Graham showed up to what they called “the shack” with the accused Bradley Joudrey.

She testified, “They came in, grabbed their beers and were socializing.”

Then she said a short while later two or three inappropriate comments were made to her by Joudrey and she said one was, “Bradley asking me who I was going home with, him or Jonathan and my response was I want to go home by myself.”

“I was not happy about the comment.... and I told Jonathan get your boy I’m done with this.”

Then she said there was a commotion, “We noticed a fight broke out and we jumped out...I think it was three punches...Jon throwing at Bradley and we broke it up.”

She went on, “He has always called Bradley one of his brothers...Jon wasn’t too fazed by it friends fight...they exchanged words and he (Bradley) left.”

The Crown ‘s theory is that minutes later both the victim and the accused met at a convenience store parking lot at Admiral Drive and Trafalgar Street.

They say Graham was doused with gasoline and set on fire. He would be rushed to hospital with thermal injuries, and would later be pronounced dead.

The Crown says Joudrey would race away from the scene and eventually crash his Dodge Journey.

He would eventually be arrested and has pled not guilty to first degree murder.

Earlier in the day the court heard from the man who operated the after hours hangout. Gauntlet Morrison testified that he witnessed the fight break out between the victim and the accused.

Morrison said he was surprised by the altercation, “Jonathan punched the other guy...the third punch he (Joudrey) fell down.”

He said following the fight he asked Joudrey to leave.

The court was also shown home security video with the victim and the accused hanging out in the backyard.

The trial resumes on Friday.

stories.title: ‘We are isolated’: Residents say large crater left unrepaired after landslide created concern over emergency services
stories.summary: Construction is finally underway at the site of a landslide that washed away a critical road and cut out a massive hole in front of the fire station in L’Ascension, Que. It took 86 days to get the work started. Mayor Jacque
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
L’ascension, QUE. - Construction is finally underway at the site of a landslide that washed away a critical road and cut out a massive hole in front of the fire station in L’Ascension, Que. It took 86 days to get the work started.

Mayor Jacques Allard says his town had to dig through a pile of red tape to obtain permits and funding to begin rebuilding. And until the road is passable again, roughly 300 people, nearly a third of the town’s residents, are cut off from the centre of the town in Quebec’s Laurentians region.

“We have one gas station, a grocery store, a church, and a post office in the village,” says Allard. “Thirty per cent of my residents were on the other side of the hole. Morale was not good. It changed our community.” Now, the town wants to help change the system and speed up emergency repairs in case of natural disasters for other municipalities.

A storm that struck on Aug. 3 caused the damage, forcing the town to declare a state of emergency. Nearly 105 millimetres of rain fell in just a few hours, oversaturating the soil, sending rushing water down rivers and causing flash floods.

A beaver dam also collapsed adding to the water pressure that eventually ripped up asphalt, destroyed a culvert, and prompted a landslide in front of the town’s municipal buildings. Where there had been an important road, a crater nearly 14 metres deep and 21 metres wide, that could hold twice as much water as two Olympic-sized swimming pools, opened up.

It stayed empty for months as the town worked to obtain permits from Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the Quebec government to begin repairs. While the crater remains open, residents have been forced to take a long detour they say add hours to their commute.

“Instead of taking me seven minutes to get to work, it takes me an hour,” says resident Melanie Bigras. Family members that were neighbours are now divided by distance and concerns are growing about emergency services. Lise Lépine and Real Carrière live less than a kilometre away from the local fire station and it would normally take just a few minutes for first responders to reach them.

Now they have to rely on help from the town of Riviere-Rouge 25 kilometres away in case of an emergency. “If I have a stroke, are they going to be here in time?” Lépine asked. “It has been worrisome.” They also now have to drive 40 minutes to reach their mailbox, and 40 minutes to return home.

Patching the hole To get the re-building work started, L’Ascension needed the go-ahead from federal and provincial departments. According to a letter reviewed by CTV News, published Oct. 15, from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, it took 53 days to greenlight the emergency repairs after the town sought authorization.

The municipality’s proposal was examined, in part, to ensure the protection of fish and its habitat. In a statement to CTV News, the DFO said that as soon as it received the request from the town, departmental officials began its review.

“The assessment determined that measures were required to address impacts to fish and fish habitat,” it read. “DFO already transmitted a letter of advice outlining the best practices to implement for the proposed work, noting that if these best practices are implemented, no permit or Fisheries Act Authorization is required.” Following the review, Quebec’s Department of Domestic Security had to sign-off, and the province had to approve funding.

The project will cost nearly $2 million, 85 per cent of which will be covered by Quebec. By early October, many residents of L’Ascension had grown exasperated with the speed of the road repairs. “It felt like something was broken,” says Allard.

“When someone has to travel 50 kilometres to get here, when a parent is on one side, a daughter on the other and they are used to get together a lot, it’s difficult.” ‘We are isolated’ There was also another pressing concern.

Erosion continued to eat away at the edges of the crater. The precipice was inching closer to an important aqueduct, prompting fears it could eventually collapse. Residents urged the town to pressure the province into fixing the problem.

In response the mayor drove to Quebec City to meet officials. The town also sent a legal letter to prove the work was urgently needed, and it organized a demonstration. On Oct. 24, hundreds of people stood on either side of the gulf and held up protest signs.

One read “Get us out of here,” while another read “We are isolated.” Four days after that protest, the municipality finally had all its permits and work began almost immediately. “It is a big relief,” says L’Ascension Director General Marc St-Pierre.

“It seemed like an uphill battle for so long.” The mayor says environmental reviews should have been done, but St-Pierre says the town had to push to speed up final approvals. With winter looming, a delay of another few weeks could have meant having to put off the project until spring.

“Regulation is absolutely important, but in certain cases it adds delays, and unfortunately there are consequences that are very real for a small community like ours,” says St-Pierre. Lightening the regulatory burden Ottawa announced new legislation for Fisheries and Oceans that streamlined the application process for some construction projects that took effect on Oct.

15, Quebec’s new government also promised to cut down on bureaucracy. L’Ascension says it wants to explore other ways to clear hurdles faster in case of any major natural disasters. Earlier this week, L’Ascension city council unanimously approved a resolution to find ways to help lighten the regulatory burden.

“We are going to offer our collaboration based on our experience so that we can find ways to speed up the process and ensure it goes as fast as possible,” says St-Pierre. He added that this could be particularly applicable in cases where the work largely involves repairing previously existing infrastructure.

In L’Ascension’s case, there have been upgrades, including to the size of the culvert to ensure it could withstand increasingly ferocious weather events. The mayor says since repair work has begun, he has seen a lot of smiles on his residents’ faces.

He drives to the site almost every day to see how the re-building is progressing and often stops to talk to those living nearby. Pierre Groulx was sitting on his porch when the mayor pulled up in his vehicle and asked how he felt about the crater now being filled.

“I am really looking forward to the reopening,” Groulx said. “My grandson lives on the other side. Now, that’s an 80 kilometre round trip so I don’t see him very much.” The mayor says plans are underway for a party in the local church for the holidays, and he hopes that will double as a party to celebrate the re-unification of the town divided by a storm.

“Regulation is absolutely important, but in certain cases it adds delays, and unfortunately there are consequences that are very real for a small community like ours,” says St-Pierre. Lightening the regulatory burden Ottawa announced new legislation for Fisheries and Oceans that streamlined the application process for some construction projects that took effect on Oct.

15, Quebec’s new government also promised to cut down on bureaucracy. L’Ascension says it wants to explore other ways to clear hurdles faster in case of any major natural disasters. “We are going to offer our collaboration based on our experience so that we can find ways to speed up the process and ensure it goes as fast as possible,” says St-Pierre. He added that this could be particularly applicable in cases where the work largely involves repairing previously existing infrastructure.

Now, that’s an 80 kilometre round trip so I don’t see him very much.” The mayor says plans are underway for a party in the local church for the holidays, and he hopes that will double as a party to celebrate the re-unification of the town divided by a storm.

content_blocks.text: L’ascension, QUE. - Construction is finally underway at the site of a landslide that washed away a critical road and cut out a massive hole in front of the fire station in L’Ascension, Que. It took 86 days to get the work started.

stories.title: Crestwood residents fear 8-plex ‘sandwiches’ being fast-tracked before provincial deadline
stories.summary: Crestwood residents fear builders and the City of Edmonton are racing the clock, trying to approve infill developments before a January deadline to roll back housing bylaws.
stories.author: Jasmine King, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
People living in Edmonton’s Crestwood neighbourhood fear a huge infill development May be coming to their community.

It comes after numerous permits were submitted to the City of Edmonton to build new eightplexes in the established, desirable west-end neighbourhood near the North Saskatchewan River Valley.

It’s become a conversation some Crestwood residents say they’re having all too often: the prospect of another infill development near their single-family homes.

“This is something that is destroying neighbourhoods. It’s pitting neighbours against each other, creating a horrible cause-and-effect,” said Crestwood resident Terry Paranych, who is real estate agent and developer.

Paranych has experience with redeveloping properties in established neighbourhoods — he’s developing single-family residential infill for 20 years and says respecting the existing look and feel of an area is important to him.

“I am for infill — but responsible infill.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "I am for infill — but responsible infill."

Earlier this year, he bought a lot slated to become an eightplex in the McQueen neighbourhood and instead is putting up a new, single-family home.

“This style of infill does not fit in the middle of residential neighbourhood,” he said of large eightplexes.

“These kinds of developments — sure, ON a corner lot on a busy road, an arterial road, leading into a community — to put four or six units, that makes sense. But to put them in the middle of the block… this is just an ideological play by a very undisciplined and poor city council.”

2023 zoning bylaw changes paved the way for housing redevelopment across much of Edmonton, in an effort to increase density, affordability, and manage population growth.

Proponents of infill argue cities need to adapt to growing populations, and multiplexes offer a way to make existing neighbourhoods denser without adding to sprawl by building out into agricultural land.

Residents of established communities who are opposed have expressed concerns about property values, lack of parking, predatory developers, quality of builds, housing affordability and the neighbourhood’s look and feel changing.

When it comes to real estate, Crestwood is a highly sought-after area where it isn’t uncommon for mid-century, single-family homes to sell for more than $1 million. It’s the seventh-most expensive neighbourhood in Edmonton , according to Honestdoor, with homes and condos selling 127 per cent above the Edmonton average.

A few areas in the historic Crestwood community have undergone some major changes in recent years, with older homes being knocked down and new ones — sometimes twice the size — going up.

When the province stepped in to the city’s infill debate last month , residents were relieved.

“We thought, wonderful, now we’re going to have the opportunity to work with the city, and the city working with the province. It’s not something that we wanted to have happen; we tried on numerous occasions, sitting down with the mayor and our councillors,” said community member Nancy Sorensen.

On Oct. 8, the provincial government ordered the City of Edmonton to revert to the previous parameters for housing types, density and height, and to restore minimum on-site parking requirements in place before 2020.

Edmonton city council was given three months, until Jan. 22, 2027, to comply.

The city said given the province’s directive and its service level timelines, it was expected (dependent on volume) that any complete applications received by Nov. 8 for development within the RS zone impacted by the changes would be able to be reviewed — put simply, make it before the cutoff to rollback the zoning rules.

But now, community members fear both builders and the city are racing against that clock — trying to approve multi-unit developments under the current rules before January, when the zoning bylaw goes back to what it used to be.

“The province had stepped in and mandated to go back to (before) the 2023 bylaws, and now we end up in this situation where we feel that these permits are being expedited,” said Crestwood resident Evan Wood.

“It feels like it’s being done in bad faith.” Share this on X Click to share quote on X: "It feels like it's being done in bad faith."

Crestwood residents say multiple permits were submitted to the city before the Nov. 8 deadline.

One could see two homes on 143 Street near 97 Avenue becoming ‘eightplex sandwiches’ — single-family homes dwarfed by much larger multi-unit builds on either side of it.

Residents point to an existing sandwich example a few streets over that became a point of contention during the infill debate.

“Eight units anywhere on this block, we feel is unacceptable and just not practical for this area,” Wood said.

Area city councillor Reed Clarke says he’s been in touch with community members over this development.

“I totally get their concerns and those mid-block large unit developments, I’ve always had an issue with. I think I’ve been pretty clear on that since the beginning,” said Clarke.

The ward Nakota Isga councillor says no permits have been approved on the street in question so far and said city administration assured him no permits are being fast-tracked.

“That timeline is not being sped up, was the understanding I got,” Clarke said.

“It’s still a pretty detailed process. I think even if they wanted to speed up, they need more resources and time — and those two things they don’t really have.”

While nothing is confirmed yet, residents say they will take action to prevent more ‘eightplex sandwiches’ if necessary.

“We’re hopeful that we can go down the appeal route, and get some sort of favourable result for us,” Wood said.

stories.title: ‘It’s a crappy full-time job’: Ontario woman documents colon cancer journey on social media
stories.summary: A Dashwood, Ont., woman is sharing her battle with stage 3 colon cancer after receiving a normal result from an at-home screening test about a year before her diagnosis.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A Dashwood, Ont., woman is sharing her battle with stage 3 colon cancer after receiving a normal result from an at-home screening test about a year before her diagnosis.

Darlene O’Rourke, 53, says she decided to complete an at-home colorectal cancer screening test after turning 50, but was also experiencing symptoms that she thought were related to perimenopause.

“I was very tired, I was bloated, foggy headed,” O’Rourke said.

The Faecal Immunochemical Test, commonly known as FIT, came back normal.

“I got it done. I literally got the copy from my doctor’s office yesterday because I wanted to see the actual date that the test results came in. It says normal in February of 2024,” she said.

But about a year later, further testing, including a colonoscopy, revealed she had advanced colon cancer.

“December 23rd, two days before Christmas, he called me to tell me I had stage three advanced colon cancer. And yeah, that was my diagnosis,” O’Rourke said.

Her cancer progressed to the point that she required emergency surgery, including an ileostomy, a procedure that creates an opening in the abdomen to allow waste to pass into an external pouch.

More recently, she underwent another major operation to remove her uterus, fallopian tubes and ovaries.

Ontario Health’s ColonCancerCheck program uses FIT to screen people at average risk for colorectal cancer every two years.

The at-home test looks for small amounts of blood in a stool sample. It is intended for people who do not have symptoms and is not designed to diagnose cancer.

In a statement to CTV News, Ontario Health said a normal FIT result means blood was not detected above the test’s threshold in that particular sample at that time.

It stressed that a normal result does not guarantee a person is cancer-free. Ontario Health declined CTV News’ request for an interview.

O’Rourke is now sharing the highs and lows of her cancer journey on social media, including footage of herself ringing the bell after completing cancer treatment.

She hopes being open about her experience will encourage others to be proactive about their health.

“The more we talk, the more proactive I think people will be on it and to get themselves checked,” she said.

“And cancer is a crappy job. It’s a crappy full-time job that you don’t get paid for. So I wanted to use my platform to share all about it.”

O’Rourke has also raised $11,000 for the Canadian Cancer Society and launched a separate fundraiser to help patients cover parking costs while attending hospital appointments for cancer treatment.

She hopes sharing her story will remind others to listen to their bodies, ask questions and advocate for their health.

stories.title: PAL Airlines pulls plane out of service after it lost a wheel in two separate flights
stories.summary: ST. John's - PAL Airlines says it is pulling a plane out of service after it lost a wheel while departing from Goose Bay in Labrador on Thursday, the second such incident for the same plane in less than two weeks.
stories.author: Sarah Smellie The Canadian Press
stories.content:
ST. John’s - PAL Airlines says it is pulling a plane out of service after it lost a wheel while departing from Goose Bay in Labrador on Thursday, the second such incident for the same plane in less than two weeks.

The flight Thursday was en route to Deer Lake in Western Newfoundland, but it was diverted to St. John’s and the airline says it landed safely without additional incident.

stories.title: Thousands in Canada affected by global Microsoft outage
stories.summary: Ottawa - Thousands of Canadians have been affected by a worldwide outage that has disrupted Microsoft platforms including Outlook and Teams.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The online tracker Downdetector suggests that there have been more than 20,000 reports in Canada of problems using Microsoft platforms.

Some federal departments reported having problems accessing emails and meetings, though it’s unclear whether any public services have been affected.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

A health-care network that runs several hospitals in Toronto has declared a code grey, indicating an infrastructure failure.

Unity Health Toronto says its teams are experiencing difficulties sending and receiving emails, but that patient and resident care is not affected by the outage.

A Microsoft spokesperson says the company is aware and investigating reports of users experiencing issues with Microsoft 365 services, primarily issues with Exchange Online.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Old East Village BIA takes stand over core responsibilities in business district
stories.summary: The Old East Village Business Improvement Area (OEV BIA) is putting London City Hall on notice — it’s re-focussing on its core responsibilities and will no longer fund programs that address the impacts of the district’s homelessness and drug crisis.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
The Old East Village Business Improvement Area (OEV BIA) is putting London City Hall on notice — it’s re-focussing on its core responsibilities and will no longer fund programs that address the impacts of the district’s homelessness and drug crisis.

“We’re going back to our mandate. We’re going back to the grass roots of what a BIA is all about,” said Executive Director Kevin Morrison.

Morrison says that means focusing on marketing, business promotion, and beautification, while leaving responsibility for addressing social challenges to city hall, the provincial government, and police.

“We’ve been taking care of the private property clean-up for our business owners. We’ve been taking care of window replacements, and we do get a lot of windows smashed. Plus the vandalism (and) graffiti removal. We also had security measures in place,” he explained. “But that funding’s gone.”

Morrison emphasizes he isn’t complaining, adding that he’s worked well with city management.

However, he wants the incoming council to understand that the BIA is staying in its lane.

“We’ll take responsibility for the mandate of a BIA. You take the responsibility for what you’re saying is safe streets,” Morrison asserted. “It was talked about in the recent election, so now it’s time to take a look at it. We’ve got a new council, so step up to the plate!”

“It’s okay to just stay in your own lane, but like (drivers), you also share that freeway. So maybe if everybody gets to the table together, and were proactive, perhaps we can get things done,” he added.

The Bia’s renewed focus includes a revitalization campaign dubbed “Why Wait?”

Morrison says last year council ignored his 44-page plan to expand the Downtown Master Plan to include Old East Village, but he says the business district can’t wait any longer.

“They’re looking at investing $48 million to revitalize downtown (called) Reimagine Downtown. So I say, why wait? That money isn’t even going to be available until probably the end of 2028. We don’t have that long (in OEV), so we’re going to invest $48,000-- and we start on Monday.”

The Bia’s “Why Wait?” campaign incorporates feedback from its members, with the goal of bringing more Londoners back to the area.

“We did a survey. People love the planters. It adds a little bit of vibrancy. You’re going to see street banners. You’re going to see many events at our local businesses, and I’m talking to local artists (about) doing mini-events,” said Morrison.

Those mini-events could see participants create two pieces of art, one to take home and a second to be used for fundraising in the district.

The BIA has also launched “Friends of OEV”, an affiliate membership program allowing those outside its official boundary to participate in the neighbourhood’s revitalization.

“There’s a lot of exciting initiatives! I say stay tuned, and why wait?” said Morrison.

stories.title: Politics Insider: Stellantis in default of funding agreement, Joly notifies automaker
stories.summary: And, Carney says he expects more European partnerships with Canada’s auto sector to come out of Ottawa’s budding relationship with the EU
stories.author: Ian Bailey
stories.content:
Hello, welcome to Politics Insider. Let’s look at what happened today.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly has officially notified automaker Stellantis NV that she considers the company in default of the federal funding agreement that gave it millions of dollars to retool the Brampton, Ont., plant it has sold to a defence contractor.

Eric Atkins reports that Joly gave the carmaker 30 days to meet the terms of the 2022 agreement , including naming a car to be built at the plant, before she will require the automaker to repay the taxpayer aid. Joly put the notification in a letter dated today to the chief executive officer of the carmaker’s Canadian division, Trevor Longley.

Stellantis idled the plant in 2023, laying off about 3,000 workers , with the intent of retooling for the Jeep Compass. But that work was halted after the U.S placed a 25-per-cent tariff on Canadian-made cars in early 2025. Stellantis, later in 2025, said the Jeep would not be built in Brampton, but at an idled plant in Belvidere, Ill.

In September, the carmaker said it had a preliminary agreement to sell the Brampton factory to Roshel, Inc., a maker of armoured vehicles. The companies said on Monday they finalized the sale for an undisclosed amount.

Details of Stellantis’s funding agreement are not public, but a heavily redacted copy of the contract obtained by The Globe and Mail shows the government gave as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont. It is not clear how much was paid.

Also today, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he expects more European partnerships with Canada’s auto sector to come out of Ottawa’s budding relationship with the European Union, but couldn’t say whether Chinese automakers are any closer to building cars here.

Steven Chase reports that, speaking to reporters at a summit of European leaders in Dublin today, the Prime Minister said Chinese investment in Canada’s auto sector will be one of the topics under discussion with China’s President Xi Jinping when the two meet next week in Shenzhen.

. It is available exclusively to our digital subscribers. You can sign up for more than 20 other newsletters on

Ontario seeks to strengthen oversight of career colleges : Students taking online-only classes at private postsecondary institutions in Ontario would no longer qualify for government loans under a package of legislative changes the Progressive Conservatives will table next week to strengthen oversight of the beleaguered career college sector.

Political Opinion: In a Data Dive, Nik Nanos says there’s hope yet for the U.S.-Canada relationship : The midterms delivered two lessons. One, the MAGA movement is bruised but far from dead. And two, to quote Democratic operative James Carville: “It’s the economy, stupid.”

On our radar

Parliamentary break: Both the House of Commons and the Senate are on a break this week.

Prime Minister’s Day: In Dublin, Mark Carney attended the European Political Community Summit and held a news conference. Carney also met with Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis. He also attended a dinner hosted by Micheál Martin, the Taoiseach of Ireland, before departing for the Philippines capital of Manila to attend the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit.

Party Leaders: In the Quebec city of Saint-Hyacinthe, Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-François Blanchet was attending a caucus meeting. Conservative Party Leader Pierre Poilievre held a news conference in Calgary. No schedules were released for other party leaders.

Ministers on the Road:

With the Commons on a break, ministers continue to travel the nation selling the federal budget.

In Halifax, Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne attended a breakfast event hosted by the Halifax Chamber of Commerce. Elsewhere in Atlantic Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab touted budget measures on worker retention in the New Brunswick city of Dieppe.

Energy Minister Tim Hodgson was in Medicine Hat, Alta., and Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski was in Edmonton. In Yellowknife, Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty talked about budget spending on culture and affordability.

“There is an assumption that if you engage with China, for example, with the Gulf countries, that you somehow are walking away from your values. That is not our point of view. Our point of view from the government of Canada’s standpoint is that the tough conversations about values occur at the table, not by walking away from the table.” - Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand , during an event at Oxford University today, where she took questions on Canadian foreign policy.

Former prime minister Justin Trudeau recently accepted a position in the Blavatnik School of Government at Oxford University’s “World Leaders Circle,” a fellowship designed for global leaders who are transitioning to “the next stage of their public leadership journey.” Which recent British prime minister joined the school’s World Leaders Circle last year?

Scroll to the bottom of this newsletter for the answer.

Perspectives

Budget 2026: What happened to restraint?

Fiscal restraint and caution were not hallmarks of Budget 2026. Cloaked by a sovereignty theme, it was notable for its wide swath of new initiatives, its big spending and its massive increase in debt. What it did provide, however, was implicit ‘forward guidance’ on what to expect from the Carney government in terms of fiscal management in the future. — Kevin Lynch, former clerk of the Privy Council and deputy minister of finance.

Quebec’s plan to ban schoolkids from wearing religious symbols is a silly but harmful distraction

The pretense for Quebec’s law banning the wearing of religious symbols by some public sector employees was, and still is, about authority, power and persuasion. — Robyn Urback, Columnist

France needs a political saviour. Could Christine Lagarde be it?

Ms. Lagarde’s Oct. 29 announcement that she will leave the ECB in February – nine months before the end of her mandate – has sent tongues wagging that she could emerge as the political saviour the French establishment has been hoping for. — Konrad Yakabuski, Columnist

The answer to today’s question: Rishi Sunak, British prime minister from 2022 to 2024, was in the Oxford program in 2025 .
