stories.title: How a Quebec town cut in half by a landslide fought red tape to reconnect neighbours and repair roads
stories.summary: Construction is finally underway at the site of a landslide that washed away a critical road and cut out a massive hole in front of the fire station in L’Ascension, Que. It took 86 days to get the work started. Mayor Jacque
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
L’ascension, QUE. - Construction is finally underway at the site of a landslide that washed away a critical road and cut out a massive hole in front of the fire station in L’Ascension, Que. It took 86 days to get the work started.

Mayor Jacques Allard says his town had to dig through a pile of red tape to obtain permits and funding to begin rebuilding. And until the road is passable again, roughly 300 people, nearly a third of the town’s residents, are cut off from the centre of the town in Quebec’s Laurentians region.

“We have one gas station, a grocery store, a church, and a post office in the village,” says Allard. “Thirty per cent of my residents were on the other side of the hole. Morale was not good. It changed our community.” Now, the town wants to help change the system and speed up emergency repairs in case of natural disasters for other municipalities.

A storm that struck on Aug. 3 caused the damage, forcing the town to declare a state of emergency. Nearly 105 millimetres of rain fell in just a few hours, oversaturating the soil, sending rushing water down rivers and causing flash floods.

A beaver dam also collapsed adding to the water pressure that eventually ripped up asphalt, destroyed a culvert, and prompted a landslide in front of the town’s municipal buildings. Where there had been an important road, a crater nearly 14 metres deep and 21 metres wide, that could hold twice as much water as two Olympic-sized swimming pools, opened up.

It stayed empty for months as the town worked to obtain permits from Fisheries and Oceans Canada and the Quebec government to begin repairs. While the crater remains open, residents have been forced to take a long detour they say add hours to their commute.

“Instead of taking me seven minutes to get to work, it takes me an hour,” says resident Melanie Bigras. Family members that were neighbours are now divided by distance and concerns are growing about emergency services. Lise Lépine and Real Carrière live less than a kilometre away from the local fire station and it would normally take just a few minutes for first responders to reach them.

Now they have to rely on help from the town of Riviere-Rouge 25 kilometres away in case of an emergency. “If I have a stroke, are they going to be here in time?” Lépine asked. “It has been worrisome.” They also now have to drive 40 minutes to reach their mailbox, and 40 minutes to return home.

Patching the hole To get the re-building work started, L’Ascension needed the go-ahead from federal and provincial departments. According to a letter reviewed by CTV News, published Oct. 15, from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, it took 53 days to greenlight the emergency repairs after the town sought authorization.

The municipality’s proposal was examined, in part, to ensure the protection of fish and its habitat. In a statement to CTV News, the DFO said that as soon as it received the request from the town, departmental officials began its review.

“The assessment determined that measures were required to address impacts to fish and fish habitat,” it read. “DFO already transmitted a letter of advice outlining the best practices to implement for the proposed work, noting that if these best practices are implemented, no permit or Fisheries Act Authorization is required.” Following the review, Quebec’s Department of Domestic Security had to sign-off, and the province had to approve funding.

The project will cost nearly $2 million, 85 per cent of which will be covered by Quebec. By early October, many residents of L’Ascension had grown exasperated with the speed of the road repairs. “It felt like something was broken,” says Allard.

“When someone has to travel 50 kilometres to get here, when a parent is on one side, a daughter on the other and they are used to get together a lot, it’s difficult.” ‘We are isolated’ There was also another pressing concern.

Erosion continued to eat away at the edges of the crater. The precipice was inching closer to an important aqueduct, prompting fears it could eventually collapse. Residents urged the town to pressure the province into fixing the problem.

In response the mayor drove to Quebec City to meet officials. The town also sent a legal letter to prove the work was urgently needed, and it organized a demonstration. On Oct. 24, hundreds of people stood on either side of the gulf and held up protest signs.

One read “Get us out of here,” while another read “We are isolated.” Four days after that protest, the municipality finally had all its permits and work began almost immediately. “It is a big relief,” says L’Ascension Director General Marc St-Pierre.

“It seemed like an uphill battle for so long.” The mayor says environmental reviews should have been done, but St-Pierre says the town had to push to speed up final approvals. With winter looming, a delay of another few weeks could have meant having to put off the project until spring.

“Regulation is absolutely important, but in certain cases it adds delays, and unfortunately there are consequences that are very real for a small community like ours,” says St-Pierre. Lightening the regulatory burden Ottawa announced new legislation for Fisheries and Oceans that streamlined the application process for some construction projects that took effect on Oct.

15, Quebec’s new government also promised to cut down on bureaucracy. L’Ascension says it wants to explore other ways to clear hurdles faster in case of any major natural disasters. Earlier this week, L’Ascension city council unanimously approved a resolution to find ways to help lighten the regulatory burden.

“We are going to offer our collaboration based on our experience so that we can find ways to speed up the process and ensure it goes as fast as possible,” says St-Pierre. He added that this could be particularly applicable in cases where the work largely involves repairing previously existing infrastructure.

In L’Ascension’s case, there have been upgrades, including to the size of the culvert to ensure it could withstand increasingly ferocious weather events. The mayor says since repair work has begun, he has seen a lot of smiles on his residents’ faces.

He drives to the site almost every day to see how the re-building is progressing and often stops to talk to those living nearby. Pierre Groulx was sitting on his porch when the mayor pulled up in his vehicle and asked how he felt about the crater now being filled.

“I am really looking forward to the reopening,” Groulx said. “My grandson lives on the other side. Now, that’s an 80 kilometre round trip so I don’t see him very much.” The mayor says plans are underway for a party in the local church for the holidays, and he hopes that will double as a party to celebrate the re-unification of the town divided by a storm.

stories.title: A deepfake video network is spreading false information about the U.S. trade war: report
stories.summary: A network that’s likely based outside of Canada is using deepfakes to spread “politically divisive” content to Canadians, says a new report released Thursday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A network that’s likely based outside of Canada is using deepfakes to spread “politically divisive” content to Canadians, says a new report released Thursday.

The report from McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy says the network uses deepfakes of real influencers. It combines the faces of real people with fake lip movements and voices generated by AI.

“We do not know what the network is for, but its operators are willing to steal faces and spread falsehoods that set Canadians against the United States, against their own government and against each other,” the report says.

Using footage of real people likely keeps the videos from being flagged as AI, the report says, noting that TikTok has only labelled four per cent of such videos as AI.

It says many of the videos focus on the U.S.-Canada trade war and the most-watched videos include false information.

They include a video about a non-existent 48-hour ultimatum from U.S. President Donald Trump which falsely says Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts.

“This never happened, but the story was shared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and played 5.1 million times,” the report says.

The people who comment on the videos don’t seem to realize they are fake, with only 6.3 per cent saying the video is inauthentic or propaganda.

“The rest agree or argue with the content in the video, and one in ten speaks to the narrator as a real person: thanking them, praising them, or telling them to check their facts,” the report says.

The videos don’t have a consistent perspective on the trade war. The report says the accounts take both sides, “and narrators switch nationality too, presenting themselves as Canadian in some videos and American in others. The effect is that Canadians are shown fabricated and misleading claims on both sides of the trade debate.”

The network includes nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts and has posted more than 3,201 videos that have been seen 22.1 million times in the past three months.

The report says it’s not clear who is behind the network but it is “almost certainly” run outside of North America.

“Its posting and registration times do not fit North American time zones,” the report says. “Activity drops off during the night in East and Southeast Asia, and some accounts carry Chinese-language settings or a registration in China, the only lead we have on a country.”

The motivation of those behind the network is also unclear.

The accounts don’t push the narratives of any foreign government and have not been monetized, the report says, adding the network could be growing audiences to use later.

It says the network could also be used for testing a tool or service, or someone May be paying those behind the operation to influence Canadians.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Elks kicker Blanchard wrote it down in 2026
stories.summary: Vincent Blanchard began writing things down this season.
stories.author: Donna Spencer
stories.content:
The Edmonton Elks kicker decided to journal his kicks and outcomes in 2026, which he hadn’t done before.

“When I have something in my mind, I write it in my book,” the 28-year-old from Quebec City said Thursday.

“When you are a kicker, you try and remove more things off your head. When I have something in my head, I just try to write it in my book and try to not think about it anymore, or to help me get some key words in order to excel on the field . . . what I need to do to kick a good ball.

“I was just trying to do something better for the mental aspect.”

Blanchard was the runner-up in voting for the CFL’s special teams award this season behind Winnipeg returner Trey Vaval.

Blanchard set a CFL record for field goals in a game with nine against Hamilton on Sept. 26.

He booted a walk-off, 57-yarder field goal July 23 against the host Saskatchewan Roughriders that silenced Mosaic Stadium and vaulted the Elks to the top of the West Division.

Blanchard led all kickers in field goals (55) and percentage made (93.2 per cent) in his second full season in the league.

“I showed what I can really do in this league, I showed my potential and my real value in this league,” Blanchard said. “I’m happy with what I put on the field, but at the end of the day we have another game to play. The job is not done.”

Kicks for points could factor into Sunday’s Grey Cup game between the Elks and Montreal Alouettes at Calgary’s McMahon Stadium, where it isn’t just notoriously windy, but those winds can shift during the game.

Blanchard says he’ll check the forecast Saturday, but acknowledged he’s had mostly calm conditions when the Elks played at McMahon.

“It’s a very windy place, but at the end of the day, it’s Canadian football. You need play in the snow and the cold and the wind and the rain,” he said.

“In this type of game, when it’s the final, it’s always a tight game. One play, two plays can make a difference. But when your name is called, you need to be ready. I was ready all year and I want to continue to be.”

Blanchard went 5-for-5 in field goals to help the University of Laval’s Rouge et Or beat the Saskatchewan Huskies for the 2022 Vanier Cup.

Drafted in the fourth round (31st) by the Alouettes in 2024, Blanchard was released from Montreal’s training camp that year, but brought back to the practice roster in October.

He was 77.8 per cent accurate on 45 field-goal attempts in his rookie season in 2025, and signed a contract extension in December.

“It’s more about the experience. When I get the experience, I can be more myself on the field,” Blanchard explained.

“At university, that was the same thing. I started, I would say slowly. My second year was better, and my third year was always better.”

“When I left last year, I told Coach Mark (Kilam) before the off-season, ‘I will be better next season. I promise you I will better because I know myself and I just need to adapt myself in this environment.'”

Kilam, who was also in his first year as head coach of the Elks in 2025, has a deep special-teams background after 14 years coaching the Calgary Stampeders in that department.

“Vin just needed to be supported. He is so talented. He needed people to believe in him,” Kilam said. “He’s a pro, he’s critical of himself in the sense that he wants to continue to get better.

“He wants to be coached. He’s sometimes too hard on himself and that’s where we can balance that out a little bit. I think the sky is the limit for Vin. I think he’s going to continue to ascend.”

Elks quarterback Cody Fajardo noticed Blanchard journaling in the locker room this season.

“Maybe it’s just he’s got this clear mentality about him but we have the utmost confidence in Vin and if the game comes down to a field goal, it doesn’t matter how long it is, we believe in Vin,” Fajardo said.

“Whether he makes it or not, it’s not going to change how much we love Vin. I told him that after he hit the walk-off against Saskatchewan.

“He’s been money for us this year. In games like this where you know it’s probably going to be close, it’s always great to have an incredible kicker like this.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

— With files from Dan Ralph.

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada dismisses bid to appeal B.C. foreign buyer tax case
stories.summary: The Supreme Court of Canada won't hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia's foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national.
stories.author: Darryl Greer The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Supreme Court of Canada won’t hear an appeal challenging the application of British Columbia’s foreign buyer tax on a real estate purchase involving joint ownership by a Canadian citizen and a foreign national.

The B.C. Court of Appeal had previously dismissed an appeal brought by a couple who jointly bought an apartment in Richmond, B.C., putting 95 per cent in the Canadian woman’s name, and five per cent in the name of her foreign partner.

stories.title: Confining kids in lockers as punishment 'unacceptable': Quebec education minister
stories.summary: QUÉBEC - Quebec Education Minister Joël Arseneau is speaking out about school personnel who allegedly confined unruly children in a locker north of Montreal.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
QUÉBEC - Quebec Education Minister Joël Arseneau is speaking out about school personnel who allegedly confined unruly children in a locker north of Montreal.

The minister says he was informed of the allegations at a school in the Laurentians and says the situation was unacceptable.

The allegations were first reported by Cogeco media outlets on Thursday.

The reports say at least three children between five and seven years old were isolated and sometimes locked in a lightly padded metal locker in order to get them to calm down.

They also say four employees, including a teacher and the school principal, were suspended following the allegations.

The alleged punishment occurred at a primary school operated by the Centre de services scolaire des Mille-Îles.

“I condemn it without reservation,” Arseneau wrote on social media. “The intervention methods used with students must meet recognized best practices and respect their safety, dignity and particular needs. Under no circumstances should students be confined in lockers.”

Local police and youth protection services are investigating the allegations.

The minister says he is in touch with authorities and will take “the necessary steps to shed full light on these practices, which we find highly problematic.”

The media reports did not name the school in order to protect the children.

The Quebec Liberals, who form the official Opposition, also condemned the alleged actions by school personnel and said the minister should be held accountable.

Marc Tanguay, the Liberal education critic, says it is Arseneau’s responsibility to be aware of what is happening in the school system and to implement best practices.

“Even if you are not the person who carried out the action, you are responsible for what happens under your authority,” he said on the sidelines of a Liberal caucus meeting at the legislature.

Tanguay is calling for a comprehensive review of the allegations.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

— with files from Patrice Bergeron in Quebec City.

stories.summary: Vancouver - A woman has been arrested and charged after allegedly impersonating a police officer during Vancouver's Remembrance Day ceremony.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Police say officers noticed the woman wearing “combat-style” camouflage clothing, body armour, tactical boots and a vest with military-style pouches.

They say the woman was also displaying a police-style badge on a chain and several police-related patches at the commemorative event at Victory Square.

Article continues below

Officers arrested the woman and found she was in possession of a replica gun.

Police say the 34-year-old woman has been charged with one count of possessing a weapon for a dangerous purpose.

Const. Megan Lui notes the force had about 120 officers deployed for Remembrance Day ceremonies across Vancouver on Wednesday.

stories.title: ‘It’s a huge financial help’: National Climate Smart Ag Program doubling enrollment in 2027
stories.summary: Sarah Alton has spent the past few years trying to modernize her family’s cattle business near Lucknow. Now, she’s turning her attention to the crops they grow.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
Sarah Alton has spent the past few years trying to modernize her family’s cattle business near Lucknow. Now, she’s turning her attention to the crops they grow. “We really want to improve them, compared to the neighboring farms.

So, when the Canza program came out, we decided this is a great opportunity for us to jump on and be a part of,” said Alton, Farm Manager at Kenruth Farms. With the help of the Canadian Alliance for Net Zero Agri-Food (Canza), Kenruth Farms used slow release nitrogen on 400 of their 1100 acres this spring.

A more expensive product, but one that’s more efficient for the plant, and better for the soil. “It’s a bit like you’re trying to make generational improvement, because you want to be sustainable for the next generation.

And, also it’s more profit in the long term of the aspect, because you’re going to generate more yield with the slow release, because the plant is being able to use that nitrogen, throughout its growing period,” said Alton, a third generation farmer.

Cost sharing new climate smart agriculture practices for Canadian farmers is the whole goal of Canza. Sharing the risk of more expensive agricultural practices on the farm level, with long term goals in mind, according to Canza officials.

This year, 32 Ontario farmers took part using new regenerative farming practices on 15,100 acres. Year Two will see double that, 60 farmers and 36000 acres, thanks in part to $10.5 million in funding from the Weston Foundation.

“We know that globally there’s a big movement towards regenerative agriculture, and there’s an initial window when farmers are asked to carry the cost and the risk of transitioning towards regenerative agriculture. So, the Million Acre Challenge is a two pronged program aimed at supporting farmers through that transition,” said Ashley Honsberger, Interim Executive Director of Canza.

Alton says taking part in the Million Acre Challenge has been one of the best decisions her family farm has made. “It’s a huge financial help on trying a new practice, because if you go out and you want to do a new practice, it’s expensive.

The financial cost, especially in agriculture today, it costs so much money to implement a new practice. Whereas if you have a supplement income from a program like this, it makes it a lot easier,” she said. Whether it’s more sustainable fertilizer, reducing methane emissions, or funding crop rotation, Canza aims to reach one Million Acres enrolled by 2032.

“According to some of the global research that says regenerative agriculture, and the subsequent improved soil health, and all of those sorts of things actually lend well to better economics on the farm, as well as the environmental benefits.

So, we’re really supporting farmers through that risky initial window,” said Honsberger.

stories.title: Generations Foundation holiday food and toy drive kicks off: Here’s where to donate
stories.summary: The Generations Foundation’s annual holiday food and toy drive is underway. Here’s where to donate toys, non-perishable food and money to support Montreal families in need.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The Generations Foundation has launched its 27th annual holiday food and toy drive, aiming to bring holiday cheer to thousands of children and families in need across Montreal.

The organization collects new toys for children and non-perishable food items for families struggling to make ends meet, as food insecurity remains one of the greatest challenges facing families today.

Founded by husband-and-wife team Adrian and Natalie Bercovici, the foundation has raised more than $12 million since its inception, according to the organization.

After 26 years of leadership, the Bercovicis stepped back last year, handing the reins to executive director Leslie Butt, who first joined the organization as a volunteer 27 years ago.

“I started to fundraise, I joined the organization, then I ended up on their board after 10 years,” Butt said. “From the board I was on at least another 15 and just last year I was nominated as executive director.”

Butt said he hopes to build on the foundation’s work while considering new ways to support the children and families it serves.

A new website is also in the works, which Butt said will make donating easier and give people more information about the foundation’s work in the community.

The organization relies exclusively on donations to operate, and Butt said it wants to ensure contributions go directly toward feeding the children it serves.

“This place exists because you donate to Generations out of your goodwill, your hearts, pockets,” he said. “And we want to make sure that when you give us 10 bucks or 10 thousand dollars, that money goes directly into the mouths of kids we’re serving and not into our pockets.”

The foundation has received support from corporate partners over the years, including Best Buy, Mattel/Mega Bloks and the Cafe Milano group.

This year, Cafe Milano will also raffle off Montreal Canadiens tickets and match every dollar raised.

The foundation is accepting new toys for the holiday season, as well as non-perishable food and monetary donations throughout the year.

Donations can be dropped off at participating Best Buy stores, Cafe Milano locations and other collection points.

Best Buy locations include stores in Anjou, downtown Montreal, Saint-Jérôme, Mascouche, Vaudreuil-Dorion, Marché Central, LaSalle, Laval, Pointe-Claire, Rosemère, Brossard and Saint-Bruno-de-Montarville.

Cafe Milano collection points are located in Saint-Léonard, Pointe-Claire, Laval and Brossard.

Other drop-off locations include the English Montreal School Board central office at 6000 Fielding Ave. in Montreal, the Montreal Gazette at 2055 Peel St., Suite 700, and Mattel/Mega Bloks at 6767 Chemin de la Côte-de-Liesse in Saint-Laurent.

stories.title: How to stay healthy during an early flu season, according to our experts
stories.summary: Readers asked how long flu season lasts, tips to prevent the spread of infection and how the vaccine is rolled out
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
On Nov. 2, Health editor Caroline Alphonso and health reporter Alanna Smith answered reader questions on this year’s flu season , how to find out about infection rates and vaccination plans in your region, and how you can prevent and manage symptoms.

The influenza virus is hitting harder and earlier this year across Canada. Rates this fall are several times higher than the numbers recorded in previous years, experts say, and some provinces are offering flu shots earlier than usual, as vulnerable populations seek to protect themselves.

Readers asked how long flu season lasts, tips to prevent the spread of infection and how the vaccine is rolled out. Here are some highlights from the Q&A.

How long does flu season typically last?

Caroline Alphonso: Typically, flu season starts in late fall (I always think of my kids going back to school and bringing home all those viruses!), peaks in the winter (it always makes our Christmas gatherings a bit eventful!) and tapers off in the spring.

This year, the flu season came a bit earlier, which prompted some provinces to adjust their vaccination plans. Tu Thanh Ha, a Health reporter on our team, had a story on the early flu season .

Why is there a flu season at all? Is it weather-dependent?

Alanna Smith: Yes, the flu season is strongly influenced by the weather. The virus is able to survive longer in colder temperatures and is constantly mutating to bypass our immune systems. Also, in the colder months, people are more likely to hang out inside, closer to one another, making it easy for the virus to jump from person to person.

We as a family are recovering from a really bad episode of cough and flu. Do we have immunity now? When do we get shots?

Alphonso: You May have some immunity now but you shouldn’t rely on it alone, and you should still get the recommended vaccines. Here’s why: Unless you were tested, you don’t know if you had the flu or COVID-19 or even some other respiratory illness. I would suggest speaking to your health care professional.

Why are flu shots unavailable for infants, and what can I do to protect my three-month-old daughter?

Alphonso: According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, the seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for almost everyone six months and older. Influenza vaccines are not approved or sufficiently protective for babies under six months of age. Health experts say that the best thing you can do to protect your daughter is to make sure everyone around her is vaccinated.

My daughter-in-law is struggling with a variant not covered by this year’s vaccine. What can be done about that?

Smith: I am assuming that you are talking about the influenza vaccine.

The seasonal shot is trivalent, which means it is designed to protect against three different strains, two different Influenza A strains and one Influenza B. Early data show that the current flu vaccine is a good match for the circulating strains. But, even if it were a mismatch, the vaccine does provide some protection, cutting the risk of severe illness and hospital admission.

Take last season, for example. While the flu vaccine was not a match for the dominant Subclade K strain, it still reduced the risk of serious illness by roughly 40 per cent compared with unvaccinated individuals. You can read more about those findings here .

How can seniors stay safe from infection during flu season, especially one that’s even longer than usual?

Alphonso: For seniors, vaccination remains the most effective protection against severe illness. Public health experts would advise seniors to stay up to date on vaccinations.

I know that masks are no longer worn by many people. However, they could be useful on public transit or crowded spaces.

And of course, ask family members to stay home if they’re sick, and practice good hand hygiene.

If we get sick, what’s a good rule of thumb on how long to take extra steps to make sure we don’t infect anybody else?

Smith: The infectious period differs depending on the respiratory illness. Additionally, the duration of sickness is typically longer when someone is not vaccinated.

For influenza, it is best to wait five days or until you feel better overall before seeing people again, according to guidance from the Public Health Agency of Canada. You are most contagious in the first three days after symptoms present.

For COVID-19, the infectious period can vary, but it is generally considered to last up to 10 days following symptom onset. That period can be longer in severe cases or for those who are immunocompromised.

Now, for the common cold, there is unfortunately quite a range. People are contagious as long as symptoms are present, which is usually between seven and 10 days but can stretch up to roughly two weeks.

Why can’t we get a flu vaccine earlier?

Smith: The flu virus hit so early and hard this season that some provinces, including Prince Edward Island and Alberta, actually had to adjust their vaccine campaigns to get shots in arms faster.

Each year, Canadian provinces and territories decide when to start offering vaccines based on federal guidance, disease surveillance and rollout logistics but, unfortunately, there is not an exact science to know when viral spread will take off. There are risks associated with starting vaccines early but also in waiting too long.

My health colleague, Tu Thanh Ha, spoke to an expert about this recently, who explained that beginning vaccine rollout too early can be problematic because protection wanes prematurely. Additionally, campaigns must be set months in advance to address manufacturing, procurement and distribution issues, making it difficult to change when the season doesn’t go as anticipated. You can read that story here .

How does each province decide how to fight the flu every year? Are there any major outliers?

Smith: Generally speaking, flu programs are similar across the country. Each province and territory, however, manages their own, so there can be differences in eligibility criteria, launch dates and rollout. The campaigns are informed by scientific and national guidance, surveillance data and vaccine procurement.

The major outlier this season is Quebec, which is the only province in Canada charging some of its residents for a flu vaccine . Only some Quebeckers are still eligible for a free shot, such as seniors, people with certain chronic conditions and those living with them, pregnant people and residents of long-term care and seniors’ homes. Everyone else has to pay between $30 and $40.

Every other province has maintained universal coverage for the flu vaccine.

Isn’t Quebec charging for flu shots asking for a lower uptake and therefore ultimately putting high risk patients at even higher risk due to lack of “herd” immunity?

Smith: You are not alone in raising these questions. Public health experts across Canada have voiced concern over Quebec’s policy, arguing that it could lower vaccine uptake and lead to more strain on hospitals and further erode vaccine confidence. But it’s too early in the viral season to be able to gauge the full impact of this move.

What is the vaccination rate by age group in B.C. and should “younger” people get vaccinated?

Smith: I have to admit, I thought those stats would live publicly online somewhere and be easy to find. . . not the case. I also reached out to the B.C. Centre for Disease Control yesterday but the agency was unable to immediately provide that data.

There is some national data , however, that shows 25.3 per cent of British Columbians aged 18 to 64 were vaccinated against the flu last season, compared to 67.1 per cent of seniors (65+).

As for the second part of your question on whether younger people should get vaccinated, I’ll point you to the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (Naci) recommendations, which are largely followed across Canada. Naci strongly recommends COVID-19 immunization for higher risk individuals, including seniors and health care workers, and that vaccines “May be offered” to all other individuals. The agency continues to recommend flu vaccination for all individuals six months and older .

Caroline Alphonso: Typically, flu season starts in late fall (I always think of my kids going back to school and bringing home all those viruses!), peaks in the winter (it always makes our Christmas gatherings a bit eventful!) and tapers off in the spring.
This year, the flu season came a bit earlier, which prompted some provinces to adjust their vaccination plans. Tu Thanh Ha, a Health reporter on our team, had a story on the early flu season .
Why is there a flu season at all? Is it weather-dependent?

Alanna Smith: Yes, the flu season is strongly influenced by the weather. The virus is able to survive longer in colder temperatures and is constantly mutating to bypass our immune systems. Also, in the colder months, people are more likely to hang out inside, closer to one another, making it easy for the virus to jump from person to person.
We as a family are recovering from a really bad episode of cough and flu. Do we have immunity now? When do we get shots?

Alphonso: You May have some immunity now but you shouldn’t rely on it alone, and you should still get the recommended vaccines. Here’s why: Unless you were tested, you don’t know if you had the flu or COVID-19 or even some other respiratory illness. I would suggest speaking to your health care professional.
Why are flu shots unavailable for infants, and what can I do to protect my three-month-old daughter?

Alphonso: According to the Public Health Agency of Canada, the seasonal flu vaccine is recommended for almost everyone six months and older. Influenza vaccines are not approved or sufficiently protective for babies under six months of age. Health experts say that the best thing you can do to protect your daughter is to make sure everyone around her is vaccinated.
My daughter-in-law is struggling with a variant not covered by this year’s vaccine. What can be done about that?
Smith: I am assuming that you are talking about the influenza vaccine.

The seasonal shot is trivalent, which means it is designed to protect against three different strains, two different Influenza A strains and one Influenza B. Early data show that the current flu vaccine is a good match for the circulating strains. But, even if it were a mismatch, the vaccine does provide some protection, cutting the risk of severe illness and hospital admission.

Take last season, for example. While the flu vaccine was not a match for the dominant Subclade K strain, it still reduced the risk of serious illness by roughly 40 per cent compared with unvaccinated individuals. You can read more about those findings here .
How can seniors stay safe from infection during flu season, especially one that’s even longer than usual?
Alphonso: For seniors, vaccination remains the most effective protection against severe illness. Public health experts would advise seniors to stay up to date on vaccinations.
I know that masks are no longer worn by many people. However, they could be useful on public transit or crowded spaces.
And of course, ask family members to stay home if they’re sick, and practice good hand hygiene.
If we get sick, what’s a good rule of thumb on how long to take extra steps to make sure we don’t infect anybody else?
Smith: The infectious period differs depending on the respiratory illness. Additionally, the duration of sickness is typically longer when someone is not vaccinated.

For influenza, it is best to wait five days or until you feel better overall before seeing people again, according to guidance from the Public Health Agency of Canada. You are most contagious in the first three days after symptoms present.

For COVID-19, the infectious period can vary, but it is generally considered to last up to 10 days following symptom onset. That period can be longer in severe cases or for those who are immunocompromised.

Now, for the common cold, there is unfortunately quite a range. People are contagious as long as symptoms are present, which is usually between seven and 10 days but can stretch up to roughly two weeks.
Why can’t we get a flu vaccine earlier?
Smith: The flu virus hit so early and hard this season that some provinces, including Prince Edward Island and Alberta, actually had to adjust their vaccine campaigns to get shots in arms faster.

Each year, Canadian provinces and territories decide when to start offering vaccines based on federal guidance, disease surveillance and rollout logistics but, unfortunately, there is not an exact science to know when viral spread will take off. There are risks associated with starting vaccines early but also in waiting too long.

My health colleague, Tu Thanh Ha, spoke to an expert about this recently, who explained that beginning vaccine rollout too early can be problematic because protection wanes prematurely. Additionally, campaigns must be set months in advance to address manufacturing, procurement and distribution issues, making it difficult to change when the season doesn’t go as anticipated. You can read that story here .
How does each province decide how to fight the flu every year? Are there any major outliers?

Smith: Generally speaking, flu programs are similar across the country. Each province and territory, however, manages their own, so there can be differences in eligibility criteria, launch dates and rollout. The campaigns are informed by scientific and national guidance, surveillance data and vaccine procurement.

The major outlier this season is Quebec, which is the only province in Canada charging some of its residents for a flu vaccine . Only some Quebeckers are still eligible for a free shot, such as seniors, people with certain chronic conditions and those living with them, pregnant people and residents of long-term care and seniors’ homes. Everyone else has to pay between $30 and $40.
Every other province has maintained universal coverage for the flu vaccine.
Isn’t Quebec charging for flu shots asking for a lower uptake and therefore ultimately putting high risk patients at even higher risk due to lack of “herd” immunity?

Smith: You are not alone in raising these questions. Public health experts across Canada have voiced concern over Quebec’s policy, arguing that it could lower vaccine uptake and lead to more strain on hospitals and further erode vaccine confidence. But it’s too early in the viral season to be able to gauge the full impact of this move.
What is the vaccination rate by age group in B.C. and should “younger” people get vaccinated?

Smith: I have to admit, I thought those stats would live publicly online somewhere and be easy to find. . . not the case. I also reached out to the B.C. Centre for Disease Control yesterday but the agency was unable to immediately provide that data.
There is some national data , however, that shows 25.3 per cent of British Columbians aged 18 to 64 were vaccinated against the flu last season, compared to 67.1 per cent of seniors (65+).

As for the second part of your question on whether younger people should get vaccinated, I’ll point you to the National Advisory Committee on Immunization (Naci) recommendations, which are largely followed across Canada. Naci strongly recommends COVID-19 immunization for higher risk individuals, including seniors and health care workers, and that vaccines “May be offered” to all other individuals. The agency continues to recommend flu vaccination for all individuals six months and older .

stories.title: N.S. municipal politicians weigh in on whether AI can speed up housing approvals
stories.summary: Municipal politicians in Nova Scotia are reacting after the federal government pitched artificial intelligence as a way of speeding up housing approvals.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
Municipal politicians in Nova Scotia are reacting after the federal government pitched artificial intelligence as a way of speeding up housing approvals.

The recent federal budget included $100 million to help communities adopt the AI technology, but many questions remain around how it will be implemented.

“AI, I think at the municipal level, it could be beneficial,” said Halifax District 5 Coun. Sam Austin.

“I think we also have to be cautious it doesn’t replace the human eye approval.”

The $100 million commitment would be spread over three years and be dedicated to helping municipalities adopt AI into their housing permitting processes. The initiative aims to reduce what can sometimes be a tedious workload.

But Austin says a human touch will still be necessary.

“I wouldn’t want to go to an AI just automatically approving a permit and issuing it without without a human somewhere in there saying, ‘Yes, this is correct,'” he said.

Halifax Mayor Andy Fillmore says he’s interested in seeing how these digital supports will help.

In a statement, he says “this is about giving our professional staff better administrative tools to do their jobs more effectively and productively — not replacing their expertise and judgement on planning decisions.”

The Federation of Canadian Municipalities is spearheading the project. The federation’s president, Tim Tierney, says AI will help communities cut back on lengthy permitting delays.

“For some of the smaller ones that don’t have the ability to have giant workforces of permitters, this will allow the smallest municipalities to be able to have that ability to speed up their processing,” said Tierney, who is also a councillor in Ottawa.

The federal government points out Edmonton is already using automated reviews and that as a result, the city is now issuing one-day approvals.

The Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities says the move could alleviate the burden on towns with limited resources but policies to govern the use of AI will be vital.

“You can’t skip steps. So we talk about efficiency, but efficiency doesn’t mean missing steps because we don’t want anyone to get hurt,” said David Mitchell, the federation’s president.

“So there’ll always be a human on the other end, whether it’s a building official and building inspector or a planner and engineer to make sure the work is done properly.”

stories.title: Saskatoon police officer who was hit by vehicle stable, still in hospital
stories.summary: The Saskatoon police officer who was stuck by a vehicle on Wednesday afternoon is still undergoing treatment in hospital, but is now stable, SPS Chief Cameron McBride said.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
The Saskatoon police officer who was seriously injured after being struck by a vehicle on Wednesday afternoon is stable and receiving treatment.

The officer, a five-year member of the Saskatoon Police Service (SPS) who was working on its traffic unit, was outside of his marked patrol vehicle and attempting to flag down a vehicle for a speed enforcement stop when he was struck by a passing vehicle at approximately 1:15 p.m. Wednesday, Saskatoon police chief Cameron McBride said.

They were in a construction zone on Circle Drive, near the 108th Street overpass when the collision occurred.

“It is our understanding that he had identified a vehicle that he wanted to pull over. And that’s what initiated the circumstance,” McBride said at a news conference, where he provided an update on the status of the injured officer .

Police are currently unsure whether the vehicle being stopped was the one that struck the officer, he noted.

“The officer sustained serious injuries and was transported to hospital, where he remains receiving treatment. We don’t know the full extent of those injuries yet. However, last we heard, he is stable and is in ongoing treatment,” McBride said.

Saskatoon police are currently not identifying the officer at his family’s request, the chief said.

No charges have been laid in relation to the collision.

In a news release shared Wednesday, police said the driver was uninjured and remained at the scene.

“There was nothing to indicate an immediate arrest or charges,” McBride told reporters.

SPS major crimes and the traffic analyst unit are conducting an investigation into the incident. The chief said police did not provide a timeline on how long that probe will take, but said it will be “thorough and complete.”

“(It) will be fully reported once it’s ready to go,” McBride added, noting that any measures recommended following the investigation will be put in place.

At the moment, no temporary safety measures have been put in place for Saskatoon police, the chief added.

He thanked the people who helped the injured officer following the incident. He asked witnesses and anyone with video or dashcam footage to contact police.

The officer, a five-year member of the Saskatoon Police Service (SPS) who was working on its traffic unit, was outside of his marked patrol vehicle and attempting to flag down a vehicle for a speed enforcement stop when he was struck by a passing vehicle at approximately 1:15 p.m. Wednesday, Saskatoon police chief Cameron McBride said.
They were in a construction zone on Circle Drive, near the 108th Street overpass when the collision occurred.

“It is our understanding that he had identified a vehicle that he wanted to pull over. And that’s what initiated the circumstance,” McBride said at a news conference, where he provided an update on the status of the injured officer .
Police are currently unsure whether the vehicle being stopped was the one that struck the officer, he noted.

“The officer sustained serious injuries and was transported to hospital, where he remains receiving treatment. We don’t know the full extent of those injuries yet. However, last we heard, he is stable and is in ongoing treatment,” McBride said.
Saskatoon police are currently not identifying the officer at his family’s request, the chief said.
No charges have been laid in relation to the collision.
In a news release shared Wednesday, police said the driver was uninjured and remained at the scene.
“There was nothing to indicate an immediate arrest or charges,” McBride told reporters.

SPS major crimes and the traffic analyst unit are conducting an investigation into the incident. The chief said police did not provide a timeline on how long that probe will take, but said it will be “thorough and complete.”
“(It) will be fully reported once it’s ready to go,” McBride added, noting that any measures recommended following the investigation will be put in place.
At the moment, no temporary safety measures have been put in place for Saskatoon police, the chief added.
He thanked the people who helped the injured officer following the incident. He asked witnesses and anyone with video or dashcam footage to contact police.

stories.title: Program that supports seniors living at home expands in rural New Brunswick
stories.summary: A new program in rural New Brunswick is bringing some of the benefits of a nursing home directly to the community.
stories.author: Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
A new program in rural New Brunswick is bringing some of the benefits of a nursing home directly to the community.

For dozens of seniors in the Fundy Rural District’s Brown Flat area, that means more support without having to leave home.

“I want to be fit, but most of all, we want to be in our homes,” said Sandy MacKinnon, 76.

MacKinnon is one of about 45 participants in the Nursing Home Without Walls program, which offers nursing home-like support and activities during the day.

The program has been running since September at the River Road Hub.

Backed by the Rocmaura Nursing Home in Saint John, it offers exercise, shared meals and social and medical assistance.

“We want to eliminate social isolation and speak about making meals and you know all of those types of things that make communities and seniors stronger,” said Christina Harvey, Greenwich Community Centre Nursing Homes Without Walls’ executive sponsor.

Five staff members support the facility, including a kinesiologist and a staff member with a nursing degree.

MacKinnon says the program gives her friendship and a reason to get out.

“Then when we go home, the emptiness is not nearly as bad, because we know we’re going to come here again,” she said.

New Brunswick Health Minister John Dornan says that kind of support could also keep some seniors out of hospitals.

“Sometimes that inability to drive or inability to get a fresh meal or inability to socialize, it’s all that’s between them and being in a hospital or nursing home,” he said.

The River Road Hub is the province’s 38th site for the program. Its annual budget has grown to $12 million, including $4 million in new funding.

“Each program is related to the needs of the seniors of their communities. Sometimes it’s different from one program to another program,” said Minister of Seniors Lyne Chantal Boudreau.

More than 7,700 seniors have used the program since its launch in 2019 and organizers say this newest site could eventually grow from 45 participants to as many as 200.

— with a file from Rebecca Lau

stories.title: Fanshawe graduate shares advice on writing and publishing a book
stories.summary: For many aspiring authors, publishing a book is a dream, but turning that dream into a reality can be challeng...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
For many aspiring authors, publishing a book is a dream, but turning that dream into a reality can be challenging, said a Fanshawe graduate who recently published his first novel.

Marty Sommers. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

“The most important thing is it’s not going to be perfect. So write it, edit it, and put it out there because you’re not going to get it perfect,” said Marty Sommers, who was on campus Thursday to showcase his book, The Dragon Within .

“You can edit it one hundred times and you’ll never have it exactly the way you want.”

Marty Sommers book. Photo Credit: Owen Schuller

Sommers was a boy when his dad introduced him to reading. Later, his dad opened a second-hand bookstore, which made books a huge part of his life.

The Dragon Within is expected to be available for sale in January. Sommers is also planning to publish more books in early 2027 called the Silver Thread of Fate and the Dragon Hearts Burn.

The most challenging part for authors isn’t just writing and publishing. It’s convincing people to buy their books, getting their name recognized and finding ways to stand out in the book market.

According to FriesenPress, a professionally published book can cost up to $6,000, between promotion, editing and other services professionals provide. Sommers admits that without professional publishers “You have to do all the footwork yourself, You have to push it yourself,” Sommers said.

stories.title: ‘What if a kid was crossing?’: New study finds about five near misses a day at crosswalks near schools
stories.summary: A study for the Canadian Automobile Association (CAA) has found an alarming number of near misses as children walk to school.
stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
A study for the Canadian Automobile Association (CAA) has found an alarming number of near misses as children walk to school.

The report found that one in 84 crossings located near schools are sites of near misses. That works out to nearly five a day across 11 cities examined.

Crossing guard Vern Jarvis of London, Ont. is not surprised by the findings.

He has been protecting kids on their way to school for seven years.

“They love to run, and they don’t make good decisions,” he said moments after finishing his shift at a busy suburban crossing.

Jarvis knows firsthand how dangerous his job can be for kids, parents and crossing guards.

Just last year, he was forced to take extraordinary measures to stop a moving vehicle.

“I ended up on the hood of his car trying to stop him because he wasn’t stopping, and I was banging on the hood of his car.”

Jarvis is fortunate. Last week, a crossing guard, a mother and two children were struck near Toronto .

The incident occurred just days before CAA released its report .

“It is not at all surprising,” repeated parent Nerissa Albert, who witnessed close calls.

“We do have near misses. We have actually almost had near misses at this exact stop when the crossing guard has not been here. This continues to be an issue.”

A point made when our cameras visited another intersection only a few blocks away, where Catherine Dockstadar recounted another close call.

“I’m trying to cross this kid and the car just kept climbing, you know, closer to me, so I have to literally shield myself between the child and the car.”

The endless stories have Albert calling out some drivers.

“A lot of people don’t stop at these school stop signs, or any kind of stop signs.”

The study also found that design can make a difference. Crossings with signals, stop signs or roundabouts had 20 times fewer near misses.

Those we spoke with agreed design changes May help, but they also suggested or supported placing more than one crossing guard at major intersections.

“That should work better, because it gets like it literally gets both sides, especially on a really busy street,” said Dockstadar.

But more crossing guards can’t stop a hurried, distracted, or dangerous driver.

stories.title: Truro deer cull to provide locally-sourced meat for food banks thanks to $30K grant
stories.summary: Nova Scotia is offering a one-time grant of $30,000 to help fund a program that donates locally-sourced meat to food banks, while also supporting Truro's annual deer cull.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Angela Capobianco
stories.content:
The Nova Scotia government is offering a one-time grant of $30,000 to help fund a program that donates locally-sourced meat to food banks, while also supporting Truro’s annual deer cull.

Officials say it’s all about ensuring people are fed and no part of an animal is wasted.

“This is leveraging the generosity of Nova Scotian hunters who would recognize that they have more than their personal need and wanting to help their neighbours,” said Opportunities and Social Development Minister Susan Corkum-Greek.

The Hunters Helping the Hungry program is an initiative between the hunting community and Feed Nova Scotia. The program has donated wild game to food banks for more than 20 years.

The partnership with Truro means meat from the annual cull will be processed through a licensed meat processor and distributed to food banks provincewide. The province’s grant will go towards the processing costs.

Hunters can register their wild game, then contact a participating registered processor and choose how much to donate.

The 2026 hunt is expected to provide about 1,200 kg of meat, which translates to roughly 12,000 meals on the table.

“Hunting and sharing harvested foods have deep roots in communities across Nova Scotia, particularly in Indigenous and rural communities where these practices are closely connected to culture, tradition, and community well-being,” said Ash Avery, executive director of Feed Nova Scotia.

Natural Resources Minister Tory Rushton says the department has been monitoring the deer cull in the Truro area over the past five years.

He says Hunters Helping the Hungry not only ensures the meat doesn’t go to waste, but also sees the animals’ hides going to Millbrook First Nation.

“I can tell you from my experience as a hunter, I would not always use the whole deer, if you will. It was shared with community,” said Rushton.

“It was shared with friends, family, and that’s sort of a pride of the hunter as well, to be able to share what they’ve worked on.”

Truro Mayor Cathy Hinton says she’s pleased to see her town playing a role in feeding the province.

“There’s children probably going to bed at night with empty bellies,” she said.

“To have protein to go to school with, to have a full stomach and to be able to sit at the table in the evening and have protein and food — that’s everything.”

The Town of Truro’s controlled urban deer hunt runs until mid-December. The cull was approved by town council in 2021 as a method of managing its urban deer population.

The town’s Deer Management Strategy says deer pose a risk to “natural ecosystems and biodiversity, citizen landscapes, public health and safety, and overall deer-human conflict.”

“Truro has an abundance of deer population. I always make a joke when new residents buy a home, you get two deer for free,” said Hinton.

“We do have an abundance of deer. And it has been problematic. Half of the town loves the deer and the other half find them a nuisance. And it’s a delicate balance between the two.”

According to the town, 88 deer were harvested in the 2025 hunt.

“Hunting and sharing harvested foods have deep roots in communities across Nova Scotia, particularly in Indigenous and rural communities where these practices are closely connected to culture, tradition, and community well-being,” said Ash Avery, executive director of Feed Nova Scotia.
Natural Resources Minister Tory Rushton says the department has been monitoring the deer cull in the Truro area over the past five years.
He says Hunters Helping the Hungry not only ensures the meat doesn’t go to waste, but also sees the animals’ hides going to Millbrook First Nation.
“I can tell you from my experience as a hunter, I would not always use the whole deer, if you will. It was shared with community,” said Rushton.
“It was shared with friends, family, and that’s sort of a pride of the hunter as well, to be able to share what they’ve worked on.”
Truro Mayor Cathy Hinton says she’s pleased to see her town playing a role in feeding the province.
“There’s children probably going to bed at night with empty bellies,” she said.
“To have protein to go to school with, to have a full stomach and to be able to sit at the table in the evening and have protein and food — that’s everything.”
The Town of Truro’s controlled urban deer hunt runs until mid-December. The cull was approved by town council in 2021 as a method of managing its urban deer population.

content_blocks.text: The town’s Deer Management Strategy says deer pose a risk to “natural ecosystems and biodiversity, citizen landscapes, public health and safety, and overall deer-human conflict.”
“Truro has an abundance of deer population. I always make a joke when new residents buy a home, you get two deer for free,” said Hinton.
“We do have an abundance of deer. And it has been problematic. Half of the town loves the deer and the other half find them a nuisance. And it’s a delicate balance between the two.”
According to the town, 88 deer were harvested in the 2025 hunt.

Advance requests for Maid are set to be decriminalized as part of a federal bill that is now before Parliament

Saskatchewan Minister of Health Jeremy Cockrill speaks during a media scrum at Saskatchewan Legislative Building in Regina, ON Nov. 9, 2026. (Heywood Yu / Regina Leader-Post)

November 12, 2026 at 4:12 p.m.

Saskatchewan intends to join Quebec in offering people the option to request a medically assisted death to be performed after they have lost the capacity to consent.

The changes to the Criminal Code come with a legislated caveat that provinces and territories, which are responsible for health-care delivery, must set up a stringent regulatory regime around how those advance requests are handled.

The Saskatchewan ministry of health said in a statement it will be doing that.

“Saskatchewan will be developing the necessary policies to safely implement advanced requests,” a spokesperson said in an emailed statement.

The statement did not provide a timeline for those policies to be developed.

Alberta has banned advance requests for Maid through provincial legislation that also bars the provision of Maid to people who are seeking an assisted death on the basis of a mental illness, as well as to people under the age of 18.

Federal law prohibits providing Maid to anyone under 18, and the legislation introduced in Parliament last month by Justice Minister Sean Fraser would also stop a planned expansion of Maid to people whose sole underlying condition is a mental illness.

Fraser’s bill goes even further, tightening what he called a gap in the current laws that has allowed health-care providers to assess a person’s suffering from a mental illness as part of their Maid evaluation. The law would ban mental illness from being considered as part of a Maid case.

Saskatchewan Health Minister Jeremy Cockrill introduced legislation this week to add safeguards to the Maid regime. Similar to Alberta’s law, it seeks to ban Maid for people under 18, those suffering from a mental illness, and for people who “in the opinion of the practitioner, lacks capacity.”

Advance requests are an exception to the requirement that a person must provide consent for Maid at the time of the procedure.

It’s long been lobbied for by advocates who say that people diagnosed with degenerative conditions like dementia who want to have Maid are forced to end their lives sooner than they wish because they risk losing capacity to consent.

The federal law proposes a series of safeguards to prohibit carrying out an advance request in cases where the person demonstrates refusal or resistance “by words, sounds or gestures,” or in a case where a medical practitioner doubts whether the person is trying to refuse. In those cases, Maid cannot be attempted for another 30 days.

The bill would also require that two medical professionals assess that a person meets the criteria, including that they are suffering.

Fraser has urged Parliament to pass the legislation quickly. Maid is set to become legal for people with a mental illness on March 17 if the law isn’t changed before then.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: No charges for officer in Brantford arrest, but other police misconduct possible: SIU
stories.summary: Ontario's police watchdog says there are no reasonable grounds to charge an officer after a man's knee was broken during an arrest in Brantford, Ont., but other officers on the scene who did not turn on their body-worn cameras should be investigated for possible misconduct.
stories.author: Maan Alhmidi The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ontario’s police watchdog says there are no reasonable grounds to charge an officer after a man’s knee was broken during an arrest in Brantford, Ont., but other officers on the scene who did not turn on their body-worn cameras should be investigated for possible misconduct.

The Special Investigations Unit says police were on the lookout for the 45-year-old man on July 10 because of warrants for his arrest.

stories.title: Carney wants to warn China about interference. But will Xi Jinping listen?
stories.summary: Carney said he would have a 'frank and open' conversation about security and interference with President Xi
stories.author: Christopher Nardi
stories.content:
Ottawa — What happens when you deliver a message to someone who refuses to hear it?

Prime Minister Mark Carney May find out when he meets with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Beijing next week.

The Nov. 17 meeting will be an opportunity for Carney to advance talks between Canada and China for a new “strategic partnership” as the prime minister vies to double Canadian exports to non-U.S. countries by 2030.

On the eve of his departure on an eight-day trip through Europe and Asia, Carney told reporters that Canada faces less risk from China than the United States.

But he also said he would have a “frank and open” conversation about security and interference with President Xi.

“It will be an opportunity for us to strengthen the importance of not allowing foreign interference in Canada. I will raise that with him,” Carney said.

But his message appears set to fall on deaf ears.

The day after Carney’s proclamation, Chinese Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Guo Jiakun issued the same response the People’s Republic of China (PRC) always has when faced with allegations of foreign interference: denial.

“China upholds the principle of non-interference in other countries’ internal affairs. We have never had any interest in interfering in Canada’s internal affairs,” Guo Jiakun told Chinese reporters Wednesday, according to a transcript published byhis department.

But an editorial about Canada-China relations published in a Chinese Communist Party mouthpiece just two days earlier made a series of thinly veiled demands for Canada ahead of the bilateral meeting.

The China Daily newspaper editorial highlighted the “cherished” and “hard-won” momentum between China and Canada after years of diplomatic freeze. Ahead of Carney’s trip to China for Apec, it argued that “the economic logic of closer ties is difficult to dispute.”

But then, the warnings.

“Canada should consistently uphold its strategic autonomy,” reads the editorial. “Ottawa should provide Chinese companies with a nondiscriminatory business environment,” as well.

And Carney should not raise “so-called ‘human rights issues'” and concerns about regional security in the Asia-Pacific at the expense of the bilateral relationship, it warned.

“Ottawa should avoid strategic miscalculation on these issues, which could affect the broader China-Canada relationship,” the editorial concluded.

Spokespeople for the Chinese embassy in Ottawa did not respond to a request for further comment on the editorial and Guo Jiakun’s statement.

For Jody Thomas, former national security advisor to former prime minister Justin Trudeau, the Prc’s denial of interference all the while issuing domestic warnings to Canada come as no surprise.

“We are slowly rebuilding a diplomatic relationship. We are slowly rebuilding an economic relationship. That’s important, but the security threat persists,” she said in an interview.

“They’re willing to speak with Prime Minister Carney differently than they spoke to prime minister Trudeau, but their intentions don’t change.”

In Ottawa, there is little doubt that China is the most sophisticated and able committer of foreign interference and transnational repression in Canada. Csis has said so in its annual report for years. The Communications Security Establishment, the federal cyber intelligence agency, has said the same.

In 2025, the public inquiry into foreign interference in Canada concluded that the People’s Republic of China (PRC) “is the most active perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canada’s democratic institution.”

The PRC targets all levels of government, uses a wide range of actors, and works towards one goal at all times: protecting and promoting the Chinese Communist Party’s power and interests in China and around the world, according to the inquiry’s final report.

Days prior to Carney’s comments, Spanish NGO Safeguard Defenders released a report detailing how at least 18 Chinese overseas associations in Canada are operating partly as secret police stations monitoring diaspora communities, a significant expansion from the five identified in a previous 2022 report.

“Rather than closing the stations and respecting the sovereignty of others, the (Chinese Communist) Party doubled down and actively instructs authorities in China to expand their covert activities abroad and to govern the ‘overseas Chinese compatriots’ by the exact same standard set at home,” reads the report.

The current Chinese government, Thomas argued, will likely never cease its interference and espionage activities abroad, including in Canada.

So it’s up to Carney to set the correct guardrails as he deepens ties with the Asian economic behemoth.

Has the prime minister done so sufficiently with the Chinese government?

“Not from what’s been made public,” Thomas said. “But that doesn’t mean that it’s not happened.”

“You have to understand what you’re getting into, which doesn’t mean that you stopped trading with them, that you stopped talking to them. We have to be able to do two things at once,” she added.

Christopher Nardi is a senior parliamentary reporter with National Post in Ottawa. He has worked in both French and English media, speaks Italian and writes about politics, national security, justice and how things work (or don't) in government.

stories.title: Youth sentenced to two years for two Toronto-area synagogue shootings, police say
stories.summary: The chief of police in a region north of Toronto says a youth has been sentenced after he pleaded guilty to shooting at two synagogues.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The chief of police in a region north of Toronto says a youth has been sentenced after he pleaded guilty to shooting at two synagogues.

Paulo Da Silva, chief of York regional police, says the youth was sentenced on Tuesday to two years in a custodial facility followed by one year of community supervision for his role in the pair of shootings in March.

stories.author: Meredith Bond

The pilot who died in a Remembrance Day plane crash south of Quebec City has been identified.

The Quebec coroner’s office has named the victim as 68-year-old Daniel Parent of Saint-Georges, Que.

Spokesperson Nic Defalco says the plane broke away from the others as a planned part of the show, but was unable to rejoin the formation and crashed in a wooded area.

stories.title: Stellantis in default of funding agreement to retool Brampton plant, Joly notifies automaker
stories.summary: Stellantis idled plant in 2023, laying off about 3,000 workers, and finalized sale to defence contractor Roshel this week
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said on Thursday that Stellantis NV Stla-N has 30 days to reverse the sale of its auto plant in Brampton, Ont., or the federal government will take it to court to recoup the money it advanced to the company to refit the factory.

Ms. Joly told reporters that the government does not have the legal authority to block the sale of the plant to Roshel, a maker of armoured vehicles, but will enforce the terms of the funding agreement it signed with the automaker in 2022 and seek “hundreds of millions of dollars.” The company has breached its commitments, she said.

“I’m fed up. Workers are fed up,” she added.

In a statement late Thursday, Trevor Longley, Stellantis Canada’s chief executive officer, said the company would voluntarily repay $24-million in federal government support it received for Brampton’s original retooling plan. He didn’t provide any further details about the amount. The company had previously offered to repay the federal government, but without giving details.

“While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use, create new jobs with priority hiring consideration for Brampton workers and secure a long-term future for the site,” he said.

A meeting earlier in the day in Toronto between Ms. Joly, officials from Stellantis, the province of Ontario and the Unifor union failed to persuade the automaker to cancel the sale, announced on Monday.

Lana Payne, Unifor’s national president, expressed frustration that Thursday’s meeting, and several before it, failed to convince the company to change course. “We are in the same place,” Ms. Payne told reporters. “The company has sold the plant.”

Stellantis idled the Brampton plant in 2023, laying off about 3,000 workers, with the intent of retooling for the Jeep Compass. But that work was halted after the U.S placed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars in early 2025. Stellantis, later that year, said the Jeep would not be built in Brampton, but at an idled plant in Belvidere, Ill.

In September 2026, the carmaker said it had a preliminary agreement to sell the Brampton factory to Roshel. The companies said on Monday they finalized the sale, for an undisclosed amount.

About 2,200 workers are on layoff benefits. Stellantis told the union during September collective bargaining talks it had a preliminary agreement to sell the plant. The union has repeatedly urged the company to let the plant sit idle until trade relations with the U.S. improved. Ms. Payne said General Motors has done so with its idled plant in Ingersoll, Ont.

“This has been an extremely difficult time for our members,” she said, referring to the 9,000 Stellantis Canada employees.

Details of Stellantis’s government funding agreement are not public, but a heavily redacted copy obtained by The Globe and Mail shows the government gave as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor.

In a Thursday letter to Stellantis, Ms. Joly said she is ending the agreement’s resolution process, in which the government and the company were meeting to find other cars for the plant to assemble. A copy of the letter was provided to The Globe.

Stellantis has “abandoned the project and closed the Brampton plant,” she said in the letter.

“At no point have I or my office indicated support for a sale to Roshel, nor given any indication that such a sale would cure Stellantis’ existing breaches of the agreement,” Ms. Joly said. “This is a clear breach of the Agreement, and you were informed that I viewed any sale as a continuation of the existing breaches.”

Stellantis and Roshel said the sale clears a “path” for manufacturing to resume at the plant, in automotive and/or defence production. The companies said they have set up a partnership to explore defence industry collaboration.

The Globe has reported Stellantis will lease back about one-quarter of the plant.

Stellantis has proposed assembling Chinese cars from kits at the plant, an idea that was rejected by the government because it would involve few jobs and contribute little to the local economy. Ms. Joly said Chinese cars are not an option for the plant.

stories.title: Quebec pilot killed in Remembrance Day plane crash is identified
stories.summary: Quebec coroner’s office names victim as 68-year-old Daniel Parent of Saint-Georges, Que.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The pilot who died in a Remembrance Day plane crash south of Quebec City has been identified.

The Quebec coroner’s office named the victim on Thursday as 68-year-old Daniel Parent of St-Georges, Que.

Parent was taking part in a Remembrance Day commemoration with other pilots when his aircraft went down near the St-Georges airport.

The City of St-Georges said Parent was a member of the local Beauce flying club, and offered condolences to his family, the wider aviation community and to any veterans who were affected.

Flags have been lowered to half-mast at city hall and the airport, it said.

The Transportation Safety Board said Parent was flying his single-engine Mooney aircraft in formation with five other planes when the crash occurred.

Spokesperson Nic Defalco said the plane broke away from the others as a planned part of the show, but was unable to rejoin them.

“When attempting to rejoin the formation, the aircraft passed beneath the other aircraft and continued on that trajectory, ultimately crashing into a wooded area,” Defalco said.

Defalco said two investigators were at the scene on Thursday, and that it was too soon to hypothesize about what caused the crash.

Provincial police spokesperson Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said officers were meeting witnesses on Thursday. She said the force is still investigating for criminal elements, though she said crashes like this are rarely linked to a crime.

She said a coroner is also investigating the causes and circumstances surrounding the death.
