stories.title: Canada-U.S. travel turnoff reversing after U.S. midterm elections
stories.summary: Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal — The Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up, travel experts say.

Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh-straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada.

However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September.

At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new leisure bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier.

Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA

“It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency.

Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies.

“We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said.

“One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.”

For now, Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations.

Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism.

“Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc.

“There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the attitude of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.”

Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips.

“We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.CA.

Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years.

“I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’”

The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether.

“We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said.

“To market the U.S. is like dynamite.”

Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots.

Corporate travel continues to hum along, Durakovic said, with virtually no drop in Flight Centre bookings over the past couple of years.

“It’s still business as usual. You can’t exactly stop travelling to the U.S. because of politics,” she said.

The broader Canadian aversion to travelling south of the border combined with the shutdown of Cuban resorts amid a fuel shortage caused by an American oil blockade has pushed sun seekers farther afield.

Mexico, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica have surged in popularity, travel agents said. Portugal and Spain have also enjoyed a recent boost in Canadian visitors.

“Air Transat flights to Malaga are full,” said Sal Lato, who owns the Voyages Marlin travel agency franchise. Meanwhile, the leisure airline has cut the 36 flights a week it operated between Canada and Florida in late 2024 down to zero.

Not all winter escapees can simply point their finger at a fresh spot on the map and jet off for a getaway, extended or otherwise.

“There are still deep ties to many U.S. snowbird destinations,” said Stephen Fine, founder of Snowbird Advisor Insurance.

“They have friends who’ve been going there for years and they want to be able to spend their winters with that community,” he said of many Canadians.

Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh-straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada.
However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September.

At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new leisure bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier.
Trade War coverage on BNNBloomberg.CA
“It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency.

Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies.
“We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said.

“One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.”
For now, Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations.

Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism.
“Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc.

“There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the attitude of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.”
Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips.
“We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.CA.
Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years.
“I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’”
The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether.
“We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said.
“To market the U.S. is like dynamite.”

Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots.
Corporate travel continues to hum along, Durakovic said, with virtually no drop in Flight Centre bookings over the past couple of years.
“It’s still business as usual. You can’t exactly stop travelling to the U.S. because of politics,” she said.

The broader Canadian aversion to travelling south of the border combined with the shutdown of Cuban resorts amid a fuel shortage caused by an American oil blockade has pushed sun seekers farther afield.
Mexico, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica have surged in popularity, travel agents said. Portugal and Spain have also enjoyed a recent boost in Canadian visitors.

“Air Transat flights to Malaga are full,” said Sal Lato, who owns the Voyages Marlin travel agency franchise. Meanwhile, the leisure airline has cut the 36 flights a week it operated between Canada and Florida in late 2024 down to zero.

“They have friends who’ve been going there for years and they want to be able to spend their winters with that community,” he said of many Canadians.
“A lot of them own properties there. People want to drive down to their destination or have their vehicles with them for the winter,” he noted. For them, America May be the only option.

stories.title: Polar vortex splitting brings uncertainty to Canada’s winter outlook
stories.summary: Typically at this time of year the polar vortex would be strengthening. But the early split could bring a flush of early-winter cold air to parts of Canada.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
With a record-breaking El Niño and the earliest recorded splitting of the polar vortex duking it out, Canada could have a very unpredictable winter.

The split in the polar vortex, which occurs when the winds change directions in the stratosphere above the North Pole, was officially recorded on Nov. 10, two weeks earlier than ever before.

Typically at this time of year the polar vortex would be strengthening, building up cold air for later in the season. But the early split could bring a flush of early-winter cold air to parts of Canada.

Global News meteorologist Anthony Farnell said an early split in the polar vortex is particularly mind boggling considering we are currently experiencing the strongest El Niño on record .

Water surface temperature in the Pacific hit at least 0.5 C above average in El Niño years but this year, the temperature has hit 3.5 C above average.

“I guess the big question is, are these two separate occurrences, these two records happening all at once, or is there some sort of a correlation? And then as a meteorologist, what does that mean?” Farnell said.

Much of Canada typically experiences a milder winter in El Niño years, but Farnell said the disruption of the polar vortex could favour some very cold air for much of December.

If the cold air does come sweeping across Canada, he said it will take a few weeks.

“Some of our computer models are now starting to bring in some snow and some colder air at the end of November and early December so I think there’s going to be a lot of back and forth coming,” he said.

Meteorologists predict the polar vortex could begin recovering within a week, with stratospheric winds expected to strengthen. But Farnell said the phenomenon still creates a lot of uncertainty.

“Picture a figure skater that’s spinning around very quickly over the North Pole in this case. They can lose their balance and get disrupted, get off of their axle, but then they often come back and they recover. But at the same time, if you watch the Olympics and a figure skater loses their balance, they’re more likely to lose their balance again,” he said.

With two record forces competing against each other, Farnell said forecasting is getting more difficult.

“You throw in climate change and there’s a lot of variables, but it keeps me busy,” he said.

stories.title: Indigenous women’s groups call out limited funding in new federal budget
stories.summary: Indigenous women's groups say the new federal budget is harming the people they represent by not including funding targeted at violence and community support services.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Indigenous women’s groups say the new federal budget is harming the people they represent by not including funding targeted at violence and community support services.

Native Women’s Association of Canada president Josie Nepinak said Thursday the safety of Indigenous women must not depend on short-term funding cycles or be treated as a secondary factor in broader programs.

“We need sustained investment, clear accountability and a meaningful role for Indigenous women’s organizations in determining how these commitments will be implemented,” Nepinak said.

The federal budget identifies $3.6 million in funding for Indigenous women, including money to address the crisis of missing and murdered Indigenous women and to fund an alert system to help find women who go missing.

Nepinak said while some of the funding in the budget is welcome, more needs to be done to ensure “Indigenous women are not an afterthought.”

The collective of Indigenous women’s organizations from across the country said Thursday they’ve met with Crown-Indigenous Relations Minister Rebecca Alty to outline their priorities, but their requests were not reflected in the budget.

When asked for comment, Crown-Indigenous Relations pointed to other funding in the budget, including for the First Nations and Inuit Policing Program and for community-led safety initiatives.

“Ensuring the safety of Indigenous women, girls and 2SLGBTQI+ people remains an urgent priority for our government, and Budget 2026 builds on significant recent progress in expanding supports and advancing solutions shaped and led by Indigenous communities,” a spokesperson said.

Ontario Native Women’s Association CEO Cora McGuire-Cyrette said funding for Indigenous women is especially important as Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government works to speed up major project development.

“Canada is mobilizing billions to respond to economic threats and expand industries that put Indigenous women’s lives at risk,” she said.

“And we have yet to see the same urgency in addressing the threats we face every day. Canada cannot be strong when we, as Indigenous women, remain unsafe.”

Amnesty International has reported that binge drinking and drug use among transient resource sector workers, combined with high housing prices and a shortage of childcare services, can lead to the exploitation of Indigenous women and girls and make it harder for them to leave abusive relationships.

A 2019 inquiry into missing and murdered Indigenous women and girls concluded Indigenous women are 12 times more likely to go missing or be murdered than their non-Indigenous counterparts.

The final report was culled from the testimony of more than 2,380 family members, survivors, experts and knowledge-keepers brought together over two years to study the crisis and propose solutions.

Family members told the inquiry how intergenerational trauma and poverty compound the threats facing Indigenous women and girls, while knowledge-keepers described how women, through colonization, have been displaced from their traditional roles.

The commission brought forward 231 calls to action to address what it described as a genocide. Seven years later, little progress has been made on implementing them.

“We need government to take up its responsibilities and act on the solutions that generations of Indigenous women have put forward over the last three decades,” McGuire-Cyrette said.

“We have an opportunity today for generational change to create safer and more prosperous communities for all, but economic prosperity requires safety first, and investments into our safety must be recognized as nation-building.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Tretiak says Russia will seek compensation if barred from world juniors in Alberta
stories.summary: Moscow — Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak is threatening to seek compensation from Canada and push for the relocation or cancellation of next month's world junior championship in Alberta if Russia is barred from competing.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Moscow — Russian hockey federation president Vladislav Tretiak is threatening to seek compensation from Canada and push for the relocation or cancellation of next month’s world junior championship in Alberta if Russia is barred from competing.

The warning comes after Ottawa confirmed Wednesday that Russian players would not be permitted to compete, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas, despite last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling ordering Russia’s reinstatement to international hockey.

Russia’s state news agency Tass reported Thursday that Tretiak told a presidential sports council meeting Russia would also seek compensation from Germany, host of the 2027 men’s world championship, if denied participation.

“There are rules: if a team does not take the ice, it receives a forfeit loss and sanctions are imposed,” Tretiak told Tass in comments translated from Russian.

“The Iihf has a way out — either allow us to participate or, if we cannot enter Canada, move the championship, not hold it at all or impose sanctions on Canada.”

Tretiak, a legendary Soviet goaltender and three-time Olympic gold medallist, also told Tass the Russian federation had asked the International Ice Hockey Federation’s ethics council to investigate and punish national federations organizing boycotts of games against Russia.

Russian President Vladimir Putin told the same sports council meeting that national federations were refusing matches against Russian teams under pressure from their governments, according to Tass, which did not identify the countries involved.

Several hockey federations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to face Russia.

The dispute follows an Oct. 30 ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport ordering the Iihf to allow Russian teams to participate in five international tournaments, beginning with the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer on Dec. 26.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes would not be permitted to represent their countries in Canada as long as the war continues.

The federal government’s earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, raising questions about whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.

Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden clarified Monday that the exemption applied only to individual athletes, not national teams.

In a statement Wednesday, van Koeverden said Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would assess Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials individually to prevent them from competing at the men’s under-20 tournament in Alberta, even if they hold valid Canadian visas.

There are Russian players with valid visas competing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country’s three major junior hockey leagues.

Russian and Belarusian players were banned from the Chl’s import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year’s draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.

The controversy has also thrown Norway’s participation into question.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the world junior tournament at Norway’s expense.

Norway qualified for the championship and has said it still hopes to compete.

The Iihf has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field, and its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams. The federation did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the possibility of cancelling or relocating the tournament.

The world junior championship will conclude on Jan. 5.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Sexual assault suspect still at large: LPS
stories.summary: The London Police Service is still looking for a suspect wanted in connection with a sexual assault investigation.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The London Police Service is still looking for a suspect wanted in connection with a sexual assault investigation.

The investigation was launched on Nov. 5 after a break-and-enter on Blythwood Road . Police have now released photos of the suspect.

He is described as a Black man, around 25 years old, five-feet-eight-inches, with short, black hair, and dark eyes. At the time of the incident, he was clean shaven, wearing a white T-shirt and dark shorts with white trim. He was seen riding a black push scooter and was described as speaking English with an accent.

Anyone who was in the area at the time of the incident, Nov. 5 around 3 p.m., or who has surveillance footage of the incident is asked to contact the LPS.

stories.title: Nova Scotia and Massachusetts team up to explore offshore wind energy
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia and Massachusetts have struck a deal to learn more about the potential for the Canadian province’s emerging offshore wind industry.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The two jurisdictions announced today what they describe as a joint request for information from a variety of sources regarding the best ways to deliver clean energy to New England markets.

They say they want to hear from offshore wind and transmission developers, utilities, researchers, supply-chain companies, Indigenous communities, fisheries representatives, environmental groups and labour organizations.

Article continues below

The request for information stems from a memorandum of understanding signed earlier this year between Nova Scotia and Massachusetts.

The agreement comes as Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston is in Boston for an annual energy conference hosted by the New England-Canada Business Council.

Houston says Nova Scotia is currently working with Hydro-Québec and the states of Massachusetts and Vermont to advance planning for transmission and supply of clean energy generated off Nova Scotia’s coast.

The partnerships are part of Wind West, which is Nova Scotia’s ambitious plan to develop Canada’s first offshore wind-energy initiative.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Outlook and Teams down as widespread Microsoft outage hits multiple services
stories.summary: Microsoft Outlook, Teams, 365, OneDrive and Copilot were among the programs potentially affected, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks digital outages.
stories.author: Joshua Smith
stories.content:
The widespread outage that took multiple Microsoft products offline — including Outlook and Teams — Thursday afternoon and Friday morning has been largely resolved, according to Microsoft.

Microsoft has seen “broad recovery and stability” across services, the company stated in a post published to X at 11:40 a.m. on Friday.

“We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners,” stated the company in the post.

The company also stated that the issue was “not related to cyber or AI/agents.”

“The incident was introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” wrote Microsoft.

Services that also experienced disruptions included Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR, the company said on its website .

“We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas,” the tech conglomerate posted from its Microsoft 365 Status account on X shortly before 1 p.m. on Thursday.

Microsoft later confirmed the issue could affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity “for users in any region.”

Then, just before 2:15 p.m., the company said it had “paused all deployments,” moved “additional traffic off the affected infrastructure,” and that they were restarting affected servers to return them to service.

About 15 minutes later, Microsoft said it had identified the cause of the disruption.

“We determined the elevated load isn’t driven by an increase in traffic, but by a number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable; straining the remaining infrastructure,” the company wrote on social media .

Just after 7 p.m., Microsoft said its servers crashed again after being brought back online, and the company was limiting traffic. At about 9 p.m., Microsoft reported some success with repairs but needed to ensure their servers were properly operating before rolling out the fixes.

As of 7 a.m. on Friday, the company had posted that it was seeing “encouraging recovery progress.”

“Some users May still experience intermittent issues as recovery actions continue,” wrote the company in a post to X .

Microsoft Outlook, Teams, 365, OneDrive and Copilot were among the programs showing high volumes of users reporting outages, according to Downdetector , a crowdsourced website displaying data about digital outages.

This Lcbo location on Bloor Street in Toronto was hit with back-to-back thefts. (Google Maps)

November 12, 2026 at 2:33 p.m.

Toronto police are investigating two reported thefts that took place at the same Lcbo store on subsequent days in the city’s west end this week.

A video posted to X by the citizen group IntegrityTO shows the second theft on Monday afternoon from the location near Bloor Street and Royal York Road in the city’s Etobicoke region.

“Yet another brazen daylight robbery of the publicly-owned Lcbo,” the post says. “The thieves nicked at least 5 bottles of Remy Martin Vsop with a sticker price of $103 each, and several bottles of Macallan 12-year valued at $144 a pop.”

Yet another brazen daylight robbery of the publicly-owned @lcbo yesterday at Bloor & Royal York. A concerned customer asks the security guard to step in, but she lacks the will or skill to stop the theft – and scurries away. Even the demoralized employee is surprised at the… pic.twitter.com/o7Sy4ut3RD — IntegrityTO (@integrity_to) November 11, 2026

Daniel Tate, executive director of IntegrityTO, told National Post that “a follower of IntegrityTO … filmed the robbery, and sent me the video, which I reposted. “

A Toronto Police spokesperson confirmed in an email to National Post that “there are two online reports for Theft Under $5,000 (not a Robbery) from the same Lcbo establishment. One theft was reported to have occurred on November 8 and the other on November 9. Both investigations are ongoing.”

Police gave the approximately times of the incidents as 12:08 p.m. Sunday and 2:15 p.m. Monday, about 26 hours apart.

Legally, theft involves taking items, whereas robbery includes force or the threat of force.

In the video, which had close to 200,000 views on X as of Thursday afternoon, two individuals in winter coats, their faces obscured by their hoods, can be seen stuffing bottles into bags and an Lcbo shopping basket. One of them says: “I apologize.”

They make their way out of the store, almost running into a security guard, who recoils and puts her hands up to her face as one of the men says: “Watch out watch out watch out.”

The person making the video then follows the two men into the street, trailing the one with the basket as they head in opposite directions.

stories.title: Widespread outage hits Outlook, other Microsoft apps
stories.summary: A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant’s suite of apps. As of around 1:30 p.m. ET, more than 120,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook — with many saying they couldn’t send and […]
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
A widespread outage hit Microsoft platforms including Outlook on Thursday, with many users encountering trouble using their email accounts and other errors across the tech giant’s suite of apps.

As of around 1:30 p.m. ET, nearly 130,000 users on outage tracker Downdetector reported problems accessing Outlook — with many saying they couldn’t send and receive emails, or encountering delays.

Thousands also reported issues with Microsoft’s workplace messaging app Teams, as well as its AI assistant Copilot and wider Microsoft 365 services.

Microsoft said that it was investigating disruptions, notably related to its email and Teams applications.

In updates posted on social media, Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft said it was aware of users “experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas.”

Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” — which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors.” The company determined a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.

Microsoft did not immediately provide more information around what might be causing that failure, but added that it was testing a fix.

“We’re aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact,” the Microsoft 365 Status account wrote on X.

Earlier in the day, the company said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

stories.title: Network of deepfake videos spreading falsehoods about trade war with U.S.: report
stories.summary: Ottawa - A new report says a network that's likely based outside of Canada is using deepfakes to spread "politically divisive" content to Canadians.
stories.author: Anja Karadeglija The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - A network that’s likely based outside of Canada is using deepfakes to spread “politically divisive” content to Canadians, says a new report released Thursday.

The report from McGill University’s Centre for Media, Technology and Democracy says the network uses deepfakes of real influencers. It combines the faces of real people with fake lip movements and voices generated by AI.

“We do not know what the network is for, but its operators are willing to steal faces and spread falsehoods that set Canadians against the United States, against their own government and against each other,” the report says.

Using footage of real people likely keeps the videos from being flagged as AI, the report says, noting that TikTok has only labelled four per cent of such videos as AI.

It says many of the videos focus on the U.S.-Canada trade war and the most-watched videos include false information.

They include a video about a non-existent 48-hour ultimatum from U.S. President Donald Trump which falsely says Prime Minister Mark Carney responded by cancelling $8 billion in U.S. defence contracts.

“This never happened, but the story was shared in 161 videos on 129 accounts and played 5.1 million times,” the report says.

The people who comment on the videos don’t seem to realize they are fake, with only 6.3 per cent saying the video is inauthentic or propaganda.

“The rest agree or argue with the content in the video, and one in ten speaks to the narrator as a real person: thanking them, praising them, or telling them to check their facts,” the report says.

The videos don’t have a consistent perspective on the trade war. The report says the accounts take both sides, “and narrators switch nationality too, presenting themselves as Canadian in some videos and American in others. The effect is that Canadians are shown fabricated and misleading claims on both sides of the trade debate.”

The network includes nearly 300 TikTok and Instagram accounts and has posted more than 3,201 videos that have been seen 22.1 million times in the past three months.

The report says it’s not clear who is behind the network but it is “almost certainly” run outside of North America.

“Its posting and registration times do not fit North American time zones,” the report says. “Activity drops off during the night in East and Southeast Asia, and some accounts carry Chinese-language settings or a registration in China, the only lead we have on a country.”

The motivation of those behind the network is also unclear.

The accounts don’t push the narratives of any foreign government and have not been monetized, the report says, adding the network could be growing audiences to use later.

It says the network could also be used for testing a tool or service, or someone May be paying those behind the operation to influence Canadians.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Using footage of real people likely keeps the videos from being flagged as AI, the report says, noting that TikTok has only labelled four per cent of such videos as AI.

It says many of the videos focus on the U.S.-Canada trade war and the most-watched videos include false information.

“Its posting and registration times do not fit North American time zones,” the report says. “Activity drops off during the night in East and Southeast Asia, and some accounts carry Chinese-language settings or a registration in China, the only lead we have on a country.”
The motivation of those behind the network is also unclear.
The accounts don’t push the narratives of any foreign government and have not been monetized, the report says, adding the network could be growing audiences to use later.
It says the network could also be used for testing a tool or service, or someone May be paying those behind the operation to influence Canadians.

stories.title: The Toronto jewellery designer putting a high-fashion spin on wearable tech
stories.summary: Steff Eleoff first launched the Elixir, a sculptural sterling silver cover that slips over the Oura Ring, in February
stories.author: Randi Bergman
stories.content:
Toronto jewellery designer Steff Eleoff wanted to wear an Oura Ring, but everything about it went against her design ethos.

The popular health tracker has found a fanbase among women seeking to better understand their menstrual cycles, fertility and hormonal changes. But its chunky metallic band leaves much to be desired. A scroll through TikTok turns up plenty of variations on the question “Why is the Oura Ring so ugly?” from those looking for something sleeker, chicer and less obviously techy.

Enter 28-year-old Eleoff, known for her liquid-metal earrings, pendants and rings. When she uploaded a TikTok video earlier this year lamenting the same, she was flooded with messages asking for her version of a stylish solution. Eleoff, it turned out, already had something in the works: a sculptural sterling silver cover, rendered in her signature drippy aesthetic, that slipped over the Oura Ring. She launched it two weeks later, in February.

“We worked around the clock to make it happen because we knew tech companies moved fast and I knew someone else was going to have this idea, too,” said the designer of her 15-person Etobicoke team. The first 100 Elixir covers sold out in 48 hours, and she followed them up with another style, the Flow, two weeks later. Eleoff sold more than 2,000 covers in those first weeks.

In 2015, the Apple Watch launched to great fanfare, with fashion industry endorsements and, later that year, an Hermès-branded edition with leather straps for the luxury consumer. Since then, the wearable tech category has boomed among biohackers, productivity obsessives and the wellness-minded: According to a 2025 report from Canadian research firm Leger, roughly 40 per cent of Canadians use wearable technology, with smartwatches being the most popular choice. Smart rings, meanwhile, are gaining ground: Oura doubled its revenue for the second year in a row in 2024. As of earlier this year, 72 per cent of the Finnish company’s members worldwide are women, with 31 per cent age 29 or younger.

Despite the mass adoption of wearable tech, there’s still a glaring divide between fashion and function. Outside of Oura’s 2022 collaboration with Gucci – a special-edition smart ring detailed with gold – options for elevating the devices are largely limited to Etsy sellers with one-off designs and a handful of fine jewellers with ring covers that push the investment to a new level. Fine jewellers Suzanne Kalan and Logan Hollowell, for example, frame the tracker with pavé diamonds . Eleoff’s tech covers, which have since expanded into a full collection of styles, start at just more than $300.

Eleoff, who has been designing jewellery since 2020, already counted celebrities such as Kylie Jenner and Olivia Rodrigo among her fans, and Selfridges in London and Kith in Tokyo among her retailers. The success of her brand’s tech ring covers has brought even more attention, resulting in Holt Renfrew pop-ups at the store’s Toronto Bloor Street and Yorkdale locations ahead of the holiday season, and a New York showcase sponsored by Shopify earlier this month.

She credits the success of her ring covers to how quickly her team was able to respond to a conversation already in full swing. But the process wasn’t without growing pains. The initial orders ballooned far beyond the studio’s capacity and the wait for a cover stretched to several months, drawing frustration from customers online.

“It was so fascinating as a business owner to learn this part of the business. We can sell so much and see all these numbers expanding, but then it’s like, ‘Oh, wait, now we’re refunding all these people. What do we do?’” she said.

The designer took to social media to explain the delays.

“We’ve been transparent from the beginning of starting the business, when I was in my parents’ basement and my mom was helping me ship packages. We filmed all of that.” With an expanded production team and interest trickling over into other areas of the brand, such as birthstone letter necklaces and new pieces inspired by bodies of water , Eleoff said she plans to keep production in Canada.

“Everything is made by hand,” she said. “We’re a team that’s slow and intentional with what we’re making.”

With Canada’s wearable tech market projected to grow by roughly 15 per cent by 2031 , there’s plenty of opportunity to bring more stylish alternatives to market. And Eleoff is open to expanding beyond rings.

“If Apple called me, I’d do it in two seconds,” she said.

stories.title: A Microsoft 365 outage is hitting users in regions around the world
stories.summary: More than a hundred thousand users are reporting issues with Microsoft systems as the company says it is working to address the problems being seen around the world.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
More than a hundred thousand users are reporting issues with Microsoft systems as the company says it is working to address the problems being seen around the world.

Reports of the apparent connectivity issues began spiking shortly after noon Eastern.

“We’re investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods in the Americas. More details can be found in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543,” Microsoft said in a statement on X.

“While we’re working to mitigate impact, we’ve confirmed the issue may affect Microsoft 365 service connectivity for users in any region, more information will be provided in the Microsoft 365 admin center under EX1550543.”

Shortly after, the company added: “We’ve determined a portion of infrastructure is experiencing elevated load across multiple regions, which is likely contributing to the connectivity errors.”

Around 1:30 pm Eastern, the website Downdetector said there were more than 100,000 reported outages.

More to come.

stories.title: Most Western Canadians say ditching time change was the ‘right move’: poll
stories.summary: After B.C., Alberta and Manitoba ditched the time change this fall, an Angus Reid Institute poll delved into how residents are reacting.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
All of Canada’s Western provinces have officially abandoned the practice of changing their clocks twice per year, and a recent survey found that most people in B.C., Alberta and Manitoba are glad it’s over.

The provincial governments of B.C. , Alberta and Manitoba separately announced they would end the semi-annual time change and adopt permanent daylight saving time in recent months. This meant that when clocks were adjusted in most of Ontario and eastward earlier this month , the time remained unchanged in the Prairies and B.C.

Stopping the practice was favoured by most people surveyed in the three provinces that ended the practice this year, according to the poll. In B.C., only 18 per cent said they favoured switching back-and-forth, according to the results of a poll released Thursday by the Angus Reid Institute. Twenty-one per cent of people in Alberta and Manitoba preferred to fall back and spring forward.

More than 70 per cent of respondents in the three provinces agreed that it was the “right move” to opt out of changing the time this fall. Results were mixed regarding if they preferred the earlier sunrises of standard time or the later sunsets of daylight time.

Forty per cent of British Columbians polled said they preferred the later sunsets. This figure has dropped by around 10 per cent when compared to a poll conducted in March.

Slightly more than 30 per cent wanted to see the sun rise earlier in that province, the fall survey found.

Manitoban opinions stayed generally the same when compared to the results from last spring, with 49 per cent in favour of permanent daylight saving time. The earlier poll said 52 per cent of people reported they would rather see the sun out later in the day.

A quarter of those surveyed earlier this month in Manitoba favoured year-round standard time.

Results in Alberta represented “a shift in public opinion compared to the spring,” Angus Reid wrote. Its March poll found 47 per cent of people in the province preferred daylight saving time. That level of approval depleted to 33 per cent in November.

Around two-fifths of people surveyed in Alberta said they would prefer always being on standard time.

Saskatchewan dropped the practice in 1966, when the province adopted permanent standard time. More than half of residents reported that they would choose to use standard time, with 41 per cent saying they would prefer switching to daylight saving time.

More than half of people in all three provinces said they have faced challenges after not turning their clocks back.

The survey found that 59 per cent of people in B.C., 64 per cent of those in Manitoba and 65 per cent of Alberta residents dealt with challenges or annoyances. The most common complaint, at 42 per cent, was that technology did not keep up. Some smart devices fell back , despite the provincial decisions.

Less than one third of respondents also cited the darker mornings and issues with calendars , meetings and scheduling as frequent annoyances they faced. Being out of the usual routines with Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes was also a point of frustration for 18 per cent of respondents.

The Angus Reid Institute conducted an online survey from Nov. 3-6, 2026, among a randomized sample of 1,634 Canadian adults. Respondents are drawn from the Angus Reid Forum , a large-scale online panel developed to include Canadian residents in each of the 343 federal ridings in Canada.

For comparison purposes only, a probability sample of this size would carry a margin of error of +/- 2 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. Discrepancies in or between totals are due to rounding. The survey was self-commissioned and paid for by the Angus Reid Institute.

Stopping the practice was favoured by most people surveyed in the three provinces that ended the practice this year, according to the poll. In B.C., only 18 per cent said they favoured switching back-and-forth, according to the results of a poll released Thursday by the Angus Reid Institute. Twenty-one per cent of people in Alberta and Manitoba preferred to fall back and spring forward.

More than 70 per cent of respondents in the three provinces agreed that it was the “right move” to opt out of changing the time this fall. Results were mixed regarding if they preferred the earlier sunrises of standard time or the later sunsets of daylight time.
Forty per cent of British Columbians polled said they preferred the later sunsets. This figure has dropped by around 10 per cent when compared to a poll conducted in March.
Slightly more than 30 per cent wanted to see the sun rise earlier in that province, the fall survey found.

Manitoban opinions stayed generally the same when compared to the results from last spring, with 49 per cent in favour of permanent daylight saving time. The earlier poll said 52 per cent of people reported they would rather see the sun out later in the day.
A quarter of those surveyed earlier this month in Manitoba favoured year-round standard time.

Results in Alberta represented “a shift in public opinion compared to the spring,” Angus Reid wrote. Its March poll found 47 per cent of people in the province preferred daylight saving time. That level of approval depleted to 33 per cent in November.
Around two-fifths of people surveyed in Alberta said they would prefer always being on standard time.

Saskatchewan dropped the practice in 1966, when the province adopted permanent standard time. More than half of residents reported that they would choose to use standard time, with 41 per cent saying they would prefer switching to daylight saving time.
More than half of people in all three provinces said they have faced challenges after not turning their clocks back.

The survey found that 59 per cent of people in B.C., 64 per cent of those in Manitoba and 65 per cent of Alberta residents dealt with challenges or annoyances. The most common complaint, at 42 per cent, was that technology did not keep up. Some smart devices fell back , despite the provincial decisions.

Less than one third of respondents also cited the darker mornings and issues with calendars , meetings and scheduling as frequent annoyances they faced. Being out of the usual routines with Ontario, Quebec and the Maritimes was also a point of frustration for 18 per cent of respondents.

The Angus Reid Institute conducted an online survey from Nov. 3-6, 2026, among a randomized sample of 1,634 Canadian adults. Respondents are drawn from the Angus Reid Forum , a large-scale online panel developed to include Canadian residents in each of the 343 federal ridings in Canada.

stories.title: Former B.C. minister Bailey says David Eby was inauthentic during failed campaign
stories.summary: Victoria - One of David Eby's former top lieutenants says he came across as inauthentic during the BC Ndp's election campaign, calling last month's crushing defeat a "harsh judgment" on the outgoing premier's leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.
stories.author: Wolfgang Depner The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - One of David Eby’s former top lieutenants said he came across as inauthentic during the BC Ndp’s failed election campaign, calling last month’s crushing defeat a “harsh judgment” on the outgoing premier’s leadership and his decision to call the snap vote.

Brenda Bailey, who served as finance and jobs minister under Eby, delivered her post-mortem on the Oct. 24 election in an interview in which she also said she had successfully undergone cancer treatment and was taking a break from politics to enter the private sector.

Bailey, who did not seek re-election in Vancouver-South Granville, said there had been “a lot of piling on Eby and it feels a little unfair” — but nevertheless contrasted Eby’s campaign persona with premier-designate Lorne Doerkson’s, calling the B.C. Conservative leader a “deeply authentic man” and “very likable.”

Doerkson’s appointment as interim leader of the Conservatives, she said, was a “brilliant” move by the party.

“I look at (the election) through the lens of authenticity, and I don’t think Eby came across as authentic,” she said Thursday.

Eby stepped down as NDP leader on election night after the scale of the Conservative victory became clear, having secured a two-thirds majority with 64 seats, while the NDP ranks were decimated from 47 to 27.

It ended nine years of NDP rule, with Eby at the helm since 2022.

Bailey singled out two moments as emblematic of Eby’s authenticity problem — his Sept. 22 announcement of the election outside Government House, and a pre-election appearance where he wore a red-and-black checked jacket and the audience was warmed up by a parody rapper who mocked U.S. President Donald Trump.

She called the election announcement where Eby justified the snap vote by citing the threat posed by Trump “perhaps the weakest presser I’ve ever seen the premier give.”

“It was kind of clear from that very first presser that Eby’s explanation of why to go now wasn’t resonating, even with him,” she said.

Bailey said Eby had “many redeeming qualities,” but the “lumber-jacket-at-the-border version of David Eby, it doesn’t work.”

“Going down to the border and wearing that coat, that’s not who David Eby is and people could tell. So it’s less a criticism of him as a human than what he specifically did during this election run, not having resonated with the public, in my opinion.”

She said Eby used explanations to justify the election that he believed would poll well, rather than what he knew to be true.

She described the election call as “quite defensible” because there was “a real sense of instability” around the government with its one-seat majority, which was hurting its ability to respond to U.S. tariffs.

Bailey said Eby was struggling to “tap dance” to keep the party together at a time when everyone in the caucus effectively had a policy veto.

But Eby’s explanation to the public that he needed to “build a firebreak” against Trump-style politics coming to British Columbia “didn’t work at all” once Doerkson became the Conservatives’ interim leader.

The day that Eby called the vote, Doerkson called Trump an “absolute bully” and said Canada would never be the 51st state.

“I think it was strategically brilliant to put Lorne Doerkson as the candidate,” Bailey said of the Conservatives’ choice after the resignation of Kerry-Lynne Findlay two days before the election call.

Bailey also said the decision to go to the polls was made at an NDP caucus meeting held on Sunday, Sept. 20, even though the Conservatives had not yet announced their interim leader.

The former minister said she did not take part in the meeting as she was “quite sick” but the decision was shared with her later.

Bailey also said her cancer treatment “was fully successful.”

“They detected it very early. I had a surgery and the surgery got all the cancer and I’ve just been recovering from surgery. I haven’t had to have chemotherapy, I haven’t had to have radiation,” she said.

“And I would say as of last week, I feel fully back to normal. So I’ve been very, very lucky.”

While she is still a member of the NDP, “time will tell” if she remains in the party, which she said runs the risk of being in opposition for a very long time if it moves too far to the left.

“I struggle with where I live politically,” she said.

“I want to be a member of a party that is fiscally responsible, and has strong social goals,” she said. “That is the party I want and I think that is the party that I think most British Columbians want and often struggle to find.”

Jennifer Whiteside has been named as the BC Ndp’s interim leader.

When Bailey was asked about the odds of her throwing her hat in the ring as leader, she said “absolutely none.”

“You couldn’t make me,” she said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. A previous version incorrectly reported that an appearance by David Eby at the United States border occurred during the British Columbia election campaign. In fact, it was in early September.

stories.title: Faster money transfers with RTR will take a while to adopt, says Scotiabank
stories.summary: A new report from Scotiabank says Payments Canada's recently announced upgraded digital payments framework could take several months or years to become the norm.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Payments Canada’s recently announced upgraded digital payments framework Real-Time Rail (RTR) aims to streamline how money moves electronically between consumers and businesses, but it could take several months or years to become the norm for most major financial institutions and banks.

That’s according to a report released Thursday from Scotiabank , and authored by senior economist David Cimon, which says Ottawa’s plans to see more “instant” payments will be anything but an instantaneous rollout across Canada.

“This system launches with a lot of promise, namely the ability to conduct instantaneous payments between both businesses and consumers, 24/7,” said Cimon in the report.

“While the option of instant payments will help, structural changes by businesses will take longer than merely activating the system.”

Payments Canada on Monday announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system, allowing consumers and businesses to send and receive payments instantly.

From gig workers getting paid instantly to Canadians being able to transfer money between their accounts much faster, the new system could have impacts on how Canadians move their money.

RTR is “an important step in modernizing Canada’s payment infrastructure,” Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Monday, as the central bank brought the new payment system under its formal oversight.

Canadians will be able to send and receive money “any hour, any day, all year round,” Finance Minister Francois-Phillipe Champagne said, adding that the RTR system was “built around international standards.”

Scotiabank’s report says the RTR system, in theory, will be beneficial to both consumers and businesses, but there will be delays in adopting it.

For one, not all banks and financial institutions will be using it immediately, and if anything, it will likely take Canada’s biggest banks the longest to utilize the RTR system.

Canada’s largest commercial bank, RBC, says it plans to introduce the RTR into its systems in the second quarter of 2027, and although most other big banks are expected to join shortly after, including Scotiabank, TD, BMO and CIBC, they have not given any specific timelines as of yet.

The only participants in the RTR’s initial launch are as follows:

Wealthsimple

Questbank

Peoples Trust Company

Paramount Commerce

KOHO

DoBusiness.com

Digital Commerce Bank

Bank of America

The big Canadian banks were excluded from this phase because Payments Canada wants to ease into the RTR system roll out by using smaller Canadian institutions along with Bank of America to test the system’s stability.

“None of the Big-5 banks are part of this wave. In general, to use RTR, both parties’ financial institutions must be a member. This will limit volumes until large institutions join and network effects occur,” said Cimon in the report.

“The entry of new participants later in 2027 will likely be a necessary condition for transaction volumes to increase meaningfully.”

“While there is understandable excitement about use cases for RTR, its real ability to transform the payments system will be limited by business’ own abilities to adapt their processes.”

Businesses and consumers who rely on cash or paper cheques for certain transactions are “dedicated users” and may also be slower to adopt the RTR system into their regular financial routines — even if the RTR makes things more efficient and convenient, the report says.

Scotiabank cites its own data along with that of Payments Canada, saying that cash payments continue to be the most popular form of physical or paper payments, but commercial cheques comprise the overwhelming majority of all paper payment values.

The average transaction size or value of cash in 2025 was roughly $24, while the average commercial cheque was around $13,600.

Cash may continue to have its benefits for some users, including non-traceability and non-dependence on an intermediary, but the report says that cheques don’t have the same value and are “a prime case for disruption.”

“Cheques are slow, both in terms of transit time from payer-to-payee and in time to clear once cashed. They also rely on either dealing directly with a financial institution or using expensive cheque-cashing services,” said Cimon in the report.

“While it’s unlikely that systems built on RTR will replace commercial cheque use entirely, this is an area with a high market value and a large degree of potential improvement.”

But getting companies to move away from paper cheques for business transactions may be a challenge, especially for larger ones, because it means rewiring how their financial back offices operate. Day-to-day bookkeeping, tracking bill payments and managing multi-day clearing times can’t just be flipped like a light switch — even if a faster option like RTR is available.

RTR also has potential benefits for employees because it can help them get paid much sooner, but the report says this will also take a while to become a reality for the majority of workers that get paid through their employer’s payroll systems.

That’s mainly because businesses will need to make structural changes to integrate RTR that will take “longer than merely activating the system.”

“The prospect of instantaneous payment of wages is unlikely for many employees, as this requires both the logistical ability to process payroll in real-time but also the willingness of employers to move off the standard 2-week payroll schedule,” said Cimon in the report.

“Similarly, in business-to-business transactions, accounts payable departments will still need time to process invoices.”

stories.title: These are the most stolen vehicles in Canada
stories.summary: Équité Association's annual ranking of the cars most targeted by thieves features many returnees
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
In its annual Top 10 most stolen vehicles in Canada list released this week, Équité Association ranked Honda’s CR-V as No. 1 most often targeted by thieves.

Last year, 2,137 of the more than 550,000 registered and insured CR-V models in Canada were stolen, the not-for-profit organization supporting Canadian property and casualty insurers said, noting that its “ongoing security weaknesses leave them vulnerable.”

The popular mid-size SUV was the most stolen on Équité’s 2021 and 2022 lists, No. 4 in 2023 and third in 2024.

Vehicle theft in Canada has been on the decline for the past couple of years, according to the federal government and the insurance industry, but plenty continue to be stolen and some, like the CR-V, far more than others.

The Civic, another Honda model and a regular on recent lists, came in second with 1,813 thefts in 2025.

Regionally, both models were in the Top 5 for most stolen in Ontario, Quebec and Atlantic Canada. All of Alberta’s most stolen vehicles were pickup trucks.

Rounding out the Top 5 are the Toyota RAV 4 (1,147 thefts), and two pickup trucks — the Ram 1500 (1,072 thefts) and the Ford 150 (1,057 thefts) models.

Not far behind was the Lexus RX Series (964), with Équité highlighting that “luxury lines … are experiencing disproportionately high theft rates (over 11 per cent ) relative to the number of insured vehicles” because they’re being specifically targeted by organized crime groups to be sold domestically and internationally.

The Lexus TX series, for example, tops Équité’s theft frequency list at 11.37 per cent, followed closely by the Toyota Land Cruiser Wagon (11.32 per cent), both of which have starting sticker prices over $70,000.

The rest of the most stolen list, in order, includes the Chevrolet/GMC Silverado and Sierra 1500 series trucks (927), Toyota Tundra (787), Jeep Wrangler (603), and Hyundai Elantra (484).

Many of those same models were highlighted in a New York Times investigative story that found Interpol received 4,798 reports of stolen Canadian vehicles turning up in Russia from February 2024 to July 2026.

“There are a lot of cars in Canada, and stealing them there is very convenient,” said Daniil Aleynik, a Russian national who was being held in Ukraine on charges of participating in an international vehicle theft plot.

In September, Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree reported that the National Action Plan onCombating Auto Theft had resulted in a 16 per cent decline in car thefts in 2024 and 2025.

About a month earlier, the RCMP reported that its Project NoCargo, launched in June 2025 with the aim of tracking down suspicious vehicle exports, “led to the interception and recovery of 392 vehicles, with an estimated total value of $28 million in Halifax, Montreal, Toronto, and Vancouver.”

The Cbsa also intercepted 1,590 stolen vehicles in railyards and ports in 2025 and 1,133 since the beginning of 2026.

As reported earlier by National Post, the Insurance Bureau of Canada said theft claims fell 24 per cent year-over-year in 2025 and the total theft-related losses fell by almost $370 million last year. However, despite the decline, the IBC also said auto theft costs remain significantly above historical levels, with claims up 38 per cent over the past decade.

Équité, in its 2025 annual report released in February, highlighted an 18 per cent year-over-year decrease in national auto thefts from 2024, but it, too, warned the costly problem persists.

“Despite considerable collective efforts to combat auto theft, criminals continue to profit from the $900 million annually in stolen vehicles,” President and CEO Heather Masterson said in a press release, noting “enforcement alone” is not enough.

Vehicles of all makes and models must be made harder to steal, she said.

“It requires a collective, preventative shift across the entire ecosystem, including working in consultation with Transport Canada to update and align the Motor Vehicle Safety Regulations with global best practices. Canadians deserve peace of mind; they deserve to feel safe.”

An Équité survey this summer found that a growing number of Canadians (66 per cent) support “a coordinated response among governments, manufacturers, law enforcement, and vehicle owners.”

The same survey found 64 per cent of Canadians say they are concerned about their family’s safety when it comes to auto theft.

“Those concerns reflect the current auto theft landscape where thieves are using key fob relay attacks and reprogramming to easily gain access to vehicles,” Équité vice-president Bryan Gast said. “Systemic vulnerabilities must be addressed at the manufacturing stage to prevent vehicles from being stolen in the first place.”

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

stories.title: Three arrested after personal data stolen and sold from Quebec's auto insurance board
stories.summary: Montreal - Three people are facing criminal charges after personal data was allegedly stolen from Quebec's auto insurance board and then sold.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
In a news release, the provincial anti-corruption unit says those arrested were a former employee and her two accomplices.

Police allege the employee in question used her position at the auto insurance board to access a confidential database and sell information to the two accomplices.

Article continues below

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

All three are facing charges of a breach of trust by a public official and unauthorized use of computers.

The former employee is also facing fraud charges.

The three accused will appear at the Montreal courthouse on Dec. 17.

According to the news release, the Canadian Border Services Agency tipped off the anti-corruption unit during a firearms smuggling investigation.

The unit collaborated with the auto insurance board’s investigation department to find the origin of the data leak.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Canadian travel to U.S. went up in October, data shows
stories.summary: October also saw more Americans travel to Canada compared to the same period in 2025, with 1.5 million trips marking an increase of 8.1 per cent compared to October 2025.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Even before the U.S. midterm elections saw Democrats sweep both houses of Congress, travel by Canadians to the U.S. was going up in October, data from Statistics Canada shows.

Canadian travel south of border had been steadily declining since U.S. President Donald Trump launched his trade war against Canada, with many vowing to buy Canadian and travel in Canada instead of going to the U.S.

In 2025, return trips by Canadians from the U.S. were down 25.4 per cent compared to 2024.

However, that trend appears to be reversing slightly.

In October, Canadians took 1.9 million trips to the United States by automobile and air, up three per cent from the same month in 2025. Return trips by road were up 2.2 per cent in the same period, with air travel going up 5.6 per cent.

While this marked the seventh consecutive month of increasing travel to the U.S., road travel was still down 29 per cent compared to 2024 while air travel was down 19 per cent.

Canadians also took more trips overseas, with one million overseas return trips by air in October 2026, up 0.5 per cent compared to October 2025.

Thanksgiving Monday, Oct. 12, was the busiest travel day, with 172,900 return trips from abroad by Canadian residents.

October also saw more Americans travel to Canada compared to the same period in 2025, with 1.5 million trips marking an increase of 8.1 per cent compared to October 2025.

Of these, 1.1 million trips (8.7 per cent increase) were by automobile and 414,400 trips were by air (6.5 per cent increase).

Friday, Oct. 9, the day before the Columbus Day long weekend in the U.S., saw the highest single day count of Americans visiting Canada at 102,100.

Travel by Canadians to the U.S. bottomed out in July 2025, with border crossing volumes nearly one-third below those reported in July 2024. Since 1972, when digital recordkeeping began for border crossings, year-over-year decline of more than 30 per cent was recorded for only other occasion.

It was for September 2001, following the Sept. 11 attacks in New York City.

stories.title: Ontario to cap Osap growth at career colleges following massive increases
stories.summary: The legislation is set to include the as-yet undefined cap, limit Osap funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Career colleges in Ontario could soon be subject to limits on the growth of students funded by financial aid, following explosive increases in the sector that prompted the government to call in the police.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that legislation will be introduced on Monday, saying the significant concerns around Ontario Student Assistance Program usage in the sector are far more widespread than first suspected and the bill is intended to increase oversight and accountability.

“What we have found here are not minor administrative concerns, but rather co-ordinated, sophisticated efforts to take advantage of students and taxpayers for personal gain,” he said Thursday at a press conference.

Career Colleges Ontario, which processes Osap applications for the schools, has removed 24 more campuses from their membership, with an additional 13 under review, Quinn said. The association has also identified concerns about backdating applications at 33 additional campuses, he said.

“This behaviour is despicable, and it must be stopped,” Quinn said.

The legislation is set to include the as-yet undefined cap, limit Osap funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location, and prohibit them from operating unrelated businesses on campus.

Quinn has said that concerns about career colleges being co-located with immigration and recruitment firms are among issues raised by an ongoing Kpmg audit of the sector.

Critics say the problem is one of the government’s own making, allowing online-only programs to qualify for Osap in the first place during the COVID-19 pandemic and not watching closely enough as growth skyrocketed.

“If the minister is indicating that this is so systemic, how come they let it get this bad?” Liberal critic Tyler Watt said.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said oversight measures proposed in the bill are important, but it never should have come to this.

“This bill is a classic case of closing the barn door after the horses are gone,” she said.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

While the Kpmg audit is ongoing, Quinn has paused Osap payments to all private post-secondary institutions, causing some students to drop out and some colleges to consider closing their doors.

Quinn has said the government is working on securing low-interest loans for students through banks until the pause is lifted in the new year, but he has so far not indicated a timeline for that.

Colleges and students are calling on the government to weed out any bad actors in a way that doesn’t also penalize institutions and students who follow the rules. Premier Doug Ford has said Kpmg auditors have been tasked with clearing low-risk schools first.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is holding innocent students hostage with the Osap pause.

“The rent doesn’t wait,” he said. “The grocery bill doesn’t wait. The kids’ clothes don’t wait, and this government’s saying, ‘wait,'” Fraser said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Apotex reports quarterly profit of $100.8-million, raises guidance for full year
stories.summary: Revenue totalled $852.9-million in second quarter, up from $843.5-million in the same quarter last year
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Apotex Health Corp. Aptx-T raised its guidance for its full year as it reported a second-quarter profit of $100.8-million, up from $82.9-million a year earlier.

The drug company says the profit amounted to 41 cents per diluted share for the quarter compared with 43 cents per diluted share a year ago when it had fewer shares outstanding.

Revenue totalled $852.9-million for the quarter, up from $843.5-million in the same quarter last year.

On an adjusted basis, Apotex says it earned 57 cents per diluted share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of 61 cents per diluted share a year earlier.

In its updated outlook, it says it now expects full-year revenue growth of nine to 10 per cent, up from earlier expectations for upper mid-single digit growth of seven to eight per cent.

Apotex also says it now expects its adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization margin to come in at about 31 per cent, up from earlier guidance for about 30 per cent.

stories.title: U of T rejects report, recommendations on anti-Muslim, anti-Arab discrimination
stories.summary: The nearly 300-page report is based on consultations with 85 people and small groups as well as 525 responses to a survey of students, staff, faculty and librarians.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio
stories.content:
A review of the University of Toronto’s policies and practices has found the school has a “general pattern of over-policing and under-protecting” Muslims, Arabs and Palestinians, with a report laying out dozens of recommendations related to academic freedom, ON-campus security methods, institutional autonomy and other concerns.

The university, however, says it cannot accept the report or recommendations issued by its Muslim, Arab, and Palestinian discrimination working group, which it says “departs significantly from past equity reports in several ways,” such as including “lengthy commentary about events abroad.”

The school nonetheless promises to take immediate actions to address discrimination against those groups at the university.

The nearly 300-page report is based on consultations with 85 people and small groups as well as 525 responses to a survey of students, staff, faculty and librarians across the school’s three campuses. These were carried out between March of last year and January.

The university says it received the working group’s final report a month ago and is releasing it as part of its commitment to transparency. Both the report and the school’s response were shared online Thursday.

The report describes restrictions on speech and events, inconsistent processes in dealing with complaints, and double standards in enforcement related to protests and postering, as well as repeated complaints about the university’s successful litigation to get rid of a pro-Palestinian encampment on campus two years ago.

Similarly, there were recurring concerns that “the university’s institutional commitment to radical, critical teaching and research suffers from a Palestine exception,” the report said.

The working group also heard about bigoted attitudes and assumptions steeped in stereotypes painting Muslims, Arabs and Palestinians as terrorists, misogynists and antisemites, it said.

“The most prevalent pattern we encountered, however, was a generalized ignorance of the histories, cultures, and lived experiences of Muslims, Arabs, and Palestinians, and the ways in which anti-Muslim, anti-Arab, and anti-Palestinian discrimination and harassment take shape,” the report said.

“Relatedly, we learned about instances when innovative research or outreach activities on issues of interest to Muslim, Arab, or Palestinian members of the university were viewed as instances of antisemitism calling for disciplinary action.”

The report lists 57 recommendations that include reviewing safety and risk metrics and how they get applied; ensuring that protests and postering are policed in a content-neutral manner; issuing stronger guidance to administrators on procedural fairness in handling complaints and regarding the cancellation or postponement of events that have already been scheduled.

Other recommendations relate to addressing concerns of bias in the university’s partnerships with organizations such as school boards that accept student-teacher placements and hospitals involved in affiliation agreements. One example cited in the report says that many clinical faculty reported “being cited for unprofessionalism when signing an open letter supporting medical workers in Gaza.”

The report makes further recommendations regarding the university’s investments, including that it “consider an absolute prohibition on investments that aid and/or abet violations of peremptory norms of international law.”

The consultations showed that “what happens around the world has implications locally on our campus, in our hallways, and in our classrooms,” the report said.

“Our consultations began in 2025 as Israel continued its campaign of large-scale violence in the Gaza Strip, the West Bank, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen and Iran. University members explained how their experiences on campus were refracted through this global conflict and its history,” it said.

“Many reflected on the university in light of published reports from human rights organizations, genocide scholars, international lawyers, and multilateral and international bodies that increasingly described Israel’s actions in Gaza as apartheid and/or genocide.”

In a written response, the university acknowledged that anti-Muslim, anti-Arab and anti-Palestinian discrimination exists at the school and said it is committed to addressing the issue.

Still, it’s understandable that the working group and the university administration wouldn’t fully agree on the range of issues raised in the report, “nor about the ideal responses to those issues – particularly given the fraught circumstances, passionate feelings, and ongoing global conflict informing many of the situations described,” it said.

“While we expect that the working group’s report will validate the experiences of many members of our community, aspects will also be offensive and upsetting to other members of our community, including some Jewish and Israeli colleagues and students,” it said.

The school cited multiple reasons for rejecting the report and its recommendations, including that some recommendations clash with collective agreements and protections related to academic freedom, some fall outside the university’s jurisdiction, and some don’t align with the university’s “position of institutional restraint.”

The university said it already offers spaces that Muslim communities can use for prayer and spiritual practice, but will do more work to ensure there are appropriate Muslim prayer spaces and multi-faith spaces on each of its three campuses.

The school’s new office of human rights, equity and inclusion will also release an e-module on discrimination against Muslims, Arabs and Palestinians, and hold an information session for members of its governing council.

“The university has supported and is committed to continued support for a range of scholarly activities, including research related to Muslim, Arab, and Palestinian communities, as well as academic initiatives focused on Palestinian history and culture,” it said.

The school’s new office of human rights, equity and inclusion will also release an e-module on discrimination against Muslims, Arabs and Palestinians, and hold an information session for members of its governing council.

“The university has supported and is committed to continued support for a range of scholarly activities, including research related to Muslim, Arab, and Palestinian communities, as well as academic initiatives focused on Palestinian history and culture,” it said.
