The school nonetheless promises to take immediate actions to address discrimination against those groups at the university.

The nearly 300-page report is based on consultations with 85 people and small groups as well as 525 responses to a survey of students, staff, faculty and librarians across the school’s three campuses. These were carried out between March of last year and January.

The university says it received the working group’s final report a month ago and is releasing it as part of its commitment to transparency. Both the report and the school’s response were shared online Thursday.

stories.title: Canada's agriculture sector divided on Mercosur free trade deal
stories.summary: Ottawa - Industries in Canada's agriculture sector are divided on whether a free trade deal with the Mercosur group will benefit the country as Canada and the South American trading bloc look to strike a deal by year's end.
stories.author: Catherine Morrison The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Industries in Canada’s agriculture sector are divided on whether a free trade deal with the Mercosur group would benefit the country as Canada and the South American trading bloc look to strike a deal by year’s end.

Representatives from the Canadian Cattle Youth Council gathered on Parliament Hill last month to warn that a free trade deal with Mercosur could jeopardize beef production in Canada and pose risks to food safety.

“The government itself warns that our food supply chains rely too heavily on foreign suppliers, and that Canada relies on imported beef to meet demand,” said Canadian Cattle Youth Council President Judson Christopherson. “You don’t fix that by making Canadians more reliant on food from abroad.”

But Michael Bourque, president and CEO of Fertilizer Canada, said in a letter to Prime Minister Mark Carney earlier this year that a trade agreement with Mercosur is a chance for Canada to strengthen its position as a global supplier of crop nutrients.

He said potash is Canada’s largest export to Brazil and Canada must ensure its potash sector remains competitive.

“At a time when Canada is advancing trade diversification as a national priority, we must pursue opportunities that expand market access and support long-term economic growth,” said Bourque.

“Few opportunities align more closely with these objectives than a trade agreement with Mercosur, one of the world’s fastest-growing economic regions and home to the world’s fifth-largest economy.”

Bourque said the Mercosur bloc includes some of the world’s most productive and fastest-growing agricultural economies. As global demand for food continues to grow, he said, the region will play an increasingly important role in “feeding the world,” creating opportunities for Canadian suppliers of crop nutrients, agricultural technology and expertise.

“Fertilizer Canada strongly urges the Government of Canada to finalize and ratify a trade agreement that positions Canada to be a long-term partner in that growth,” he said.

Keith Currie, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, said any Canada-Mercosur agreement must account for significant differences in production scale, cost structures, regulatory frameworks and market conditions.

Currie said while opportunities May exist in some sectors, the benefits for Canadian agriculture are likely to be uneven and it’s important that any deal protects Canadian farmers.

The Mercosur trading bloc includes Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay. In 2024, Canada’s merchandise trade with Mercosur totalled $15.8 billion, with Canada’s exports valued at $3.1 billion and imports valued at $12.8 billion.

International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu has said the government is looking to sign three major trade deals before the end of the year — with Mercosur, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and India.

Canada and Mercosur launched free trade negotiations in March 2018. Talks were paused for years due to the pandemic and only resumed in October 2025.

Brazil, which recently held a general election, is Mercosur’s co-ordinator for free trade negotiations with Canada.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Association of Quebec farmers challenges costs of high-speed rail in new study
stories.summary: Research suggests it would be possible to link Quebec City and Toronto at a fraction of the estimated cost, environmental impact of Alto project
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud
stories.content:
The Crown corporation behind a proposed high-speed train between Quebec City and Toronto says a new study proposing a cheaper and slower alternative is not as simple as it sounds.

The study, released by Vision Transport and agricultural group Union des producteurs agricoles, says these savings could be made by modernizing existing tracks.

The study was conducted by Vincent Duguay, a master’s student in research at the École nationale d’administration publique, and Pierre DuSablon, an expert with extensive experience in the rail industry.

It examines two scenarios: a route serving the same 22 stations currently served by Via Rail, and an express route with stops only in major cities.

The authors say a modernized route serving intermediate stations, such as Saint-Hyacinthe or Drummondville, would reduce travel time to six hours and 40 minutes, while an express route would take five hours and 50 minutes.

Alto’s high-speed rail proposal promises to connect Quebec City to Toronto in four hours and 30 minutes.

Currently, it takes eight hours and 40 minutes to travel from Quebec City to Toronto by rail, which is slightly longer than it takes by car.

The study’s authors say their proposed project would still be faster than travelling by car.

“Farmers don’t want to have their land expropriated only to find out, in the end, that it doesn’t happen because it’s going to cost too much,” UPA president Martin Caron said. “So, can we look at other alternatives that will have much less of an impact and be much less expensive?”

Alto says it “cannot simply add more passenger trains to existing tracks” owned by other railway companies such as CN, Cpkc or Cfqg.

“Freight trains have priority on these tracks,” Alto said in a statement.

“Slowing or interrupting freight trains during construction or operation would have serious consequences for the Canadian economy, including for businesses’ ability to export goods, and for Canadian farm operations.”

On its website, Alto says it chose to proceed with high-speed rail “based on an in-depth analysis that clearly demonstrated that only high-speed rail can fully meet the current and future mobility needs of the Toronto to Quebec City corridor.”

Alto also says that speeds offered by a high-frequency service would not be fast enough to make commuters choose rail over driving or flying.

The new study includes five major proposals. The biggest and most costly includes doubling existing tracks along the entire route, which would involve adding tracks over 407 kilometres.

Currently, 37 per cent of the corridor has only one track, and passenger trains are regularly forced to pull onto a siding to let a freight train pass.

The second element of the plan involves upgrading the signalling system to reduce the distance between trains and increase maximum speeds to 177 km/h, up from 153 km/h. The third proposal would strengthen the Canadian Transportation Agency’s authority to give passenger trains priority over freight.

Unlike the high-speed proposal, which would fence in both sides of the track and eliminate level crossings, Vision Transport’s plan would retain the current 924 level crossings but require 533 of them to be secured with full barriers. Alternatively, it says it could be possible to replace one-third of the level crossings with overpasses, suggesting that would reduce the travel time between Montreal and Toronto by an additional eight minutes.

Finally, the fifth element of the plan is to replace the current rolling stock with tilting trains and tracks with steeper bank angles on curves, which would allow them to travel at higher speeds.

Alto estimates the cost of the high-speed rail project at between $60-billion and $90-billion. The parliamentary budget officer estimates a cost of $73-billion to $113-billion, while other independent industry sources put the price tag at $150-billion.

The modernization project presented by Vision Transport comes in at a cost of $9-billion to $9.4-billion, to which it adds a 20 per cent contingency reserve, bringing the initial cost to $11-billion – a fraction of the Alto project.

The alternative proposal’s costs would increase by $8.2-billion if it includes the cost of eliminating one-third of the level crossings “for reasons of acceptability, co-existence with local residents, and corridor modernization.” With a 20 per cent contingency allowance, the total cost would be about $21-billion.

The project’s authors also examined the electrification of the train they are proposing for the modernized line, which would represent an additional investment of $3-billion to $7-billion for overhead wires and rolling stock, for a total of approximately $30-billion.

Alto estimates that the cost of a high frequency rail project could be much higher than the numbers cited in the study, ranging from $45-billion to $75-billion.

Via Rail does not currently control all of the rights-of-way along its routes between Quebec City and Toronto.

“If we’re already using the tracks and doubling them in various places, it’s more accessible to people, and naturally, in terms of cost, it’s much less expensive and will have a much smaller impact on everyone,” Caron said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has also opposed the Alto high-speed rail development, and campaigned against it before the Parti Québécois was elected to form a minority government. The premier has said it could be a financial fiasco, noting that the Bloc Québécois has estimated the project will end up costing $200-billion.

The UPA and its members oppose a route on the north shore, which would involve expropriations of farmland and traffic headaches. Caron recalls the massive expropriations in the 1960s to make way for the ill-fated Mirabel airport project. The airport never caught on with passengers, and its terminal was demolished in 2014.

stories.title: Association of Quebec farmers releases study challenging costs of high-speed rail
stories.summary: The study conducted by Vision Transport and agricultural group Union des producteurs agricoles say these savings could be made by modernizing existing tracks.
stories.author: Pierre Saint-Arnaud
stories.content:
A new study suggests it would be possible to build a rail link between Quebec City and Toronto at a fraction of the estimated cost and environmental impact of the high-speed train project being developed by the Crown corporation Alto, although it would be slower.

The study conducted by Vision Transport and agricultural group Union des producteurs agricoles say these savings could be made by modernizing existing tracks.

The study was conducted by Vincent Duguay, a master’s student in research at the École nationale d’administration publique, and Pierre DuSablon, an expert with extensive experience in the rail industry.

It examines two scenarios: a route serving the same 22 stations currently served by Via Rail, and an express route with stops only in major cities.

The authors say a modernized route serving intermediate stations, such as Saint-Hyacinthe or Drummondville, would reduce this time to six hours and 40 minutes, while an express route would take five hours and 50 minutes.

Alto’s high-speed rail proposal promises to connect Quebec City to Toronto in 4 hours and 30 minutes.

Currently, it takes eight hours and 40 minutes by train to travel from Quebec City to Toronto by rail, which is slightly longer than it takes by car.

The study’s authors say their proposed project, while slower, would still be faster than travelling by car.

“Farmers don’t want to have their land expropriated only to find out, in the end, that it doesn’t happen because it’s going to cost too much,” UPA president Martin Caron said. “So, can we look at other alternatives that will have much less of an impact and be much less expensive?”

The new study includes five major proposals. The biggest and most costly includes doubling existing tracks along the entire route, which would involve adding tracks over 407 kilometres. Currently, 37 per cent of the corridor has only one track, and passenger trains are regularly forced to pull onto a siding to let a freight train pass.

The authors say double tracks would also make it possible to increase ridership by operating both an express service connecting only the major cities and a local service serving all 22 stations.

The second element of the plan involves upgrading the signalling system to reduce the distance between trains and increase maximum speeds from 153 km/h to 177 km/h, while the third proposes strengthening the Canadian Transportation Agency’s authority to give passenger trains priority over freight.

Unlike the high-speed proposal, which would require fencing in both sides of the track and eliminating level crossings, Vision Transport’s proposed train would retain the current 924 level crossings but would require 533 of them to be secured with full barriers. Optionally, it would also be possible to eliminate one-third of the crossings by building overpasses, which would reduce the travel time between Montreal and Toronto by an additional eight minutes.

Finally, the fifth element of the plan is to replace the current rolling stock with tilting trains and tracks with steeper bank angles on curves, which would allow them to travel at higher speeds.

Alto estimates the cost of the high-speed rail project at between $60 billion and $90 billion. The parliamentary budget officer estimates a cost of $73 billion to $113 billion, while other independent industry sources put the price tag at $150 billion.

The modernization project presented by Vision Transport comes in at a cost of $9 billion to $9.4 billion, to which it adds a 20 per cent contingency reserve, bringing the initial cost to $11 billion — a fraction of the Alto project.

The alternative proposal’s costs would also increase by $8.2 billion if it includes the cost of eliminating one-third of the level crossings “for reasons of acceptability, coexistence with local residents, and corridor modernization.” With a 20 per cent contingency allowance, the total cost would be about $21 billion.

The project’s authors also examined the electrification of the train they are proposing for the modernized line, which would represent an additional investment of $3 billion to $7 billion for overhead wires and rolling stock, for a total of approximately $30 billion.

Caron has expressed concerns around electrification, given the difficulties Montreal’s light-rail system has faced with winter conditions. However, he applauds the idea of staying on the existing railroad tracks and rights-of-way on the south shore of the St. Lawrence River.

Via Rail does not currently control all of the rights-of-way along its routes between Quebec City and Toronto.

“If we’re already using the tracks and doubling them in various places, it’s more accessible to people, and naturally, in terms of cost, it’s much less expensive and will have a much smaller impact on everyone,” he said in an interview with The Canadian Press.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has also opposed the Alto high-speed rail development, and campaigned against it before the Parti Québécois was elected to form a minority government. The premier has said it could be a financial fiasco, noting that the Bloc Québécois has estimated the project will end up costing $200 billion.

The UPA and its members oppose a route on the north shore, which would involve expropriations of farmland and traffic headaches. Caron recalls the massive expropriations in the 1960s to make way for the ill-fated Mirabel airport project. The airport never caught on with passengers, and its terminal was demolished in 2014.

Caron finds it hard to understand Ottawa’s stubbornness when it comes to the project, which he describes as costly and disruptive: “They say, ‘Let’s just go ahead with it, and it’ll cost whatever it costs.’ But I don’t think we’re at that point anymore in Canada — or even in Quebec. Instead, we’ve reached a point where we’re developing projects that can garner social acceptance.”

stories.title: Encouraging news in fight against opioid addiction: Raam
stories.summary: A London physician has found that one opioid treatment appears to be more effective at preventing overdoses than three other commonly used therapies.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
There is encouraging news for people struggling with fentanyl addiction.

A London physician has found that one opioid treatment appears to be more effective at preventing overdoses than three other commonly used therapies.

The treatment, known as Sublocade, was first administered in Canada at London’s Rapid Access Addiction Medicine (Raam) Clinic in 2019. Now, research led by the clinic’s medical director suggests Sublocade not only helps reduce fentanyl cravings, but also offers the strongest protection against overdose when compared with methadone, Suboxone and Kadian.

“What it means is, if people are on methadone or Suboxone, you can still overdose. Whereas if you’re on Sublocade, you don’t overdose,” said Dr. Kenneth Lee, medical director of the London Raam Clinic.

Researchers analyzed data from 45,243 people who experienced one or more opioid-related overdoses between 2022 and 2024.

Among those receiving opioid agonist therapy, 4,109 people, or 9.1 per cent, experienced a non-fatal overdose, while 770 people, or 1.7 per cent, died from an overdose.

Of those 770 deaths, 58 occurred while patients were receiving methadone, 37 while receiving Suboxone and 18 while receiving Kadian. Fewer than five deaths were recorded among patients receiving Sublocade. Among people not enrolled in an opioid agonist therapy program, 640 died from an overdose.

“That’s the thought, that if you block the receptors and not allow fentanyl to get in, that people will use less fentanyl,” Lee said. “But the beauty of this is that we have the secondary benefit of overdose protection.”

Unlike other opioid agonist therapies that require daily medication, Sublocade is administered as a once-monthly injection.

Rachel Gosling, co-ordinator of addiction medicine at the Raam Clinic, said patients have responded positively to the treatment.

“We’ve had individuals who were really afraid of overdose, and of that potential consequence of their use, and we were able to support them reducing that anxiety while they’re still in recovery,” she said.

Lee cautioned that Sublocade’s protective effects apply specifically to fentanyl addiction and not necessarily to other substances.

“We’re doing better in terms of opioid deaths, fentanyl overdose deaths, but that doesn’t mean you can’t overdose from other things,” he said.

Lee described the findings as the first significant piece of positive news in the fight against opioid addiction in several years.

The study has been published in Frontiers in Public Health . Lee has also presented the findings at conferences in San Diego and Portland and is scheduled to share the results at the Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine conference in Calgary on Nov. 21.

“There’s the older treatments with methadone, Suboxone, but this is something that’s new on the horizon,” Lee said. “We’re trying to spread the word.”

Among those receiving opioid agonist therapy, 4,109 people, or 9.1 per cent, experienced a non-fatal overdose, while 770 people, or 1.7 per cent, died from an overdose.

content_blocks.caption: Dr. Kenneth Lee, medical director of the London Rapid Access Addiction Medicine Clinic (RAAM), displays a box of Sublocade in London, Ont. Nov. 11, 2026. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: Of those 770 deaths, 58 occurred while patients were receiving methadone, 37 while receiving Suboxone and 18 while receiving Kadian. Fewer than five deaths were recorded among patients receiving Sublocade. Among people not enrolled in an opioid agonist therapy program, 640 died from an overdose.

“That’s the thought, that if you block the receptors and not allow fentanyl to get in, that people will use less fentanyl,” Lee said. “But the beauty of this is that we have the secondary benefit of overdose protection.”
Unlike other opioid agonist therapies that require daily medication, Sublocade is administered as a once-monthly injection.
Rachel Gosling, co-ordinator of addiction medicine at the Raam Clinic, said patients have responded positively to the treatment.

“We’ve had individuals who were really afraid of overdose, and of that potential consequence of their use, and we were able to support them reducing that anxiety while they’re still in recovery,” she said.

content_blocks.alt: sublocade - london - nov 2026
content_blocks.caption: Rachel Gosling, co-ordinator of addiction medicine at the Rapid Access Addiction Medicine (RAAM) Clinic, speaks with CTV News in London, Ont. on Nov. 11, 2026. (Bryan Bicknell/CTV News London)

content_blocks.text: Lee cautioned that Sublocade’s protective effects apply specifically to fentanyl addiction and not necessarily to other substances.
“We’re doing better in terms of opioid deaths, fentanyl overdose deaths, but that doesn’t mean you can’t overdose from other things,” he said.
Lee described the findings as the first significant piece of positive news in the fight against opioid addiction in several years.

The study has been published in Frontiers in Public Health . Lee has also presented the findings at conferences in San Diego and Portland and is scheduled to share the results at the Canadian Society of Addiction Medicine conference in Calgary on Nov. 21.
“There’s the older treatments with methadone, Suboxone, but this is something that’s new on the horizon,” Lee said. “We’re trying to spread the word.”

stories.title: Western University business school reviewing use of AI tutor by professors
stories.summary: The business school at Western University says it’s reviewing the use of an artificial intelligence tutor in one course after students raised concerns about the cost and reliability of the chatbot.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The business school at Western University says it’s reviewing the use of an artificial intelligence tutor in one course after students raised concerns about the cost and reliability of the chatbot.

Ivey Business School’s associate dean for programs, Martha Maznevski, says in a statement the school is aware of the concerns surrounding course materials for the global macroeconomics for managers class and is reviewing the matter.

Forth-year student Daniel Wang says the class textbook was replaced earlier this fall with an AI tutor called Ask GMM and students have been asked to pay $72 to access the chatbot after they have already paid a $750 course materials fee.

Wang says students who took the class in previous years accessed the same course materials through the university’s learning system, but this year’s class materials are available behind a separate paywall.

He says students need to create external accounts on a separate website to access class materials, which raises concerns about the privacy and safety of their data and how their interactions with the AI tool are collected, stored and accessed.

Professors Kirsten Cornelson and Tony Frost say they are piloting the AI tool in their class this year and the fee students must pay covers the cost of building and using the AI.

Cornelson and Frost didn’t respond to questions about the potential risks of the new AI tool to the students’ privacy and data security.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Maan Alhmidi, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Champagne says energy investments set the stage for Canada's future economic growth
stories.summary: Halifax - Canada’s finance minister says Ottawa is investing in energy infrastructure to create a foundational base for the new technologies that will power the 21st century economy.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Canada’s finance minister says Ottawa is investing in energy infrastructure to create a foundational base for the new technologies that will power the 21st century economy.

François-Philippe Champagne told a group of business people in Halifax Thursday that history has shown economies with plenty of energy resources do better in the long run. He said the world is moving toward electrification in almost every area of the economy, including the transport, manufacturing and industrial sectors.

stories.title: Pilot killed in Quebec Remembrance Day plane crash identified
stories.summary: A pilot who died Wednesday when his plane crashed after participating in a Remembrance Day ceremony south of Quebec City has been identified.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A pilot who died Wednesday when his plane crashed after participating in a Remembrance Day ceremony south of Quebec City has been identified.

The City of Saint-Georges said Thursday the victim was Daniel Parent, a member of a local flying club.

Mayor Manon Bougie offered her condolences and said the city was lowering flags to half-mast at city hall and the Saint-Georges airport.

Parent was the only person aboard the plane when it went down around 11 a.m. Wednesday, Quebec provincial police (SQ) said. He was declared dead at the scene.

SQ spokesperson Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said the pilot had been flying with several other aircraft when his plane crashed.

The small plane came down in a wooded area near the Saint-Georges airport and caught fire after the crash. The pilot had been approaching the airport to land.

Police described Parent as a man in his 60s who lived in the region.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon offered his condolences following the crash.

St-Pierre Plamondon said he was working with the province’s domestic security minister to gather more information about what happened.

Transportation Safety Board investigators have been deployed to the scene to gather information and assess what happened.

The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) told Global News that the aircraft did not belong to the military and no CAF personnel were involved.

“Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the pilot who tragically lost their life. We extend our deepest condolences to all those affected by this tragic incident,” CAF said in a statement.

National Defence Minister David McGuinty also issued a statement expressing his condolences to the pilot’s family and loved ones, saying his thoughts were with everyone affected by the tragedy.

The cause of the crash is not yet known.

Bilodeau said the SQ’s major crime unit was investigating the crash for any possible criminal elements, though she noted crashes such as this are rarely linked to a crime.

Saint-Georges is located roughly 100 kilometres southeast of Quebec City.

— with files from Alessia Simona Maratta

stories.title: Ontario seeks to strengthen oversight of career colleges through limits on Osap, enrolment
stories.summary: Bill coming next week to propose overhaul that includes requiring a physical location and prohibiting third-party recruiters from setting up shop on campus
stories.author: Kelly Grant, Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Students taking online-only classes at private postsecondary institutions in Ontario would no longer qualify for government loans under a package of legislative changes the Progressive Conservatives will table next week to strengthen oversight of the beleaguered career college sector.

The proposed overhaul will also require career colleges to have a physical location, prohibit third-party recruiters such as immigration consultants from setting up shop on campus and limit the runaway enrolment growth that sparked concerns about suspicious activity at half a dozen Greater Toronto Area private colleges.

However, the province will not lift a freeze on loan disbursements to career colleges and their students earlier than next year, after the rules are tightened from the overhaul. Several career colleges say they won’t survive that long without their chief source of revenue: tuition paid through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, the province’s needs-based financial aid plan.

Nolan Quinn, Ontario’s Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, unveiled the proposed changes at a news conference Thursday.

“Our legislation includes a suite of measures that will give the province stronger legislative powers to crack down on fraud, prevent abuse before it occurs and require transparent, student-focused results,” he said.

Mr. Quinn paused Osap payouts to private career colleges and their students in early October, after the initial findings of a third-party audit turned up serious concerns about how government aid was being used in the sector. Some of those concerns were forwarded to the Ontario Provincial Police .

On Thursday, Mr. Quinn revealed that Career Colleges Ontario, the sector’s industry association, informed his office last week that it removed 24 campuses from its membership rolls and is reviewing the status of another 13. He did not say why the association took those steps. Career Colleges Ontario did not immediately respond to a request for comment Thursday.

Mr. Quinn also said Career Colleges Ontario informed his office of another 33 campuses that are alleged to have backdated enrolment to before Aug. 1, when the rules barring Osap grants kicked in. From that point forward, career college students were only eligible for repayable loans.

“Let me be very clear: What we have found here are not minor administrative concerns, but rather co-ordinated, sophisticated efforts to take advantage of students and taxpayers for personal gain. It is systematic and widespread,” Mr. Quinn said.

Career Colleges Ontario warned provincial officials as early as January 2023 that enrolment had skyrocketed at a small number of schools in a manner that smacked of “suspicious activity.”

The association has been urging the government to resume Osap payments to private colleges that are not suspected of wrongdoing as soon as possible.

“We remain extremely concerned about the impact on students, and we continue to call on the government to restore Osap immediately for students at compliant institutions,” association spokeswoman Taylor Buck said by e-mail Wednesday, before Mr. Quinn’s latest announcement.

“We support strong oversight and action where there are legitimate compliance concerns, but that can be done without penalizing students who have followed the rules.”

Opposition politicians at Queen’s Park said that the proposed changes were a case of too little too late, and that the government was ignoring both the many legitimate students left without promised Osap loans and the innocent colleges that could be forced to shut their doors.

“What we saw this morning is that the government is intent on putting forward what I would say is a cover-your-ass bill,” interim Ontario Liberal leader John Fraser told reporters. “The toothpaste is already out of the tube, and the problem is … that thousands of thousands of honest, hard-working students and their families have been penalized.”

The Ontario Ndp’s postsecondary education critic, Peggy Sattler, called on the government to fire Mr. Quinn, restore Osap and provide a timeline for a return to normal for legitimate students and colleges caught up in the aid freeze – a freeze she said would never have been necessary if the government had basic controls in place.

“This bill is a classic case of closing the barn door after the horses are gone,” she said. “So yes, we need better oversight. But it should never have come to this.”

stories.title: Shelter-in-place advisory issued near Squamish, B.C., due to flooding from heavy rain
stories.summary: Some areas saw a lull in rain Wednesday, although orange rainfall warnings remain in place for west and inland Vancouver Island
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Peter Spitzer is among residents of Paradise Valley Road who are sheltering in place north of Squamish, B.C., after their homes were cut off by river waters swollen by drenching rains and a dam discharge that followed.

He’s been at his property near the confluence of the Cheakamus River and Culliton Creek for nearly 40 years and has seen flood waters break their banks before.

Spitzer and his neighbours in the flood zone about 16 kilometres from Squamish know the drill.

“We all stay put and help the neighbours out if somebody needs anything. We usually have food and water for quite a few days before we run out,” he said Thursday.

A procession of storms has drenched parts of southwest British Columbia with more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours leading to multiple evacuation orders and alerts, as well as the shelter-in-place decree that was issued by the District of Squamish on Thursday morning.

The entire village of Pemberton, population 3,400, is under an evacuation alert “out of an abundance of caution.”

But rains have eased for most of the province, including Metro Vancouver.

Environment Canada had lowered most rainfall warnings by Thursday, although yellow warnings were still active for west and inland Vancouver Island, where heavy rains were forecast to last into Friday afternoon.

But the impacts of the deluge continue. Spitzer said parts of Paradise Valley Road were flooded and water under the now-closed Bailey Bridge out of the community is “very close to the top.”

“At the moment there’s no way out of the valley,” he said.

Spitzer said the water hadn’t reached his home but others were surrounded or their basements were flooded.

Video posted online shows trucks driving down roads covered in fast-flowing water. Another shows a resident standing at the front door of his home, which is under several feet of water, while a friend on the opposite bank calls across the water to make sure he is OK.

The District of Squamish said in a statement Thursday that the spill level from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked at approximately 5 a.m. and was expected to decrease slowly throughout the day.

The district said that would create room in the reservoir for more rain, and eventually allow for roads to be reopened, adding that river levels were also expected to peak Thursday.

The flooding came after the discharge rate from the dam more than tripled expectations, due to back-to-back storms.

Whitney Deane, a spokesperson for B.C. Hydro, said forecasters were originally expecting the discharge rate to peak at a manageable 235 cubic metres per second by midday Thursday.

But at 11 p.m. on Wednesday, the hydro company issued a flood warning and about an hour later, discharge peaked at 735 cubic metres per second, she said.

“That’s roughly three times the forecast coming at a much shorter window,” she said.

The string of weather systems that slammed southwestern B.C. since last week brought 306 millimetres of rain to Port Mellon in the Howe Sound region since Tuesday, while 261 millimetres fell at Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island.

The rain forced evacuation orders for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil’wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Pemberton’s evacuation order covers properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, waste water treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course. The B.C. Ministry of Transportation’s DriveBC website says Highway 99 east of Pemberton has been shut in both directions.

The Lilʼwat Nation has expanded an evacuation order and alert for the area from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake.

Elsewhere, the Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the village of Sayward on the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, as high flows in Newcastle Creek led to extra sediment in the water, and an evacuation order due to flooding and landslide risks remains in place for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

“A strong frontal system over the area will weaken today. Rain will continue to ease as the front weakens,” Environment Canada said Thursday.

Environment Canada said several locations reported more than 100 millimetres of rain in the last 48 hours, including Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island (248 mm), Port Alberni (123 mm), Porteau Cove on the Sea to Sky Highway (140 mm), Whistler (138 mm), and Squamish (134 mm).

The storms have been associated with a spike in temperatures which saw daily records fall in more than 30 locations on Wednesday, including Abbotsford, where the mercury reached 20.1 Celsius, smashing a 45-year-old record by three degrees.

stories.title: Csis foreign powers could help Canada navigate an unreliable U.S.: experts
stories.summary: The federal government has strongly hinted that Canada’s spy service is getting an expanded mandate alongside billions in new funding.
stories.author: Alex Boutilier
stories.content:
A foreign intelligence mandate for Canada’s spy service May help the country plot its own course amid an increasingly choppy geopolitical climate and an increasingly unreliable America, national security experts say.

The Liberal government has strongly hinted that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) will be getting an expanded mission alongside $6 billion in new funding over the next decade, and there is growing speculation among national security experts that role could focus ongathering information from foreign nationals abroad to feed back to Ottawa.

Canada relies heavily on security partners — especially the U.S. — for much of its foreign intelligence needs. Csis has a limited ability to collect intelligence globally, but that information must be related to threats to Canadian security.

Successive Canadian governments have viewed that situation as good enough, and balked at the suggestion — and cost — of setting up a foreign intelligence service akin to the U.K.’s MI6 or the U.S. CIA.

But with the U.S. becoming a dubious economic and security partner under President Donald Trump’s administration, experts told Global News Canada’s reliance on America for intelligence is a questionable strategy.

“We are pursuing our own sovereign interests in a way that the government has not in the past, where our interests in trade, who we might partner with … we’re pursuing very much our own interests, as opposed to the interests of the United States and we’re tagging along,” said Leah West, a national security law professor at Carleton University.

“So as we’re looking to (invest) and partner with foreign countries on defence, and technology, and critical minerals in a way that we didn’t before, we need to have a good sense of what’s happening on the ground in those countries, with those governments, with those companies. So there is a need for greater foreign intelligence.”

Csis was created in the 1980s after allegations of serious misconduct were levelled against the RCMP’s intelligence branch, leading to the federal McDonald Commission. That independent probe recommended splitting law enforcement and intelligence gathering into two different agencies.

The report also strongly cautioned, however, against giving the newly formed Csis a foreign intelligence mandate. Foreign intelligence agencies routinely violate the law of other countries, and the commission worried about that “contagion” reaching domestic security investigations.

Domestic and foreign intelligence agencies collect different kinds of information, with domestic agencies focused more on security threats than issues like economic intelligence.

The McDonald Commission also expressed concerns about creating a “security and intelligence monolith in a democratic state” — giving one agency responsibility for both domestic and foreign intelligence.

West noted that the commission was writing in the early 1980s in a very different world, and that political oversight and public scrutiny over intelligence agencies’ activities is much stronger now than it was 40 years ago.

“Those criticisms arise from a very different era, when there wasn’t a lot of legal constraint and required reporting and transparency built into the mandates of our spy services,” West said.

Wesley Wark, a longtime national security observer and a senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation, said there remain crucial roles for “human” intelligence even with the advent of invasive surveillance technology and digital spying.

“You can’t take a spy satellite image of what a foreign leader is thinking about (an issue). And very often you won’t be able to use signals intelligence to give you a clear picture of that,” Wark said in a recent interview.

“(Human intelligence) is very much a business of trying to tap into human knowledge about adversary state plans and potentialities. And the gold mine is being able to have sources of information that are close to decision makers, who are in the know, in a foreign state.”

Wark added that a foreign intelligence capability could augment other, more modern types of intelligence gathering. For instance, having “a close ear on the ground” in a foreign state could help the Communications Security Establishment (CSE) determine who to target for electronic surveillance, or help identify important facilities to keep watch using spy satellites.

But Wark said the current government might be most interested in intelligence that can inform its trade agenda.

“One of the clear indications we have from the prime minister on his outlook on the world is that … Mark Carney is very interested in economic intelligence,” Wark said.

West noted that the commission was writing in the early 1980s in a very different world, and that political oversight and public scrutiny over intelligence agencies’ activities is much stronger now than it was 40 years ago.
“Those criticisms arise from a very different era, when there wasn’t a lot of legal constraint and required reporting and transparency built into the mandates of our spy services,” West said.

“You can’t take a spy satellite image of what a foreign leader is thinking about (an issue). And very often you won’t be able to use signals intelligence to give you a clear picture of that,” Wark said in a recent interview.

“(Human intelligence) is very much a business of trying to tap into human knowledge about adversary state plans and potentialities. And the gold mine is being able to have sources of information that are close to decision makers, who are in the know, in a foreign state.”

Wark added that a foreign intelligence capability could augment other, more modern types of intelligence gathering. For instance, having “a close ear on the ground” in a foreign state could help the Communications Security Establishment (CSE) determine who to target for electronic surveillance, or help identify important facilities to keep watch using spy satellites.
But Wark said the current government might be most interested in intelligence that can inform its trade agenda.
“One of the clear indications we have from the prime minister on his outlook on the world is that … Mark Carney is very interested in economic intelligence,” Wark said.

content_blocks.text: A foreign intelligence mandate for Canada’s spy service May help the country plot its own course amid an increasingly choppy geopolitical climate and an increasingly unreliable America, national security experts say.
content_blocks.html: A foreign intelligence mandate for Canada’s spy service may help the country plot its own course amid an increasingly choppy geopolitical climate and an increasingly unreliable America, national security experts say.

content_blocks.text: The Liberal government has strongly hinted that the Canadian Security Intelligence Service (Csis) will be getting an expanded mission alongside $6 billion in new funding over the next decade, and there is growing speculation among national security experts that role could focus ongathering information from foreign nationals abroad to feed back to Ottawa.

Canada relies heavily on security partners — especially the U.S. — for much of its foreign intelligence needs. Csis has a limited ability to collect intelligence globally, but that information must be related to threats to Canadian security.

Successive Canadian governments have viewed that situation as good enough, and balked at the suggestion — and cost — of setting up a foreign intelligence service akin to the U.K.’s MI6 or the U.S. CIA.

But with the U.S. becoming a dubious economic and security partner under President Donald Trump’s administration, experts told Global News Canada’s reliance on America for intelligence is a questionable strategy.

“We are pursuing our own sovereign interests in a way that the government has not in the past, where our interests in trade, who we might partner with … we’re pursuing very much our own interests, as opposed to the interests of the United States and we’re tagging along,” said Leah West, a national security law professor at Carleton University.

“So as we’re looking to (invest) and partner with foreign countries on defence, and technology, and critical minerals in a way that we didn’t before, we need to have a good sense of what’s happening on the ground in those countries, with those governments, with those companies. So there is a need for greater foreign intelligence.”

Csis was created in the 1980s after allegations of serious misconduct were levelled against the RCMP’s intelligence branch, leading to the federal McDonald Commission. That independent probe recommended splitting law enforcement and intelligence gathering into two different agencies.

The report also strongly cautioned, however, against giving the newly formed Csis a foreign intelligence mandate. Foreign intelligence agencies routinely violate the law of other countries, and the commission worried about that “contagion” reaching domestic security investigations.
Domestic and foreign intelligence agencies collect different kinds of information, with domestic agencies focused more on security threats than issues like economic intelligence.

stories.title: Canada faces ‘gradual and bumpy recovery,’ Kpmg economic outlook says
stories.summary: Growth in 2026 is expected to be 'tepid' and 'sub-par' with U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war weighing on Canada, Kmpg's Fall Economic Outlook says.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
The Canadian economy is facing a “gradual and bumpy recovery” over the next couple of years, Kpmg’s economic outlook said.

The Canadian economy is forecast to grow at one per cent in 2026, with GDP growth ramping up to 1.8 per cent in 2027 and two per cent in 2028, Kpmg’s Fall 2026 Economic Outlook said.

“Business is not as good as in the U.S., but our view is that the Canadian economy will see a gradual and bumpy recovery,” the report said.

The Kpmg forecast does not account for the possibility of a trade deal with the U.S.

“A thaw in trade tensions looks likely, particularly after the midterms, but we have not baked it in given past head fakes,” it said.

Growth in 2026 is expected to be “tepid” and “sub-par” with U.S. President Donald Trump’s trade war weighing on Canada.

However, continued consumer spending, rising investments in AI-related infrastructure, Canadian “adaptation” to U.S. tariffs and “modest” population growth will mean a resilient Canadian economy, the forecast said.

“While that May not be eye-popping growth, our expectation is that the quality of Canada’s growth will improve,” it said.

So far, however, AI investment has failed to spur economic growth in Canada, analysis shows.

Analysis from Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) economists says they don’t expect rising AI investments to add to Canada’s GDP growth in the same way as in the United States.

Claire Fan, a senior economist with RBC, said Canada is beginning to invest more in AI infrastructure, but those investments are being made in computer and peripheral equipment made in other countries.

Over the first half of 2026, these purchases surged 28 per cent, according to national accounts data.

However, Fan said 75 per cent of this equipment is imported from outside of Canada.

The economy is still facing headwinds, the Kmpg report said, with markets being nervous about higher investment in AI, the Bank of Canada raising interest rates and bond yields skyrocketing across the world, including here in Canada, Kpmg said.

The federal budget for 2026 will provide some “modest stimulus” for growth and pave the path for higher immigration, it added.

The prairie provinces are expected to be drivers of regional growth, with Alberta and Saskatchewan benefiting from higher oil prices, major projects investment as well as data centre build out.

Ontario’s economy is expected to rebound in 2027, but growth in Quebec will “remain subdued amid soft population growth.”

The economy in Ontario and Quebec, which rely heavily on manufacturing, could rebound faster in the event of a trade deal.

The Canadian dollar is expected to average between $1.40 and $1.42 compared to the U.S. Dollar in the near term, with the Loonie expected to pick up steam in the back half of 2027.

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.

Middlesex County Library Facility Master Plan

The Middlesex County Library Board received an overview of the proposed Library Facility Master Plan, a long-range planning document examining how library facilities can continue to support residents over the next two and half decades.

The study highlights strong community engagement, with more than 450 public responses helping to shape priorities and identify opportunities for library spaces across the County.

The Library has seen continued growth with branch visits increasing 21% since 2023 to 243,000 annual visits and borrowing increasing 19% to nearly 460,000 items. Digital borrowing now accounts for 42% of overall circulation, demonstrating the Library’s ability to meet evolving user needs.

The plan outlines opportunities to enhance library spaces across the system, including accessibility improvements, integrated libraries, expanded teen and makerspace areas, outdoor gathering spaces, and new ways to connect residents with library services. The recommendations provide a framework to help guide future discussions as Middlesex County continues to grow.

See theLibrary Facility Master Plan presentation") for more information.

Updated Human Resources Policy Handbook

The Library Board adopted the Middlesex County Human Resources Handbook, which streamlines and consolidates existing policies into a more user-friendly structure, organized around employment, benefits, workplace expectations, and health and safety.

The updated handbook strengthens consistency, supports legislative compliance, reduces duplication, and provides clearer guidance for employees and management. It also aligns Human Resources policies with current organizational practices and digital systems. Implementation will include modernization and standardization of the supporting forms, templates, and administrative tools associated with the policies. The policies will continue to be reviewed in response to legislative and regulatory amendments, collective agreement changes, and evolving operational practices and circumstances.

For more information, read theMiddlesex County Human Resources Policy Handbook report").

Library Branches Support Community Safety and Seasonal Programming

This fall, the Library is drawing attention to the No Excuses Bus Safety Campaign, a community-wide initiative reminding drivers to stop for a school bus with flashing lights. The Library will be raising awareness at the branches and online, and promotional materials, including lawn signs, will be available to residents free of charge, while supplies last.

The Library is also offering a variety of seasonal programs and events for residents of all ages, including a community book sale at the Thorndale Branch, a family-friendly Holiday Open House at the Mount Brydges Branch, a festive Winter Lantern Walk at the Strathroy Branch, and a holiday greenery workshop at the Melbourne Branch. These initiatives highlight the Library’s role in bringing residents together through learning, creativity, community connections, and public awareness programming

Read the latest Library Activity Report")for more information.

Library Board Highlights is an informal summary of selected actions taken by the Middlesex Library Board at business meetings. The Library Board Highlights are not an official record of Board proceedings.To view official agendas and minutes, please visit Middlesex Meetings and Minutes.
Middlesex County Library Facility Master Plan

The Middlesex County Library Board received an overview of the proposed Library Facility Master Plan, a long-range planning document examining how library facilities can continue to support residents over the next two and half decades.
The study highlights strong community engagement, with more than 450 public responses helping to shape priorities and identify opportunities for library spaces across the County.

The Library has seen continued growth with branch visits increasing 21% since 2023 to 243,000 annual visits and borrowing increasing 19% to nearly 460,000 items. Digital borrowing now accounts for 42% of overall circulation, demonstrating the Library’s ability to meet evolving user needs.

The plan outlines opportunities to enhance library spaces across the system, including accessibility improvements, integrated libraries, expanded teen and makerspace areas, outdoor gathering spaces, and new ways to connect residents with library services. The recommendations provide a framework to help guide future discussions as Middlesex County continues to grow.
See theLibrary Facility Master Plan presentation") for more information.
Updated Human Resources Policy Handbook

The Library Board adopted the Middlesex County Human Resources Handbook, which streamlines and consolidates existing policies into a more user-friendly structure, organized around employment, benefits, workplace expectations, and health and safety.

The updated handbook strengthens consistency, supports legislative compliance, reduces duplication, and provides clearer guidance for employees and management. It also aligns Human Resources policies with current organizational practices and digital systems. Implementation will include modernization and standardization of the supporting forms, templates, and administrative tools associated with the policies. The policies will continue to be reviewed in response to legislative and regulatory amendments, collective agreement changes, and evolving operational practices and circumstances.
For more information, read theMiddlesex County Human Resources Policy Handbook report").
Library Branches Support Community Safety and Seasonal Programming

This fall, the Library is drawing attention to the No Excuses Bus Safety Campaign, a community-wide initiative reminding drivers to stop for a school bus with flashing lights. The Library will be raising awareness at the branches and online, and promotional materials, including lawn signs, will be available to residents free of charge, while supplies last.

The Library is also offering a variety of seasonal programs and events for residents of all ages, including a community book sale at the Thorndale Branch, a family-friendly Holiday Open House at the Mount Brydges Branch, a festive Winter Lantern Walk at the Strathroy Branch, and a holiday greenery workshop at the Melbourne Branch. These initiatives highlight the Library’s role in bringing residents together through learning, creativity, community connections, and public awareness programming
Read the latest Library Activity Report")for more information.

stories.title: Democrats’ blue tsunami could be reversing travel turnoff of Canada-U.S. trade war
stories.summary: Montreal — Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Montreal — The Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up, travel experts say.

Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh-straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada.

However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September.

At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new leisure bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier.

“It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency.

Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies.

“We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said.

“One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.”

For now, Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations.

Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism.

“Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc.

“There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the attitude of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.”

Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips.

“We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.CA.

Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years.

“I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’”

The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether.

“We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said.

“To market the U.S. is like dynamite.”

Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots.

Corporate travel continues to hum along, Durakovic said, with virtually no drop in Flight Centre bookings over the past couple of years.

“It’s still business as usual. You can’t exactly stop travelling to the U.S. because of politics,” she said.

The broader Canadian aversion to travelling south of the border combined with the shutdown of Cuban resorts amid a fuel shortage caused by an American oil blockade has pushed sun seekers farther afield.

Mexico, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica have surged in popularity, travel agents said. Portugal and Spain have also enjoyed a recent boost in Canadian visitors.

“Air Transat flights to Malaga are full,” said Sal Lato, who owns the Voyages Marlin travel agency franchise. Meanwhile, the leisure airline has cut the 36 flights a week it operated between Canada and Florida in late 2024 down to zero.

Not all winter escapees can simply point their finger at a fresh spot on the map and jet off for a getaway, extended or otherwise.

“There are still deep ties to many U.S. snowbird destinations,” said Stephen Fine, founder of Snowbird Advisor Insurance.

“They have friends who’ve been going there for years and they want to be able to spend their winters with that community,” he said of many Canadians.

“A lot of them own properties there. People want to drive down to their destination or have their vehicles with them for the winter,” he noted. For them, America May be the only option.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

The prime minister had to be ushered away from the U.S. ambassador following a ceremony in Ottawa Wednesday

Prime Minister Mark Carney greets veterans during the National Remembrance Day ceremony at the National War Memorial in Ottawa Nov. 11, 2026. (Blair Gable / Postmedia)

National Post staff

November 12, 2026 at 9:57 a.m.

Canadians watching Wednesday’s Remembrance Day ceremonies in Ottawa witnessed a rare moment between two political antagonists, Prime Minister Mark Carney and Pete Hoekstra, the U.S. Ambassador to Canada.

As Carney and Governor General Louise Arbour left the cenotaph at the National War Memorial following the ceremony, both dignitaries stopped briefly to greet people nearby, mostly veterans, including some of the oldest living ones.

As seen on Cpac, Carney, accompanied by his wife, Diana Fox Carney, stopped for several moments to speak with an elderly veteran seated in an assisted walking device and bundled against the cold. During their chat, Carney learns the man is “three months away from turning 101” years old.

looks like Pete Hoekstra was keen to have a word with the PM pic.twitter.com/JVTDL98ZB0 — Scott Robertson (@sarobertson_) November 11, 2026

A few steps later, another veteran hands the prime minister a piece of paper, which he puts in his pocket after a few more handshakes with awaiting veterans. Just before he reaches Hoekstra, another said: “Mr. Prime Minister, I couldn’t be prouder of you.”

Upon reaching Hoekstra, the ambassador is seen leaning in to say something undiscernible to Carney while shaking his hand. Carney responds and motions that he’s moving forward as Hoekstra’s grip lingers.

As Hoekstra says something to Carney that elicits a chuckle from the next people in line, an officer with the prime minister pipes in.

“We’re going to miss the March,” he says.

“Yeah, we’ll get going,” Carney says, breaking free from Hoekstra. “Sorry, Randy. I apologize.”

That’s the last time either is seen in Cpac’s video.

Like U.S. President Donald Trump, who gave Hoekstra the ambassadorship at his own request, the diplomat has been a polarizing figure amidst the efforts to stabilize the tenuous trade between the neighbouring nations.

Leading into the U.S. midterm elections, Hoekstra warned Canadian politicians to “keep your nose out of American politics,” alleging Canadian interference in the form of lobbying and retaliatory tariffs, though he provided no evidence.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra has claimed that Canada paying to construct the Gordie Howe International Bridge is a “big myth.” Tony Caldwell/Postmedia

In August, he told iPolitics that Carney and Canadians shouldn’t expect more Democratic power in the halls of U.S. government to make an immediate and meaningful difference in trade negotiations. He also disputed Canada’s “leverage.”

“I’ve heard the arguments for 16, 18 months. I’ve heard we’ve got the leverage. It’s time for America to come to their knees,” he said.

“It’s the president’s call, but I don’t think you’re going to find the president coming back to Canada on his knees as much as Canadians might like that.”

Earlier this summer, he also embroiled himself in the debate over the new Gordie Howe International Bridge between Windsor and Detroit, claiming that it’s a “big myth” that Canada paid for its construction. (Canada did pay the estimated CA$6.4 billion for the crossing and anticipates recovering the investment via tolls over time.)

Meanwhile, a parliamentary petition calling for Hoekstra’s to be declared “persona non grata” and to request his removal as ambassador, accusing him of undermining Canada-U.S. diplomatic relations and normalizing “51st state” language, now sits at 284,635 signatures.

stories.title: Blue Jays eye versatile Jazz Chisholm Jr. in search for offence
stories.summary: Chisholm initially broke into the majors as an infielder with the Miami Marlins, but was moved to centre field in 2023.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Shi Davidi, Sportsnet

Posted November 12, 2026 9:56 am.

The Toronto Blue Jays are prioritizing offence as they explore all areas of the off-season market and while they see adding to the outfield as the cleanest fit, they’re taking a long look at available infielders, too.

Having already expressed interest in free-agent second baseman Brandon Lowe as the GM Meetings opened, they met Wednesday with representatives for Jazz Chisholm Jr., and are monitoring what the Arizona Diamondbacks do with Ketel Marte, who landed on the restricted list this season and has no-trade protection as a 10-and-5 player.

All of that is standard operating procedure for the Blue Jays as they gauge where the opportunities lie for them in the coming weeks. But Chisholm, intriguingly, is open to a versatile defensive role in which he moves between multiple positions, including the outfield, after being used almost exclusively in the infield, mostly second base, by the New York Yankees over the past two-and-a-half seasons.

The 28-year-old initially broke into the majors as an infielder with the Miami Marlins, but was moved to centre field in 2023 and stayed there until they sent him to the Yankees at the 2024 trade deadline. In New York, he played two games in centre while logging 74 at third base and 237 at second, where in 2026, his defence was eight outs above average.

That positional flexibility, along with his power-speed profile, match up well with traits the Blue Jays value and could potentially jolt an offence that ranked last in the majors with 648 runs. And unlike Lowe, who mashed 35 home runs for the Pittsburgh Pirates and offers the type of production they’re seeking, Chisholm isn’t saddled with a qualifying offer, so the team that signs him won’t have to surrender a compensatory draft pick.

Marte, owed $76 million over the next four seasons, would cost both money and trade assets, but his price should be lower than when the Blue Jays checked on him in previous winters, as he was placed on the restricted list after an initially unexplained no-show for an August game at Boston. That strained his relationship with the club, which may be more willing to trade him, although the switch-hitting second baseman, a three-time all-star, controls the process having reached 10 years of big-league service, five consecutive with his current team.

That Marte’s wife is Vladimir Guerrero Jr.’s first cousin could entice him to accept the Blue Jays as a trade destination, should the other elements line up. Another big-ticket trade option could be Texas Rangers shortstop Corey Seager, although he’s owed $157.5 million over the next five years, likely making him prohibitively expensive.

The Blue Jays have Guerrero, Ernie Clement, Andres Gimenez, Kazuma Okamoto, Josh Smith and Charles McAdoo for the infield along with Addison Barger, who can toggle between right field and third base, so any adds there would create surplus, even with the DH spot open.

Their outfield mix includes Barger, Nathan Lukes, Brett Bateman, Anthony Santander, McAdoo and Davis Schneider. A reliable right-handed hitter like Seiya Suzuki, whom they are pursuing and appears to be one of their clearest fits, makes sense. Another target is Teruaki Sato, who like Barger is a left-handed hitting third baseman/outfielder, but has enough upside to negate concerns about roster redundancy.

Like Suzuki, Randy Arozarena bats right-handed and fits their offensive needs. Agent Scott Boras described him as “a model of consistency and he’s done it in a market (Seattle) where right-handed hitters go to die. He is 20-20 every year, multiple all-star teams. I think you’d say he was Seattle’s best hitter this season. Essentially, this rose has no thorns. And all the teams, frankly, they’re feeling really randy.”

Maybe so, but the slew of deal-making expected before the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1 is yet to begin. As the GM Meetings conclude Thursday, the Blue Jays’ preference list may still be somewhat uncertain, but their determination to add offence in some form remains clear.

Short hops :

The Blue Jays intend to add a starter and they’ve done lots of background work on Kaima Taira, the intriguing five-foot-eight, 209-pound righty who posted a 1.36 ERA in 146 innings with the NPB’s Seibu Lions. Taira isn’t visiting the cities of interested clubs since he’s currently in Japan and instead, “we’re doing a lot of Zooms with all the teams and that’s how they’re doing the introductions,” said Boras, his agent. “He’s got a fastball that few major-leaguers have. It has very late movement, and it’s up in the zone. He has the ability to be an upper-level pitcher in a rotation, no question.” …

Has the way the Blue Jays handled Kazuma Okamato’s transition to the big-leagues and helped Yusei Kikuchi find his way helped their perception among Japanese players? “Toronto has a vast sports-science process, an international process,” replied Boras. “I can’t think of any Japanese pitcher I’ve had that’s interacted with the Blue Jays and has not had a great experience.”

A good line from Boras on Max Scherzer’s future that hints at his plans but doesn’t provide a definitive answer: “If you saw Scherzer’s last game, I think you understand he’s far from maxed out.”

stories.title: Lab equipment upgrades to speed up patient test results: LHSC
stories.summary: Patients at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) are expected to have faster access to test results following a major upgrade to laboratory equipment at University Hospital and Victoria Hospital.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Patients at London Health Sciences Centre (LHSC) are expected to have faster access to test results following a major upgrade to laboratory equipment at University Hospital and Victoria Hospital.

LHSC says its Core Labs, which process patient bloodwork, can now handle more than 15,000 tests per hour combined, an increase of just over 24 per cent from previous capacity. Equipment used to prepare samples for testing was also upgraded, extending its lifespan by another five years.

The installation took place over the spring and summer and was funded through LHSC’s existing budget. The new equipment was fully operational by the end of August.

The Core Labs are responsible for processing tests used to diagnose and monitor a wide range of conditions, including diabetes, infections, and heart, kidney and liver disease.

Samples analyzed in the Core Labs can also be sent to specialized laboratories at LHSC for further testing when required.

Hospital officials say the new equipment provides greater automation, faster processing, increased testing capacity and improved reliability. The technology also requires less hands-on maintenance, allowing staff to focus on patient care.

stories.title: Tesla driver found asleep on Highway 417 during Ottawa rush hour: OPP
stories.summary: A driver has been charged with careless driving after allegedly falling asleep behind the wheel of a Tesla during Ottawa rush-hour traffic.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A driver has been charged with careless driving after allegedly falling asleep behind the wheel of a Tesla during Ottawa rush-hour traffic.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said an officer spotted the driver sleeping at the wheel of a Tesla SUV Tuesday afternoon on Highway 417.

The OPP said in a Facebook post Wednesday that even if a vehicle is equipped with self-driving capabilities, drivers are still required to exercise reasonable care and attention while driving.

The driver, whose identity was not released, faces a fine of up to $490 and six demerit points if convicted of careless driving.

stories.title: St. Thomas man charged after fire at community pool
stories.summary: St. Thomas police said officers on community patrol spotted an active fire and signs of forced entry at Jaycees Community Pool on Inkerman Street on Wednesday night.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A St. Thomas man is facing several charges after police responding to a fire at a community pool reported finding evidence of a break-in.

St. Thomas police said officers on community patrol spotted an active fire and signs of forced entry at Jaycees Community Pool on Inkerman Street on Wednesday night.

According to police, two people were seen running from the area when officers arrived — the fire was extinguished and no injuries were reported.

Investigators said a description of the suspects was shared with officers, who quickly located a 21-year-old man on Balaclava Street. Police allege the man provided a false name when approached.

The accused has been charged with arson, break and enter, mischief and obstructing a peace officer.

Police said a second suspect has been identified but has not yet been located.

stories.title: Carney to meet European leaders in Ireland before heading to Asia
stories.summary: Carney is attending the European Political Community summit, where leaders discuss geopolitical issues every six months, ever since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Dublin for an informal meeting with European leaders, ahead of summits in Asia.

Carney is attending the European Political Community summit, where leaders discuss geopolitical issues every six months, ever since Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The prime minister will be among more than a dozen leaders gathering today to hear from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy about the state of negotiations with Russia.

Carney is set to leave for Asia Thursday evening, possibly before the arrival of U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law, Jared Kushner, to brief Zelenskyy on talks with Russia.

Carney says attending today’s summit is meant to boost affordability and economic opportunity for Canada through new partnerships with Europe.

Carney is also set to have bilateral discussions today with his counterparts from Greece and Cyprus, two European Union countries that haven’t ratified a decade-old trade deal with Europe.

stories.title: Brookfield reports third-quarter profit up from year ago
stories.summary: Revenue for the quarter totalled $20.69-billion
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Brookfield Corp. BN-T reported a profit attributable to shareholders of US$1.31-billion for its latest quarter, up from US$219-million in the same quarter last year.

The company, which keeps its books in U.S. dollars, says the profit amounted to 54 US cents per diluted share for three-month period ended Sept. 30.

The result compared with a profit of eight US cents per diluted share in the same quarter last year.

Revenue for what was Brookfield’s third quarter totalled US$20.69-billion, up from US$18.92-billion in the third quarter of 2025.

Brookfield says its distributable earnings per share amounted to 73 US cents per share, up from 63 US cents per share a year ago.

Brookfield president Nick Goodman said the company’s focus on real assets with inflation-linked revenues, pricing power and durable cash flows positions its well for continued growth.
