stories.title: AI is not adding to Canada’s GDP like it is in the U.S., new analysis says
stories.summary: A slower adoption of artificial intelligence has had a net-neutral effect on Canada’s GDP, new analysis says. But long-term productivity gains are still possible.
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
A slower adoption of artificial intelligence has had a net-neutral effect on Canada’s GDP, new analysis says. But long-term productivity gains are still possible.

Analysis from Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) economists says they don’t expect rising AI investments to add to Canada’s GDP growth in the same way as in the United States.

Claire Fan, a senior economist with RBC, said Canada is beginning to invest more in AI infrastructure, but those investments are being made in computer and peripheral equipment made in other countries.

Over the first half of 2026, these purchases surged 28 per cent, according to national accounts data.

However, Fan said 75 per cent of this equipment is imported from outside of Canada.

“We are a little bit behind. Canadian businesses are adopting at a slower pace than American businesses,” Joël Blit, an economics professor at the University of Waterloo as well as co-founder and co-director of the Canadian AI Adoption Centre, told Global News.

While Blit said he agrees that investments into AI infrastructure are directly benefitting the economies that produce them, not Canada’s, he said that is not the most important question economists should be asking.

“Productivity, I expect, is gonna rise significantly,” he said. “But that is going to take a little bit longer because you need to make these investments and then they have to work their way through until you can actually produce in these new ways with this new technology.”

Blit studies disruptive technologies which include things like electricity, computers and the internet. He said the first stage involves inserting the new technology into the current workflow as a direct replacement.

“An example of that might be a human computer was a person who sat at desks all day and did arithmetic for a living. Well, you were still doing everything the same way you always did, but now instead of asking the person to do that arithmetic, you go and ask the computer,” he said.

This only improves productivity slightly , he said.

He said real gains come when people “reimagine how they do their business.”

“Barnes and Noble used the internet to better track inventories, to help people find books on shelves. But Amazon re-imagined the book-selling industry as a whole,” he said.

But in order for that kind of reimagination to be possible, Blit said complimentary investments are needed .

“You also have to retrain people and you May need to re-engineer your processes to take full advantage of the new technology,” he said.

Public opinion polling shows that the majority of Canadians hold a negative view of AI.

Data from Angus Reid collected in the first half of the year shows 43 per cent of Canadians view AI negatively and 24 per cent are critical of it.

Despite the negative perceptions, Canadians are still using AI. The same survey found that 41 per cent of Canadians use AI more than once per week, compared to 30 per cent who don’t use AI at all.

Blit said this individual use could help Canada in the long run as much of the adoption in businesses is not coming “top down.”

“A lot of what’s happening in organizations is not that the head boss is saying, ‘hey, let’s adopt this technology’. It’s that if they provide the guardrail, if they provide access to the technology and the guardrails, people are gonna use them,” he said.

Fan said AI investments over the past year have amounted to just over one per cent of GDP per hour worked. But Blit said this emphasizes the importance of increasing AI literacy and exploration.

“It’s so important for us as a country to invest in AI literacy so that we can empower as many Canadians as possible to experiment and find ways to use these tools,” he said.

content_blocks.text: “You also have to retrain people and you May need to re-engineer your processes to take full advantage of the new technology,” he said.
Public opinion polling shows that the majority of Canadians hold a negative view of AI.
Data from Angus Reid collected in the first half of the year shows 43 per cent of Canadians view AI negatively and 24 per cent are critical of it.
Despite the negative perceptions, Canadians are still using AI. The same survey found that 41 per cent of Canadians use AI more than once per week, compared to 30 per cent who don’t use AI at all.
Blit said this individual use could help Canada in the long run as much of the adoption in businesses is not coming “top down.”

“A lot of what’s happening in organizations is not that the head boss is saying, ‘hey, let’s adopt this technology’. It’s that if they provide the guardrail, if they provide access to the technology and the guardrails, people are gonna use them,” he said.
Fan said AI investments over the past year have amounted to just over one per cent of GDP per hour worked. But Blit said this emphasizes the importance of increasing AI literacy and exploration.
“It’s so important for us as a country to invest in AI literacy so that we can empower as many Canadians as possible to experiment and find ways to use these tools,” he said.

stories.title: Carney sees Ottawa’s growing ties with EU leading to more partnerships with Canada’s auto sector
stories.summary: Speaking at a summit in Dublin, Prime Minister declined to say whether Canada was any closer to welcoming Chinese investment in the sector
stories.author: Steven Chase
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney says he expects more European partnerships with Canada’s auto sector coming out of Ottawa’s budding relationship with the European Union but couldn’t say whether Chinese automakers are any closer to building cars here.

Speaking to reporters at a summit of European leaders in Dublin, the Prime Minister said Chinese investment in Canada’s auto sector will be one of the topics under discussion with China’s President Xi Jinping when the two meet next week in Shenzhen.

Mr. Carney’s visit to the European Political Community summit in Ireland on Thursday is his first trip to the continent since it was confirmed last month that Canada is working toward becoming the first “associate member” of the European Union.

Back in January, Mr. Carney’s government announced a strategic partnership with China and said it expected significant Chinese auto investment in Canada “within three years.”

But on Thursday, Mr. Carney declined to say whether Canada was any closer to welcoming Chinese investment in the auto sector 10 months after the Beijing announcement with Mr. Xi .

“Canadian auto workers are some of the most productive auto workers in the world, are certainly the most productive in North America, and so we want real opportunity for those workers,” the Prime Minister said.

He noted South Korea, Japan and countries in Europe have made or pledged investments in Canada’s auto sector, including within the electric vehicle industry. Toyota and Honda have car plants in Canada, and other companies have pledged battery facilities.

“I think you will see more European partnerships coming out of this,” the Prime Minister said, referring to growing Canada-EU relations.

He hedged on China, though, saying “the extent to which there’s Chinese investment depends on a variety of factors. It’ll be one of the discussions with President Xi.”

He said he was also mindful of the fact that talks about Chinese auto investment have implications for relations with the United States. Canada-China co-operation on autos “also is relevant to our ongoing discussions with the United States,” Mr. Carney said.

The U.S. has a 100-per-cent tariff in place on Chinese-made electric vehicles. Canada, which imposed the same tariff back in 2024 in tandem with the former Joe Biden administration, broke with the United States in January to scale back 100-per-cent tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles in return for Beijing sharply reducing retaliatory levies on canola products and other agricultural shipments from Canada.

The United States, during negotiations on a new trade deal with Canada and Mexico, has been pressing Ottawa into aligning its tariffs with the steep U.S. levies on China.

The Canadian government offered a more optimistic projection for Chinese auto investment in Canada. Back in January, the Prime Minister’s Office said it expected within three years, the new partnership with Beijing “will drive considerable new Chinese joint-venture investment in Canada with trusted partners to protect and create new auto manufacturing careers for Canadian workers, and ensure a robust build-out of Canada’s EV supply chain.”

Mr. Carney is due to meet with Mr. Xi on Nov. 17 in Shenzhen, where China is hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

In June, Industry Minister Mélanie Joly met with four Chinese companies in China about the possibility of them building electric vehicles in Canada.

The four companies – BYD, Chery, Geely and Shanghai Launch Automotive Technology – had been examining possible investments in Canada. Ms. Joly said Shanghai Launch’s proposal includes a partnership with British automaker Austin Motor Co.

The push to attract Chinese investment was an effort by the Carney government to save the Canadian auto industry as it faces an uncertain future because of protectionist United States trade policy.

The federal government has been repairing ties with China as it seeks to reduce dependence on U.S. trade.

In April, Ms. Joly rejected Stellantis NV’s plan to assemble electric cars with kits shipped from China at the automaker’s idled factory near Toronto, saying she wants cars to be made with Canadian parts and Canadian labour.

Asked Thursday in Dublin, Mr. Carney said his government still rejects kit car assembly plants.

The Prime Minister also reiterated earlier comments that automaker Stellantis’s decision to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant amounted to a “betrayal” of thousands of Canadian workers.

He said Stellantis is violating obligations it made under several agreements, including a battery production deal.

“The betrayal is not fulfilling all the obligations for all of the workers. That’s the responsibility of Stellantis. That’s the responsibility they made multiple times, including in the battery deal that they signed with the government,” he said.

“We will pursue all of this. A partial solution is a step. It is not a global solution.”

stories.title: Engineering team creates 3D-printed raptor puppets to help wildlife rehabilitation
stories.summary: Western Engineering team worked with Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre on 3D-printed puppets to help baby birds in rehab
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
Four new feeding puppets at Salthaven Wildlife Rehabilitation and Education Centre will help caregivers feed young raptors while reducing their contact with people when baby season returns next year.

Created through a collaboration with Western Engineering, the 3D-printed puppets resemble a great horned owl, merlin falcon, red-tailed hawk and American kestrel. They are designed to encourage nestlings to associate food with their own species rather than people – an important part of preparing these young patients for a return to the wild.

“Birds get along in the wild by learning from one another by example and when they don’t have one another to learn from, then their chances of survival are pretty slim,” said Salthaven founder Brian Salt. “Our mission is to help rehabilitate sick, injured or orphaned wildlife and return them to the wild so that they can sustain themselves there.”

The 3D-printed raptor puppets designed by a Western Engineering team for their capstone project. (Submitted)

The puppets help preserve that connection to their own species by giving young birds a familiar-looking face at feeding time. Caregivers can offer food through the puppet’s beak while keeping their hands concealed, and recordings of parent birds’ calls help make the experience more realistic.

“Feeding them with a puppet, it takes away that human element and allows them to relate to their own kind a whole lot better,” said Salt. “It increases their chances of survivability in the wild substantially.”

Previously, caregivers wore reflective masks and gowns to obscure their human form during repeated daily feedings. Salthaven also used a rudimentary great horned owl puppet, but feeding required reaching around its face to offer food. The new designs allow feeding forceps to pass through the head and out beneath the beak.

The project is the latest development in a partnership that connects hands-on student learning with the needs of a local wildlife rehabilitation centre.

The collaboration began with a Western Engineering capstone team that designed specialized leg splints for injured Canada geese and mallard ducks. Thanks to a donated 3D printer, Salthaven is now able to reproduce the splints itself.

That relationship opened the door to the feeding puppets. Joel Sierra, an undergraduate student from Lima, Peru, designed and printed the puppet heads while at Western as a visiting researcher, incorporating feedback from Salt.

A local artist then painted the heads and canvas sleeves to match each species, transforming the printed forms into convincing stand-ins for raptor parents. Salthaven also received the digital designs so it can print additional heads as needed.

“Working with Salthaven is always interesting, enriching and a lot of fun,” said Ryan Willing, professor in the department of mechanical and materials engineering, who supervised the engineering teams for both projects.

“From designing 3D printable splints for waterfowl, to creating realistic bird head puppets for feeding fledglings, it’s wonderful to watch students spread their wings and apply their engineering expertise to solve challenging real-world problems impacting wildlife in our local communities.”

Learn more about how Western is preparing future leaders and global citizens.

stories.title: Owner rents out Regent Park condo, but jumps at chance to sell
stories.summary: This one-bedroom unit sat on the market for about five weeks last fall but this time, got a conditional offer in 10 days
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
170 Sumach St., No. 307, Toronto

Asking price: $449,900 (September 2026)

Selling price: $439,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling price: $271,768 (April 2014)

Taxes: $2,332 (2026)

Days on the market: 16

Listing agent: Christopher Bibby, Re/Max Hallmark Bibby Group Realty

At One Park Place, across from Regent Park Athletic Grounds and Pam McConnell Aquatic Centre, this one-bedroom unit was listed in the $500,000s last fall and sat on the market for about five weeks. The owner found a renter instead but resumed their search for buyers this fall. With a lower price of $449,900, the condo got a conditional offer within 10 days. The deal was finalized for $439,000 the next week.

“It sold a little faster than what was expected or planned because the conditions today are unpredictable,” said agent Christopher Bibby.

“We looked at other sales in the building for similar size units, and we felt it was priced fairly, even if someone would try to negotiate a bit.”

Mr. Bibby also notes that this 568-square-foot space, built in 2014, has a functional plan that end-users like.

“In a lot of new buildings in the immediate area, the one-bedroom units are quite a bit smaller, mostly under 500 square feet,” Mr. Bibby said.

“[Here] you could have a dining table and a full-size sofa. There was a balcony right at the tree line, and there was a window in the bedroom.”

This unit has floor-to-ceiling windows and a balcony with access from the bedroom and living room.

There is a four-piece bathroom, a closet for stacked laundry machines, and a U-shaped kitchen with stainless-steel appliances.

The unit has a storage locker, but no parking spot. Monthly fees of $540 cover heating and water. Common areas include a gym, sports courts, theatre and party room, as well as a rooftop terrace.

“It feels more like you’re in a neighbourhood rather than downtown,” Mr. Bibby said.

“You step outside and there’s a playground, a soccer field, a kids’ school and a community centre.”

At One Park Place, across from Regent Park Athletic Grounds and Pam McConnell Aquatic Centre, this one-bedroom unit was listed in the $500,000s last fall and sat on the market for about five weeks. The owner found a renter instead but resumed their search for buyers this fall. With a lower price of $449,900, the condo got a conditional offer within 10 days. The deal was finalized for $439,000 the next week.
“It sold a little faster than what was expected or planned because the conditions today are unpredictable,” said agent Christopher Bibby.
“We looked at other sales in the building for similar size units, and we felt it was priced fairly, even if someone would try to negotiate a bit.”
Mr. Bibby also notes that this 568-square-foot space, built in 2014, has a functional plan that end-users like.
“In a lot of new buildings in the immediate area, the one-bedroom units are quite a bit smaller, mostly under 500 square feet,” Mr. Bibby said.
“[Here] you could have a dining table and a full-size sofa. There was a balcony right at the tree line, and there was a window in the bedroom.”
This unit has floor-to-ceiling windows and a balcony with access from the bedroom and living room.
There is a four-piece bathroom, a closet for stacked laundry machines, and a U-shaped kitchen with stainless-steel appliances.
The unit has a storage locker, but no parking spot. Monthly fees of $540 cover heating and water. Common areas include a gym, sports courts, theatre and party room, as well as a rooftop terrace.
“It feels more like you’re in a neighbourhood rather than downtown,” Mr. Bibby said.
“You step outside and there’s a playground, a soccer field, a kids’ school and a community centre.”

stories.title: North York home next to a church receives duelling offers
stories.summary: Some horse trading for this four-bedroom home before sellers accepted $3.38-million package
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
67 Dunblaine Ave., Toronto

Asking price: $3,595,000 (August 2026)

Selling price: $3.38-million (August 2026)

Previous selling price: $2,975,000 (May 2019)

Taxes: $16,696 (2026)

Days on the market: 13

Listing agent: Andre Kutyan, Harvey Kalles Real Estate Ltd.

Agent Andre Kutyan was enlisted to sell this four-bedroom home on a 42- by 130-foot lot near Avenue Road about three months after he sold a similar property for $4-million a few streets away. The differentiating feature with this home was its location next to a church. Mr. Kutyan considered that in pricing the property at $3,595,000 this summer.

“Any time you’re next to something that’s not a house – whether it’s a church, school, or commercial property – there has to be a discount for that,” Mr. Kutyan said.

He also believed that price was something of a sweet spot for the neighbourhood.

“Properties in the mid to low $3-million range are very hard to come by in the area. ... There’s a lot of stuff sitting in the $4-million plus [range].”

One buyer submitted a bid, but on hearing that another party offered more money, though with conditions, they raised their price and removed their conditions. The sellers accepted their $3.38-million package.

“As a seller, you want to go with a firm deal,” said Mr. Kutyan.

“If the [price] difference is nominal – maybe 1 or 2 per cent or less – it’s not worth taking a chance on a conditional deal.”

Custom-built in 2019, this two-storey house has 3,647 square feet of living space, plus a finished basement with access into the double garage.

Ceiling heights are 10 feet in the office, living and dining areas, as well as the eat-in kitchen. The family room also has a gas fireplace and sliding doors to a two-tiered deck and yard.

There are five bathrooms, most with heated flooring.

“It was designed by Peter Higgins, one of the premier architects in central and midtown Toronto, with a really good layout and design,” Mr. Kutyan said.

“For example, this house has a rough-in for an elevator.”

stories.title: A home that zigs and zags to catch the light
stories.summary: Arranged in a zigzag, or Z-shaped, configuration, this Ottawa home uses aesthetics and symmetry to create a warm atmosphere
stories.author: Matthew Hague
stories.content:
For many people, the office is where they discover things they dislike: the frustration of paper jams, the discomfort of cramped cubicles, the pitfalls of petty corporate politics. But when IBK Ajila worked at Shopify’s Ottawa headquarters, a space lined with so much warm wood that it almost resembled a sauna, he discovered something he loved: design. “I didn’t realize that architecture could actually make you feel so good,” he says.

Although Mr. Ajila eventually left tech for a career as a therapist, he kept that office in mind when it came time to hire an architect for his own design project. After he and his wife, Lisa, found a prime lot in Ottawa’s west end, bordering a National Capital Commission park, they approached Linebox Studios to design a custom home.

Linebox had designed not only Shopify’s office but also the houses of several of the couple’s friends, including a former manager. “Initially, I actually said I didn’t want the space to feel too Linebox,” said Mr. Ajila. “They often use symmetry, or sets of three windows together. I said I didn’t want that.”

At the outset, Linebox founder Andrew Reeves and project architect Jennifer Jabs focused less on aesthetics and symmetry than on the atmosphere the couple wanted to create. “Light was part of Lisa and Ibk’s description of what they wanted for the home,” Mr. Reeves said. “At one point, they said they imagined having a house where you never needed to turn the lights on during the day.”

“It was actually an off-the-cuff remark,” Mr. Ajila said. “But Andrew took that and really turned it into the thesis of the whole house.”

The challenge was that the lot ran east-west, with a neighbouring house directly to the south, blocking the sun. The parkland lay to the north. “We wanted to have certain views, certain light conditions,” Mr. Reeves said. “But there were zoning and code limitations on the number of windows we could have close to the lot lines.”

Rather than opt for a conventional rectangular floor plan, Mr. Reeves and Ms. Jabs arranged the house in a zigzag, or Z-shaped, configuration – a first for the firm. By alternating between projections toward and recesses away from the lot lines, they could accommodate the large windows needed to capture sunlight as it moved across the southern side of the house while framing views of the park to the north. “We didn’t need any variances,” Mr. Reeves said. “It’s not conventional, but it works with the zoning.”

The design also creates a beautiful interior environment. The main floor, with its open, flowing kitchen, dining, and living areas, is suffused with sunshine and picture-perfect views, not only of the nearby forest but also of the outdoor spaces tucked into the house’s architectural zigzags. “We have a backyard with a pool we use a lot during the summer,” Mr. Ajila said. “There’s a courtyard along the side of the house with a hot tub we use more in the winter.”

Mr. Ajila also appreciates how the house’s unconventional, criss-crossing footprint allows him to catch glimpses of the building from different windows. “You wouldn’t get that with a rectangle,” he said. “We spent a lot of time picking the cladding materials – the brick, the wood. They’re nice to see.”

On the second floor, the bedrooms are divided into two wings, separated by a skylit atrium. During the planning process, Mr. Ajila mentioned that he liked to get up early and cycle along the nearby Ottawa River. But he didn’t want to disturb his family as he got ready. He and Lisa had one young child at the time of construction and were expecting their second.

“To reduce noise, Linebox proposed putting the primary bedroom at one end of the house and the kids’ rooms at the other,” Mr. Ajila says. “It was a thoughtful way to ensure my morning wouldn’t affect the whole family.”

Still, the separation gave Mr. Ajila pause. “I wasn’t sure I wanted my room to be too far from the kids,” he said. But Linebox built a virtual-reality model that allowed him to explore the design. “Some people read plans, but it wasn’t until I saw the space in VR that I was sold on the proportions, the way the whole house would come together.”

The children aren’t relegated to a forgotten corner. They have the pool and a basement play space equipped with climbing walls and a slide. “The playroom was originally supposed to be a kitchenette,” Mr. Ajila said. “But we realized we would never use it. We ended up with a much more fun alternative. And when the children are older, there’s plumbing hidden behind the climbing bars so the space can be converted into an actual bar if we want.”

As the design process progressed, Mr. Ajila relaxed one of his original requirements. Linebox incorporated its signature grouping of three windows in a couple of places after all. “If somebody sees those three parallel lines and said, ‘I wonder if that’s Linebox,’ I’m actually happy,” he said. “I realize that their motifs aren’t taking away from the fact that this is our home. It’s idiosyncratic to us.”

stories.title: Impacts from B.C. drenching mount as water levels rise
stories.summary: The impacts of the drenching on B.C.'s south coast have been increasing as rain triggers evacuation orders and alerts, flood warnings and the shutdown of a water treatment plant.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The impacts of the drenching on British Columbia’s south coast have been increasing as heavy rain triggers evacuation orders and alerts, flood warnings and the shutdown of a water treatment plant.

The Village of Pemberton has issued an evacuation order for properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, wastewater treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course due to flooding and “high-risk river levels.”

The Lilʼwat Nation has also issued an evacuation order and an evacuation alert for the area from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake due to flooding.

The Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the Village of Sayward on the northeast coast of Vancouver Island as high flows in Newcastle Creek lead to extra sediment in the water.

An evacuation order due to flooding and landslide risks remains in place for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

Some areas saw a lull in the rain on Wednesday, though orange rainfall warnings remain in place for west and inland Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky region, with downpours expected today.

The designation means severe storms are likely to cause significant damage and disruption.

stories.title: What happens when your face becomes data?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses who sets the thresholds for obedience and what happens when facial recognition data collection is non-negotiable.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Facial recognition is marketed as convenient, but it seems like the ease comes at a cost.

Biometric surveillance has become central to security information systems across government agencies including border patrol, policing and immigration. These are instances where choice and consent come at the price of life and liberty.

Host Maria Kestane speaks to Aaron Tucker, author and associate professor at Memorial University of Newfoundland. They discuss who sets the thresholds for obedience, and what happens when data collection is non-negotiable.

stories.title: Author Kate Cayley, playwright Jordan Tannahill win Governor General's Literary Awards
stories.summary: Toronto - Works about a gentrifying neighbourhood struck by tragedy and a provocative fictionalization of a member of the Royal Family are among the Governor General's Literary Award winners.
stories.author: Kaitlyn McGrath The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - Works about a gentrifying neighbourhood struck by tragedy and a provocative fictionalization of a member of the Royal Family are among this year’s Governor General’s Literary Award winners.

Toronto author Kate Cayley received the fiction prize for her debut novel “Property,” which follows characters living in the city’s west end during a spring day as their lives become increasingly interconnected following a death.

“It feels like you’ve suddenly found yourself in one of your own daydreams,” Cayley said about learning she had won the prestigious prize.

The Canada Council for the Arts recognized 14 English and French winners on Thursday that represent outstanding literary works in Canada.

Each winner receives $25,000, while publishers get $3,000 to promote the winning books. Finalists receive $1,000 each.

The drama award went to playwright Jordan Tannahill for his play set in a future where Prince George, the eldest son of the Prince and Princess of Wales, is a gay man. This is the third Governor General’s Literary Award for the 38-year-old playwright, who also won the drama prize in 2014 and 2018.

The non-fiction winner was Trina Moyles for her memoir “Black Bear: A Story of Siblinghood and Survival,” in which she writes about her evolving attitudes toward the animal alongside her relationship with her late brother.

Meanwhile, the poetry award went to Gillian Sze for “An Orange, A Syllable” while “Together by the Sea” by Katia Grubisic won the French-to-English translation award. “Touching Grass” by Kristy Jackson received the young people’s text award, while Matthew Forsythe received the young people’s illustrated books category for “Aggie and the Ghost.”

There are separate French-language categories for francophone writing.

Cayley, who is also a poet and playwright, said she felt “incredibly lucky and grateful” to be recognized by one of the country’s oldest and most prestigious literary awards.

“These kinds of awards mean that you keep writing,” she said. “That you feel both supported in your writing, recognized by your peers, and also the fact that it’s monetary means that you can just keep going.”

“Property” was inspired by Virginia Woolf’s “Mrs. Dalloway,” Cayley said, calling it “almost a rewriting” of the classic stream-of-consciousness novel.

“I wanted to write a novel in which you are really feeling the weight of the kind of ordinary interior,” said Cayley, who began writing the novel in 2022 during a COVID-19 lockdown. “You’re having the same thoughts over again. You are sort of half-thinking about a fight with your partner and half-thinking about your grocery list.

“But we as the reader are hovering above it knowing that something is going to happen to one of these people and we sort of see it coming, and I like to think that when it does come, it’s not quite what we expected,” she said.

The honour is the second of the week for Cayley’s “Property,” which also took home the $20,000 Toronto Book Award, presented by the City of Toronto and the Toronto Public Library. Indeed, Cayley called it a “very Toronto book” and said it was inspired “partly by a rat infestation in my house.”

“Rats are a big part of this novel,” said Cayley who calls the city’s west end home.

Meanwhile, Tannahill said each time he’s won the prize it’s been “an extraordinary honour.”

“I’m in a different place in my life now than when I won it back in 2018 or 2014,” the Ottawa-born writer said, referring to his wins for plays “Age of Minority” and “Botticelli in the Fire.”

He added it felt like a “really profound validation from my peers, from the theatre community, about what I’m up to at this moment in time in my writing.”

The play, “Prince Faggot,” which Tannahill wrote in 2020 while living in London, was initially inspired by a 2017 photograph of a young Prince George smiling with his hands resting on his face, which Tannahill said reminded him of pictures of himself as a child.

Tannahill said the photos were a jumping off point to “meditate on this idea of queer childhood” and “give language to this, particularly at a time in which the very idea of this is such a politically volatile discourse.”

The photos also led to a bold thought experiment that created a fictionalized narrative of the heir to the British throne identifying as a gay man that “really resembled very much my own (life) and very much the struggle that I went through as a gay man,” Tannahill said.

As for the play’s title, Tannahill said it came to him very early in the creative process. He referred to its name as an invitation “for an audience to consider their relationship with that word.”

“And I’m not offended if people say the title and I also understand if they don’t,” he said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2027.

stories.title: Video: Small businesses targeted with racist and vulgar graffiti, adding insult to road construction pains
stories.summary: It been tough for the family-run small businesses on Dundas Street east of Kellogg Lane ever since construction of London’s bus rapid transit (BRT) route closed all four lanes connecting to Highbury Avenue.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
It been tough for the family-run small businesses on Dundas Street east of Kellogg Lane ever since construction of London’s bus rapid transit (BRT) route closed all four lanes connecting to Highbury Avenue.

Arriving to work on Wednesday morning, things went from bad to worse.

At least three businesses were victimized by an overnight vandalism spree that was caught on security video.

At Dundas Auto Sales, Mario Fatibene spent much of the day cleaning graffiti from the front of his dealership, including racial slurs, and vulgar references to the LGBTQ2S+ community written in both blue paint and black marker.

“They tried to kick the door down. They couldn’t get in the building, we got them on camera,” he tells CTV News. [It] didn’t break [because] we got tempered glass there. Thank God, because they would have hurt themselves. But the whole glass front of our building has been tagged.”

Security footage captured four vandals spray painting the dealership before moving down the block to deface other businesses and a commercial van.

Fatibene says the long-vacant former McCormick Beta Brands cookie factory has become a magnet for graffiti in the area.

“Tear it down for God’s sake!” he urges city officials.

He says the situation worsened when Dundas Street was closed in both directions between McCormick Boulevard and Highbury Avenue for construction of the bus rapid transit (BRT) system.

Fatibene explains there are fewer eyes on the street, “There’s no traffic along here, so in the middle of the night anybody can be walking along [Dundas] causing all sorts of trouble.”

In fact, the security video shows the vandals temporarily stop spray painting when a pedestrian approached the area on the sidewalk.

Once the pedestrian rounded the corner, they resumed their attack on the businesses.

Fatibene believes the four vandals came to the area to spray graffiti on the former cookie factory, then traveled west down Dundas targeting the small businesses.

He points out a four-letter tag ‘D-O-L-O’ was spayed in blue paint on a crane in front of the factory.

The same tag, in the same colour, was painted on the front of his car dealership before the vandals walked westbound out of the camera’s field of view.

“What’s this mayor doing about it? Nothing. Absolutely nothing,” Fatibene fumes about the latest impact to his business, after surviving years of road construction, “You’re the head of the city. You’re responsible to do something about this!”

In a statement, London Mayor Josh Morgan said he fully understands the frustration, and will reach out to Fatibene to begin a dialogue.

Morgan wrote, “The behaviour described, the property damage and graffiti is unacceptable. There are options available to help address these issues, and I am always ready to find solutions.”

In the meantime, the businesses continue to take steps to protect their properties.

“We can’t even leave our cars outside in the parking lot like a normal dealership. We are forced to bring them inside at night,” Fatibene explained.

CTV News has yet to receive a response from London Police Service about whether an investigation has been launched into the vandalism spree.

stories.title: Who’s responsible? Pearson tag-switching victims sue across the system
stories.summary: More than two dozen Canadians accused of international drug smuggling are now turning to a personal injury lawyer, claiming they were victims of a bag tag switching scheme.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part two of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

More than two dozen Canadians accused of international drug smuggling are now turning to a personal injury lawyer, claiming they were victims of a bag tag switching scheme. Some say the airlines offered them peanuts after they were detained abroad in nightmarish conditions.

W5 has now identified more than two dozen cases of travellers being detained after their airline luggage tag was swapped from their bag and put onto another bag, containing drugs, allegedly by corrupt workers at Pearson Airport.

When the scheme goes as planned, an accomplice picks up the drug bag at the destination airport. But, if the drugs are detected, the pickup is aborted, and the innocent passenger is left trying to explain why their luggage tag is on a bag of drugs.

Canadian seniors victimized

Following W5’s initial investigation into the bag tag switching scheme operating at Pearson Airport more travellers have come forward — including Kristian Gjoni, a Toronto I.T. businessman facing up to 15 years in Albanian prison — and at least three Toronto women in their 60s or 70s.

Leila Drakes, who uses a wheelchair, said Barbados police spoke to her in 2024 about “a very large suitcase of cannabis” with her name on it .

Grace Merano spent 24 hellish nights behind bars in the Philippines after being accused of importing 24 kilograms of methamphetamine.

And Naomi, who requested anonymity, said she was detained at Narita Airport in Japan last year for allegedly smuggling 21 kilograms of meth.

All three women flew out of Toronto Pearson International Airport.

A total of 11 people are now launching legal action in a bid to be compensated for what they went through.

Toronto lawyer Paul Miller is representing them. Miller, who has practiced personal injury law for 25 years, told W5 he’d never heard anything like the stories his clients told him.

“This was shocking,” he said. “This was right out of a James Bond type of movie.”

Being detained abroad is particularly traumatic, he noted.

“That’s not your home country anymore. Who’s there to help you? Who do you call?” he said.

Victims seeking up to $1M

Despite their ordeals, Miller said his clients were “basically told to go away” by the airlines.

Merano said her 24 nights in Filipino jail were spent sharing a three-by-five-metre space with three others.

“You can see cockroaches crawling all over the place, big and small. All I can do is just pray,” she said.

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA .

Merano said Cathay Pacific Airways offered her about $22,000 — roughly half of what she says the ordeal cost her in legal fees and upended travel plans.

Drakes, the 77-year-old wheelchair user, said she got a terrifying call after joining her brother in Barbados. The drug squad was looking for her.

Cops came to her hotel, “very much to my embarrassment,” she wrote in a statement for police. They explained that her bag tag was on a suitcase full of cannabis.

“Can you imagine how the rest of my vacation was spent? When I got back to Canada I was a basket case,” she wrote.

Drakes was never charged with a crime.

She said WestJet offered her a $300 flight credit.

Jan Baumann and Charlene Ranadheera, from Winnipeg, were detained on an Air Canada flight to Germany after their baggage tags were switched onto luggage containing 33 kilograms of marijuana.

After being handcuffed and detained at Pearson for 12 hours, then released without charges, Ranadheera said the airline offered them about $2,000.

“And we were like, ‘Haha, thank you, but no,’” she said.

Miller said his clients are looking for a little bit more — somewhere in the range of $100,000 to $1 million in each case.

‘You guys can fight it out’

In an airport the size of Pearson, where hundreds of organizations employ thousands of workers — many subcontracted by the airlines themselves — it’s complicated to figure out exactly who’s at fault, Miller said.

“Is the baggage handler [the airline’s] employee? Was it hired by Pearson, which is the Greater Toronto Airports Authority? Was it hired by a third party?” he said.

Miller said most of his tag switching cases will involve suing several organizations, including the airline, Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson.

Ultimately, the airline is responsible, he argues, because that’s who took his clients’ bags from them.

“So, my attitude is, ‘Okay, I’ll sue a whole bunch of parties,’” he said. “You guys can fight it out.”

Spokespeople for Air Canada, Air Transat and WestJet said the airlines take security seriously but noted the many other organizations involved in the system.

Luggage moves through “a complex network of infrastructure operated and overseen by various third parties, from check-in to delivery,” said Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson.

Who is liable for bags that are tampered with comes down to “circumstances and applicable law, including an assessment of the role of each party,” he added.

Cathay Pacific did not comment by press time.

Miller said it would be better for the airlines to pony up now rather than let these cases run through the courts.

“Putting your head in the sand never works out well…the cover-up is always worse than the crime. If something bad happened and it’s under your company, deal with it,” he said.

The Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson, said it “does not direct or oversee baggage security,” and pointed to federal agencies and police.

The Canada Border Services Agency said it is “working with Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority to make airport security stronger. For security and operational reasons, we are not in a position to share more information.”

Majority of Canadians concerned about bag tag switching

Two-thirds of Canadians say they’re concerned about tag switching, according to a Nanos Research poll done for W5 in September.

Nearly half (45 per cent) of respondents say they’ve heard news coverage of tag switching in the past six months.

Part 1: Pearson luggage tag switch leaves Toronto man facing 15 years in Albania

And 44 per cent of those say they’ve changed their airport behaviours — like holding onto their luggage receipt or putting a tracker in their bag, like an AirTag.

Almost half of those surveyed (48 per cent) said they were less confident in checked luggage systems than they were a year ago.

Watch the one-hour special presentation of W5’s Avery Haines Investigates Sunday at 10 p.m. ET live on W5’s official YouTube channel and on CTV and Crave following the Grey Cup.

“Is the baggage handler [the airline’s] employee? Was it hired by Pearson, which is the Greater Toronto Airports Authority? Was it hired by a third party?” he said.
Miller said most of his tag switching cases will involve suing several organizations, including the airline, Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson.

content_blocks.caption: International passengers arrive at Pearson International Airport in Toronto, Ont. on Wednesday, Feb. 11, 2026. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Jon Blacker

content_blocks.text: Ultimately, the airline is responsible, he argues, because that’s who took his clients’ bags from them.
“So, my attitude is, ‘Okay, I’ll sue a whole bunch of parties,’” he said. “You guys can fight it out.”
Spokespeople for Air Canada, Air Transat and WestJet said the airlines take security seriously but noted the many other organizations involved in the system.
Luggage moves through “a complex network of infrastructure operated and overseen by various third parties, from check-in to delivery,” said Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson.
Who is liable for bags that are tampered with comes down to “circumstances and applicable law, including an assessment of the role of each party,” he added.
Cathay Pacific did not comment by press time.
Miller said it would be better for the airlines to pony up now rather than let these cases run through the courts.
“Putting your head in the sand never works out well…the cover-up is always worse than the crime. If something bad happened and it’s under your company, deal with it,” he said.
The Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson, said it “does not direct or oversee baggage security,” and pointed to federal agencies and police.

The Canada Border Services Agency said it is “working with Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority to make airport security stronger. For security and operational reasons, we are not in a position to share more information.”

content_blocks.text: Majority of Canadians concerned about bag tag switching
Two-thirds of Canadians say they’re concerned about tag switching, according to a Nanos Research poll done for W5 in September.
Nearly half (45 per cent) of respondents say they’ve heard news coverage of tag switching in the past six months.
Part 1: Pearson luggage tag switch leaves Toronto man facing 15 years in Albania
And 44 per cent of those say they’ve changed their airport behaviours — like holding onto their luggage receipt or putting a tracker in their bag, like an AirTag.
Almost half of those surveyed (48 per cent) said they were less confident in checked luggage systems than they were a year ago.

stories.title: When it comes to rare earth minerals, Canada is leaving its riches in the ground: Benchmark Canada
stories.summary: 'It's not because we're slow at permitting that we can't get these projects built. It's because you can't attract money into them'
stories.author: David George-Cosh
stories.content:
Countries don’t typically get report cards, but there are hard facts that can be collated, assessed and compared. Enter Benchmark Canada, a new project from the Macdonald-Laurier Institute that brings together more than 40 different metrics that measure this nation’s performance. This fall, the National Post is examining many of those findings.

Canada sits on some of the world’s biggest rare earth deposits, minerals vital to products ranging from smartphones to electric vehicles. Yet it mined none last year or the year before.

That lack of mining development exposes a weakness in Prime Minister Mark Carney’s ambition to make Canada a critical minerals powerhouse, according to Benchmark Canada, a Macdonald-Laurier Institute project comparing the country’s performance against its peers.

The project finds Canada holds more than 14 million tonnes of identified rare earth resources, compared with 3.6 million in the U.S., according to U.S. Geological Survey data. While Canada’s rare earth production remained bare, China mined 270,000 tonnes in 2025 and Americans mined 51,000 tonnes.

Rare earth minerals like neodymium or terbium are used in powerful magnets for electric vehicles, wind turbines and weapons systems. China controls most of that supply, and Canada and its allies are scrambling to build alternatives.

“We’re potentially a great provider, particularly as we reorganize international supply chains, but there’s a long, long way to go,” said John Steen, director of the University of British Columbia’s Bradshaw Research Institute for Minerals and Mining.

Canada is a major producer of some critical mineral production. It supplies 30.6 per cent of the world’s potash, a vital fertilizer component, and 23.1 per cent of its uranium, according to Benchmark Canada.

Beyond those, Canada’s critical mineral advantage remains underdeveloped. Canada holds significant lithium, graphite and cobalt reserves, but production is relatively scant, the Benchmark Canada data show. Canada holds 4.3 per cent of the world’s lithium reserves but accounts for just 1.9 per cent of production. For graphite, it has a 1.9 per cent share of global reserves, but just 0.44 per cent of output.

Pierre Gratton, president and chief executive of the Mining Association of Canada, said that while Canada has focused on expanding its uranium and potash operations and opened new gold mines over the past two decades, exploration for critical minerals has lagged.

“We have lost ground in the last 30 years as a producer of some of the critical minerals the world is crying out for, whether it be copper, nickel or cobalt,” he said.

For rare earth developers, China’s dominance has made financing new mines in Canada particularly difficult. Small Canadian companies must persuade investors to back projects whose economics could be undermined by a surge in Chinese supply, Gratton said.

“A company developing a rare earths mine in Canada can be killed overnight by China flooding the market,” he said.

Even if Canada were to rubber-stamp permits to make development quicker, that alone would do little to solve the China problem.

“It’s not because we’re slow at permitting that we can’t get these projects built. It’s because you can’t attract money into them,” Gratton said.

Government purchase commitments and stockpiling could provide developers with a guaranteed customer that would help them raise private capital to get shovels in the ground, he said. Public support would be crucial for projects competing against China’s state-backed producers.

“You’re not going to build a rare earths mine or a processing facility without some form of support from governments, because you’re competing against state-owned enterprises, and they dominate the market,” he said.

Gratton also thinks Ottawa should broaden its clean technology manufacturing tax credit to cover mine development expenses, such as sinking shafts, while finding ways to encourage miners to expand mines that already have established infrastructure and customer relationships.

Meanwhile, Steen said Canada desperately needs increased mining processing and training. China spent decades developing the expertise to turn mined material into products manufacturers can use, leaving countries like Canada on the back foot when figuring out how to process rare earth minerals laden with complex chemistries.

“They’re the technology leaders. They’re way ahead of us,” Steen said.

While Canada’s rare earth production remained bare, China mined 270,000 tonnes in 2025 and Americans mined 51,000 tonnes. STR/AFP/Getty Images

He said Canada should take a page from Australia, which created cooperative research centres to train a new generation of metallurgists, miners and geologists, and brought universities and companies together on research.

Some progress is happening. The Saskatchewan Research Council said its rare earth processing facility achieved commercial-scale metals production in 2024, with plans to process raw materials into magnet-grade metals and oxides in 2027.

The growth of artificial intelligence could also create a sustained market for Canadian miners, particularly copper producers. The U.S. Geological Survey identifies copper as an essential material in data centres and cooling equipment.

Steen cautioned against concluding that Canada’s critical mineral production shortfall should be viewed as a government failure. Mines take years to develop, and today’s minimal output reflects investment decisions made long before critical minerals became a political priority.

“There are minerals where (Canada) is underrepresented, but that’s more of a time effect than a negligence effect,” he said.

stories.title: Ford, feds, Unifor set for high-stakes meeting with Stellantis
stories.summary: At the heart of the issue is whether Stellantis is obligated to hold up its end of a funding agreement that saw millions in taxpayer dollars being given to the company.
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford is expected to attend a high-stakes meeting with international automaker Stellantis, ON Thursday, as the province reels from the sale of the Brampton auto assembly plant that could put thousands of people permanently out of work.

Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Stellantis workers across the country, said the meeting between Ottawa, the province, the manufacturer and the union will take place at a downtown Toronto hotel.

Prime Minister Carney, who derided the company’s decision to sell the idled Brampton plant to Roshel , a Canadian defence manufacturer, emphasized that Ottawa plans to “enforce our rights, absolutely, in protection of those workers,” suggesting an action plan would be the subject of discussion at Thursday’s meeting.

At the heart of the issue is whether Stellantis is obligated to hold up its end of a funding agreement that saw millions in taxpayer dollars being given to the company to retool its facilities in Brampton and Windsor.

In 2023, Stellantis was promised a $1.5 billion joint commitment between the federal and Ontario provincial governments over 10 years as a performance incentive, to revive an electric vehicle battery facility in Windsor and prevent it from being moved to the U.S.

The agreement required Stellantis to maintain its footprint in Ontario through 2035, which includes the Brampton plant.

That agreement was on top of a billion dollar pledge from both the provincial and federal governments to upgrade its production lines and prepare them for electric vehicles. Ontario pledged $132 million for the Brampton re-tooling plans.

Stellantis told Global News ahead of the meeting that it recognizes that “Canadians expect accountability for public funding and that is why Stellantis has offered to voluntarily return the government support received for Brampton Assembly’s original retooling plan.”

“Confidentiality provisions in our agreements prevent us from disclosing further details,” it said in a statement.

Public records show Ontario’s Ministry of Economic Development paid FCA Canada (now Stellantis) a total of $55.4 million between 2022 and 2025. It’s unclear how much of that was specifically for the Brampton upgrades.

The plant’s sale has also been condemned by Unifor, which said the Roshel takeover will jeopardize the jobs of more than 2,000 laid-off Brampton workers who have been waiting to return to the plant since it halted operations in 2023.

Ahead of the sale, Stellantis workers also voted overwhelmingly in favour of a strike mandate in October, with 97.3 per cent voting yes. Unifor said a strike would be a last resort but bargaining has been at an impasse over several key issues including job security.

The financial terms of the sale to Roshel have not been made public.

stories.title: Scattered showers, cooler temperatures expected Friday
stories.summary: Cooler temperatures and lingering showers are expected across the region Thursday, with lake-effect precipitation developing near Lake Huron, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Cooler temperatures and lingering showers are expected across the region Thursday, with lake-effect precipitation developing near Lake Huron, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

The day will start overcast, with a chance of showers and possible mixed precipitation in parts of midwestern Ontario. Most areas are expected to see rainfall taper off around noon, with some breaks of sunshine developing in the afternoon.

London is forecast to reach a high of 6 C, with northeast winds bringing cooler conditions.

Atchison says lake-effect precipitation could bring additional showers and even some snowflakes to areas near Georgian Bay and Grey County.

Friday will bring a mix of sun and cloud, but temperatures will drop to a high of just 3 C.

Saturday will remain mainly cloudy, with a 60 per cent chance of scattered lake-effect showers. The risk of precipitation could affect the Santa Claus parade.

Sunday is expected to bring a mix of sun and cloud and a high of 7 C, with sunshine returning early next week.

stories.title: Toronto lawyer helps win Lgbtq rights victory in Trinidad at top London court
stories.summary: Rare appearance for a Canadian at U.K.’s Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
For decades following Confederation, Canadian lawyers made their way to London to plead final appeals at the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council. Canada’s own Supreme Court wasn’t fully supreme until after the Second World War. The last Canadian case heard in the British capital happened in 1959.

In July, however, a Canadian made a rare appearance at the Judicial Committee, across from Parliament and beside Westminster Abbey.

Adam Goldenberg, a McCarthy Tétrault LLP partner who is fighting several high-profile Lgbtq rights cases in Canada, was among the lawyers seeking to overturn a long-standing “buggery” law in Trinidad and Tobago that criminalizes gay sex. The Judicial Committee remains the final court of appeal for Trinidad and some other Caribbean countries.

On Tuesday, the Judicial Committee delivered a historic victory for Lgbtq rights in Trinidad, a legal decision that could resonate more widely in legal challenges in places such as Guyana, Grenada and Jamaica that have similar discriminatory laws rooted in the colonial era.

Lord Philip James Sales declared the prohibition in Trinidad could not be reasonably justified “in a society that has a proper respect for the rights and freedoms of an individual.”

It is the culmination of a decade-long legal odyssey for Jason Jones, a 62-year-old who was born and raised in Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago’s capital. He came out when he was 16 but suffered harassment and discrimination in the country before moving to England in his 30s. He moved back for several years in the early 2010s and won an initial court victory in Trinidad in 2018 against the anti-gay law.

The country’s appeal court overturned that ruling in early 2025 – a defeat that propelled the quest to London.

It was then that Mr. Goldenberg’s phone rang. The 39-year-old is a commercial litigator at McCarthy but has long devoted free pro bono services to Lgbtq cases. Among them is UR Pride, currently at the Supreme Court of Canada, a Charter of Rights and Freedoms case defending transgender youth and challenging Saskatchewan’s 2023 pronouns and parental rights law.

Mr. Goldenberg grew up in Vancouver and came out when he was 14, in the early 2000s. “It was not as difficult as it is for many people,” he said in an interview.

He came of age when Lgbtq rights were on the March, often through the courts, led by the generational victory for marriage equality.

Mr. Goldenberg took the helm of a group of interveners on Mr. Jones’s appeal in London, representing close to 200 organizations in the Caribbean.

The criminalization of gay sex in Trinidad goes back to a 1925 law against “unnatural offences,” including the “abominable crime of buggery,” that threatened five years of imprisonment. In 1986, a quarter-century after independence, the country doubled down on the old law with new legislation, increasing the potential jail time to 10 years and eventually to 25. No consenting gay men had ever been prosecuted but the spectre of criminal sanction for simply living’s one life loomed.

During a daylong hearing on July 8 at the Privy Council, Mr. Goldenberg felt a “strangely familiar” atmosphere, given the shared legal history, though everyone was in business attire, rather than the robes worn in Canada’s Supreme Court, and there was no elevated bench. Interveners provide written arguments but aren’t offered time to speak, unless the lords present a question.

“I was ready to leap to my feet,” said Mr. Goldenberg, but he wasn’t called upon.

The Trinidad government argued the law is protected from constitutional challenges and also asserted it is constitutionally valid, because a parliamentary supermajority passed the 1986 legislation and it was at that time reasonably justifiable.

In their written arguments, Mr. Goldenberg and this team stated: “Criminalisation of whom a person loves – and with whom they May express that love through physical intimacy – does not merely limit a person’s ambit of actions: it denies them a core feature of their identity.”

On Tuesday, the Judicial Committee in its ruling noted the assistance of the interveners’ filing and thanked the lawyers for their pro bono work. “I know English members of our team were quite chuffed to see that shoutout,” Mr. Goldenberg said.

To Mr. Goldenberg, who called it disgraceful that some countries still criminalize Lgbtq people, one of the lessons of the experience was what Canada has achieved and where human rights remain at risk.

He pointed to the UR Pride Saskatchewan case and similar laws in Alberta that place restrictions on transgender youth, which is also involved in legal challenges. Conservative governments in both provinces shielded their laws with the Charter’s notwithstanding clause, which allows legislators to override numerous constitutional rights such as security of the person and equality.

“I’d much rather live in Canada than a place that criminalizes homosexuality, but we are far from perfect,” Mr. Goldenberg said.

In 1959, the last Canadian case at the Privy Council, a 25-year-old William Stevenson was among the lawyers on a civil appeal over a financial disagreement from the nascent days of Alberta’s oil industry. Mr. Stevenson served on the Supreme Court of Canada for several years in the early 1990s.

And while Mr. Goldenberg’s appearance in London is a rare one, there was another Canadian at the Privy Council recently. Al Meghji, head of tax litigation at Osler, Hoskin & Harcourt LLP, was there in 2024 for a case from Trinidad connected with Vancouver-based Methanex Corp.

In the Lgbtq victory for Trinidadians, the country’s government stood behind the discriminatory law, but the lead lawyer for appellant Mr. Jones was Anand Ramlogan, a former attorney-general of Trinidad and Tobago.

“Gay rights form part of the wider struggle for human rights,” Mr. Ramlogan’s law firm said in a statement. “Every person is entitled to the protection of the Constitution, regardless of their sexual orientation.”

stories.title: Alberta’s new family law system draws complaints from lawyers
stories.summary: Reforms aim to settle more cases before they reach a trial
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
A new system in Alberta designed to settle more family law disputes outside of court has led to access-to-justice issues, some lawyers in the province say.

At the start of the year, the Alberta Court of King’s Bench launched what it calls the Family Focused Protocol. The changes are in part inspired by successful reforms instituted several years ago in Manitoba, where the number of family law trials has been significantly reduced.

The Alberta court says the new rules aim to reduce the amount of time family law disputes spend in a courtroom to minimize the “toxicity of adversarial litigation” on families as they undergo proceedings related to divorce, division of property, and questions such as child and spousal support. One early requirement is an alternative dispute resolution process.

But lawyers who work on divorce cases in Alberta say the new system has been cumbersome and convoluted, with several months of paperwork and other prerequisites necessary before they can make an initial appearance in front of a judge on behalf of their clients.

Marc Massie, a partner at Vogel LLP in Calgary, said he has been in front of a judge about five times this year, as of October, less than a quarter of the number of appearances he would have made under the old system.

“When you can get in front of a judge, it was really helpful,” Mr. Massie said of the new system. “Getting in has been close to a nightmare. That’s the challenge.”

Canada’s justice system has struggled for years with delays, a problem that gets the most attention in the criminal courts. But the country’s civil courts – and family law cases in particular – are also plagued by delays, which have led chief justices across Canada to consider better ways to organize the system.

Alberta’s new Family Focused Protocol starts with requirements such as a course on parenting after separation and an alternative dispute resolution process. The eventual first step in front of a judge, after an array of forms are processed, is called the mandatory intake triage.

The new protocol also aims to assign a single judge to each family throughout their entire process. The Court of King’s Bench has about 30 judges spending a substantial portion of their time on family law.

But Mr. Massie and other lawyers say the early steps in the system have not yet worked well. The court issued a lengthy 89-page manual on the new protocol, and in some situations has rejected legal filings because an item wasn’t submitted in the exact specifications cited in the manual.

“There was a lot of hope,” said lawyer Sierra Yanush of Yanush + Abusow LLP in Calgary. “The idea had been to move through the system faster.”

Ms. Yanush said judges are trying to make the new system successful, but lawyers are finding it challenging and costly for clients. She estimated the work required to get to the first judicial appearance at the triage meeting would cost clients at least $5,000.

Other lawyers have expressed frustration on social media about the inability to get time in court to see a judge. “Access to justice is a real concern, especially in matters involving children,” Marcus Sixta, founder of Crossroads Law in Calgary, posted on LinkedIn in the spring.

In late October, the Alberta government moved to increase the number of available judges. The government does not have oversight of the court’s daily management, but on Oct. 27 tabled legislative amendments to the Court of King’s Bench Act to allow 10 applications judges to help “more effectively resolve issues” in familial disputes.

The Court of King’s Bench, meanwhile, is working with lawyers to better navigate the new system and on Nov. 9, published an updated guide that aims to reduce logistical problems. It is now 248 pages and is meant to be a detailed reference guide.

“Many early form rejections and related problems could have been avoided by following the instructions in the manual,” Darryl Ruether, the court’s executive legal counsel, said in an e-mailed response to questions.

Mr. Ruether noted that the new Alberta system is based in part on reforms the Manitoba courts put in place in 2019, where the goal was to reduce the number of cases that went to trial and instead settle disputes before that point.

“We are hopeful that the resolution-focused approach will pay off for Alberta families in time,” Mr. Ruether said.

Justice Glenn Joyal of the Supreme Court of Canada cited the Manitoba reforms as part of his application to the country’s top court, to which he was named in June.

Justice Joyal had been chief justice of the Manitoba Court of King’s Bench from 2011 until this year. In his Supreme Court application, he said the family law changes in Manitoba revolved around reducing the “adversarial reality of needlessly protracted legal proceedings.”

He said that in Manitoba, 70 per cent of family cases are now resolved, either completely or substantially, at an initial triage meeting. Before the reforms, the Manitoba court previously scheduled 300 family trials each year, with about a third of those proceeding to the actual hearing. Now, only about 20 trials proceed each year.

“The financial and psychological savings to families of early and lasting judicially assisted resolution is obvious,” Justice Joyal stated in his application.

In Ontario, the province’s Court of Justice is also working on a five-year plan to overhaul family court. The court’s Chief Justice, Sharon Nicklas, in September said one part of the plan is to enact the principle of “one judge, one family,” the same as a goal of Alberta’s new system.

One factor across the country is the variable availability of what’s called unified family courts, said Hadley Friedland, a law professor at the University of Alberta. Some family law falls under provincial legislation and is handled at the provincial court level, whereas divorces are governed by federal legislation and dealt with at the superior court level, such as Alberta’s Court of King’s Bench. Unified family courts help streamline cases by handling all issues in one court rather than two. Manitoba uses the unified system, but Alberta does not.

Prof. Friedland said the reforms at the Alberta Court of King’s Bench are a step in the right direction, even as the changes have caused some problems this year. She said the goal of having more families reach a settlement before a trial makes sense.

“I’ve heard that it’s convoluted and difficult, but something needed to change,” said Prof. Friedland. “Because the family law system has not been working for families and children for a very long time.”

To Mr. Massie, the lawyer at Vogel in Calgary, the new system needs to strike a balance where families are able to access a judge when necessary. He said the push for alternative dispute resolution makes sense, but stressed that people still need answers from a judge on difficult questions that cases of divorce often involve.

“There are certain things,” said Mr. Massie, “that just can’t avoid a fight.”

Ms. Yanush said judges are trying to make the new system successful, but lawyers are finding it challenging and costly for clients. She estimated the work required to get to the first judicial appearance at the triage meeting would cost clients at least $5,000.

Other lawyers have expressed frustration on social media about the inability to get time in court to see a judge. “Access to justice is a real concern, especially in matters involving children,” Marcus Sixta, founder of Crossroads Law in Calgary, posted on LinkedIn in the spring.

In late October, the Alberta government moved to increase the number of available judges. The government does not have oversight of the court’s daily management, but on Oct. 27 tabled legislative amendments to the Court of King’s Bench Act to allow 10 applications judges to help “more effectively resolve issues” in familial disputes.

The Court of King’s Bench, meanwhile, is working with lawyers to better navigate the new system and on Nov. 9, published an updated guide that aims to reduce logistical problems. It is now 248 pages and is meant to be a detailed reference guide.

“Many early form rejections and related problems could have been avoided by following the instructions in the manual,” Darryl Ruether, the court’s executive legal counsel, said in an e-mailed response to questions.

Mr. Ruether noted that the new Alberta system is based in part on reforms the Manitoba courts put in place in 2019, where the goal was to reduce the number of cases that went to trial and instead settle disputes before that point.
“We are hopeful that the resolution-focused approach will pay off for Alberta families in time,” Mr. Ruether said.
Justice Glenn Joyal of the Supreme Court of Canada cited the Manitoba reforms as part of his application to the country’s top court, to which he was named in June.

Justice Joyal had been chief justice of the Manitoba Court of King’s Bench from 2011 until this year. In his Supreme Court application, he said the family law changes in Manitoba revolved around reducing the “adversarial reality of needlessly protracted legal proceedings.”

He said that in Manitoba, 70 per cent of family cases are now resolved, either completely or substantially, at an initial triage meeting. Before the reforms, the Manitoba court previously scheduled 300 family trials each year, with about a third of those proceeding to the actual hearing. Now, only about 20 trials proceed each year.
“The financial and psychological savings to families of early and lasting judicially assisted resolution is obvious,” Justice Joyal stated in his application.

In Ontario, the province’s Court of Justice is also working on a five-year plan to overhaul family court. The court’s Chief Justice, Sharon Nicklas, in September said one part of the plan is to enact the principle of “one judge, one family,” the same as a goal of Alberta’s new system.

One factor across the country is the variable availability of what’s called unified family courts, said Hadley Friedland, a law professor at the University of Alberta. Some family law falls under provincial legislation and is handled at the provincial court level, whereas divorces are governed by federal legislation and dealt with at the superior court level, such as Alberta’s Court of King’s Bench. Unified family courts help streamline cases by handling all issues in one court rather than two. Manitoba uses the unified system, but Alberta does not.

Prof. Friedland said the reforms at the Alberta Court of King’s Bench are a step in the right direction, even as the changes have caused some problems this year. She said the goal of having more families reach a settlement before a trial makes sense.

“I’ve heard that it’s convoluted and difficult, but something needed to change,” said Prof. Friedland. “Because the family law system has not been working for families and children for a very long time.”

To Mr. Massie, the lawyer at Vogel in Calgary, the new system needs to strike a balance where families are able to access a judge when necessary. He said the push for alternative dispute resolution makes sense, but stressed that people still need answers from a judge on difficult questions that cases of divorce often involve.
“There are certain things,” said Mr. Massie, “that just can’t avoid a fight.”
