stories.title: How a 67-year-old B.C. retiree’s large-cap Tfsa trounced the market
stories.summary: And why he’s now holding a great deal of cash in the account
stories.author: Larry MacDonald
stories.content:
This is Tfsa Trouncers, a series that profiles how Canadian investors invest their tax-free savings accounts. Whether you’ve been successful in growing your Tfsa or not, we’d like to hear from you. Please fill out this form to contribute. You May choose to be anonymous, but we do require an e-mail address and May request a screengrab of your portfolio for fact-checking purposes.

Bob, a 67-year-old retiree residing in British Columbia, opened a tax-free savings account in 2009 and contributed the maximum amount at the start of each year (totalling $109,000), investing almost exclusively in large-cap dividend stocks.

His Tfsa now has a value of more than $610,000.

When Bob was building his Tfsa portfolio, he was mainly interested in solid stocks with good dividends, not so much their potential for capital gains. Nonetheless, a number of his stocks had capital gains of several hundred per cent.

When TFSAs were introduced in 2009, the timing was good for buying stocks. They had just been assigned to the bargain bin by the financial crisis and recession of 2008 and 2009. Bob was a fan of Warren Buffett and acted on his advice to “be greedy when others are fearful.”

The first three annual contributions to his Tfsa were invested in downtrodden U.S. large-cap stocks, such as Ford Motor Co. F-N , General Electric Co. GE-N and Altria Group MO-N . Insolvency risk was a concern but the companies had debt under control or were backstopped by the U.S. government.

By the end of 2011, his $15,000 of contributions had soared in value to $70,000, as the economy rebounded and dividends were raised. Not liking the claw backs on his U.S. dividends, he began shifting to large-cap Canadian dividend stocks in 2012.

He bought into Canadian companies in the banking, energy, pipeline, insurance and telecom sectors. His Tfsa now holds twelve stocks from those sectors.

The banks are the major position. Their shares climbed every year since 2012 to notch a sixfold gain as a group. The energy stocks also scored a sixfold increase – in just the past six years. Other sectors have been strong too, except for telecom in recent years.

Bob did have a considerable number of shares in Telus Corp. T-T . But as competition heated up in the telecom sector and the stock of Telus sank, he began unwinding his position and was out by early 2026. He dodged the dividend cut in July of 2026.

His portfolio returns were augmented by reinvesting dividends. Several of his companies also had dividend reinvestment plans that bought shares at discounts to market prices. And there were many dividend increases.

However, Bob stopped reinvesting dividends last year. They now go to his cash position, which sits near $90,000. He is concerned about a bear market around the corner and wants to pick up some bargains if and when it arrives.

As Bob’s example shows, a Tfsa with large-cap companies can outperform. What helped was buying when the shares sold off during panics or unexpected shocks. “I had a bit of luck too,” he says.

A recent example of a buy opportunity was the U.S. money laundering scandal in 2024 that rocked Toronto-Dominion Bank TD-T . The bank’s stock was down a lot, which left the dividend yield near 5 per cent. Since then, the shares have more than doubled.

Bob never expected the value of his Tfsa to become so large. When his estate is settled, the plan will pass to his granddaughter and grandson. Hopefully, his talks about saving and investing will help them grow the Tfsa and their own savings.

We asked Ian Calvert (CFP, CIM), principal, head of wealth planning at Highview Financial Group, for his thoughts on Bob’s Tfsa.

It’s an impressive value in his Tfsa, considering the lifetime contribution amount is $109,000. Taking advantage and having cash to deploy during the equity selloff in 2008 and 2009 has provided a great start to the account.

I like his approach of holding equities that provide both growth and income, however the withholding taxes on U.S. dividends presents a small hurdle within the Tfsa. When U.S. dividends are held in a non-registered account, there is relief through the foreign tax credit; when held in an Rrsp, there is no withholding tax at all.

U.S. dividends received in the Tfsa are taxed 15 per cent, deducted at source, with no ability for any recovery. The lack of recovery should be known, and is certainly a small drag on performance, but it shouldn’t dictate all investment decisions.

To optimize the benefits of the Tfsa, the ultimate goal should still be to maximize long-term growth in a tax-exempt environment. Making the decision to switch to all Canadian equities has fixed the dividend issue and will allow Bob to reinvest and compound 100 per cent of the income within the account.

Having a large weighting to Canadian financials has been an excellent boost. The performance of the Canadian banks has been great and outpaced expectations over the past few years while continuing to pay strong dividends. Given the Canadian blue-chip dividend machine Bob has built in his Tfsa, he should continue to see the benefit of the account with minimal need for active and tactical trading.

However, keeping some cash available for the next selloff in equities could provide some future benefits. Making sure both his beneficiary and contingent beneficiaries are up to date is another important item to maximize the benefits of his Tfsa.

Larry MacDonald is author of The Shopify Story and blogs at Shopify’s Journey .

stories.title: More than 60% of First Nations support Carney’s plans to ramp up fossil fuel output, exclusive poll finds
stories.summary: The poll also found that the prime minister has more than 50 per cent support among Indigenous people
stories.author: Jesse Snyder
stories.content:
More than 60 per cent of First Nations people who responded to an exclusive survey said they back Prime Minister Mark Carney’s efforts to ramp up natural resource production, suggesting widespread support for Ottawa’s plans to build major projects as a way to grow the economy.

In a Postmedia-Leger poll of Indigenous Canadians, 63 per cent of respondents said they either “strongly support” or “somewhat support” Carney’s plan to develop more oil and gas resources, compared with 22 per cent saying they “somewhat oppose” or “strongly oppose.” The other 15 per cent of respondents said they “don’t know.”

The poll, which relied solely on First Nations respondents, offers a rare insight into Indigenous perspectives on issues such as fossil fuel development and political preferences.

The survey also asked about respondents’ views toward federal political leaders, and found significantly higher trust among Indigenous people in Carney compared with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre and NDP Leader Avi Lewis. Indigenous respondents also reported a relatively low level of trust in Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak, National Chief of the Assembly of First Nations, an Ottawa-based lobby group.

Canada’s First Nations people hold widely varying views toward oil and gas development, with many communities supporting various projects and occasionally taking direct equity stakes in pipelines, storage facilities and other assets. But others, particularly some of those in northern B.C., have been among the most outspoken critics of large-scale energy proposals, and have hindered their development through sustained opposition in the courts.

Thomas Isaac, a law partner at Cassels Brock & Blackwell who specializes in Indigenous affairs, said First Nations are often far more supportive of economic proposals than media reports tend to suggest.

“That doesn’t surprise me at all,” Isaac said of the survey results.

Isaac has worked closely with many Indigenous leaders in his work, and said that they are unanimously focused on securing jobs and revenue for their communities.

“People have to understand there’s a political side of this discussion, and then there’s the reality,” he said. “I’ve met with so many Indigenous groups, either with them or across the table from them, who are just trying to make their lives better. I see it every day in my practice, and I haven’t met a single Indigenous government that isn’t concerned about the environment — but they’re also concerned about their economic well-being.”

Leger conducted the online survey of Indigenous Canadians between Oct. 8 and 16, with respondents spread more or less equally across the provinces. Respondents were split roughly evenly between male and female, and across age ranges from 18 to older than 75. A margin of error can’t be assigned to an online survey.

Canada’s energy sector has made increasing efforts to give First Nations direct equity stakes in major projects, saying it would give them more direct control over project decisions, environmental designs and how they allocate the capital they generate.

Asked whether their support was contingent on First Nations having an equity stake in a given project, however, respondents to the Leger poll were evenly split. Forty-five per cent of First Nations said they would be more likely to support a project that has some Indigenous ownership, whereas 42 per cent said it “makes no difference.” The remaining 13 per cent said they didn’t know.

On the issue of how to redistribute the capital flowing back to communities, respondents were also fairly divided. Asked if they would prefer any potential benefits from a major resource development to “be directed as monetary payments to individuals of the community,” 45 per cent of First Nations agreed. By comparison, 21 per cent said monetary payments should go “directly to your local band, council or governing organization,” while 34 per cent said communities should, rather than receive monetary payments, get “a certain percentage of jobs for the project being available to Indigenous peoples.”

As for their political preferences, First Nations respondents were broadly supportive of the current government in Ottawa. Fifty-four per cent of respondents said they were satisfied with the Carney government, with 19 per cent saying they were “very satisfied.” By comparison, 38 per cent said they were dissatisfied, and nine per cent said they did not know. That satisfaction was higher in eastern provinces (60 per cent), Leger found, compared with Western ones (47 per cent).

Carney also enjoyed the most support among First Nations when asked if they trusted him to “promote the rights of Indigenous people in Canada,” with 52 per cent saying they trusted him. In comparison, the lowest number of respondents (27 per cent) said they trusted Poilievre or Trudeau. Thirty-six per cent said they supported the NDP leader, Lewis. (Trust in Carney’s ability to protect First Nations’ rights was also higher in the east, at 58 per cent, compared with 45 per cent in Western provinces).

The low levels of trust in Trudeau come despite his government’s constant political posturing in favour of various First Nations issues. The former prime minister had said that the treatment of Indigenous people at Canada’s residential schools amounted to “cultural genocide,” and his Liberal government ramped up land-claim payments to First Nations communities to the tune of tens of billions.

Asked whether they trust Woodhouse Nepinak, the head of the Assembly of First Nations and a member of Manitoba’s Pinaymootang First Nation, 37 per cent of respondents who were familiar with her said they did. Polling also showed a lack of awareness of the Assembly of First Nations, however, with 57 per cent saying they did not know whether they trusted Woodhouse Nepinak to protect their rights and interests.

The Postmedia-Leger poll also noted in one question that the combined budget for the Indigenous Services and Crown-Indigenous Relations departments has quadrupled from $8 billion in 2015 to $39 billion in 2026. It then asked First Nations respondents whether their day-to-day lives were getting better, to which 55 per cent said they were, while 27 per cent said they were getting worse. The other 18 per cent said they did not know.

Of the First Nations respondents, 42 per cent said they feel that they “get good value for the money spent by the government,” while 36 per cent said they get poor value. Another 21 per cent said they did not know.

stories.title: Accused of smuggling, now they’re suing over Pearson tag switches
stories.summary: More than two dozen Canadians accused of international drug smuggling are now turning to a personal injury lawyer, claiming they were victims of a bag tag switching scheme.
stories.author: Jack Hauen, Avery Haines
stories.content:
What happens when a simple trip turns into a nightmare? Part two of W5’s five-part investigation on CTVNews.CA follows travellers who say they went from passenger to prisoner, caught in a scheme that crossed borders and changed lives forever.

More than two dozen Canadians accused of international drug smuggling are now turning to a personal injury lawyer, claiming they were victims of a bag tag switching scheme. Some say the airlines offered them peanuts after they were detained abroad in nightmarish conditions.

W5 has now identified more than two dozen cases of travellers being detained after their airline luggage tag was swapped from their bag and put onto another bag, containing drugs, allegedly by corrupt workers at Pearson Airport.

Part 1: Pearson luggage tag switch leaves Toronto man facing 15 years in Albania

When the scheme goes as planned, an accomplice picks up the drug bag at the destination airport. But, if the drugs are detected, the pickup is aborted, and the innocent passenger is left trying to explain why their luggage tag is on a bag of drugs.

Canadian seniors victimized

Following W5’s initial investigation into the bag tag switching scheme operating at Pearson Airport more travellers have come forward — including Kristian Gjoni, a Toronto I.T. businessman facing up to 15 years in Albanian prison — and at least three Toronto women in their 60s or 70s.

Leila Drakes, who uses a wheelchair, said Barbados police spoke to her in 2024 about “a very large suitcase of cannabis” with her name on it .

Grace Merano spent 24 hellish nights behind bars in the Philippines after being accused of importing 24 kilograms of methamphetamine.

And Naomi, who requested anonymity, said she was detained at Narita Airport in Japan last year for allegedly smuggling 21 kilograms of meth.

All three women flew out of Toronto Pearson International Airport.

A total of 11 people are now launching legal action in a bid to be compensated for what they went through.

Toronto lawyer Paul Miller is representing them. Miller, who has practiced personal injury law for 25 years, told W5 he’d never heard anything like the stories his clients told him.

“This was shocking,” he said. “This was right out of a James Bond type of movie.”

Being detained abroad is particularly traumatic, he noted.

“That’s not your home country anymore. Who’s there to help you? Who do you call?” he said.

Victims seeking up to $1M

Despite their ordeals, Miller said his clients were “basically told to go away” by the airlines.

Merano said her 24 nights in Filipino jail were spent sharing a three-by-five-metre space with three others.

“You can see cockroaches crawling all over the place, big and small. All I can do is just pray,” she said.

If you have any information regarding tag switching or corruption at Canadian airports, please reach out to avery.haines@bellmedia.CA and jack.hauen@bellmedia.CA .

Merano said Cathay Pacific Airways offered her about $22,000 — roughly half of what she says the ordeal cost her in legal fees and upended travel plans.

Drakes, the 77-year-old wheelchair user, said she got a terrifying call after joining her brother in Barbados. The drug squad was looking for her.

Cops came to her hotel, “very much to my embarrassment,” she wrote in a statement for police. They explained that her bag tag was on a suitcase full of cannabis.

“Can you imagine how the rest of my vacation was spent? When I got back to Canada I was a basket case,” she wrote.

Drakes was never charged with a crime.

She said WestJet offered her a $300 flight credit.

Jan Baumann and Charlene Ranadheera, from Winnipeg, were detained on an Air Canada flight to Germany after their baggage tags were switched onto luggage containing 33 kilograms of marijuana.

After being handcuffed and detained at Pearson for 12 hours, then released without charges, Ranadheera said the airline offered them about $2,000.

“And we were like, ‘Haha, thank you, but no,’” she said.

Miller said his clients are looking for a little bit more — somewhere in the range of $100,000 to $1 million in each case.

‘You guys can fight it out’

In an airport the size of Pearson, where hundreds of organizations employ thousands of workers — many subcontracted by the airlines themselves — it’s complicated to figure out exactly who’s at fault, Miller said.

“Is the baggage handler [the airline’s] employee? Was it hired by Pearson, which is the Greater Toronto Airports Authority? Was it hired by a third party?” he said.

Miller said most of his tag switching cases will involve suing several organizations, including the airline, Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson.

Ultimately, the airline is responsible, he argues, because that’s who took his clients’ bags from them.

“So, my attitude is, ‘Okay, I’ll sue a whole bunch of parties,’” he said. “You guys can fight it out.”

Spokespeople for Air Canada, Air Transat and WestJet said the airlines take security seriously but noted the many other organizations involved in the system.

Luggage moves through “a complex network of infrastructure operated and overseen by various third parties, from check-in to delivery,” said Air Canada spokesperson Sean Davidson.

Who is liable for bags that are tampered with comes down to “circumstances and applicable law, including an assessment of the role of each party,” he added.

Cathay Pacific did not comment by press time.

Miller said it would be better for the airlines to pony up now rather than let these cases run through the courts.

“Putting your head in the sand never works out well…the cover-up is always worse than the crime. If something bad happened and it’s under your company, deal with it,” he said.

The Greater Toronto Airports Authority, which runs Pearson, said it “does not direct or oversee baggage security,” and pointed to federal agencies and police.

The Canada Border Services Agency said it is “working with Transport Canada and the Greater Toronto Airports Authority to make airport security stronger. For security and operational reasons, we are not in a position to share more information.”

Majority of Canadians concerned about bag tag switching

Two-thirds of Canadians say they’re concerned about tag switching, according to a Nanos Research poll done for W5 in September.

Nearly half (45 per cent) of respondents say they’ve heard news coverage of tag switching in the past six months.

And 44 per cent of those say they’ve changed their airport behaviours — like holding onto their luggage receipt or putting a tracker in their bag, like an AirTag.

Almost half of those surveyed (48 per cent) said they were less confident in checked luggage systems than they were a year ago.

“You can see cockroaches crawling all over the place, big and small. All I can do is just pray,” she said.

Merano said Cathay Pacific Airways offered her about $22,000 — roughly half of what she says the ordeal cost her in legal fees and upended travel plans.

stories.title: From VHS to iPods, retro tech is driving this year’s holiday shopping season
stories.summary: In the age of endless online streaming, Canadians want to return to physical media and tech, a new survey from Best Buy Canada shows.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Like the Carpenters song promised, “it’s yesterday once more.” Nostalgia is driving a holiday shopping spree for many, with younger Canadians looking for retro tech as presents.

In the age of endless online streaming, Canadians want to return to physical media and tech, a new survey from Best Buy Canada shows.

Four in 10 (40 per cent) Canadians said they are likely to buy a holiday gift out of nostalgia, with the number jumping to around half for both millennial (53 per cent) and Gen Z (49 per cent) Canadians.

“We’re seeing younger Canadians rediscover technology many of us grew up with, but this isn’t nostalgia for nostalgia’s sake,” says Kushal Samy, director of brand marketing at Best Buy Canada.

One-third (33 per cent) of respondents to the survey conducted by Angus Reid said they’re drawn to old tech because they value owning physical media, like vinyl records and video game cartridges.

“People want technology that feels personal and unlocks possibilities. Sometimes that means the newest device, and sometimes it means rediscovering a format or product they love,” Samy said.

This comes as Canadians are increasingly souring on streaming services, according to another Angus Reid survey . Nearly two-in-five Canadians (37 per cent) say they’ve cancelled at least one streaming service in the past six months, up from 32 per cent four years ago, a survey released last month found.

The return to physical media is being led by younger Canadians, according to the Best Buy survey.

Nearly one in four (23 per cent) Canadians said they bought music, movies or games in a physical format in the last year, rising to 32 per cent for millennials and 30 per cent for Gen Z, the survey showed.

At 12 per cent, Boomers still lagged their younger counterparts.

The most popular retro product making a comeback is the Apple iPod, with Gen Z most interested in it. This is followed by the Blackberry phone, with its physical keyboard.

Millennials, though, favour old gaming consoles like the Nintendo 64 or Super Nintendo, while Boomers were most nostalgic for VCRs and VHS tapes.

Headphones, earbuds, video game consoles and turntables or vinyl records are all popular categories this year, Best Buy said.

Are you a retail owner seeing a surge in requests for analog or physical media right now? Are you a consumer ditching streaming for DVDs, CDs, Game Boys or iPods — or whose kids are on the hunt for these types of retro tech? stories.title: Canada Disability Benefit payments go out next week. Here's what you need to know
stories.summary: What to know about eligibility, payment amounts and how to apply for the montly federal benefit.
stories.author: Samm Mohibuddin
stories.content:
Eligible Canadians with disabilities are set to receive another Canada Disability Benefit payment this month.

The payment is scheduled for Thursday, Nov. 19, according to the government’s benefit payment calendar. Payments are generally issued on the third Thursday of each month.

The benefit provides monthly financial support to working-age Canadians with disabilities and is administered by Service Canada.

Here’s what you need to know about the November payment, eligibility requirements and how to apply.

The maximum payment for the July 2026 to June 2027 benefit period is $204.20 per month, up from $200 during the previous benefit year.

The amount a person receives depends on their adjusted family net income and other factors, meaning not everyone qualifies for the maximum. The benefit is adjusted annually for inflation, with payments for the current benefit period calculated using income reported on 2025 federal tax returns.

The federal government also offers an online Canada Disability Benefit estimator to help applicants determine how much they could receive.

Applicants generally must be between 18 and 64 years old, have been approved for the Disability Tax Credit and be Canadians residents for income tax purposes.

They must also have filed their 2025 federal income tax return, along with their spouse or common-law partner, if applicable.

Applicants must meet citizenship or immigration status requirements. Eligible groups include Canadian citizens, permanent residents, protected persons, people registered or entitled to be registered under the Indian Act, and temporary residents who have lived in Canada throughout the previous 19 months.

Full details about eligibility to see if you qualify can be found on the Canadian Disability Benefit eligibility webpage.

Once an application is approved, benefit payments generally begin the following month and are issued on the third Thursday.

Some recipients May qualify for retroactive months of eligibility. Payments can be made by direct deposit or cheque and are not taxable.

The federal government advises that payments May take a few days to arrive, with mailed cheques potentially taking longer than direct deposit.

The federal government introduced a separate $150 supplemental payment to help cover costs associated with obtaining the Disability Tax Credit, which is required to qualify for the Canada Disability Benefit.

The one-time payment began rolling out in September and is separate from the regular monthly benefit.

People who received a Canada Disability Benefit before September 2026 May qualify for the supplement, even if they are no longer receiving monthly payments.

Recipients do not need to apply separately for the additional money.

Applicants generally need their Social Insurance Number and information about their status in Canada.

Approval for the Disability Tax Credit does not automatically enrol someone in the Canada Disability Benefit. A separate application is required.

The final regular payment of the year is scheduled for Dec. 17.

stories.title: His wife died by suicide. He wants the government to reconsider its Maid bill
stories.summary: If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Hannah Alberga, The Canadian Press

Posted November 12, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 12, 2026 5:18 am.

If you or someone you know is thinking about suicide, support is available 24-7 by calling or texting 988, Canada’s national suicide prevention helpline.

Poring over photographs spilled across his kitchen table, David Slater picks one up that captured his late wife mid-laughter.

She’s posing at an ancient temple in Greece, holding out a navy skirt in one hand, as if preparing for a curtsy. There are dozens more like it: Diane McDowell draped in a pink pashmina outside the Taj Mahal; sunglasses hanging from her neck as she grins with a family of elephants in Botswana.

Travel was an escape from the depression she kept at bay for decades with therapy, medication and exploration. “She had kept it in remission,” as Slater put it. “But when the time came, it wasn’t going to go back. She had passed the point of remission.”

Things she once loved — gardening for hours in her Toronto backyard, slipping on a pair of shiny loafers, sailing through the Caribbean — became reminders of her lost joy, out of reach.

McDowell, 71, wanted a medically assisted death, but was not eligible, Slater said.

She died by suicide on Oct. 25.

Slater recalls a conversation they had about a month and a half earlier, when his wife of 36 years said, “I don’t want to die, but I don’t want to live like this.” He pauses as a rush of tears spills from his eyes. “And that’s MAID in a nutshell.”

He believes MAID should be an option for mental illness, and he wants members of Parliament to consider the potential consequences of new legislation introduced by Justice Minister Sean Fraser in late October, which, if passed into law in the coming months, would ban people with mental illness as a sole underlying condition from accessing MAID.

Slater said he knows his wife’s life would have ended either way, but with MAID, “the dignity with which she lived her life would have been maintained.”

The justice minister read McDowell’s obituary and was moved by the tragedy. He recently lost a friend who also struggled with mental illness. However, Fraser said he had to make a decision on MAID in the absence of consensus from the medical community, and erred on the side of caution because of the permanence of the decision to end one’s life.

“And you do your best to, in the presence of a wide range of opinions, take decisions that have the potential to preserve life where possible, without being inconsiderate towards people who don’t see a path for themselves,” Fraser told The Canadian Press in a quiet room on Parliament Hill.

“People whose experience has been characterized by extraordinary pain and suffering, but who I can’t say with certainty, after having spoken to experts and people with lived experience, that there’s not a possibility for a recovery.”

Fraser said he was heeding concerns from many psychiatrists who said there was no way to parse out if someone could get better with the right treatment, even if it appeared they had tried everything. He also said he spoke to people who would not be alive today if MAID had been an option, and were happy to still be here.

Some experts in the field, meanwhile, have warned that restricting access to MAID for mental illness would result in people dying by suicide, instead of surrounded by family on their own terms. Obituaries published over the past several years, during which a planned expansion of MAID access was delayed, suggest there have been such cases.

Fraser said this policy decision was not “an accounting exercise,” weighing the fatal stakes of either withholding or granting MAID to people with mental illness.

“I’m not blind to the struggle that people have when they live with mental illness with deadly consequences,” Fraser said, pausing and becoming visibly emotional as he spoke about his close childhood friend, who he lost just weeks ago after a more than 20-year battle with mental illness. They had grown apart as adults, but remembers him as smart, funny, and talented, on a path to immense success before his life changed.

“And they tried everything, too,” he said, speaking of his friend and clarifying that MAID was not a part of his story.

MCDOWELL’S STORY

Depression was a part of McDowell’s life before she met Slater in her early thirties. She managed it with medication and therapy. Slater says she was quieter at low periods, but never cancelled social plans or missed a day at the litigation firm, where she was a founding partner and worked for more than 30 years. At the office, she had a reputation for her grace, empathy and professionalism.

McDowell retired from the law firm in 2012. The couple did not have children — “we have holidays,” Slater said they liked to quip.

They spent the winters sailing the Caribbean, summers back home in Toronto, and then rented an apartment for about three months in the south of France.

McDowell’s father was in the Air Force and she lived in Germany, France and across Canada throughout her childhood. She was one of the first in her family to graduate from university and managed the pub at Queen’s University to pay for summer travels, Slater said with pride.

Several years into retirement, feeling good in her golden years, McDowell asked her family doctor to go off of her medication for depression and began tapering her dose, her husband said.

They were on a boat in Grenada when she woke up one morning and told Slater she had to go home. “Something is not right,” he recalls her saying. That was the beginning of this “more difficult journey.”

She immediately went back on medication. It didn’t help, nor would any of the treatments her doctors tried in the coming years, including transcranial magnetic stimulation, electroconvulsive therapy or ketamine.

“It came on like a ton of bricks. It was shocking,” he said.

Slater recalls waking one night to the sound of their brass headboard banging against the wall. “She was shaking so hard that I thought she was actually having an epileptic fit,” he said.

He later learned she had had an anxiety attack. It sometimes took eight or nine hours for her surge of panic to subside.

“They say the actual attacks are usually like only four or five minutes, but it’s the getting over them that takes a huge drain,” he said.

Six months after Grenada, McDowell spent a month in the psychiatric ward at Toronto General Hospital. Not long after she was discharged, Slater recalls his wife — someone who would not even answer the door in sweatpants — not getting dressed.

“It took me a long time to understand. Probably. I knew she was ill and, you know, you’ve heard the old, ‘oh, just snap out of it.’ Well, there’s no snapping out of it. And why would a woman who has had the life she had — had the most amazing retirement — why would she choose to lie on the bed and suffer?”

It finally sunk in, he said. His wife had a fatal illness.

She spent another three months back in the psychiatric ward under intense supervision, balancing medications and lots of one-on-one therapy. She also went to Homewood Health Centre, a mental health treatment facility in an old mansion on a river in Guelph, for about nine weeks.

“There was no stone left unturned,” Slater said.

“When things really started to look poor, she did talk about MAID. I would have supported her in that. I told her I would,” he added. MAID was not unfamiliar to Slater. His father received the end-of-life procedure at the age of 89 after a stroke.

“My dad’s quality of life, when he was approved, was way better than Diane’s quality of life when she wasn’t even allowed to apply,” he said.

But as a lawyer and a pragmatic person who read the newspaper every day, McDowell knew she was not eligible, and she was not hopeful that would change in the near future.

They looked at going to Switzerland, which has an end-of-life program that receives international applicants. McDowell feared she would be hospitalized again if her doctors found out she wanted MAID.

FUNERAL REMARKS BY MP

McDowell’s funeral took place Nov. 7 and everyone — from her psychiatrist to her hairdresser — showed up, along with Liberal member of Parliament Robert Oliphant, her neighbour for 16 years on their midtown cul-de-sac.

Oliphant co-chaired a parliamentary committee tasked with making recommendations to the government on MAID in 2016. He spoke at McDowell’s funeral, saying he would commit once again to drawing attention to and pushing for fair and rightful access to MAID for people with mental illness.

“Diane’s death is something that I think makes it, again, personal for me,” Oliphant said in an interview from his house, kitty-corner from where she lived.

Soon, he is to vote on the government’s MAID legislation. It won’t be a straightforward decision, he said, as a vote in favour would close the door on mental illness but open the door to advance requests for people with dementia and other conditions that take away their capacity to consent. “I will have to decide on where ultimately I come down on it,” he said.

“Maybe it does take the death of an innocent person to spark us to say, no, we have to help this to not happen to another person.”

‘IT COULD HAVE BEEN DIGNIFIED’

If MAID was an option, Slater said, his wife could have been surrounded by family when she died. They could have talked about the little café they adored on the back side of the Notre-Dame, where they would end up at 2 a.m. for an ice cream and coffee after wandering the streets of Paris.

“The fact that I couldn’t sit and talk to her about that on her deathbed. You know? That’s wrong,” he said.

He imagines that she would have said, “I do not want to do this, but I have to because I have no choice. She would’ve said, ‘I love you very much.’ I could have held her hand,” he said, breaking into a deep, sorrowful sob.

stories.title: Carney in Ireland for meetings with European leaders, ahead of Asia summits
stories.summary: Dublin — Prime Minister Mark Carney is in Dublin for an informal meeting with European leaders, ahead of summits in Asia.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Dublin — Prime Minister Mark Carney continued his push for closer economic and security ties between Canada and Europe at a political summit in Ireland on Thursday.

The prime minister also met with the leaders of two of the nine European nations that have yet to ratify a decade-old trade deal.

Carney was in Dublin for a meeting of the European Political Community, an informal gathering of leaders from around Europe that has occurred every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

On the sidelines, he sat down with both Cyprus President Nikos Christodoulides and Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis to discuss negotiations to strengthen Canadian-European ties.

Greece and Cyprus have not yet ratified the Canada-European Union Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement. Christodoulides indicated that could soon change, at least for his nation.

“I want to mention this publicly. We are doing whatever is necessary in order to pass the agreement, (the) free trade agreement between the European Union and Canada, which is very important for both of us,” he said during a photo op ahead of his private conversation with Carney.

Both countries have held back for reasons that include questions about protected origins for cheeses — such as whether Canadian-made products can be called feta or halloumi.

Christodoulides said the meeting was the first between a Canadian prime minister and a Cypriot president in 80 years. He said it reflects the “pro-European Canadian approach” under Carney’s leadership.

Carney also had informal discussions, known as pull-asides, with French President Emmanuel Macron and the leaders of Latvia, Ireland and Denmark. France and Ireland also have not ratified Ceta, which effectively has been in place since 2017.

Carney’s trip to Dublin marks the second time Canada has been invited to the European Political Community meeting. And for the second time, Canada was the only non-European country represented at the table.

Since the last meeting in May in Armenia, Carney and European Union leaders have pitched making Canada an “associate member” of the EU — a title they have yet to define.

Carney told reporters Thursday morning that the summit could help advance his goal of boosting affordability and economic opportunities for Canadians through new partnerships with Europe.

“It delivers opportunity — opportunity for our youth, for our artists, for companies. It will deliver affordability, cutting red tape, more competition in Canada, more goods, more choice and security,” he said in English.

Thursday’s summit included Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who briefed Carney and a dozen European leaders on the state of negotiations with Russia.

The Ukrainian leader discussed this week’s talks in Abu Dhabi with Russian officials organized by U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Zelenskyy had not presented a public summary of those talks by Thursday evening. His briefing took place as Witkoff and Kushner were in Moscow to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Witkoff and Kushner are expected to fly to Dublin to meet with Zelenskyy.

Carney said it’s up to Europe to craft arrangements that will secure an eventual peace, with support from countries like Canada.

These “security guarantees” can include promises to provide troops to ensure a ceasefire holds, or to defend a country if it is invaded.

“Security guarantees are a European responsibility, with Canada, with the United States. So there are tiers for security guarantees,” Carney said in French.

The Associated Press reports that Nato Secretary-General Mark Rutte said Thursday that the U.S., Europe and Ukraine are “very much aligned” on what the security guarantees should look like once a viable peace is established.

The United Kingdom has convened Canada, Australia, Japan and numerous EU countries in what it calls a coalition of the willing aimed at providing military support to Ukraine once a ceasefire is in place.

Carney spoke briefly with reporters at the start of Thursday’s meetings, but most of the plenary was not broadcast. He is expected to give a press conference in coming days.

The summit’s Irish hosts have locked down a section of central Dublin for what they are calling its largest ever gathering of international leaders. Police boats have been patrolling the River Liffey and there is a visible security presence across the city.

Schools, newsrooms and an airline have reported receiving bomb threats which local authorities have said are not credible.

Carney is set to leave for Asia Thursday evening.

He will attend a summit in the Philippines focused on regional issues, followed by the Francophonie summit in Cambodia.

The Francophonie summit will also include Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, whose minority government was elected on a sovereigntist platform.

Plamondon has said he wants to conduct diplomacy on Quebec’s behalf instead of leaving it to the prime minister.

On the sidelines of Thursday’s meeting, Macron said he looks forward to speaking with all representatives to the Francophonie at the upcoming summit.

“It is not my place to interfere in Canadian affairs, but rather to continue supporting our shared affinities, including our cultural and linguistic ties,” he said in French.

Carney said he did not attend this week’s UN Climate Conference in Turkey — better known as COP31 — because the leaders’ day fell on Nov. 11.

“It was more important to be at Remembrance Day to honour the women and men of the Canadian Forces who served our country, who stood for democracy, often in Europe, [and] supported our rights,” he said.

Carney added that his environment minister will help advance Canadian interests on electrification, saying it’s a major theme of the summit in Turkey.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario wobbles on ending municipalities’ veto over new landfills
stories.summary: Provincial Environment Minister open to ‘tweaks’ to proposal to remove local say over dumps
stories.author: Jeff Gray
stories.content:
Ontario Environment Minister Todd McCarthy says he is open to changes to his proposal to eliminate a municipal veto on new landfills, despite initially insisting the move is necessary, as the province stares down a shortage of places to put its garbage.

When Mr. McCarthy first unveiled his plan last month, as part of an omnibus bill aimed at reducing red tape, he said Ontario has less than 10 years of landfill space left. He warned that a new 50-per-cent U.S. tariff imposed by President Donald Trump on trash that crosses the border would make the situation worse, adding that Ontario sends 40 per cent of its commercial waste to Michigan and New York State.

The proposal, which has alarmed some rural municipal leaders and environmentalists, would remove a section from the province’s Environmental Assessment Act that requires landfill proponents to show they have the support of the host municipality and others within 3.5 kilometres of the site.

The provision was inserted into the legislation by the same Progressive Conservative government just six years ago, when it sided with a swath of rural municipalities that opposed being stuck with big-city waste against their will.

In an interview with The Globe and Mail, Mr. McCarthy said striking the section would be a “housekeeping amendment,” a term that generally refers to an insignificant change in legislation – despite saying when he introduced the bill that it was key to streamlining the approval of new landfills. He also said he is open to “tweaks.”

“Technically, that veto is being removed. That’s a proposal,” he said, adding that once the bill goes before a legislative committee “some consideration will be given to different alternatives.”

Mr. McCarthy said municipalities will retain input and their existing permitting powers, which can be overridden by the province’s land tribunal. But he said he expects there will be enough willing communities for both new landfills and new “energy-from-waste” incinerators, for which he is also proposing an easier approval process. That’s also a flashpoint for environmentalists, who warn of pollution and greenhouse gas emissions.

Mr. McCarthy’s previous public statements about the landfill veto have also sent mixed messages. When asked by reporters late last month if he would force a municipality to accept a landfill site, he left the door open. But the next day, he repeatedly declared that no municipality would be forced to accept trash.

The latest back-and-forth is taking place in the shadow of a move the provincial government made just last year, when it passed special legislation to override local opposition and allow proponents seeking to revive and expand a landfill site in the Southwestern Ontario town of Dresden to skip the environmental assessment process.

The PC government’s original promise of a local veto followed an anti-dump battle that began more than a decade ago, when a proposal to put 17.4 million tonnes of waste in a quarry just two kilometres from the heart of small town Ingersoll, Ont., became a rallying cry for rural municipalities.

Local leaders, activists and a coalition of 150 municipalities pushed for a formal veto. Mr. Ford and his party then campaigned in 2018 on giving communities one – and got around to amending the Environmental Assessment Act to include it in 2020.

The potential reversal is the latest in a spate of policies from the Ford government that have alarmed environmentalists. It has also caught the attention of local politicians in Oxford County, which was ground zero for the landfill battle that prompted the veto clause in the first place.

The county issued a statement on Nov. 2, signed by 12 local mayors and mayors-elect, reaffirming their belief that municipalities should retain the right to say no to landfills. They warn that the changes “would leave municipalities without leverage or meaningful voice at the table, with little to no opportunity to negotiate the necessary terms to safeguard their communities.”

Marcus Ryan, the outgoing warden of Oxford County and mayor of Zorra Township, said he and other local politicians intend to meet with Mr. McCarthy to see if the veto can be preserved. He blames the proposed change on lobbying by the waste industry, which has advocated against the veto.

“We wish it wasn’t happening,” he said, adding that there is no indication the owners of the quarry in Oxford intend to revive their landfill proposal. “But this is the world of government. And our level of government will talk to their level of government and we’ll see if we can work it out.”

Bryan Smith, chair of the Oxford Coalition for Social Justice, who helped lead the fight against the landfill, said the provincial government appears to be talking out of both sides of its mouth.

“What they are writing and what they are saying are two different things,” he said, warning that citizens’ groups and local politicians would restage their fight if the government goes ahead.

Long-time local Oxford PC MPP Ernie Hardeman had previously championed the municipal veto. Now, he says he hopes a new system can be worked out at the committee stage that would preserve a say for municipalities, yet still make it easier to create new landfills.

He said it doesn’t make sense that municipalities can decide where a Tim Hortons goes, but not a landfill, and that being unable to say no leaves them with very little leverage in negotiating with landfill companies.

But he also said the clause that he worked to insert into the Environmental Assessment Act in 2020 went too far by extending the veto to some neighbouring municipalities, not just the prospective host.

“Hopefully we’re going to see some amendments,” he said. “I think the challenge is we know landfill has to be somewhere.”

Waste to Resource Ontario, which represents the waste industry, warned in a statement sent by the group’s manager of member services and events, Lauryn Weinberger, that the province faces a landfill capacity crisis.

The group said the province must act now to find new sites and increase diversion and recycling, as new landfills take eight to 10 years to become operational. The statement said if the U.S. border were to close completely for trash, Ontario could run out of space by 2034.

stories.title: Canadian court gives fresh hope to Afghan family, split by smugglers and bureaucracy, trying to reunite in Canada
stories.summary: A judge rules the refusal in the brother’s case was unreasonable, and sends the case back to the Immigration Department.
stories.author: Nicholas Keung
stories.content:
Mo Youssufi has spent more than 15 years filing applications, appealing decisions and fighting an immigration system that seemed determined to keep his family apart.

Last week, the Federal Court threw the family a lifeline, sending their reunification case back to the Immigration Department for a new decision, offering fresh hope to a family split by smugglers and separated by bureaucracy.

“After so many years of waiting, uncertainty, and disappointment, it was incredibly emotional to finally receive some positive news,” said Youssufi, an Afghan who was resettled in Toronto by the Canadian government from Turkey in 2008.

“For the first time in a long while, it felt like our voices had truly been heard and that there was still hope for our family to be together again.”

The family’s ordeal started in 2006, when Youssufi’s mother fled Herat, in Western Afghanistan, with her four children and two grandkids after they were targeted by the Taliban following the U.S.-led intervention, because their father worked for the government. He was threatened and then vanished.

After arriving in Turkey, they were separated in 2007 when smugglers split them into two groups. Youssufi’s mother, Tooba Gholan Hasan, and youngest brother, Mehran Youssufi, ended up in Denmark where they have been granted temporary status; the rest of the family were rescued by United Nations officials and later sponsored to go to Canada.

Family sent back to Honduras accuses Ottawa of violating rights by handing them to U.S. — despite what they claim is Trump administration's abuses.

In 2009, Youssufi finally located his mother and sibling through a grapevine of people over the internet and an Afghan TV program in the U.S. The family would spend the following 15 years trying, without success, to reunite in Canada .

They have tried everything: getting their mother and brother visitor visas; sponsoring them for permanent residence; and even once flying them to the United States to enter via the land border.

In 2023, the family resorted to the last option for reunification by submitting permanent resident applications for Hasan and Mehran, now 26, under humanitarian and compassionate grounds. Among the reasons was the mother’s and son’s precarious status in Denmark, which has strict requirements for permanent settlement for refugees.

They were rejected the following year, and the family appealed the decisions in court. A federal judge refused to hear the mother’s case, but a different judge allowed a separate challenge by the brother to proceed.

On Friday, the Federal Court quashed the immigration decision against Mehran Youssufi, ruling the refusal was unreasonable because the officer failed to consider the fact that the family was separated against their will during their flight from Afghanistan, an event the court said was at the root of nearly two decades of “involuntary separation.”

“Failing to account for this history led the officer to view the applicant’s circumstances, especially his alleged establishment in Denmark and his family’s efforts to maintain contact and to reunite, through an unduly negative lens,” Judge François Joyal wrote in his ruling.

Treating an applicant’s ability to cope with separation as a reason to refuse relief went against the spirit of the humanitarian immigration scheme, the judge noted.

Toronto lawyer Adam Hummel, who represented the family, said he was heartened by the court’s decision to reopen the file.

“The family’s efforts to stay in contact through calls, visits and other means did not diminish the emotional hardship of the separation,” Hummel said. “In fact, those efforts supported the strength of their family ties and their desire to reunite.”

Despite the good news, there is still uncertainty about what will happen next.

“More than anything, we dream of the day when both Mehran and my mother can finally come to Canada and our entire family can be reunited,” said Mo Youssufi, now a police officer here.

“We have already missed so many precious moments together, and all we want is the chance to create new memories without being separated by borders.”

stories.title: Q&A: Hidden studies, broken promises and Ontario’s gambling problem
stories.summary: Submit your questions on Ontario’s online gambling scandal, the study the government didn’t want you to see and what comes next.
stories.author: Brendan Kennedy
stories.content:
This live event has ended.

When Ontario opened its online gambling market in 2022, it vowed to share data with researchers to reduce problem gambling — but it never did.

The province also secretly shelved a study it commissioned to track rates of problem gambling when executives didn’t like what researchers found. These are the findings from two of my recent investigations into online gambling policy in Ontario.

In just a few years, online gambling has become incredibly lucrative for the province. Ontarians wagered more than $82 billion last fiscal year, with more than $574 million of that added to provincial coffers.

Critics say that windfall has come at a cost to public health. Emergency department visits for gambling disorders have doubled since Ontario opened its legal market. Insolvencies in which gambling is identified as one of the causes have more than tripled. Suicides by people with gambling issues have also increased. Meanwhile, we are inundated with gambling advertisements.

Do you have questions about the province’s approach to gambling policy? Wondering how much the gambling companies take home in comparison to the province?

I want to hear all of it. I’ll be answering your questions in the comments on Friday, Nov. 13 at 11 a.m. in a live Q&A.

The live Q&A will take place in the comment section below. There is no live stream video. I will instead respond to questions by replying to individual comments.

To ask a question, log into our site or app and submit you query via the comment section. When your question is answered, there will be a button below your comment that says “Show reply.” Click to see the reporter’s response.

Any reader can ask a question as long as they are registered and logged in to the Star. Nonregistered readers can still view the live chat.

stories.title: Improving patient care one test at a time: LHSC Core Lab upgrades boost capacity, efficiency
stories.summary: November 12, 2026London Health Sciences Centre's (LHSC) Core Labs have powered up their capacity thanks to a significant upgrade to testing equipment that will mean faster access to results for patients.
stories.content:
Kristen Mendonca, medical laboratory technologist stands in front of automated lab equipment at Victoria and Children's Hospital Core Labs.

November 12, 2026

London Health Sciences Centre's (LHSC) Core Labs have powered up their capacity thanks to a significant upgrade to testing equipment that will mean faster access to results for patients.

The labs at University Hospital and Victoria Hospital, which are the main intake for patient bloodwork, now have the ability to process more than a combined 15,000 tests an hour thanks to the upgrades. That’s an increase of a little more than 24 per cent from previous levels. Additional equipment used to prepare samples for testing was also refreshed, extending its useful life by five years.

The work to install the new equipment took place over the spring and summer months and was funded through LHSC's existing budget. By the end of August, the new technology was firing on all cylinders, helping to diagnose and monitor more patients faster.

The upgrades to the Core Labs help the dedicated staff members within the Pathology and Laboratory Medicine (PaLM) department ensure care teams and patients have access to the health information they need as quickly as possible.

“Although we work behind the scenes, the results we generate play a critical role in diagnosis and treatment decisions,” says Kristen Mendonca, a medical laboratory technologist who works within the Core Labs. She helped test the new equipment after it was installed and supported her coworkers' training.

The tests that Mendonca and her colleagues process and analyze are used by physicians to diagnose patients with conditions including diabetes and infections as well as heart, kidney and liver disease; all ailments that require timely interventions and treatments.

Samples that are first tested in the Core Labs are also sent to other specialized laboratories at LHSC for further analysis when necessary.

“I enjoy knowing that my work directly supports patient care and contributes to positive patient outcomes,” Mendonca says.

Even though the new and refreshed equipment has only been up and running fully for a few months, the difference is noticeable.

“Compared with previous models, the new equipment offers improved automation, faster processing, increased testing capacity and greater reliability,” explains Jade Bolsover, manager of Core Laboratories, Flow Cytometry, Transfusion Medicine and Transplant Immunology within the broader PaLM team. The new machines also require less hands-on maintenance from staff.

Since coming online at Victoria Hospital, which also provides testing for Children's Hospital, the team has noted that the new equipment is active and available for use more often.

“While turnaround time data is still being monitored, early results show a positive trend,” Bolsover says.

PaLM is a joint venture between LHSC and St. Joseph’s Health Care London (St. Joseph's). St. Joseph's has also upgraded part of its Core Lab facility.

LHSC has 21 laboratories across all its sites that diagnose everything from common ailments to rare diseases

The Core Labs are the main intake for bloodwork from patients in LHSC’s three Emergency Departments as well as in-patient units and clinics across University Hospital, Victoria Hospital and Children’s Hospital

The Core Labs run 24 hours a day, 365 days a year

Specialized LHSC laboratories include Biochemistry, Microbiology, Molecular Diagnostics, Pathology, Transfusion Medicine and Transplant Immunology

More than eight million tests are performed per year for patients across Southwestern Ontario within PaLM’s labs

Approximately 60 medical laboratory technologists and 50 medical laboratory assistants work diligently to process and analyze test samples 24 hours a day, seven days a week

stories.title: London Knights defeated by Guelph Storm on home ice
stories.summary: The London Knights faced off against the Guelph Storm at Canada Life Place Wednesday night in one of the most anticipated matchups in the Ontario Hockey League this season.
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights faced off against the Guelph Storm at Canada Life Place Wednesday night in one of the most anticipated matchups in the Ontario Hockey League this season.

Juho Piiparinen opened the scoring early in the second period to give the Knights a one-goal lead.

Guelph responded, scoring three unanswered goals.

Marcus Nordmark added his ninth of the season, scoring on the Knight’s power play in the third period.

Trailing by one in the third, the Knights needed a late push to even the score but couldn’t find the equalizer.

Guelph would go on to seal the win, taking it 5-2.

stories.title: London family says insurance settlement falls short after alleged drunk driver crashes into backyard
stories.summary: A London family says they’re facing thousands of dollars in additional expenses after an alleged drunk driver crashed into their backyard, leaving their fence, deck and patio door damaged.
stories.author: Reta Ismail
stories.content:
A London family says they’re facing thousands of dollars in additional expenses after an alleged drunk driver crashed into their backyard, leaving their fence, deck and patio door damaged.

Sargon Koshaba says he contacted TD Insurance immediately after the March 6, 2026, crash, expecting the damages to be repaired.

“I’m not asking for a betterment on my property from the insurance company. I’m just asking for my house to be put back the way it was prior to the accident,” he said.

But months later, the couple says they’re still dealing with a dispute over the cost of repairs.

Janet Koshaba was sleeping inside the home when the vehicle came through the backyard fence, drove across the deck and slammed into the patio door.

TD Insurance sent its own contractor to assess the damage. The resulting estimate was approximately $13,000.

The Koshabas say three other contractors provided estimates in the range of $40,000 to replace their damaged fence, lawn and backyard deck.

The Koshaba’s say the contractor selected by TD was unable to complete the work for at least a year. Unwilling to wait that long, the homeowners found another contractor willing to do the work for approximately $20,000.

However, they say the repairs will not fully restore the backyard to its original condition, and they’re concerned the differences could affect the property’s resale value.

The fence has only been repaired in the section where the vehicle crashed through, and the replacement does not match the rest of the existing fence.

The couple says they’ve paid their $2,000 insurance deductible and are covering additional costs out of pocket. Ammer Esho, with General Restoration Services, is now completing some of the repairs.

He says rising material and labour costs can make delays particularly difficult for contractors and homeowners.

“Today I went to one of the suppliers to pick up material. And prices gone up 10 per cent,” Esho said. He says contractors can be left absorbing those increases when projects are delayed while waiting for insurance approval.

In an email to the homeowners, TD outlined a cash-settlement option of $13,193.73, after taxes and the $2,000 deductible were factored in.

The offer was based on TD’s approved repair estimate of $13,445.78, plus applicable taxes. The insurer also indicated it could reimburse withheld contractor overhead and profit costs up to $2,279.06 if the homeowners’ licensed general contractor charged those fees.

Gabriel Murray, a lawyer who handles insurance disputes, says delays involving insurance-approved contractors are becoming an increasingly common problem.

He says homeowners are often left choosing between waiting for an insurer’s contractor or accepting a cash settlement and hiring someone themselves.

The difficulty, Murray says, comes when the homeowner’s preferred contractor charges more than the insurer is willing to pay.

Homeowners May also have the option of pursuing the at-fault driver to recover additional costs, but Murray says that route can be expensive.

In a statement to CTV News, Megan Sampson, manager of corporate and public affairs at TD Bank Group, said the company understands how difficult it can be when a home is damaged.

“TD Insurance is working closely with the client to review the information provided to make sure their claim is assessed based on the coverage available to them and remain committed to supporting our client the best we can throughout the process,” Sampson said.

The Koshabas say they aren’t looking for an upgrade to their property. They want their backyard restored to the condition it was in before the crash.

The Koshabas say three other contractors provided estimates in the range of $40,000 to replace their damaged fence, lawn and backyard deck.

The Koshaba’s say the contractor selected by TD was unable to complete the work for at least a year. Unwilling to wait that long, the homeowners found another contractor willing to do the work for approximately $20,000.
However, they say the repairs will not fully restore the backyard to its original condition, and they’re concerned the differences could affect the property’s resale value.
The fence has only been repaired in the section where the vehicle crashed through, and the replacement does not match the rest of the existing fence.
The couple says they’ve paid their $2,000 insurance deductible and are covering additional costs out of pocket. Ammer Esho, with General Restoration Services, is now completing some of the repairs.
He says rising material and labour costs can make delays particularly difficult for contractors and homeowners.

“Today I went to one of the suppliers to pick up material. And prices gone up 10 per cent,” Esho said. He says contractors can be left absorbing those increases when projects are delayed while waiting for insurance approval.
In an email to the homeowners, TD outlined a cash-settlement option of $13,193.73, after taxes and the $2,000 deductible were factored in.

The offer was based on TD’s approved repair estimate of $13,445.78, plus applicable taxes. The insurer also indicated it could reimburse withheld contractor overhead and profit costs up to $2,279.06 if the homeowners’ licensed general contractor charged those fees.
Gabriel Murray, a lawyer who handles insurance disputes, says delays involving insurance-approved contractors are becoming an increasingly common problem.
He says homeowners are often left choosing between waiting for an insurer’s contractor or accepting a cash settlement and hiring someone themselves.
The difficulty, Murray says, comes when the homeowner’s preferred contractor charges more than the insurer is willing to pay.
Homeowners May also have the option of pursuing the at-fault driver to recover additional costs, but Murray says that route can be expensive.
In a statement to CTV News, Megan Sampson, manager of corporate and public affairs at TD Bank Group, said the company understands how difficult it can be when a home is damaged.

“TD Insurance is working closely with the client to review the information provided to make sure their claim is assessed based on the coverage available to them and remain committed to supporting our client the best we can throughout the process,” Sampson said.
The Koshabas say they aren’t looking for an upgrade to their property. They want their backyard restored to the condition it was in before the crash.

stories.title: Three Ontario private career colleges lay off staff as Osap pause continues
stories.summary: One school has also paused classes for roughly 300 students
stories.author: Kelly Grant
stories.content:
Anderson College has laid off just more than 100 staff and paused classes for about 300 recently enrolled students. Computek College laid off 25 employees this week. The Academy of Applied Pharmaceutical Sciences has laid off 10 people so far.

And the owners of all three say they fear worse is to come if the Ontario government doesn’t lift a blanket freeze on loan disbursements to schools and students in the private career college sector sooner than its previously announced timeline of next year.

“We are operating, as you can imagine, at a huge loss,” said Laleh Bighash, president of the Academy of Applied Pharmaceutical Sciences, a private college in the Greater Toronto Area that trains university graduates for careers in the pharmaceutical and food-safety industries. If the pause endures, she added, the school can survive for “maybe weeks, maybe maximum a month, but we wouldn’t be able to operate beyond that.”

Layoffs, class suspensions and other consequences are mounting for Ontario’s private career colleges as they struggle to stay afloat without their main source of revenue: tuition fees paid through the Ontario Student Assistance Program, the province’s needs-based student aid program.

The Progressive Conservative government has said it had no choice but to pause Osap disbursements after a preliminary audit identified “serious concerns” with the integrity of student aid in the private postsecondary sector. Some of those concerns were forwarded to the Ontario Provincial Police.

Private career colleges offer quick diplomas for jobs such as personal support workers, early childhood assistants, community service workers, medical office assistants and dental hygienists, among others. They generally charge higher tuition than their publicly-funded counterparts because they aren’t subsidized by taxpayers.

They also tend to attract low-income students, such as new Canadians and working parents. As a result, their students rely heavily on government loans to cover tuition and to help defray their living costs. Normally, Osap sends tuition fees directly to postsecondary institutions, but that didn’t happen for private colleges this fall.

At least one private college in Toronto, the Harris Institute for music industry education, said the Osap pause played a part in its decision to close , while another, Trillium College, has responded by suspending classes at all five of its campuses.

The freeze is also chilling business for career college marketers and suppliers, some of whom are sitting on niche textbooks and branded uniforms their clients can no longer afford.

“My clients, they’re not under investigation. But they’ve been cut off anyways,” said Eddy Della Mora, owner of Campus Bookstore, a business that sells books and clothing to private colleges. His sales were down 96 per cent in October compared to the same month last year.

Premier Doug Ford said earlier this week that his government is “moving as quickly as we possibly can” to reform Osap rules for the private postsecondary sector. Nolan Quinn, the Minister of Colleges, Universities, Research Excellence and Security, is scheduled to make an announcement about the program on Thursday.

“We’re going to catch these bad actors, and they need to go to jail,” Mr. Ford said at an unrelated news event on Monday. “Simple as that. We need to get the money back and invest it into good actors.”

In May, the province issued notices of Osap non-renewal to six GTA career colleges that had recorded unusually large spikes in Osap-funded students in online-only courses. Three of those schools took the government to court, a move that put provincial inspection reports and other internal documents on the public record.

Inspectors allege they found suspicious activities such as asynchronous courses being completed in a day or two and exams written in less than five minutes, often from IP addresses outside North America, which suggest third parties May have completed the coursework. They also noted that thousands of Osap applications for the schools came from a handful of IP addresses.

None of the allegations have been proven in court.

In August, the province brought in Kpmg to conduct the wider audit that triggered the freeze.

It’s not yet clear how many private postsecondary institutions have laid off staff or suspended classes, according to Career Colleges Ontario, an association that represents about 280 career college campuses. Spokeswoman Taylor Buck said the organization is actively gathering data from its members about the ramifications.

“We continue to hear from students about the very real impact this is having on their education and their ability to cover basic living expenses. If funding is not restored quickly, we expect more institutions will have to pause programs or close, putting even more students at risk of disrupted education,” she said by e-mail.

Muraly Srinarayanathas, the owner and chairman of Computek College, laid off 25 of his 120 staff starting on Monday. The school, which offers mainly health, business and technology programs at its campuses in Scarborough, Markham and Ajax, has avoided suspending classes for now.

But Mr. Srinarayanathas worries about having to take that step, and having to consider another round of layoffs. And he worries just as much about the students and the workplaces they serve, including nursing homes, hospitals and daycares.

“I think it’s going to be horrific,” especially for health-care employers, he said.

At Anderson College, which has 10 campuses in the GTA and in southern Ontario, students in at least one class broke into tears when they learned their course was being suspended, according to Heather Yang, the college’s president and chief executive officer.

Late last month, Anderson paused classes for students newly enrolled in August and September.

“They were working hard. They studied really well despite uncertainty,” Ms. Yang said. “They bonded with their classmates. They bonded with their instructors, and to just have this news announced, through no fault of their own. It’s just very devastating.”

Bianca Giacoboni, a spokeswoman for Mr. Quinn, emphasized in a statement on Wednesday that the preliminary findings of the independent audit compelled the government to enact the pause to “protect taxpayer dollars and hold bad actors accountable.”

She added that, “We recognize the impact that this pause is having on hard-working students and good institutions. We are pursuing options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions for students, while concurrently working as quickly as possible to get good actors back into the Osap system.”

She also said the day-to-day operations of postsecondary institutions, including private colleges, are the responsibilities of those institutions.

stories.title: Montrealers pay tribute to war veterans at annual Remembrance Day ceremony
stories.summary: Retired lieutenant-colonel Colin Robinson said Remembrance Day is an opportunity for Canadians to reflect on the dangers of war, particularly amid current global tensions.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
About a hundred people gathered under sunny skies in downtown Montreal on Wednesday for a Remembrance Day ceremony honouring Canada’s war veterans and those who died serving their country.

Retired lieutenant-colonel Colin Robinson, who attended the ceremony at Place du Canada, said Remembrance Day is an opportunity for Canadians to reflect on the dangers of war, particularly amid current global tensions.

“These things can spiral out of control relatively quickly,” he said, drawing parallels between the events leading up to the two world wars and the state of the world today.

“I think that sense of awareness will probably lead to us having less conflict and less war.”

A military parade was followed by the national anthem shortly before 11 a.m., with some in the crowd singing along as bells rang from nearby St. George’s Anglican Church.

A 21-gun salute echoed through the area, sending flocks of birds into the sky, as bagpipes played near the war memorial.

Organizers had warned that the blank rounds used during the salute could cause temporary hearing discomfort but posed no danger.

Dignitaries and military representatives took turns laying wreaths at the foot of the monument, including Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada, who laid one on behalf of the city. Some offered military salutes while others bowed their heads.

One wreath honoured the four soldiers killed in a training accident at CFB Wainwright, Alta., last month, when a grass fire swept through a training area, injuring 39 others.

“Serving in the military is inherently risky. What happened in Wainwright last month is another reminder,” said retired lieutenant-colonel Colin Robinson.

Decorated with red poppies, a purple ribbon and autumn leaves, the wreaths gradually lined the base of the memorial.

During the ceremony, Col. Lisa Pacarynuk, chaplain general of the Canadian Armed Forces, spoke of lives cut short, families separated and the lasting physical and emotional wounds of war.

“Their experiences remind us that peace is precious, that freedom must never be taken for granted and that the consequences of conflict extend far beyond the battlefield,” she said.

Those attending were also asked to observe two minutes of silence at 11 a.m., marking the moment fighting ended in the First World War on Nov. 11, 1918.

Robinson reflected on the passing of generations of veterans. When he joined his regiment in 1989, he recalled regularly meeting Second World War veterans.

“I think we kind of took it for granted,” he said. “You don’t realize that it’s going to go away.”

Also attending the ceremony, Pierre Saint-Louis, who served in the Canadian Navy and infantry before becoming a lawyer, had tears in his eyes as he explained what attending the Remembrance Day ceremony meant to him.

“It’s hard to explain; you just feel it, there are things you believe in,” he said.

He said remembrance should also mean supporting veterans who are still alive and the families of military personnel serving overseas.

A member of the Royal Canadian Legion, an organization that supports veterans and their families, Saint-Louis said he wants it to do more to help military families, particularly those whose loved ones are deployed overseas.

As the ceremony came to an end shortly before noon, some attendees removed the red poppies from their coats and left them at the foot of the monument.

Remembrance Day ceremonies took place across the country Wednesday to honour the men and women who served or died in uniform.
