stories.title: Quebec woman with ALS hears her own voice again thanks to AI app
stories.summary: A new AI tool is helping people with ALS regain a version of their voice, making conversations faster and more personal.
stories.author: Charlotte Glorieux
stories.content:
When Anne-Marie Poirier speaks at family gatherings, her nieces and nephews hear a familiar voice — one they thought they might never hear again.

Poirier has amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS , a progressive neurological disease that has robbed her of her ability to speak and affected her ability to swallow.

But a new artificial intelligence tool has brought a simulated version of her voice back into the lives of her loved ones, reinvigorating her family conversations and interactions.

“They are so happy. It’s as though they forget that my life is slowly coming to an end,” she said, using the AI tool during an interview with The Canadian Press.

Poirier first experienced symptoms in August 2024 and was diagnosed with ALS a year later. She began losing her voice in October 2025 and has relied on communication applications since January.

In May, she started using Vocality, an application developed by two young Montreal entrepreneurs that allows her to turn a few keywords into complete sentences, spoken aloud in a voice resembling her own.

Users can download the tool and use it after getting a paid subscription.

Eligible users May also qualify for financial assistance through ALS Québec, a non-profit organization that supports people living with the disease and their families.

“It gives me energy, a feeling of being alive,” she said.

ALS, also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease, is an incurable neurological disease that progressively destroys nerve cells controlling voluntary movement.

As it advances, patients can lose their ability to walk, speak, swallow and eventually breathe, even as their ability to think and understand others often remains intact.

Nearly 4,000 Canadians live with ALS, and about 1,000 are diagnosed each year, according to the ALS Society of Canada.

For those who lose their ability to speak, even a simple exchange can become a painstaking process, with conversations moving faster than they can write or type.

Thomas Houlachi saw that frustration firsthand. In 2021, two members of his family were diagnosed with ALS. By 2023, both had lost their ability to speak.

They tried using communication applications on an iPad, but typing messages letter by letter was slow and increasingly difficult as their motor skills deteriorated. At times, they found it easier to write on paper.

“Speech is something so fundamental to the human experience. If you lose it, you lose half of that experience,” Houlachi said.

Houlachi, then beginning his biomedical engineering studies at Polytechnique Montréal, wondered whether he could make communicating less of a struggle.

He teamed up with David Ruiz, who studied software engineering at Concordia University, and the two founded Vocality in 2023.

Houlachi’s relatives died before the pair finalized the application, so they never got to use the finished product.

After more than two years of development and testing with people living with ALS, Vocality launched on iPhones and iPads in June, with an Android version expected next week, according to Houlachi.

Instead of typing out entire sentences, users can enter a few keywords and have the application fill in the rest. It can also listen to conversations and suggest responses based on what others are saying.

Houlachi said Vocality uses AI technology designed specifically for people with speech impairments, allowing the application to learn their vocabulary and expressions over time.

Houlachi acknowledged the tool is being introduced at a time of growing public concerns about artificial intelligence and its use in health care. But he said his firm was working with leading experts to ensure the AI was being introduced in a safe and ethical way.

“We often talk about AI replacing what humans do, but Vocality is the exact opposite,” he said. “It’s a tool that gives people control, allowing them to continue expressing themselves authentically, while helping them communicate faster and more smoothly.”

Some of the AI processing takes place directly on users’ devices, reducing the need to send personal information to external servers.

More than 100 people across North America now use the application daily, according to Houlachi.

Vocality is also compatible with eye-tracking equipment, allowing people with limited mobility to select words and phrases using their eyes rather than their fingers.

The application also allows users to communicate in a digital recreation of their own voice. Using recordings of their speech, technology developed by AI company ElevenLabs can create a synthetic voice that Vocality uses to read messages aloud.

For Poirier, the voice combines recordings of her actual speech with digitally generated words.

Poirier, who had previously used other communication applications, said Vocality is easier to use.

“It’s so much simpler, more intuitive,” she said. “The application allows you to correct mistakes, and with just a few words, it generates sentences.”

Poirier learned about the project through ALS Québec, which helped recruit users to test the application.

She has since regularly shared feedback with Houlachi. For example, when someone asked her to repeat a sentence, she sometimes had to type it again because the application had erased it after reading it aloud.

The current version of Vocality allows users to save frequently used phrases in their library. It also has a feature that allows users to repeat sentences when needed.

That close relationship with users is part of what makes Vocality stand out, according to Paul Shenouda, a partnerships manager at Propolys, Polytechnique Montréal’s technology incubator.

Vocality has received business training, coaching, and $16,000 in financial support from Propolys, Polytechnique Montréal’s technology incubator. Houlachi said the firm also earned an additional $150,000 through fundraising and prize money from two contests.

Shenouda said the founders’ willingness to involve patients early in the development process caught his attention.

He said entrepreneurs sometimes become so focused on developing their technology that they lose sight of the people who will eventually use it.

“It’s rather rare to have a story that’s so sincere,” Shenouda said.

Vocality is now available in six languages and is being used by people with other conditions affecting speech, including cerebral palsy and some forms of aphasia.

For Poirier, the technology has opened up another unexpected possibility: communicating with her partner in Italian.

Although she understands the language, she doesn’t normally speak it. Vocality allows her to generate sentences in Italian and have them read aloud to her partner, who speaks the language fluently.

Despite the progression of her disease, Poirier says she wants to make the most of the time she has.

“No one can guarantee they will live a long time,” she said. “You have to enjoy every moment of life and be as happy as possible.”

A video posted to Instagram by Schnitzel bakery in Montreal shows broken glass at its entrance. (Schnitzel / Instagram)

November 11, 2026 at 8:54 p.m.

A Montreal kosher restaurant was broken into and robbed in the early hours of Wednesday, adding to a string of incidents at Jewish-owned businesses in the city in recent days.

The break-in at Schnitzel, a café and restaurant on Queen Mary Rd., occurred two days after a window was smashed at Pizza Pita in Décarie Square and following two suspected arson attacks at Mimimelon, a kosher bakery in St-Laurent.

Joseph Cohen, the owner of Schnitzel, which serves everything from schnitzel sandwiches and homemade soups to fresh pastries and traditional Shabbat dinners, said someone shattered the restaurant's glass door and stole between $700 and $800 in cash, along with personal receipts.

It's the second time the restaurant had been damaged in recent months. An earlier attempt to break through its front window was unsuccessful.

“We are truly just devastated that this is happening to all these Jewish-owned businesses,” Cohen told The Gazette. “Really sad!”

Asked whether the break-in was motivated by antisemitism: “I don't necessarily believe it was directed. But it's been happening to a lot of them recently. We work in a very popular area for cafés and food places. Why us?”

Mouna Sougratti, a Montreal police spokesperson, confirmed officers were investigating the break-in but said no arrests had yet been made.

The hate-crimes unit was not involved in the investigation at present, though that could change if evidence emerged, she said.

Police have also not established an antisemitic motive in Monday's vandalism at Pizza Pita. Its owner, Uri Peretz, told The Gazette on Tuesday that there was no evidence to suggest his restaurant had been targeted because it was Jewish-owned.

The two suspected arson attacks at Mimimelon are being investigated with the involvement of the police hate-crimes unit.

Cohen said nobody was injured in the latest break-in and that the restaurant remained open.

“We are thankful nothing else was damaged,” he said.

stories.title: Joly didn't meet with Roshel before deal signed with Stellantis: minister's office
stories.summary: A spokesperson for Joly's office said the industry minister took part in discussions between Stellantis and Unifor to find a way forward after the company decided to move production previously earmarked for the Brampton plant to the United States.
stories.author: Sammy Hudes The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s office is disputing media reports that characterized the federal government as having played an active role in negotiations that led to automaker Stellantis selling its Brampton, Ont. assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Mathis Denis, a spokesperson for Joly’s office, said Wednesday evening that reporting that Joly “was involved in the deal is false.”

“The minister had no part in negotiating with Stellantis or Roshel on the deal,” he said.

“The minister was in a conflict resolution (role) between Stellantis and the union. That’s it. The minister didn’t meet Roshel.”

Denis said the minister took part in discussions between Stellantis and Unifor, which represents more than 9,000 Canadian workers for the automaker, to find a way forward after the company decided to move production previously earmarked for the Brampton plant to the United States.

Company says it will repay government its ‘retooling’ money, but Unifor says deal betrays its workers with an ‘underhanded deal to sell the plant

He said the move, announced in October 2025, was in violation of Stellantis’ commitments to Ottawa tied to a federal commitment of up to $529 million through the Strategic Response Fund (SRF).

“Reporting that the minister was involved in the (Roshel) deal is false because the minister, the department and the team would have never approved or agreed to a deal that, first, did not honour their commitment under the SRF, but, second, lacked the union’s approval,” said Denis.

“We have already made it clear to Stellantis that if they were going to move forward with a sale or a deal ... that did not honour their commitment under the SRF, we would use the tools at our disposal to respond.”

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said that selling the Brampton plant “violates the obligations that Stellantis has under several agreements,” as he called the move “unacceptable.”

“But to be more fundamental, it’s a betrayal of the workers as it is a betrayal of the obligations to Canada and by extension to all Canadians,” Carney said.

Later that day, CTV News reported — citing three unnamed sources with “direct knowledge” of the talks between Stellantis and Roshel — that Ottawa “was actively and intensively part” of those discussions. The news outlet reported that the federal government engaged “directly” with both companies, knew the terms surrounding the sale and “did not stand in the way of it.”

CBC News also reported the federal government was aware for months about the possibility that Stellantis would sell the facility to Roshel and that it was “engaged regularly” since August.

Stellantis announced the sale of the facility and associated equipment to Roshel for an undisclosed amount late Monday afternoon. The companies say they expect the transaction to close by the end of this year, however it is subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov has said his Brampton-based company is willing to hire back some of the 2,000 Stellantis employees who were laid off from the plant when it halted operations in 2023.

The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before Stellantis paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

Joly is set to convene a meeting Thursday in Toronto with the leadership of Stellantis and Unifor, along with Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli.

“This is not the outcome we wanted and we have no choice but to find Stellantis in default of their obligation,” said Denis.

With files from Alessia Passafiume in Ottawa

stories.title: In Wainwright, Remembrance Day takes a new meaning in the wake of tragedy
stories.summary: Weeks after four soldiers were killed in the CFB Wainwright fire, the community gathered to honour Canada’s veterans and fallen troops
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
As the sun began to shine in Wainwright, melting away frost on the face of the Memorial Clock Tower, members of the local Legion walked down the Alberta town’s main street on Wednesday to lay a wreath at the base of the monument that commemorates fallen soldiers.

Just weeks earlier, flowers of all colours were placed on the same cenotaph to honour the four military members who died, and dozens more injured, during the Oct. 17 fire at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright. It was one of Canada’s worst peacetime tragedies on home soil, bringing new meaning to Remembrance Day this year.

The community, still trying to make sense of the devastating event, showed up in droves to ceremonies hosted by the local branch of the Royal Canadian Legion, where military and political dignitaries offered their condolences to the affected families and wished the injured a swift recovery.

Alberta Senator Scott Tannas, at the Wainwright Legion where a large Canadian flag at half-mast flapped in the wind, said Remembrance Day is a time to commemorate those who made the ultimate sacrifice in wars and conflicts of the past. But he said there was a deeper poignancy in Wainwright this year.

“The grief you carry is not found only in history books or memorials. It’s personal, it’s recent,” he said.

“We remember those who served Canada and did not return home from battlefields far away and we remember those very close to home whose lives ended too soon, whose service to Canada was cut short and whose memory remains close to our hearts.”

The small Prairie town of Wainwright and the Canadian military have a rich history stretching back nearly a century. In 1940, an army training camp was established just outside of town under a wartime order, eventually evolving to what is known today as CFB Wainwright.

With no more than a kilometre between the base and the town, the lives of soldiers and civilians have been intrinsically woven together, making the October fire a shared tragedy. On Wednesday, some people let tears fall down their cheeks as speakers honoured the young men killed last month: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , whose federal riding covers Wainwright, spoke about meeting Pte. Goulding and other young soldiers in the summer. He said they were in the prime of their lives – rambunctious, excited and strong – and chose bravely to serve their country.

Mr. Poilievre said he has heard stories about firefighters running into the flames on Oct. 17, of nurses and doctors who worked around the clock to help burn victims and of soldiers peeling off the scorched uniforms of their wounded friends.

“We imagine hell as a ball of flames, which means that these men literally went to hell and back to save their brothers and sisters in harm’s way,” he said.

Scattered on tables inside the Legion were Remembrance Day-themed postcards with handwritten messages from kids at Wainwright High School.

English teacher Mary Claire Belanger said her Grade 7 students have been penning such cards annually for seven years but that the messages have evolved from generic thank-yous to more thoughtful notes, especially after the recent tragedy.

She said her students, many of whom have close ties to the military, wrote their cards after watching community members line the roads in a Highway of Heroes-style vigil after the fire. This helped the kids “take it more to heart,” said Ms. Belanger.

One card read: “As a Canadian, I acknowledge the sacrifices you all made to make this country free and safe. When I’m older, I would love to follow your footsteps and serve this country.”

On the military base, charred ground stretches into the horizon, a scar left behind by the smouldering grass fire that transformed into a wind-whipped “wall of flame ,” overwhelming soldiers from The Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry last month.

Within minutes, the local hospital became a scene of horrors and heroism as staff worked to stabilize and treat soldiers with severe burns and other critical wounds. More than half of the 39 soldiers who were injured still remain in hospital .

Several people laid flowers and wreaths at the cenotaph in Wainwright, Alta., ON Remembrance Day. Some said the day was different this year as they paid their respects to the four so…

Prime Minister Mark Carney , who was in Ottawa on Wednesday, said in a statement that Canada will remember the four soldiers who died at CFB Wainwright.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” he said.

Inside Wainwright’s Peace Memorial Multiplex, residents filled the circular arena to pay respect to Canada’s fallen soldiers, watching as red poppies were pinned to a cross covered in white fabric, which said, “Lest we forget,” as the names of fallen soldiers echoed in the rink.

CFB Wainwright Base Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Dustin MacLeod, speaking to the crowd, said the recent losses have deeply affected the military base and surrounding community but also revealed acts of “extraordinary compassion and generosity.”

“You have reminded us that service and care are not exclusive to any particular uniform and that the strength of community is most evident in how it comes together during difficult times,” he said.

“As we remember those who have given their lives, let us recognize that their legacy lives on in the values we uphold, the choices we make and, most importantly, how we care for one another.”

Steps down the road, a symbol of the community coming together was outside for all to see.

Days after the fatal blaze, Chelsey McBride went into a wooded area near her home to cut down limbs and branches from trees, taking “from Mother Nature for what it took from the fire.”

She then hand wired each piece of greenery to a metal mannequin to form a dress and train before meticulously covering it with roughly 250 red silk poppies. Attached to a black bow that drapes across the skirt are also four white flowers, one each for the soldiers killed on Oct. 17.

The figure, which Ms. McBride calls “Poppy,” is displayed outside of her shop, the Wainwright Flower Cart. She says it is a symbol of remembrance, love and the lives that will not be forgotten.

Holding back tears on Tuesday, Ms. McBride said the fire has rattled the close-knit community, especially those who saw firsthand the horrific injuries suffered by soldiers. She said many questions must still be answered surrounding the tragic event.

There are multiple investigations under way into the fire, including by Alberta’s Chief Medical Examiner and the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service, a military police unit.
paragraphs: As the sun began to shine in Wainwright, melting away frost on the face of the Memorial Clock Tower, members of the local Legion walked down the Alberta town’s main street on Wednesday to lay a wreath at the base of the monument that commemorates fallen soldiers.

Just weeks earlier, flowers of all colours were placed on the same cenotaph to honour the four military members who died, and dozens more injured, during the Oct. 17 fire at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright. It was one of Canada’s worst peacetime tragedies on home soil, bringing new meaning to Remembrance Day this year.

The community, still trying to make sense of the devastating event, showed up in droves to ceremonies hosted by the local branch of the Royal Canadian Legion, where military and political dignitaries offered their condolences to the affected families and wished the injured a swift recovery.

Alberta Senator Scott Tannas, at the Wainwright Legion where a large Canadian flag at half-mast flapped in the wind, said Remembrance Day is a time to commemorate those who made the ultimate sacrifice in wars and conflicts of the past. But he said there was a deeper poignancy in Wainwright this year.
“The grief you carry is not found only in history books or memorials. It’s personal, it’s recent,” he said.

“We remember those who served Canada and did not return home from battlefields far away and we remember those very close to home whose lives ended too soon, whose service to Canada was cut short and whose memory remains close to our hearts.”

The small Prairie town of Wainwright and the Canadian military have a rich history stretching back nearly a century. In 1940, an army training camp was established just outside of town under a wartime order, eventually evolving to what is known today as CFB Wainwright.

With no more than a kilometre between the base and the town, the lives of soldiers and civilians have been intrinsically woven together, making the October fire a shared tragedy. On Wednesday, some people let tears fall down their cheeks as speakers honoured the young men killed last month: Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre , whose federal riding covers Wainwright, spoke about meeting Pte. Goulding and other young soldiers in the summer. He said they were in the prime of their lives – rambunctious, excited and strong – and chose bravely to serve their country.

Mr. Poilievre said he has heard stories about firefighters running into the flames on Oct. 17, of nurses and doctors who worked around the clock to help burn victims and of soldiers peeling off the scorched uniforms of their wounded friends.
“We imagine hell as a ball of flames, which means that these men literally went to hell and back to save their brothers and sisters in harm’s way,” he said.
Scattered on tables inside the Legion were Remembrance Day-themed postcards with handwritten messages from kids at Wainwright High School.

English teacher Mary Claire Belanger said her Grade 7 students have been penning such cards annually for seven years but that the messages have evolved from generic thank-yous to more thoughtful notes, especially after the recent tragedy.

She said her students, many of whom have close ties to the military, wrote their cards after watching community members line the roads in a Highway of Heroes-style vigil after the fire. This helped the kids “take it more to heart,” said Ms. Belanger.
One card read: “As a Canadian, I acknowledge the sacrifices you all made to make this country free and safe. When I’m older, I would love to follow your footsteps and serve this country.”

On the military base, charred ground stretches into the horizon, a scar left behind by the smouldering grass fire that transformed into a wind-whipped “wall of flame ,” overwhelming soldiers from The Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry last month.

Within minutes, the local hospital became a scene of horrors and heroism as staff worked to stabilize and treat soldiers with severe burns and other critical wounds. More than half of the 39 soldiers who were injured still remain in hospital .
Several people laid flowers and wreaths at the cenotaph in Wainwright, Alta., ON Remembrance Day. Some said the day was different this year as they paid their respects to the four so…
Prime Minister Mark Carney , who was in Ottawa on Wednesday, said in a statement that Canada will remember the four soldiers who died at CFB Wainwright.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” he said.

Inside Wainwright’s Peace Memorial Multiplex, residents filled the circular arena to pay respect to Canada’s fallen soldiers, watching as red poppies were pinned to a cross covered in white fabric, which said, “Lest we forget,” as the names of fallen soldiers echoed in the rink.

CFB Wainwright Base Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Dustin MacLeod, speaking to the crowd, said the recent losses have deeply affected the military base and surrounding community but also revealed acts of “extraordinary compassion and generosity.”
“You have reminded us that service and care are not exclusive to any particular uniform and that the strength of community is most evident in how it comes together during difficult times,” he said.
“As we remember those who have given their lives, let us recognize that their legacy lives on in the values we uphold, the choices we make and, most importantly, how we care for one another.”
Steps down the road, a symbol of the community coming together was outside for all to see.
Days after the fatal blaze, Chelsey McBride went into a wooded area near her home to cut down limbs and branches from trees, taking “from Mother Nature for what it took from the fire.”

She then hand wired each piece of greenery to a metal mannequin to form a dress and train before meticulously covering it with roughly 250 red silk poppies. Attached to a black bow that drapes across the skirt are also four white flowers, one each for the soldiers killed on Oct. 17.
The figure, which Ms. McBride calls “Poppy,” is displayed outside of her shop, the Wainwright Flower Cart. She says it is a symbol of remembrance, love and the lives that will not be forgotten.

Holding back tears on Tuesday, Ms. McBride said the fire has rattled the close-knit community, especially those who saw firsthand the horrific injuries suffered by soldiers. She said many questions must still be answered surrounding the tragic event.
There are multiple investigations under way into the fire, including by Alberta’s Chief Medical Examiner and the Canadian Forces National Investigation Service, a military police unit.

stories.title: Sale of Brampton auto plant from Stellantis to Roshel leaves laid-off workers in the lurch
stories.summary: Unifor chairperson says news has devastated employees, 3,000 of whom were sent home when Stellantis idled the plant in 2023
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Ardis Snow stands on the windswept sidewalk in Brampton, Ont., outside the Stellantis NV Stla-N auto plant and points to the weeds poking through the cracks in the employee parking lot, empty since late 2023.

That’s when the automaker idled the plant and sent almost 3,000 employees home to wait out a retooling that was expected to take 22 months.

Almost three years later, nothing has changed, and everything has changed.

The assembly line remains silent and the workers are still on layoff. But Stellantis has shifted production of the vehicle planned for the plant to Illinois and sold the plant to a defence contractor, ending 40 years of automaking at the factory northwest of Toronto.

Mr. Snow, a 38-year Stellantis employee and the plant’s Unifor chairperson, said the news was devastating for the workers who have been waiting to return to their jobs. They face financial hardship and mental-health challenges and, in some cases, have sold their houses and moved.

“They just want to come back to work,” Mr. Snow said at a coffee shop near the plant.

Stellantis, maker of Chrysler, Ram, Fiat and several other brands, closed the plant in late 2023 to retool the assembly line for the Jeep Compass. But after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed tariffs of 25-per-cent on Canadian-made cars in 2025, Stellantis halted the work before moving the Jeep Compass, to Belvidere, Ill.

The sale of the plant to Roshel Inc. , announced this week, angered the union and federal politicians, who said the carmaker violated terms of the agreement that gave the company taxpayer money to work on the plant.

Stellantis said this week it has offered to return the undisclosed amount of money. Stellantis’s global operations are struggling to make a profit amid weak sales, a move away from EVs and overcapacity at its manufacturing sites.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly’s spokesman, Mathis Denis, said the government has been negotiating with Stellantis for a year, but has determined the carmaker has violated the terms of the agreement that allowed it to tap taxpayers’ money for the retool of the plant.

Details of the funding arrangement are confidential. The federal government gave as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor, Ont., according to the 2022 agreement obtained by The Globe and Mail.

“The minister believes that Stellantis is no longer acting in good faith to address the breach of their agreement and advance the resolution process,” Mr. Denis told The Globe on Wednesday. “This is not the outcome we wanted, and we have no choice but find Stellantis in default of their obligation.”

Stellantis did not respond to a request for comment.

Ms. Joly will convene a meeting in Toronto on Thursday with Unifor, Stellantis and Ontario government officials.

About 2,200 Stellantis employees remain on layoff, receiving what amounts to about 70 per cent of what they would make in a 40-hour week, Mr. Snow said. Also gone is overtime pay, a regular income supplement at a plant with a 300-day backlog.

In the Greater Toronto Area, the money laid-off workers are paid doesn’t go far, he said, and many have moved to more affordable regions, some as far away as New Brunswick.

“Our members are struggling,” Mr. Snow said. “I’ve cried with my members. I’ve cried for my members.”

Some of those who have tried to find new jobs are offered work that pays $25 an hour, compared to the $45 they made at Stellantis, he said. Others see a path to a full pension disappearing.

“There is no way to replace these jobs,” Mr. Snow said. “Manufacturing is what makes the middle class. We’re just becoming a service-industry country.”

Brampton-based Roshel, which has factories in several countries, says it will pursue defence and automotive contracts for the plant, using the existing assembly line and equipment. The plant could once again employ thousands, paying taxes and contributing to the economy with a buy-Canadian ethos, company owner Roman Shimonov told The Globe. He is pursuing the federal government’s light utility vehicle contract, worth $4.9-billion.

Mr. Snow said Roshel’s plants do not pay close to what Unifor members make at car plants, and he vowed to lead efforts to unionize any work force hired at the Brampton plant.

The 2.95-million-square-foot plant, built by American Motors Corp., sits on 269 acres. Stellantis, or Chrysler as it was then known, acquired the plant in 1987 when it bought AMC.

The Stellantis plant’s final products were the Dodge Charger and Challenger, muscle cars beloved by their owners. Mr. Snow said he would regularly arrange plant tours for the buyers, some of whom would fly in from the U.S. to watch their dream car being assembled.

Brampton employees knew they were making coveted cars and took great pride in the quality awards the plant received, he said.

“Our employees cared about the cars,” he said. “We were just so proud of what we built.”

Mr. Snow talks about the generosity and closeness of the employees – how they would collect donations at the plant gate for the family of a member who died too soon, or, say, had their home damaged in a storm.

Every Halloween, the women’s committee collects costumes and candy at the plant and takes them to a local women’s shelter, the temporary home for families and children who cannot trick or treat for safety reasons.

The costume collection and dropoff happened again a couple weeks ago, almost three years after the workers clocked out after what would be their final shift.

stories.title: High School Roundup: Okkerse wins cross country gold, Lady Panthers win field hockey silver, Trojans earn berth at Wossaa
stories.summary: Nash Okkerse is bringing another Ofsaa gold medal back to St. Thomas, Ont.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
Nash Okkerse is bringing another Ofsaa gold medal back to St. Thomas, Ont.

The grade 10 student at Parkside Collegiate capped off an amazing running season with a gold medal in the junior boys cross country race at Kivi Park in Sudbury, Ont.

He finished the five-kilometre race in just under 17 minutes, to win the provincial title for the second straight year. In 2025, Okkerse won the novice boys race by 12 seconds.

This time, he dominated the competition with a win by seven seconds in 16 minutes and 59.46 seconds.

This win capped off a massive year with three gold medals at Legion Nationals in Saskatchewan, two gold medals at the Ontario Summer Games, two first place finishes in Legion Provincials in Sudbury and the Jr. Boys Tvra Cross Country division to extend an 11-race win streak.

Lady Panthers win Ofsaa field hockey silver medal

The South Huron District High School (Shdhs) Lady Panthers from Exeter, Ont. are Ofsaa silver medallists in Girls Field Hockey.

The Panthers made it to the gold medal game in Milton, Ont. losing 2-1 to Westdale SS from Hamilton.

“Coming from a small town, it’s been very exciting and a great accomplishment for Grade 12,” said Mady Rader.

The Panthers finished 2-1 in the round robin portion of the tournament. The knocked off London Medway in the quarterfinals and then Bluevale CI from Waterloo to reach the championship game.

“Right from the get-go I could tell how well we were doing, you could tell how strong they were and worked together,” said Kim Campbell, a volunteer coach, and former player at Shdhs.

“We were a small roster of 14, so they were fatigued for sure at Ofsaa, but our goal was to get there and we did it, so we’re pretty proud of these girls.”

The only two losses the girls suffered all season were at Ofsaa, finishing with a 24-2 overall record.

“We came out strong for every game, of course we were nervous when they came in with their big buses and all their equipment and uniforms, absolutely, but we held to it and we didn’t let that bother us, so we came out strong,” said Campbelll, ON facing opponents from much larger cities.

“The coaching staff and the players are certainly proud to get the South Huron Panthers back on that map.”

Clarke Road Trojans win AA Girls Basketball; advance to Wossaa

The Clarke Road Trojans are headed back to the Wossaa tournament for the second straight year after winning the Tvra Senior Girls Basketball final 40-35 over John Paul II.

After losing 44-43 in the regular season to the same Jaguars, the Trojans got revenge Tuesday in the AA title game.

“I think it was pretty exciting on us like it was for most of us, it’s our last year,” said co-captain Sophie Herrera.

“A lot of us are grade 12 and just knowing that like it was our last year, especially because we played them a lot and we’re usually underdog in the season. Being able to go to Wossaa one last time and it’s our third time so it is just really nice for us.”

The atmosphere was electric with about 40 rowdy fans cheering on each set of bleachers.

“It was definitely a lot, and you just have to tune it out,” added Youden-Richard.

The Lucas Vikings are the Senior Boys AA Volleyball champions after a nail-biting three-set win over Oakridge. The Vikings won the grueling match 26-24, 25-21, 25-23 to advance to Wossaa.

Saunders defeated Mother Teresa in the third-place game.

The E.S. Monseigneur-Bruyere Pantheres won the Senior Girls A Basketball Championship with a 40-19 win over London Christian High School to advance to Wossaa.

The Senior Boys Football AA Final will have London South taking on St. Thomas Parkside Friday under the lights at 1Password Park in St. Thomas. The AAA semifinals Friday will pit Catholic Central against Lucas at 11 a.m. and Mother Teresa vs Oakridge at 2:15 p.m. at Citywide Field.

stories.title: London region has lowest living wage in Ontario, midwestern Ontario has 2nd highest
stories.summary: London-Elgin-Oxford can boast the lowest living wage in Ontario.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
London-Elgin-Oxford can boast the lowest living wage in Ontario.

The annual calculation of how much it takes an average Ontarian to earn each hour to cover their basic needs, shows a slight increase in living wages for every community in Ontario.

London and area was the lowest at $21.15/hour. Midwestern Ontario, including Huron, Perth, Bruce and Grey Counties has the second highest living wage in the province at $24.75.

The lack of less expensive, public transportation, considered one of the main reasons for the high number, according to researchers.

The Greater Toronto Area has the highest living wage, at $27.60.

stories.title: Sombre Remembrance Day in Wainwright as town honours soldiers killed in military training fire
stories.summary: Remembrance Day carried added significance in the Alberta town of Wainwright on Wednesday, as the community gathered to honour Canada’s fallen soldiers while mourning four military members killed in a training fire at a nearby Canadian Forces base last month.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Wainwright, Alta. - Remembrance Day carried added significance in the Alberta town of Wainwright on Wednesday, as the community gathered to honour Canada’s fallen soldiers while mourning four military members killed in a training fire at a nearby Canadian Forces Base last month.

The fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17 left dozens of soldiers injured. Twenty-one remain in hospital, including nine in critical condition.

The tragedy cast a shadow over Wednesday’s ceremony, where residents, veterans and military personnel gathered to pay their respects.

“Their loss has deeply affected this base and our entire community,” said Lt.-Col. Dustin MacLeod, base commander of CFB Wainwright.

Among those killed was 23-year-old Aidan Goulding.

His mother, Sonia Monk, spoke to CTV News on Wednesday about a photograph of her son shared by one of his close friends.

Monk said she became emotional after seeing the image.

“It was just such a beautiful photo. It looked like he was... like heaven was just behind him,” she said. “That picture is the most treasured picture that I have.”

Back in Wainwright, the military’s longstanding connection to the town made this year’s Remembrance Day particularly emotional.

“It’s a very large crowd today. And it’s very quiet because everyone is thinking about what happened,” said ceremony attendee Charlene Drever.

Wainwright acting deputy mayor Will Challenger said he hoped the ceremony would help the community heal.

“I’m hoping it brings some closure,” he said. “I’m really hoping, and I’m thinking this will maybe help bring some closure on some of the events that transpired.”

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was also among those attending the ceremony, laying a wreath at the cenotaph earlier in the day.

“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends,” Poilievre said.

For retired warrant officer Tim Franz, who lives in Wainwright, Remembrance Day also brings back painful memories of his own military service.

Franz served for more than 30 years, including a deployment to Afghanistan, where he helped carry the remains of fallen Canadian soldiers onto aircraft for their final journey home.

He offered condolences to the families affected by last month’s tragedy and encouraged injured soldiers to seek support.

“So sorry for your loss. Speedy recovery, and get the help you need early,” he said.

Franz became tearful as he reflected on the fallen soldiers he helped bring home.

“It’s bittersweet. I mean, not everybody could be standing here,” he said.

Following the ceremony, people continued to leave their poppies at the cenotaph, a small gesture honouring generations of fallen soldiers as Wainwright continues to grapple with the recent tragedy.

His mother, Sonia Monk, spoke to CTV News on Wednesday about a photograph of her son shared by one of his close friends.
Monk said she became emotional after seeing the image.
“It was just such a beautiful photo. It looked like he was... like heaven was just behind him,” she said. “That picture is the most treasured picture that I have.”
Back in Wainwright, the military’s longstanding connection to the town made this year’s Remembrance Day particularly emotional.
“It’s a very large crowd today. And it’s very quiet because everyone is thinking about what happened,” said ceremony attendee Charlene Drever.
Wainwright acting deputy mayor Will Challenger said he hoped the ceremony would help the community heal.
“I’m hoping it brings some closure,” he said. “I’m really hoping, and I’m thinking this will maybe help bring some closure on some of the events that transpired.”
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre was also among those attending the ceremony, laying a wreath at the cenotaph earlier in the day.
“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends,” Poilievre said.
For retired warrant officer Tim Franz, who lives in Wainwright, Remembrance Day also brings back painful memories of his own military service.
Franz served for more than 30 years, including a deployment to Afghanistan, where he helped carry the remains of fallen Canadian soldiers onto aircraft for their final journey home.
He offered condolences to the families affected by last month’s tragedy and encouraged injured soldiers to seek support.
“So sorry for your loss. Speedy recovery, and get the help you need early,” he said.
Franz became tearful as he reflected on the fallen soldiers he helped bring home.
“It’s bittersweet. I mean, not everybody could be standing here,” he said.
Following the ceremony, people continued to leave their poppies at the cenotaph, a small gesture honouring generations of fallen soldiers as Wainwright continues to grapple with the recent tragedy.

stories.title: Canada says Russian players with visas will still be barred from World Juniors
stories.summary: The statement appears to close the door on Russia's return to the world juniors after last month's court ruling that the Iihf must reinstate the country in international hockey.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says Russian hockey players will not be permitted to compete at next month’s world juniors championship in Alberta, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas.

A statement provided Wednesday by Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden says Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete.

There are Russians with valid visas playing in the Canadian Hockey League, the umbrella organization for the country’s three top major junior hockey leagues.

Russians and Belarusians were banned from the Chl’s import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year’s draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.

Wednesday’s statement appears to close the door on Russia’s return to the world juniors following last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that the International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf) must reinstate the country in international hockey.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the tournament at Norway’s expense.

Norway qualified for the tournament and has said it still hopes to compete.

The Iihf has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field. Its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams.

Hockey federations from several nations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to compete against Russian players.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes could not compete in Canada while representing their countries as long as the war continues.

0:55 Carney says Russia won’t be able to participate in World Juniors

The government’s earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, leaving open the question of whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.

Van Koeverden clarified Monday that the neutral designation applied to individual athletes, not teams.

The government said its position would not change as long as Russia continues its war in Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity.

The world junior championship begins Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

stories.title: Nuisance bear delays winter camping at national park
stories.summary: A bear that’s caused camping cancellations all year long at the Bruce Peninsula National Park has forced a delay in the start of winter camping at the popular park.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
A bear that’s caused camping cancellations all year long at the Bruce Peninsula National Park has forced a delay in the start of winter camping at the popular park.

Overnight camping has been closed at Cyprus Lake campground part of the Bruce Peninsula National Park since the end of August.

A bear that as officials say “lost it’s fear of humans” prompted the closure.

While officials are hoping that impending hibernation will help the bear situation, they’d decided to delay winter camping at the National Park until mid-December.

Park officials say they hope to re-open camping next summer, but will have to monitor the bear situation come springtime.

stories.summary: The federal government says Russian hockey players will not be permitted to compete at next month's world junior championship in Alberta, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The federal government says Russian hockey players will not be permitted to compete at next month’s world junior championship in Alberta, even if they already hold valid Canadian visas.

A statement provided Wednesday by Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden says Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada will take measures to individually assess and prevent Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials from entering Canada to compete.

Russians and Belarusians were banned from the Chl’s import draft from 2022-24 before being allowed back in. According to the CHL, Russia led this year’s draft with 32 of the 114 players selected.

Wednesday’s statement appears to close the door on Russia’s return to the world juniors following last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that the International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf) must reinstate the country in international hockey.

However, Russian sports broadcaster Match TV reported Wednesday that the country’s hockey federation has demanded the Iihf allow Russia to compete at the 2027 world junior hockey championship in Canada or move the tournament to another country. Citing an unnamed source, Match TV said the federation made the demand in a letter sent Tuesday to the Iihf.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the tournament at Norway’s expense.

Norway qualified for the tournament and has said it still hopes to compete.

The Iihf has not formally announced any changes to the tournament field. Its website continues to list Norway among the 10 participating teams.

Hockey federations from several nations, including Finland, Sweden, Czechia and Norway, have said their teams will refuse to compete against Russian players.

Russia and Belarus have been banned from international hockey competition since Russia invaded Ukraine with Belarusian assistance in 2022.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week that Russian and Belarusian athletes could not compete in Canada while representing their countries as long as the war continues.

The government’s earlier position allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals, leaving open the question of whether a Russian team could participate under a neutral designation.

Van Koeverden clarified Monday that the neutral designation applied to individual athletes, not teams.

The government said its position would not change as long as Russia continues its war in Ukraine with Belarus’s complicity.

The world junior championship begins Dec. 26 in Edmonton and Red Deer.

stories.title: Wainwright honours soldiers killed, injured in fire: ‘Tragedy befell this small town’
stories.summary: Hundreds gathered at the Wainwright arena for a Remembrance Day ceremony that hit closer to home for the central Alberta military community, still shaken from last month's tragedy.
stories.author: Bill Graveland
stories.content:
Hundreds in a hockey arena stood for a moment of silence before Rev. Mokwadi Basele led them in prayer.

His thoughts were of the four soldiers killed more than three weeks ago in a wind-propelled grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

“God, we come closer to home, we come to Wainwright, as we remember the tragedy that befell this small town,” said the minister with Grace United Church at Wednesday’s Remembrance Day service in the town southeast of Edmonton.

The minister also prayed for a quick recovery for the many others still in hospital with severe burns.

“We lift up those who were injured and all who continue to heal in hospitals and at home, as well as comrades from the base and friends who live with shock and grief.”

The four who died were honoured at ceremonies across Alberta and Canada.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the Oct. 17 blaze.

A few blocks from the Peace Memorial Multiplex, some left flowers and wreaths at the base of a historic, century-old fieldstone tower commemorating Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.

“We come every year,” said Wainwright resident Reimer Nielsen.

“This (Remembrance Day) is a little more sombre and more important to be here for the four.”

Veteran Sean Hansen said Remembrance Day is always special in the town, but it feels different this year because of the fire.

“Unfortunately, some paid with their lives and some are horribly scarred,” he said.

About 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training on Oct. 17, when a windstorm shot flames from a grass fire and onto the troops.

Another 39 soldiers were injured and 21 are still recovering in hospital, as of Nov. 5.

“These young people literally ran into balls of fire to save their brothers and sisters in arms,” federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said after attending the Wainwright ceremony.

He represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.

“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends, and there are dozens of others who recovering from the most horrendous wounds imaginable,” he said.

“Third-degree burns on 80 to 90 per cent of their bodies. We reflect on the courage of the people on that day.”

Northwest of Edmonton, at least 2,000 lined a road leading to the St. Albert Cenotaph, a war memorial for local soldiers who died in combat.

Roughly 300 members of the same regiment caught in the Wainwright fire marched to the site.

Farrell’s family was also there, and they laid a wreath in his honour.

1:44 Family of soldier burned at CFB Wainwright attends Remembrance Day ceremony

“We May not know much about the lives of the people who were recently killed or injured in Wainwright, yet each one of them lived and breathed among us,” Rev. Ken MacRae, a retired Armed Forces chaplain, told the crowd.

“They had or still have dreams of their own. They had or still have friends and family who love them.”

He said the names of the four killed in Wainwright are to be added to some cenotaphs and memorial sites across the country.

“God has not forgotten them, nor should any of us forget these individuals.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney, at a ceremony in Ottawa, honoured those in Wainwright.

He has called the deadly fire at the base one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Rabbi Idan Scher gave the benediction at the Ottawa service. He said Canadians united after the fire.

“Canadians lined up to donate blood, prepared meals for emergency crews, opened their homes and worked tirelessly to care for the injured,” Scher said.

“At a time when our world feels increasingly divided, these Canadians reminded us of what truly matters. They did not ask what their neighbours believed, where they came from, or whether they saw the world the same way.

“They simply asked, ‘How can I help?'”

2:26 Youth and victims of CFB Wainwright fire honoured at the Field of Crosses

The minister also prayed for a quick recovery for the many others still in hospital with severe burns.
“We lift up those who were injured and all who continue to heal in hospitals and at home, as well as comrades from the base and friends who live with shock and grief.”
The four who died were honoured at ceremonies across Alberta and Canada.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the Oct. 17 blaze.

A few blocks from the Peace Memorial Multiplex, some left flowers and wreaths at the base of a historic, century-old fieldstone tower commemorating Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.
“We come every year,” said Wainwright resident Reimer Nielsen.
“This (Remembrance Day) is a little more sombre and more important to be here for the four.”
Veteran Sean Hansen said Remembrance Day is always special in the town, but it feels different this year because of the fire.
“Unfortunately, some paid with their lives and some are horribly scarred,” he said.

About 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training on Oct. 17, when a windstorm shot flames from a grass fire and onto the troops.
Another 39 soldiers were injured and 21 are still recovering in hospital, as of Nov. 5.
“These young people literally ran into balls of fire to save their brothers and sisters in arms,” federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said after attending the Wainwright ceremony.
He represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.
“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends, and there are dozens of others who recovering from the most horrendous wounds imaginable,” he said.
“Third-degree burns on 80 to 90 per cent of their bodies. We reflect on the courage of the people on that day.”
Northwest of Edmonton, at least 2,000 lined a road leading to the St. Albert Cenotaph, a war memorial for local soldiers who died in combat.
Roughly 300 members of the same regiment caught in the Wainwright fire marched to the site.
Farrell’s family was also there, and they laid a wreath in his honour.

“We May not know much about the lives of the people who were recently killed or injured in Wainwright, yet each one of them lived and breathed among us,” Rev. Ken MacRae, a retired Armed Forces chaplain, told the crowd.
“They had or still have dreams of their own. They had or still have friends and family who love them.”
He said the names of the four killed in Wainwright are to be added to some cenotaphs and memorial sites across the country.
“God has not forgotten them, nor should any of us forget these individuals.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney, at a ceremony in Ottawa, honoured those in Wainwright.
He has called the deadly fire at the base one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.
Rabbi Idan Scher gave the benediction at the Ottawa service. He said Canadians united after the fire.
“Canadians lined up to donate blood, prepared meals for emergency crews, opened their homes and worked tirelessly to care for the injured,” Scher said.

“At a time when our world feels increasingly divided, these Canadians reminded us of what truly matters. They did not ask what their neighbours believed, where they came from, or whether they saw the world the same way.
“They simply asked, ‘How can I help?'”

stories.title: Childhood health issues led to a life in medicine for Paralympian Francine Lemire
stories.summary: Despite a leg amputation, she won Paralympic gold medals for Canada in cross-country skiing and became an award-winning family doctor, medical educator and global leader in her field
stories.author: Monte Stewart
stories.content:
When Francine Lemire was 11 years old, doctors amputated her left leg above the knee because of complications resulting from a benign tumour.

It was the last of many annual surgeries on the leg after its growth was stunted when she was a toddler. But she did not let the disability deter her from realizing big dreams.

She became a two-time Paralympian cross-country skier, competing at the Winter Paralympics in Innsbruck in 1984 and 1988, and winning a pair of gold medals.

Off the snow, she became an award-winning family doctor, medical educator and family-medicine leader, aiding Canadian and international doctors and health organizations. She was both the first woman and the first francophone to serve as CEO and executive director of the College of Family Physicians of Canada, a management position, after previously serving as its volunteer president. In 2023, she was named a member of the Order of Canada for her contributions to sport, medicine and her community.

Dr. Lemire died on Oct. 11 in Corner Brook, N.L., after a brief battle with ovarian cancer. She was 74.

“[Her disability] didn’t prevent her from doing anything,” said Dr. Sarah Funnell, the Cfpc’s current president.

Francine Lise Lemire was born in Montreal on Aug. 14, 1952. She was the only child of Robert Lemire, a grocery store owner, and Alice Lemire (née Jacob), who worked in the women’s clothing department at Eaton’s department store.

Doctors removed a tumour from Francine’s left knee when she was about three, but damage to the growth plate surrounding the knee inhibited the leg’s development, so as her other leg grew normally, the difference between the two legs increased.

She underwent years of bone-extension procedures and increasingly elevated shoes before doctors recommended amputation and a prosthesis to improve her mobility.

Francine’s health issues sparked her interest in family medicine and her desire to become a doctor. After taking her early schooling in French, she sought to learn English, so she studied medicine at McGill University. Her medical-school preceptor advised her to launch a family-medicine practice in either Newfoundland and Labrador or British Columbia. She knew a Newfoundland-based doctor and decided to do her residency in St. John’s. Her rotations took her to the emergency ward of Western Memorial Hospital, in Corner Brook, where she met cardiologist Jamie Graham, her future husband.

“I was taken with her right away,” Dr. Graham said. “My own first marriage was on the rocks and I was looking around [for a new relationship]. … The first time I met her, she told me about her problems with physical activity in her prosthesis. She said that she always wanted to learn skiing. That was my hobby. I’ve been skiing since the age of three. I was an instructor in cross-country skiing. I invited her to take a few lessons from me, which she started off in January of 1980.”

She learned to ski by holding onto a broomstick for support while Dr. Graham and his daughter, Jeri, held each end. Advancing quickly, Dr. Lemire soon excelled in competitions, winning several medals. One of Dr. Lemire’s coaches, Margaret (Muggs) Tibbo, also managed Canada’s disabled skiing team and invited her to a camp in Banff, Alta., where she improved her technique, earning a spot on the 1984 Canadian Paralympic team. She barely missed the medal podium, placing fourth in both of her disability classification’s five-kilometre and 10-kilometre events in Innsbruck. Four years later, again in Innsbruck, she captured Paralympic gold medals in the two events at the age of 36.

Later in 1988, Dr. Lemire was named Newfoundland’s female athlete of the year, topping disabled and able-bodied athletes alike. In 2014, she was inducted into the Cross Country Newfoundland and Labrador Hall of Fame

While operating a full-scope (i.e., birth-to-death) family practice between 1979 and 2002, she also served as an anesthetist and obstetrician, delivering approximately 1,500 babies.

Dr. Lemire served as the elected president of the Cfpc’s Newfoundland chapter from 1989 to 1990 and the group’s national president from 1998 to 1999.

During her two decades in Cfpc management, from 2002 to 2022, Dr. Lemire worked weekdays in Mississauga, Ont., at the headquarters of the 47,000-member organization, returning to Corner Brook on weekends. During her first decade as membership director, she also supervised family-medicine residents at Toronto Western Hospital. From 1997 to 2003, she oversaw a Memorial University program that assessed and provided clinical training to internationally educated physicians preparing to practise in Canada. She served on the World Organization of Family Doctors (Wonca) board from 2010 to 2013, joined several committees from 2018 to 2020 and chaired its membership and voting task force from 2023 to 2024.

“Family medicine has lost a leader and we will miss her voice deeply,” said Harris Lygidakis, CEO of Wonca in a tribute issued by the organization.

Dr. Lemire also wrote a column in the medical journal Canadian Family Physician (2013 to 2022). She served as Cfpc’s top executive during this same period, and her accomplishments include spearheading the creation of the Besrour Centre for Global Family Medicine, a hub based at the organization’s headquarters in Mississauga; changing Cfpc’s governance model; and heading its charitable foundation, for which she raised millions of dollars.

Dr. Lemire also oversaw Canadian family-physician certification, a role that became particularly challenging for the Cfpc during the COVID-19 outbreak.

With in-person gatherings restricted, the college had to find alternative ways to examine 4,100 medical residents and osteopaths who were already Cfpc members and eligible to practise family medicine while ensuring they met its rigorous standards.

“Francine led the organization to quickly pivot to have the examinations be held in different ways through virtual platforms,” Dr. Funnell said. “It was a big shift.”

In March 2021, Dr. Lemire spoke out against racism in family medicine at a federal online anti-racism town hall convened after the death of Joyce Echaquan, a 37-year-old Atikamekw woman who was verbally abused by hospital staff and denied appropriate care before dying in a Montreal-area hospital in 2020. A Quebec coroner subsequently concluded that racism and prejudice contributed to her death, which could have been prevented with proper assessment and monitoring.

Dr. Funnell, a Kingston, Ont.-based family doctor and member of the Kitigan Zibi First Nation, greatly appreciated Dr. Lemire’s invitation to speak with her at the town hall.

In September 2021, Dr. Lemire co-authored an article in Canadian Family Physician acknowledging that Cfpc had engaged in systemic racism. The Cfpc also updated its action plan to integrate Indigenous health and cultural safety into family-medicine residency-training standards and help racialized-group leaders address systemic racism in areas where the college has responsibility and influence.

As a leader, Dr. Lemire was collaborative and decisive, said Dr. Funnell. As a teacher and family doctor, Dr. Lemire was kind, caring and compassionate, according to former colleagues and patients who posted online tributes to her.

“She was an incredible mentor,” wrote McMaster University medical professor Lynda Redwood-Campbell on LinkedIn. “She believed in us when we didn’t believe in ourselves.”

Former patient Catherine Meaney appreciated the way Dr. Lemire was “completely interested” in what she had to say every time she saw her.

“Just as I turned 18, I started to become very ill. She followed me intently and was always available to see me when an episode would take place. Her follow-up with tests and procedures was always prompt and I always knew she was in my corner,” Ms. Meaney wrote in a tribute on the Fillatre’s Funeral Homes’ webpage containing Dr. Lemire’s death notice. “Five months later, I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease. She saw me regularly and ensured I got what I needed. I think of her often as she was always there for me, especially at a very scary time in my life. I’ll never forget her.”

After retiring from the Cfpc in 2022, Dr. Lemire served as a Newfoundland and Labrador Health Services trustee and chaired its Western regional health council. She also sat on the boards of Canadian Doctors for Medicare, Vision Loss Rehabilitation Canada and the Canadian Alliance of Physiotherapy Regulators, while advocating for better eldercare and more health human resources before parliamentary committees.

Dr. Lemire remained active in cross-country skiing, coaching young skiers with disabilities, serving on Cross Country NL’s board and volunteering at events. She also oversaw medical services at the 1999 Canada Winter Games in Corner Brook.

In retirement, Dr. Lemire remained an avid swimmer, enjoyed time at her family’s cottage near Parry Sound, Ont., and continued to entertain family and friends with dinners and wine tastings, indulging her long-time passion for cooking.

She and Dr. Graham, 86, also cross-country skied in Norway, Sweden, northern Italy, Alberta, B.C., and New Hampshire, in addition to paddling a canoe and kayak in waterways located across Canada while he maintained his cardiology work before retiring in September.

“Toward the end, we were skiing 800 kilometres a year,” Dr. Graham said.

Dr. Lemire died through Medical Assistance in Dying (Maid) in Western Memorial Regional Hospital’s palliative-care unit 27 days after receiving her diagnosis of inoperable cancer. As her symptoms rapidly worsened, the procedure date was moved up twice. Prolonging the inevitable “felt useless,” Dr. Graham said.

“She just didn’t have anything to live for,” he said. “All the family were around, so it would have been what she would call a good death. She was always interested in having a good death. She didn’t want to be suffering for months.”

Dr. Lemire leaves her husband of 42 years, Jamie Graham; stepchildren, Jeri, Philip and Ian Graham; cousin, Nancy Dessureault; and step-grandchildren, Sarah Graham, Graham Zilkowsky and James Graham.

Dr. Funnell said Dr. Lemire lived and died the same way – with great determination. “[She was] very determined to make decisions for herself – even in death.”

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com .

She served on the World Organization of Family Doctors (Wonca) board from 2010 to 2013, joined several committees from 2018 to 2020 and chaired its membership and voting task force from 2023 to 2024.
“Family medicine has lost a leader and we will miss her voice deeply,” said Harris Lygidakis, CEO of Wonca in a tribute issued by the organization.

Dr. Lemire also wrote a column in the medical journal Canadian Family Physician (2013 to 2022). She served as Cfpc’s top executive during this same period, and her accomplishments include spearheading the creation of the Besrour Centre for Global Family Medicine, a hub based at the organization’s headquarters in Mississauga; changing Cfpc’s governance model; and heading its charitable foundation, for which she raised millions of dollars.
Dr. Lemire also oversaw Canadian family-physician certification, a role that became particularly challenging for the Cfpc during the COVID-19 outbreak.

With in-person gatherings restricted, the college had to find alternative ways to examine 4,100 medical residents and osteopaths who were already Cfpc members and eligible to practise family medicine while ensuring they met its rigorous standards.
“Francine led the organization to quickly pivot to have the examinations be held in different ways through virtual platforms,” Dr. Funnell said. “It was a big shift.”

In March 2021, Dr. Lemire spoke out against racism in family medicine at a federal online anti-racism town hall convened after the death of Joyce Echaquan, a 37-year-old Atikamekw woman who was verbally abused by hospital staff and denied appropriate care before dying in a Montreal-area hospital in 2020. A Quebec coroner subsequently concluded that racism and prejudice contributed to her death, which could have been prevented with proper assessment and monitoring.
Dr. Funnell, a Kingston, Ont.-based family doctor and member of the Kitigan Zibi First Nation, greatly appreciated Dr. Lemire’s invitation to speak with her at the town hall.

In September 2021, Dr. Lemire co-authored an article in Canadian Family Physician acknowledging that Cfpc had engaged in systemic racism. The Cfpc also updated its action plan to integrate Indigenous health and cultural safety into family-medicine residency-training standards and help racialized-group leaders address systemic racism in areas where the college has responsibility and influence.

As a leader, Dr. Lemire was collaborative and decisive, said Dr. Funnell. As a teacher and family doctor, Dr. Lemire was kind, caring and compassionate, according to former colleagues and patients who posted online tributes to her.
“She was an incredible mentor,” wrote McMaster University medical professor Lynda Redwood-Campbell on LinkedIn. “She believed in us when we didn’t believe in ourselves.”
Former patient Catherine Meaney appreciated the way Dr. Lemire was “completely interested” in what she had to say every time she saw her.

“Just as I turned 18, I started to become very ill. She followed me intently and was always available to see me when an episode would take place. Her follow-up with tests and procedures was always prompt and I always knew she was in my corner,” Ms. Meaney wrote in a tribute on the Fillatre’s Funeral Homes’ webpage containing Dr. Lemire’s death notice. “Five months later, I was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease. She saw me regularly and ensured I got what I needed. I think of her often as she was always there for me, especially at a very scary time in my life. I’ll never forget her.”

After retiring from the Cfpc in 2022, Dr. Lemire served as a Newfoundland and Labrador Health Services trustee and chaired its Western regional health council. She also sat on the boards of Canadian Doctors for Medicare, Vision Loss Rehabilitation Canada and the Canadian Alliance of Physiotherapy Regulators, while advocating for better eldercare and more health human resources before parliamentary committees.

Dr. Lemire remained active in cross-country skiing, coaching young skiers with disabilities, serving on Cross Country NL’s board and volunteering at events. She also oversaw medical services at the 1999 Canada Winter Games in Corner Brook.

In retirement, Dr. Lemire remained an avid swimmer, enjoyed time at her family’s cottage near Parry Sound, Ont., and continued to entertain family and friends with dinners and wine tastings, indulging her long-time passion for cooking.

She and Dr. Graham, 86, also cross-country skied in Norway, Sweden, northern Italy, Alberta, B.C., and New Hampshire, in addition to paddling a canoe and kayak in waterways located across Canada while he maintained his cardiology work before retiring in September.
“Toward the end, we were skiing 800 kilometres a year,” Dr. Graham said.

Dr. Lemire died through Medical Assistance in Dying (Maid) in Western Memorial Regional Hospital’s palliative-care unit 27 days after receiving her diagnosis of inoperable cancer. As her symptoms rapidly worsened, the procedure date was moved up twice. Prolonging the inevitable “felt useless,” Dr. Graham said.

“She just didn’t have anything to live for,” he said. “All the family were around, so it would have been what she would call a good death. She was always interested in having a good death. She didn’t want to be suffering for months.”
Dr. Lemire leaves her husband of 42 years, Jamie Graham; stepchildren, Jeri, Philip and Ian Graham; cousin, Nancy Dessureault; and step-grandchildren, Sarah Graham, Graham Zilkowsky and James Graham.
Dr. Funnell said Dr. Lemire lived and died the same way – with great determination. “[She was] very determined to make decisions for herself – even in death.”

content_blocks.text: Francine Lise Lemire was born in Montreal on Aug. 14, 1952. She was the only child of Robert Lemire, a grocery store owner, and Alice Lemire (née Jacob), who worked in the women’s clothing department at Eaton’s department store.

content_blocks.text: Doctors removed a tumour from Francine’s left knee when she was about three, but damage to the growth plate surrounding the knee inhibited the leg’s development, so as her other leg grew normally, the difference between the two legs increased.

content_blocks.text: She underwent years of bone-extension procedures and increasingly elevated shoes before doctors recommended amputation and a prosthesis to improve her mobility.

content_blocks.text: Francine’s health issues sparked her interest in family medicine and her desire to become a doctor. After taking her early schooling in French, she sought to learn English, so she studied medicine at McGill University. Her medical-school preceptor advised her to launch a family-medicine practice in either Newfoundland and Labrador or British Columbia. She knew a Newfoundland-based doctor and decided to do her residency in St. John’s. Her rotations took her to the emergency ward of Western Memorial Hospital, in Corner Brook, where she met cardiologist Jamie Graham, her future husband.

I invited her to take a few lessons from me, which she started off in January of 1980.”

One of Dr. Lemire’s coaches, Margaret (Muggs) Tibbo, also managed Canada’s disabled skiing team and invited her to a camp in Banff, Alta., where she improved her technique, earning a spot on the 1984 Canadian Paralympic team. stories.title: Remembrance Day ceremony in New Ross steeped in military tradition
stories.summary: About 300 people gathered around what's considered Nova Scotia's oldest cenotaph this Remembrance Day to pay tribute to the men and women who served and died in the line of duty.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Ella Macdonald
stories.content:
About 300 people gathered around what’s considered Nova Scotia’s oldest cenotaph this Remembrance Day to pay tribute to the men and women who served and died in the line of duty.

The ceremony was hosted by Royal Canadian Legion Branch 79.

“We like to call it the best little legion in New Ross,” said Ron Langevin, the branch’s services officer.

“New Ross was formed by the military, by Captain Ross. And we have a long history of military right from the Louis Riel uprising to the Boer War and so on. So New Ross has a very strong military presence and we take it very seriously.”

The base stones for the cenotaph were placed at the village crossroads in 1917, and the original monument was erected to honour soldiers who served in the First World War. Later additions were made to honour Second World War veterans.

Langevin said the cenotaph originally sat at the centre of town in a roundabout but it was struck a few times by vehicles.

“So the town people decided they wanted to move it to a different area. Unfortunately, the World War II veterans didn’t agree with that, so in the middle of the night, a group of them hooked up a bulldozer, put a chain around it and dragged it up to the Legion and since that day, we have been the caretakers of the monument,” he said.

Over the years, pieces have been replaced but the message at the structure’s core remains the same: ‘Lest we forget.’

Community members laid wreaths Wednesday at that cenotaph, honouring the sacrifices made both past and present.

At 11 a.m., attendees observed a moment of silence. Then, they held an extra minute of silence in honour of the four soldiers killed during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17.

“Recently our nation lost four soldiers who were training in Wainwright, Alberta,” said Master of Ceremonies Keith Carter during the ceremony.

“I would like an additional minute at this time to recognize the sacrifice that all of our Canadian forces members make, every day they go to work. Even here on Canadian soil, as they train to serve their duties overseas and around the world.”

When asked how he reflects this Remembrance Day, Langevin said his thoughts are “all-encompassing.”

“I’m looking at the veterans that are still serving today. I reflect on the sacrifices of the fallen. But then I look at the families who lost their loved ones, the mothers, the fathers, the brothers, and the sisters. So I try to take it all in,” he said.
