stories.title: Hamilton police looking for three suspects in home invasion
stories.summary: Police say officers responded to the home invasion on Weathering Heights in the Stoney Creek Mountain neighbourhood shortly before 2 a.m.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
By Staff The Canadian Press

Posted November 11, 2026 4:47 pm

Updated November 11, 2026 5:52 pm

Hamilton police say they are looking for three suspects after a home invasion in the city early this morning.

Police say officers responded to the home invasion on Weathering Heights in the Stoney Creek Mountain neighbourhood shortly before 2 a.m.

They say three male suspects forced their way in and assaulted three occupants before fleeing the area in a black Honda Civic.

Police say the victims sustained non-life-threatening injuries and they were taken to hospital.

They say the motive behind the home invasion is unknown.

Police are asking anyone with information to contact them.

stories.title: What a solo production of Shakespeare’s Macbeth can teach us about the perils of AI
stories.summary: Evan Buliung stars in an AI-inspired take on the Bard’s tragedy at Crow’s Theatre
stories.author: Aisling Murphy
stories.content:
In the age of artificial intelligence, what’s left for live theatre to tell us about ourselves that we can’t discover faster elsewhere?

This month, two artists at Crow’s Theatre in Toronto hope to answer that question with the words of the playwright they know best: William Shakespeare. In their one-act spin on Macbeth , actor Evan Buliung and director Christopher Manousos (also the associate artistic director of Crow’s) comment on the enticing promise of artificial intelligence by reimagining Shakespeare’s witches as sycophantic chatbots – all without altering a single line of the original play. (The only changes to Shakespeare’s text are cuts for length.)

In the lead-up to Macbeth ’s opening night on Nov. 11, The Globe and Mail spoke with Buliung and Manousos, the production’s co-creators, to discuss the increasingly complex relationship between theatre and AI – and why, no matter the technological landscape, our culture will never stop coming back to Shakespeare.

How and when did the idea for this production come together?

Evan Buliung: I had been interested in directing a production of Macbeth , and I was in a position where I had to very quickly pitch how I would do it, with the witches as AI agents. I cut the script down to one act. But I was interested in this idea of influence. I was watching a lot of true crime – a lot of stuff about Jodi Hildebrandt in the U.S. – and thinking about her influence, and the crimes that were committed because of it. How does influence spiral out of control?

I eventually brought it to Crow’s and was teamed up with Christopher – I had seen his Measure for Measure and thought his aesthetic would be perfect for this. My only condition after that was that we had to have sound designer Thomas Ryder Payne. He’s the best in the business. When we heard his first test run of what he thought would work for the witches, it really illuminated what we were doing, and we went from there.

The conceit of the production brings to mind news stories in which AI chatbots allegedly encouraged users to take their own lives. Can you talk about how the darker side of AI might fit into the existing narrative of Macbeth ?

EB: There’s certainly that mental health angle in the original play. One of my favourite lines in the play is from Lady Macbeth: “Thou wouldst be great, Art not without ambition, but without the illness should attend it.” What she’s saying is that she understands the nature of what a person needs in order to achieve the power they want to achieve. We see it in politicians: The vast majority of them are narcissistic monsters.

Christopher Manousos: The mental health aspect, I think, comes as a byproduct of searching for a place in the world, and searching for companionship. You can ask these things: Where do I fit in the world? How do I move ahead? How do I get what I want? For people who are isolated and don’t feel like they have access to community, to people, to friends, to intimacy, they start to look for that through AI agents, and build personal relationships with them. Through the pursuit of humanity is how so much of that humanity gets lost.

There’s a trope in modern productions of Shakespeare’s work in which directors will say, “It’s Shakespeare, but it’s _,” and add some gimmick to make a play newly relevant. Why isn’t that what’s happening here? Why is Macbeth the scaffolding that’s needed to tell this particular story?

CM: I’ve been watching and reading a lot of plays lately that are trying to be of the moment of AI, that are trying to be in the dialogue of what’s happening right now, but because that technology is moving at such a velocity, those plays feel behind the moment.

In this piece, we’re not chasing something that’s happening right now. We’re looking at these human relationships and letting this thing speak for itself. We then get to draw our own mirror, and give a lot of autonomy to the audience to draw their own parallels.

EB: I love Shakespeare. It’s my bread and butter. I teach it. I love the universality of it and playing with the line between masculine and feminine, especially in a play like Macbeth . Of course, I didn’t really like Shakespeare when I was young – none of us do. But if I saw something like this when I was younger, I might have identified with it, that modern sort of invitation.

Can you talk more about navigating the line between masculine and feminine in Shakespeare’s work?

EB: We keep shifting ground on that. I’ve played women before – playing Titania in A Midsummer Night’s Dream was the first time I went, ‘Oh, wow, this is what you guys have to deal with.’ It was quite an eye-opening experience, being drugged, all those things that happen to Titania in that play.

The tricky thing with Macbeth , and having done it a few times, is trying to contain those multitudes. I’m trying to find a reasoning behind Lady Macbeth’s descent into evil, in a way. I think sometimes we want to make her more of a compassionate character, but then I come back to true crime, to people such as Fred and Rose West . Is Lady Macbeth having a mental health crisis? Or is she just a bad apple? It’s really been a fine balance trying to navigate that world.

CM: When [artistic director Chris Abraham] and I were talking about programming this play, we discussed whether this would be a three-hander, a two-hander or a solo. The deciding factor was that Evan plays women really well – there’s a thoughtfulness and rigour there. We knew he’d have it in the bag.

It seems that theatre and AI ought to be incompatible – they exist at the extremes of human and non-human ways of interacting with the world. How do you see these forms of expression informing each other as technology continues to evolve?

CM: We talk about this lots in rehearsal – I’m really hoping we see theatre have this kind of glorious golden age. Theatre works most successfully when people feel like they’re gathered together, experiencing something as a unit. At its most successful, theatre generates passion, and a sense of life, and a sense of singular personhood within a greater society. I think good theatre will continue to acknowledge that, even if AI is involved. But if AI is involved, it has to be without disrupting that golden thread of what theatre is at its core. I think audiences are smart enough to feel that disruption.

EB: I’ve been thinking a lot about Station Eleven. That book was so influential on me – this idea that, when the world ends, the things that surface are classical music and Shakespeare. Those things are distillations of the truest human connection. No matter what, there’s an analogue aspect that the theatre will always have to hold onto in order to be successful.

I’m trying to find a reasoning behind Lady Macbeth’s descent into evil, in a way. I think sometimes we want to make her more of a compassionate character, but then I come back to true crime, to people such as Fred and Rose West . Is Lady Macbeth having a mental health crisis? Or is she just a bad apple? It’s really been a fine balance trying to navigate that world.

content_blocks.text: CM: We talk about this lots in rehearsal – I’m really hoping we see theatre have this kind of glorious golden age. Theatre works most successfully when people feel like they’re gathered together, experiencing something as a unit. At its most successful, theatre generates passion, and a sense of life, and a sense of singular personhood within a greater society. I think good theatre will continue to acknowledge that, even if AI is involved. But if AI is involved, it has to be without disrupting that golden thread of what theatre is at its core. I think audiences are smart enough to feel that disruption.

stories.title: Fanshawe dedicated new memorial in recently named ‘Valour Court’
stories.summary: Hundreds of Fanshawe's staff and students gathered at the school's newly named "Valour Court" Wednesday...
stories.author: Samantha Luis
stories.content:
Hundreds of Fanshawe’s staff and students gathered at the school’s newly named “Valour Court” Wednesday, to show gratitude to veterans at a Remembrance Day ceremony.

A new memorial in the courtyard outside D Building has been designated as a place of reflection to honour Canada’s service members. Fanshawe’s Poppy Project and Veterans Affairs Canada’s Commemoration Program funded the memorial.

Several speakers at the ceremony asked attendees to honour those who made the ultimate sacrifice and veterans who fought in the military.

Reservist Andrew Malison, career consultant for Fanshawe’s military-connected students (Credit: Owen Schuller/ XFM News)

“I think of my father, who also served albeit in the British military. I think of everyone that has served, everyone that has given a part of themselves to our country or countries, and I do that with great gratitude,” said Peter Devlin, president of Fanshawe College.

The designation of Valour Court is the latest initiative related to making Fanshawe a military-connected school.

Peter Devlin, Fanshawe President (Credit: Owen Schuller/ XFM News)

“Remembrance day is a very delicate topic. A strict focus on those who chose to serve and made the ultimate sacrifice, and those who continue to serve and make that sacrifice,” said reservist Andrew Malison, career consultant for Fanshawe’s military-connected students.

Terry Kelly, Juno Canadian award-winning music artist performed his heart-warming piece; A Pittance of Time and Safe Home.

Private Benjamin Gyorkos a student in the paramedic program, read the poem In Flanders Fields

Fanshawe TV live streamed the ceremony at: Live — Fanshawe TV

stories.title: Thousands gather at Remembrance Day ceremony held at Victoria Park
stories.summary: Thousands of Londoners gathered Wednesday at Victoria Park to remember those who served for Canada. The...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Thousands of Londoners gathered Wednesday at Victoria Park to remember those who served for Canada.

The Remembrance Day ceremonies began with a March from the Delta Armouries hotel on Dundas Street to the Cenotaph on Dufferin Street. Opening remarks started at 10:45 a.m., followed by O Canada, then the last post.

RCMP officers March down Dufferin Street after the ceremony on Nov, 11. Callum Contursi/XFM News .

Despite the large crowds, one could hear a pin drop during the two minutes of silence.

Shawn Irvine from CTV News was the Master of Ceremony and Col. Right Reverend Nigel Shaw was the Parade Chaplain.

The Salvation Army Jubilee Brass conducted by bandmaster David Rosell and the Catholic Central Chamber Choir conducted by Shannon Swain provided the music for the ceremony.

The event finished with Mayor Josh Morgan, Police Chief Thai Truong and several other politicians and officials laying wreaths.

The parade, including motorists, cadets, veterans and RCMP officers marched back down Dufferin Street with bagpipes playing in the background.

Those who attended the ceremony took photos with the wreaths in front of the Cenotaph after the ceremony.

stories.title: Saskatoon police officer seriously injured after being hit by vehicle
stories.summary: The Saskatoon Police Service has confirmed to Global News that an officer is seriously injured after being hit by a vehicle in a construction zone on Circle Drive.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A member of the Saskatoon Police Service was hit by a vehicle while conducting traffic enforcement on Circle Drive on Wednesday afternoon, police have confirmed to Global News.

The collision occurred Wednesday around 1:15 p.m. while the officer conducted traffic enforcement in the southbound lanes along a construction zone on Circle Drive near the 108th Street overpass. The speed limit in that area is 60 km/h.

The officer was taken to hospital with serious injuries, according to police.

The vehicle’s driver was not injured and remained at the scene.

Circle Drive East was closed in the southbound lanes from Attridge Drive to College Drive as of 2:30 p.m. Traffic was rerouted onto 108th Street for detours to allow the police collision analyst unit to investigate.

stories.title: Vancouver Island war museum closing as visitors drop — but staff not giving up hope
stories.summary: 'Until about two years ago, we had no idea that we would be in this situation,' Lewis Bartholomew, founder and executive director of the Hmcs Alberni museum, told Global News.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
A museum on Vancouver Island to honour ship crew members who lost their lives during the Second World War is marking its final operating day on Nov. 11.

The Hmcs Alberni Museum and Memorial in Courtenay pays tribute to the 59 men who died when their warship, the Corvette Hmcs Alberni, was sunk off the coast of England during the Second World War.

But now, the museum says it has to close after years of declining visits and revenue.

“Until about two years ago, we had no idea that we would be in this situation,” Lewis Bartholomew, founder and executive director of the museum, told Global News.

“We’ve been in similar situations in the past when, for instance, a landlord would want our space and then we’d have to scramble for a new space — but we always knew that we would open if we moved to somewhere else.”

Bartholomew said the museum has faced a lot of challenges over the years, but has managed to survive them all.

“We’ve had three flash floods in this building that have closed us down for short terms,” he said.

“We’ve had two arson attacks against us here. We survived through the COVID pandemic. We’ve also survived moving probably 18 times since 2012 for various reasons.

“But this one here sort of came out of the blue for us. We weren’t expecting the new changes to have affected us so much.”

The museum is located inside a small mall on Cliffe Avenue, next to the Connect Temporary Shelter and Service Hub.

The building that was leased from the city was intended as a temporary space for the area’s homeless population, but that was six years ago.

The museum operators say they know there is a need for housing, but the expectation when Connect moved in was that it would be there for six to 12 months before a new location would be found.

1:57 Vancouver Island war museum moving due to shelter

Bartholomew said the museum dropped from 6,000 to 7,000 visitors per year to only 759 visitors last year and the majority of their income comes from donations.

“Two years ago, the board saw the writing on the wall, that the three of us that work here or volunteer here could not keep paying the bills out of our own pocket,” he said.

“And so plans were made originally to completely liquidate, which really hurt me personally because this is my child, I guess you would call it. And then we realized that we could not possibly close completely.

“First of all, we’re an official Canadian Veterans Memorial for the crew who served on Hmcs Alberni. The other thing is that over the years, people have families that have entrusted us with their own family’s personal history, with their personal remembrances that they have that they’ve wanted to make public.”

Bartholomew said the museum has so many artifacts that mean so much to many families that they didn’t want to pass them on to another museum or a private collector.

So they are giving themselves at least two years to restructure and reevaluate their programs, including for veterans and children, and to convert exhibits into portable ones to tour museums and other festivals on Vancouver Island.

“We just won’t have a physical presence for a while,” Bartholomew said.

He added the community has always stepped up to help in times of need, but they would require more funding from a foundation or an individual benefactor to secure a permanent location.

Bartholomew said the museum will be open until sunset on Remembrance Day.

“We’ll start our ceremony of bells of peace and that will start right about 5:30 in our hallway, of which we will ring the bell 100 times, naming off a random list of names, veterans, and we’ll also allow members of the public who are attending this to ring the bell for themselves for their own particular loved ones,” he added.

stories.title: ‘A lasting way to recognize’: Program honours 305 Canadians for service
stories.summary: A new program is recognizing the more than 300 veterans, military spouses and RCMP members who live in All Seniors Care Living Centres Canada-wide.
stories.author: Tavi Dhillon
stories.content:
A new program is recognizing more than 300 Canadian veterans, military spouses and retired RCMP members who are living in care facilities for older adults.

Dubbed “The Proud 305” by All Seniors Care Living Centres, the initiative honours veterans, spouses of Canadian Armed Forces members and RCMP workers who live in its homes. The company said the project title comes from the fact that there are 305 people being recognized in 2026 — the program’s inaugural year.

All Seniors Care Living Centres operates across Canada, with locations in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec.

David Rosnar was one of the people honoured. He served as an army reserve lieutenant in the early 1960s.

“We have freedoms now. We can walk the streets and not have to worry about things. And I used to wear my poppy more than one day because I thought we shouldn’t just remember these things (for) one day,” Rosnar told Global News.

He, along with the hundreds of others being recognized this year, is among the people the organization is calling The Proud 305’s “founding members.” That title can only be held by the people being honoured this year, the company said in a news release. Founding members each received a certificate.

On top of acknowledging the groups’ broader contributions to Canada, The Proud 305 also notes the impacts they had on the communities they lived in.

In Rosnar’s case, he used to be a teacher. Among the lessons his students learned was the importance of remembrance, he said.

All Seniors Care Living Centres is a division of Castle Living Group. Lily Goodman, CEO of Castle Living Group, said that the founding members “represent an extraordinary legacy of service, sacrifice, courage and resilience.”

“We wanted to create something that goes beyond an annual day of remembrance – a lasting way to recognize the people among us who have served our country and supported those who did,” Goodman added in the news release.

stories.title: Muskoka regional chair ‘deeply disappointed’ after being ousted by Ford government
stories.summary: Muskoka’s outgoing regional chair says he’s “deeply disappointed” after the Ford government ousted him from the role in favour of Scott Aitchison, a current Conservative MP who plans to step away from Parliament Hill. Jeff Lehman, the former Mayor of Barrie who was elected as the regional council chair in December 2022, found himself out...
stories.author: Colin D'Mello, Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
Muskoka’s outgoing regional chair says he’s “deeply disappointed” after the Ford government ousted him from the role in favour of Scott Aitchison, a current Conservative MP who plans to step away from Parliament Hill.

Jeff Lehman, the former Mayor of Barrie who was elected as the regional council chair in December 2022, found himself out of a job after Premier Doug Ford unveiled hand-picked eight appointees who would serve as the heads of upper tier councils.

In a social media post, Lehman said he “pursued” the appointment as part of the province’s application process and was backed by fellow council members and “many voices in Muskoka” who advocated for a term extension.

Ultimately, the government said it chose a candidate who “brings a deep understanding of their municipalities and a proven record of performance and public service.”

Lehman, however, defended his record over the past four years and pushed back on the process.

“The District has delivered a 3x increase in the amount of affordable housing built in Muskoka, faster paramedics, more child care, less garbage, and better roads – all while delivering the second-lowest tax increase of the regional municipalities in Ontario,” Lehman said in the post.

Lehman, who has been affiliated with the Ontario Liberal Party, also called out the politics of “partisanship [and] patronage.”

“There is no Conservative or Liberal way to snowplow a road, build a home, or treat drinking water. Heads of Council should always be selected by their communities and their local elected representatives,” he said.

The Ford government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo and also extended an existing power to appoint the chairs in Niagara, Peel and York Regions.

The regional chairs will also get so-called strong chair powers, including to appoint or fire the chief administrative officer and division heads, direct staff, veto certain bylaws and propose the municipal budget.

Critics have slammed the Ford government this week, particularly for its appointment of Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca as the Chair of York Region, stating that it’s a conflict of interest.

Aitchison is a Conservative MP for Parry Sound-Muskoka, but said he plans to step down in November and will be sworn in as chair of the District of Muskoka on Dec 1.

Global News has reached out to Lehman for comment.

stories.title: Pilot dead after plane in Remembrance Day ceremony crashes in Quebec
stories.summary: The pilot, a man in his 60s, was preparing to land when the plane crashed and caught fire near the airport in Saint-Georges
stories.author: Maura Forrest
stories.content:
A Remembrance Day ceremony south of Quebec City ended in tragedy Wednesday when a pilot died in a small plane crash after taking part in an aerial salute.

The plane went down after completing a flypast with five other aircraft, part of an annual tradition in Saint-Georges, a small city about 100 kilometres from the provincial capital.

The victim, a man in his 60s, was part of a group of local pilots who perform the same aerial formation every year, said Mayor Manon Bougie.

“It’s terrible,” she said. “Remembrance Day will never be the same for us.”

Ms. Bougie said a small crowd had assembled for the ceremony, and watched as the six planes flew past. They performed the Missing Man formation, in which one aircraft pulls away from the others, leaving a gap to commemorate fallen soldiers.

Everything seemed normal at the time, Ms. Bougie said. But shortly afterward, emergency vehicles started driving past in the direction of the airport.

She later learned the plane had crashed as it was preparing to land, catching fire and sending up a column of smoke. She also learned the victim was the pilot who detached from the Missing Man formation. “It’s the height of irony,” she said.

Provincial police have not confirmed the identity of the pilot.

Yvon Thibodeau, a member of the Royal Canadian Legion who attended the ceremony, said the pilots are members of a local group called the Club Aéronautique de Beauce. He said it’s mostly the same pilots who perform the formation each year.

“They practise a lot in the summer,” he said. “You often see them going by.”

The Department of National Defence has confirmed that the plane did not belong to the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the pilot was not a member of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau, a spokesperson for the provincial police force, said the crash occurred in a wooded area near the airport at around 11 a.m., and the pilot was pronounced dead at the scene.

She said the pilot was alone in the plane and no one else was injured.

Mr. Thibodeau said the host of the event, a retired lieutenant-colonel who was one of the pilots in years past, received the news of the crash and shared it with the crowd.

“He started crying because it was one of his close friends,” Mr. Thibodeau said. “He broke down.”

Ms. Bougie said many of the people in attendance seemed to be in shock upon hearing the news. “There was definitely confusion,” she said. “The situation seemed unreal – it was impossible to imagine it happening.”

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon addressed the incident in a social media post, saying he is in contact with the province’s domestic security minister.

“I would like to offer my sincere condolences to his family and loved ones,” he said of the pilot.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said Wednesday afternoon that investigators were on their way to the site.

stories.title: Stopping GLP-1 drugs could increase heart attack risk for some, study says
stories.summary: The study showed those considered medically obese showed an even higher risk when they stopped using the drug, than those considered a normal weight.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
Stopping treatment of type 2 diabetes with GLP-1 weight loss medications May lead to a doubled risk of heart attack, stroke or death, a new study shows.

The study, published Monday in the Lancet Regional Health Europe, looked at more than 80,000 Italians with type 2 diabetes and no established heart disease. Data was collected between 2004 and 2024.

Researchers found four in every 100 of those people a year who stopped taking GLP-1 treatments had a non-fatal heart attack or stroke, or died, compared to about two in 100 of the people who stayed on the medication.

Those with a body mass index of 30 or more, people considered medically obese, also showed a higher risk among those who stopped treatment than those under that BMI range.

Of the more than 80,000 people who started GLP-1s, those who stayed on treatment did so for about three years. The group that did not stay on treatment, about 60 per cent, is reported to have stopped use after about one year.

But while the study raises questions about what factors could be behind that increase for some, researchers caution that as an observational study there are certain factors they couldn’t determine.

An analysis by the British Medical Journal notes the study could not determine if discontinuing GLP-1 drugs directly caused the increased risk, or if people who experienced a higher risk of health events were already in poorer health.

The BMJ also cautioned the study did not analyze why people stopped taking the drugs, such as potential gastrointestinal side effects, the high cost some drugs have, or potential illnesses. Some patients May have stopped because they were already in poor health, the journal added.

4:25 Ask an Expert: Maintaining your health on a GLP-1 medication

Dr. Christopher Labos, cardiologist and epidemiologist at McGill University, stressed the Lancet study compared two groups of diabetic patients.

“In one sense, what you’re saying is that these medications actually have a very clear cardiovascular benefit, which is known, and if you stop them, you don’t get that cardiovascular benefit,” Labos said.

Receive the latest medical news and health information delivered to you every Sunday.

Some previous studies have shown weight-loss drugs could lead to regaining weight when people stop using the medication.

A study published in the BMJ in January 2026 showed weight-loss drug users on average regain weight at a rate of 0.4 kilograms or 0.88 pounds per month after they stop. That study reviewed 63 trials covering more than 9,000 individuals up to February 2025.

Patients who went on the drugs then stopped them regained their entire baseline weight on average about 20 months after they stopped taking the medications.

Labos noted the Lancet study further underscores these are chronic medications for chronic conditions and should only be stopped due to issues such as side effects or ineffectiveness.

“If you’re stopping them just because you think they’ve worked and now you want to stop, number one, you are probably going to see a regain of the weight,” he said. “Number two, you’re putting yourself to an increased risk because you no longer are having the metabolic benefits that are coming from the weight loss and the cardiovascular protection that goes with it.”

The Lancet study says it only included a small group of semaglutide users, with most patients using liraglutide or dulaglutide: all of which are types of GLP-1 medications.

Tirzepatide, also known as Mounjaro for type 2 diabetes users and Zepbound for weight loss, was released after the period of the study and was not included.

Type 2 diabetes patients who stopped GLP-1 treatment found their weight, blood sugar concentrations and blood pressure changed “only modestly,” the study says. Similar amounts were seen in patients whether they went on to have a heart attack, stroke, or died.

6:50 Generic Ozempic arrives in Canada: How to know if it’s right for you

Researchers also cautioned the heightened risk of heart attack, stroke or death if you stop taking GLP-1s May not affect people without type 2 diabetes who take the drugs for weight loss or other conditions.

Further research is needed into whether stopping GLP-1 medications can directly cause increased cardiovascular risk or if it instead represents “a marker of higher underlying risk rather than a direct cause of adverse outcomes,” the study says.

The study should not be taken to imply the drugs are dangerous, instead Labos said people should understand it outlines how the GLP-1 medications should be taken.

“If the interpretation that you draw from this is that, oh, these medications are potentially dangerous I think that’s the wrong interpretation,” he said. “If the interpretation you draw from this is that you shouldn’t just be starting and stopping these medications on a whim, I think that’s the correct interpretation.”

stories.title: Molson, Coors Light and other beers recalled in Canada over metal pieces
stories.summary: Molson Canadian, Coors Light, Blue Moon and other popular beer brands are being recalled across Canada due to the presence of metal.
stories.author: Daniel Otis
stories.content:
Molson Canadian, Coors Light, Blue Moon and other popular beer brands are being recalled across Canada due to the presence of metal pieces.

According to a recall notice published by the Canadian Food Inspection Agency, the recall covers several alcoholic and non-alcoholic beers made by parent company Molson Canada 2005.

Impacted brands include Molson Canadian, Coors Light, Blue Moon, Hop Valley, Brasseur de Montréal, Black Horse and India Beer.

“Various brands of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer recalled due to pieces of metal,” the national recall notice warns. “Do not use, sell, serve or distribute the affected products,”

Molson Canada 2005 is the Canadian subsidiary of Molson Coors Beverage Company, which was formed in a 2005 merger between Coors, a U.S. company, and Molson, which was founded in Canada in 1786.

The affected products and formats are:

Black Horse Beer – 8 x 355 mL

Blue Moon Non-Alcoholic Belgian White Belgian-Style Wheat Ale Beer – 6 x 355 mL and 24 x 355 mL

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-Style Wheat Ale Beer – 24 x 355 mL

Blue Moon Light Citrus Wheat Beer with natural flavour – 12 x 355 mL

Blue Moon Belgian White Belgian-Style Wheat Ale Beer – 473 mL, 4 x 473 mL, 24 x 473 mL and 12 x 355 mL

Blue Moon Mango Wheat Beer with natural flavour – 473 mL, 4 x 473 mL and 24 x 473 mL

Brasseur de Montréal Neighbourhood’s Pick – 12 x 355 mL

Brasseur de Montréal Bonsecours Lager Light Beer – 4 x 473 mL and 12 x 355 mL

Brasseur de Montréal Normanville Hazy IPA Beer – 4 x 473 mL and 12 x 355 mL

Brasseur de Montréal Petite-Bourgogne Red Ale Beer – 12 x 355mL

Brasseur de Montréal Griffintown Blonde Ale Beer – 12 x 355mL

Coors Light – 8 x 355mL, 12 x 355 mL, 15 x 355mL and 24 x 355mL

Hop Valley Bubble Stash IPA Strong Beer – 12 x 355 mL

India Beer – 12 x 355 mL

Molson Canadian – 473 mL, 12 x 355mL, 15 x 355mL and 24 x 473 mL

For a full list of specific recalled product codes, read the Canadian Food Inspection Agency recall notice .

stories.title: Intimate partner violence up 15% over 8 years in Canada, StatCan says
stories.summary: Intimate partner violence rates are rising across the country, according to Statistics Canada, following an influx of what some experts are calling "anti-feminist backlash."
stories.author: Rachel Morgan
stories.content:
The average rate of intimate partner violence (IPV) across the country has risen for the eighth straight year, according to Statistics Canada, following a surge of what some experts are calling “anti-feminist backlash.”

Data released by the agency on Tuesday shows the average rate of police-reported intimate partner violence was two per cent higher in 2025 compared to 2024. The most recent numbers were up 15 per cent from 2018.

“We know things like IPV are chronically under-reported, so I’m not surprised that the numbers are rising,” said Kaitlynn Mendes, interim director of the Centre for Research and Education on Violence Against Women and Children at Western University.

She said movements like #MeToo and an increase in community support have sparked an increase in the number of victims coming forward. A greater understanding of what constitutes intimate partner violence, which Mendes said can include anything between physical, psychological, emotional or financial violence, could also be sparking this rise.

While it is hard to pinpoint whether the increases come from a rise in instances of violence or if the increased numbers represent more people coming forward to file police reports, Mendes said she wouldn’t be surprised if the increase reflects more cases, not just better reporting.

“We’re in this anti-feminist backlash, I would say. We have these influencers who are really promoting things like aggressiveness: ‘if you want to show that you’re like a real man, you do that by being really aggressive, being dominant,’” she said.

“I think that the numbers that we see from Statistics Canada, we should regard as the floor, not the ceiling,” she added. “It’s an underestimation.”

A rise in reports of intimate partner violence could also be linked to the ongoing socioeconomic climate, said Alexa Yakubovich, an associate professor in the department of community health and epidemiology at Dalhousie University.

The COVID-19 pandemic and the economic turmoil that followed created a “collision of factors” including inadequate housing, food insecurity, economic insecurity and unemployment, she said.

“All of that together increases the risk for intimate partner violence,” she added.

Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Quebec and Saskatchewan saw the rate drop between 2024 and 2025, but all saw a sizable increase over the eight-year period.

Records of intimate partner violence in 2025 were highest in the territories with rates three to 19 times higher than the national average. Rates in Manitoba and Saskatchewan were nearly two times the national average.

Mendes said one reason for these higher rates could be the number of communities that operate in isolation. Many remote communities do not have the same access to social supports, she said.

“There is also the issue of privacy in terms of it can be easier to commit because there aren’t potentially as many witnesses,” she added.

According to Statistics Canada, one in six Indigenous women have experienced at least one form of intimate partner violence. While Indigenous women account for just five percent of all women in Canada, federal data shows they made up approximately 26 per cent of all women killed by an intimate partner in 2022.

Yakubovich said while rural and remote communities have higher risk factors for bearing the brunt of violence, indicators for a wide range of gender-based violence are evident all across the country.

Nova Scotia was the first province to declare intimate partner violence an epidemic in 2024. New Brunswick followed suit in 2025 and Newfoundland and Labrador labelled it an epidemic in May.

There have been repeated calls in Ontario to make the same declaration.

But Yakubovich said a declaration alone will do nothing to stop epidemic levels of violence.

She said a declaration of an epidemic needs to come with funding “elevated to epidemic proportions” for community support services as well as the healthcare system.

“The most common formal service that is accessed by victims before they are killed is healthcare, whether we’re looking at mental health, hospitals, primary care, et cetera. So the health system plays a really important identification point that we might not ever have the opportunity to utilize otherwise,” she said. “So we need healthcare providers to be aware of the red flags for intimate partner violence.”

Mendes said there also needs to be greater awareness and education at the community level so people are not afraid to access help.

“Taking it seriously, I think that is the first step,” she said. “And then really trying to resist these narratives that are really prominent on social media about how women lie.”

“Because again, we know that there’s often shame, there’s stigma, there are real barriers to reaching out for help. And educating the community to help spot some signs and to be an upstander and to call it out, to break past those things.”

stories.title: Atlantic Canadian padres honour Wainwright soldiers in Remembrance Day speeches
stories.summary: Two padres in Atlantic Canada led their Remembrance Day speeches on Wednesday with reflections on the recent deadly fire at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Two padres in Atlantic Canada led their Remembrance Day speeches on Wednesday with reflections on the recent deadly fire at CFB Wainwright, in Alberta.

In downtown Halifax, Padre Steven Cochrane honoured Canadian Armed Forces members and the sacrifices they make during training exercises, pointing in particular to members in Wainwright.

Padre Stephen Courtney led his speech at the National War Memorial in St. John’s, N.L., with a reflection on the four soldiers killed in the fire, and the dozens of others who were hurt.

“We remember those who died, the injured, especially those who remain in hospital at this time,” Courtney said to a quiet crowd of hundreds. “We remember the families.”

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed at the Alberta training base last month when strong winds propelled a nearby grass fire across the training area.

Thirty-nine others were injured, and many are still recovering in hospital.

The weather indigital St. John’s on Wednesday was rainy and cold, but people packed the two downtown streets on either side of the National War Memorial, as well as the stairs connecting them. Bright red poppies stood out against the thick, dark jackets in the shoulder-to-shoulder crowds.

Newfoundland and Labrador is still marked by its deep military history. This year is the 110th anniversary of the Battle of Beaumont-Hamel, in the First World War, which saw hundreds of Royal Newfoundland Regiment soldiers mowed down by German fire.

Leo Knox and his family laid a wreath at the foot of the war memorial in honour of his father, Leo F. Knox, who was a gunner with the 166th Royal Newfoundland Field Artillery Regiment in the Second World War. Leo F. Knox died about five years ago, at the age of 93, and he was a well known and widely respected veteran in St. John’s.

Knox said he and his family promised his father they would lay a wreath for him every year at the war memorial. He was joined on Wednesday by several generations of the Knox family.

“Dad just passed away not too long ago and I still find it really tough, but the truth is that this is probably the most special, solemn day for us every year,” Knox said.

“It’s the one day of the year that I really like to do nothing except reflect on not only my dad, but all the other veterans,” he added. “I’m not for war, but the sacrifices they made for us are really appreciated. That’s why we do this every year.”

Remembrance Day ceremonies were scheduled across Atlantic Canada on Wednesday.

In Halifax, hundreds gathered at the Grand Parade downtown to bow their heads and honour those lost to battle.

“At the 11th hour of the 11th month, the 11th day, time stands still for a moment,” Padre Cochrane said. “We remember those who died not for war, but for a world that (would) be free and at peace.”

stories.title: Family of CFB Wainwright burn victim honour him at Remembrance Day in St. Albert
stories.summary: The wife and mom of Liam Ramage attended Remembrance Day on behalf of the soldier who has burns across 40 per cent of his body and is hospitalized in the University of Alberta ICU.
stories.author: Karen Bartko, Sarah Ryan
stories.content:
Families of soldiers injured at CFB Wainwright were amongst the hundreds of people gathered for a Remembrance Day ceremony in St. Albert to honour Canadian troops who have served and died for Canada.

The Ramage family was one of many that attended the ceremony in the bedroom community northwest of Edmonton.

Pte. Liam Ramage from Red Deer County suffered severe burns to 40 per cent of his body in the fire and remains in the University of Alberta Hospital.

He was amongst the roughly 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry based at CFB Edmonton who were taking part in attack training at CFB Wainwright in central Alberta on Oct. 17 when a windstorm sent flames from a grass fire onto the troops.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 more were injured. Many are still recovering in hospitals across Alberta, including in the province’s two highly specialized burn units.

Roughly 300 members of their regiment marched into the Remembrance Day service Wednesday morning in St. Albert, which is right next door to the Edmonton military base.

With a family history steeped in military service, Cheryl Ramage has always attended Remembrance Day ceremonies, but Wednesday’s gathering hit much closer to home this year.

Her son, Liam, suffered terrible injuries in the fire at CFB Wainwright. Covered in burns, he remains in the intensive care unit in critical, but stable condition.

Despite being seriously wounded himself, Liam was still trying to save his fellow soldiers when first responders arrived at the scene in Wainwright three weeks ago.

Liam was then rushed to Edmonton, where he was so badly injured his wife and mother had to identify him by his feet .

He suffered extensive burns to his face, head and neck. His family said both sides of his hands were in bad condition, and he was burnt on his arms, legs and some on his back as well.

The extent of his injuries forced doctors to make difficult decisions.

“He’s got lots of skin grafts, another surgery and unfortunately had partial and full amputations of all of his fingers,” Cheryl said.

After suffering a trio of strokes, the infantryman was paralyzed on one side and his family says he’s slowly regaining some movement.

The 27-year-old has been taken off a ventilator that had been sustaining him for nearly a month. Liam is now able to breathe on his own and has been speaking to his loved ones.

“He’s nonstop talking,” said his wife of three years, Marisa Ramage.

“I had a great conversation with him yesterday, it was great. It’s nice to be able to talk to him and have him answer me.”

Despite those developments, Marisa said her husband’s progress often feels like one step forward — five steps back.

His mother said as Liam regains consciousness, her son is in a lot of pain — crying out, despite painkillers and the best efforts of hospital staff.

His cries are horrible to hear, Cheryl said.

Pte. Ramage was supposed to have finished his weapons training at CFB Wainwright on Nov. 5 and Marisa said they’d planned to attend the St. Albert Remembrance Day ceremony together.

Instead, his loved ones gathered in St. Albert in his honour as he lies in a hospital bed, working on his recovery.

Ramage enlisted in the Canadian Armed Forces in 2024 after participating in cadets as a youth, where he advanced to the top as a regimental sergeant major.

Since joining the military two years ago, Ramage has served in Latvia and at the G7 gathering in Kananaskis, Alta.

The family is collecting donations in a GoFundMe campaign to help his loved ones remain by his side and fund his future rehabilitation.

The family is collecting donations in a GoFundMe campaign to help his loved ones remain by his side and fund his future rehabilitation.

Recell uses a small sample of a patient’s healthy skin to prepare a liquid mixture that is sprayed onto a burn wound

Veteran Shayne Jewitt stands with Royal Canadian Legion Pembroke Branch 72 president Stan Halliday at a candlelight vigil honouring the victims of the CFB Wainwright fire. (File photo)

November 11, 2026 at 1:32 p.m.

As Canada spends the day remembering the military sacrifices of past conflicts, soldiers injured in the CFB Wainwright fire in mid-October are benefiting from a new medical treatment not normally available in this country.

The treatment, known as Recell, uses a small sample of a patient’s healthy skin to prepare a liquid mixture known as an autologous skin cell suspension that is sprayed onto a burn wound.

“Because a small sample of skin can cover a much larger wound area, burn surgeons use Recell across a range of burns, including the face, hands and joints,” explains Andrea Sampson, spokesperson for Avita Medical, the treatment manufacturer.

Recell was approved for use in the U.S. back in 2018. But it is not commercially available in Canada, Sampson says.

However, she adds, Avita worked with Canadian clinicians and Health Canada to provide about three dozen Recell units through Health Canada’s special access program.

Avita also sent three of its people to burn centres in Calgary and Edmonton, where they began work within days and continued in the following weeks. “They remain available as needed,” Sampson says.

This medical aid came about as the result of a call from the American Burn Association to the Avita team, “who responded immediately to the request to support surgeons in Canada,” Sampson adds.

At present, there are 21 patients from the CFB Wainwright fire undergoing treatment in Alberta hospitals, Jennifer Vanderlan from Acute Care Alberta told National Post in an email. She added that “nine are in critical condition.”

Clinicians harvest a thin sample of the patient’s skin and process it in the Recell device to create spray-on skin cells. This procedure can be used alone or in combination with a skin graft.

Recell was designed to treat burns as well as trauma and surgical wounds, according to the manufacturer. It supports the regrowth of skin and minimizes the need for large skin grafts.

“One of (the) greatest challenges in treating very large burns is the shortage of healthy skin available for grafting,” says Dr. Alan Rogers, burn and plastic surgeon with Sunnybrook Hospital in Toronto, who has been involved in the medical response to the CFB Wainwright fire victims.

“Every area from which we harvest skin creates another wound that needs to heal. Techniques that allow us to cover more of the burn with less donor skin can therefore be particularly valuable.”

Rogers says that in “full-thickness burns, where the entire depth of the skin has been destroyed, it is used alongside skin grafts. Its principal contribution is to help achieve wound closure while reducing the amount of skin that must be harvested.”

Rogers notes that his colleagues, Dr. David Wallace and Dr. Stephanie Mason, used Recell during fellowships in the United States and bring first-hand experience of its application to Canada.

For him, “the broader message is that these developments are most valuable when incorporated into a carefully coordinated treatment plan: removing damaged tissue, preparing the wounds, conserving donor skin and supporting recovery through intensive care, meticulous nursing, nutrition and rehabilitation.

“In extensive burns, every centimetre of healthy skin matters. Recell offers another way to make that limited resource go further,” Rogers says.

Stewart Lewis is a writer and editor with National Post. A journalist and lawyer, he has worked in newspapers, radio and TV, and served a legal stint with Global Affairs Canada at the United Nations in New York City.

stories.title: Pilot of Quebec plane scheduled for Remembrance Day ceremony killed in crash
stories.summary: Police say there was only one person aboard the aircraft
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Remembrance Day ceremony south of Quebec City ended in tragedy Wednesday when a pilot died in a small plane crash after taking part in an aerial salute.

The plane went down after completing a flypast with five other aircraft, part of an annual tradition in Saint-Georges, a small city about 100 kilometres from the provincial capital.

The victim, a man in his 60s, was part of a group of local pilots who perform the same aerial formation every year, said Mayor Manon Bougie.

“It’s terrible,” she said. “Remembrance Day will never be the same for us.”

Ms. Bougie said a small crowd had assembled for the ceremony, and watched as the six planes flew past. They performed the Missing Man formation, in which one aircraft pulls away from the others, leaving a gap to commemorate fallen soldiers.

Everything seemed normal at the time, Ms. Bougie said. But shortly afterward, emergency vehicles started driving past in the direction of the airport.

She later learned the plane had crashed as it was preparing to land, catching fire and sending up a column of smoke. She also learned the victim was the pilot who detached from the Missing Man formation. “It’s the height of irony,” she said.

Provincial police have not confirmed the identity of the pilot.

Yvon Thibodeau, a member of the Royal Canadian Legion who attended the ceremony, said the pilots are members of a local group called the Club Aéronautique de Beauce. He said it’s mostly the same pilots who perform the formation each year.

“They practise a lot in the summer,” he said. “You often see them going by.”

The Department of National Defence has confirmed that the plane did not belong to the Royal Canadian Air Force, and the pilot was not a member of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau, a spokesperson for the provincial police force, said the crash occurred in a wooded area near the airport at around 11 a.m., and the pilot was pronounced dead at the scene.

She said the pilot was alone in the plane and no one else was injured.

Mr. Thibodeau said the host of the event, a retired lieutenant-colonel who was one of the pilots in years past, received the news of the crash and shared it with the crowd.

“He started crying because it was one of his close friends,” Mr. Thibodeau said. “He broke down.”

Ms. Bougie said many of the people in attendance seemed to be in shock upon hearing the news. “There was definitely confusion,” she said. “The situation seemed unreal – it was impossible to imagine it happening.”

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon addressed the incident in a social media post, saying he is in contact with the province’s domestic security minister.

“I would like to offer my sincere condolences to his family and loved ones,” he said of the pilot.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said Wednesday afternoon that investigators were on their way to the site.

stories.title: Pilot dead in crash near Quebec City involving plane intended for Remembrance Day ceremony: premier
stories.summary: The pilot of a plane that was intended for a Remembrance Day ceremony has died in a crash near Quebec City, according to the province’s premier. Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says the plan crashed in Saint-Georges, in the Beauce region, ON Wednesday morning. “I would like to extend my sincere condolences to their family and loved […]
stories.author: Kelsey Patterson
stories.content:
A pilot returning to the airport after participating in a Remembrance Day ceremony has died in a plane crash in a town south of Quebec City.

The small aircraft crashed into a wooded area near the airport in Saint-Georges, in Quebec’s Beauce region, around 11:01 a.m. Wednesday.

The pilot has been identified by the Sûreté du Québec as a man in his 60s who lived in the region. A spokesperson for the provincial police, Audrey-Anne Bilodeau, says he was the lone occupant of the plane and he was declared dead at the scene.

“What has just happened is truly sad and terrible,” said Saint-Georges Mayor Manon Bougie in a news release. “Our hearts go out to the family and loved ones affected by this tragedy. All our thoughts and prayers are with them at this time.”

The municipality of Saint-Georges says the crash appears to have happened while the pilot was preparing to land, and the plane reportedly caught fire upon impact.

Bilodeau says it is too early in the investigation to confirm those exact details.

“Regarding all the circumstances, whether it happened during landing or takeoff, there are many questions you might be asking,” Bilodeau told reporters. “Was there an operational error, or was there a mechanical failure in the aircraft? You will understand that the investigation will reveal this, working in conjunction with our partners at the Transportation Safety Board (TSB).”

The TSB indeed dispatched a team of investigators to the scene, which is about 100 kilometres south of Quebec City.

“Their expertise lies precisely in determining whether there was a breakage, a mechanical failure, or an operational error that could have led to a loss of control — resulting in the tragic outcome,” the SQ spokesperson said.

Bilodeau said the police force will speak to witnesses. She said she could not speak to the pilot’s level of experience.

Politicians across Quebec and the country extended their condolences to the pilot and his family.

In a post on X, Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said he is in contact with Quebec Domestic Security Minister Guy Jr. Lapointe “to obtain further details and to determine whether the Government of Quebec can provide any assistance.”

The leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, Charles Milliard, offered his condolences to the pilot’s family and loved ones. “My thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy,” he wrote on X.

At the federal level, Quebec lieutenant Joël Lightbound said: “On this day, as we pay tribute to those who have served us, my thoughts are with the pilot’s family, his loved ones, and the entire Beauce region.”

Federal Transport Minister Steven MacKinnon said he was saddened to hear of the pilot’s passing.

The leader of the Conservative Party of Canada, Pierre Poilievre, also expressed his sympathies. “Thank you to the courageous emergency responders who answered the call,” he said on X.

–With files from La Presse Canadienne

stories.title: Mortgage rules need to change for first-time home buyers, report says
stories.summary: A new report suggests specific policy changes could help many first-time home buyers who find it challenging to get into home ownership.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
Housing affordability continues to be a key issue for millions of Canadians, and a new report suggests specific policy changes could help many first-time home buyers get into home ownership.

The National Housing and Investment Initiative, a collaboration of members from some of Canada’s biggest banks and real estate groups, released its November report with several recommendations for what it says can help create a more sustainable housing market.

This comes as sales dwindle in some of Canada’s biggest markets, like Toronto , as prices remain high and available supply is falling behind demand.

But some experts are skeptical about the report’s proposed potential benefits outweighing the risks for the housing market and overall affordability.

“We have to ask, are there any risks coming from these recommendations that could undermine the other factors that are happening right now to put a downward pressure on home values, which is what we want to restore affordability over the medium and long term,” says Paul Kershaw, policy professor at the University of British Columbia and the founder of the advocacy think tank Generation Squeeze.

“Even if we implement most or all of these recommendations, we’re still not talking about restoring housing affordability throughout our housing market, our housing system for many, many years.”

These are the recommendations outlined in the report.

One of the report’s recommendations is to make it easier for young Canadian first-time home buyers to afford a down payment on newly constructed homes. This includes both by lowering the required down payment for first-time buyers and establishing an assistance program, like a low-interest loan, to help these potential buyers afford their down payment.

But making it easier for buyers to get into the housing market without increasing supply simultaneously can risk higher prices for homes in the long term.

The report says that by limiting these financial supports to new homes, it will avoid inflating the resale market.

“There’s a worry right now that we’re not getting enough of those newly built homes because there isn’t enough demand for them at their current price points,” says Kershaw.

“It worries me that that does risk refueling the housing market more generally, but because it is being honed in specifically on new builds, it might be the kind of thing that’s just like walking the tightrope carefully enough that it’s going to help us get more supply without over-fueling the inflation of the market more generally.”

Once a home-buyer has enough money for a down payment, they likely will still need a mortgage to finance the remaining balance on that home.

The report recommends refining mortgage stress tests — which require buyers to qualify at a higher mortgage rate than they May initially get — to allow for more nuance and flexibility.

For example, introducing a sliding qualifying rate based on the term of the mortgage or the type of buyer, and offering lower qualifying rates for both new builds and first-time buyers in general.

“Easing the stress test a little bit certainly allows first-time buyers to afford a little more,” says John Pasalis, real estate broker and president of Move Smartly Realty.

“In particular, if they’re going to relax it, for example, for new housing, it kind of makes it a little bit more affordable, drives more supply and kind of pushes buyers more into that market — that’s the segment that’s struggling.”

The report also recommends young Canadians and first-time buyers be able to write off some of their mortgage interest on newly built homes so they can more easily afford them. However, that tax break would be balanced by reducing the capital-gains tax exemption on primary residences if they sell and make a profit.

Builders have largely pulled back on construction plans in recent years mainly because of a combination of higher costs to build and a lack of private investment.

The report cites an RBC study from last year , which estimates Canada’s real estate market needs about $2 trillion of capital deployment over the next five years to meet the current need for affordable housing, which is about 3.5 million homes.

With condo construction, developers usually have to wait to sell the majority of units before building can commence, and although federal incentives are available for new construction, it is mainly geared towards purpose-built rentals and houses.

“If they only need to pre-sale 40 per cent of the units, that changes so much for them,” says Pasalis.

“They can build a lot faster. They can start building units that they believe the end user market needs upon completion rather than just waiting for investors to buy them.”

To entice the private sector into building more housing, the report calls for expanding federal financing measures to include qualifying condo projects, speeding up project approvals both at the federal and municipal level, and adjusting the foreign buyers’ ban to allow for more international investors.

The federal foreign home buyers ban expires on Jan. 1, 2027 , and Budget 2026 proposed extending this for two years but would also except newly built homes from the ban.

The report also recommends maintaining sustainable and predictable immigration targets and reforms that are conducive to growing the housing market.

High immigration levels can add to overall housing demand, which can lead to higher prices. At the same time, the report says that focused immigration policies can help ensure builders have enough of the skilled workers they need to get these projects built efficiently.

Finally, the report says that keeping accurate and consistent housing sector data is key to tracking progress, keeping all sides accountable and creating more predictability for both builders and buyers.

stories.title: Aircraft being used for Remembrance Day ceremony crashes in Quebec: premier
stories.summary: An aircraft that was being used for Remembrance Day ceremonies has crashed in Quebec, Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon says.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
The pilot of an aircraft that participated in a Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday died after it crashed near Saint-Georges, south of Quebec City, officials confirmed.

Quebec provincial police (SQ) said the crash happened at around 11 a.m. and there was only one person aboard the aircraft.

The pilot was declared dead at the scene. Police said there were no other victims.

The crash involved a small aircraft that had just participated in a Remembrance Day commemoration, the City of Saint-Georges said in a statement.

SQ spokesperson Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said the pilot had been flying with a group of other planes when his aircraft went down.

The small plane came down in a wooded area near the Saint-Georges airport and caught fire after the crash, the city said. The crash happened as the pilot was approaching the airport to land.

Police identified the victim as a man in his 60s who lived in the region.

Dominique Maheux, who lives near the Saint-Georges airport, said she looked outside after hearing the sound of planes flying by and saw one of them veer to the right before plunging toward the ground.

“I thought, ‘Where is it going?’” Maheux said. “Then it disappeared into the trees, and I saw a ball of fire, followed by black smoke.”

“It all happened in three seconds.”

“What happened is really sad and terrible,” Saint-Georges Mayor Manon Bougie said.

Beauce resident Mélanie Quirion said she saw six planes flying overhead at about 10:50 a.m., roughly 10 minutes before the crash. At that point, “everything seemed normal,” she said.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon offered his condolences following the crash.

“I have just learned of the death of the plane’s pilot,” St-Pierre Plamondon wrote on social media. “I would like to express my sincere condolences to their family and loved ones.”

St-Pierre Plamondon said he was working with the province’s domestic security minister to gather more information about what happened.

The Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) said Transportation Safety Board investigators have been deployed to the scene of the small aircraft accident to gather information and assess what happened.

CAF told Global News the aircraft did not belong to them and no Armed Forces personnel were involved.

“Our thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the pilot who tragically lost their life. We extend our deepest condolences to all those affected by this tragic incident,” the CAF said in a statement.

Federal National Defence Minister David McGuinty also issued a statement expressing his condolences to the pilot’s family and loved ones, saying his thoughts were with everyone affected by the tragedy.

The cause of the crash is not yet known.

Bilodeau said the SQ’s major crime unit was investigating the crash for any possible criminal elements, though she noted crashes such as this are rarely linked to a crime.

Saint-Georges is located roughly 100 kilometres southeast of Quebec City.

'There was some moments and some things that happened to my family that, for me, crossed the line '

Goaltender Connor Hellebuyck during a warm-up with his New Jersey Devils teammates at Canada Life Centre on Nov. 10, 2026 in Winnipeg. (Cameron Bartlett / Getty Images)

November 11, 2026 at 12:46 p.m.

Former Winnipeg Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has told reporters he had several reasons for wanting to leave the team where he’d played for more than a decade. But on Tuesday night he revealed that threats made against him and his family last season were the final straw.

As reported in the New York Times and elsewhere, Hellebuyck didn’t disclose the exact nature of the threats, but said: “There was some moments and some things that happened to my family that, for me, crossed the line and, as a husband and a father, I felt made that decision very certain.”

He added that he didn’t want to “ruin the relationship I have with the city,” but said: “There are a few moments that I don’t want to see happen again. It is more than just online death threats, and I’m going to ask you to respect my privacy and my family’s privacy. I won’t go deeper than that.” He and his wife have two young children.

In August, Hellebuyck revealed that he had requested a trade from the Jets “several months ago,” adding: “With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request.” He called the decision “the best path forward for me and my family.”

On Sept. 16, he was suspended by the Jets for failing to report to the team’s training camp. A fan website, hellebuck.com, was created to track the salary he was losing as a result. The suspension was slated to end on Oct. 23, but that was also the day he was drafted by the New Jersey Devils.

In a letter to Jets fans posted to Instagram this week, Hellebuyck said he would “always be grateful for the life my family and I built there and for the people who became such an important part of it.”

View this post on Instagram

He spoke fondly of the outdoor activities Manitoba offered, but added: “There were several things that went into the decision including some very challenging circumstances involving my family … We’ve chosen to keep those personal circumstances private, and I hope people can respect that.”

The 33-year-old, who was born near Detroit, Michigan, is a three-time winner of the Vezina Trophy (2019, 2023 and 2024), awarded to the best goalie in the NHL. He also won the Hart Trophy as the League’s most valuable player in 2024.

Hellebuyck would not say whether he believed the harassment his family received came from within the city.

“I feel like the media will probably eat me alive, regardless of what I say,” he said. “So, I feel like if I answer that question, it’s pitting someone against each other, and I don’t want this to be about that. I’ve made my decision. I’ve made it clear, and I’ve sacrificed a lot to live by that decision.”

Hellebuyck did not play in the Devils’ game against the Jets on Tuesday, though he said he wanted to. It’s the only matchup in Winnipeg between the two teams this year. They next meet at Prudential Center in New Jersey on Nov. 28. [](https://nationalpost.com/news/u-s-hockey-star-connor-hellebuyck-says-death-threats-motivated-trade-request-out-of-Canada/)

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: One airlifted with life-altering injuries after Perth East crash
stories.summary: Police said the collision involved a commercial motor vehicle and a passenger vehicle.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A person suffered serious injuries in a two-vehicle collision south of Milverton on Tuesday morning, provincial police say.

Members of the Perth County Ontario Provincial Police, the Perth East Fire Department and Perth County Emergency Medical Services responded to the crash at the intersection of Perth Line 55 and Perth Road 119 shortly before 9:30 a.m.

Police said the collision involved a commercial motor vehicle and a passenger vehicle.

The driver of the commercial vehicle was not injured. The driver of the passenger vehicle suffered serious, life-altering injuries and was airlifted by Ornge to a trauma centre.

Police are asking anyone with information or video footage related to the crash to contact the Perth County OPP.

stories.title: Sarnia police warn of targeted thefts of Toyota, Lexus vehicles
stories.summary: Investigators believe they are using sophisticated electronic methods that allow vehicles to be started and stolen within minutes.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The Sarnia Police Service is warning residents after several thefts and attempted thefts involving newer-model Toyota and Lexus vehicles over the past two nights.

Investigators believe the incidents are connected and that suspects are targeting specific Toyota and Lexus models. Police say the offenders appear to be organized, travelling to the community from outside the area and leaving shortly after stealing a vehicle.

According to police, the thieves are not relying on access to owners’ keys. Instead, investigators believe they are using sophisticated electronic methods that allow vehicles to be started and stolen within minutes.

Police are urging residents to take precautions to reduce the risk of theft, including parking vehicles in locked garages, using visible steering wheel locks, installing approved aftermarket immobilizers and parking another vehicle behind a targeted vehicle when at home.

Residents are also encouraged to park in well-lit areas, ensure home security cameras are functioning and keep keys and key fobs secured inside their homes.

Police are asking anyone who sees suspicious activity, including individuals checking vehicle doors or using electronic devices near parked vehicles, to report it immediately. Anyone witnessing a vehicle theft in progress is urged to call 911.

The Sarnia Police Service said it is actively investigating the thefts and attempted thefts and is working with other police services and law enforcement agencies to identify those responsible and prevent further incidents.

stories.title: Magna looks to grow faster than overall automotive market
stories.summary: Auto parts company eyes compounded adjusted-earnings-per-share growth of at least 15% through 2030
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Magna International Inc. MG-T says it’s aiming for compounded annual growth for its adjusted earnings per share of at least 15 per cent through 2030.

In releasing its latest financial targets, the auto parts company says it’s also looking for organic sales growth of 2 to 4 per cent above market on a compounded annual basis over the same time period.

Magna says the targets reflect a strategy to grow faster than the overall automotive market.

The company says the increase is expected to come from expanding its content per vehicle with its current customers, adding new customers and regions and growth in markets beyond the automotive sector.

It is also looking to raise its profitability with an increase in its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes margin of 200 basis points or more from 2026 through 2030.

Magna CEO Swamy Kotagiri says the targets represent the company’s confidence in its strategy, capabilities and the opportunities that lie ahead.

Magna says the targets reflect a strategy to grow faster than the overall automotive market.

The company says the increase is expected to come from expanding its content per vehicle with its current customers, adding new customers and regions and growth in markets beyond the automotive sector.
It is also looking to raise its profitability with an increase in its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes margin of 200 basis points or more from 2026 through 2030.
Magna CEO Swamy Kotagiri says the targets represent the company’s confidence in its strategy, capabilities and the opportunities that lie ahead.

stories.title: Montreal's LaSalle College gets more time to repay debts amid language fines dispute
stories.summary: Montreal - A private college in Montreal that is facing $30 million in fines from the Quebec government says it is getting more time to settle its debts with creditors.
stories.author: Marieke Glorieux-Stryckman The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Montreal - A private college in Montreal that is facing $30 million in fines from the Quebec government is getting more time to settle its debts with creditors.

A Quebec Superior Court judge ruled on Tuesday to extend LaSalle College’s protection from creditors until Jan. 29, 2027.

The Quebec government fined the college under provincial language legislation for having too many students in its English-language programs.

The government also ordered the college to reimburse about $18 million in subsidies from last year, pushing its total debt to close to $48 million.

“The College is contesting (the fines),” said spokesperson Laurie Saindon.

The provincial education ministry declined to comment.

Tuesday’s decision set the hearing on the fines for Jan. 21 and 22.

The penalties stem from a 2022 language law passed by the provincial government, which imposed limits on the number of students in English-language college programs.

In the 2023-24 school year — the first year the new limits were applied — LaSalle College exceeded its quota by 716 students and received a fine of $8.8 million. The following year, the college surpassed its quota by 1,066 students, and was fined an additional $21 million.

LaSalle College first requested protection from its creditors in August, getting a 10-day reprieve from the court on Aug. 24.

At the time, the school’s director called the fine unfair and unprecedented, suggesting that no company in Quebec could survive such a penalty.

“If you impose a quota that is lower than the number of students we already have in our classrooms, we are doomed from day one. … It’s like you’re on the highway, you’re going 100 kilometres an hour, suddenly there’s a sign at 60 kilometres an hour, and then you get a fine of $30 million,” he said.

Marchand said LaSalle College now respects the limits on students in English-language programs.

The college delayed the beginning of classes by one week because of these fines.

In a decision on Sept. 3, a judge reinstated government subsidies to the college, which reopened its doors the following day.

The court also extended the creditor protection on the same day, and again on Sept. 24. Tuesday’s decision was the third extension.

LaSalle College is a subsidized private school and one of the few institutions in Quebec offering both English-language and French-language programs.

Saindon said students will continue to attend classes and prepare for the winter semester as the dispute with the government plays out in court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: Report: Blue Jays to meet with star free agent Tarik Skubal
stories.summary: Skubal will meet with the Blue Jays next week in California, Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported on Wednesday.
stories.author: Sportsnet
stories.content:
The Toronto Blue Jays are going big-game hunting again.

Star free agent Tarik Skubal will meet with the Blue Jays next week in California, Jon Heyman of the New York Post reported on Wednesday.

Skubal will also meet with the New York Mets, Los Angeles Dodgers and San Diego Padres, per Heyman.

Starting pitching has emerged as the Blue Jays’ top priority in the free-agent market, Sportsnet reported Tuesday, with the team “seriously exploring fits for some prominent arms,” per Ben Nicholson-Smith.

“We’re going to look to add to our offence and add to our starting pitching,” general manager Ross Atkins said Tuesday.

Now, it seems they have their eyes on the top starter on the market in Skubal, who finished last season with the Dodgers after a mid-season trade from the Detroit Tigers, where he had previously played his entire career.

Between the two clubs last season, Skubal posted a 12-7 record, 2.72 ERA and 0.96 Whip with 186 strikeouts in 158.2 innings.

The left-hander won the AL Cy Young as a member of the Tigers in each of the 2024 and 2025 seasons.

In Toronto, he would join a rotation that already features Cy Young finalist Dylan Cease, Jose Soriano and Trey Yesavage.

When asked about the possibility of being aggressive in free agency, Atkins said that’s not the driving force behind the team’s moves.

“For us, it’s about being prepared and not about being aggressive,” he clarified. “And you only can be aggressive and effective if you are prepared.”

Meanwhile, if there’s one segment of free agency that could move sooner than the rest, it could be the left-handed relief market according to some agents. Speaking in general terms, Atkins acknowledged that the Blue Jays are aiming to add to their bullpen.

“In an ideal world, we get through an off-season where we can add to every aspect of our team.”

With files from Sportsnet’s Ben Nicholson-Smith
