stories.title: Canadian manufacturer eyes U.S. as firms 'cannot hold off for too long anymore'
stories.summary: A Canadian textile maker battered by U.S. tariffs is looking to expand south of the border, illustrating how the trade war could leave a lasting mark on the country's manufacturing sector.
stories.author: Brett Bundale The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A Canadian textile maker battered by U.S. tariffs is looking to expand south of the border, illustrating how the trade war could leave a lasting mark on the country’s manufacturing sector.

Fine Cotton Factory Inc. produces fabrics for clothing, mattresses and bedding at its Toronto mill, with roughly half of its sales tied to U.S. customers.

The company saw those sales tumble as tariffs of up to 50 per cent on some products prompted American buyers to delay orders and run down inventories, said Skip Kann, executive vice-president of sales and marketing at Fine Cotton Factory.

Orders are now starting to recover, but he said uncertainty over the Canada-U.S. trade relationship has the company already moving some production to the United States.

Kann said Fine Cotton Factory is shipping some unfinished fabrics to U.S. contractors for additional processing, reducing its exposure to tariffs on finished products, as it lays the groundwork for a larger American expansion.

“There’s been damage done to the relationship between the U.S. and Canada,” he said in an interview.

“We are going to put some form of our business in the U.S. as a long-term plan so that this can never happen to our company again.”

Kann said he plans to open a U.S. warehouse before sourcing equipment and beginning production early next year.

Even the removal of tariffs or a new Canada-U.S. trade agreement May not alter those expansion plans, he said.

“There could always be that niggling little doubt from customers that don’t fully trust the supply chain out of Canada,” Kann said.

That erosion of confidence could have consequences beyond individual companies, said Pau Pujolás, associate professor of economics at McMaster University.

He said the loss of trust in cross-border supply chains could potentially influence where manufacturers invest for years to come.

“Just the fear is enough to generate those suboptimal decisions,” said Pujolás, who specializes in international trade.

“The fact that they are scared, the fact they are thinking of this possibility of a trade disruption when they are taking these investment decisions, that’s the real harm.”

Even if a new free trade agreement is reached, he said businesses May continue to worry that a future U.S. administration could impose new trade barriers.

“The worst thing that you can do to a bunch of business decision-makers is to tell them policies May or May not change,” Pujolás said.

When U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods took effect in March 2025, some manufacturers put expansion plans on hold and adjusted supply chains to limit their exposure.

But as the trade war drags on, some companies are reaching a point where they can no longer delay decisions about where to invest, said Ari Van Assche, a professor of international business at HEC Montréal.

He said he knows of another Canadian manufacturer that is now seriously considering a new U.S. plant after facing steep tariffs, although a shortage of skilled workers is complicating plans.

Still, Van Assche said the broader economic picture does not yet point to a major shift of Canadian manufacturing investment south of the border.

“In the aggregate data, we don’t see a lot of ... companies moving away,” he said. “There’s no uptick in foreign investment in the manufacturing sector in the United States coming from Canada.”

Statistics Canada figures show Canadian direct investment in the United States was down slightly at the end of 2025.

But Van Assche warned that could change.

“It might well be that other companies, even if they’re not facing this, are saying, ‘Look, we cannot hold off for too long anymore.’”

paragraphs: A Canadian textile maker battered by U.S. tariffs is looking to expand south of the border, illustrating how the trade war could leave a lasting mark on the country’s manufacturing sector.
Fine Cotton Factory Inc. produces fabrics for clothing, mattresses and bedding at its Toronto mill, with roughly half of its sales tied to U.S. customers.

The company saw those sales tumble as tariffs of up to 50 per cent on some products prompted American buyers to delay orders and run down inventories, said Skip Kann, executive vice-president of sales and marketing at Fine Cotton Factory.
Orders are now starting to recover, but he said uncertainty over the Canada-U.S. trade relationship has the company already moving some production to the United States.

Kann said Fine Cotton Factory is shipping some unfinished fabrics to U.S. contractors for additional processing, reducing its exposure to tariffs on finished products, as it lays the groundwork for a larger American expansion.
“There’s been damage done to the relationship between the U.S. and Canada,” he said in an interview.
“We are going to put some form of our business in the U.S. as a long-term plan so that this can never happen to our company again.”
Kann said he plans to open a U.S. warehouse before sourcing equipment and beginning production early next year.
Even the removal of tariffs or a new Canada-U.S. trade agreement May not alter those expansion plans, he said.
“There could always be that niggling little doubt from customers that don’t fully trust the supply chain out of Canada,” Kann said.
That erosion of confidence could have consequences beyond individual companies, said Pau Pujolás, associate professor of economics at McMaster University.
He said the loss of trust in cross-border supply chains could potentially influence where manufacturers invest for years to come.
“Just the fear is enough to generate those suboptimal decisions,” said Pujolás, who specializes in international trade.
“The fact that they are scared, the fact they are thinking of this possibility of a trade disruption when they are taking these investment decisions, that’s the real harm.”
Even if a new free trade agreement is reached, he said businesses May continue to worry that a future U.S. administration could impose new trade barriers.

stories.title: Soldiers gave ‘their todays for our tomorrows’: Canadians remember war dead
stories.summary: Canadians will bow their heads to honour those who served and sacrificed for their country as they gather across the country to mark Remembrance Day, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa -- Guns boomed, bagpipes wailed and CF-18 Hornets thundered overhead as Canadians paused at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Wednesday to remember those who served and died defending this country.

This Remembrance Day comes just weeks after a deadly training accident at Canadian Forces Wainwright left four dead and dozens of other soldiers with burn injuries.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement released to media on Wednesday.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed at the Alberta training base last month.

They died and dozens of others were injured when strong winds suddenly swept up a grass fire that was burning on the automatic grenade launcher range and carried it across the training area.

“We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Carney said.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said this year’s service carries extra weight because it comes just weeks after the deadly fire.

“Our thoughts remain with the soldiers we lost, those who were wounded, as well as the families, friends, comrades and all others affected by this tragic event,” Arbour said.

“Such moments remind us that behind every uniform is a human being: someone who serves with dedication, accepts risk on behalf of others and is supported by loved ones who share in the sacrifices that service often demands.”

The last update from National Defence on Nov. 4 said of the 39 injured, 14 had been released from hospital while another 25 remained in hospital.

Dave Edwards, who works in operations with the Connaught Cadet Training Centre in Ottawa and was in attendance for the national ceremony, said the Wainwright tragedy serves as a reminder that armed forces members do dangerous jobs.

“We do take risks and sometimes that’s the result and it’s unfortunate, very, very unfortunate, and I know that they’ll be missed,” he said. “We should remember them just as we remember any others.”

A separate ceremony is planned at CFB Wainwright. Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend that event alongside other dignitaries, military members and veterans.

Canadians are also marking 25 years since the start of the Afghanistan war, a conflict in which 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members served. Veterans Affairs Canada says 158 Canadian Armed Forces members and seven Canadian civilians -- a diplomat, four aid workers, a government contractor and a journalist -- lost their lives in Afghanistan.

Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch his son March in his first Remembrance Day parade as a member of the Canadian Armed Forces after joining last year.

“My father was in World War II, my mother was in World War II, I served for about 28 years in the Hastings and Prince Edward Regiment, and he thought it was just time for him to pay a little price for Canadians to be free,” he said.

McGill said his job during the Afghanistan war was to notify next of kin when soldiers were killed, so the day has a lot of meaning for him.

“It’s a pretty powerful day and gives us an opportunity to come out and pay tribute to those who can’t be here today,” he said.

“Those guys gave their todays for our tomorrows.”

The Afghanistan conflict, which lasted more than 12 years, was the longest in Canadian history and saw the largest deployment of Canadian troops since the Second World War.

This year is also the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Royal Canadian Legion -- created in 1926 to serve as the main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits -- and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

By Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

With files from Nick Murray

stories.title: OPP charges two cops with obstruction after 19-year-old's carbon monoxide death
stories.summary: Sudbury - Police in Greater Sudbury say two of its police officers have been charged by the OPP with obstructing an investigation into the sudden death of a 19-year-old last year.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
SUDBURY - Police in Greater Sudbury say two of its police officers have been charged by the OPP with obstructing an investigation into the sudden death of a 19-year-old last year.

By The Canadian Press

Both Sudbury police and the OPP declined to give additional details about the nature of the obstruction of justice charges.

The investigation at the heart of the case involves the death of Roch (Rocco) Renaud, who police say died of carbon monoxide poisoning inside a home in Lively, a community southwest of Sudbury, in May 2025.

ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW

Angine de Poitrine debut third member in Toronto

The OPP say they took over the investigation at the request of Sudbury police in June 2025 and laid criminal negligence charges last month against two people and a company in the 19-year-old’s death.

After additional investigation, the OPP says it laid obstruction charges against three more individuals, including a Sudbury police sergeant and constable this week.

Sudbury police said in a release the allegations concern off-duty conduct and the force remains committed to the highest standards of professionalism and accountability.

Last year, Sudbury police said two police officers had been suspended with pay after a complaint by the force’s chief prompted an investigation into their off-duty actions.

They said at the time the OPP assumed responsibility of the investigation after it was determined there was an institutional conflict of interest.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

The investigation at the heart of the case involves the death of Roch (Rocco) Renaud, who police say died of carbon monoxide poisoning inside a home in Lively, a community southwest of Sudbury, in May 2025.

Sudbury police said in a release the allegations concern off-duty conduct and the force remains committed to the highest standards of professionalism and accountability.
Last year, Sudbury police said two police officers had been suspended with pay after a complaint by the force’s chief prompted an investigation into their off-duty actions.

stories.title: Body found at motel south of Ingersoll; OPP investigates suspicious death
stories.summary: The circumstances surrounding the death prompted an investigation by the OPP crime unit, with assistance from the Ontario Coroner’s Office.
stories.author: Gerry Dewan
stories.content:
Police remain at a motel south of Ingersoll after a body was discovered Tuesday morning, prompting a suspicious death investigation by the Oxford County detachment of the Ontario Provincial Police.

Officers were called to the property on Plank Line at about 11:20 a.m. and found one person deceased. The circumstances surrounding the death prompted an investigation by the OPP crime unit, with assistance from the Ontario Coroner’s Office.

Police tape surrounded a vehicle and the entrance to a motel room at the scene.

In a news release issued Tuesday evening, the OPP said preliminary information suggests the incident is isolated and there is no threat to public safety.

The investigation is being conducted by the OPP Criminal Investigation Branch, under the direction of the Office of the Chief Coroner for Ontario and the Ontario Forensic Pathology Service. OPP Forensic Identification Services is also assisting.

Residents can expect an increased police presence in the area as the investigation continues.

Police have not released the identity of the deceased or additional details about the circumstances of the death.

stories.title: Dorothy Myo named new commissioner of Indigenous languages
stories.summary: Ottawa - Dorothy Myo has been named the new commissioner of Indigenous languages, replacing interim commissioner Candice St-Aubin.
stories.author: Alessia Passafiume The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - Dorothy Myo has been named the new commissioner of Indigenous languages, replacing interim commissioner Candice St-Aubin.

Myo, who was raised in Saulteaux First Nation in Saskatchewan, will serve in the role for five years.

Her LinkedIn profile says she is a fluent speaker of Saulteaux, Cree and English and recently worked as the deputy chief of self-government and senior director of policy and research at the Métis Nation-Saskatchewan.

She also led the Saskatchewan Indian Cultural Centre, where she worked to preserve, protect and promote First Nations languages and cultures.

A cabinet decision announcing her appointment says Myo was selected for the role after consultations with Indigenous governments and organizations.

The selection process for a new, permanent commissioner was delayed and St-Aubin’s 90-day term was extended last month.

The term of Ron Ignace, the previous commissioner, ended in July, along with the terms of the office’s directors.

The Canadian Press reported earlier this year an audit is being conducted on the office, which is tasked with helping to preserve at-risk Indigenous languages.

Half a dozen sources, including former employees, told The Canadian Press that over the five years of its existence, the commissioner’s office has failed to move the needle on strengthening Indigenous languages and supporting research.

Instead, they said, the office focused on extensive travel and hosting one big conference in Ottawa that cost $10 million. They also alleged a toxic work environment, bullying and uncompleted projects, and staff quitting in frustration.

The Canadian Press agreed not to name the sources because they feared reprisals.

In a media statement at the time, Ignace said the office has faced challenges but “we succeeded in laying the foundation for an office capable of carrying forward this significant work.”

Canadian Heritage Minister Marc Miller described allegations against the office as serious.

“But part of holding people to account is giving people the benefit of the doubt, and that includes making sure the due process is respected,” he said in June.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: Most stolen vehicles in Canada in 2025: Honda CR-V tops national list as Ontario remains auto theft hotspot
stories.summary: The national rankings are also reflected in Ontario, where the Honda CR-V once again topped the 2025 list.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Lucas Casaletto

Posted November 11, 2026 11:05 am.

The Honda CR-V remains the most stolen vehicle in Canada, according to a new report that highlights how SUVs and pickup trucks continue to be prime targets for organized auto theft rings despite government and industry efforts to curb the crime.

New data released by Équité Association found the Honda CR-V ranked first among the country’s most frequently stolen vehicles in 2025, with 2,137 reported thefts among more than 550,000 insured vehicles nationwide.

While the latest figures suggest Canada’s vehicle theft crisis has begun to stabilize after reaching record levels in recent years, industry experts say thieves remain focused on high-demand models that can be quickly exported overseas, resold using fraudulent documentation or dismantled for parts.

According to the report, six of the 10 most-stolen vehicles in Canada were SUVs, led by the Honda CR-V.

The top 10 most stolen vehicles nationally in 2025 were:

Honda CR-V – 2,137 thefts

Honda Civic – 1,813 thefts

Toyota RAV4 – 1,147 thefts

Ram 1500 Series – 1,072 thefts

Ford F-150 Series – 1,057 thefts

Lexus RX Series – 964 thefts

Chevrolet Silverado/GMC Sierra 1500 Series – 927 thefts

Toyota Tundra – 787 thefts

Jeep Wrangler – 603 thefts

Hyundai Elantra – 484 thefts

The Honda Civic was the highest-ranked passenger car on the list, while pickup trucks accounted for four of the top 10 positions.

The national rankings are reflected in Ontario, where the Honda CR-V once again topped the list of the province’s most frequently stolen vehicles in 2025.

According to Équité Association, 1,598 Honda CR-Vs were reported stolen in Ontario, accounting for nearly three-quarters of all CR-V thefts recorded across Canada.

The Honda Civic ranked second with 1,041 thefts, followed by the Lexus RX Series with 863 stolen vehicles. The Toyota Tundra and Toyota RAV4 rounded out the top five, with 593 and 591 thefts respectively.

Rounding out Ontario’s top 10 most-stolen vehicles were the Ford F-150 Series (532 thefts), Toyota Grand Highlander (459), Ram 1500 Series (457), Jeep Wrangler (365) and Toyota Highlander (314).

While the Honda CR-V recorded the highest number of thefts overall, several other vehicles were targeted at significantly higher rates relative to the number of insured vehicles on the road.

The Toyota Grand Highlander posted the province’s highest theft rate at 8.63 per cent, with 459 thefts among just 5,320 insured vehicles. The Toyota Tundra followed with a theft rate of 2.06 per cent, while the Lexus RX Series recorded a theft frequency of 1.45 per cent.

Ontario’s top 10 most stolen vehicles in 2025

Honda CR-V (1,598 thefts)

Honda Civic (1,041)

Lexus RX Series (863)

Toyota Tundra (593)

Toyota RAV4 (591)

Ford F-150 Series (532)

Toyota Grand Highlander (459)

Ram 1500 Series (457)

Jeep Wrangler (365)

Toyota Highlander (314)

Federal, provincial and municipal governments have introduced a series of anti-theft measures over the past two years , including increased border inspections, enhanced law-enforcement coordination and investments in vehicle-tracking technologies.

Automakers have also begun implementing stronger security measures, including improved encryption systems and anti-theft software updates.

Despite those efforts, Équité says the continued concentration of thefts among a relatively small group of vehicles demonstrates that organized criminal networks remain highly active and adaptable.

stories.title: Canadians warming to U.S. following midterm elections: poll
stories.summary: Canadians are overall pleased with U.S. midterm results, but many remain wary of actual impact on trade negotiations, according to a Leger survey
stories.author: Kenn Oliver
stories.content:
In the wake of the Democratic Party’s wave of wins in last week’s U.S. midterm elections, Canadians’ perception of their southerly neighbour has softened somewhat, according to a new poll.

Before probing respondents on their midterm thoughts, Leger first sought to understand their perspective of the U.S., finding 38 per cent see it as an enemy country — down three per cent from similar polling in August, but still up eight points over a June 1 survey.

Perception of the U.S. as a neutral nation was at 27 per cent this time up, up from 22 per cent in August, and those who see it as an ally counted 20 per cent, a drop of two per cent. A further 14 per cent are unsure.

Leger executive vice-president Andrew Enns reasons that “rhetoric” about Canada in the final month of the elections — particularly in border states Michigan, Ohio and Maine, where trade relationships became part of the campaign — May have played a part, but so did the overall result.

Some people May have leaned more toward neutrality, he told National Post, “because it looks like Congress, at least, will be a little more friendly towards Canada, at least you know on the outward side.”

“We’ll see from the policy side where that goes,” he said.

“Maybe there’s going to be a bit more of a reset of the relationship, and it won’t be as antagonistic and we won’t feel like … everything wrong in America is somehow Canada’s fault.”

While people 55 and over (45 per cent) and Quebecers (44 per cent) are the most inclined to consider the U.S. an enemy, both cohorts’ opinions have similarly tempered since August polling.

Enns says Quebecers, coming off their own provincial election where no clear majority was awarded, May be expecting “a little friendlier” tone from trading partners following the midterms.

Asked about their level of satisfaction with the result of last Monday’s vote, 80 per cent of those who see the U.S. as an enemy were pleased, most of them very (56 per cent).

That sentiment was highest in Quebec (75 per cent) and among 55-plus respondents (78 per cent).

Meanwhile, a mere seven per cent cumulatively were disappointed, led by respondents in Manitoba and Saskatchewan (14 per cent) and those who see the U.S. as an ally (20 per cent), most of whom were very disappointed (13 per cent).

Of note, 14 per cent expressed no feelings about the U.S. and 12 per cent didn’t know enough about the elections to confidently express an opinion.

As for how the historic results might impact Canada, 72 per cent consider it very (23 per cent) or somewhat (49 per cent) good news.

Again, 80 per cent ~~oft~~ofthose who see the U.S. an enemy expect it to be good for Canada, as do 78 per cent who see it as neutral. Quebecers and the oldest cohort (79 per cent, respectively) led the way demographically.

Just eight per cent think it’s bad news for Canada, led by Manitobans and people in Saskatchewan (14 per cent), and those who see an ally in the U.S. (19 per cent), most of whom see it as very bad (13 per cent).

Another 20 per cent responded that they don’t know enough about the results to say.

Among those who see the U.S. as an enemy, however, only half (50 per cent) expect the power shift will make it easier for “Canada to negotiate favourable trade terms” with its largest trading partner.

That’s on par with the 48 per cent of all respondents dubious about the impact on trade negotiations, only 10 per cent of whom think it’ll be “much easier.” Quebecers (53 per cent) are the most hopeful in that regard, while Manitobans and Saskatchewan residents (14 per cent) are the most pessimistic.

Only seven per cent think more Democrats in the mix will make talks more difficult, 30 per cent expect it won’t matter, and 16 per cent don’t know enough about the results to opine.

Enns said that while Canadians’ satisfaction with the results probably comes as no surprise to Ottawa, the apprehension around trade talks signals “cautious optimism” about the tangible impact coming out of Nov. 4.

“Canadians think it’s an improved environment, but it’s by no means a slam dunk,” he said, adding that the media’s emphasis on the negotiations demonstrates the need to get a deal in place so companies can start planning for a more certain economic environment.

Almost two-thirds (63 per cent) of Canadians admitted to following the elections very (24 per cent) or somewhat (39 per cent) closely this year. It was most closely observed in B.C. and Atlantic Canada (68 per cent, respectively), while those in Alberta and Quebec (41 per cent, respectively) had the highest percentages not dialed in.

More men (73 per cent) than women (54 per cent) followed closely, while more women (46 per cent) than men (27 per cent) were checked out. Respondents 55 and over were the most invested (73 per cent), followed by the 18-34 cohort (60 per cent).

The survey of 1,527 respondents in Canada was conducted by Leger between Nov. 6 and 9. For comparison purposes, a probability sample of this size yields a margin of error of plus or minus 2.5 per cent, 19 times out of 20.

Kenn Oliver is a web editor and writer for National Post. He is a career journalist of more than 20 years, the bulk of which was spent as a sports writer, business reporter and web editor for the Telegram in St. John's, N.L.

stories.title: Two Mississauga men charged after $86K in coffee machines stolen
stories.summary: In July, police said officers responded to a call for a break-and-enter at Mississauga building. Investigators found that nine-high commercial coffee machines had been stolen.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
Police in Peel Region said it has charged two Mississauga men after officers recovered nearly $86,000 in stolen high-end coffee machines following a commercial break-and-enter investigation.

On July 11 at around 6:40 a.m., police said officers responded to a call for a break-and-enter at a commercial building in Mississauga. Investigators found that nine high-end commercial coffee machines had been stolen.

Officers later found the stolen coffee machines had been listed for sale on an online marketplace. Two suspects were identified and on Nov.1 and a search warrant was executed at a residence near Bloor Street and Fieldgate Drive in Mississauga.

Six of the nine stolen coffee machines were recovered. Police believe the remaining three machines were sold online before police executed the search warrant.

Two men from Mississauga, aged 45 and 57, have been charged with possession of property obtained by crime. Police said they are scheduled to appear in court at a later date.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: New Canada Post stamp honours Chinese Canadians who volunteered for covert operations in World War II
stories.summary: The Canada Post stamp honours the legacy of a group of 150 Chinese Canadians who were recruited for their language skills.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
Even though they were barred from serving in the Canadian military at the start of World War II, Chinese Canadians stepped up to volunteer for dangerous covert operations when called upon in 1944, and their contributions are being commemorated with a new Canada Post Remembrance Day stamp issued earlier this month.

The stamp honours the legacy of a group of 150 Chinese Canadians who were recruited for their language skills and ability to blend in for secret missions behind enemy lines in Japanese-occupied Asia.

Chinese Canadians who stepped forward to serve in these missions were either on Force 136 – part of Britain’s Special Operations Executive – or with Australia’s Services Reconnaissance Department and underwent intense specialized training in espionage, sabotage, guerrilla warfare, parachuting and intelligence gathering.

At a time when Chinese Canadians faced discrimination, were denied basic rights and considered second-class citizens, many saw enlistment as a way to demonstrate their commitment to the country and change the way immigrants were viewed and treated.

The stamp was unveiled in Vancouver on Nov. 3 and a ceremony was also held in Toronto on Tuesday ahead of Remembrance Day by Canada Post, alongside the Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto, attended by family and friends of those who volunteered for Force 136.

“Their sacrifice at the time when the Chinese in Canada were still underneath the 1923 Chinese Exclusion Act is actually kind of extraordinary,” said Rick Wong, the son of Hank Wong who served in Operation Oblivion. “At the time, my father didn’t think it was a big thing – he just said ‘you gotta do what you gotta do’ – but when you look at it in hindsight he was willing to sign up for essentially a suicide mission when Chinese in Canada did not have full rights.

Historians say the contributions of Force 136 members extended far beyond the battlefield. Their service helped advance the Allied war effort and strengthen the push for equality at home.

Two years after the war ended, the Chinese Exclusion Act was repealed and Chinese Canadians gained full citizenship rights, including the right to vote.

The new stamp features a historic black-and-white photograph of Force 136 members awaiting repatriation in 1945, overlaid with the red phoenix insignia of Force 136, whose name appears in English, French and traditional Chinese. It’s meant to serve as a lasting tribute to their courage, sacrifice and role in breaking down barriers in Canada.

“For Canada Post to recognize that immigrants built Canada and also fought in the war is so very important. That’s a legacy – these are stories that we’re going to tell to our next generation – and not just to Chinese [people] but to Canadians at large,” said Sharifa Khan, Chinese Cultural Centre of Greater Toronto.

content_blocks.text: Chinese Canadians who stepped forward to serve in these missions were either on Force 136 – part of Britain’s Special Operations Executive – or with Australia’s Services Reconnaissance Department and underwent intense specialized training in espionage, sabotage, guerrilla warfare, parachuting and intelligence gathering.

content_blocks.text: At a time when Chinese Canadians faced discrimination, were denied basic rights and considered second-class citizens, many saw enlistment as a way to demonstrate their commitment to the country and change the way immigrants were viewed and treated.

stories.title: Watch Live: London’s 2026 Remembrance Day ceremony
stories.summary: Motorists should expect several road closures in downtown London on Remembrance Day as the city hosts its annual ceremony and parade.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Motorists should expect several road closures in downtown London on Remembrance Day as the city hosts its annual ceremony and parade.

The City of London says temporary closures will be in effect from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday to accommodate Remembrance Day events.

From 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., the following roads will be closed:

Dufferin Avenue from Clarence Street to Picton Street.

Wellington Street from Central Avenue to Queens Avenue.

Additional closures will be in place from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.:

Dundas Street from Wellington Street to Waterloo Street.

Waterloo Street from Dundas Street to Dufferin Avenue.

Dufferin Avenue from Waterloo Street to Clarence Street.

The city says access to the public parking garage at City Hall will remain available before the parade arrives at approximately 10:30 a.m.

Employees and visitors will be able to enter the garage by travelling westbound on Dufferin Avenue through the Waterloo Street intersection. However, access in and out of the garage will not be possible during the parade and ceremony.

stories.title: Genetic genealogy helps Toronto police identify man found dead in 1992
stories.summary: Derek is the 14th person identified through an initiative called 'Project 31,' which began in the summer of 2022 and uses investigative genetic genealogy.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau
stories.content:
Police in Toronto have identified the remains of a man who was found dead in 1992 as part of a project using investigative genetic genealogy.

First responders were called to the area of Queen and Church streets on Sept. 15, 1992 to a report of an unresponsive man on the lawn of a church.

According to Toronto police , crews were unable to revive him and his cause of death was not considered suspicious.

However, the man did not have any identification and investigators at the time were unable to identify him.

More than three decades later, his case was selected for investigation using genetic genealogy, and a DNA profile for him was uploaded to public-facing databases on Jan. 8, 2026.

“The man’s closest matches were very distant, but they suggested he was from the United Kingdom,” police said in a release.

“Months of work by the Toronto Police Service genealogy team and TPS investigators determined that the man was likely a man named Derek.”

It was learned that Derek had moved to Toronto from the UK in the 1970s.

He was reported missing by his lawyer in December 1993 — nearly 15 months after the unidentified man had died — but the connection wasn’t made between the two cases at the time.

Toronto police were able to find a copy of Derek’s fingerprints in another country, according to the release. When compared, they matched those of the unidentified man found in 1992.

“They confirmed that the unknown man was Derek,” police said.

“Derek’s family in the UK was contacted and notified of his identification by members of the Toronto Police Service.”

Derek is the 14th person identified through an initiative called ‘Project 31,’ which began in the summer of 2022. It was named after the 31 open Toronto Police Service cases involving long-term unidentified deceased people for whom DNA material is readily available.

Last year, a man from Portugal named Alcides was identified as the unknown deceased man in a 2008 case .

stories.title: ‘I’ve lost soldiers on a mission’: What Remembrance Day is like for active-duty soldiers
stories.summary: Members of the Canadian Armed Forces deployed thousands of kilometres from home are sharing their Remembrance Day reflections.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Camp Adazi, Latvia – Members of the Canadian Armed Forces deployed thousands of kilometres from home are sharing their Remembrance Day reflections.

“Sacrifice isn’t just measured in casualties in the military,” said Col. David Brassard, the Canadian commander of Nato’s Multinational Brigade in Latvia. “When our soldiers deploy here (to Latvia) for six months, they’re away from their families and loved ones. That’s a type of sacrifice we don’t talk about as much.”

CTV News spent the last week embedded with the multinational brigade in eastern Latvia along the border with Russia and Belarus. It is there that CTV News spoke with multiple soldiers about the personal sacrifice.

“I joined the military because I wanted to serve Canada,” said one Canadian commanding a Nato tank squadron.“We have a lot of freedoms, we’re very fortunate (in Canada) and we want to be able to protect that and help provide security for other countries.”

CTV News is withholding the names of some the service members interviewed for this story, to ensure their safety and security while on deployment in eastern Latvia.

“I’m here doing something meaningful, it’s meaningful to me as well,” said one Canadian lieutenant helping lead a battle brigade into a training exercise just 30 kilometres from the border of Belarus.

The memory of fallen comrades remains heavy for the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia.

The last name ‘Hornburg’ hangs along the side of a Canadian Leopard tank in honour of Cpl. Nathan Hornburg, who was killed in September 2007 in Afghanistan after he was hit by a mortar shell while fixing a tank west of Kandahar.

Troops in Latvia are also mourning those injured and killed by an October deadly fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. The unit at Wainwright had been training to deploy to Latvia and form a light infantry unit.

“There are always risks involved, even in training,” said Lt.-Col. Simon Mailloux, the commander of the brigade’s multinational infantry battle group.

and I was previously injured myself.”

Canadian soldiers in Latvia are training for any possibility with tensions running high between Nato and Russia. Adrian Ghobrial reports.

Mailloux, a 25-year veteran, was a platoon commander in Afghanistan when Pte. Simon Longtin was killed by an improvised explosive device (IED) in August 2007.

Three months later, another roadside bomb cost Mailloux part of his left leg and killed Cpl. Nicolas Beauchamp and Pte. Michel Lévesque.

“It’s still hard to process, even during Remembrance Day,” Mailloux said.”

Mailloux later became the first Canadian amputee to return to active duty in Afghanistan.

A Canadian commander is overseeing 3,000 troops as Canada takes a leadership role in Nato's defence mission in Latvia. Adrian Ghobrial takes a closer look.

Speaking to CTV National News just 30 kilometres from the Russian border, Mailloux says his current soldiers understand the gravity of their mission.

“We are here now, very close to a border (with Russia), my troops know it, they can feel it,” Mailloux said. “That’s what their job is asking of them right now.”

On this Remembrance Day, those we spoke with had messages to share with their loved ones back home. Many are sending their love and thanks to their parents, siblings, spouses and children.

Most Canadian soldiers in Latvia are here on a six-month deployment scheduled to end in December, leaving many looking forward to returning home for the holidays. Asked why they joined the Canadian Armed Forces, the majority of those who spoke to CTV News shared a similar thought, they love the military and they love their country.

stories.title: Saskatoon judge delivers 20-year sentence for ‘absolutely abhorrent’ killing
stories.summary: One of the three people responsible for a gruesome 2024 Saskatoon homicide has been sentenced to 20 years behind bars on charges of manslaughter and indignity to human remains.
stories.author: Grace Miller
stories.content:
Warning: This story contains content that May be disturbing to some readers. Discretion is advised.

One of the three people responsible for a gruesome 2024 Saskatoon homicide has been sentenced to 20 years behind bars on charges of manslaughter and indignity to human remains.

Edin Vrazalica received his sentence Justice Richard Danyliuk calling the crime “absolutely abhorrent.” Vrazalica is one of three who have pleaded guilty for playing a role in Perkins’ death.

Crown prosecutor Cory Bliss said it is evident from what the judge had to say while giving his sentence that this case is about more than a death.

“It’s very rare in the Crown’s experience to hear a judge speak so strongly and frankly calling this an atrocity, referring to Mr. Vrazalica as monstrous, referencing his cowardice for not even watching the terrible things he did when they were displayed in the courtroom,” said Bliss.

“The judge basically pointed to Mr. Vrazalica as the ringleader based on everything he had been shown. Certainly that’s always been the Crown’s view, unfortunately, we have limitations in what we can present to the court by way of witnesses.”

The courtroom heard tearful victim impact statements from Perkins’ family before the judge’s decision.

She says she cautioned Perkins about befriending Vrazalica when they met in the spring of 2022.

Perkins’ sister-in-law, Natasha Perkins, said she is left questioning how humanity could fall so far into the depths of its own evil.

His father, Cameron Perkins, said he thinks no one who butchers another human should be allowed to walk in public again.

The agreed facts of the case show Vrazalica, as well as co-accused Dillon Singler and Chantel McLaren, were trafficking drugs from Vancouver to Saskatoon in 2024.

Saskatoon Police Service officers responded to a disturbance call at 610 Lisgar Ave. on Feb. 1, 2024, and found Perkins intoxicated and seemingly unharmed. Some drugs matching those the accused were trafficking were seized, but police did not arrest Perkins

Snapchat videos from later in the day showed Perkins on the ground beaten and covered in blood with Vrazalica cutting off four of his fingers over the missing drugs.

Bliss says Vrazalica was also angry with Perkins, thinking he gave some pills to McLaren, Vrazalica’s girlfriend at the time.

The next day, Vrazalica and McLaren were seen on security camera video purchasing cleaning supplies and large plastic containers.

On Feb. 2, 2024, police received an anonymous report of Vrazalica assaulting an unknown male and proceeded to stake out the same address they previously attended.

McLaren and another woman were arrested trying to escape and Vrazalica was shot by police after sprinting out of the house holding what is described as a cylindrical object.

Police found Perkins’ remains wrapped in plastic inside of a plastic container on top of a tarp.

The autopsy found Perkins died of blood loss from a large slash to his throat.

The following investigation showed significant amounts of blood present in the home in the areas Snapchat videos showed Perkins being assaulted.

stories.title: Performance Of The Year Film Debut at the Hyland Cinema in London
stories.summary: After nearly eight years of development, an independent film rooted in London's creative community is hitting ...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
After nearly eight years of development, an independent film rooted in London’s creative community is hitting the big screen.

Performance of the Year, produced by London-based Orange Hat Film Production premiered, Nov. 7 at London’s Hyland Cinema. About 100 people turned out for the screening, which was followed by a Q & A with cast and crew.

Fanshawe advanced film graduate Darryl Ayles directed and co-wrote the film alongside Tad Brock and Jamara Forbes. Performance of the Year follows the story of Olivia Billings, an aspiring actress navigating the pressures of an industry where one opportunity could change her career.

People filing in before the screening of Performance Of The Year at the Hyland Cinema on November 7. Sloane Geofroy/Instagram

Ayles said he would return to film in London because the city is rich with rising talent and interesting architecture that offers a variety of settings.

“I’ve always made the joke that I consider London to be ‘Hollywood South’ as opposed to Toronto’s ‘Hollywood North,'” Ayles said.

Inspired by the MeToo movement, the psychological thriller explores themes of power, vulnerability, and exploitation.

For Sloane Geofroy, who portrays Olivia, the character’s experiences were personally relatable.

“I can resonate with this so much. I am her,” Geofroy said.

Geofroy, an actor from Hamilton, said Olivia’s experiences reflect the challenges many performers face while pursuing careers in a competitive industry.

“So many of us artists and actors and everyone out there can resonate with Olivia and can resonate with how much rejection she feels on a daily basis,” she said.

Darryl Ayles and Sloane Geofroy in Performance of the Year (2026) Photo by Devon King – © Orange Hat Film Productions

Preparing for the role involved extensive collaboration with Ayles. Geofroy said the two spent hours discussing the script, reviewing Olivia’s motivations and making adjustments to develop the character.

“For the most part, it was very creative and collaborative, which I really enjoy,” Geofroy said.

Although Geofroy travelled from Hamilton to London for filming, she said the experience allowed her to build meaningful relationships with the cast and crew.

Sloane Geofroy photographed with the Performance Of The Year poster at the Hyland Cinema on November, 7. Sloane Geofroy/Instagram

“I like to consider myself like an unofficial official member of the London film community,” she said.

Filmmaker and graphic designer Michael Doyle also contributed to the production, designing its movie poster and assisting with several aspects of filmmaking.

“This was the first time, I guess you could say, I designed a professional movie poster,” Doyle said.

The idea for the poster came while Doyle was watching an early version of the film with members of Orange Hat.

Doyle said seeing his design displayed in the Hyland Cinema lobby was surreal. The artwork was also featured on T-shirts and smaller promotional materials.

His involvement extended beyond graphic design. Doyle contributed to auditions, storyboarding, costumes, on-set work and advertising.

“That’s the case with independent films, man. Everybody has to wear multiple hats, you know?” Doyle said.

Doyle said the production had one of the largest crews he and his fellow filmmakers had worked with, demonstrating the collaboration required to bring an independent project to completion.

Michael Doyle posing in front of the Performance Of The Year poster at the Hyland Cinema on November, 7. Michael Doyle/Instagram

For Geofroy, the experience strengthened her connection to London’s filmmaking community. For Doyle, it provided an opportunity to develop his creative skills and see his work presented to an audience.

With more than 100 tickets sold for its Hyland Cinema premiere, Performance of the Year marked a milestone for the cast and crew.

For Ayles, the production also reinforced London’s potential as a filming destination.

His willingness to return to the city, combined with the contributions of actors and filmmakers from across southwestern Ontario, highlights the opportunities available to independent productions outside larger filmmaking centres.

stories.title: Knights host Storm Wednesday, Easton Cowan greets hundreds of fans in Toronto
stories.summary: The Knights have reached the quarter mark of the Ontario Hockey League season with an 11-4-1-1 record but still sit six points behind the Storm for first place in the Midwest Division.
stories.author: Brent Lale
stories.content:
It’s a rare Wednesday night game at Canada Life Place as the Guelph Storm visit the London Knights.

The Knights have reached the quarter mark of the Ontario Hockey League season with an 11-4-1-1 record but still sit six points behind the Storm for first place in the Midwest Division.

“We’re just thinking of it like a playoff game,” Knights assistant coach Rick Steadman said.

The Knights are set to unveil new throwback uniforms Wednesday night and will recognize veterans from Parkwood Hospital during a Remembrance Day ceremony before puck drop.

The club says a limited number of tickets remain available.

Sokolovskii returns to practice in non-contact jersey

The 6-foot-8 Russian defenceman has appeared in just one game for the London Knights this season. He suffered a lower-body injury in a 7-4 victory over the Owen Sound Attack on Sept. 25.

The Philadelphia Flyers’ 2026 first-round pick drew attention in that game after delivering a heavy hit on an Attack player before immediately fighting Julian Brown in response to the check.

Knights general manager Mark Hunter told CTV News he expects Sokolovskii will be a couple of weeks away from returning to game action, unless he is able to quickly regain strength and muscle in his injured leg.

Former Knight Easton Cowan greets hundreds of fans at Sports Card Expo

The lineup to meet former London Knight Easton Cowan stretched through the Toronto Sports Card Expo, with a queue wrapping around one area and extending down an aisle on the event’s opening day in Mississauga.

Cowan spent part of the day signing autographs and posing for photos with Toronto Maple Leafs fans.

“I remember being a young guy trying to meet the Leafs too, so I’m super excited to meet the fans,” he told CTV News backstage.

Cowan scored his seventh goal of the season and added an assist Tuesday night in Toronto’s 6-3 loss to the Colorado Avalanche.

The Mt. Brydges, Ont., native is averaging nearly 16 minutes of ice time per game in his second NHL season. He has seven goals through 20 games after scoring 11 during his entire rookie campaign.

“Obviously being my second year, you feel a bit more comfortable and you know the guys a bit better,” Cowan said.

“I think you just start to learn a lot about the game and lifestyle. So just trying to adapt and get better every day, but the vibes are high.”

The Philadelphia Flyers’ 2026 first-round pick drew attention in that game after delivering a heavy hit on an Attack player before immediately fighting Julian Brown in response to the check.

Knights general manager Mark Hunter told CTV News he expects Sokolovskii will be a couple of weeks away from returning to game action, unless he is able to quickly regain strength and muscle in his injured leg.
Former Knight Easton Cowan greets hundreds of fans at Sports Card Expo

The lineup to meet former London Knight Easton Cowan stretched through the Toronto Sports Card Expo, with a queue wrapping around one area and extending down an aisle on the event’s opening day in Mississauga.
Cowan spent part of the day signing autographs and posing for photos with Toronto Maple Leafs fans.
“I remember being a young guy trying to meet the Leafs too, so I’m super excited to meet the fans,” he told CTV News backstage.

The Mt. Brydges, Ont., native is averaging nearly 16 minutes of ice time per game in his second NHL season. He has seven goals through 20 games after scoring 11 during his entire rookie campaign.
“Obviously being my second year, you feel a bit more comfortable and you know the guys a bit better,” Cowan said.
“I think you just start to learn a lot about the game and lifestyle. So just trying to adapt and get better every day, but the vibes are high.”

stories.title: The Latest: Canadians gather to mark Remembrance Day
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadians across the country will pause at 11 a.m. to reflect on the sacrifices and service of Canadian Armed Forces members to mark Remembrance Day.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Canadians across the country are reflecting on the sacrifices and service of Canadian Armed Forces members today as they mark Remembrance Day.

This year is also the 25th anniversary of the start of the Afghanistan war in which 40,000 Canadians served. Veterans Affairs Canada says 158 Canadian Armed Forces members and seven Canadian civilians — a diplomat, four aid workers, a government contractor and a journalist — lost their lives while in Afghanistan.

This year’s ceremonies take place just weeks after the tragic fire at Canadian Armed Forces Base Wainwright. Four soldiers were killed and dozens were injured when a wildfire suddenly overtook a training exercise.

All times are listed in Eastern Standard Time.

12:10 p.m. — At least 2,000 people have lined a street in downtown St. Albert, Alta., to pay their respects at a Remembrance Day service.

More than 300 members of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry marched to the service, along with cadets and RCMP officers.

The regiment was taking part in attack training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month, when wind whipped a grass fire into a group of soldiers. Four were killed and dozens were injured.

12:00 p.m. — A moment of silence is held in Alberta, where there is extra attention on Remembrance Day in that province after a wildfire killed four soldiers at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright during a training exercise and injured dozens more. They were Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

Hundreds gathered for the ceremony in Wainwright, Alta. a small community about two kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

11:40 a.m. — Governor General Louise Arbour and Prime Minister Mark Carney greet veterans and other dignitaries as the national Remembrance Day Ceremony comes to a close.

Carney shakes hands with U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra during this time, and the two have a brief exchange.

11:30 a.m. — In Ottawa, Rabbi Idan Scher said the people of Wainwright exemplified the military spirit of stepping up to serve in the wake of the deadly fire during by asking “how can I help?”

“In those four simple words, lies the very spirit of service we honour today. The choice to look beyond ourselves, to recognize our responsibility to one another. And to place the needs of others before our own,” he said while giving the benediction at the national ceremony.

“Today, we remember those who never came home. We honour those who returned bearing the scars of service, some visible to the world, others carried silently deep within. And we stand with the families whose sacrifices continue long after the uniforms have been put away.”

11:25 a.m. — Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow commemorated the Legion on its 100th anniversary during her remarks at today’s Remembrance Day ceremony. The Legion, she said, has supported veterans and kept their stories alive. “The Legion shows us the city we can be. A city where no one carries the burden alone. A city where we take care of each other and stand up for each other,” she said.

11:17 a.m. Brig.-Gen. Éric Landry, who has served in Afghanistan, told a Remembrance Day ceremony outside Queen’s Park in Toronto that Canada is a country worth defending.

11:15 a.m. — After the bell struck 11 atop Toronto’s Old City Hall, Rev. Levi Samson Beardy read the act of remembrance in Ojibwe. Before he stepped away from the podium, he addressed the crowd gathered around the cenotaph for the Remembrance Day ceremony.

“As we think of remembering the past, let us look to the future that there may be peace. And if you’re praying person, pray for peace. So that our children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren will not to have to endure the horrors of war,” he said.

11:15 a.m. — After the clock on Toronto’s Old City Hall strikes 11, Rev. Levi Samson Beardy reads the act of remembrance in Ojibwe. Before he steps away from the podium, he addresses the crowd gathered around the cenotaph for the Remembrance Day ceremony.

“As we think of remembering the past, let us look to the future that there may be peace. And if you’re praying person, pray for peace. So that our children, grandchildren, and great grandchildren will not to have to endure the horrors of war,” he says.

11:11 a.m. — Gov. Gen. General Louise Arbour lays the first wreath at the national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa on behalf of “the people of Canada.” She is followed by Virginia Hicks, this year’s Silver Cross mother, who lays a wreath on behalf of “the mothers of Canada.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney then lays a wreath on behalf of the government of Canada. More dignitaries continue to lay wreaths at the cenotaph.

11:10 a.m. — A prayer for the Wainwright victims is read out as the sound of cannon fire rolls over Montreal during the Remembrance Day ceremony.

The official laying of wreaths begins at the foot of the monument.

11 a.m. — The national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa observes two minutes of silence.

10:52 a.m. — Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa, her first as commander-in-chief.

Arbour is wearing a uniform. The governor general always wears a military uniform for the ceremony.

10:50 a.m. — Virginia Hicks, this year’s Silver Cross mother, arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony, where she will lay a wreath on behalf of all mothers who have lost children in military service.

Her daughter, Sapper Mariebeth Short, was killed in a training exercise on Sept. 23, 2002 in Petawawa, Ont.

Hicks is a veteran herself, working in supply and logistics for 29 years.

10:45 a.m. — Prime Minister Mark Carney and his wife Diana Fox arrive at the National War Memorial for the national Remembrance Day ceremony. He shakes hands with the assembled dignitaries, including Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan.

10:40 a.m. — A Remembrance Day procession arrives at the war memorial at Place du Canada in Montreal.

About a hundred people gather under sunny skies for the ceremony, including many young people.

Many chat in small groups ahead of the ceremony, with red poppies pinned to their coats.

Several wreaths are laid on the ground on behalf of different organizations, including one honouring the victims of Wainwright

10:30 a.m. — The national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa gets underway as military bands and veterans march to the National War Memorial near Parliament. Thousands of people line the streets to watch the ceremony.

10 a.m. — NDP Leader Avi Lewis issues a Remembrance Day message and, like other leaders, he pays special attention to those who died in the fire at CFB Wainwright last month.

“This Remembrance Day, we reinforce our commitment to a Canada where every veteran has a roof over their head, honour the legacy of those who defeated fascism by standing against hate, and rededicate ourselves to the task of building a peaceful world,” Lewis said.

9:20 a.m. — Prime Minister Mark Carney issues a Remembrance Day message saying “rights and freedoms do not defend themselves” in an increasingly “dangerous and divided world.”

He says today is about honouring those who stepped up to serve their country through the generations. He reads the names of the victims of the Wainwright fire: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Carney said.

9:10 a.m. — A Remembrance Day procession arrives at the National War Memorial in Newfoundland and Labrador’s capital city. Hundreds of people gather at the monument in St. John’s, despite the rain. The hushed crowd prepares for the two minutes of silence.

9:10 a.m. — In a video clip released today of a speech she made in the legislature earlier this week, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith says “wearing a uniform from the Canadian Armed Forces is a declaration that you will lay down your life for the values of this nation.”

8:30 a.m. — People begin to gather along the fence line at the national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa.

8:15 a.m. — Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour releases a Remembrance Day message calling on all Canadians to reflect on the courage and dedication of Canada Armed Forces members and the sacrifices made by their families and communities.

She says the Wainwright fire is a reminder that everyone who serves is a human being who “accepts risk on behalf of others and is supported by loved ones who share in the sacrifices that service often demands.”

7:45 a.m. — In a video message honouring veterans, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the “cost of service has been brought home” in the wake of the Wainwright fire.

Poilievre also makes special mention of soldiers who served and died in Afghanistan on the 25th anniversary of the start of that conflict.

Poilievre’s Alberta riding includes the community of Wainwright.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version misspelled the name of Sapper Mariebeth Short.

stories.title: Artists Sharon Lockhart and Zadie Xa show two sides of reality at Toronto’s Power Plant
stories.summary: The slow-burn contemplation of Fogo Island contrasts the futuristic exhibition
stories.author: Tatum Dooley
stories.content:
Sharon Lockhart’s exhibition, a photography and film installation aptly titled Fogo, feels like an ad for Fogo Island’s tourism board. Now screening at the Power Plant Contemporary Art Gallery in Toronto as part of its fall programming, in collaboration with the Vega Foundation, the film, titled Windward , follows the landscape of the tiny island off Newfoundland’s northeast coast. With a population of just over 2,000, Fogo Island holds an outsized place in the arts’ imagination, with the esteemed Fogo Island Arts residency bringing world-renowned artists to the island and into the public eye. Lockhart, an American artist who participated in the residency in 2022, spent four summers on the island to shoot the project.

Like any effective tourism commercial, I’m left wishing I were there instead of watching in a darkened room. In each vignette, children play idly. A girl feeds a pack of seagulls on the shoreline from buckets of discarded fish; when she leaves, the birds rush to take her place; preteens jump into torrent water; a kid flies a kite; and, my favourite, a child walks on stilts. Between each scene, an abrupt cut to dark, before much of the same: children in the distance, greenery, the Atlantic Ocean, a windy soundtrack.

Every time a child gets too close to the ocean, I feel a jolt of anxiety. The stress is unfounded. I’m projecting drama onto a film that has none, my brain fabricating excitement. In reality, the film is idyllic bordering on tedious. No phones, no adults, just moments of slow, monotonous play. Like a friend who insists on showing you every moment of their vacation, you get the picture pretty fast.

After reading the didactic text, I learned that Lockhart directs the children’s play. Directed play! The phrase feels like an oxymoron. Lockhart’s inspiration for Windward was the 1967 short film Children of Fogo Island , directed by Colin Low as part of a package of 27 films shot for the National Film Board of Canada.

Through Low’s lens, a group of boys inexplicably move a wooden structure along the shoreline. Children stumble on homemade stilts as the camera zooms in and out. A group of kids launch into the ocean on a makeshift raft. The location is the same as Lockhart’s, but there’s so much more texture to dig your teeth into. Garbles of children’s conversation in distinct East Coast accents and the chaos of real children playing bring a sense of joy. While the films differ, they share the same goal: to depict the community of Fogo Island in a meaningful way.

Despite the lack of drama, or perhaps because of it, it was nice to sit in the room and watch the scenes unfold. The physical installation has lovely moments. Behind the block of ascending seats, photographs of children from the island stand solemnly at attention. The seven photographs are life-sized, a product of Lockhart’s open invitation to her makeshift studio on the island.

Similarly life-sized, the film is the same scale as the landscape it depicts. Lake Ontario, seen out the window, lines up with the coastline in the film. At one point, I walk past the screen to look out the window where a version of the film unfolds in real time. Someone is painting the mast of a ship docked in the water. A woman sits with her young baby watching birds fly past. Perhaps this is the beauty of the film; it lets you see art everywhere and with abandon.

On the other side of the Power Plant’s clerestory, which splits the two exhibitions, a very different scene unfolds. Canadian artist Zadie Xa works with her long-time collaborator, Benito Mayor Vallejo, to transport the viewer into another dimension in their exhibition, Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes. It’s as if I’ve become a player in a video game full of magical creatures, hidden treasures and shells that speak. Gone are all subtleties, and in their place, a room of jewel tones and a gold floor that reflects. I’ve a feeling we’re not in Fogo anymore.

The colours, sounds and characters ignite the imagination in a childlike way. Under this veneer of play, Xa explores heady issues of socio-political conditions and diasporic identities. She’s specifically interested in spotlighting narratives of Korean heritage that have been erased or repressed. This can be seen in the recurring motifs she paints: Korean patchwork quilting, matriarchal subjects, hybrid figures participating in the Korean spirit-cleansing dance, Salpuri.

Without that context, the exhibition reads much less serious on a casual walk-through.

There are two distinct painting styles in Moonlit Confessions Across Deep Sea Echoes . On one hand, heavily rendered depictions of anthropomorphs that wouldn’t be out of place in a pack of Magic: The Gathering cards. These are fantastical and rendered so precisely that they become less about the feat of application and more about the content. These land flat alongside canvases that embrace their materiality: patchworks of thickly applied paint that show their layers and span from simple still lifes to operatic tableaus. These are paintings you want to step into and stay a while.

Before you walk across the shiny gold floor, you’re asked to remove your shoes or put on foot covers. There’s something ingenuous about taking your shoes off in public. My immediate reaction was to hope that I was wearing nice socks. I wasn’t; they had holes. It turns out being barefoot is a great way to view art, providing a simple remove from everyday life.

Inside this room, a levitating conch made of bells is surrounded by four shells rigged to play audio, hugged by large-scale paintings. One shell gurgles and creaks. From another, a dial tone. A particularly spiky shell recites lines from Octavia E. Butler’s Parable of the Sower and Ursula K. Le Guin’s The Ones Who Walk Away from Omelas . A game of telephone with the sea ensues. This is world-building on full display.

Xa has created a world only accessible within the exhibition, whereas Lockhart’s muse is a plane and ferry ride away. Both artists have very different approaches to subtlety and immersion, which begs the question: What is art’s obligation to entertain? It’s my own fault, a side effect of today’s culture that feeds us content in 15-second batches, that I even think that should be a question. The goal, or art, isn’t to entertain, but to see the world differently. Both artists succeed, albeit for very different attention spans.

These are paintings you want to step into and stay a while.

Both artists have very different approaches to subtlety and immersion, which begs the question: What is art’s obligation to entertain? stories.title: 3 more charged in Guelph homecoming investigation, bringing arrests to 15
stories.summary: Three more people are facing charges in connection with September’s rowdy homecoming party near the University of Guelph.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Three more people are facing charges in connection with September’s rowdy homecoming party near the University of Guelph.

Fifteen people have been arrested so far, and police continue to search for more suspects.

The three new accused have been identified as men from York Region and Hamilton. They each face two counts of assault causing bodily harm and mischief under $5,000.

Twelve people arrested last week each face charges of assault with a weapon, causing a disturbance and two counts of mischief. One man faces an additional charge of assaulting a police officer with a weapon.

All the accused are between the ages of 17 and 26.

The Sept. 26 party drew up to 15,000 people and resulted in roughly $91,000 in policing costs, a report presented to the Guelph Police Service Board last month showed.

Video from the event showed partygoers throwing objects into large crowds, while students described glass bottles, metal water bottles, sticks and other debris being hurled through the air.

Some students told Global News they chose to leave when the situation escalated.

Police were out in full force during the gathering and eventually deployed tactical officers to help restore order.

Emergency responders treated multiple people for injuries, including cuts and lacerations, and responded to several intoxication-related medical calls.

The report identified 11 criminal incidents associated with the gathering, including seven assaults, one offensive weapons occurrence, one disturb-the-peace occurrence, one mischief involving public property and one mischief involving a vehicle.

Six arrests were made during the event. Four involved public intoxication, one involved an alleged assault and one involved causing a disturbance.

Roughly 70 provincial offence notices were issued as well, with most involving open liquor.

Four property damage reports were made, including damage to a Guelph Transit bus shelter, two vehicles on Chancellor’s Way and other personal property. Several businesses also filed complaints that remain under investigation, the report said.

The investigation remains ongoing.

Police have announced they’re forming a working group with the city, the University of Guelph and Guelph General Hospital to help manage large, unsanctioned gatherings.

stories.title: Watch Live: Road closures planned for Remembrance Day ceremony in London
stories.summary: Motorists should expect several road closures in downtown London on Remembrance Day as the city hosts its annual ceremony and parade.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Motorists should expect several road closures in downtown London on Remembrance Day as the city hosts its annual ceremony and parade.

The City of London says temporary closures will be in effect from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday to accommodate Remembrance Day events.

CTV News will livestream today’s ceremony starting around 10:45 a.m.

From 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m., the following roads will be closed:

Dufferin Avenue from Clarence Street to Picton Street.

Wellington Street from Central Avenue to Queens Avenue.

Additional closures will be in place from 10 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.:

Dundas Street from Wellington Street to Waterloo Street.

Waterloo Street from Dundas Street to Dufferin Avenue.

Dufferin Avenue from Waterloo Street to Clarence Street.

The city says access to the public parking garage at City Hall will remain available before the parade arrives at approximately 10:30 a.m.

Employees and visitors will be able to enter the garage by travelling westbound on Dufferin Avenue through the Waterloo Street intersection. However, access in and out of the garage will not be possible during the parade and ceremony.

stories.title: Remembrance Day: What, and who, Canada’s soldiers in Latvia are thinking of today
stories.summary: Members of the Canadian Armed Forces deployed thousands of kilometres from home are sharing their Remembrance Day reflections.
stories.author: Adrian Ghobrial
stories.content:
Camp Adazi, Latvia – Members of the Canadian Armed Forces deployed thousands of kilometres from home are sharing their Remembrance Day reflections.

“Sacrifice isn’t just measured in casualties in the military,” said Col. David Brassard, the Canadian commander of Nato’s Multinational Brigade in Latvia. “When our soldiers deploy here (to Latvia) for six months, they’re away from their families and loved ones. That’s a type of sacrifice we don’t talk about as much.”

CTV News spent the last week embedded with the multinational brigade in eastern Latvia along the border with Russia and Belarus. It is there that CTV News spoke with multiple soldiers about the personal sacrifice.

“I joined the military because I wanted to serve Canada,” said one Canadian commanding a Nato tank squadron.“We have a lot of freedoms, we’re very fortunate (in Canada) and we want to be able to protect that and help provide security for other countries.”

CTV News is withholding the names of some the service members interviewed for this story, to ensure their safety and security while on deployment in eastern Latvia.

“I’m here doing something meaningful, it’s meaningful to me as well,” said one Canadian lieutenant helping lead a battle brigade into a training exercise just 30 kilometres from the border of Belarus.

The memory of fallen comrades remains heavy for the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia.

The last name ‘Hornburg’ hangs along the side of a Canadian Leopard tank in honour of Cpl. Nathan Hornburg, who was killed in September 2007 in Afghanistan after he was hit by a mortar shell while fixing a tank west of Kandahar.

Troops in Latvia are also mourning those injured and killed by an October deadly fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright in Alberta. The unit at Wainwright had been training to deploy to Latvia and form a light infantry unit.

“There are always risks involved, even in training,” said Lt.-Col. Simon Mailloux, the commander of the brigade’s multinational infantry battle group.

“I’ve lost soldiers on a mission, and I was previously injured myself.”

Canadian soldiers in Latvia are training for any possibility with tensions running high between Nato and Russia. Adrian Ghobrial reports.

Mailloux, a 25-year veteran, was a platoon commander in Afghanistan when Pte. Simon Longtin was killed by an improvised explosive device (IED) in August 2007.

Three months later, another roadside bomb cost Mailloux part of his left leg and killed Cpl. Nicolas Beauchamp and Pte. Michel Lévesque.

“It’s still hard to process, even during Remembrance Day,” Mailloux said.”

Mailloux later became the first Canadian amputee to return to active duty in Afghanistan.

A Canadian commander is overseeing 3,000 troops as Canada takes a leadership role in Nato's defence mission in Latvia. Adrian Ghobrial takes a closer look.

Speaking to CTV National News just 30 kilometres from the Russian border, Mailloux says his current soldiers understand the gravity of their mission.

“We are here now, very close to a border (with Russia), my troops know it, they can feel it,” Mailloux said. “That’s what their job is asking of them right now.”

On this Remembrance Day, those we spoke with had messages to share with their loved ones back home. Many are sending their love and thanks to their parents, siblings, spouses and children.

Most Canadian soldiers in Latvia are here on a six-month deployment scheduled to end in December, leaving many looking forward to returning home for the holidays. Asked why they joined the Canadian Armed Forces, the majority of those who spoke to CTV News shared a similar thought, they love the military and they love their country.

stories.title: Remembrance Day ceremonies set to get underway in Ottawa
stories.summary: The National Remembrance Day ceremony is being held at the National War Memorial in downtown Ottawa, where Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to attend at 10:45 am Eastern.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Canadians across the country are marking Remembrance Day , honouring those who died in military service.

The National Remembrance Day ceremony is being held at the National War Memorial in downtown Ottawa, where Prime Minister Mark Carney is scheduled to attend at 10:45 a.m. Eastern.

The ceremony will begin with a veterans’ march, followed by the arrival of various dignitaries including the Speakers of the House of Commons and the Senate, the minister of veterans affairs, the chief of the defence staff, the Silver Cross Mother and the governor general, who will receive the vice-regal salute and inspect the assembled troops for the commemoration.

Global News will be streaming special live coverage of the national ceremony here.

The marching contingent is scheduled to form up at 10:10 a.m. Eastern, with the step off scheduled at 10:30 a.m.

The ceremony will conclude with the veterans’ march-past at 11:30 a.m. Eastern.

More to come.
