stories.title: Carney heading for summits in Ireland, Asia after Remembrance Day ceremony
stories.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he'll look to advance trade and security ties.
stories.author: Dylan Robertson and Caroline Plante
stories.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he’ll look to advance trade and security ties.

His travels will take him to four countries and put him on the ground as high-stakes diplomacy takes place between the United States, China and Russia.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the trip is Canada’s chance to build on new agreements and partnerships it has signed with countries around the world.

“We’re now entering a much more consequential phase of actually implementing and delivering on all of these agreements, and sustaining the momentum,” she said.

“When Prime Minister Carney speaks about diversifying our relationships, it’s not just about Europe.”

The prime minister is set to depart for Dublin shortly after the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa.

Carney will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, set for Nov. 12. For the second time, Canada will be the only non-European country represented at the table. Carney joined the group’s last meeting in Armenia in May.

The EPC summits have taken place roughly every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The informal meetings are aimed at discussing strategic co-operation in politics, security and infrastructure.

Carney and European Union leaders have floated Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU since the last summit — a title they have yet to define.

After Dublin, Carney will cross both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans to visit Manila, where the Philippines is hosting Canada as a guest at the Nov. 15–18 summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

Asean is a bloc of 11 countries that focuses on trade, regional peace and international norms. Canada is set to finalize negotiations on two trade deals while Carney is in Manila, one with the Asean bloc and another bilateral deal with the Philippines. He could even sign one of them while he’s there.

The prime minister has a meeting scheduled for Saturday with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and will address Asean leaders on Sunday.

Queen’s University professor Stéphanie Martel, who studies Southeast Asia and the Asia-Pacific, said the visit will help shape the Indo-Pacific strategy the Trudeau government released four years ago. That strategy focused on making Ottawa a relevant partner in the region after years of sporadic engagement.

“It’s becoming kind of a cliché to refer to Canada as this fairweather friend,” she said.

Martel said Carney has focused on trade and maritime defence but less on local concerns about climate change resilience and gender-inclusive militaries.

“There’s a lot of action in terms of specific trade deals and specific sectors. But the overall engagement and the ability of Canada to be seen as this serious, comprehensive contributor to the region is still up for debate,” she said.

In the Philippines, Carney will be joined by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and Gender Minister Rechie Valdez, who is of Filipino origin.

Carney will then visit the Francophonie summit in Cambodia set for Nov. 14 to 16. He’s expected to meet with leaders from Africa and other continents while in the capital Phnom Penh.

Canada is hosting the next Francophonie summit in 2028 in the Ottawa area. Carney is expected to use the gathering to advance Canada’s strategic autonomy and protect the role of French in the growing digital economy.

Francophonie members will elect their next leader in Cambodia and Ottawa says it is staying neutral to avoid affecting the next summit.

On Sunday, the prime minister is set to address CEOs at the FrancoTech innovation event at the summit. On Monday, he is set to give plenary remarks.

Dominique Caouette, Indo-Pacific studies chair at the University of Montreal’s political science department, said the Francophonie summit is an opportunity for Canada and Quebec to advance economic interests.

“The Francophonie could also serve as a platform for Mr. Carney toward the middle powers. There are several that are part of the Francophonie. It’s another space where Canada could play an influential role,” Caouette said in a French-language interview.

The summit will feature both Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who was elected on a sovereigntist mandate aimed at pushing back on Ottawa. Caouette said he doesn’t expect the two to clash.

“It’s not in the Canadian or Quebec tradition to air one’s dirty laundry in public,” he said.

Carney will be joined in Cambodia by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her parliamentary secretary Mona Fortier. Before his arrival, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will lead Canada’s delegation at the summit.

Carney’s last stop will be China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 to 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Nadjibulla said the summit allows for bilateral and “minilateral” discussions that bring leaders together in small groups to advance common goals. She said the Apec meetings themselves have taken on less importance, thanks to the diverging interests of Russia, the U.S. and China.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit.

The meeting has European leaders worried about a possible impact on Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Analysts are also watching for any updates on Trump’s war on Iran.

Carney’s visit will come just days after China extended a deal to provide market access to Canadian imports such as canola meal and lobster, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday and he will address business leaders the next day.

Nadjibulla said she’ll be watching for any economic announcements, such as a move to allow more Chinese vehicles into Canada or new Chinese investments in energy and technology.

“The warming, the recalibration of the relationship has been moving at a rapid pace,” Nadjibulla said, adding that any moves could affect trade talks with the U.S.

In China, Carney will be joined by his parliamentary secretary Kody Blois and Anand.

Carney is set to return to Ottawa on Nov. 19.

The federal Conservatives have criticized Carney’s overseas deals, arguing that the signed agreements have not yielded significant gains and are distracting the government’s attention from the affordability crisis.

The Liberals argue facetime between leaders is critical to diversifying trade and building more resilient supply chains and security partnerships.

stories.title: Schulich Medicine & Dentistry reflects on legacy of military service
stories.summary: From the First World War to today, Western students carry a legacy of military service through medicine and CAF training.
stories.author: Emily Leighton
stories.content:
In August 1916, a group of physicians, nurses and medical trainees from Western University sailed to England aboard the H.M. Troopship 2810.

Led by surgeon and anatomy professor Dr. Edwin Seaborn, the No. 10 Canadian Stationary Hospital would spend the next three years treating soldiers wounded on the frontlines of the First World War.

Though only 12 physicians were needed, more than 70 had volunteered.

“The organization of Stationary Hospital No. 10 has a serious bearing upon the work of Western University, drawing heavily upon faculty and students in all departments,” wrote Rev. Edward Ernest Braithwaite, Western’s president at the time.

In the decades that followed, military service became woven into Schulich School of Medicine & Dentistry’s history. The Medicine Class of 1950, known as the Veterans Class, was comprised entirely of veterans from the Second World War – an idea put forward by then dean of medicine Dr. Edward G. Hall, a veteran himself. More recently, Schulich & Medicine established the Office of Military Academic Medicine, strengthening partnerships in education, research and training.

Today, students like Jessica Girard and Michael Hutchison are writing the next chapter. As members of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) enrolled in the Military Medical Training Program (Mmtp), they are preparing to care for those who serve.

For more than a decade, Jessica Girard built a military career that took her from infantry training to maintaining CF-18 fighter jets.

But medicine was never far from her mind.

Growing up in Quebec, and later Peterborough, Ont., medicine was an ambition she carried through high school and into her undergraduate studies in forensic science at Trent University.

Along the way, she joined the reserves and quickly found a sense of purpose in military life.

Jessica Girard (Megan Morris/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

“I’ve always challenged gender stereotypes, and I found the military setting to be empowering,” she said. “Everyone was held to the same standard, men and women.”

Girard served in the Canadian Army and the Royal Canadian Air Force, eventually specializing as an aviation technician. She rose quickly through the ranks, earning the highest technician qualification, Level A, in record time.

An unexpected posting to an administrative position prompted her to revisit a dream she had set aside years earlier.

“Maybe this is the perfect opportunity to pursue medicine while staying under the umbrella of the military,” she recalled thinking.

Now in her third year of medical school, Girard says medicine offers the ideal combination of scientific discovery and patient care.

“I love understanding how things work,” she said. “Being able to use that knowledge to help people is incredibly rewarding.”

She has also found opportunities to bridge her military experience with health research.

Working with military surgeon and associate professor Dr. Rich Hilsden, Girard is studying how prolonged exposure to extreme cold affects menstruation among military personnel – research inspired by her own experience during an Arctic training exercise.

“I got to observe a phenomenon firsthand,” she said. “When I looked into whether it had been studied, it hadn’t.”

The project addresses a gap in knowledge about women serving in operational environments, an area she hopes to continue exploring throughout her career.

After residency, Girard will return to military service as a family physician.

By the time he arrived at medical school, Michael Hutchison had already built a career, raised a family and served in the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) as a military medic.

The first person in his family to attend university, he also earned an undergraduate degree while working full-time in the military.

Medicine had not always been part of the plan.

Michael Hutchison (Megan Morris/Schulich Medicine & Dentistry)

“I honestly thought medicine was out of reach for me,” he says. “I never considered it because I never thought I could get here.”

Growing up in London, Ont., Hutchison joined the army cadets at age 11, drawn to activities like camping and navigation. By 17, he enlisted in the reserves. Soon after high school, he left for Alberta to serve full-time as an infantry soldier.

Away from home for the first time, he began rethinking what he wanted from a career.

He returned to Ontario and spent months trying different jobs – construction, cooking and factory work – before rejoining the military as a medical technician, a role similar to a paramedic.

It would become a 15-year career.

Hutchison served across Canada and overseas, embracing every opportunity that came his way. He developed expertise in winter medicine, supporting military operations in some of the country’s most remote environments.

As his career progressed, he began exploring the military’s physician assistant pathway, which required post-secondary education. To qualify, he enrolled in Queen’s University’s online health sciences program as a mature student.

Encouraged by his wife, military colleagues and physician mentors, he applied to medical school through the Mmtp.

Now in his second year at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, he plans to return to military service as a family physician, ideally in Petawawa, where he and his family spent eight years building a life.

“I just love meeting people,” he said. “I pull on that one thread, ask the right question, and all of a sudden I get to know who they are.”

This story originally appeared in Rapport, Schulich Medicine & Dentistry’s alumni magazine, in the 2026 issue.

Growing up in London, Ont., Hutchison joined the army cadets at age 11, drawn to activities like camping and navigation. By 17, he enlisted in the reserves. Soon after high school, he left for Alberta to serve full-time as an infantry soldier.
Away from home for the first time, he began rethinking what he wanted from a career.
He returned to Ontario and spent months trying different jobs – construction, cooking and factory work – before rejoining the military as a medical technician, a role similar to a paramedic.
It would become a 15-year career.

Hutchison served across Canada and overseas, embracing every opportunity that came his way. He developed expertise in winter medicine, supporting military operations in some of the country’s most remote environments.

As his career progressed, he began exploring the military’s physician assistant pathway, which required post-secondary education. To qualify, he enrolled in Queen’s University’s online health sciences program as a mature student.
Encouraged by his wife, military colleagues and physician mentors, he applied to medical school through the Mmtp.
Now in his second year at Schulich Medicine & Dentistry, he plans to return to military service as a family physician, ideally in Petawawa, where he and his family spent eight years building a life.
“I just love meeting people,” he said. “I pull on that one thread, ask the right question, and all of a sudden I get to know who they are.”
This story originally appeared in Rapport, Schulich Medicine & Dentistry’s alumni magazine, in the 2026 issue.

stories.title: Remembrance Day live updates: Where to watch ceremonies, and what’s open and closed
stories.summary: This year marks the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion, founded in 1926 to create one main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits
stories.author: Globe staff
stories.content:
– Globe staff

The poppy is a symbol of remembrance that is worn to honour the veterans who have died in service, and is inspired by Canadian John McCrae’s famous poem, In Flanders Fields . The Royal Canadian Legion offers a guide on its website of the appropriate and respectful ways to wear a poppy, as well as how to dispose of it.

It is common to leave the poppy on the cenotaph or a wreath as a sign of respect at the end of a Remembrance Day ceremony. For example, thousands of poppies are placed on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Ottawa on Remembrance Day each year. Other ways to respectfully dispose of a poppy include storing it away or discarding it in the garbage or recycling after the Remembrance period ends on Nov. 11.

– Marcus Gee

In a corner of Toronto’s Prospect Cemetery, a collection of granite headstones stand in a broad lawn shaded by tall, old trees. Most bear the Maple Leaf logo that identifies them as fallen warriors of the First World War.

On a gentle fall afternoon last week, Helen Williams walked among them, stopping to scrape lichen from the stone. Facing budget and environmental constraints, the Commonwealth War Graves Commission put out a call for volunteer grave tenders last year, a program spokeswoman Katrielle Ethier says has been a “resounding success.”

More than 600 people have stepped up. Like sons and daughters caring for the resting place of a beloved parent, they look after the graves of long-dead warriors, scrubbing their headstones and trimming the weeds around their plots.

Williams, 59, joined the program just after her husband of nearly 40 years, Richard Williams, retired from the army. The couple were moved by the care put into war graves they visited around the world during Richard’s 36 years of service, and wanted to help make sure that fallen soldiers buried at home in Canada got the same measure of respect.

He says the work gives them the chance to honour those who gave their lives and to “make sure they’re remembered in some way, shape or form.” These Canadians made the “ultimate sacrifice,” he says, and we need to “reflect on that every time we get a chance.”

- Sarah Wallace

The history of Canada’s military medals is as storied as the country itself. Thousands of medals have been awarded for both military members and civilians since the country’s inception, and continue to be handed out today.

“The orders, decorations and medals that are awarded to Canadian military personnel are just one of the ways in which we honour the service and sacrifice of those who protect our country both at home and abroad,” said Caitlin Pilkington, a collection specialist for medals, ceremonial and photos at the Canadian War Museum.

“They can recognize outstanding achievements, acts of bravery and courage or service in a particular conflict or operation, but they can also commemorate important events in Canadian history or acknowledge long service and devotion to duty.”

From the Victoria Cross to the Sacrifice Medal, here’s a guide to six of the rare medals service members and civilians can earn, and what they represent.

- Alanna Smith

It’s been less than a month since a deadly fire swept through a Canadian military base, killing four soldiers and badly injuring 39 more.

As I found Wednesday, the recent tragedy made the Remembrance Day ceremonies in the adjacent town of Wainwright, Alta., where everyone has some connection to the military, that much more poignant.

– Mira Miller

When Maggie Burns suggested to friends at her local curling club that their town of Bobcaygeon, Ont., should knit and crochet poppies for Remembrance Day, she never imagined how it would take off.

Last January, 74-year-old Burns, and her friends Alison Williams and Andrea DeFalco, 61 and 71, kick-started the initiative, making a Facebook group to spread word of the project and share the patterns. The group has since grown to 449 members and helped to organize poppy-making events and local business participation.

Now, after almost a year of hard work, the town of just 3,576 people has made nearly 11,000 poppies. At the beginning of November, volunteers set up thousands of poppies on display at seven different locations throughout Bobcaygeon, where they’ll remain for all to admire until Nov. 15.

“The way everybody jumped on board, I was shocked, really,” Burns said. “The participation was just unbelievable.”

Read the full story .

– The Canadian Press

Two padres, also known as military chaplains, in Atlantic Canada led their Remembrance Day speeches on Wednesday with reflections on the recent deadly fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta.

In downtown Halifax, Padre Steven Cochrane honoured Canadian Armed Forces members and the sacrifices they make during training exercises, pointing in particular to members in Wainwright.

Padre Stephen Courtney led his speech at the National War Memorial in St. John’s, N.L., with a reflection on the four soldiers killed in the fire, and the dozens of others who were hurt there.

“We remember those who died, the injured, especially those who remain in hospital at this time,” Courtney said to a quiet crowd of hundreds. “We remember the families.”

– Arisa Valyear

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty expressed his “heartfelt condolences” to the family of the pilot who died Wednesday in a crash near Saint-Georges, Que. The plane had been part of a Remembrance Day ceremony nearby.

“My heartfelt condolences go out to his family and loved ones. My thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy,” he wrote in a statement on X.

Retired lieutenant-colonel Colin Robinson, who attended the ceremony at Place du Canada in downtown Montreal, said Remembrance Day is an opportunity for Canadians to reflect on the dangers of war, particularly amid current global tensions.

“These things can spiral out of control relatively quickly,” he said, drawing parallels between the events leading up to the two world wars and the state of the world today.

“I think that sense of awareness will probably lead to us having less conflict and less war.”

A military parade was followed by the national anthem shortly before 11 a.m., with some in the crowd of around one hundred people singing along as bells rang from nearby St. George’s Anglican Church.

A 21-gun salute echoed through the area, sending flocks of birds into the sky, as bagpipes played near the war memorial.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he was “deeply saddened” to hear a plane had crashed after it participated in a Remembrance Day ceremony in Beauce, Que., on Wednesday.

“My heartfelt condolences go to the family and loved ones of the pilot who lost his life. My thoughts and prayers are with all those affected, and I thank the first responders who were on the scene,” he said in a post on X.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow commemorated the Legion on its 100th anniversary during her remarks at a ceremony at Toronto’s Old City Hall.

“The Legion shows us the city we can be. A city where no one carries the burden alone. A city where we take care of each other and stand up for each other ,” she said.

Earlier this morning in British Columbia, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson posted a statement of remembrance on X to commemorate “those who served our country, those who sacrificed, and those who never came home.”

“The debt we owe those who served can never truly be repaid,” Doerkson said in the post . “But we can honour them by caring for our veterans, supporting the members of the Canadian Armed Forces and their families, and never taking for granted the peace, freedom and democracy they helped secure.”

South of the border, Rear-Admiral Kristjan Monaghan spoke at the Canadian Embassy on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., about those who died in Alberta last month.

“The loss experienced there has been felt across the Canadian Forces family, across the nation and beyond,” Monaghan said.

“It reminds us that sacrifice is not defined solely by geography. Service members accept risks, not only when deployed overseas but also while preparing themselves to serve their country.”

- Maura Forrest

A pilot has died after a plane involved in a Remembrance Day ceremony crashed south of Quebec City, in the province’s Beauce region.

Provincial police confirmed the death of a man in his 60s after they were called to the site around 11 a.m. on Wednesday.

Spokesperson Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said the crash occurred in a wooded area near the airport in Saint-Georges, a small city about 100 kilometres from the provincial capital. The pilot was pronounced dead at the scene.

In a statement posted to social media , the city of Saint-Georges said the pilot had just participated in a Remembrance Day ceremony and was preparing to land when it crashed and caught fire.

“What has just happened is truly sad and terrible,” Saint-Georges Mayor Manon Bougie said in the statement. “Our hearts go out to the family and loved ones affected by this tragedy. All our thoughts and prayers are with them at this time.”

Sgt. Bilodeau said she believed the plane was a private aircraft and that the pilot was not a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was alone in the plane, she added, and no one else was injured.

Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, shared his condolences to the family of the pilot who died in a crash earlier Wednesday south of Quebec City. The plane was supposed to take part in Remembrance Day ceremonies today, according to Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.

In a statement posted to X, Milliard said his thoughts were with those affected by the crash.

Quebec provincial police confirmed one person is dead after a plane crashed south of Quebec City at around 11 a.m.

Police say there was only one person aboard the aircraft and they were declared dead at the scene.

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon identifies the victim as the pilot and the plane as one scheduled to take part in Remembrance Day commemorations on Wednesday.

Police spokesperson Frédéric Deshaies said the crash happened near St-Georges-de-Beauce, in the Chaudière-Appalaches region south of the provincial capital.

St-Pierre Plamondon says he is working with the province’s domestic security minister to gather more information on the crash.

The pilot of a plane set to be used for Remembrance Day commemorations has died after the aircraft crashed, according to a post by Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on X.

“I would like to extend my sincere condolences to his family and loved ones,” Plamondon wrote.

Quebec Police say there was only one person aboard the aircraft.

In an earlier social media post, Plamondon said the aircraft crashed in St-Georges-de-Beauce, south of Quebec City, earlier this morning and the situation is being closely monitored.

At a ceremony outside Queen’s Park, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said this Remembrance Day “is especially poignant” after the devastating fire last month at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in.

“I want to thank all the heroic Ontario health care workers who were deployed to support recovery efforts and continue to pray for those impacted by the fire,” he said while attending one of several ceremonies held in Toronto.

“Whether it’s a family member or a friend who answered the call to serve, or someone who came home with wounds, visible and invisible, Remembrance Day holds a special meaning for each of us.”

At least 2,000 people have lined a street in downtown St. Albert, Alta., to pay their respects at a Remembrance Day service.

More than 300 members of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry marched to the service, along with cadets and RCMP officers.

The regiment was taking part in attack training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month, when wind whipped a grass fire into a group of soldiers.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the blaze.

Thirty-nine others were injured, and many are still recovering in hospital.

A moment of silence is held in Alberta, where there is extra attention on Remembrance Day in that province after a wildfire killed four soldiers at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month during a training exercise and injured dozens more.

They were Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

As the sun rose into the sky, with birds flying overhead, two wreaths were carefully placed at the base of the Wainwright Memorial Clock Tower on Wednesday morning.

Dozens of locals, many with red poppies pinned to their collars, watched as members of the local legion and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took a moment of silence in front of the commemorative arrangements.

A short distance away, hundreds were filling into the Peace Memorial Multiplex for the community’s Remembrance Day ceremony.

Guns boomed, bagpipes wailed and CF-18 Hornets thundered overhead as Canadians paused at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Wednesday to remember those who served and died defending this country.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said this year’s service carries extra weight because it comes just weeks after the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Wainwright.

“Our thoughts remain with the soldiers we lost, those who were wounded, as well as the families, friends, comrades and all others affected by this tragic event,” Arbour said.

“Such moments remind us that behind every uniform is a human being: someone who serves with dedication, accepts risk on behalf of others and is supported by loved ones who share in the sacrifices that service often demands.”

Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch his son march in his first Remembrance Day parade as a member of the Canadian Armed Forces after joining last year.

“My father was in World War II, my mother was in World War II, I served for about 28 years in the Hastings and Prince Edward Regiment, and he thought it was just time for him to pay a little price for Canadians to be free,” he said.

Virginia Hicks, this year’s Silver Cross mother , arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony to lay a wreath on behalf of all mothers who have lost children in military service.

Her daughter, Sapper Mareibeth Short, was killed in a training exercise on Sept. 23, 2002 in Petawawa, Ont.

Hicks is a veteran herself, working in supply and logistics for 29 years.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith released a video message ahead of the province’s Remembrance Day ceremonies, saying it was a “civic duty” to remember the veterans who have served in Canada.

“Wearing a uniform from the Canadian Armed Forces is a declaration that you will lay down your life for the values of this nation,” she said in the video.

At the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, Canadians gathered at the National War Memorial in Ottawa are pausing for a moment of silence to remember those who served and died defending this country.

The Last Post is a traditional military bugle call that is used at military funerals and at ceremonies commemorating those who have died in battle. It signifies the calling home of the spirits of fallen soldiers to rest.

It was originally played to signal to soldiers that the camp was secured for the night. It was also played to call out to wounded or separated soldiers at the end of a battle, to guide them home to safety.

For Remembrance Day ceremonies, a bugler plays the Last Post and the last note marks the beginning of the two minutes of silence.

Governor-General Louise Arbour arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa, her first as commander-in-chief. Arbour is wearing a uniform. The governor general always wears a military uniform for the ceremony.

– Stephanie Levitz

Prime Minister Mark Carney and his wife, Diana Fox Carney, have arrived at the National War Memorial on this chilly but bright morning in Ottawa.

In a statement to mark Remembrance Day, the Prime Minister paid tribute specifically to the four soldiers killed in the accident at CFB Wainwright, as well as the generations of women and men who have served in the military.

“In an increasingly dangerous and divided world, our rights and freedoms do not defend themselves,” Carney said in his statement.

“They are earned every single day. Our remembrance is more than an expression of gratitude. It is an act of vigilance and determination. And it is a promise: that what they defended, we will defend; that what they won, we will keep, forever cherish and pass on.”

– Erin Anderssen

Every year, Virginia Hicks places red roses in the branches of a lonely maple tree growing on the Mattawa Plains at CFB Petawawa in Ontario.

The tree marks the place where her daughter, 22-year-old Private Mariebeth Short, died in 2002 during a training exercise while serving as a sapper in the 2 Combat Engineer Regiment. Mrs. Hicks remembers seeing the little sapling, randomly sprouting in the grass when she visited the site the day after the accident. Now bushy and tall, the maple is waiting there every Sept. 23, when she returns with flowers and memories.

This year, Royal Canadian Legion chose Mrs. Hicks, a veteran herself, to be Canada’s Silver Cross Mother. On Remembrance Day, the retired sergeant from Trenton, Ont., will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa.

She will kneel there for a moment, she says, and think about her daughter and what she might have accomplished. She’ll think about all the military families, past and present, grieving sons and daughters.

In a video message honouring veterans, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the “cost of service has been brought home” in the wake of the Wainwright fire.

Poilievre also makes special mention of soldiers who served and died in Afghanistan on the 25th anniversary of the start of that conflict.

Poilievre’s Alberta riding includes the community of Wainwright.

A Remembrance Day procession has arrived at the National War Memorial in Ottawa, beginning with military marching bands and a veterans march. Thousands of people line the streets to watch the ceremony.

The program includes a playing of the Last Post and two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. ET. At approximately 11 a.m. ET, there will be a 21-gun salute fired from the east side of Parliament Hill, near the Rideau Canal.

CF-18 fighter jets and a Black Hawk helicopter will perform flypasts over the national ceremony.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Governor-General Louise Arbour and Silver Cross Mother Virginia Hicks will all lay wreaths at the National War Memorial.

Hicks lost her daughter during a training incident at CFB Petawawa in 2002. She was chosen by the Royal Canadian Legion months before the Wainwright accident took place.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford issued a statement ahead of the province’s Remembrance Day ceremonies, saying that his government had introduced new guidelines for teachers to help students understand the significance of the day.

“As the years pass, it’s more important than ever that their stories of selflessness and bravery are passed on to Ontario’s young people,” Ford said in the statement.

Some of the guidelines include encouraging students to wear poppies and that school flags should be lowered to half-mast - things most schools already implement. The new guidelines also outline specific lessons and themes by grade.

Shortly after the fatal blaze at CFB Wainwright, Chelsey McBride went into a wooded area near her home to cut down limbs and branches from trees, taking “from Mother Nature for what it took from the fire.”

She then hand wired each piece of greenery to a metal mannequin to form a dress and train before meticulously covering it with roughly 250 red silk poppies. Attached to a black bow that drapes across the skirt are also four white flowers, one each for the soldiers killed on Oct. 17 - Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

The figure, which McBride calls “Poppy,” is displayed outside of her shop, the Wainwright Flower Cart in the town’s centre. She says it is a symbol of remembrance, love and the lives that will not be forgotten.

Holding back tears, McBride said the fire has rattled the close-knit community, especially those who saw firsthand the horrific injuries suffered by soldiers. She said many questions must still be answered surrounding the tragic event.

Municipalities across Canada – in smaller communities and major cities – such as Toronto , Ottawa , Edmonton , Vancouver , Victoria and Montreal – are set to hold Remembrance Day ceremonies to honour Canada’s fallen soldiers. The local ceremonies will take place at city halls, universities, schools, city cenotaphs and war memorials.

The Royal Canadian Legion will hold ceremonies at local branches across the country and worldwide. You can use their locator tool to find your local Remembrance Day ceremony. Most provinces or local municipalities also share a map or list of locations for this year’s events on their websites.

Canadian and Allied forces landed at Normandy on June 6, 1944. Jim Parks, with the Royal Winnipeg Rifles, was among those storming Juno Beach. He would go on to fight in numerous bat…

Good morning, I’m Alanna Smith, an Alberta-based Globe reporter. I’m in Wainwright, a small prairie town southeast of Edmonton where Remembrance Day is taking on new meaning after a fatal fire last month killed four soldiers and injured dozens at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

The town of Wainwright and the Canadian military have a rich history stretching back nearly a century. Later this morning, flowers and wreaths will be placed under the town centre’s Memorial Clock Tower, a monument dedicated to Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.

Dignitaries, including CFB Wainwright Base Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Dustin MacLeod and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, are to deliver remarks at a ceremony hosted by the local legion after the wreath laying.

“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told The Canadian Press on Tuesday. “I get a sense that things will never be the same.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a Remembrance Day message saying “rights and freedoms do not defend themselves” in an increasingly “dangerous and divided world.”

He said Remembrance Day is about honouring those who stepped up to serve their country through the generations. He also read the names of the victims of the Wainwright fire: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Carney said.

In Canada, Remembrance Day is a federal statutory holiday, meaning workers and employees of federal government organizations receive the day off with pay. Provinces and territories that also recognize Remembrance Day as a paid statutory holiday include British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Yukon.

In Ontario and Quebec, Nov. 11 is considered a regular work day for most private-sector workers and provincial government employees.

Manitoba and Nova Scotia have distinct legislation that regulates what types of businesses can and can’t operate on Remembrance Day. Manitoba’s Remembrance Day Act , for example, stipulates that most industries must shut down operations for the day, excluding essential services such as hospitals, emergency responders, some trade workers, restaurants and hotels. Retailers are permitted to remain open in Manitoba, but cannot operate between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. The Remembrance Day Act in Nova Scotia provides similar exceptions for essential services, but most grocery stores, retailers and malls must close.

Marches and ceremonies are planned across Atlantic Canada on Wednesday to honour those lost in battle.

In downtown St. John’s, N.L., a sombre parade is scheduled to arrive at Newfoundland’s National War Memorial before a ceremony and a moment of silence at 11 a.m.

The annual event attracts hundreds of people in a place deeply marked by its military history.

In Halifax, people will gather downtown at the Grand Parade square, and at legions and cenotaphs across the regional municipality.

Events are also scheduled throughout New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, including TD Station in Saint John and and the cenotaph in Charlottetown.

Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise are among those being honoured Wednesday at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Wainwright, Alta.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend along with other dignitaries, military members and veterans.

On Oct. 17, a strong wind sent flames from a grass fire racing onto troops at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright , southeast of Edmonton.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s annual Remembrance Day service is expected to be the most solemn one in its recent history.

Roughly 300 members of the regiment are set to attend a Remembrance Day service in St. Albert, a bedroom community northwest of Edmonton.

The military says they are to march in a parade to the city’s cenotaph. There will also be a memorial Air Force flypast.

Banks, Canada Post, Service Canada, passport offices, Parliament and other federal government offices are all closed across the country on Nov. 11.

Grocery stores and other retailers may be open in some provinces and territories including Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, potentially with reduced hours. For the most up to date information, consult official provincial and municipal websites, and call local businesses to verify correct hours of operation.

Remembrance Day is commemorated on Nov. 11 to mark the signing of the armistice to cease First World War hostilities at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918.

This year marks the 81st anniversary of the end of the Second World War. It is also the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion , which celebrates a century of service to Canadian veterans and military families since it was officially incorporated by Parliament on July 17, 1926.

Remembrance Day, also called Armistice Day, is celebrated in the U.K., France, Belgium and many Commonwealth countries. In the United States, it is called Veterans’ Day.

Canadians will mark this year’s Remembrance Day with a series of ceremonies and events across the country, including two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. local time.

The Royal Canadian Legion has organized a national Remembrance Day service at the National War Memorial in Ottawa. The ceremony begins at approximately 10:30 a.m. with a program that includes a veterans’ march, a playing of the Last Post , two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. ET and a 21-gun salute.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Governor-General Louise Arbour and Minister of Veterans Affairs Jill McKnight are expected to attend and take part in the wreath-placing ceremony. This year’s National Silver Cross Mother is Virginia Hicks, who will place a wreath on behalf of all Canadian mothers who have lost a child in military service to Canada.

Road closures around the National War Memorial will affect traffic and OC Transpo service before and during the Remembrance Day ceremony.

The national ceremony will be live-streamed on the Legion’s Facebook page , and will also be shown on TV by Canada’s national news networks.

Canadians across the country are gathering Wednesday to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.

Canadians will mark 25 years since the start of the Afghanistan war, a conflict in which 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members served and 159 lost their lives.

The Afghanistan conflict, which lasted more than 12 years, was the longest in Canadian history and saw the largest deployment of Canadian troops since the Second World War.

Three Second World War veterans are expected to attend the ceremony in Ottawa and Prime Minister Mark Carney, Govenor-General Louise Arbour and other dignitaries will lay wreaths at the National War Memorial.

CF-18 fighter jets and a Black Hawk helicopter will perform flypasts over the national ceremony, while Griffon, Chinook and Cormorant helicopters and other RCAF aircraft will conduct flyovers at local ceremonies across the country.

This year is also the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion – founded in 1926 to create one main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits – and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.

Some 300 cadets are expected to attend the parade to mark that anniversary, which is about 200 more cadets than usual.

Padre Stephen Courtney led his speech at the National War Memorial in St. John’s, N.L., with a reflection on the four soldiers killed in the fire, and the dozens of others who were hurt there.
“We remember those who died, the injured, especially those who remain in hospital at this time,” Courtney said to a quiet crowd of hundreds. “We remember the families.”
– Arisa Valyear

Minister of National Defence David McGuinty expressed his “heartfelt condolences” to the family of the pilot who died Wednesday in a crash near Saint-Georges, Que. The plane had been part of a Remembrance Day ceremony nearby.
“My heartfelt condolences go out to his family and loved ones. My thoughts are with everyone affected by this tragedy,” he wrote in a statement on X.

Retired lieutenant-colonel Colin Robinson, who attended the ceremony at Place du Canada in downtown Montreal, said Remembrance Day is an opportunity for Canadians to reflect on the dangers of war, particularly amid current global tensions.
“These things can spiral out of control relatively quickly,” he said, drawing parallels between the events leading up to the two world wars and the state of the world today.
“I think that sense of awareness will probably lead to us having less conflict and less war.”
A military parade was followed by the national anthem shortly before 11 a.m., with some in the crowd of around one hundred people singing along as bells rang from nearby St. George’s Anglican Church.
A 21-gun salute echoed through the area, sending flocks of birds into the sky, as bagpipes played near the war memorial.
Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said he was “deeply saddened” to hear a plane had crashed after it participated in a Remembrance Day ceremony in Beauce, Que., on Wednesday.

“My heartfelt condolences go to the family and loved ones of the pilot who lost his life. My thoughts and prayers are with all those affected, and I thank the first responders who were on the scene,” he said in a post on X.
Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow commemorated the Legion on its 100th anniversary during her remarks at a ceremony at Toronto’s Old City Hall.
“The Legion shows us the city we can be. A city where no one carries the burden alone. A city where we take care of each other and stand up for each other ,” she said.

Earlier this morning in British Columbia, premier-designate Lorne Doerkson posted a statement of remembrance on X to commemorate “those who served our country, those who sacrificed, and those who never came home.”

“The debt we owe those who served can never truly be repaid,” Doerkson said in the post . “But we can honour them by caring for our veterans, supporting the members of the Canadian Armed Forces and their families, and never taking for granted the peace, freedom and democracy they helped secure.”
South of the border, Rear-Admiral Kristjan Monaghan spoke at the Canadian Embassy on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., about those who died in Alberta last month.
“The loss experienced there has been felt across the Canadian Forces family, across the nation and beyond,” Monaghan said.
“It reminds us that sacrifice is not defined solely by geography. Service members accept risks, not only when deployed overseas but also while preparing themselves to serve their country.”
- Maura Forrest
A pilot has died after a plane involved in a Remembrance Day ceremony crashed south of Quebec City, in the province’s Beauce region.
Provincial police confirmed the death of a man in his 60s after they were called to the site around 11 a.m. on Wednesday.

Spokesperson Sergeant Audrey-Anne Bilodeau said the crash occurred in a wooded area near the airport in Saint-Georges, a small city about 100 kilometres from the provincial capital. The pilot was pronounced dead at the scene.
In a statement posted to social media , the city of Saint-Georges said the pilot had just participated in a Remembrance Day ceremony and was preparing to land when it crashed and caught fire.

“What has just happened is truly sad and terrible,” Saint-Georges Mayor Manon Bougie said in the statement. “Our hearts go out to the family and loved ones affected by this tragedy. All our thoughts and prayers are with them at this time.”

Sgt. Bilodeau said she believed the plane was a private aircraft and that the pilot was not a member of the Royal Canadian Air Force. He was alone in the plane, she added, and no one else was injured.

Charles Milliard, leader of the Quebec Liberal Party, shared his condolences to the family of the pilot who died in a crash earlier Wednesday south of Quebec City. The plane was supposed to take part in Remembrance Day ceremonies today, according to Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon.
In a statement posted to X, Milliard said his thoughts were with those affected by the crash.
Quebec provincial police confirmed one person is dead after a plane crashed south of Quebec City at around 11 a.m.
Police say there was only one person aboard the aircraft and they were declared dead at the scene.
Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon identifies the victim as the pilot and the plane as one scheduled to take part in Remembrance Day commemorations on Wednesday.
Police spokesperson Frédéric Deshaies said the crash happened near St-Georges-de-Beauce, in the Chaudière-Appalaches region south of the provincial capital.
St-Pierre Plamondon says he is working with the province’s domestic security minister to gather more information on the crash.
The pilot of a plane set to be used for Remembrance Day commemorations has died after the aircraft crashed, according to a post by Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon on X.
“I would like to extend my sincere condolences to his family and loved ones,” Plamondon wrote.
Quebec Police say there was only one person aboard the aircraft.
In an earlier social media post, Plamondon said the aircraft crashed in St-Georges-de-Beauce, south of Quebec City, earlier this morning and the situation is being closely monitored.
At a ceremony outside Queen’s Park, Ontario Premier Doug Ford said this Remembrance Day “is especially poignant” after the devastating fire last month at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in.

“I want to thank all the heroic Ontario health care workers who were deployed to support recovery efforts and continue to pray for those impacted by the fire,” he said while attending one of several ceremonies held in Toronto.
“Whether it’s a family member or a friend who answered the call to serve, or someone who came home with wounds, visible and invisible, Remembrance Day holds a special meaning for each of us.”
At least 2,000 people have lined a street in downtown St. Albert, Alta., to pay their respects at a Remembrance Day service.
More than 300 members of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry marched to the service, along with cadets and RCMP officers.
The regiment was taking part in attack training at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month, when wind whipped a grass fire into a group of soldiers.
Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the blaze.
Thirty-nine others were injured, and many are still recovering in hospital.

A moment of silence is held in Alberta, where there is extra attention on Remembrance Day in that province after a wildfire killed four soldiers at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright last month during a training exercise and injured dozens more.
They were Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.
As the sun rose into the sky, with birds flying overhead, two wreaths were carefully placed at the base of the Wainwright Memorial Clock Tower on Wednesday morning.

Dozens of locals, many with red poppies pinned to their collars, watched as members of the local legion and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre took a moment of silence in front of the commemorative arrangements.
A short distance away, hundreds were filling into the Peace Memorial Multiplex for the community’s Remembrance Day ceremony.
Guns boomed, bagpipes wailed and CF-18 Hornets thundered overhead as Canadians paused at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Wednesday to remember those who served and died defending this country.
Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said this year’s service carries extra weight because it comes just weeks after the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Wainwright.
“Our thoughts remain with the soldiers we lost, those who were wounded, as well as the families, friends, comrades and all others affected by this tragic event,” Arbour said.

“Such moments remind us that behind every uniform is a human being: someone who serves with dedication, accepts risk on behalf of others and is supported by loved ones who share in the sacrifices that service often demands.”
Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch his son march in his first Remembrance Day parade as a member of the Canadian Armed Forces after joining last year.

“My father was in World War II, my mother was in World War II, I served for about 28 years in the Hastings and Prince Edward Regiment, and he thought it was just time for him to pay a little price for Canadians to be free,” he said.
Virginia Hicks, this year’s Silver Cross mother , arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony to lay a wreath on behalf of all mothers who have lost children in military service.
Her daughter, Sapper Mareibeth Short, was killed in a training exercise on Sept. 23, 2002 in Petawawa, Ont.
Hicks is a veteran herself, working in supply and logistics for 29 years.
Alberta Premier Danielle Smith released a video message ahead of the province’s Remembrance Day ceremonies, saying it was a “civic duty” to remember the veterans who have served in Canada.
“Wearing a uniform from the Canadian Armed Forces is a declaration that you will lay down your life for the values of this nation,” she said in the video.

At the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, Canadians gathered at the National War Memorial in Ottawa are pausing for a moment of silence to remember those who served and died defending this country.

The Last Post is a traditional military bugle call that is used at military funerals and at ceremonies commemorating those who have died in battle. It signifies the calling home of the spirits of fallen soldiers to rest.

It was originally played to signal to soldiers that the camp was secured for the night. It was also played to call out to wounded or separated soldiers at the end of a battle, to guide them home to safety.
For Remembrance Day ceremonies, a bugler plays the Last Post and the last note marks the beginning of the two minutes of silence.

Governor-General Louise Arbour arrives at the national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa, her first as commander-in-chief. Arbour is wearing a uniform. The governor general always wears a military uniform for the ceremony.
– Stephanie Levitz
Prime Minister Mark Carney and his wife, Diana Fox Carney, have arrived at the National War Memorial on this chilly but bright morning in Ottawa.

In a statement to mark Remembrance Day, the Prime Minister paid tribute specifically to the four soldiers killed in the accident at CFB Wainwright, as well as the generations of women and men who have served in the military.
“In an increasingly dangerous and divided world, our rights and freedoms do not defend themselves,” Carney said in his statement.

“They are earned every single day. Our remembrance is more than an expression of gratitude. It is an act of vigilance and determination. And it is a promise: that what they defended, we will defend; that what they won, we will keep, forever cherish and pass on.”
– Erin Anderssen
Every year, Virginia Hicks places red roses in the branches of a lonely maple tree growing on the Mattawa Plains at CFB Petawawa in Ontario.

The tree marks the place where her daughter, 22-year-old Private Mariebeth Short, died in 2002 during a training exercise while serving as a sapper in the 2 Combat Engineer Regiment. Mrs. Hicks remembers seeing the little sapling, randomly sprouting in the grass when she visited the site the day after the accident. Now bushy and tall, the maple is waiting there every Sept. 23, when she returns with flowers and memories.

This year, Royal Canadian Legion chose Mrs. Hicks, a veteran herself, to be Canada’s Silver Cross Mother. On Remembrance Day, the retired sergeant from Trenton, Ont., will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial in Ottawa.

She will kneel there for a moment, she says, and think about her daughter and what she might have accomplished. She’ll think about all the military families, past and present, grieving sons and daughters.
In a video message honouring veterans, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre says the “cost of service has been brought home” in the wake of the Wainwright fire.
Poilievre also makes special mention of soldiers who served and died in Afghanistan on the 25th anniversary of the start of that conflict.
Poilievre’s Alberta riding includes the community of Wainwright.

A Remembrance Day procession has arrived at the National War Memorial in Ottawa, beginning with military marching bands and a veterans march. Thousands of people line the streets to watch the ceremony.

The program includes a playing of the Last Post and two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. ET. At approximately 11 a.m. ET, there will be a 21-gun salute fired from the east side of Parliament Hill, near the Rideau Canal.
CF-18 fighter jets and a Black Hawk helicopter will perform flypasts over the national ceremony.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, Governor-General Louise Arbour and Silver Cross Mother Virginia Hicks will all lay wreaths at the National War Memorial.
Hicks lost her daughter during a training incident at CFB Petawawa in 2002. She was chosen by the Royal Canadian Legion months before the Wainwright accident took place.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford issued a statement ahead of the province’s Remembrance Day ceremonies, saying that his government had introduced new guidelines for teachers to help students understand the significance of the day.
“As the years pass, it’s more important than ever that their stories of selflessness and bravery are passed on to Ontario’s young people,” Ford said in the statement.

Some of the guidelines include encouraging students to wear poppies and that school flags should be lowered to half-mast - things most schools already implement. The new guidelines also outline specific lessons and themes by grade.

Shortly after the fatal blaze at CFB Wainwright, Chelsey McBride went into a wooded area near her home to cut down limbs and branches from trees, taking “from Mother Nature for what it took from the fire.”

She then hand wired each piece of greenery to a metal mannequin to form a dress and train before meticulously covering it with roughly 250 red silk poppies. Attached to a black bow that drapes across the skirt are also four white flowers, one each for the soldiers killed on Oct. 17 - Sergeant Morgan Wong, Private Shaun Farrell, Private Aidan Goulding and Private Hayden Lykkemark.

The figure, which McBride calls “Poppy,” is displayed outside of her shop, the Wainwright Flower Cart in the town’s centre. She says it is a symbol of remembrance, love and the lives that will not be forgotten.

Holding back tears, McBride said the fire has rattled the close-knit community, especially those who saw firsthand the horrific injuries suffered by soldiers. She said many questions must still be answered surrounding the tragic event.

Municipalities across Canada – in smaller communities and major cities – such as Toronto , Ottawa , Edmonton , Vancouver , Victoria and Montreal – are set to hold Remembrance Day ceremonies to honour Canada’s fallen soldiers. The local ceremonies will take place at city halls, universities, schools, city cenotaphs and war memorials.

The Royal Canadian Legion will hold ceremonies at local branches across the country and worldwide. You can use their locator tool to find your local Remembrance Day ceremony. Most provinces or local municipalities also share a map or list of locations for this year’s events on their websites.

Good morning, I’m Alanna Smith, an Alberta-based Globe reporter. I’m in Wainwright, a small prairie town southeast of Edmonton where Remembrance Day is taking on new meaning after a fatal fire last month killed four soldiers and injured dozens at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

The town of Wainwright and the Canadian military have a rich history stretching back nearly a century. Later this morning, flowers and wreaths will be placed under the town centre’s Memorial Clock Tower, a monument dedicated to Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.

Dignitaries, including CFB Wainwright Base Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Dustin MacLeod and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, are to deliver remarks at a ceremony hosted by the local legion after the wreath laying.
“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh told The Canadian Press on Tuesday. “I get a sense that things will never be the same.”
Prime Minister Mark Carney issued a Remembrance Day message saying “rights and freedoms do not defend themselves” in an increasingly “dangerous and divided world.”

He said Remembrance Day is about honouring those who stepped up to serve their country through the generations. He also read the names of the victims of the Wainwright fire: Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding, and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark.

“With their bright futures still before them, they chose to safeguard ours. We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Carney said.

In Canada, Remembrance Day is a federal statutory holiday, meaning workers and employees of federal government organizations receive the day off with pay. Provinces and territories that also recognize Remembrance Day as a paid statutory holiday include British Columbia, Alberta, Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Prince Edward Island, Northwest Territories, Nunavut and Yukon.
In Ontario and Quebec, Nov. 11 is considered a regular work day for most private-sector workers and provincial government employees.

Manitoba and Nova Scotia have distinct legislation that regulates what types of businesses can and can’t operate on Remembrance Day. Manitoba’s Remembrance Day Act , for example, stipulates that most industries must shut down operations for the day, excluding essential services such as hospitals, emergency responders, some trade workers, restaurants and hotels. Retailers are permitted to remain open in Manitoba, but cannot operate between 9 a.m. and 1 p.m. The Remembrance Day Act in Nova Scotia provides similar exceptions for essential services, but most grocery stores, retailers and malls must close.
Marches and ceremonies are planned across Atlantic Canada on Wednesday to honour those lost in battle.
In downtown St. John’s, N.L., a sombre parade is scheduled to arrive at Newfoundland’s National War Memorial before a ceremony and a moment of silence at 11 a.m.
The annual event attracts hundreds of people in a place deeply marked by its military history.
In Halifax, people will gather downtown at the Grand Parade square, and at legions and cenotaphs across the regional municipality.
Events are also scheduled throughout New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island, including TD Station in Saint John and and the cenotaph in Charlottetown.
Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise are among those being honoured Wednesday at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Wainwright, Alta.
Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to attend along with other dignitaries, military members and veterans.
On Oct. 17, a strong wind sent flames from a grass fire racing onto troops at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright , southeast of Edmonton.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.
Wainwright Mayor Bruce Pugh said the town’s annual Remembrance Day service is expected to be the most solemn one in its recent history.
Roughly 300 members of the regiment are set to attend a Remembrance Day service in St. Albert, a bedroom community northwest of Edmonton.
The military says they are to march in a parade to the city’s cenotaph. There will also be a memorial Air Force flypast.
Banks, Canada Post, Service Canada, passport offices, Parliament and other federal government offices are all closed across the country on Nov. 11.

Grocery stores and other retailers may be open in some provinces and territories including Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan, potentially with reduced hours. For the most up to date information, consult official provincial and municipal websites, and call local businesses to verify correct hours of operation.
Remembrance Day is commemorated on Nov. 11 to mark the signing of the armistice to cease First World War hostilities at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month in 1918.

This year marks the 81st anniversary of the end of the Second World War. It is also the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion , which celebrates a century of service to Canadian veterans and military families since it was officially incorporated by Parliament on July 17, 1926.
Remembrance Day, also called Armistice Day, is celebrated in the U.K., France, Belgium and many Commonwealth countries. In the United States, it is called Veterans’ Day.
Canadians will mark this year’s Remembrance Day with a series of ceremonies and events across the country, including two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. local time.

The Royal Canadian Legion has organized a national Remembrance Day service at the National War Memorial in Ottawa. The ceremony begins at approximately 10:30 a.m. with a program that includes a veterans’ march, a playing of the Last Post , two minutes of silence at 11 a.m. ET and a 21-gun salute.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, Governor-General Louise Arbour and Minister of Veterans Affairs Jill McKnight are expected to attend and take part in the wreath-placing ceremony. This year’s National Silver Cross Mother is Virginia Hicks, who will place a wreath on behalf of all Canadian mothers who have lost a child in military service to Canada.
Road closures around the National War Memorial will affect traffic and OC Transpo service before and during the Remembrance Day ceremony.
The national ceremony will be live-streamed on the Legion’s Facebook page , and will also be shown on TV by Canada’s national news networks.
Canadians across the country are gathering Wednesday to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.
Canadians will mark 25 years since the start of the Afghanistan war, a conflict in which 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members served and 159 lost their lives.
The Afghanistan conflict, which lasted more than 12 years, was the longest in Canadian history and saw the largest deployment of Canadian troops since the Second World War.

Three Second World War veterans are expected to attend the ceremony in Ottawa and Prime Minister Mark Carney, Govenor-General Louise Arbour and other dignitaries will lay wreaths at the National War Memorial.

CF-18 fighter jets and a Black Hawk helicopter will perform flypasts over the national ceremony, while Griffon, Chinook and Cormorant helicopters and other RCAF aircraft will conduct flyovers at local ceremonies across the country.

This year is also the 100th anniversary of the Royal Canadian Legion – founded in 1926 to create one main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits – and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.
Some 300 cadets are expected to attend the parade to mark that anniversary, which is about 200 more cadets than usual.

content_blocks.text: It is common to leave the poppy on the cenotaph or a wreath as a sign of respect at the end of a Remembrance Day ceremony. For example, thousands of poppies are placed on the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Ottawa on Remembrance Day each year. Other ways to respectfully dispose of a poppy include storing it away or discarding it in the garbage or recycling after the Remembrance period ends on Nov. 11.

The group has since grown to 449 members and helped to organize poppy-making events and local business participation.

stories.title: Remembrance Day ceremony will honour CFB Wainwright fire victims
stories.summary: Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright will be honoured at a community Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright will be honoured at a community Remembrance Day ceremony Wednesday.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19 and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, died in the Oct. 17 blaze at the military base, which is southeast of Edmonton.

Thirty-nine others were injured, and 21 are still recovering in hospital as of Nov. 5.

Roughly 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training when the fire occured. The Canadian Armed Forces said strong winds sent flames from a grass fire basically on top of them.

Roughly 300 members of the regiment are set to attend the Remembrance Day service in St. Albert, which is northwest of Edmonton.

The regiment will March in a parade to the cenotaph. There will also be a memorial Air Force flypast.

Globalnews.CA will live stream the ceremony beginning at 10:30 a.m. local time.

— with files from The Canadian Press

content_blocks.text: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19 and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, died in the Oct. 17 blaze at the military base, which is southeast of Edmonton.
Thirty-nine others were injured, and 21 are still recovering in hospital as of Nov. 5.

stories.title: Buyers attracted to Hamilton home priced under $550,000
stories.summary: Three-bedroom home was built 80 years ago and is close to the city’s iconic Sam Lawrence Park
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
74 East 12th St., Hamilton

Asking price: $549,999 (September 2026)

Selling price: $547,000 (September 2026)

Previous selling price: $500,000 (May 2020); $380,000 (February 2018); $195,000 (December 2006); $119,000 (June 1999); $110,000 (November 1992)

Taxes: $4,251 (2025)

Days on the market : 13

Listing agents: Michael St. Jean and Andrew Hart, Michael St. Jean Realty Inc.

This three-bedroom house with a private driveway on a 40- by 81-foot lot met the needs of many first-time buyers aiming to spend less than $550,000 in Hamilton. During one week in September, more than a dozen buyers, not including open house guests, roamed through the detached home. As the second week of showings began, the seller welcomed a buyer’s conditional offer just $2,999 shy of their asking price.

“To get this product in and around $550,000 is pretty good for a first-time home buyer,” agent Michael St. Jean said.

“The average days on market is probably 40 days in the area. This [home] went pretty fast.”

According to Mr. St. Jean, properties close to amenities along the Niagara Escarpment tend to be in short supply.

“It’s a pretty desirable pocket on the Hamilton Mountain, so you’re never going to have a lot of inventory,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“A block or two away is Sam Lawrence Park. It’s probably the most notable, iconic park in all of Hamilton Region because it’s a prime, central park, right on the mountain brow. A lot of people go there to hang out, and you can see the entire city of Hamilton, Lake Ontario and the CN Tower.”

This 80-year-old house has 1,028 square feet of living space, including one bedroom by the kitchen and living room.

An updated bathroom is next to the exit to the yard and the staircase leading up to two bedrooms.

Downstairs, there is a recreation area with a gas fireplace, one bathroom and new laundry machines.

“It’s an all-brick home, one-and-a-half storeys, with nice curb appeal,” Mr. St. Jean said.

“It had many updates in recent years, and it’s move-in ready, yet it’s got character.”

stories.title: Luxury Kingsway condo buyer takes $25,000 off the top
stories.summary: Large, corner unit in a building near the historic Old Mill Inn on the Humber River has an east-facing balcony and two parking spots
stories.author: Sydnia Yu
stories.content:
4 The Kingsway, No. 302, Toronto

Asking price: $2,188,000 (September 2026)

Selling price: $2,163,000 (October 2026)

Previous selling prices: $2.13-million (August 2022); $1,510,048 (April 2020)

Taxes: $11,716 (2026)

Days on the market: 16

Listing agent: Luisa Piccirilli, Re/Max West Realty Inc.

This eight-storey luxury condo building designed by architect Richard Wengle sits near the historic Old Mill Inn on the Humber River. Agent Luisa Piccirilli, who sold another of the building’s 38 units a year ago, also represented the seller of this unit with an east-facing balcony.

“It’s in a triangular-shaped building, and this unit is a corner unit right where the circular part of the building is,” Ms. Piccirilli said.

“The last one sold was technically the same unit, but it did not have a balcony, and this one did have a balcony.”

Over two weeks, the 1,986-square-foot space had 10 visitors, and sold at a $25,000 discount to the asking price.

“The builder, North Drive, does really nice finishes where a lot of other builders would say those are all upgrades and you have to pay extra for them,” Ms. Piccirilli said.

“Because of the square footage, being over 1,800 square feet, there’s a demand for that type of unit, plus it had two parking spots, and those were all big pluses.”

This unit has windows in both bedrooms and the kitchen, and a balcony off the living room. It also has a gas fireplace.

There are three bathrooms and a laundry closet with a sink.

The unit has two storage lockers. Monthly fees of $3,000 cover water, concierge and valet parking, along with the use of a gym and rooftop terrace.

“There is a demand to get into that building because it’s in a prime Kingsway area,” Ms. Piccirilli said.

“The architecture was by Richard Wengle, a well-known architect, especially in Etobicoke and all of Toronto. The design of the building is beautiful.”
