stories.title: GTA housing market riled by homes under power of sale
stories.summary: Distressed properties often come with a steep discount, setting new neighbourhood benchmarks
stories.author: Carolyn Ireland
stories.content:
Some home sellers in the Toronto area face an added challenge in the current market doldrums: their property May be competing with a listing in the hands of an unsentimental lender or distressed homeowner.

Houses and condo units listed under “power of sale” by a bank or finance company are appearing more frequently, agents say, and those properties often come with a steep discount to the asking price.

Some debt-burdened homeowners list before the lender takes charge, which can be motivation to accept a fire sale price.

Robin Pope, broker with Pope Real Estate, recently sold a Toronto townhouse for $1.12-million after four turbulent months on the market.

“Property values dropped like a stone,” he said of the process, which began when he listed the three-bedroom townhouse in late spring with an asking price just below $1.28-million.

House hunters circulated through the three-bedroom home in a sought-after pocket of Etobicoke near Islington Avenue, Mr. Pope said, but they didn’t appear to feel any urgency.

One buyer came forward with an offer, and the sellers agreed to an amount not far below the asking price. But there were conditions on the offer, and the buyer did not firm up.

Mr. Pope later learned the same buyer had walked away from another agreement six months earlier.

Then, seller competition in the enclave ramped up.

“All of a sudden, there were seven [other homes] for sale,” he said of the unusual surge. By June, the pocket became a “dead zone,” continuing into July and August.

One buyer’s agent began polling the listing agents, trying to suss out who might be willing to strike a deal. One seller, who started out with an asking price close to $1.3-million, had clearly become very motivated, Mr. Pope said.

“They ended up dropping their pants and selling for $1.058-million. It shocked everyone.”

The next two properties to sell fetched only slightly more – all a noticeable decline for the area, where homes changed hands at prices as high as $1.325-million at the market peak. More recently, comparable properties sold for $1.25-million and $1.275-million.

The situation was stressful for the other sellers in the enclave, said Mr. Pope, who trimmed about $30,000 from the asking price of his listing.

When the property sold in September, the final price was about 10 per cent below the deal that came undone.

“It was certainly, for my clients, an emotional roller coaster,” he said. The couple had recently retired and regretted that they hadn’t acted faster to get the property on the market.

“They still made a lot of money, but not as much as they hoped.”

In another case, Mr. Pope listed a house in Rexdale with an asking price around the $800,000 mark. Two comparable homes in the neighbourhood were listed under power of sale.

“They put downward pressure on my price,” he says.

The property he listed had quite a few improvements, including a new kitchen installed the previous year. Lenders make no effort to spruce up a property before listing, Mr. Pope added, so he recommends that sellers make their home as move-in ready as possible.

“The one advantage you May have over any other seller is if it’s turnkey. Make sure your property shines more than anybody else’s out there.”

Cheri Dorsey McCann, broker with McCann Realty Group, noted that a property selling at a bargain price under power of sale sets a new benchmark for the neighbourhood.

“That becomes the new market value,” said Ms. McCann. “It reduces the price for all the comparables.”

Ms. McCann recently kept an eye on the progress of one homeowner who set an asking price above the $2-million mark for a semi-detached house. Around the same time, the other half of the semi was listed under power of sale for $1.99-million.

A buyer agreed to pay $1.715-million for the vacant power-of-sale property during the summer, but the deal did not close, said Ms. McCann.

The property was relisted in late September with an asking price of $1.725-million, intended to spark competition, she said. It sold for $1.8-million.

Meanwhile, the owner of the other semi had to convince buyers of the value of a well-maintained property with a more polished appearance and attractive landscaping, said Ms. McCann.

That property eventually sold for $2.1-million.

“When people are losing everything, they’re not as happy,” she said of owners under duress, who May neglect the property.

By contrast, a seller who lives in the house and wants to sell is more likely to keep the property in top shape. The various motives of rival sellers create constant shifts in the landscape, she said.

“It is challenging to price because the listings are all over the map,” she said. “The market changes month by month and week by week. You really need your finger on the pulse.”

Sales in the Greater Toronto Area dropped 7.9 per cent in October compared with the same month last year, according to the Toronto Regional Real Estate Board. New listings declined 11.9 per cent in the same period.

The average price dipped 2.7 per cent last month compared with October 2025 to stand at $1,024,108.

Many consumers are concerned about the outlook for the economy.

At National Bank of Canada, Matthieu Arseneau, deputy chief economist, and Alexandra Ducharme, senior economist, say October’s employment data for Canada was disappointing on all fronts.

The figures confirm that the labour market is undergoing a more pronounced deterioration, according to Mr. Arseneau and Ms. Ducharme.

The manufacturing sector appears to be losing momentum amid renewed trade tensions, while the real estate market is experiencing another bout of weakness with rising interest rates that are also likely to weigh on activity in other sectors of the economy, they said in a note to clients.

Against that backdrop, sellers often encounter buyers who become frozen with indecision.

“Nobody feels like ‘I’d better buy this because it might be more tomorrow,’” said Mr. Pope of the inertia.

In his view, the ease with which deals fall apart indicates faltering consumer confidence.

People are concerned about grocery prices, interest rates, employment and – for some – the effect artificial intelligence May have on their jobs.

“There’s this fear of the unknown,” he says. “There are so many factors that are making people feel uneasy.”

stories.title: ‘Sometimes, I just feel like he’s still on training’: Father remembers son who died at CFB Wainwright
stories.summary: As Canadians mark Remembrance Day, one father is remembering his 26-year-old son, Sgt. Morgan Wong. Wong was among four Canadian soldiers killed in a training fire at CFB Wainwright last month
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Edmonton, Alta.- As Canadians mark Remembrance Day, one father is remembering his 26-year-old son, Sgt. Morgan Wong.

Morgan was among four Canadian soldiers killed in a training fire at CFB Wainwright last month. Dozens of others were injured, leaving families across the country facing an uncertain road ahead.

” said Morgan’s father, Chek Wong. “But when the reality hits ... he’s not coming back.”

For Chek, the tragedy compounded his family’s loss. His wife, Hong Tan, died of lung cancer in 2020, leaving him to raise their two children, Morgan and his sister, without her.

Now, six years later, he is mourning their son.

“Losing him, it’s just like ... take a part of me,” Chek said, struggling to find the words. “I’ll stay strong for my daughter ... family.”

The impact of the fire isstill being felt in Alberta hospitals.

According to Acute Care Alberta, 21 patients injured in the CFB Wainwright fire remained in hospital as of Nov. 6, including nine in critical condition.

The Canadian Armed Forces is sending 15 registered nurses with specialized burn and intensive care training to Alberta to help care for the injured. The nurses are expected to arrive beginning Nov. 10 and remain until Jan. 15, 2027.

“This offers well-deserved respite to civilian staff who have been working around the clock to provide this highly specialized care,” Acute Care Alberta said in an emailed statement.

A late-night knock

For Chek, the events that changed his family forever began with an unexpected knock at the door.

Three military officers had arrived at his Edmonton home late at night.

“I peeked out the window,” he recalled. “That’s not a good sign.”

He remembers wishing it were all a dream.

His partner, Kelly Fairweather, said Chek was overwhelmed by the news.

“I just remember ... him passing me his phone and saying, ‘I don’t know who to call. I don’t know what to do next.’”

Fairweather said family members and friends have been helping Chek navigate the weeks since Morgan’s death.

Some of Morgan’s closest friends have continued visiting, sharing memories and stories that occasionally bring laughter amid the sadness.

To those who knew him, Morgan was a reserved young man who revealed a different side of himself around the people he loved.

“Morgan is (a) very quiet person. But if you know him, he (opens) up and is really nice,” Chek said.

Chek also remembers the little things, like preparing home-cooked meals for Morgan before he left for work and when he returned home.

“He loved the curry,” Chek recalled. “He really enjoyed almost all those homemade food things (he) can’t get anywhere else.”

His father remembers a son who cared deeply for others and was always willing to help.

Morgan volunteered with St. John Ambulance and developed an interest in military service while still in school.

A ‘remarkable’ soldier

Chek recalled Morgan coming home at 17 and expressing an interest in joining the army reserve.

“I was like ‘well, let him try. Let’s give him a chance. It’s an opportunity he likes to do ... he likes to serve his country.’ Well, I said go for it,” Chek recalled.

Over the years, that interest developed into a career of service that made his father immensely proud.

“He was a remarkable soldier and a great leader,” Chek said. “He liked to help people and he’s very genuine.”

Morgan was also a newlywed.

He met his wife, Laura Karzinina, in Riga, Latvia, while deployed overseas. The couple married in December 2025, less than a year before his death.

“We haven’t had a big wedding yet, so we just had an intimate ceremony with his dad and his friends,” Karzinina recalled.

For Morgan’s uncle, George, who travelled from Hong Kong to support his brother and the family, the news was almost impossible to comprehend.

He recalled being on a street in Hong Kong when he received the call.

“I couldn’t believe it,” he said. “I lived in denial for a couple of days.”

George also reflected on Morgan’s deployment to Latvia.

“On the one hand, I’m concerned. But on the other hand, I’m very proud because there is the Wong name representing Nato,” he recalled.

Neighbours come to help

As the Wong family navigates its grief, neighbours and community organizations have been finding ways to show their support.

Former Edmonton city councillor Jennifer Rice helped organize a community gathering on Oct. 22.

Residents brought flowers, signed cards and shared their condolences with Chek and his loved ones.

Rice said the response extended beyond those who personally knew the family, with local organizations and community members offering help.

Community members have also rallied online to provide financial support to the Wong family.

“I need the family [to] know ... they’re not alone. They have the community behind them,” Rice said.

She said that continued support will be important in the months ahead.

The Legacy of Peace Society is also planning a commemorative tree planting in Morgan’s honour, with hopes that members of the public will be able to participate.

Morgan’s former elementary school also held a Remembrance Day ceremony Tuesday, which Chek and his family attended.

Chek described the ceremony as beautiful and touching, particularly because it took place at a school where his son had once been a student.

Despite his own grief, Chek said he continues to think about the other military families whose lives were changed by the fire.

“My heart goes to the family ... all the families that are impacted by this tragedy,” he said through tears.

He hopes they can find comfort in supporting one another through the difficult months ahead.

Chek hopes his son will be remembered for his service and everything he accomplished.

“I want everybody to ... remember him as a hero, that he was serving his country,” he said.

With files from CTV News’ Kristen Yu

Community members have also rallied online to provide financial support to the Wong family.
“I need the family [to] know ... they’re not alone. They have the community behind them,” Rice said.
She said that continued support will be important in the months ahead.
The Legacy of Peace Society is also planning a commemorative tree planting in Morgan’s honour, with hopes that members of the public will be able to participate.

content_blocks.text: Morgan’s former elementary school also held a Remembrance Day ceremony Tuesday, which Chek and his family attended.
Chek described the ceremony as beautiful and touching, particularly because it took place at a school where his son had once been a student.
Despite his own grief, Chek said he continues to think about the other military families whose lives were changed by the fire.
“My heart goes to the family ... all the families that are impacted by this tragedy,” he said through tears.
He hopes they can find comfort in supporting one another through the difficult months ahead.
Chek hopes his son will be remembered for his service and everything he accomplished.
“I want everybody to ... remember him as a hero, that he was serving his country,” he said.

stories.title: Wealth gap between Montreal and Toronto remains steady, report finds
stories.summary: A new report has found that Quebec’s regions have closed the economic gap with Ontario, even as the wealth gap between Toronto and Montreal remains.
stories.author: Stéphane Rolland
stories.content:
A new report has found that Quebec’s regions have closed the economic gap with Ontario, even as the wealth gap between Toronto and Montreal remains.

The report by the Institut du Québec research group finds that Quebec’s gross domestic product per capita was 91 per cent of Ontario’s in 2011, when Toronto and Montreal were excluded.

The group says that gap was nearly closed by 2022, when the per capita GDP of Quebec’s regions reached 99 per cent of Ontario’s.

However, the report found the spread between the two Canadian metropolitan areas did not narrow, with per capita GDP in Montreal remaining at about 80 per cent of Toronto’s.

Institut du Québec economist Jean-Baptiste Vallantin-Dulac says Montreal hasn’t necessarily performed poorly, but that Toronto’s economy is heavily based on the lucrative finance and insurance sectors.

The research group warns that the gap between Montreal and Toronto May widen if Quebec doesn’t reverse its immigration policies to attract a highly-skilled workforce.

stories.title: Pensions warned that LNG stakes could expose them to climate-related legal action
stories.summary: Advocacy group Stand.earth enlists Quebec law firm to warn pension funds against investing in LNG Canada, Ksi Lisims LNG
stories.author: Lauren Krugel
stories.content:
Environmental advocacy group Stand.earth has enlisted a high-profile law firm to warn six major pension funds against investing in liquefied natural gas megaprojects, saying climate-related and other risks could expose plan administrators to legal action.

The letter from Anne-Julie Asselin, partner at Trudel Johnston & Lespérance, was sent last week to trustees of the Canada Pension Plan Investment Board, Public Sector Pension Investment Board, Ontario Municipal Employees’ Retirement System, Ontario Teachers’ Pension Plan, University Pension Plan and Healthcare of Ontario Pension Plan.

Montreal-based Trudel Johnston & Lespérance specializes in class action and public interest cases, including a decades-long legal battle against major tobacco companies that resulted in a $32.5-billion settlement approved last year, as well as an ongoing fight against opioid makers. Lawyers at the firm were also involved in a lawsuit over the defunct Energy East pipeline’s potential impact on whale habitats in the Gulf of St. Lawrence.

“As the financial risks associated with fossil fuel investments become more significant, more foreseeable and better understood, prudence demands an increasingly rigorous assessment of those investments,” Asselin wrote in the letter. “Disregarding such risks becomes more difficult to justify and May carry legal consequences.”

She urged pensions to “refrain from investing, either directly or via a private fund, in LNG Canada, Ksi Lisims LNG or comparable Canadian LNG projects unless and until it can demonstrate, ON the basis of a rigorous and transparent assessment, that such investments are consistent with its statutory and fiduciary obligations.”

Stand.earth and its legal counsel had the letters drafted and ready to send when news broke last week that four pension funds plan to invest in LNG Canada.

U.S. asset manager Blackstone BX-N is leading a group, which includes Cppib , Omers, the Investment Management Corp. of Ontario and the PSP Investment board, planning to acquire a non-controlling stake in the Mitsubishi Corp. subsidiary that holds an interest in LNG Canada.

Asselin said it’s not clear how final the Mitsubishi deal is, so the warning was still worthwhile.

“We will definitely be looking at what are the next steps, that’s for sure,” Asselin said in an interview. “We weren’t expecting (decisions to make LNG investments) that quickly. And we were hoping that it would never happen.”

LNG Canada is the first natural gas export facility to start up on Canada’s West Coast. The partners, which also include Shell Shel-N and Korean, Chinese and Malaysian companies, decided last month to go ahead with an expansion to double the output at the plant in Kitimat, B.C. LNG Canada Phase 2 has also been deemed a national-interest project under federal legislation passed last year that aims to speed along new infrastructure.

Richard Brooks, climate finance director at Stand.earth, said attempts to communicate concerns directly with pension plans amid rumours they were looking to invest in LNG gained little traction.

He said the letters are “an attempt to remind them in the language that they should be paying attention to, which is legal language, about what they are accountable for and what they’re responsible for.”

He said the pension funds collectively manage $1.6-trillion in investments on behalf of millions of workers.

“There is probably no larger class in Canada than workers covered under these pensions,” Brooks said. “So (Trudel Johnston & Lespérance’s) experience with class-action lawsuits, particularly the tobacco one, really spoke to us.”

Geoff Souter, managing director at CPP Investments, said in a Nov. 2 news release on the LNG Canada investment that the project “is a high-quality, globally strategic asset with strong long-term fundamentals and attractive return potential for the CPP Fund.”

A spokesperson for Cppib did not respond to a request for further comment by late Tuesday, nor did representatives with Ontario Teachers and the University Pension Plan. Omers and Hoopp declined to comment.

PSP confirmed it has received the letter and said it does not share Stand.earth’s views on the risks of LNG investments.

“PSP Investments’ investment decisions, including those referenced by Stand.earth, are made in accordance with applicable statutory and legal obligations,” it said.

“They are made in furtherance of PSP Investments’ mandate, which is to manage amounts transferred to it by the Government of Canada in the best interests of contributors and beneficiaries under plans designated in PSP Investments’ governing statute, and to invest its assets with a view to achieving a maximum rate of return, without undue risk of loss, having regard to the funding, policies and requirements of the plans, and to the ability of the plans to meet their financial obligations.”

Separately, four young Canadians launched a lawsuit last year against Cppib alleging the fund is failing to protect the long-term interests of contributors who are set to retire decades from now with its fossil fuel-related investments.

In a news release Tuesday, the group Shift: Action for Pension Wealth and Planet Health, said CPP members and environmental advocates plan to gather outside Ontario Superior Court on Thursday as Cppib asks a judge to strike the suit.

Legal action has been a “tool of last resort” among groups concerned about pension funds’ investments in fossil fuels, Brooks said.

“We’re certainly prepared to go there if the pension funds move ahead with investments (in LNG), particularly after they’ve been duly warned and reminded of their responsibilities.”

stories.title: Carney’s budget tackles homelessness. Will it work?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses what sets this plan apart from the previous government's commitment to tackle homelessness in Canada.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
Ottawa is pledging to end homelessness within 10 years, and is investing tens of billions of dollars to do so.

The investment will manifest across several housing and health-care initiatives, including $2 billion for mental health and addictions infrastructure, a new Centre for Mental Health and Addictions in Winnipeg, as well as renewing the Canada Housing Benefit.

Besides the investment, the promise requires heavy buy-in from provinces and territories.

Host Caryn Ceolin speaks to Steve Pomeroy, industry professor at McMaster University with the Canadian Housing Evidence Collaborative. The discuss what sets this plan apart from the 2017 Trudeau government commitment to slash homelessness by 50 per cent in 10 years, and what else is needed for the pledge to actually meet Canadians where they’re at.

stories.title: Toronto’s Reel Asian film festival marks 30 years with a renewed call for change
stories.summary: This year’s festival also celebrates long-time executive director Deanna Wong, who is leaving the organization
stories.author: Barry Hertz
stories.content:
There was something in the air when Anita Lee started the Toronto Reel Asian International Film Festival in 1997.

That same year, the Vancouver Asian Film Festival also sprang up, with programmers buoyed by a new wave of independent Asian-American films bursting onto the scene (including Rea Tajiri’s Strawberry Fields , Chris Chan Lee’s Yellow , and Quentin Lee and Justin Lin’s Shopping for Fangs ).

At the time, Lee never imagined that her festival would make it past a decade, let alone three. But this week, Reel Asian kicks off its 30th edition by celebrating its past at the same time that it has its eye trained on the future. In addition to its anniversary milestone, the festival is marking the departure of long-time executive director Deanna Wong, with associate director Kelly Lui succeeding her.

Ahead of this year’s fest, which runs Nov. 11-29, The Globe and Mail sat down with Wong and Lee (who is now the chief programming officer for the Toronto International Film Festival) to talk about a generational run.

Anita, when you started the festival, did you have a roadmap in mind as to where it might go?

Anita Lee: Well, did I think that the CN Tower would be turning red to celebrate Reel Asian? No, I did not. But I think that speaks to the community and the audience that have supported us over the years to come to this landmark time. My roadmap or vision, though, when I started was during when a few things converged. I had just made a short film, I had held a position at the Canadian Filmmakers Distribution Centre, which was an important experimental hub, and there were also a lot of identity politics happening at the time. I wanted to create a space where we were no longer defining what Asian diasporic stories are, but to create a space where we can support the work that was being made. This work was being created in the margins, but not being programmed in festivals.

It’s funny thinking about 1997, because that’s when the Vancouver Asian Film Festival also started.

Lee: Yes, and Barbara Lee from Vancouver’s festival, I ran into her that same year in San Francisco for that city’s Asian-American film festival, and she and I witnessed that moment together. It was almost that Asian-American new wave movement of feature films that were travelling all over the circuit. It was groundbreaking.

Deanna, when you first joined the organization in 2005, how would you say Anita had built up the institution?

Deanna Wong: I moved to Toronto from Winnipeg around the end of ’96, and I stumbled onto the festival that first year, not knowing Anita or the community. I was just going as an Asian-Canadian person who loved movies and craved some representation on screen. I remember seeing Yellow , and being hooked immediately. I eventually joined the board, and then decided to apply for the job of executive director. I was just thrilled that there was a festival full of films like this, it was so rare. I could count on one hand the number of times I’d seen any American or Canadian movie that starred more than one or two Asian people.

Anita, what was the transition like for you to have built this up and then hand it over to others?

Lee: I ran the festival hands-on as executive director and director of programming for three years, and had never planned to do that as a career. But I wanted to set it up as a not-for-profit organization, so I’d spent that time looking for baseline operational funding, and that fourth year I moved onto the board and served as chair for 10 years. It was about growing the festival incrementally. At that time, I remember Cameron Bailey asked me, “Does success mean that Reel Asian would not need to exist in the future?” But even more than ever, we need this festival. There’s so much more that the festival supports year-round.

Wong: I had left the festival for a bit, but when I came back in 2019, that was at the height of the Crazy Rich Asians phenomenon, and there was a lot of excitement about what the success of that film meant. Have we arrived in the mainstream? But we also had this peak of DEI initiatives of creating film and television projects that’s now been waning. So what has remained this whole time is the need for the community to support each other in writing and directing stories that reflect their own experiences.

Lee: Every time there’s a wave of Asian cinema from Asia, there’s a similar question that arises. When there was the time of John Woo and Hong Kong action films, there was that question of do you need places like Reel Asian. But today, Reel Asian, in terms of the programming and the audience development and the community, it’s still in advance of the industry in general. I don’t feel that the presence of Asian-Canadian filmmakers has grown in a significant way. There hasn’t been significant support for this community to develop at the rate that they should have. We joke about how there’s always support given for emerging directors, but not looking at how you bring those people through the industry. The first wave of Asian-Canadian directors are emerging, but into retirement.

We see certainly a lot more opportunity, and then success, with Asian-Canadian filmmakers working in the U.S. system.

Lee: Look at Celine Song, who has made one of the biggest American independent movies with Past Lives . Maggie Kang with KPop Demon Hunters . Domee Shi with Turning Red . There’s a gap, and what have we not been able to do in Canada that they, for example, have been not able to have those careers here? I’m thrilled they have made it in Hollywood, but there are so many other directors here who, given the opportunity, could be working in a much more significant way. For some reason that nut has not been cracked.

Wong: And we’re aware of that by developing our year-round programming to address that. We’ve stopped emphasizing our kind of Filmmaking 101 parts of our industry series so we can create something like our Fire Horse Award, whose $25,000 allows those filmmakers to continue doing their work in Canada. We’re not trying to create a star system necessarily, but providing the opportunity for experienced filmmakers to be recognized and keep the spotlight on them.

Deanna, why did you feel now was the right time to depart?

Wong: I feel like all organizations need to grow and have fresh blood to keep things going. Thirty is a nice round number, too. Also, it is a tough time for non-profit arts organizations and we’ve weathered a number of minor crises along with everybody else. We’re in a relatively strong position and have staff, including Kelly, who have a lot of institutional memory. I can leave and make space for the next wave, wherever the next 30 years go.

stories.title: Younger Canadians, Quebec residents less likely to find military service important: poll
stories.summary: Those aged 18 to 24 'May have grown up with the expectation that international conflict can almost always be resolved through negotiation,' says Jack Jedwab
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
Younger Canadians and residents of Quebec proved to be the most hesitant groups when it comes to believing military service is important in a time of need, according to a recent poll.

Only five per cent of those surveyed between 18 and 24 years old strongly agreed that it was crucial to serve their country.

That group in particular “May have grown up with the expectation that international conflict can almost always be resolved through negotiation,” Jack Jedwab told National Post. He is the president and CEO of the Association for Canadian Studies and the Metropolis Institute, which released the poll by the Ekos research group.

Meanwhile, those living in Quebec were least likely to agree in the importance of serving compared to the rest of the country — even though it was still over half, at 55 per cent.

The poll, released to mark Remembrance Day, is based on a weighted national total of 1,232 respondents who participated between Oct. 9 and 15.

The sacrifices of those who served invite reflection on what Canadians today — 108 years after the First World War ended — believe they owe their country, said researchers.

Overall, it found that 22 per cent of Canadians strongly agreed with serving in the army, while 40 per cent somewhat agreed. The remaining 33 per cent disagreed, while five per cent weren’t sure or didn’t respond.

The willingness to serve, which is not an indication of whether Canadians will actually enlist, said Jedwab, is viewed differently based on where respondents were born.

Many refugees and diaspora communities were more likely to strongly agree with military service (27 per cent) versus those born in Canada (21 per cent).

“Most Canadians have come to think of war that is always happening somewhere else in the world that affects them unevenly,” he said. “When people do not feel directly threatened, it becomes harder to imagine the urgency that could make military service necessary.”

Broken down by province, those living in Atlantic Canada had the strongest beliefs in serving during a time of need, at 71 per cent. British Columbia was a close second (66 per cent), while Manitoba and Saskatchewan combined had the same result. Residents of Ontario and Alberta weren’t far behind, at 63 and 62 per cent, respectively. Quebec came in last (55 per cent).

Age played a major role in how Canadians think of military service. The older Canadians are, the more likely they believe in the importance of joining the army.

Part of the reluctance of the youngest group, 18 to 24, to endorse military service could be because they have difficulty imagining circumstances in which a negotiation would fail, said Jedwab. However, he cautioned against treating the responses in the poll as a “definitive prediction of how young Canadians would react to an actual threat.”

Eleven per cent of the next age group, 25 to 34, strongly agreed with military service, followed by 35 to 44 year olds at 14 per cent, 45 to 54 (21 per cent), and 55 to 64 (26 per cent).

By the time Canadians reached the 65-plus category, 35 per cent strongly believed in joining the army during a time of need.

There are nearly half a million veterans living in Canada, according to data from the 2021 Census. The largest proportion of them — 192,960 men and women — are 65 and older.

“The challenge for the future is how to preserve Canada’s commitment to peace while helping younger generations understand the obligations that could arise if that peace were threatened,” said Jedwab.

In comparison to other countries, a 2023 International Social Survey Program report found that Canada ranked 25 out of 29 countries included in the survey when asked about willingness to serve.

“My interpretation is that Canada’s relatively lesser commitment mainly reflects the distance most Canadians feel from an immediate military threat and have felt that way for many decades,” said Jedwab.

The margin of error for the total sample is ±2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. Margins of error are larger for subgroups, including individual age groups.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

There are nearly half a million veterans living in Canada, according to data from the 2021 Census. The largest proportion of them — 192,960 men and women — are 65 and older.

stories.title: ‘I can’t falter’: For 20 years Daniel Ferland has stood perfectly still in silent vigil on Remembrance Day
stories.summary: 'We’re a reflection of the old generation using the old uniforms, shadowing the younger generations'
stories.author: Adrian Humphreys
stories.content:
Silent, still and solemn.

At a Remembrance Day ceremony one year ago in Kingston, Ont., a solitary figure stood motionless in the snow from the start of the service until the end. He caught the eye of a photographer, Julia McKay with the Kingston Whig-Standard. The stance she captured in a photo — head bowed, disciplined and respectful in an old-fashioned military battle dress — was strikingly emblematic of the occasion.

The man in uniform is 58-year-old Daniel Ferland, who retired from the Canadian Armed Forces in 2020 after 32 years of service. Although retired, he continued a duty he volunteered for each Remembrance Day over two decades, standing in silent vigil at cenotaph ceremonies around the country.

“I put myself in place before it starts and then I stay there until it ends. I don’t move,” Ferland said. Most ceremonies these days feature some movement for soldiers and cadets, such as during the national anthem. “But myself, I don’t move because that’s part of it. I’m a traditionalist and I feel that it shows better.”

Ferland stands virtually motionless. Sometimes it’s a service of 30 minutes, usually it’s the better part of an hour. His longest was one hour and 35 minutes. It takes a lot to stand still. Once at a high school ceremony, he heard a student ask a teacher if the soldier was a mannequin. That was mission accomplished for Ferland.

Daniel Ferland, a master warrant officer who retired in 2020 after serving for 32 years, stands vigil in his Second World War battle dress uniform at a Remembrance Day service last year in Kingston, Ont. Julia McKay/Postmedia

In military terms, the drill is called Rest On Your Arms Reversed. The arms in this case are weapons, not limbs. A soldier thrusts their rifle forward as far as their arm can take it and then rotates the barrel forward and down, vertically, until the muzzle rests on the toe of the soldier’s left boot. Their hands are then rested on the top of the rifle’s butt, and the elbows drop to the side.

The head is lowered until the chin touches the chest, completing the contemplative and respectful pose.

“Because you have that time by yourself, you got time to think,” he said of his vigils.

His thoughts range from the practical to the emotional.

“I am thinking: ‘Stand still. I can’t falter. This means so much. Look sharp,’” he said. “I look at a spot on the ground so that way I don’t waver. If you start getting tunnel vision, it starts going a little bit black — I don’t want to go down, you know.”

But he is also listening to the ceremony. Its meaning can’t be avoided, its importance, its messages of loss, sacrifice, service. The haunting Last Post bugle call, used at military funerals and commemorations, hits him every time.

“Last Post is always the worst because I’ve been to many funeral parades, some for people known, some for people unknown. There’s some stuff that triggers the emotion. I try not to get too emotional there, because, well, I’m kind of stuck, but it reminds me why I am there.”

Ferland has encountered many people and places over his military service that serve as personal reminders.

For most of 2008, he was deployed in Afghanistan as a weapons technician with the Royal Canadian Electrical and Mechanical Engineers.

“It felt like you were walking in an Easy-Bake Oven. It was incredibly hot. But we were well trained,” he said of Afghanistan. Ferland and his unit rushed from place to place fixing or replacing damaged weapons used in battle — pistols, rifles, machine guns, anti-tank guns, mortars, armoured vehicles; everything but tanks. Some of the equipment he was trained to fix are now museum pieces. “That makes me feel old.”

I try not to get too emotional there, because, well, I’m kind of stuck, but it reminds me why I am there

While there, he was also a part of 17 ramp ceremonies, the solemn services at Kandahar Airfield when the body of a Canadian soldier, in a flag-covered casket, is loaded onto an aircraft to be brought back to Canada.

“There’s a few tearjerker moments there,” he said.

All around Ferland that day in Kingston were reminders of that time.

The Legion branch he was visiting on Remembrance Day last year is dedicated to Capt. Matthew J. Dawe, who was 27 when he was killed on deployment to Afghanistan in 2007. A platoon commander, Dawe was hit by a remotely detonated explosive while on an operation he had planned and named for his son, who was turning two on the day of his mission.

Sometimes Ferland is in a squad of four for a vigil, sometimes two. In Kingston, he was solo. He picked a place that was visible but out of the spotlight.

He wore his authentically recreated Second World War battle dress uniform, with light fighting orders, in military lingo. That means he doesn’t carry the extra weight of a heavy pack. His green uniform blended with the greenery of a cedar behind him, a red poppy on his chest adding colour.

“Most of the stuff is authentic, except for the boots and my underwear,” he said of his 1940s uniform. On his shoulder is the patch of the Rceme, which was created a month before the deadly D-Day landing.

McKay, the photographer, said she was struck by Ferland’s stillness for the entire ceremony.

He has had a lot of practice.

It was a couple of decades ago when Ferland started doing vigils in period uniform. When he was posted to the Canadian Forces Base Gagetown in New Brunswick, the second-largest military base in Canada, he and a few other amateur historians who recreated authentic uniforms stood vigil at a Remembrance Day ceremony.

Bugler Larry Stafford plays Last Post leading into the moment of silence during a Remembrance Day service in Kingston, Ont., in 2025. Julia McKay/Postmedia

They called it a “shadow vigil” because they stood by a cenotaph but not at it, allowing young cadets to fulfill the central role of remembrance.

“We’re a reflection of the old generation using the old uniforms, shadowing the younger generations,” he said. He said it was well received.

“I thought it was important. And I kept that tradition going.”

He usually arrives with a display of military memorabilia, often curated to match the focus of the ceremony. For last year’s, because the service was based in a hall dedicated to a soldier killed in Afghanistan, he brought a display emphasizing the modern era.

This year, Ferland can’t perform his formal silent vigil.

“Unfortunately, I got a pinched sciatic nerve. I’m walking with a limp at best right now. Three months ago, I could barely walk,” he said.

He will still be remembering on November 11. He will be at his Legion ceremony in Ottawa. “I’ll still be standing, but not in a vigil. I’ll be standing with other veterans. I guess it’s my body’s way of telling me to take a break this year and heal, and then next year I can get back into action.”

Adrian Humphreys, a founding journalist at National Post in 1998, is a senior national reporter focusing on crime, policing and justice stories, and investigative journalism. He is the author of three non-fiction bestsellers about organized crime, and runs a popular YouTube channel about global gangsters.

stories.title: B.C. could get a brief reprieve from heavy rain before the next storm arrives
stories.summary: Flood watches continue to cover much of Vancouver Island and the South Coast
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Gregory Whittaker said he was up half the night in Pemberton Meadows, B.C., listening to rain pound down outside, while nearby Miller Creek was “getting angry.”

A series of atmospheric rivers have been battering B.C.’s south coast, and after Whittaker’s sleepless night, the province’s River Forecast Centre upgraded flood watches to warnings on Wednesday in the Pemberton Valley, as well as Howe Sound, Sea to Sky and the North Shore of Metro Vancouver.

The drenching that saw more than 200 millimetres of rain fall in some places in a 24-hour period also forced an evacuation for parts of the Village of Pemberton, just south of Whittaker’s home.

The order issued Wednesday afternoon covers properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, its waste water treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course.

“All persons within the affected area are required to leave immediately and follow the directions of emergency personnel,” the village’s order said, citing “immediate danger to life safety caused by flooding.”

The community about 160 kilometres north of Vancouver said on social media Wednesday morning that flooding had happened around One Mile Lake, including sections of trail, and urged residents to stay clear of flooded areas and flowing water.

Despite the warning, 50-year-old Whittaker went out on a rainy Remembrance Day hike to check out the levels of Miller Creek, which converges with the Lillooet River northwest of Pemberton.

Videos he shot show the creek as a roaring torrent of white water.

“It’s more of a spectacle at this point,” he said of the rising water levels, noting he lives above the floodplain so is generally not concerned about his property flooding.

But Whittaker acknowledged conditions could change overnight.

“We’re supposed to get round three of heavy rain this evening so, you know, it could be a whole other story tomorrow. We’ll have to see what happens,” he said Wednesday.

Environment Canada meteorologist Jennifer Hay said in an interview that 24-hour rainfall reached 214 millimetres in Port Mellon, about 50 kilometres northwest of Vancouver, by Wednesday morning, while Howe Sound had received 79 millimetres and West Vancouver Island-Kennedy Lake nearly 140 millimetres.

“The system is coming across, so it’s currently along the coast (and) lots of areas are still getting rain,” she said Wednesday morning.

She said a rainfall warning over the Vancouver and Fraser Valley regions had been dropped, although it could be reissued as another system moved in.

While parts of the province including Metro Vancouver experienced a morning lull in the storms that have been sweeping across the region since last week, the River Forecast Centre said more rain was forecast throughout Wednesday, with weather models indicating another 100 millimetres through the Sea to Sky corridor, and up to 100 millimetres through west and central Vancouver Island.

The centre said rivers in the South Coast region had been “rising rapidly,” with the Stawamus, Clowhom, and Squamish rivers and Tofino Creek all exhibiting high flow rates.

Orange rainfall warnings that were raised by Environment Canada on Monday remained in place for Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions.

The weather office warned residents of central B.C. that the “strong and slow-moving” system would bring damaging winds, with gusts reaching around 100 kilometres an hour in some areas, before easing Wednesday night.

It said utility outages were likely and driving May be difficult, with risk of injury due to falling debris.

The River Forecast Centre said in its warning that people should continue to stay away from river banks as the fast flow of water increases the risk of bank instability.

“Continued rises in river levels are expected into Thursday in response to additional rainfall,” the warning said.

B.C.’s Transportation Ministry urged drivers to monitor conditions and prepare for high winds, heavy rainfall and possible flooding in southern coastal regions for the rest of the week.

Hay said there was a “break coming” on Thursday or early Friday, though “another quite strong system” was expected between Friday and Sunday.

“It looks it’s not until well into the 15th or the 16th where we do see a change of pattern, everything dries out and the temperatures probably will drop ,” she said.

While parts of the province including Metro Vancouver experienced a morning lull in the storms that have been sweeping across the region since last week, the River Forecast Centre said more rain was forecast throughout Wednesday, with weather models indicating another 100 millimetres through the Sea to Sky corridor, and up to 100 millimetres through west and central Vancouver Island.
The centre said rivers in the South Coast region had been “rising rapidly,” with the Stawamus, Clowhom, and Squamish rivers and Tofino Creek all exhibiting high flow rates.
Orange rainfall warnings that were raised by Environment Canada on Monday remained in place for Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions.

The weather office warned residents of central B.C. that the “strong and slow-moving” system would bring damaging winds, with gusts reaching around 100 kilometres an hour in some areas, before easing Wednesday night.
It said utility outages were likely and driving May be difficult, with risk of injury due to falling debris.
The River Forecast Centre said in its warning that people should continue to stay away from river banks as the fast flow of water increases the risk of bank instability.
“Continued rises in river levels are expected into Thursday in response to additional rainfall,” the warning said.
B.C.’s Transportation Ministry urged drivers to monitor conditions and prepare for high winds, heavy rainfall and possible flooding in southern coastal regions for the rest of the week.
Hay said there was a “break coming” on Thursday or early Friday, though “another quite strong system” was expected between Friday and Sunday.
“It looks it’s not until well into the 15th or the 16th where we do see a change of pattern, everything dries out and the temperatures probably will drop ,” she said.

stories.title: Their families came to Canada seeking safety. They chose to serve for their new home
stories.summary: Ten years after immigrating to Canada, Yousef Shaath gave up his job as an accountant to enlist in the army. He was 45 years old, going through basic training with recruits who had just entered adulthood.
stories.author: Judy Trinh
stories.content:
Ottawa – The most recent data from the Department of National Defence show that 28 per cent of new recruits are visible minorities.

Many of them joined the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF) because of a fierce sense of patriotism instilled in them by their immigrant parents.

That’s the case for Palestinian Canadians Yousef Shaath, 66, and George Al-Koura, 39. The veterans are a generation apart but both found a shared purpose through military service.

Ten years after immigrating to Canada, Shaath gave up his job as an accountant to enlist in the army.

He was 45 years old, going through basic training with recruits who had just entered adulthood.

Shaath said he was inspired by his cousin, Wafa Dabbagh, the first Muslim woman wearing a hijab in CAF . He was determined to “embed his footsteps” into Canada, energized by his fellow recruits who were more than half his age.

“I enjoyed every minute of it … if there’s a hurdle, you persist,” Shaath said in an interview with CTV News.

Over his 14-year career as a logistics officer, Shaath was deployed in Kuwait and Lebanon. He helped move weapons and equipment out of Afghanistan after Canada wound down its combat operation in Kandahar.

Shaath said his last deployment was the most meaningful to him. In 2015, he was sent to Lebanon to help the federal government conduct security checks on Syrian refugees.

Displaced by escalating violence in their homeland, Shaath’s parents fled from Palestine to Egypt in 1936. Shaath said his family history impressed upon him the importance of the work he was doing in helping Canada vet Syrian refugees for its sponsorship group.

“It was most rewarding … being helpful, to put up a hand to help others – that made me more loyal, more loving to the Canadian Forces.”

‘I’m Canadian first’

That shared sense of being uprooted – then falling in love with a new country – is a feeling that is also ingrained in Al-Koura.

In 2005, he joined the military just a few weeks before turning 18 years old. He sought adventure and to put into practice the lessons his parents taught him.

His parents, also Palestinian refugees, instilled in him the importance of protecting the freedom they found in the “cultural mosaic” of Canada.

“I’m proud to be ethnic Palestinian, but I’m Canadian first,” said Al-Koura, who was born in Montreal and raised Catholic. He followed in his sister’s footsteps and joined the CAF.

“I remember the ice storm of ’97. We have inconveniences, but Canada allows us to be ourselves and gives us the freedom to live without essentially warfare in the background of our lives.”

Al-Koura became a signals intelligence officer. He was also involved in Operation Impact, the U.S.-led mission against the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria. He used his fluency in Arabic to analyze the military manoeuvres of Isis.

He retired from the CAF last year and has transitioned into the private sector. In his 20-year career, he has lost colleagues in the line of duty. For Al-Koura, the most painful loss came during the War in Afghanistan. After Canada’s mission ended in 2014, a childhood friend took his own life.

“He died when he got back (to Kingston.) His reintegration process wasn’t the easiest of things. The Afghan years were hard for lots of people. It was really hard for people to understand what they went through,” he said. “When (the soldiers) came back, we as a society didn’t really know how to help.”

Like Al-Koura, Shaath also lost a close friend. His colleagues died during a Nato training mission.

On Nov. 11, he will be thinking of that friend and others who have served and those still on the front lines.

“On Remembrance Day, I think of everybody. Ever soldier that went there and came back. I think of the people who are away from their homes. It’s not easy.”

With files from CTV News’ Kristen Yu

stories.title: Jeff Rath sold $6.6M estate amid court fight over First Nation fee refund
stories.summary: Global News examined Rath’s sworn testimony and financial records, uncovering unreported property deals and longstanding debts he sought urgent court approval to pay.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
Alberta lawyer Jeffrey Rath and his wife sold a waterfront estate in B.C. for $6.6 million – more than $4 million above its purchase price – while his firm fought a court order to refund millions to a First Nation client, Global News has found.

In March 2021, an Alberta judge ordered Rath’s firm to refund $8.5 million in legal fees to Tallcree First Nation. Rath and his firm appealed, and three months later, while the lawsuit continued, the couple sold their Galiano Island estate.

In the months that followed that sale, Rath signed documents transferring his interest in the couple’s Calgary home to his wife, Dayna Laverick-Rath, for a stated $1 and granting her a $10-million collateral mortgage over his Foothills ranch, property records show.

What happened to the proceeds of the Galiano sale, and the financial implications of the subsequent property transactions, remain unclear. Five years later, however, Tallcree is still fighting for that refund.

As Global News previously reported , Tallcree chief Rupert Meneen is suing Rath and his firm, RathPC, for nearly $15 million over disputed trust withdrawals, including the $8.5-million refund and millions in administration fees. The First Nation has now asked a court to expand an investigative receiver’s powers from investigating Rath’s finances to taking control of assets and recovering the money.

The lawsuit sparked further legal battles with other First Nations and American litigation funders , with more than $150 million in disputed debts, legal fees and allegedly unauthorized trust withdrawals at stake.

As lawyers scrutinize Rath’s finances and asset disclosures, Global examined records beyond his sworn testimony.

That investigation uncovered the Galiano estate sale and Calgary property transfer, which have not surfaced in court proceedings.

Rath has been questioned in court about the $10 million mortgage, however. He said it arose from a matrimonial property agreement and denied it was intended to protect assets from creditors.

Rath did not respond to questions for this story. However, he briefly spoke to Global on Oct. 17 during the lead-up to the Alberta referendum, characterizing the litigation as a “fee dispute” and saying First Nations had agreed to payments for legal services under agreed terms.

“Everybody understands what it is that they’ve agreed to pay,” he said. “At the end of the day, you know, they want to fight about it.”

Global also uncovered a 2019 letter, recently filed in court, in which Rath promised Tallcree beneficiaries his firm would charge no trustee fees — despite RathPC later billing the trust millions.

The investigation also examined court filings Rath submitted in September seeking the urgent release of $280,000 for horse-related expenses.

Rath warned that his horses’ health and safety were “in peril,” but several creditors told Global they had gone unpaid long before his assets were frozen.”

The horses are not worth what he owes me, I’ve been trying to get him to send me a transfer to take them to the sales,” Wilson said.

“For several months, he would just not pick up the phone,” Renee Wilson of Crawford Racing told Global.

Wilson said Rath owed her about US$50,000 for horse care dating back to February, although he only included a US$13,000 invoice from her in his September application.

But Wilson also criticized the government for freezing Rath’s assets, saying it unfairly burdened those caring for his horses.

“That’s wrong for the animals,” she said. “I don’t care who’s a bad person or not a bad person.”

Rath’s financial disclosures have been under the microscope in recent months, after an Alberta court froze his assets under a Mareva injunction and appointed an investigative receiver to trace the disputed funds.

Silver Gold Bull, a precious-metals trading platform, has emerged as a central player in the financial dealings. Documents show it received most of the $8.5-million million that was ordered to be refunded to Tallcree , while Rath continued trading through the platform. Meneen alleges those later transactions involved disputed trust funds.

Among the transactions now being examined are approximately $200,000 worth of silver coins, prompting a contentious exchange in court over their whereabouts. Rath testified that he gave the coins to Laverick-Rath as a Christmas Eve gift in 2025.

“She filed for divorce, and we lived in separate residences, and I was hoping to reconcile, but we were still separated,” he said, during an October cross-examination.

However, purchase records show about $100,000 worth of those coins were bought after Christmas, ON Dec. 27 and Jan. 7.

Questioning about the coins grew acrimonious. When Meneen’s lawyer asked how Rath had brought the boxes home, he replied: “I flew like a fairy. I drove in my car.”

He then called the questions “stupid” and “such a waste of time.”

Laverick-Rath died in June.

Rath maintained that the coins he gave his wife belonged to her estate. “It’s not mine to hand over to the receiver,” he testified.

Requests for her will and probate records remain unanswered, according to court filings.

Her estate has also come under scrutiny over Rath’s Alberta property holdings and mortgage arrangements.

During a September cross-examination, Rath said he had owned property in Vancouver but could not recall when he sold it, for how much or to whom, later estimating the sale was more than five or six years ago.

Global could not identify that property but found one Rath sold about five years ago on picturesque Galiano Island, off the B.C. coast.

Rath and Laverick-Rath jointly acquired two properties on the island for a combined $2.49 million in 2006 and 2008, according to land-title records.

Together, the properties formed Blue Raven Estate, a 9.4-acre waterfront compound featuring a nearly 5,000-square-foot main house, two guest houses, two deep-water docks, a helipad and a private four-hole golf course, archived real estate listings state.

The estate was listed for $8.58 million in December 2018. That was four months after another First Nation client, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation , sought a review of Rath’s legal fees, according to court documents. However, records show his lawyers were not formally served until later that December.

That same month, an American litigation funder registered a broad-based security interest over Rath’s professional corporation and advanced an initial $10 million under a funding agreement, separate documents show.

The estate was still advertised for the same price more than two years later .

The couple sold it in July 2021 for $6.6 million — $2 million below asking but $4.11 million above their combined purchase prices, land-title records show.

Within weeks of the sale, Rath transferred his interest in the couple’s $1.7-million Calgary home to Laverick-Rath for a stated $1. Three months later, she was granted a $10-million collateral mortgage against three properties at his Foothills ranch.

Rath did not respond to Global News questions about the property transactions.

Meneen is also challenging more than $4.8 million in administration fees charged by Rath, but a recent court-filed letter reveals a pledge at odds with those charges.

The original 2017 Tallcree trust agreement allowed RathPC to charge trustee fees.

But in March 2019, beneficiaries were preparing to vote on whether to retain Rath’s firm as trustee or transfer control of the settlement funds to the Bank of Montreal.

In a letter accompanying the ballots, Rath said his firms “do not charge a fee for acting as Trustee.

“Should Jeffrey R. W. Rath Professional Corporation continue to administer the Trust, it will continue to charge no fee in accordance with its practice to date.”

Beneficiaries voted 59-32 to keep Rath.

A month later, according to court documents, Rath allegedly told a Tallcree beneficiary his firm charged no administration fees and had “no intention of doing so,” claiming the Law Society monitored trust withdrawals.

The regulator told Global it does not.

Asked in September why he had no time records to justify $4.8 million in fees, Rath said he stopped tracking his hours in February 2018, because he planned to charge a percentage instead.

Confronted with the apparent contradiction related to the trustee fees, Rath insisted his statement had been “true at the time” and denied misleading beneficiaries. However, he said he could not recall correcting or updating the written promise.

On Sept. 11, Rath asked an Alberta court to unfreeze nearly $800,000 for personal and legal expenses, including almost $280,000 for overdue horse-related bills. He warned that his horses’ health and safety were “in peril,” submitting urgent invoices from trainers, veterinarians and others in Canada and the U.S.

But when Global contacted the creditors, several described bills that had gone unpaid for more than a year — long before Rath’s assets were frozen.

“I call him and he doesn’t answer the phone,” said Angel Diaz, a horse trainer in Menifee, California, who said Rath owed him more than $5,200, and the debt had accumulated over about a year.

Judy Hicks of Brookstown Farm, near Versailles, Kentucky, said: “He’s never been paid up for the two years he was here.”

“The reason was that, while his wife was alive, he told me it was because he didn’t want her to know he had horses. Because she did not approve of him having horses.”

Candice Foster, an Oklahoma horse hauler, said repeated attempts to collect a $1,000 bill for transporting one of Rath’s horses in December 2025 had gone unanswered.

But trainer John Ennis, who received a payment from RathPC in February, according to court-filed financial records, said his dealings with Rath had been “really good.”

“I’m sure Rath will get around to paying. He’s a good guy.”

Justice Lorena Harris rejected Rath’s application, finding his financial disclosures were “materially incomplete.”

Rath described his racehorses, which have earned nearly $500,000 in gross winnings since 2021 according to Equibase, as a “hobby,” but acknowledged using them for business purposes. Tallcree alleges trust funds helped finance the horses, a claim Rath disputes.

His troubles have since extended beyond the courtroom. In October, Alberta Prosperity Project board members voted to remove him from his roles, a decision Rath disputes, while the United Conservative Party expelled him on Oct. 29.

Rath remains defiant, accusing Premier Danielle Smith’s office of orchestrating a media campaign against him.

In March 2021, an Alberta judge ordered Rath’s firm to refund $8.5 million in legal fees to Tallcree First Nation. Rath and his firm appealed, and three months later, while the lawsuit continued, the couple sold their Galiano Island estate.

In the months that followed that sale, Rath signed documents transferring his interest in the couple’s Calgary home to his wife, Dayna Laverick-Rath, for a stated $1 and granting her a $10-million collateral mortgage over his Foothills ranch, property records show.

What happened to the proceeds of the Galiano sale, and the financial implications of the subsequent property transactions, remain unclear. Five years later, however, Tallcree is still fighting for that refund.

As Global News previously reported , Tallcree chief Rupert Meneen is suing Rath and his firm, RathPC, for nearly $15 million over disputed trust withdrawals, including the $8.5-million refund and millions in administration fees. The First Nation has now asked a court to expand an investigative receiver’s powers from investigating Rath’s finances to taking control of assets and recovering the money.

The lawsuit sparked further legal battles with other First Nations and American litigation funders , with more than $150 million in disputed debts, legal fees and allegedly unauthorized trust withdrawals at stake.
As lawyers scrutinize Rath’s finances and asset disclosures, Global examined records beyond his sworn testimony.
That investigation uncovered the Galiano estate sale and Calgary property transfer, which have not surfaced in court proceedings.
Rath has been questioned in court about the $10 million mortgage, however. He said it arose from a matrimonial property agreement and denied it was intended to protect assets from creditors.

Rath did not respond to questions for this story. However, he briefly spoke to Global on Oct. 17 during the lead-up to the Alberta referendum, characterizing the litigation as a “fee dispute” and saying First Nations had agreed to payments for legal services under agreed terms.
“Everybody understands what it is that they’ve agreed to pay,” he said. “At the end of the day, you know, they want to fight about it.”
Global also uncovered a 2019 letter, recently filed in court, in which Rath promised Tallcree beneficiaries his firm would charge no trustee fees — despite RathPC later billing the trust millions.
The investigation also examined court filings Rath submitted in September seeking the urgent release of $280,000 for horse-related expenses.
Rath warned that his horses’ health and safety were “in peril,” but several creditors told Global they had gone unpaid long before his assets were frozen.”
The horses are not worth what he owes me, I’ve been trying to get him to send me a transfer to take them to the sales,” Wilson said.
“For several months, he would just not pick up the phone,” Renee Wilson of Crawford Racing told Global.
Wilson said Rath owed her about US$50,000 for horse care dating back to February, although he only included a US$13,000 invoice from her in his September application.
But Wilson also criticized the government for freezing Rath’s assets, saying it unfairly burdened those caring for his horses.
“That’s wrong for the animals,” she said. “I don’t care who’s a bad person or not a bad person.”

Rath’s financial disclosures have been under the microscope in recent months, after an Alberta court froze his assets under a Mareva injunction and appointed an investigative receiver to trace the disputed funds.

Silver Gold Bull, a precious-metals trading platform, has emerged as a central player in the financial dealings. Documents show it received most of the $8.5-million million that was ordered to be refunded to Tallcree , while Rath continued trading through the platform. Meneen alleges those later transactions involved disputed trust funds.

Among the transactions now being examined are approximately $200,000 worth of silver coins, prompting a contentious exchange in court over their whereabouts. Rath testified that he gave the coins to Laverick-Rath as a Christmas Eve gift in 2025.
“She filed for divorce, and we lived in separate residences, and I was hoping to reconcile, but we were still separated,” he said, during an October cross-examination.
However, purchase records show about $100,000 worth of those coins were bought after Christmas, ON Dec. 27 and Jan. 7.
Questioning about the coins grew acrimonious. When Meneen’s lawyer asked how Rath had brought the boxes home, he replied: “I flew like a fairy. I drove in my car.”
He then called the questions “stupid” and “such a waste of time.”
Laverick-Rath died in June.
Rath maintained that the coins he gave his wife belonged to her estate. “It’s not mine to hand over to the receiver,” he testified.
Requests for her will and probate records remain unanswered, according to court filings.
Her estate has also come under scrutiny over Rath’s Alberta property holdings and mortgage arrangements.

During a September cross-examination, Rath said he had owned property in Vancouver but could not recall when he sold it, for how much or to whom, later estimating the sale was more than five or six years ago.
Global could not identify that property but found one Rath sold about five years ago on picturesque Galiano Island, off the B.C. coast.
Rath and Laverick-Rath jointly acquired two properties on the island for a combined $2.49 million in 2006 and 2008, according to land-title records.

Together, the properties formed Blue Raven Estate, a 9.4-acre waterfront compound featuring a nearly 5,000-square-foot main house, two guest houses, two deep-water docks, a helipad and a private four-hole golf course, archived real estate listings state.

The estate was listed for $8.58 million in December 2018. That was four months after another First Nation client, Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation , sought a review of Rath’s legal fees, according to court documents. However, records show his lawyers were not formally served until later that December.

That same month, an American litigation funder registered a broad-based security interest over Rath’s professional corporation and advanced an initial $10 million under a funding agreement, separate documents show.
The estate was still advertised for the same price more than two years later .
The couple sold it in July 2021 for $6.6 million — $2 million below asking but $4.11 million above their combined purchase prices, land-title records show.

Within weeks of the sale, Rath transferred his interest in the couple’s $1.7-million Calgary home to Laverick-Rath for a stated $1. Three months later, she was granted a $10-million collateral mortgage against three properties at his Foothills ranch.
Rath did not respond to Global News questions about the property transactions.
Meneen is also challenging more than $4.8 million in administration fees charged by Rath, but a recent court-filed letter reveals a pledge at odds with those charges.
The original 2017 Tallcree trust agreement allowed RathPC to charge trustee fees.
But in March 2019, beneficiaries were preparing to vote on whether to retain Rath’s firm as trustee or transfer control of the settlement funds to the Bank of Montreal.
In a letter accompanying the ballots, Rath said his firms “do not charge a fee for acting as Trustee.
“Should Jeffrey R. W. Rath Professional Corporation continue to administer the Trust, it will continue to charge no fee in accordance with its practice to date.”
Beneficiaries voted 59-32 to keep Rath.

A month later, according to court documents, Rath allegedly told a Tallcree beneficiary his firm charged no administration fees and had “no intention of doing so,” claiming the Law Society monitored trust withdrawals.
The regulator told Global it does not.
Asked in September why he had no time records to justify $4.8 million in fees, Rath said he stopped tracking his hours in February 2018, because he planned to charge a percentage instead.

Confronted with the apparent contradiction related to the trustee fees, Rath insisted his statement had been “true at the time” and denied misleading beneficiaries. However, he said he could not recall correcting or updating the written promise.

On Sept. 11, Rath asked an Alberta court to unfreeze nearly $800,000 for personal and legal expenses, including almost $280,000 for overdue horse-related bills. He warned that his horses’ health and safety were “in peril,” submitting urgent invoices from trainers, veterinarians and others in Canada and the U.S.

Judy Hicks of Brookstown Farm, near Versailles, Kentucky, said: “He’s never been paid up for the two years he was here.”
“The reason was that, while his wife was alive, he told me it was because he didn’t want her to know he had horses. Because she did not approve of him having horses.”
Candice Foster, an Oklahoma horse hauler, said repeated attempts to collect a $1,000 bill for transporting one of Rath’s horses in December 2025 had gone unanswered.
But trainer John Ennis, who received a payment from RathPC in February, according to court-filed financial records, said his dealings with Rath had been “really good.”
“I’m sure Rath will get around to paying. He’s a good guy.”
Justice Lorena Harris rejected Rath’s application, finding his financial disclosures were “materially incomplete.”

Rath described his racehorses, which have earned nearly $500,000 in gross winnings since 2021 according to Equibase, as a “hobby,” but acknowledged using them for business purposes. Tallcree alleges trust funds helped finance the horses, a claim Rath disputes.

His troubles have since extended beyond the courtroom. In October, Alberta Prosperity Project board members voted to remove him from his roles, a decision Rath disputes, while the United Conservative Party expelled him on Oct. 29.
Rath remains defiant, accusing Premier Danielle Smith’s office of orchestrating a media campaign against him.

stories.title: Rain expected after mild start to Remembrance Day
stories.summary: A mix of sun and cloud will give way to increasing cloud cover and rain Wednesday, with temperatures reaching 11 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
A mix of sun and cloud will give way to increasing cloud cover and chance of rain Wednesday, with temperatures reaching 11 C, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.

The day will have a frosty start with light winds, with temperatures hovering between 6 C and 9 C as people head out to Remembrance Day ceremonies across the region.

Cloud cover will increase through the afternoon, with showers possible by late afternoon and early evening before periods of rain develop overnight.

Atchison says some light drizzle is possible in parts of midwestern Ontario during morning ceremonies, with more widespread rain moving in later in the day.

Showers are expected to continue into Thursday, when temperatures will reach just 7 C under mainly cloudy skies.

Cooler air will follow, bringing a slight chance of lake-effect precipitation. London is expected to only see about a 30 per cent chance of precipitation heading into the weekend.

Saturday’s Santa Claus parade forecast is looking pleasant, with a mix of sun and cloud with temperatures in the low single digits, dropping closer to the freezing mark after sunset.
