stories.title: Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Ireland, Philippines, Cambodia and China
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he'll look to advance trade and security ties.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted November 11, 2026 4:00 am.

Last Updated November 11, 2026 5:17 am.

OTTAWA — Prime Minister Mark Carney takes off Wednesday for summits in Asia and Ireland where he’ll look to advance trade and security ties.

His travels will take him to four countries and put him on the ground as high-stakes diplomacy takes place between the United States, China and Russia.

Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, said the trip is Canada’s chance to build on new agreements and partnerships it has signed with countries around the world.

“We’re now entering a much more consequential phase of actually implementing and delivering on all of these agreements, and sustaining the momentum,” she said.

“When Prime Minister Carney speaks about diversifying our relationships, it’s not just about Europe.”

The prime minister is set to depart for Dublin shortly after the Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa.

Carney will attend the European Political Community summit in Dublin, set for Nov. 12. For the second time, Canada will be the only non-European country represented at the table. Carney joined the group’s last meeting in Armenia in May.

The EPC summits have taken place roughly every six months since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

The informal meetings are aimed at discussing strategic co-operation in politics, security and infrastructure.

Carney and European Union leaders have floated Canada becoming an “associate member” of the EU since the last summit — a title they have yet to define.

The Philippines

After Dublin, Carney will cross both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans to visit Manila, where the Philippines is hosting Canada as a guest at the Nov. 15–18 summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations.

ASEAN is a bloc of 11 countries that focuses on trade, regional peace and international norms. Canada is set to finalize negotiations on two trade deals while Carney is in Manila, one with the ASEAN bloc and another bilateral deal with the Philippines. He could even sign one of them while he’s there.

The prime minister has a meeting scheduled for Saturday with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and will address ASEAN leaders on Sunday.

Queen’s University professor Stéphanie Martel, who studies Southeast Asia and the Asia-Pacific, said the visit will help shape the Indo-Pacific strategy the Trudeau government released four years ago. That strategy focused on making Ottawa a relevant partner in the region after years of sporadic engagement.

“It’s becoming kind of a cliché to refer to Canada as this fairweather friend,” she said.

Martel said Carney has focused on trade and maritime defence but less on local concerns about climate change resilience and gender-inclusive militaries.

“There’s a lot of action in terms of specific trade deals and specific sectors. But the overall engagement and the ability of Canada to be seen as this serious, comprehensive contributor to the region is still up for debate,” she said.

In the Philippines, Carney will be joined by Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu and Gender Minister Rechie Valdez, who is of Filipino origin.

Carney will then visit the Francophonie summit in Cambodia set for Nov. 14 to 16. He’s expected to meet with leaders from Africa and other continents while in the capital Phnom Penh.

Canada is hosting the next Francophonie summit in 2028 in the Ottawa area. Carney is expected to use the gathering to advance Canada’s strategic autonomy and protect the role of French in the growing digital economy.

Francophonie members will elect their next leader in Cambodia and Ottawa says it is staying neutral to avoid affecting the next summit.

On Sunday, the prime minister is set to address CEOs at the FrancoTech innovation event at the summit. On Monday, he is set to give plenary remarks.

Dominique Caouette, Indo-Pacific studies chair at the University of Montreal’s political science department, said the Francophonie summit is an opportunity for Canada and Quebec to advance economic interests.

“The Francophonie could also serve as a platform for Mr. Carney toward the middle powers. There are several that are part of the Francophonie. It’s another space where Canada could play an influential role,” Caouette said in a French-language interview.

The summit will feature both Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, who was elected on a sovereigntist mandate aimed at pushing back on Ottawa. Caouette said he doesn’t expect the two to clash.

“It’s not in the Canadian or Quebec tradition to air one’s dirty laundry in public,” he said.

Carney will be joined in Cambodia by Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand and her parliamentary secretary Mona Fortier. Before his arrival, Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour will lead Canada’s delegation at the summit.

Carney’s last stop will be China’s tech hub of Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation summit, set for Nov. 18 to 19. Leaders from across the Pacific Rim will gather in the city bordering Hong Kong to take stock of an increasingly disordered trading system.

Nadjibulla said the summit allows for bilateral and “minilateral” discussions that bring leaders together in small groups to advance common goals. She said the APEC meetings themselves have taken on less importance, thanks to the diverging interests of Russia, the U.S. and China.

U.S. President Donald Trump is set to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin at the summit.

The meeting has European leaders worried about a possible impact on Moscow’s war against Ukraine. Analysts are also watching for any updates on Trump’s war on Iran.

Carney’s visit will come just days after China extended a deal to provide market access to Canadian imports such as canola meal and lobster, in exchange for Canadian market access for Chinese steel and aluminum.

Xi and Carney are set to meet Tuesday and he will address business leaders the next day.

Nadjibulla said she’ll be watching for any economic announcements, such as a move to allow more Chinese vehicles into Canada or new Chinese investments in energy and technology.

“The warming, the recalibration of the relationship has been moving at a rapid pace,” Nadjibulla said, adding that any moves could affect trade talks with the U.S.

In China, Carney will be joined by his parliamentary secretary Kody Blois and Anand.

Carney is set to return to Ottawa on Nov. 19.

The federal Conservatives have criticized Carney’s overseas deals, arguing that the signed agreements have not yielded significant gains and are distracting the government’s attention from the affordability crisis.

The Liberals argue facetime between leaders is critical to diversifying trade and building more resilient supply chains and security partnerships.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

— With files from Caroline Plante in Quebec City

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Budget 2026 shifts Liberal government’s language on home construction targets
stories.summary: Ottawa — The federal housing minister's office is reasserting Ottawa's goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals' hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The federal housing minister’s office is reasserting Ottawa’s goal of doubling the pace of home construction — even though references to the Liberals’ hallmark affordability pledge were missing from Budget 2026.

The budget, which was tabled last week, dropped any mention of that original target, which was introduced in the Liberals’ 2025 election platform and repeated numerous times in that year’s budget.

Instead, the 511-page document outlines a new plan to triple the pace of non-market housing construction to 24,000 starts per year over the next decade.

Non-market housing is usually more affordable and relies on government support to get built, but those homes account for only a small share of the overall number of units built in a year.

The Canadian Press asked Housing Minister Gregor Robertson’s office whether Ottawa is abandoning its goal of doubling the annual pace of overall home building.

After repeated requests, his office pointed to a six-month-old statement given to The Canadian Press in May confirming that the government was still “working toward doubling homebuilding over the next decade.”

At the time, The Canadian Press had asked Robertson’s office about Ottawa’s commitment to the target because April’s spring economic update also lacked references to the goal.

Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan pointed out then that while the government’s fiscal update included plenty of talk about affordability supports, “no specific targets or metrics for the pace of home building were provided.”

Housing affordability has been a hot-button issue since the COVID-19 pandemic, which saw rents and resale prices rapidly escalate — boxing out many young Canadians trying to become homeowners.

On Tuesday, Robertson’s office pointed to statistics showing national housing starts are up more than 20 per cent since the pre-pandemic period, rental construction is setting a record pace and rents have trended lower over the past few years.

“Since forming government, we launched an ambitious national plan to focus our efforts and spur co-ordinated action between governments, homebuilders, and communities. We moved quickly to increase housing supply and improve access to safe, warm, affordable homes,” his office said.

MP Scott Aitchison, the Conservative housing critic, accused the Liberals of quietly dropping the promise to double home building and replacing it with the smaller non-market target.

“Their announcements and promises have turned into another Liberal housing illusion. Tripling the speed of slow is still unbearably slow and will not restore affordability,” Aitchison said in a statement to The Canadian Press.

“Canadians need homes they can afford, not more failed Liberal targets and broken promises.”

In its fall housing supply report, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp. wrote that the country is entering a “new phase” where slowing population growth is leading to more balance in Canadian rental markets.

But the Crown corporation warned that the annual pace of housing starts is well short of levels needed to restore pre-pandemic affordability to the market in the next 10 years.

The Cmhc’s “business-as-usual” forecast sees Canada breaking ground on 231,000 homes per year, which it estimates would leave the market up to 238,000 homes short of affordable levels by 2036.

Affordability will remain out of reach if Canada fails to take advantage of this moment to rapidly build housing supply ahead of the next surge in demand, the Cmhc said.

Mike Moffatt, founding director of the Missing Middle Institute, said he always viewed the Liberals’ goal of doubling home building levels as a tough one to achieve. It would mean bringing the annual number of housing starts up to 500,000 in a given year, when Canada has so far topped out around 300,000.

Moffatt said the target May also be “excessive,” given that the government can effectively control the pace of population growth, which dictates how much supply is really needed to serve the Canadian market.

The headline number also doesn’t specify what kinds of homes Canada needs to build to actually meet Canadians’ needs, he added.

“I never loved the target. I felt it was probably too high and missed some important nuances,” Moffatt said.

The federal Liberals have instituted a number of policy changes aimed at stimulating home building since Prime Minister Mark Carney came to office in March 2025.

They include waiving the GST on many newly built homes, establishing new funds for local infrastructure and setting up Build Canada Homes, a new Crown corporation tasked with reversing years of lagging non-market home construction.

Budget 2026 proposed giving another $13 billion over 10 years to Build Canada Homes and pledged tens of billions of dollars over the coming decade to an effort to end homelessness across the country.

Andy Yan, director of the City Program at Simon Fraser University, also said he considered Ottawa’s original home building goal “more aspirational than realistic.”

“You can set a target, but do you have the capacity to meet those targets?” he said.

Yan said policies like the Housing Accelerator Fund and the Apartment Construction Loan Program have been “fairly successful” in getting more homes built, particularly on the rental side.

The Housing Accelerator Fund, which ties federal cash to pro-development policy changes, was one of Ottawa’s tools for addressing the fact that barriers to building often lie at the municipal level.

Many of the other levers for stimulating home building are also not directly in the federal government’s hands.

Building material costs have grown in response to U.S. tariffs, while a soft labour market is dampening buyer demand for new homes.

Interest rates — a critical factor for developers weighing the business case for a new build — are set independently by the Bank of Canada. The central bank delivered its first rate hike in more than three years last month and signalled more could be on the way.

Moffatt warned that many of the constraints holding back broader construction apply to social housing as well.

“There’s no non-market drywall, right? There’s no non-market lumber, there’s no non market electrician,” he said.

“A non-market social housing target is more in the government’s control, but it’s hardly a slam dunk.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Remembrance Day ceremonies to honour CFB Wainwright fire victims
stories.summary: Wainwright - Four soldiers killed in a fire during a training exercise are among those being honoured today at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Wainwright, Alta.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Wainwright - Hundreds in a hockey arena stood for a moment of silence before Rev. Mokwadi Basele led them in prayer.

His thoughts were of the four soldiers killed more than three weeks ago in a wind-propelled grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright.

And he hoped for a quick recovery for the many others still in hospital with severe burns.

“God, we come closer to home, we come to Wainwright, as we remember the tragedy that befell this small town,” said the minister with Grace United Church at Wednesday’s Remembrance Day service in the town southeast of Edmonton.

“We lift up those who were injured and all who continue to heal in hospitals and at home, as well as comrades from the base and friends who live with shock and grief.”

The four who died were honoured at ceremonies across Alberta and Canada.

Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton died in the Oct. 17 blaze.

A few blocks from the Peace Memorial Multiplex, some left flowers and wreaths at the base of a historic, century-old fieldstone tower commemorating Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars.

“We come every year,” said Wainwright resident Reimer Nielsen.

“This (Remembrance Day) is a little more sombre and more important to be here for the four.”

Veteran Sean Hansen said Remembrance Day is always special in the town, but it feels different this year because of the fire.

“Unfortunately, some paid with their lives and some are horribly scarred,” he said.

About 84 soldiers with the Charlie Company unit of the 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in attack training on Oct. 17, when a windstorm shot flames from a grass fire and onto the troops.

Thirty-nine others were injured. As of last week, the military said 25 were still recovering in hospital.

“These young people literally ran into balls of fire to save their brothers and sisters in arms,” federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said after attending the Wainwright ceremony.

He represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.

“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends, and there are dozens of others who recovering from the most horrendous wounds imaginable,” he said.

“Third-degree burns on 80 to 90 per cent of their bodies. We reflect on the courage of the people on that day.”

Northwest of Edmonton, at least 2,000 lined a road leading to the St. Albert Cenotaph, a war memorial for local soldiers who died in combat.

Roughly 300 members of the same regiment caught in the Wainwright fire marched to the site.

Farrell’s family was also there, and they laid a wreath in his honour.

“We May not know much about the lives of the people who were recently killed or injured in Wainwright, yet each one of them lived and breathed among us,” Rev. Ken MacRae, a retired Armed Forces chaplain, told the crowd.

“They had or still have dreams of their own. They had or still have friends and family who love them.”

He said the names of the four killed in Wainwright are to be added to some cenotaphs and memorial sites across the country.

“God has not forgotten them, nor should any of us forget these individuals.”

Prime Minister Mark Carney, at a ceremony in Ottawa, honoured those in Wainwright.

He has called the deadly fire at the base one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

Rabbi Idan Scher gave the benediction at the Ottawa service. He said Canadians united after the fire.

“Canadians lined up to donate blood, prepared meals for emergency crews, opened their homes and worked tirelessly to care for the injured,” Scher said.

“At a time when our world feels increasingly divided, these Canadians reminded us of what truly matters. They did not ask what their neighbours believed, where they came from, or whether they saw the world the same way.

“They simply asked, ‘How can I help?’”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

— With files from Jack Farrell in St. Albert, Alta.

He represents the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, which includes the base.

“We think of their mothers, their fathers, their sisters, their brothers, their friends, and there are dozens of others who recovering from the most horrendous wounds imaginable,” he said.

“They simply asked, ‘How can I help?'”

stories.title: Toronto ceremonies at Queen's Park, Old City Hall among those marking Remembrance Day
stories.summary: Toronto - Provincial and municipal dignitaries are set to join veterans and their families today at Remembrance Day ceremonies in Toronto.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Toronto - As John Anderson prepared to lay a wreath at a Remembrance Day ceremony in Toronto, the retired Canadian Navy lieutenant said he would be thinking of people who were part of his service “brotherhood.”

The Cambridge, Ont., resident who was in the navy for more than 40 years said taking part in the solemn ceremonies every year is a particular honour.

“It honours the people who served to give us what we have today and the current people that are serving,” he said. “You bring them together, it’s like one big brotherhood.”

The 79-year-old, who said he helps connect veterans with the services they need, was in the large crowd gathered around the Old City Hall Cenotaph on Wednesday to honour the sacrifices of Canada’s veterans and soldiers.

Toronto Mayor Olivia Chow also commemorated the Legion on its 100th anniversary during her remarks at the event.

“The Legion shows us the city we can be. A city where no one carries the burden alone. A city where we take care of each other and stand up for each other,” she said.

About two kilometres away, many more joined a ceremony outside Queen’s Park, where Ontario Premier Doug Ford said this Remembrance Day “is especially poignant” after the devastating fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta that killed four soldiers and injured dozens of others.

“I want to thank all the heroic Ontario health-care workers who were deployed to support recovery efforts and continue to pray for those impacted by the fire,” he said.

“Whether it’s a family member or a friend who answered the call to serve, or someone who came home with wounds, visible and invisible, Remembrance Day holds a special meaning for each of us.”

Brig.-Gen. Éric Landry, who has served in Afghanistan in leadership roles, thanked every member of the Canadian Armed Forces who has chosen to defend the country.

“We are a very reliable ally. We are the neighbour every country (wishes) they had,” he told the crowd at Queen’s Park.

Landry spoke of Canada’s role in the U.S.-led war in Afghanistan, 25 years after it began.

“We deployed 40,000 troops to Afghanistan over 15 years; 158 of us never came back. And all of us who did come back were changed forever,” he said.

“So I want to thank everybody, but I want to tell them also that this is worth it. Canada is worth defending.”

Landry also honoured the four soldiers who died in the Wainwright fire, saying they will never be forgotten.

Other Remembrance Day ceremonies were also held in Toronto, including at the Fort York National Historic Site and the Toronto Zoo.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

stories.title: From activist to academic, Bessie Borwein never stopped connecting people
stories.summary: Her family remembers her as a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them
stories.author: The Globe and Mail
stories.content:
Bessie Borwein: Matriarch. Scientist. Communicator. Connector. Born March 17, 1927, in Johannesburg, South Africa; died June 9, 2026, in London, Ont., of natural causes; aged 99.

Bessie Flax – not short for Elizabeth or Beatrice, just Bessie − grew up under the dual shadows of apartheid and the Holocaust, danced with Nelson Mandela in her student activist days, married at 19 and spent the next 75 years building a life defined by a relentless impulse to make the world a better place.

Bessie and David Borwein grew up together in the Johannesburg Jewish community. David was three years older and tutored her in math when she was an undergrad at University of Witwatersrand in Johannesburg. They married in 1946.

The couple left South Africa two years later to live in London where David pursued a DPhil in mathematics and Bessie started a PhD in botany. After the Nationalist Party came to power in 1948, David used to say that they could never go back as Bessie would have spent her life in jail – a statement he made with equal parts pride and genuine assessment of the risks.

David’s first teaching position was at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland. Bessie cried when she heard the news – she did not want to go somewhere so cold and dark and small. In the end, they loved it and spent 15 happy years there, welcoming three children, Jon, Peter and Sarah. Bessie and her family also became British citizens.

Ever adventurous, in the 1960s, the family of five immigrated to Canada – to London, Ont., a place they had never heard of – for a one-year sabbatical at Western University. They decided to make Canada their home and became Canadian citizens in 1982.

In London, Bessie began working as a lab technician and a professor at the university encouraged her to pursue graduate work. She completed her PhD in anatomy in 1973. Bessie studied the eyes of Anableps anableps , a quirky fish that swims at the water’s surface and thus sees two worlds at once. This was something that her daughter always found fitting.

Bessie was the answer to anyone who ever said it was too late to start. She had an extraordinary, illustrious career that didn’t start until she was nearly 50. She became an associate professor at Western University then associate dean of medical research. She served on the Research Ethics Review Board, founded a non-profit that educated the public on science, worked with the Alzheimer’s Society in Ontario, the Ontario Breast Screening Program, Madame Vanier Children’s Services and the Youth Science Foundation, among other gigs. She also won a list of awards and recognitions too long to recount here.

Bessie was a do-er. If there was a problem, she needed to help solve it. In 1968, when a neighbourhood child went missing, she spearheaded the Block Parent program, a network of safe homes each marked by a sign in the window. London was the first city in Canada to have it and it spread across the country.

She never stopped connecting people to each other – spotting the invisible thread between two people and pulling until they met. Bessie often sent packages of random newspaper clippings to her children, simply to say she was thinking of them. She signed every note “YDM” (for Your Devoted Mother). She also took in a cousin’s daughter and rewrote two futures in a single act of kindness – hers, and Sarah’s, as they became as close as sisters.

Bessie took infectious joy in her grandchildren and became a devoted and loving grandmother to all nine of them. Her home was a haven, full of warmth, heated political argument and David’s dry wit. He used to say their 75-year marriage worked because of the division of labour: He did the division, she did the labour.

She outlived her sons Jon and Peter, and David. Bessie carried those profound losses in her body and over the years, slipped away from the world. But the Bessie her family remembers was a fierce, brilliant, loving woman who made lives better by her presence in them.

Bessie was close to 100 before she died. Had she been a little more present, she might have held on for that telegram from the king.

Sarah Borwein is Bessie Borwein’s daughter.

content_blocks.text: Bessie was the answer to anyone who ever said it was too late to start. She had an extraordinary, illustrious career that didn’t start until she was nearly 50. She became an associate professor at Western University then associate dean of medical research. She served on the Research Ethics Review Board, founded a non-profit that educated the public on science, worked with the Alzheimer’s Society in Ontario, the Ontario Breast Screening Program, Madame Vanier Children’s Services and the Youth Science Foundation, among other gigs. She also won a list of awards and recognitions too long to recount here.

content_blocks.text: Bessie was a do-er. If there was a problem, she needed to help solve it. In 1968, when a neighbourhood child went missing, she spearheaded the Block Parent program, a network of safe homes each marked by a sign in the window. London was the first city in Canada to have it and it spread across the country.

content_blocks.text: She never stopped connecting people to each other – spotting the invisible thread between two people and pulling until they met. Bessie often sent packages of random newspaper clippings to her children, simply to say she was thinking of them. She signed every note “YDM” (for Your Devoted Mother). She also took in a cousin’s daughter and rewrote two futures in a single act of kindness – hers, and Sarah’s, as they became as close as sisters.

He used to say their 75-year marriage worked because of the division of labour: He did the division, she did the labour.

stories.title: ‘Normal is back’: Federal Conservatives get a lesson in unity from their B.C. cousins
stories.summary: 'The biggest lesson you can take away from B.C. politics is that things can change quickly, and expect the unexpected,' MP Aaron Gunn said
stories.author: Sarah Ritchie
stories.content:
Ottawa — When Aaron Gunn first walked into the House of Commons after the provincial B.C. Conservatives won their election last month, he was met with high-fives and claps on the back from his colleagues.

The victory offered a morale boost to a federal Conservative caucus that’s had few of those in the last year.

Gunn said the win is evidence the Conservative brand is “alive and well” in Canada, but the B.C. MP isn’t convinced the federal party can draw much from the success, given the strange set of circumstances that preceded the election.

“The biggest lesson you can take away from B.C. politics is that things can change quickly, and expect the unexpected,” Gunn said.

B.C. Conservative Leader Lorne Doerkson rose from being a backbench MLA to the office of British Columbia premier in a matter of weeks, after NDP premier David Eby gambled an early election call on the turmoil within the conservative movement.

Doerkson’s first order of business after learning his colleagues had chosen him to succeed ousted leader Kerry-Lynne Findlay — after flying home from South Africa — was to get everyone into the same room.

After months of vicious infighting, Doerkson’s party pulled together in a hurry.

That happened, in part, because everyone knew an election was coming whether they were ready or not. It was also a deliberate strategy: unity was campaign director Katy Merrifield’s “biggest priority.”

“We in B.C. on the centre-right are very accustomed to doing exactly (that): focus on the 70 per cent of things you can agree on, drop egos. Everyone get inside the tent and work together,” she said.

That’s a lesson Merrifield said can apply to any political party.

Gunn, a first-time MP who was a key part of building the current version of the B.C. Conservatives, was “very close” to running for the provincial party leadership last winter. He had to sit back and watch as the party’s spring leadership race turned nasty.

B.C. Conservative Party Leader Lorne Doerkson on election night in Vancouver on Oct. 24, 2026. Arlen Redekop / Postmedia

Findlay won narrowly at the end of May, but bitterness lingered between her supporters and those who’d backed her primary opponent, Caroline Elliott.

Federal Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre waded into the fray over the summer by taking a verbal shot at the “Liberal lobbyists from out east” who’d worked against Findlay (a shot intended for Ontario Premier Doug Ford and his former campaign manager, Kory Teneycke, but one that landed hard among the rest of Team Elliott).

Elliott responded with a social media video calling on everyone to “unite, not divide.”

The fractures cracked wide open in the early fall, with a chaotic stretch of staff hirings followed swiftly by firings and the departure of 13 MLAs. It became clear Findlay couldn’t continue.

When the election was called and Doerkson was chosen as leader, many of those recently departed MLAs were brought back into the fold.

“Everybody showed up, and it’s like, ‘Let’s see if we can put Humpty Dumpty back together again,’” Gunn said.

Anthony Koch, who was a senior adviser on Doerkson’s campaign, was among those who jumped back into the fray after working on Elliott’s leadership run. A key takeaway for him is that tone matters.

“Yes, you need to motivate your people. Yes, you need to be a real conservative. But you also need to present yourself in such a way that no one’s scared by the prospect of you forming government,” said Koch, who was communications director for Poilievre’s 2022 leadership campaign.

Doerkson’s Conservatives didn’t compromise on principles, Merrifield said. The party pledged to get rid of Dripa, the controversial NDP law to enact the UN Convention on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and end the sexual orientation and gender identity policy in education.

“I can’t point to any policy that Kerry-Lynne Findlay announced that Lorne Doerkson came in and reversed and abandoned,” said Gunn.

“But the tone and how those issues were communicated, I think, did change significantly.”

Insiders describe Doerkson as a “happy warrior,” a consensus builder and a regular guy.

Merrifield said she thinks his appeal, similar to that of Prime Minister Mark Carney, demonstrates that the era of anger-driven politics is out, at least for the moment.

“Normal is back,” Koch said.

Politicians like Justin Trudeau, who energized progressives, or Donald Trump, who ignited the Maga base, are falling out of favour with an electorate that’s now looking for “more calm, competent, normal, adult-like politicians,” he said.

Merrifield, who was Poilievre’s communications director last year, was credited with encouraging the Tory leader to change his strategy and tone after losing the 2025 election. For a brief period during her tenure, he spoke more with mainstream media and sat down with popular podcasters like Joe Rogan. But the party continues to struggle in the polls.

Gunn acknowledged Poilievre has tried to shift his tone — a number of times, in fact — over the last two years, but maintains that another adjustment is not what’s needed.

“What I think we need to continue focusing on is staying true to your values, principles and beliefs, while also trying to be as welcoming to as many Canadians as possible,” he said.

Koch is still firmly in the camp of those who believe Poilievre is the best person to lead right now. He has the support of caucus, and earned the support of delegates at this year’s leadership review.

But caucus morale took a series of blows over the last year as four MPs crossed the floor, and a fifth joined the Senate. Two others have left, and byelections to replace them in Yorkton-Melville and Brantford-Brant South on Dec. 7 are being closely watched.

Poilievre already weighed in on the Ontario race, installing a candidate instead of allowing an open nomination, and in the process blocked a local party organizer who had the backing of outgoing MP Larry Brock. Dave Carrol is now running as an independent in what’s expected to be a tight race.

With polls continuing to place the Conservatives a distant second to Carney’s Liberals, losing Brantford-Brant South could be another mark against Poilievre.

Koch said there is another cautionary tale for federal Conservatives in all of this: if you rewind the clock to early September, British Columbia’s centre-right looked like it had been cleaved into at least three parts.

For some Tories, the disastrous outcome the B.C. Conservatives narrowly avoided is just as instructive as the party’s electoral triumph.

Sarah Ritchie joined National Post’s politics bureau after four years covering breaking news on Parliament Hill for The Canadian Press, where she worked as a reporter and editor. Before that, she was an anchor and investigative reporter at Global News in Halifax and covered the Nova Scotia legislature for CTV Atlantic.

stories.title: ‘Crypto King’ kidnapping trial opens with tape of desperate call ‘begging’ Toronto hotel magnate for money
stories.summary: 'I wouldn't be calling you begging you for money right now at one o'clock in the morning if it wasn't something serious.'
stories.author: Betsy Powell
stories.content:
A group of men allegedly kidnapped, tortured and tried to extort “Crypto King” Aiden Pleterski over three days across Ontario in late 2022 after one of them failed to recover money he believed he was owed.

That’s the picture Crown attorney Julia De Vuono painted for jurors Tuesday as the trial of three of the alleged participants got underway in downtown Toronto.

“The evidence will show that a dispute over money escalated into a violent kidnapping carried out over three days across Ontario,” De Vuono said in her opening address. “During that time, Pleterski was abducted, confined, assaulted and held while his captors attempted to obtain money from him.”

During the alleged kidnapping, a video was released on social media of Pleterski appearing badly beaten and making a false explanation of what happened with the investment money, De Vuono told the jury. Pleterski was eventually released on Dec. 8, 2022, and will testify he was repeatedly threatened, assaulted, burned, cut and waterboarded and was led to believe that he was going to be killed, she said.

Pleterski, 27, was recently convicted of fraud in the same courthouse and is awaiting sentencing.

Pleterski had taken in millions in investments on the promise of surefire returns trading cryptocurrency. By 2022, tensions were growing, and many investors were demanding repayment.

Akil Heywood, who lost a substantial sum in Pleterski’s investment scheme, was the “driving force” behind the kidnapping plot, De Vuono said. A prominent figure in the ensuing bankruptcy proceedings, Heywood had repeatedly confronted Pleterski about money in the months leading up to the alleged abduction, she said.

The Crown is not alleging Heywood, who has pleaded not guilty to kidnapping and extortion, was present during the three days.

Rakeem Henry and Alfredo Paladino — two of three men who allegedly carried out the abduction — have all pleaded not guilty to kidnapping, extortion and other charges. Deren Akyeam-Pong, whom De Vuono called the “lead” kidnapper, is not on trial.

On Dec. 5, 2022, the night of the alleged kidnapping, Pleterski called Sandeep Gupta, whose family owned the $10-million Burlington mansion where Pleterski was living under a lease-to-own arrangement costing him around $45,000 a month.

Gupta — the president of the hotel division of Sunray Group, which operates 75 hotels across Canada — was the Crown’s first witness Tuesday.

Jurors heard a recording of Pleterski pleading by phone with Gupta to come up with $2 to $3 million. Gupta didn’t record the call, but he put Pleterski on speakerphone and separately called 911. The call was captured by the operator, who was familiar with the high-profile case.

“I wouldn’t be calling you begging you for money right now at one o’clock in the morning if it wasn’t something serious ... OK,” Pleterski told Gupta, speaking in an increasingly urgent tone.

“I totally get that, and that’s why I’m trying to figure out how to help you,” Gupta responded, telling Pleterski there is no way he can come up with the cash in the middle of the night.

During his combative cross-examination, Hussein Aly, the defence lawyer representing Heywood, suggested to Gupta that he was either in on Pleterski’s schemes, or was trying to get whatever funds he could when the “gig” was up.

“Mr. Gupta, did you know that Aiden Pleterski stole $30 or $40 million ... from hard-working people,” Aly asked.

“When I had my dealings with him, I didn’t know it was stolen money. To me ... he had an investment company and people invested with him.”

“You say you had no part in any of this,” Aly continued.

“Let’s talk about some of the support Aiden Pleterski got along the way,” the lawyer continued. He zeroed in on the word “mentor” that Gupta used when describing his relationship with the younger man to police.

“Mentor was a wrong choice of words,” Gupta responded. “I was a sounding board for him.”

Aly noted that Pleterski put down a $500,000 deposit on the mansion and, when he could no longer cover the rent, provided Gupta with a $1 million car as collateral. Gupta also arranged for Pleterski to stay in a rental unit near Barrie after angry investors began showing up at the property.

“All types of bad things happened, right?” Aly asked.

“Correct,” he replied.

“And you’re saying you did this at the goodness of your heart?”

“When somebody calls you in a possibly life-or-death situation, I didn’t want to hang up the phone.”

“The truth is, you had to be involved because you’re too smart to associate with this fraudster. What did you get out of this?”

“I got nothing out of it,” he said — except “misery.”

The trial resumes Thursday.

Jurors heard a recording of Pleterski pleading by phone with Gupta to come up with $2 to $3 million. Gupta didn’t record the call, but he put Pleterski on speakerphone and separately called 911. The call was captured by the operator, who was familiar with the high-profile case.
“I wouldn’t be calling you begging you for money right now at one o’clock in the morning if it wasn’t something serious ... OK,” Pleterski told Gupta, speaking in an increasingly urgent tone.
“I totally get that, and that’s why I’m trying to figure out how to help you,” Gupta responded, telling Pleterski there is no way he can come up with the cash in the middle of the night.

During his combative cross-examination, Hussein Aly, the defence lawyer representing Heywood, suggested to Gupta that he was either in on Pleterski’s schemes, or was trying to get whatever funds he could when the “gig” was up.
“Mr. Gupta, did you know that Aiden Pleterski stole $30 or $40 million ... from hard-working people,” Aly asked.
“When I had my dealings with him, I didn’t know it was stolen money. To me ... he had an investment company and people invested with him.”
“You say you had no part in any of this,” Aly continued.

“Let’s talk about some of the support Aiden Pleterski got along the way,” the lawyer continued. He zeroed in on the word “mentor” that Gupta used when describing his relationship with the younger man to police.
“Mentor was a wrong choice of words,” Gupta responded. “I was a sounding board for him.”

Aly noted that Pleterski put down a $500,000 deposit on the mansion and, when he could no longer cover the rent, provided Gupta with a $1 million car as collateral. Gupta also arranged for Pleterski to stay in a rental unit near Barrie after angry investors began showing up at the property.
“All types of bad things happened, right?” Aly asked.
“Correct,” he replied.
“And you’re saying you did this at the goodness of your heart?”
“When somebody calls you in a possibly life-or-death situation, I didn’t want to hang up the phone.”
“The truth is, you had to be involved because you’re too smart to associate with this fraudster. What did you get out of this?”
“I got nothing out of it,” he said — except “misery.”
The trial resumes Thursday.

Wednesday, November 11, 2026

Lane restrictions are currently in place on Wonderland Road between Beaverbrook Avenue and Farrah Road as crews address breaks to the watermain.

Two different leaks have been repaired on the watermain, and crews are currently preparing to repave the area. The road is expected to be reopened this evening.

Motorists should avoid the area, expect delays, and follow posted signs.

A map showing temporary lane restrictions on Wonderland Road between Beaverbrook Avenue and Farrah Road.

stories.content:
A separate campaign to pressure the University of B.C. into overhauling how it handles sexual-assault complaints following multiple allegations against a PhD student in its history department was intensifying around the time allegations against bestselling author Steven Galloway exploded, an advocate for victims of sexual violence testified Tuesday.

Glynnis Kirchmeier testified in her own defence in B.C. Supreme Court as to how, in the fall of 2015, some in the school community began conflating her efforts and those of others to hold the university to account with a separate push by a former student to get the university to investigate allegations Mr. Galloway sexually harassed and sexually assaulted her.

Mr. Galloway, who was the chair of Ubc’s creative-writing program, launched a lawsuit against almost two dozen defendants in 2018. He claims that a woman, known as A.B. because of a publication ban on her identity, made allegations that ruined his reputation , cost him his job and destroyed his personal life.

Tuesday’s testimony painted a picture of an institution embroiled in scandal at the dawning of the #MeToo era and a growing call for systemic change across society to combat sexual violence.

Ms. Kirchmeier told the court that as she held a Nov. 22, 2015, press conference about the complaints related to the history student, local media asked about Mr. Galloway, who the university had announced four days earlier it was suspending because of “serious allegations.”

She testified the university was also fielding questions from the CBC’s the fifth estate about an episode involving the history student that was set to air at the end of November, with other outlets also contacting the CBC wondering if the coming TV documentary promoted by the national broadcaster involved Mr. Galloway.

“The journalists who came to the press conference - which took place at the UBC campus - I do recall some asking if Mr. Galloway was included in the documentary, but one of the other women said ‘no,’ and ‘we don’t know anything about that,’” said Ms. Kirchmeier, who participated in the CBC documentary.

Ms. Kirchmeier testified that she first met A.B. in the spring of 2016 and began helping advise her how to hold the university accountable.

Only A.B., Ms. Kirchmeier and two others are on trial. The rest have settled with Mr. Galloway, who has never been charged with a criminal offence and has always denied he sexually assaulted A.B., with whom he was having a two-year affair.

Ms. Kirchmeier, who is attending law school in the United States, is representing herself in the trial and claiming a defence of fair comment against Mr. Galloway’s assertion that her 2018 post on the social-media site X, then known as Twitter, defamed him. In that tweet, she called out The Walrus magazine for publishing a news feature for which, she testified, she believed that Mr. Galloway was the main source.

“That piece said Galloway had an ‘affair,’ which we now know is what he calls raping/sexually harassing a student. But it set the narrative for 1 + year,” the tweet read.

Ms. Kirchmeier contends that, per the Chicago style citation guidelines she used as a history student, the slash in that tweet meant either sexually assaulting or harassing a student not both acts, which Mr. Galloway’s lawyers reject.

The cross-examination of Ms. Kirchmeier by Daniel Coles became heated in the afternoon when he brought up personal e-mails between her, A.B. and fellow defendant Mandi Gray , a Trent University assistant professor of criminology. In those e-mails, Ms. Kirchmeier vented about the findings of former B.C. Supreme Court justice Mary Ellen Boyd, whom the school hired in late 2015 to investigate A.B.’s allegations.

In 2016 Ms. Boyd found that, ON a balance of probabilities, it could not be established that he committed sexual assault or assault, but that he had sexually harassed her and committed other misconduct.

During cross-examination, Mr. Coles read out one of Ms. Kirchmeier’s e-mails: “This all sucks. SG sucks. UBC sucks. Boyd’s a shill. The Walrus is nasty and uncritical.”

Mr. Coles then pressed her on whether she believed UBC hired the retired judge “for a predetermined outcome.”

Ms. Kirchmeier said she did, based on her experience with another investigation into the allegations into her fellow history student.

Earlier in the day, Ms. Kirchmeier detailed how she made efforts to influence the university.

On Nov. 10, 2015, Ms. Kirchmeier sent an open letter to her network of students and professors in the history department, from which she had just graduated, calling out UBC for not acting on complaints about a male PhD student that stretched out over years, which led to more women becoming his victims, she told court.

Her letter found its way into the inbox of Mr. Galloway’s accuser. The next day, A.B., a former creative writing student, forwarded it to Mr. Galloway and another senior professor in her program, Ms. Kirchmeier testified.

Witness testimony is expected to finish this week, with the trial resuming Friday when Ubc’s then-dean of arts Gage Averill takes the stand at the behest of the defence.

stories.title: 90-year-old veteran selling poppies says he was ‘harassed’ by Montreal metro security
stories.summary: 90-year-old Carl Andersen has been selling poppies in the Montreal metro since 2007, but he says he recently ran into a bit of an obstacle.
stories.author: Dan Spector
stories.content:
A Montreal man who’s been selling poppies at the Vendôme metro station for two decades says he was recently hassled by security guards.

The 90-year-old Carl Andersen is a Canadian Forces veteran who volunteers his early November mornings raising money for the Royal Canadian Legion.

Recently, he ran into a bit of an obstacle. Andersen says last week two Société de transport de Montréal (STM) transit agency security officers asked him if he had permission to sell poppies at Vendôme.

“I said, I’ve been doing it for 20 years, I’ve never had to ask permission. He said, ‘well, we’re trying to get rid of people asking for money in the subway,'” Andersen recounted to Global News.

Andersen said it’s the first time he’s ever been hassled by security. He said after consulting with their supervisors, the officers told him they would “tolerate” his presence.

“I felt a little harassed,” he said. “The thing is, I didn’t like the word ‘tolerate,’ which meant that they could change that toleration at any moment.”

The STM told Global News it is permitted to solicit donations outside the paid zone.

“If Mr. Andersen does not solicit customers, but rather waits for customers to come to him and it is considered a donation, there should not be a problem, as long as he complies with the other rules concerning traffic flow, civic conduct, etc,” STM spokesperson Amelie Regis said in an emailed statement.

He hasn’t had any trouble since, and the people he was pinning poppies on Tuesday appeared happy to see him, according to Global News staff.

Some buy from him year after year, pausing their commutes for a warm greeting and a story.

“There are veterans that are in real need, and for them, this is why we do it,” he said.

Charity is a vital part of who Andersen is. It’s something the Canadian Forces veteran says he learned from his mom. “My mother was very giving and we weren’t brought up with a hell of a lot of bucks,” he said.

Andersen says he lied about his age to join the forces at 15. He served in Canada during the tail end of the Korean War. He claims eventually his lie was discovered, and he was honourably discharged.

Andersen used to be a big runner. He says he’s completed 97 marathons in his life, and he’s done more fundraising runs than he can count. He’s raised money for breast cancer research, the Terry Fox Foundation and the War Amps, among others.

“I’m close to, if not over, a million dollars in charity done through my running,” he said.

Andersen said he hopes to keep volunteering for the Legion at Vendôme until he’s at least 100.

stories.title: Ontario court sides with tow-truck drivers ousted by Ford government’s rules
stories.summary: Court of Appeal rules that new law cannot permanently ban people with historic drug-trafficking convictions
stories.author: Colin Freeze
stories.content:
The Ontario government cannot permanently ban people who have drug-trafficking convictions from driving tow trucks, according to the Court of Appeal.

In a decision issued Monday by a three-judge panel, the Ontario Court of Appeal sided with two tow-truck drivers who alleged Premier Doug Ford’s government had been unfairly barring them from seeking certification under a new law intended to keep criminals out of the tow-truck industry.

As The Globe and Mail previously reported, André Thibault and Sean Ramsay alleged the new rules cast too wide a net.

The Ontario government passed a law in 2021 giving it control over tow-truck certifications. New screening requirements imposed in July 2024 bar drivers with certain kinds of criminal histories – including those who have weapons bans – from holding certifications.

When the regime started, it began screening out people convicted of drug-trafficking offences – regardless of the date or nature of the crime committed – because such convictions in court automatically impose a lifetime weapons ban.

However, the appeal court has now ruled that permanently barring these drivers from certification is “illogical,” given how the same regulations spell out a punishment written specifically for convicted drug dealers.

There can be no certification in such cases only if “a person has been convicted or found guilty in the preceding ten years of an offence,” these regulations say.

The Court of Appeal did not overturn the new regulation or the Ministry of Transportation’s previous decision to deny the drivers certification. But the ruling does say that such applicants “should be certifiable once 10 years have elapsed since their conviction.”

stories.title: B.C. storm delays search for missing canoeist
stories.summary: Dakota Smith, 35, was reported missing last Friday after going fishing
stories.author: Brieanna Charlebois
stories.content:
Wild weather that is slamming into the south coast of British Columbia has forced the suspension of search-and-rescue efforts for a missing canoeist off Vancouver Island, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides triggered by drenching rains.

A series of atmospheric rivers has been hitting southwest B.C. since last week, with the latest storms forecast to bring up to 250 millimetres of rain in some places.

The storms had already turned deadly, with the deaths of a driver in Surrey, B.C., whose car was crushed by a falling tree on Saturday, and a Vancouver pedestrian who was hit by a car during what police called a heavy rainstorm last Friday.

RCMP in Sayward, B.C., said worsening weather had made it unsafe for water and shoreline searches for 35-year old Dakota Smith, who was reported missing last Friday after going fishing.

Smith’s capsized canoe had been found in waters off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, but police said the chances of his survival had been “drastically reduced” by “high unpredictable winds, heavy rainfalls and the frigid water temperature.”

The Ma’amtagila Nation community indicated members were continuing to look for Smith despite the end of the official search.

Environment Canada recorded high winds the day Smith went missing, and the province was being struck by storm systems that are continuing.

Environment Canada meteorologist Michael Gismondi said in an interview Tuesday that the drenching from the atmospheric river storms is “fairly typical for this time of year.”

“Typically we get a few every year, so it’s not unusual for this to happen.”

Gismondi said he does not expect “catastrophic” impacts, but flooding was possible as the rain continued across the region for a day or more.

“It kind of taps into some warm tropical air from the lower latitudes and it brings it right up to the B.C. coast,” he said of the atmospheric river. “So we’ll expect heavy rain, mild conditions, high freezing levels and then there’s another system coming in that will sort of re-intensify that front as we go into Wednesday.”

Environment Canada has raised orange rainfall warnings in west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky regions, meaning the “severe” storms were likely to cause significant damage and disruption.

The agency said parts of Vancouver Island could see more than 250 millimetres of rain, while Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions could see upwards of 160 millimetres.

Parts of Metro Vancouver could receive 160 millimetres, while Haida Gwaii and north Vancouver Island could get wind gusts of up to 110 kilometres an hour.

Grouse Mountain Regional Park in North Vancouver closed early on Tuesday due to inclement weather, and the mountain’s website says both the Grouse Grind and Bcmc trail will be closed on Wednesday due to heavy rains.

The mountain’s website said park staff will assess conditions over the coming days to determine when it can safely reopen.

The forecaster also issued orange warnings for potentially “damaging winds” in central B.C., ON Tuesday. It said the southeasterly wind would increase into Wednesday, with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour expected in some regions before easing Wednesday evening.

British Columbia’s River Forecast Centre issued ongoing flood watches on Monday for much of Vancouver Island and the South Coast, with the worst weather expected to last into Wednesday before tapering off Thursday.

The agency issued high streamflow advisories for southern Vancouver Island, the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon on Tuesday.

BC Hydro said in a news release Tuesday that its crews were working to restore power to customers “following a series of damaging storms that affected approximately 415,000 customers across the province since Friday.”

It noted some of the most extensive storm damage happened in the northern and central Interior, adding that about 2,300 properties remained without power as of Tuesday.

Gismondi said the precipitation along B.C.’s coastal regions is expected to slow early Wednesday before the next system is forecast to pass through the region. That, he said, is expected to continue until Friday, when another short break is expected.

“It kind of looks like another system coming for the weekend – so probably back into some rain for the weekend,” he said.

B.C.’s Transportation Ministry issued a news release late Tuesday, advising drivers travelling along the south coast to monitor conditions and prepare for heavy rain, wind and possible flooding through the rest of the week.

“Ministry contractors are actively preparing by clearing debris from roadways and drainage infrastructure,” the statement said. “They will continue monitoring corridors throughout the storm and be ready to respond immediately to issues.”

Gismondi suggested people take steps to try to mitigate flooding, including making sure their storm drains are clear and to ensure loose objects are put away as heavy winds are also expected in the region.

“If you’re driving, watch for water pooling on the roads, try not to drive through any deep water,” he warned.

“Be aware of possible hydroplaning, keep your headlights on, keep a safe distance and slow down. Just try and be careful out there, and stay safe.”

stories.title: More disturbing evidence at murder trial of London man accused of setting his best friend on fire
stories.summary: The Crown produced text messages that were extracted from a cellphone registered to the accused.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Despite being best friends, The Crown’s theory is that in the hours before 29-year-old Jonathan Graham was set on fire, he and Bradley Joudrey were upset with each other after the victim punch the accused.

The trial has heard the pair was supposed to meet at a convenience store parking lot at Trafalgar Street and Admiral Drive in the early morning hours of July 12, 2022.

The Crown produced text messages that were extracted from a cellphone registered to Joudrey that were sent just seconds before the fire.

At 2:06:39 a.m., the first text asked, “Where’d you go?” Then seconds later, “Call me.”

At 2:08:02 a.m., “Watch you and your car.” And then seconds later, “Don’t be a b**** call me.”

Finally, at 2:15:12 a.m., “Better be there.”

The Crown has told the court that minutes after the two met, Graham was set on fire.

Witness Shane Woolner testified that he was outside having a cigarette at the time when he her a commotion and rushed to the scene.

He saw the victim and the burned clothes on the ground, saying, “I asked if he was okay and he said, ‘No.’ Someone had poured gasoline on him.”

Minutes after that, London Police Const. Cassidy Wattie showed up, and testified that he did his best to preserve the scene for evidence because it started raining, “Some clothing on the grass was slightly smoking.”

He added, “My main concern was the charred area and the piece of skin.”

When retired London Police Forensic Officer Richard Terrio arrived at the fire scene to collect evidence, he testified, “I saw a Pepsi bottle … I smelled an accelerant and it smelled like gasoline to me.”

Graham was rushed to hospital and was later pronounced dead from thermal injuries.

The Crown says the 36-year-old Graham drove off from the scene, crashed his vehicle, and ran home where he was later arrested.

He has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder.

The court was shown photos of Joudrey following his arrest which included injuries and abrasions to his face, neck, legs, and feet.

The trial and the Crown’s case resume on Thursday.

stories.title: Zak Jones, Robert Moor among Writers’ Trust prize winners
stories.summary: Country’s most generous literary event gave away more than $400,000 to Canadian writers on Tuesday
stories.author: Brad Wheeler
stories.content:
Snazzier book galas get the glory, but the country’s most generous literary event gave away more than $400,000 to Canadian writers on Tuesday evening at the annual Writers’ Trust Awards in Toronto.

Among the winners announced at the CBC’s Glenn Gould Studio was Zak Jones, who received the $70,000 Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize for his debut novel Fancy Gap , published by Hamish Hamilton Canada. Jones is a U.S. Army veteran and dual Canadian-American citizen who grew up between rural North Carolina and Toronto.

The jury of Canadian fiction writers, David Chariandy, Conor Kerr and Kathleen Winter, cited the Appalachia-set saga about poverty, substance abuse and apocalyptic Christianity as an uncanny read: “Jones brings the setting alive through sound, taste, smell, and imagery in a slow burn that leaves readers feeling as if they, too, are in detox from a world they’ve only ever heard whispered about.”

On the non-fiction side, Robert Moor was awarded the $75,000 Hilary Weston Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction for In Trees: An Exploration , published by Simon & Schuster Canada. The American magazine writer is based in Halfmoon Bay, B.C.

His winning book is a sequel to 2016’s On Trails: An Exploration , inspired by a hike through the Appalachian Trail. For In Trees , he branched out to scale a giant sequoia with Sir David Attenborough and travelled to Tanzania to spend a night sleeping in a chimpanzee nest.

In its citation, the jury of Canadian non-fiction writers, Katherine Ashenburg, Debra Thompson and Joshua Whitehead, said Moor wrote with the “sensibility of a poet and the relentless curiosity of a philosopher,” and that his book is a “sophisticated and moving analysis that asks his audience to think carefully and expansively about what we might learn from these quiet, ancient, surrounding forms of life that grow slowly, endure catastrophe, and exist in complicated and profound interdependence.”

Six other Writers’ Trust prizes were presented at an event hosted by poet Moez Surani.

Métis author Cherie Dimaline, whose The Marrow Thieves was named by Time magazine as one of the top 100 young-adult books of all time in 2021, took home the $40,000 Vicky Metcalf Award for Literature for Young People.

Vancouver author Rachel Rose received the inaugural $25,000 Nancy Flight Writers’ Trust Prize for Nonfiction Editing for Humanitarienne: A Doctor’s Stories from the Conflict Zone by Kirsten Johnson, published by Douglas & McIntyre.

Toronto’s Margaret Christakos won the $60,000 Latner Griffin Writers’ Trust Poetry Prize, a career honour.

Métis author and playwright Maria Campbell was given the $40,000 Matt Cohen Award recognizing a commitment to the writing life that has spanned 50 years.

Montreal poet Misha Solomon was awarded the $12,000 Dayne Ogilvie Prize for LGBTQ2S+ Emerging Writers for My Great-Grandfather Danced Ballet , published by Brick Books.

Vancouver novelist Shaena Lambert won the $25,000 Writers’ Trust Engel Findley Award recognizing an outstanding writer of fiction in mid-career.

The Writers’ Trust also hosted a presentation from the founders of the Andrew Pyper Prize for Genre Fiction. The career prize recognizes the writing legacy of the late thriller novelist . Speculative fiction writer Nalo Hopkinson was announced as the inaugural winner of the $20,000 award.

November is the high season for literary events in Canada. On Thursday, the Canada Council for the Arts will announce the 2026 winners of the Governor-General’s Literary Awards , which honour works published in Canada, in English and French, across seven categories. The Globe and Mail’s Greg Mercer is a finalist for his non-fiction book The Lobster Trap.

The country’s richest fiction award, the $100,000 Giller Prize, will be presented at a Toronto gala hosted by Rick Mercer and televised and streamed across CBC platforms on Nov. 16. The nominees are Toronto’s Patmeena Sabit, Regina’s Tara Gereaux, Vancouver’s Nazanine Hozar , Pei’s Nicholas Herring and Saskatchewan’s Michelle Good .

Globe reporter and photojournalist Jesse Winter is shortlisted for Canada’s Balsillie Prize for Public Policy , an annual $70,000 award that recognizes books that advance policy discussions on social, political, economic and cultural topics. His Wild Fire: Dispatches from a Country Ablaze covers three Canadian wildfires from the front lines.

The four other finalists are Tim Wu, Rick Westhead, Moira Welsh and Dennis Molinaro, with the winner revealed on Nov. 24.

stories.title: Tensions emerge at first Kelowna council meeting over board appointments
stories.summary: The regional district board is the only one of more than a dozen for which councillors receive compensation.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
Tensions are already emerging on Kelowna’s newly elected city council, with councillor Gord Lovegrove challenging mayor Tom Dyas over appointments to the regional district board.

“You’re breaking with tradition and putting that trust at risk again,” said Lovegrove at Monday’s council meeting, directing the comment at Dyas. “I think this sets the tone for the next four years in council. I am very concerned.”

Lovegrove, who topped council votes in the municipal election, is questioning why he wasn’t among the councillors recommended by Dyas for a seat at the regional table.

“I’ve seen no precedent where the top vote-getter, the top qualified by the voters themselves councillor, is not appointed to the regional district,” Lovegrove told Global News on Tuesday.

The two-term councillor suspects politics May have played a role in the decision.

Lovegrove supported Dyas’ mayoral rival, Ron Cannan, during the election campaign.

“I think there is political payback involved,” Lovegrove said.

Dyas denied any personal vendetta, saying his recommendations were based on skills identified during council orientation-a session Lovegrove missed due to a family vacation.

“I have great confidence with regards to the individuals within Kelowna who elected council,” Dyas said. “They all have skills that will be extremely valuable on all of the different boards.”

Dyas added that the mayor does not have unilateral say on appointments.

“What a mayor does is make a recommendation and then council needs to vote on that,” Dyas said.

But Lovegrove said new councillors May feel reluctant to challenge the mayor’s recommendation.

“With five new councillors, the mayor made a recommendation and they are not necessarily going to go against that,” Lovegrove said.

The regional district board is the only one of more than a dozen for which councillors receive compensation.

Other notable appointments include Dyas returning himself to the uptown Rutland Business Association board, an area where residents have long voiced concerns about feeling overlooked.

Dyas also recommended downtown business owner Brady Rogers for the Downtown Kelowna Association board.

Todd Daniels, owner of Gallery Streetwear, says he believes Rogers is the right person for the position.

Daniels previously took to social media to call for more city action on downtown social disorder.

“After we made our video back in January, we saw an uptick in the police force, the bylaw for maybe a month and then it went away,” Daniels said.

As for the regional district appointments, Lovegrove says he isn’t letting the issue rest.

He plans to bring forward a motion that would see future appointments determined by election vote counts, rather than recommendations from the mayor.

“Let’s just remove the politics from this,” Lovegrove said.

content_blocks.text: “You’re breaking with tradition and putting that trust at risk again,” said Lovegrove at Monday’s council meeting, directing the comment at Dyas. “I think this sets the tone for the next four years in council. I am very concerned.”
Lovegrove, who topped council votes in the municipal election, is questioning why he wasn’t among the councillors recommended by Dyas for a seat at the regional table.
“I’ve seen no precedent where the top vote-getter, the top qualified by the voters themselves councillor, is not appointed to the regional district,” Lovegrove told Global News on Tuesday.

stories.summary: Vancouver - A defendant in Steven Galloway's defamation lawsuit has testified how unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author and writing professor came to light in late 2015 against a backdrop of criticism over how Galloway's employer, the University of British Columbia, was handling such complaints.
stories.author: Brenna Owen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - A defendant in Steven Galloway’s defamation lawsuit has testified how unproven allegations of rape and sexual assault against the author and writing professor came to light in late 2015 against a backdrop of criticism over how Galloway’s employer, the University of British Columbia, was handling such complaints.

Glynnis Kirchmeier, a former graduate student who is representing herself at the B.C. Supreme Court trial, outlined her involvement in calls for the university to improve processes for complaints of sexual misconduct, including contacting David Eby years before he became premier.

stories.title: Rural N.S. patients worry as medical ride program comes to an end
stories.summary: Nova Scotia Health said that "between exhausting federal funds and the complexities of rural, non-medical transportation, the program quickly became unsustainable."
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Mitchell Bailey
stories.content:
People in some northern Nova Scotia communities say they’re worried about losing access to health care as a pilot program that offers rides to appointments is coming to an end on Dec. 1.

For three years now, the Northern Zone Transportation Pilot has helped people in East Hants, Colchester, Cumberland and Pictou counties get to non-urgent health-care appointments.

It’s offered through Nova Scotia Health and was intended to help improve access to care.

News that the rides won’t be available after this month is concerning to patients like Wanda Tingley, who has a traumatic brain injury and requires many doctors’ appointments that have her travelling from her home in Lantz, N.S. to the city.

“To take a cab from here to Halifax for my head treatment is $123 one way,” said Tingley. “I’m 65 years old on old age security.”

Tingley points out there are no public transit options in the area. When the program began in 2023, she says she used it “pretty much almost daily.” Now, she depends on it a couple of times a week.

“I do have medical appointments in December, but I’ll have to cancel them,” she said.

Andrew Doughty, the owner of Handy Cabs, has been working under the program to drive patients to medical appointments. He estimates his company makes 250 trips a month.

“We’re picking up people that physically can’t get to the hospital, whether it’s for financial reasons. We’ve got people that can’t drive, that aren’t legally allowed to drive anymore,” he said.

“There’s been customers I’ve picked up that haven’t even been into the city for 20 years and they’re going in for cancer treatment.”

Those patients are now calling him and wondering what the change will mean.

“We’ve got people calling and they’re like, ‘What do I do now?’ And I literally don’t have an answer,” he said.

The service was offered through federal and provincial support.

In a statement, Nova Scotia Health said that “between exhausting federal funds and the complexities of rural, non-medical transportation, the program quickly became unsustainable.”

Cumberland North MLA Elizabeth Smith-McCrossin said the service is vital for rural communities and she wants to see it reinstated.

“Most people in our area, there’s a lot of seniors, there’s high incidence of people with disabilities. Poverty is a real thing and cancellation of this program will mean people will not be able to access health care,” she said.

“It’s the wrong decision and on behalf of all of the people, I’m calling on the premier to reverse this decision immediately.”

Nova Scotia Health says it is reaching out to impacted patients to inform them of alternative transportation options.

stories.title: P.E.I.’s minimum wage is $17.30, but living wage tops $24. Does the new capital budget help?
stories.summary: The P.E.I. government unveiled a smaller plan for long-term investments Tuesday afternoon, as some Islanders struggle to afford housing and other essentials.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – The P.E.I. government unveiled a smaller plan for long-term investments Tuesday afternoon, as some Islanders struggle to afford housing and other essentials. The 2027-28 capital budget earmarks $1.34 billion over five years, $289 million less than last year’s plan.

Nearly 60 per cent of the funding is dedicated to health care and education, with a focus on maintaining existing assets and building new infrastructure where the government sees urgent and critical needs. “We are doing the most we can, inside our guardrails,” said Finance and Affordability Minister Jill Burridge.

She said the lower total partly reflects major projects nearing completion. Other work is being deferred as the province prioritizes finishing what it already started. With demand for skilled labour and building materials high, Burridge said scheduling too many projects at once could drive up costs and delay delivery.

Additional projects would also increase borrowing and interest payments, putting pressure on future budgets, she said. Two credit rating agencies, Moody’s and S&P, have assigned negative outlooks to the province’s credit ratings, signalling a risk of downgrades.

In the legislature, Premier Rob Lantz said every project had to pass a test: is it needed or wanted? “Every dollar we spend on capital investments is another dollar in debt,” he said. Highlights from the budget Highlights from the capital budget include $418 million to improve the safety and reliability of the health-care system and $380 million for education, with funding for construction and upgrades, including a new school in Summerside.

Another $285 million is allocated to rehabilitating and improving roads, bridges and highways, while $60 million is set aside for housing. That housing commitment “pales in comparison” to what’s needed, said Christine Saulnier, a director with the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives (Ccpa).

“When you’re seeing a target in housing that isn’t even half of what you’re spending on roads, where are your priorities?” she asked. While capital spending is not designed to provide immediate relief from grocery bills or raise wages, it can help reduce housing, transportation, and childcare costs over time.

Saulnier pointed to 2021 census data showing more than 4,000 P.E.I. households were in need of core housing. That means their homes needed major repairs, were too crowded or unaffordable. That number has likely risen since the census, Saulnier said.

Figures provided by the Finance Department show the province added 262 government-owned social housing units in the last two years and plans to build another 42 over the next five. Living wage rises A new report from the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives released this week, suggests Islanders need to make about $24 an hour on average to cover basic living expenses.

That’s nearly $7 more than the province’s minimum wage, which was raised to $17.30 in October. The living wage calculation increased by 5.75 per cent this year, reflecting higher rent and fuel costs, along with a revised transportation budget.

P.E.I. recorded the highest inflation rate among provinces at 5.7 per cent in September, well above the national rate of 3.1 per cent. “If you’re earning less than that, then you are making difficult choices,” Saulnier said.

The reference is a family of two parents working full time, raising a couple children, aged two and seven. It assumes the household relies on full-time childcare, plus care before and after school and during breaks, with the parents using three weeks of vacation to cover some of those needs.

But it doesn’t account for every real-world situation, like someone living with a chronic illness or disability. An earlier Ccpa analysis found nearly one in four P.E.I. workers earned less than $20 an hour in 2025, the minimum wage the organization has been advocating for.

Responding to concerns about housing, Minister Burridge pointed to what she called record investments over the past three years, citing higher vacancy rates as a sign of progress. The Finance Department said it’s also seeking clarity from the federal government on how the Build Communities Strong Fund could help pay for road and bridge work in the capital plan.

Saulnier credited the province with investing in buses and regional transportation, which can help families spend less on gas. But she said she’s hearing that services aren’t frequent or accessible enough for some people to get to work on time.

She also welcomed the province’s child benefit and essentials benefit, along with the addition of a tax bracket for higher income earners. “All those things together could actually make a difference,” she said. “But we need to see more of that coming forward so that households are actually receiving some benefits.”
