stories.title: Dresden keeps up landfill battle as project seeks Ontario approvals
stories.summary: A southwestern Ontario town is pushing back on the latest step to advance a controversial landfill and transfer station project, as Premier Doug Ford's government ramps up a search for garbage space.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A southwestern Ontario town is pushing back on the latest step to advance a controversial landfill and waste transfer station project, as Premier Doug Ford’s government ramps up a search for garbage space.

Waste company York1 wants to revive and expand a dormant landfill less than a kilometre from Dresden and pack it over the next decade with enough waste to fill Toronto’s Rogers Centre, despite local opposition.

“It’s a beautiful town, fantastic community, and this is just a few hundred metres north of town,” said Dave Taylor, deputy chief administrative officer for Chatham-Kent, the municipality encompassing Dresden.

“Our council has been unanimously opposed to the project since York1 proposed it.”

The landfill would be mostly soils, such as excavated earth from worksites along with other construction waste, according to the company’s site plans. The proposed transfer station would also sort and clean up construction debris, scrap wood, blue box material and dirt, before sending it to recyclers or landfillers.

Municipal officials have argued the company relied on outdated permits, granted decades ago, to bypass a full environmental assessment. The Ford government, which backtracked last year on a promise to complete that assessment, is now seeking public comment on whether to amend the permits.

“The York1 project is an expansion of an existing facility and can mobilize quickly to expand Ontario’s waste management capacity, as active landfill waste permissions are already in place, and it would not require a new environmental assessment that would take nearly a decade to complete,” Juliana Wilson, spokesperson for Environment Minister Todd McCarthy, said in a statement.

A spokesperson for York1 said “nothing is more important than safety” and encouraged people to take part in the public review.

“Ontario is running short of landfill space, and keeping recyclable materials out of landfill is part of the answer. We think this site can do that safely, and the provincial review is where that gets tested,” their statement read.

The proposal comes as the province prepares to overhaul landfill approvals, and as the minister warns Ontario could hit its capacity in the next 10 years, or sooner if the United States keeps up tariffs on Canadian garbage. Ontario shipped about a quarter of its landfill waste to the United States in 2024, an industry report said.

New omnibus legislation would repeal a municipal veto over new dumps, initially granted by the Ford government in 2020. Under recent regulatory changes, landfills looking to expand their service area or increase how much waste they take no longer need to undergo an environmental assessment, and would instead only be subject to amendments to narrower environmental compliance approvals.

Environmental assessments decide if a landfill project should happen at all, weighing environmental, social and economic impacts together and exploring alternatives. A compliance approval governs how it operates, by setting limits on garbage intake, air pollution or stormwater runoff.

While the Dresden site’s existing approvals are still in place, the municipality says the small landfill has been dormant so long it should be treated as a new project.

Under the proposal, the small landfill dating back to the 1960s, which holds an estimated 40,000 cubic metres of waste, would expand to a maximum capacity of 1.6 million cubic metres, the volume of the Rogers Centre. Up to 3,000 tonnes of waste per day would be accepted and then sorted at the site’s proposed waste transfer station. About 20 two-way truck trips would pass through the site each hour during peak times, a traffic report commissioned by the company suggests.

Locals have balked at the site’s proximity to homes and schools and raised a number of concerns, including about traffic and water impacts. A tributary to the Sydenham River runs along the site.

“We still hold out hope that by us raising those issues that we know are there, that will still factor into the provincial decision as to whether or not to ultimately grant the environmental compliance approvals,” Taylor, the municipality’s deputy chief administrative officer, said in an interview this week.

The public comment period on the amended permits is open until Dec. 21. If greenlit, the municipality says the landfill will still be subject to local zoning requirements, after York1 recently dropped a lawsuit where it argued those local approvals should not apply.

The province initially announced in March 2024 it would pursue an environmental assessment for the project, citing community concerns. Shortly after that, the premier called a byelection in the local riding of Lambton-Kent-Middlesex, where the successful Progressive Conservative candidate Steve Pinsonneault campaigned against the expansion.

paragraphs: A southwestern Ontario town is pushing back on the latest step to advance a controversial landfill and waste transfer station project, as Premier Doug Ford’s government ramps up a search for garbage space.

Waste company York1 wants to revive and expand a dormant landfill less than a kilometre from Dresden and pack it over the next decade with enough waste to fill Toronto’s Rogers Centre, despite local opposition.

“It’s a beautiful town, fantastic community, and this is just a few hundred metres north of town,” said Dave Taylor, deputy chief administrative officer for Chatham-Kent, the municipality encompassing Dresden.
“Our council has been unanimously opposed to the project since York1 proposed it.”

The landfill would be mostly soils, such as excavated earth from worksites along with other construction waste, according to the company’s site plans. The proposed transfer station would also sort and clean up construction debris, scrap wood, blue box material and dirt, before sending it to recyclers or landfillers.

Municipal officials have argued the company relied on outdated permits, granted decades ago, to bypass a full environmental assessment. The Ford government, which backtracked last year on a promise to complete that assessment, is now seeking public comment on whether to amend the permits.

“The York1 project is an expansion of an existing facility and can mobilize quickly to expand Ontario’s waste management capacity, as active landfill waste permissions are already in place, and it would not require a new environmental assessment that would take nearly a decade to complete,” Juliana Wilson, spokesperson for Environment Minister Todd McCarthy, said in a statement.
A spokesperson for York1 said “nothing is more important than safety” and encouraged people to take part in the public review.

“Ontario is running short of landfill space, and keeping recyclable materials out of landfill is part of the answer. We think this site can do that safely, and the provincial review is where that gets tested,” their statement read.

The proposal comes as the province prepares to overhaul landfill approvals, and as the minister warns Ontario could hit its capacity in the next 10 years, or sooner if the United States keeps up tariffs on Canadian garbage. Ontario shipped about a quarter of its landfill waste to the United States in 2024, an industry report said.

New omnibus legislation would repeal a municipal veto over new dumps, initially granted by the Ford government in 2020. Under recent regulatory changes, landfills looking to expand their service area or increase how much waste they take no longer need to undergo an environmental assessment, and would instead only be subject to amendments to narrower environmental compliance approvals.

Environmental assessments decide if a landfill project should happen at all, weighing environmental, social and economic impacts together and exploring alternatives. A compliance approval governs how it operates, by setting limits on garbage intake, air pollution or stormwater runoff.
While the Dresden site’s existing approvals are still in place, the municipality says the small landfill has been dormant so long it should be treated as a new project.

Under the proposal, the small landfill dating back to the 1960s, which holds an estimated 40,000 cubic metres of waste, would expand to a maximum capacity of 1.6 million cubic metres, the volume of the Rogers Centre. Up to 3,000 tonnes of waste per day would be accepted and then sorted at the site’s proposed waste transfer station. About 20 two-way truck trips would pass through the site each hour during peak times, a traffic report commissioned by the company suggests.
Locals have balked at the site’s proximity to homes and schools and raised a number of concerns, including about traffic and water impacts. A tributary to the Sydenham River runs along the site.

“We still hold out hope that by us raising those issues that we know are there, that will still factor into the provincial decision as to whether or not to ultimately grant the environmental compliance approvals,” Taylor, the municipality’s deputy chief administrative officer, said in an interview this week.

The public comment period on the amended permits is open until Dec. 21. If greenlit, the municipality says the landfill will still be subject to local zoning requirements, after York1 recently dropped a lawsuit where it argued those local approvals should not apply.

The province initially announced in March 2024 it would pursue an environmental assessment for the project, citing community concerns. Shortly after that, the premier called a byelection in the local riding of Lambton-Kent-Middlesex, where the successful Progressive Conservative candidate Steve Pinsonneault campaigned against the expansion.

Then, in a surprise after the election last year, the government cancelled that assessment as part of an omnibus bill. Pinsonneault spoke out against the decision but was absent from the legislature when it was voted on.
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Warm, sunny weather to continue before cooler temperatures arrive later this week
stories.summary: Another mild day is expected across southern Ontario Tuesday, with temperatures reaching 14 C in London before cooler air moves in later this week, according to CTV News meteorologist Julie Atchison.
stories.author: Koylan Azofeifa Rueda
stories.content:
Southern Ontario is enjoying temperatures well above seasonal norms this week, with sunshine and mild conditions expected to continue through Remembrance Day, according to CTV News London meteorologist Julie Atchison.

“It’s nice and mild out there in London,” Atchison said, noting temperatures had reached 14 C in London by Tuesday afternoon, while Sarnia and Windsor were already reporting 17 C.

The sunny weather is expected to continue through Tuesday before skies become partly cloudy overnight. Residents can expect a mix of sun and cloud Wednesday morning, with increasing cloud cover developing through the afternoon.

Atchison said moisture moving out of the American Midwest will bring mainly cloudy skies for Remembrance Day ceremonies on Wednesday, but conditions should remain pleasant.

“There is a slight chance for some showers towards Grey and Bruce County,” she said. “However, I am expecting the majority of the rainfall to hold off until later in the day.”

Steadier rain is expected to develop north of London, including parts of Huron and Perth counties, by late afternoon, with Grey and Bruce counties also expected to see rainfall. London faces only a 40 per cent chance of showers, Atchison said.

Temperatures are expected to reach about 9 C by late Wednesday morning, with light and variable winds, generally from the south.

A significant cool-down is forecast to arrive later in the week. Thursday’s high is expected to reach just 7 C, followed by 4 C on Friday under a mix of sun and cloud.

Overnight temperatures are forecast to fall between -2 C and 1 C, creating the potential for lake-effect precipitation, particularly in areas north of London.

“Any time you get that cold flow coming off Lake Huron, we could get into some mixing,” Atchison said.

While a slight chance of lake-effect rain or snow will remain in the forecast through the weekend, Atchison said residents planning outdoor activities should still be able to enjoy some sunshine.

stories.title: Fatal B.C. attack involved 4 bears displaying ‘predatory behaviour,’ officials say
stories.summary: A GoFundMe page identified the victims as Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed. One person’s remains were found in the Snooka West Trail area last Monday.
stories.author: Amy Judd
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four bears were involved in the deadly attack in Bella Coola last week in which a mother and her daughter were killed .

The service said the bears have been “dispatched.”

“Evidence from the investigation, as well as animal DNA, was analyzed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring,” Insp. Jeff Tyre with the BC Conservation Officer Service said at an update on Tuesday.

“After considering all the evidence and in accordance with provincial human wildlife conflict response guidelines, these bears have been dispatched to protect the public.”

Tyre also said this attack “likely involved predatory behaviour,” which is very rare.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how ended,” he said.

One person’s remains were found in the Snooka West Trail area last Monday.

The second person’s remains were found on Tuesday afternoon during search efforts by conservation officers and the RCMP.

A GoFundMe page identified the victims as Jenny Balcarras and her daughter, Selah Reed.

A family member started the fundraiser and said Balcarras recently moved to Bella Coola to start a new career and begin a new chapter in her life.

“Selah was just 20 years old, with her whole life ahead of her. She was only beginning her journey into adulthood, making this loss even more heartbreaking,” the crowdfunding campaign reads.

“Jenny leaves behind three young adult children — a son and two daughters — as well as a grandchild. They are now faced with the devastating loss of their mother and sister while also having to navigate the unexpected financial burden of arranging funeral services and covering the associated expenses for both Jenny and Selah.”

Tyre said the four bears were not involved in the 2025 attack in the same area, whith involved school children .

More to come.

stories.title: Four bears involved in fatal B.C. attack that left mother and daughter dead
stories.summary: DNA tests link female grizzly and three yearling cubs to deadly attack, with all four killed to protect public, authorities say
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.

“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”

The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.

Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says a rare predatory attack by a grizzly sow and her three yearling cubs was behind the deaths of Jenny Balcarra and her adult daughter, Selah …

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.’s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

paragraphs: The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.
Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.
“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.
“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”
The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.
Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.
Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”
“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”
Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”
“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says a rare predatory attack by a grizzly sow and her three yearling cubs was behind the deaths of Jenny Balcarra and her adult daughter, Selah …
The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.
Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.
He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”
Scapillati said B.C.’s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.
But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.
He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.
“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”
He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.
Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.
The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

stories.title: How a small poppy project bloomed into a community event and nearly 11,000 handmade flowers
stories.summary: An initiative kick-started by three friends for Remembrance Day sparks fellowship in the Ontario town of Bobcaygeon
stories.author: Mira Miller, Photography by Justine Rines
stories.content:
When Maggie Burns suggested to friends at her local curling club that their town of Bobcaygeon, Ont., should knit and crochet poppies for Remembrance Day , she never imagined how it would take off.

Last January, 74-year-old Burns, and her friends Alison Williams and Andrea DeFalco, 61 and 71, kick-started the initiative, making a Facebook group to spread word of the project and share the patterns. The group has since grown to 449 members and helped to organize poppy-making events and local business participation.

Now, after almost a year of hard work, the town of just 3,576 people has made nearly 11,000 poppies. At the beginning of November, volunteers set up thousands of poppies on display at seven different locations throughout Bobcaygeon, where they’ll remain for all to admire until Nov. 15.

“The way everybody jumped on board, I was shocked, really,” Burns said. “The participation was just unbelievable.”

Burns took part in a similar poppy project a few years ago, when she briefly lived in St. Marys, Ont. She had also heard of similar installations in other Ontario cities, including Stratford and Niagara Falls . When she returned to Bobcaygeon in September 2025, she was inspired to bring the project home with her.

Burns first requested and received the necessary approvals from the Royal Canadian Legion, the City of Kawartha Lakes and Parks Canada. She needed permission to use the red poppy, as it is a registered trademark owned by the Legion, and because the poppies would be displayed on public property. She got the go-ahead without issue and began recruiting her friends, involving others soon after.

The historic stone archway entrance to the Boyd Heritage Museum and the swing bridge crossing the Trent-Severn Waterway are decorated with poppies.

“It just snowballed and the poppies started pouring in,” said Burns, a retired software-test manager who picked up crochet again during the pandemic, after first learning it in the seventies. The poppies are about four inches across and each take roughly 30 minutes to make, depending on whether they’re crocheted or knitted and the crafter’s skill level.

Throughout the winter, the trio held monthly social events at local businesses where people could gather to knit and crochet together. Several of those businesses also operated as drop-off locations, so residents could leave their poppies to be collected when they were done.

Williams, Burns and DeFalco have been putting their time and talents into creating the poppies as a tribute to those who served and sacrificed.

“It became very social,” Williams said. “People loved it because it was just a tiny thing they could do to be part of a great big community event.”

The initial goal was 5,000 poppies, a target the volunteers reached by July, so they set a new objective of 10,000. They hit that by the end of September.

The final official count at the end of October came in at 10,899, though Williams said they’ve received even more since then.

In September, Burns, Williams, DeFalco and other volunteers started meeting up twice a week to sew the poppies onto pieces of mesh for display.

“We’d just sit and chat and stitch and a lot of the ladies became friends,” Burns said. “They were exchanging numbers at the end.”

Burns said the town is proud to pay their respects to veterans in this way and pass down important history to younger generations.

“It’s just a really good feeling,” she said. “My father was in the services and it’s an honour to do this on behalf of the Legion and the veterans who sacrificed so much for us.”

Volunteers also made poppy garlands and 100 poppy sticks that have been placed behind the town’s cenotaph, where the Remembrance Day ceremony is held, to honour the 100th anniversary of the Legion.

The project was met with enthusiasm from community members of all kinds, from residents at the local retirement home to children as young as eight years old. Many also got involved by donating yarn from Granny Bird’s Wool Shoppe in town.

Janet Wilson, 69, hadn’t crocheted in more than 40 years when she heard of the initiative at the curling club – so she decided to relearn. “I made around 180 poppies and really enjoyed the participation of our town in this unique project,” she said.

stories.title: Silver Cross mother calls Wainwright tragedy ‘cold water’ after daughter’s death
stories.summary: Canada's Silver Cross mother says Canadians can support the victims of CFB Wainwright and all military by wearing their poppies and thanking them for their service.
stories.author: Sean Previl
stories.content:
When Virginia Hicks, Canada’s Silver Cross mother , heard of the fatal tragedy at CFB Wainwright she says it was “like somebody dumped a bucket of cold water” as her daughter also died in a training exercise.

Four soldiers died and dozens more were injured last month when a nearby grass fire overwhelmed soldiers taking part in live-fire training at the base southeast of Edmonton.

“It’s like somebody dumped a bucket of cold water, you could just… Oh my God, not again, and you have to feel for the families that this is not something that anybody wants ever to happen to their loved ones,” Hicks said in an interview with Global News. “When they go to work, they want them to come home.”

A veteran herself, Hicks lost her daughter Mariebeth Short in 2002 during a training exercise on the Matawa Plains in Petawawa, Ont.

As an investigation is ongoing into the Wainwright tragedy, Hicks encouraged families to “stay patient” and allow the Canadian Armed Forces to do its investigation.

It was the same thing her family had to do when her daughter died.

Mariebeth Short was a sapper who served with 2 Combat Engineering Regiment based in Petawawa. Both Hicks and her stepfather Brian were serving already, which piqued her interest.

Originally interested in becoming a navigator, Hicks said due to math scores Short had to look at alternatives and decided she wanted to become a combat engineer which gave her parents pause.

“Brian goes, ‘combat engineer? Are you crazy?’ He said, ‘you are four-foot-11, you weigh 95 pounds when you’re soaking wet, do you realize that a combat arms trade is really heavy work,'” Hicks explained.

But their daughter was “feisty” and “liked a challenge,” prompting her to move ahead with her goal.

Short graduated second in her class and was eventually stationed at Petawawa.

On Sept. 23, 2002, she called her mother to let her know she’d get to drive first during a training exercise. She promised to call them once the exercise was done, likely later that week on Friday.

A full military funeral was held for Short in Trenton, Ont., her mother’s hometown, with hundreds of soldiers in attendance. She now rests in the same Trenton graveyard as members of her family.

Each year on the anniversary of her death, Hicks said the family returns to Petawawa and is taken to the crash site by the military.

“We take roses and there was a little tiny tree the day of the crash … That kind of gives us a point of remembrance because that’s where her body laid when they took her out of the LAV, was by this tree,” Hicks said. “So every year we go back with roses and we stick roses in the tree. Well, back in 2002 the tree was about six to eight inches tall, now it’s like 25 feet tall.”

She added they put a rose at a monument put together for all members of the unit who were killed in Kandahar, Kabal and others killed in the service of Canada.

On Remembrance Day, Hicks will lay a wreath at the National War Memorial on behalf of mothers whose children died while serving the military.

Hicks said she’s honoured to be chosen as this year’s Silver Cross mother because it’s not only her daughter who she’ll be remembering.

“It is a remembrance of Mariebeth, but it’s also a remembrance of all of the fallen, all of the mothers, the families, and you think of them daily and especially on Remembrance Day,” Hicks said. “When I lay the wreath I know I’m allowed to go up, I’m going to kneel and I always kiss my hand and then put my hand on the wreath and that’s like, my heart going out to them.”

As the victims and families of Wainwright observe the first Remembrance Day following the tragedy, Hicks stressed they have a large group of people they can lean on.

“I feel very badly for all the parents, even the parents of the ones that are still in hospital, they have a long road ahead of them,” Hicks said. “If there’s anything they ever need or want, there is a large group of Silver Cross mothers out there that, reach out to any of us, I’m sure we’ll help you as best as we can.”

stories.title: CP NewsAlert: Four bears involved in deadly attack in Bella Coola, B.C.
stories.summary: Bella Coola - The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.

“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.

The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says a rare predatory attack by a grizzly sow and her three yearling cubs was behind the deaths of Jenny Balcarra and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, in Bella Coola, B.C., this month. Insp. Jeff Tyre says the four bears were trapped and have been killed after DNA conclusively linked them to the attack. (Nov. 10, 2026)

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”

The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.

Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.‘s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: 15-year-old faces impaired driving charges after fatal crash
stories.summary: Oneida Police Service and Middlesex County OPP say officers responded to a crash on Oneida Road at about 6:40 a.m. on Nov. 7.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 17-year-old from London has been identified as the person killed in a single-vehicle crash on Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation.

Oneida Police Service and Middlesex County OPP say officers responded to a crash on Oneida Road at about 6:40 a.m. on Nov. 7.

Police said one passenger was pronounced dead at the scene. The victim has been identified as a 17-year-old from London.

Three other occupants of the vehicle were taken to hospital.

Investigators allege the driver, a 15-year-old from Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation, was impaired at the time of the crash.

The youth has been charged with operation while impaired with a blood-alcohol concentration exceeding the legal limit, operation while impaired causing death, dangerous operation causing death, driving without a licence, driving with a blood-alcohol concentration above zero as a novice driver, using a licence plate not authorized for the vehicle, and driving a motor vehicle with liquor readily available.

The accused was held for a bail hearing.

The identity of the accused is protected under the Youth Criminal Justice Act.

Police are asking anyone with information or dashcam footage of the vehicle involved before the collision to contact the Oneida Police Service or OPP.

Oneida Police Service and Middlesex County OPP say officers responded to a crash on Oneida Road at about 6:40 a.m. on Nov. 7.

Investigators allege the driver, a 15-year-old from Oneida Nation of the Thames First Nation, was impaired at the time of the crash.

stories.title: Four grizzly bears involved in deadly attack on mother and daughter in B.C.
stories.summary: Bella Coola — The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The B.C. Conservation Officer Service says four grizzly bears that it captured in Bella Coola in recent days were all involved in a deadly attack that claimed the lives of a mother and daughter in the community this month.

Insp. Jeff Tyre with the service said DNA tests had conclusively linked the female grizzly and her three yearling cubs to the attack and all had been killed to protect the public.

“Our investigation also found that this attack likely involved predatory behaviour, which I can tell you is very rare,” Tyre told an online briefing.

“That is to say, we don’t know how it started, but we know how it ended.”

The bodies of art therapist Jenny Balcarras and her adult daughter, Selah Reed, were found last week about 150 metres apart after they were reported missing on Nov. 1.

Their remains were found in an area of trails outside the northern B.C. community, where local authorities imposed a voluntary curfew and police had been escorting children to school last week in the wake of the attack.

Tyre said the DNA tests showed the bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a group of schoolchildren in the same area of Bella Coola, which is about 1,000 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Tlhmtimut Samuel Schooner, elected Chief Councillor of the Nuxalk Nation, said the investigation into the recent attack “was carried out with the utmost care and respect.”

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” he told the briefing.

“Our thoughts remain with the victims’ family. We still have community supports in place, and they will remain there until we feel the time is right to remove them. Our community is rightly still deeply affected and will be for generations.”

Tyre said bears involved in fatal attacks on people “cannot be rehabilitated or relocated.”

“This type of behaviour represents an extreme risk to the public, and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”

The 2025 attack by a grizzly on a group of about 20 elementary school students and teachers last November left an adult and three children badly injured.

Nicholas Scapillati, executive director of the B.C.-based Grizzly Bear Foundation, said in an interview on Tuesday that the tragedy in Bella Coola was an “extremely challenging” situation.

He commended the Conservation Officer Service for their investigation, and “helping these rural communities where they clearly need our help in co-existing with the bears.”

“Rural communities co-existing or working to co-exist with grizzly bears in Western North America have great challenges and they need our help,” Scapillati said. Education was necessary, he said, “but we also need community programs that further co-existence and safety.”

Scapillati said B.C.’s Bear Smart program, which helps educate communities about staying safe and co-existing with bears, is effective.

But “this past year, the B.C. government stopped putting energy into that program and actually paused it,” he said.

He said the timing of the attack was significant.

“Bears are heading toward hibernation. Their behaviour is significantly different at this time of year and communities need to be safe and that’s a critical message for everyone in Western Canada, in Western North America right now that lives close to a grizzly bear,” he said.

“In the fall, it’s a more challenging time to co-exist with them.”

He said the incoming B.C. Conservative provincial government could have a “great opportunity” to do more to help rural communities avoid similar tragedies.

Schoone said in a statement on Tuesday that the First Nation was thankful to the conservation officer service for finding the bears and bringing some resolution to the community.

The statement said community members should “take all necessary precautions outdoors, stay close to young children, and ensure our spaces are free of any attractants.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Darryl Greer, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Jury convicts Canadian woman who ‘answered Isis’s call’
stories.summary: The trial of Ammara Amjad was a test of whether Canada could bring to justice women who served the Islamic State.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A Canadian woman who spent four years with Isis and married two of its fighters is guilty of terrorism, a jury in Brampton, Ont. ruled on Tuesday.

Ammara Amjad, 32, was the first woman to go on trial in Canada for her role in the Islamic State in Syria as it committed widespread atrocities.

The case was a test of whether Canada could bring to justice the women who played support roles in Isis as wives and mothers but were not armed fighters.

The jury began deliberations on Monday and returned after one day to find Amjad guilty of participating in, or contributing to, the activities of a terrorist group.

A former York University student and Walmart employee, Amjad was living a life of “comfort” in Ontario when Isis summoned women to Syria, according to the Crown.

The Pakistan-born Canadian flew to Turkey in March 2015, crossed into Isis territory and remained with the terror group until she was captured four years later.

“She answered Isis’s call,” the Crown argued in its closing arguments on Friday, as the two week trial came to an end in a courtroom north of Toronto.

Amjad faces a possible sentence of ten years in prison. She was not detained during the trial, having been released on bail after she was charged in 2023.

She did not testify in her defence and her lawyer did not present any evidence, instead arguing the Crown had not proved what Amjad did in Syria.

European and American courts have convicted dozens of women who flocked to Syria to live under Isis rule. As recently as Oct. 27, a U.S. woman was convicted .

But Canadian authorities have struggled to prosecute citizens for their part in overseas terrorist groups, citing the challenges of collecting evidence in foreign conflict zones.

At least 11 Canadian women suspected of joining Isis were caught in Syria. Nine were repatriated by the government from 2021 to 2023, but only three have been charged.

Oumaima Chaouay of Montreal pleaded guilty to participating in Isis last year. She was sentenced to one day, ON top of the 110 days she had spent in pre-trial custody.

Kimberly Polman pleaded guilty to the same charge in October. The B.C. resident, who allegedly received weapons training in Syria, is scheduled for sentencing on Nov 30.

Amjad opted to let a jury decide her fate, turning the case into a test of whether Canada could hold to account women accused of joining the terror group.

The defence depicted her as a naive youth who went to Syria to join her boyfriend, and argued that prosecutors had not shown she had knowingly contributed to Isis.

“Do not convict her because of the place where she lived. Do not convict her because of who she married,” her lawyer Ayeman Kenaway told the jurors.

But the Crown said that not all terrorists carried weapons, and the evidence showed Amjad had participated in Isis by taking on the domestic tasks it assigned to her.

Amjad married an Isis fighter, Bilal Khan of Mississauga, Ont. When he died, she married another, British citizen Hamza Parvez, with whom she had two children.

She was on the Isis payroll, espoused its ideology to family and friends in Canada, and pestered them repeatedly for money, according to the Crown.

“She fulfilled the role of the wife of Isis fighters and mother to the next generation,” the Crown said, arguing Amjad knew Isis was a terrorist group before she joined.

“Amjad made a considered, deliberate decision to migrate to Syria and fulfill the role of women in Isis for the purpose of helping Isis carry out its terrorist activities.”

Canadian women left B.C., Alberta, Ontario and Quebec to join Isis after the terror group seized parts of Syria and Iraq that it proclaimed a puritanical Islamic State.

The RCMP was unaware of Amjad until she was captured in March 2019 near Baghouz, the Syrian town where the hardcore of Isis made their last stand.

The Integrated National Security Enforcement Team was unable to locate any record of her travel because so much time had elapsed since she had left Canada.

But the investigators found she had renewed her Canadian passport in March 2015, bought a plane ticket to Turkey, and allegedly left her parents to pay her credit card debt.

At the time of what she called her “hijra,” Arabic for migration, Isis was the topic of blanket news coverage, and had left no doubt about what it stood for.

It had called for terrorist attacks in Canada, beheaded prisoners on video, massacred Iraq’s Yazidi minority and abducted young girls to serve as sex slaves.

The abhorrent abuses had led Canada to join an international military coalition assembled to fight the terrorist group, which had emerged from the Al Qaeda branch in Iraq.

“By 2015, Isis was a notorious terrorist group. It was a listed terrorist entity in Canada for a year before Ms. Amjad made her way to the Isis territory,” the Crown said.

It was “completely implausible and unbelievable” that Amjad was unaware of that, according to the Crown, adding there was no evidence she was compelled to join Isis.

“This was a woman committed to her own choices from the beginning to the end, not someone who was forced to do anything against her will,” the Crown said.

The evidence collected by police was described by the judge as circumstantial, but included documents on Parvez that were found in Syria, and which the FBI shared with the RCMP.

The U.K. government, meanwhile, notified the RCMP it had revoked Parvez’s citizenship after he left London, where he was born, to join Isis, the Crown said.

The RCMP also found thousands of WhatsApp text and audio messages on a phone seized during a search at Amjad’s parents’ house.

The messages show that, while in Syria, Amjad had told her family and friends she was happy, had done the right thing and they had a religious duty to follow in her footsteps.

In November 2015, she contacted Khan’s family in Ontario to announce he’d been “martyred” in a Russian airstrike. As proof, she allegedly sent a photo of his body.

She allegedly later called them back to ask for permission to marry another Isis fighter, Parvez, a British-Pakistani extremist.

The defence challenged the RCMP translations of her messages, which were mostly in Urdu, and at one point argued unsuccessfully for a mistrial.

Amjad made no effort to leave Isis until the terror group was surrounded by U.S.-backed Syrian-Kurdish fighters, who captured her and Parvez in March 2019.

For the next four years, she lived at the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for the families of Isis fighters, until Global Affairs Canada secured her release in April 2023.

Her sentencing has been scheduled for Feb. 2.

Amjad opted to let a jury decide her fate, turning the case into a test of whether Canada could hold to account women accused of joining the terror group.
The defence depicted her as a naive youth who went to Syria to join her boyfriend, and argued that prosecutors had not shown she had knowingly contributed to Isis.
“Do not convict her because of the place where she lived. Do not convict her because of who she married,” her lawyer Ayeman Kenaway told the jurors.
But the Crown said that not all terrorists carried weapons, and the evidence showed Amjad had participated in Isis by taking on the domestic tasks it assigned to her.
Amjad married an Isis fighter, Bilal Khan of Mississauga, Ont. When he died, she married another, British citizen Hamza Parvez, with whom she had two children.
She was on the Isis payroll, espoused its ideology to family and friends in Canada, and pestered them repeatedly for money, according to the Crown.
“She fulfilled the role of the wife of Isis fighters and mother to the next generation,” the Crown said, arguing Amjad knew Isis was a terrorist group before she joined.
“Amjad made a considered, deliberate decision to migrate to Syria and fulfill the role of women in Isis for the purpose of helping Isis carry out its terrorist activities.”
Captured with Isis ‘hardcore’
Canadian women left B.C., Alberta, Ontario and Quebec to join Isis after the terror group seized parts of Syria and Iraq that it proclaimed a puritanical Islamic State.
The RCMP was unaware of Amjad until she was captured in March 2019 near Baghouz, the Syrian town where the hardcore of Isis made their last stand.
The Integrated National Security Enforcement Team was unable to locate any record of her travel because so much time had elapsed since she had left Canada.
But the investigators found she had renewed her Canadian passport in March 2015, bought a plane ticket to Turkey, and allegedly left her parents to pay her credit card debt.
At the time of what she called her “hijra,” Arabic for migration, Isis was the topic of blanket news coverage, and had left no doubt about what it stood for.
It had called for terrorist attacks in Canada, beheaded prisoners on video, massacred Iraq’s Yazidi minority and abducted young girls to serve as sex slaves.
The abhorrent abuses had led Canada to join an international military coalition assembled to fight the terrorist group, which had emerged from the Al Qaeda branch in Iraq.
“By 2015, Isis was a notorious terrorist group. It was a listed terrorist entity in Canada for a year before Ms. Amjad made her way to the Isis territory,” the Crown said.
It was “completely implausible and unbelievable” that Amjad was unaware of that, according to the Crown, adding there was no evidence she was compelled to join Isis.
“This was a woman committed to her own choices from the beginning to the end, not someone who was forced to do anything against her will,” the Crown said.
Texts and battlefield evidence
The evidence collected by police was described by the judge as circumstantial, but included documents on Parvez that were found in Syria, and which the FBI shared with the RCMP.
The U.K. government, meanwhile, notified the RCMP it had revoked Parvez’s citizenship after he left London, where he was born, to join Isis, the Crown said.
The RCMP also found thousands of WhatsApp text and audio messages on a phone seized during a search at Amjad’s parents’ house.
The messages show that, while in Syria, Amjad had told her family and friends she was happy, had done the right thing and they had a religious duty to follow in her footsteps.
In November 2015, she contacted Khan’s family in Ontario to announce he’d been “martyred” in a Russian airstrike. As proof, she allegedly sent a photo of his body.
She allegedly later called them back to ask for permission to marry another Isis fighter, Parvez, a British-Pakistani extremist.
The defence challenged the RCMP translations of her messages, which were mostly in Urdu, and at one point argued unsuccessfully for a mistrial.
Amjad made no effort to leave Isis until the terror group was surrounded by U.S.-backed Syrian-Kurdish fighters, who captured her and Parvez in March 2019.
For the next four years, she lived at the Al Hol and Al Roj detention camps for the families of Isis fighters, until Global Affairs Canada secured her release in April 2023.
Her sentencing has been scheduled for Feb. 2.

stories.title: Carney to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping next week
stories.summary: Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney says he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — Prime Minister Mark Carney said Tuesday he will raise concerns about foreign interference in Canada when he meets next week with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Carney and Xi are expected to meet in person at the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

“The advantage of these meetings is you can raise issues directly and frankly,” Carney told a press conference in Montreal.

Carney said he would bring up with Xi the importance Canada attaches “to the non-interference in our affairs by China and other countries.”

The prime minister said he also will discuss with Xi the global security climate and the economic partnership between the two countries. He said that partnership “is something that is deepening but has clear guardrails in terms of the areas in which we’re involved.”

Carney last met with Xi in January. The two leaders also spoke at last year’s Apec summit — the first formal meeting between the leaders of Canada and China since 2017.

Carney said at the time he and Xi discussed foreign interference but Beijing didn’t understand how seriously Canadians take the issue.

Carney’s government has been rebuilding Canada’s relationship with China and is pursuing increased trade between the two nations.

In January 2025, a public inquiry identified China as the top perpetrator of foreign interference targeting Canadian democratic institutions, and concluded Beijing tried to meddle in some Canadian elections.

A recent report by the organization Safeguard Defenders said China has expanded the network of illegal police stations it operates around the world, including in Canada. The Spain-based non-governmental organization said the stations are used by China to monitor the diaspora in a bid to control them.

Carney also told reporters in Montreal that his government has chosen a new ambassador to China and will announce the appointment soon. The post has been vacant since the spring.

“It’s a little longer than we would have liked. We wanted to get the right person and we have found that right person,” he said.

U.S. President Donald Trump will also be at the summit. Carney said he and Trump are expected to have a conversation at Apec or at the Asean summit in the Philippines, which takes place a few days earlier.

“I have an ability to engage with the president in multiple occasions and on a running basis, so yes, it’s good to sit down but it’s not absolutely necessary,” Carney said.

Carney said he spoke briefly with Trump over the weekend.

That conversation came a few days after the U.S. midterm elections where Trump’s Republicans lost badly in a vote widely believed to be a referendum on many of his policies, including the tariffs on Canada.

Trade talks between Canada and the U.S. collapsed in August. In the days since the U.S. midterm elections gave the Democrats firm control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, several party officials have indicated repealing Trump’s tariffs on Canadian products is a priority.

Carney told reporters last week that “more intense” trade negotiations with the United States have restarted.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations, or Asean, summit will take place in the Philippines from Nov. 16 to 18. The Apec summit will bring leaders from across Asia, South America and the South Pacific together in Shenzhen, China from Nov. 18 to 19.

China has confirmed that it is discussing a possible meeting between Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, which would take place at the Apec summit.

Carney was in Montreal Tuesday to tout the $4 billion in funding for culture and recreation outlined in last week’s federal budget. It includes new tax credits, and $600 million in annual funding for Canadian content.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

— With files from The Associated Press and Catherine Morrison

Anja Karadeglija, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Ontario appoints eight regional chairs, including outgoing Conservative MP Scott Aitchison
stories.summary: Ford’s government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford’s government has appointed eight regional heads of council, including Conservative MP Scott Aitchison.

Aitchison had announced he would resign his Parry Sound-Muskoka seat at the end of the fall sitting of Parliament, and the Ontario government says he will be sworn in as Muskoka District chair on Dec. 1.

Ford’s government recently gave itself powers to appoint regional chairs in Durham, Halton, Muskoka and Waterloo, also extending an existing power to appoint the chairs in Niagara, Peel and York regions.

The regional chairs will also get so-called strong chair powers, including to appoint or fire the chief administrative officer and division heads, direct staff, veto certain bylaws and propose the municipal budget.

Appointed chairs who are serving as mayors in their communities will hold both roles, including Pickering Mayor Kevin Ashe as Durham regional chair and Vaughan Mayor Steven Del Duca as York regional chair.

Former Oakville mayor Ann Mulvale will become Halton regional chair, outgoing Orillia Mayor Don McIsaac will serve as Simcoe County chair, outgoing Welland Mayor Frank Campion will serve as Niagara regional chair, Kitchener city Coun. Scott Davey will serve as Waterloo regional chair, and current Peel regional chair Nando Iannicca will stay in the role.

stories.title: Two charged after $70,000 worth of construction equipment stolen in Strathroy-Caradoc
stories.summary: The Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service says the investigation began on Sept. 28 after officers received a report that construction equipment and materials had been stolen several days earlier.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
Two people are facing charges after an investigation into the theft of approximately $70,000 worth of construction equipment and materials in Strathroy-Caradoc.

The Strathroy-Caradoc Police Service says the investigation began on Sept. 28 after officers received a report that construction equipment and materials had been stolen several days earlier.

The case was later assigned to the force’s criminal investigation division.

As a result of the investigation, police arrested a 48-year-old Thedford resident and a 28-year-old Lambton Shores resident.

Both men have been charged with possession of property obtained by crime and trafficking in property obtained by crime.

Police say several stolen items were recovered during the investigation, including a significant amount of copper wire.

The accused are scheduled to appear in a London court in late December.

stories.title: Global conflict pushes countries to focus on domestic energy security, report finds
stories.summary: Shift to nuclear and other renewable sources stands to reduce carbon emissions, according to Wood Mackenzie analysis
stories.author: Joy SpearChief-Morris
stories.content:
Global conflicts and supply-chain pressures are pushing some countries to shift away from a dependency on fossil fuels and helping to reduce their carbon emissions more than with climate-specific policies alone, a new report finds.

Research group Wood Mackenzie’s annual Energy Transition Outlook found trade conflict and the U.S.-Iran war have led some major economies to become less reliant on global energy markets, focusing more on domestically produced energy, including nuclear and other low-carbon sources.

“The world now confronts an energy landscape of unprecedented complexity, where emissions trajectories continue deteriorating, climate targets drift further from reach, and market volatility has reached extraordinary levels,” said Prakash Sharma, Wood Mackenzie vice-president and head of scenarios and technologies and one of the report’s lead authors.

“We believe the government thinking has moved in parallel with these market pressures.”

Mr. Sharma said climate policy and net-zero objectives require stronger policy supports and incentives, and “the current global order, we believe, is not designed to support that alternative.”

Canada is one of almost 200 countries that have committed to net zero carbon emissions by 2050 as signatories to the 2015 Paris Agreement, which seeks to limit a global average temperature rise to between 1.5 and 2 degrees above preindustrial levels.

Wood Mackenzie’s independent assessment, which outlines five distinct energy transition scenarios across 105 energy markets to 2060, found the energy security scenario – one which focuses on domestic renewable sources – would result in a projected warming of 2.5 degrees by 2100, lower than their base-case scenario of 2.6 degrees.

The security scenario accounts for a boost in investment in nuclear and geothermal energy sources over technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, which it said rely on stronger climate policies and incentives.

The scenario that accounts for countries choosing to focus on economic expansion, such as major investments in data centres for artificial intelligence and robotics, is projected to lead to warming of 3 degrees since fossil fuel usage continues longer, delaying investment in renewable sources.

The report states electricity demand is expected to grow by 15 per cent between now and 2030, with data centres accounting for about one-third of that increase.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been shifting Canada’s policies away from a climate-focused approach to one prioritizing investment in major projects, including fossil fuels, with new oil and natural gas pipelines to the West Coast announced recently.

However, the 2026 federal budget tabled Nov. 5 outlined billions in new money for Canada’s electricity system, including $40-billion over 10 years starting in 2027-28 for infrastructure expansion.

It also extended tax credits for clean electricity investment through 2040, with an expected cost of $2.4-billion from 2027-28 to 2030-31 and $36.1-billion from 2031-32 to 2041-42.

Lindsey Entwistle, Wood Mackenzie’s principal analyst of scenarios and technologies and another of the report’s lead authors, said electrification is “clearly the solution to many of the challenges of energy security, decarbonization, and economic growth.”

The Canadian Climate Institute’s annual early emissions report found the country was well short of its carbon-emissions-reduction goals for 2030, and also turned to clean electrification as a solution.

Sachi Gibson, mitigation research director at the environmental think tank, said technology such as electric vehicles and heat pumps has driven power demand in Canada, although the transition has not been as rapid as in other countries.

“Folks are electrifying for many reasons, not just climate concerns,” Ms. Gibson said.

“There’s multiple drivers at play. It can be climate policy, it can be energy security concerns, it could also be affordability.”

Wood Mackenzie said data centres and AI are expected to double global power demand by 2060, with the U.S., China and India accounting for more than half of that growth.

“There’s an immediate scramble for electricity supply and real fears around high energy prices,” Ms. Entwistle said.

The federal budget also included a commitment to support data centre developers to build 500 megawatts of processing power for Canadian AI companies, though it did not put a dollar figure behind the program.

Wood Mackenzie’s independent assessment, which outlines five distinct energy transition scenarios across 105 energy markets to 2060, found the energy security scenario – one which focuses on domestic renewable sources – would result in a projected warming of 2.5 degrees by 2100, lower than their base-case scenario of 2.6 degrees.

The security scenario accounts for a boost in investment in nuclear and geothermal energy sources over technologies such as hydrogen and carbon capture, which it said rely on stronger climate policies and incentives.

The scenario that accounts for countries choosing to focus on economic expansion, such as major investments in data centres for artificial intelligence and robotics, is projected to lead to warming of 3 degrees since fossil fuel usage continues longer, delaying investment in renewable sources.
The report states electricity demand is expected to grow by 15 per cent between now and 2030, with data centres accounting for about one-third of that increase.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has been shifting Canada’s policies away from a climate-focused approach to one prioritizing investment in major projects, including fossil fuels, with new oil and natural gas pipelines to the West Coast announced recently.
However, the 2026 federal budget tabled Nov. 5 outlined billions in new money for Canada’s electricity system, including $40-billion over 10 years starting in 2027-28 for infrastructure expansion.
It also extended tax credits for clean electricity investment through 2040, with an expected cost of $2.4-billion from 2027-28 to 2030-31 and $36.1-billion from 2031-32 to 2041-42.

Lindsey Entwistle, Wood Mackenzie’s principal analyst of scenarios and technologies and another of the report’s lead authors, said electrification is “clearly the solution to many of the challenges of energy security, decarbonization, and economic growth.”

The Canadian Climate Institute’s annual early emissions report found the country was well short of its carbon-emissions-reduction goals for 2030, and also turned to clean electrification as a solution.

Sachi Gibson, mitigation research director at the environmental think tank, said technology such as electric vehicles and heat pumps has driven power demand in Canada, although the transition has not been as rapid as in other countries.
“Folks are electrifying for many reasons, not just climate concerns,” Ms. Gibson said.
“There’s multiple drivers at play. It can be climate policy, it can be energy security concerns, it could also be affordability.”
Wood Mackenzie said data centres and AI are expected to double global power demand by 2060, with the U.S., China and India accounting for more than half of that growth.
“There’s an immediate scramble for electricity supply and real fears around high energy prices,” Ms. Entwistle said.

The federal budget also included a commitment to support data centre developers to build 500 megawatts of processing power for Canadian AI companies, though it did not put a dollar figure behind the program.

November 10, 2026 at 12:53 p.m.

Ottawa — Since the spring, two separate groups have asked Parliament to reconsider how we honour our veterans. The first wants Canada to finally award the Victoria Cross, our highest military decoration for valour. The second campaign wants the government to reclassify past conflicts as wars, elevating veterans of those fights as war veterans.

In this video, we explain why this is happening now and what it will mean for veterans.

Let’s start with the Victoria Cross. The original medal was struck by Queen Victoria in 1856 to award valour in the Crimean War. Echoing present conflicts, that was a war where the allies tried to evict Russian occupiers out of the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea.

These medals are highly prized and worth about a half million dollars on the open market though they rarely go up for sale. Lord Michael Ashcroft has 245 of them that he collected to preserve the legacy that they honour.

The Canadian War Museum purchased Robert Shankland’s VC when it came up for auction in 2009. Shankland is part of a trio of Victoria Cross winners, coincidentally all born in the 700 block of Winnipeg’s Pine Street. The museum was also able to acquire the medals of Leo Clarke and Frederick William Hall to celebrate the heroism of the men who May never have physically met, but all performed the greatest acts of bravery. In 1925, Winnipeg renamed Pine Street Valour Road in their honour.

The VC was Britain’s highest honour, and as a former colony, it was also Canada’s. Our winners had to visit Buckingham Palace to receive their award. Ninety-nine Canadians would be awarded this ultimate honour, the last one in the dying days of World War II.

Then, in 1993, Canada created its own version, the Canadian Victoria Cross. But not a single one was ever awarded.

Aghan vet Bruce Moncur made it his personal mission to change this, and he enlisted his former boss Chief Of Defence Staff Rick Hillier to help.

Moncur’s team strategized that the best way to win this battle was to pick a single hero to champion for a VC, and they chose North Bay Ontario’s Jess Larochelle.

North Bay MP Pauline Rochefort entered the fray after an earlier bill by former Conservative leader Erin O’Toole failed to convince the Trudeau government to act. This time the request was for a review of past honours, not just VCs.

Her bill was referred to committee where it would receive unanimous consent.

Upon returning to the House, it passed, also with unanimous consent. On Nov. 2, Defence Minister David McGuinty announced that in the coming months, the government will begin developing a process to consult with veterans, serving members, stakeholders and historians to examine potential criteria for the review and classification of past conflicts and military operations.

Canada has not officially designated any military operation as “wartime service” since the Korean War, which ended in 1953. Everything after that, including the Gulf War and the war in Afghanistan, have been classified as “special duty service.” While changing the designation won’t affect benefits or pensions, for those affected, this is a badge of honour of great importance to them.

Mick Gzowski is a video reporter for the National Post's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa.

stories.title: Stegh president and CEO announces retirement
stories.summary: In a statement, Karen Davies informed the hospital’s board of directors of her decision to step down from the role.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
The president and chief executive officer of St. Thomas Elgin General Hospital has announced plans to retire.

In a statement, Karen Davies informed the hospital’s board of directors of her decision to step down from the role. Davies said she will remain in the position during the transition period and continue supporting the hospital’s strategic priorities while assisting with the onboarding of new leadership.

Board chair Amy Dale praised Davies’ leadership and contributions to the hospital.

“Karen has provided transformational leadership at Stegh, and her vision, steadfastness, calm nature and commitment to putting people first have created a very strong hospital and bright future for care in our community,” Dale said in a statement.

Davies joined the hospital in 2012 as chief nursing executive and vice-president. She served in that position for nine years before becoming president and CEO in 2021.

According to the hospital, Davies helped strengthen its focus on quality of care, emergency department performance, patient experience, staff experience and operational excellence during her tenure.

“Serving this hospital and community has been one of the greatest privileges of my life,” Davies said in a statement.

“I have been fortunate to work alongside exceptional staff, physicians, volunteers, leaders, board members and community partners who share an unwavering commitment to providing exemplary care.”

The hospital’s board of directors said it will begin a search for a new president and CEO in the coming weeks.

stories.title: Morgan proposes dividing London’s deputy mayor role, nominates new budget chair, in council re-organization
stories.summary: Morgan is nominating two councillors to become his deputy mayors, Coun. Shawn Lewis and Coun. Corrine Rahman, and Coun. Steve Lehman to be his new Budget Chair.
stories.author: Daryl Newcombe
stories.content:
Mayor Josh Morgan will ask the newly elected city council to endorse his re-organization of senior council positions at the start of the new term.

Morgan is nominating two councillors to become his deputy mayors, Coun. Shawn Lewis and Coun. Corrine Rahman, and Coun. Steve Lehman to be his new Budget Chair.

Lewis served as the city’s sole deputy mayor throughout the four-year term.

“Having a second deputy mayor position is going to allow us to spread the work across multiple individuals,” Morgan explained. “At a very high level, one of the deputy mayors would be helping with a lot of advocacy and organization of external groups.”

Morgan said the second deputy mayor position will have a greater focus on council decision-making, “Making sure our meetings are efficient, that we’re getting the things done that people want us to work on. This is an opportunity for leadership in a way to help reinforce that, and to be very streamlined and focused on those things.”

The mayor’s decision to add a second deputy mayor position, and his nominations for the three roles, will all require endorsement from city council.

Lewis says he’s honoured to be nominated for a second consecutive four-year term.

However, his role would evolve, “I’ll be doing a little bit more outside the walls of City Hall. That will include some engagement with AMO (Association of Municipalities of Ontario) and provincial leadership. It will also include some advocacy and some work with leadership within our community.”

Some of his previous role, including chairing the Strategic Priorities and Policy Committee (Sppc) would become the responsibility of the other deputy mayor he added, “One of the things I’ve talked to the mayor about already is setting up a process improvement table with the construction trades and our (city) staff to start to sort out these traffic issues so that we can move London around better.”

She emphasized that improving the efficiency of committee meetings will be high on her priority list.

Asked about being London’s first female deputy mayor in about a decade she replies, “I’m a visible minority woman. So, that’s not something that we have experienced in the city in a deputy mayor role. So, it will be different from that perspective, but we bring our identities to the table with us and that’s something that I bring.”

Lehman says he’s excited about being nominated to be budget chair, but recognizes there are expectations from the public to achieve the mayor’s tax pledge that would keep increases in the three per cent range.

“It’s going to be a challenge. There’s no question,” Lehman acknowledged. “We’re going to get out of the gate right now with the final year of our four year budget, and then we get into the really heavy lifting for crafting the next four year budget.”

He added, “I think affordability was top of priority list, not just for the mayor, but for myself. I think people that have been elected. But also I looked at the campaign platforms of those running across the city, and it was there as well.

Coun. Elizabeth Peloza was the previous budget chair from 2020 until 2026.

Regarding his decision to change his budget chair Morgan said, “I think [councillor] Peloza served the city very well in the budget chair position. She’s got a constituency that’s got a lot of work to do. She’s got BRT [bus rapid transit] coming to fruition, she’s got a lot of development in her ward. She’s a great leader on council and I think she’ll continue to lead in many different ways.”

In a statement to CTV News, Peloza expressed gratitude for serving in the role, and that it has been a privilege to play a part in upholding London’s AAA credit rating that keeps borrowing costs low.

Peloza offered Lehman her congratulations and best wishes.

She added, “My commitment to London and its residents remains unwavering. Public service has never been about a title or a position, it is about the responsibility we have to our community and the difference we can make.”

Each of the three roles would pay $101,759 per year, an eight per cent top-up above the new $94,222 base pay of a city councillor.

Since the elimination of London’s Board of Control, mayors have structured senior council leadership positions differently each term.

From 2010 to 2014, the city had no deputy mayor and instead used a rotating acting mayor system. From 2014 to 2018, there were two deputy mayors. Between 2018 and 2022, council had one deputy mayor and one budget chair serving two-year terms, while the 2022-26 term featured one deputy mayor and one budget chair serving four-year terms.
