stories.title: New Kelowna ‘Home for Belonging’ gives neurodivergent community a permanent place to connect
stories.summary: A home in Kelowna is giving neurodivergent people and their caregivers a permanent place to build community, make friends and take part in programs centred around their interests
stories.author: Cohan Sassaman
stories.content:
A new home in Kelowna is giving neurodivergent people and their caregivers a permanent place to build community, make friends and take part in programs centred around their interests.

Autism Okanagan officially opened its new ‘Home for Belonging on Monday, after more than 13 months of work to turn the property into a community space.

The home was donated by the Hall family, who saw an opportunity to help the organization move away from relying on rented community spaces.

“Now, all of our programs will be in the same place,” said Autism Okanagan executive director Christy Phillips. “All the kids will come, and all the kids will now have a regular routine.”

For years, Autism Okanagan ran programs out of places such as recreation centres and libraries. The new home is intended to provide a consistent space where members can return each week.

But getting the property ready was not without challenges.

The organization worked with the City of Kelowna for more than a year to rezone the property. During the process, the home was also broken into and equipment used for programming was stolen.

Phillips says the community stepped up to help replace what was lost.

The space will host programs including Lego, digital arts, comics and drawing, Dungeons & Dragons, cosplay and social groups.

Autism Okanagan currently serves about 1,000 people between the ages of four and 40 across the Okanagan. The organization says the new space could eventually help double that number.

While the organization is called Autism Okanagan, any neurodivergent person is welcome to take part – a formal diagnosis is not required.

Programs are offered as full-session programs, with courses typically running for two to five months, giving participants time to build relationships and routines.

Programs currently run after school during the week and on weekends, with additional programming planned as funding becomes available. A new group for parents and caregivers is also planned, providing families with an opportunity to connect and build their own community.

For Autism Okanagan, the goal is simple: create a place where people can feel they belong.

“As they age, they will grow up in the house, and it will just become a place that is theirs and where they always belong,” Phillips said.

content_blocks.text: Autism Okanagan currently serves about 1,000 people between the ages of four and 40 across the Okanagan. The organization says the new space could eventually help double that number.
While the organization is called Autism Okanagan, any neurodivergent person is welcome to take part – a formal diagnosis is not required.
Programs are offered as full-session programs, with courses typically running for two to five months, giving participants time to build relationships and routines.

Programs currently run after school during the week and on weekends, with additional programming planned as funding becomes available. A new group for parents and caregivers is also planned, providing families with an opportunity to connect and build their own community.

stories.title: B.C. battered by storms as unusually warm weather grips other parts of Canada
stories.summary: Forecasters warn of flooding and landslides as another powerful storm approaches the west coast
stories.author: Jesse Winter, Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Christina Lepore was awoken in the middle of the night by the sound of crashing trees and howling winds. The second of three major storms had blown in off the Pacific Ocean, crashing ashore over her small town of Zeballos, ON Vancouver Island’s remote northwestern coast.

“Around 3 o’clock in the morning, we heard quite loud noises. And when I went to look outside, we were surrounded by water,” Ms. Lepore said.

The winds were strong enough to have blown the window out of her pick-up truck’s rear canopy, and that of her neighbour’s as well, she said. Trees came down, knocking out power and blocking a creek, she said, leading to a flood.

“There’s still pieces of siding and roofs scattered about,” said Ms. Lepore, who runs the small town’s convenience store. “There’s a lot of debris on the road, rocks from the rockslide and branches.”

North Vancouver woman rescued after being swept into creek during B.C. storm

The Village of Zeballos ordered the evacuation of 22 properties Friday owing to landslide risks that it said posed a threat to life and safety. Parts of that order were downgraded to an evacuation alert Monday, but a statement from the regional district said residents should expect some restrictions to remain in place for the remainder of the week.

Elsewhere the wild weather wreaked havoc across southwestern British Columbia. The storm was linked to two deaths in Metro Vancouver. On Friday, the driver of a sedan struck a 78-year-old woman who was attempting to cross the street during heavy rain, according to Vancouver Police.

On Saturday, a driver was killed when a falling tree struck two vehicles in Surrey, B.C. A canoeist has been missing in stormy waters off northern Vancouver Island since Friday.

According to BC Hydro, nearly 415,000 customers experienced power outages since Friday. Outages in hard-hit rural areas around Prince George are expected to last several days, with the earliest restoration expected by late Tuesday, the utility said. Access has made some repairs more difficult.

By late Monday afternoon, about 13,300 customers remained without power.

And there is more on the way. On Monday afternoon, forecasters escalated rainfall warnings in southwest British Columbia, saying some areas could receive a deluge topping 250 millimetres in a new parade of storms that is set to drench the region.

Orange warnings have been raised for west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky region, with Environment Canada warning of flooding and landslides after the “very robust” frontal system makes landfall Tuesday morning.

The province’s River Forecast Centre has also issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C.

“The heaviest rain is forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, with lingering rainfall continuing through the rest of the week,” the centre said on Monday.

Residents are being asked to stay away from riverbanks of fast-moving water and to never cross flooded roads or bridges.

Communities have begun preparing for the coming storms, with the City of Vancouver opening additional shelter spaces on Monday and Tuesday.

“This rainfall event comes on the heels of several low-pressure systems that have moved through the region in recent days, already bringing substantial amounts of precipitation to parts of the coast,” Environment Canada said.

Meanwhile other parts of Canada have seen unseasonable weather of a different sort.

Rhythm Reet, a meteorologist at the Weather Network, said Canada is experiencing what’s called an “omega block,” a weather pattern characterized by a high-pressure ridge sandwiched between two low-pressure troughs, to resemble the Greek letter.

Over the next 10 days, the Pacific storms will bring warm winds across the Rocky Mountains and push temperatures in Alberta and Saskatchewan up between seven and 10 degrees above seasonal, Ms. Reet said.

But the most significant temperature anomalies are expected in Yukon and the Northwest Territories, extending into a portion of Nunavut, where a ridge of high pressure will drive temperatures up 10 to 15 degrees above the seasonal average.

“To put numbers to that: Yellowknife, this Thursday, Nov. 12, the average daytime high is around -7 C, and the low around -15 C,” Ms. Reet said. “Our forecast is indicating that it’s going to be 3 C as a high for Yellowknife, and the low is going to be -1 C.”

Opinion: El Niño is coming for our skating rinks (and that’s not all)

Ms. Reet said she couldn’t comment on the possible connection between recent weather and climate change but she did say that it has been somewhat influenced by the growing El Niño pattern, which is gathering strength in the Pacific Ocean.

“The general pattern we end up seeing in the winter as well is the fact that the jet stream is further toward the north, allowing for this ridging pattern to hold steady toward Western Canada,” she said.

A study published in August suggests that El Niño patterns are getting stronger because of climate change.

El Niños are more than 36-per-cent stronger than they were before the industrial age began in the mid-1800s, with a 16-per-cent jump in just the last 40 years showing that the increase is accelerating, according to a study in Thursday’s journal Science .

stories.title: Vancouver’s illegal rental houses reminiscent of Hong Kong’s coffin apartments
stories.summary: Simon Fraser University's city program director, Andy Yan, told Global News the dividing of homes in Vancouver reminds him of Hong Kong's coffin apartments.
stories.author: Kristen Robinson, Amy Judd
stories.content:
A new Vancouver city councillor and former legal advocate for tenants says the discovery that landlords have been fined $90,000 after they subdivided a single-family home into a rooming house operation is sad — but not too surprising.

“The practices that I saw described in this decision are regrettably practices that I have seen elsewhere over the course of my time representing tenants, and then more recently from tenants in the Vancouver Tenants Union who have been organizing in buildings,” Stephanie Smith told Global News.

She said the scale of this house is extreme, but there are situations like this across Vancouver.

An inspection of the home in July 2025 found the house near Commercial Drive had been subdivided into 21 rooms with at least 17 tenants, plus multiple bathrooms and plumbing fixtures were added without permits.

That August, the City of Vancouver issued an order to vacate.

“The practice (of) subdividing without permits, making unpermitted renovations, making un-permited changes to electrical and plumbing, egress issues, like all of these life safety issues — these are things that I’ve seen in multiple buildings across the city over decades,” Smith added.

Following an investigation, the Residential Tenancy Branch found the landlords did not maintain the rental property in compliance with health, safety and housing standards required by law and failed to complete urgent plumbing and electrical repairs.

They were ordered to pay $85,000 for the first violation and a $5,000 penalty for the second .

The decision showed, however, that the rental home had to the capacity to generate $11,000 a month in revenue for the landlords.

Smith said the $90,000 fine is a large one, but only represents about eight months of income for the property that’s now listed for sale for $1.4 million .

“I have noted and tenant advocates have noted, that the penalties that can be assigned by the RTB (Residential Tenancy Branch) Compliance and Enforcement Unit are not proportional to the harms that can be done to tenants,” Smith said.

“And when you have a larger landlord who May be breaching bylaws or the Residential Tenancy Act in multiple properties, that can amount to a cost of doing business.”

Simon Fraser University’s city program director, Andy Yan, told Global News the dividing of homes in Vancouver reminds him of Hong Kong’s coffin apartments or home — which are essentially wooden boxes with a single bed.

“I think that this is a scene that actually is something out of Vancouver’s past from the 1800s, when they used to just stack people, new and young Canadians, into these places,” Yan said.

Yan added this issue highlights the need for local governments to ensure that landlords are not allowed to do these practices and then pay fines as the cost of doing business.

stories.title: ‘People here are warm and welcoming’: How a string of suspected arsons have shaken a Quebec town
stories.summary: Police will step up patrols in Ormstown after a string of suspected arsons shook the small community about 70 kilometres southwest of Montreal.
stories.author: Genevieve Beauchemin
stories.content:
Ormstown, Que. - Police will step up patrols in Ormstown after a string of suspected arsons shook the small community about 70 kilometres southwest of Montreal.

The increased presence is a bid to support residents after Sara Pizzeria was reduced to rubble on Sunday morning. It is the latest alleged attack on restaurants located within metres of each other on a small street called rue Lambton.

Summer Eastwood, a lifelong Ormstown resident and owner of the nearby Taverne de la Ferme, a few blocks from the scene of the fires, said the situation is frightening.

“It’s scary,” Eastwood said. “I think both as a citizen and as a business owner, this is not the kind of environment we want to be living in. It’s very disconcerting not to know who is behind these attacks in our otherwise very peaceful and supportive community.”

A trend of suspicious attacks

Police said this is the second suspicious fire at Sara Pizzeria this month. Last week, a 27-year-old man was arrested moments after the first incident. He was suspected of throwing a Molotov cocktail at the restaurant. He remains in custody.

The recent fires follow one in September at an Italian restaurant doors away on rue Lambton and a July fire at another pizzeria across the street. No one has been injured in any of the suspected arsons.

“This is the first time since I have been in the department that we’ve had a serious problem like this,” said Ormstown Fire Chief Michael Greig, who has been a firefighter in town for 17 years.

Ormstown Mayor Philippe Besombes called on the provincial government to help his town.

“It’s very difficult because we are a little community,” Besombes said. “People don’t understand what happened.”

Quebec’s Minister of Domestic Security Guy Jr. Lapointe, a former police officer, travelled to Ormstown on Monday to meet with the mayor and to reassure the population.

“We are seeing more and more violent situations in regions, whether it is fires, or arsons,” Lapointe said after the meeting. “We are here for support, to have citizens feel safer. I think it is very important. We said we would have more police officers. We will do that. We are working on that presently.”

Arsons targeting restaurants in Montreal and other major cities are frequently linked to extortion attempts and organized crime. However, the Surete du Quebec, which is investigating the Ormstown fires, has not confirmed any links to criminal organizations or evidence of extortion.

Eastwood, a 20-year veteran of the restaurant industry, said her specialty is welcoming guests, offering diners top-tier service, and that she is not a security expert.

“I really hope our government is going to step up and look out for us,” she said. “I don’t think it is the job of restaurant owners to protect their businesses.”

She added that Ormstown remains one of the most beautiful places in Quebec, filled with warm and welcoming people, and she hopes people know that the arsons do not reflect the spirit of her town.

The recent fires follow one in September at an Italian restaurant doors away on rue Lambton and a July fire at another pizzeria across the street. No one has been injured in any of the suspected arsons.
“This is the first time since I have been in the department that we’ve had a serious problem like this,” said Ormstown Fire Chief Michael Greig, who has been a firefighter in town for 17 years.
Ormstown Mayor Philippe Besombes called on the provincial government to help his town.
“It’s very difficult because we are a little community,” Besombes said. “People don’t understand what happened.”
Quebec’s Minister of Domestic Security Guy Jr. Lapointe, a former police officer, travelled to Ormstown on Monday to meet with the mayor and to reassure the population.

“We are seeing more and more violent situations in regions, whether it is fires, or arsons,” Lapointe said after the meeting. “We are here for support, to have citizens feel safer. I think it is very important. We said we would have more police officers. We will do that. We are working on that presently.”

Arsons targeting restaurants in Montreal and other major cities are frequently linked to extortion attempts and organized crime. However, the Surete du Quebec, which is investigating the Ormstown fires, has not confirmed any links to criminal organizations or evidence of extortion.
Eastwood, a 20-year veteran of the restaurant industry, said her specialty is welcoming guests, offering diners top-tier service, and that she is not a security expert.
“I really hope our government is going to step up and look out for us,” she said. “I don’t think it is the job of restaurant owners to protect their businesses.”
She added that Ormstown remains one of the most beautiful places in Quebec, filled with warm and welcoming people, and she hopes people know that the arsons do not reflect the spirit of her town.

stories.title: Why thousands of Canadian students are leaving poppies on veterans’ graves today
stories.summary: P.E.I. fourth graders spent part of Monday morning placing poppies on the graves of veterans, joining other children across the country ahead of Remembrance Day.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – Fourth graders on P.E.I. spent part of Monday morning placing poppies on the graves of veterans, joining other children across the country ahead of Remembrance Day.

The ‘No Stone Left Alone’ initiative began 15 years ago in Edmonton and has grown into an international movement. Last year, about 17,500 students participated in 220 communities across six countries, honouring nearly 115,000 veterans, according to the organization.

“They gave peace to us, and now we don’t have war in Canada,” said nine-year-old Nova-Lee MacPhee in Charlottetown.

“Soldiers are one of the strongest people. And they bring peace to our world,” said Nora Bruce.

Bags of poppies in hand, the students fanned out across Sherwood Cemetery, taking time to learn about the veterans buried there.

At Sgt. Cyril Bertram Crummey’s headstone, two young girls learned about the airman from Newfoundland and Labrador. In 1943 his plane went missing during a training flight and his body was later recovered from the sea. Crummey was buried on P.E.I. at just 23.

“He did something he loved and he died doing it,” said nine-year-old Gwen Christian.

Passing remembrance to the next generation

The organization’s P.E.I. co-ordinator, Bill Crabb, was part of the military group that helped get the initiative started while he was posted in Edmonton.

He recalls attending similar events when he was younger and listening to veterans of the world wars describe their experiences. With the First World War generation gone and so few Second World War veterans remaining, he says the responsibility now falls on those who served in modern conflicts to keep their message alive.

“It’s important to let them know what generations before them endured,” he said. “To kneel at their gravesite, to say their name, to have a moment of reflection, I think it’s very touching.”

Crabb, a retired chief warrant officer, was an armoured soldier who worked with tanks. His overseas missions included trips to Bosnia and Afghanistan, as well as Israel and Syria.

The lessons weren’t lost on the fourth graders, who were left thinking about how much courage had been asked of such young people.

“For soldiers, it was a really hard life for them since they were in the army, and I realized that it’s very nice to put poppies on their gravestone,” said Ruby Dunning.

The visit brought mixed emotions, from sadness to happiness at being part of the ceremony. For Wiley Stewart, it was a chance to show his gratitude.

“We’re honouring the soldiers that died fighting for our freedom,” he said.

On Wednesday, Canadians of all ages will come together again to mark Remembrance Day.

stories.title: What Winnipeg can learn from Toronto’s housing model
stories.summary: A new mental health and addictions hospital and housing units will be built in Winnipeg replicating a housing project based in Toronto.
stories.author: Toni De Guzman
stories.content:
A new mental health and addictions hospital and 2,000 housing units will be built in Winnipeg replicating a housing project based in Toronto that saw a decrease in ER visits and millions of savings.

Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to end homelessness across the country within a decade, at a news conference at Wehwehneh Bahgahkinahgohn on Friday. Winnipeg is set to receive $1 billion to build a Winnipeg Centre for Mental Health and Addictions and transitional homes, according to the 2026 federal budget.

The location for the housing and hospital has not been determined.

Dunn House, the housing project in Toronto that Winnipeg will , reported a 52 per cent reduction in emergency room visits and more than $2 million of savings, according to the budget.

“There is a huge cost to the status quo. The status quo is not working,” said Kinew. “We’re gonna get it done right, and we’re gonna get it done quick — and the housing similarly for us to stand up 2,000 housing units and get people settled in by 2031 means we’re going to be looking everywhere.”

The housing units will have rooms, medical offices, and shared spaces like the kitchen and community room, said Doug Rollins, the City of Toronto’s executive director housing secretariat.

Watch the video above for the full story.

stories.title: Expert insight: Scientists predicted Nov. 13, 2026 will be ‘doomsday.’ Should we worry?
stories.summary: Western expert says 1960 'doomsday' prediction for Nov. 13 was a mathematical projection, not a credible forecast.
stories.author: Special to Western News
stories.content:
In 1960, Science, one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026. It predicted that on this future date – just over a month from today – the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself.

The outlandishness of the claim landed the article widespread public attention. More surprisingly – because its underlying research and math seemed sound – it also received careful and sustained scientific attention.The authors – Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot – argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one.

“Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.”

The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate – until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts.

Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half what it was in 1960. Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to staggering effect.

The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself.

In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans May be exceptional.

Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one.

They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations.

Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity.

Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.

This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times. It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.

Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work – calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd” – the authors responded with spirited defences that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions.

Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited – usually at face value – in textbooks on genetics, ecology and demography.

It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian Parliamentary committee, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favour increased population.

The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate – at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts – because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.

We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13 “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on – prepping for the next doomsday scenario – it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.

For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.

Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.

To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity – that’s a good trick.Image 1: The Conversation

Alan MacEachern, Professor, History, Western University

Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half.

This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times. It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears.

Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work – calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd” – the authors responded with spirited defences that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions.
Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited – usually at face value – in textbooks on genetics, ecology and demography.

It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian Parliamentary committee, for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favour increased population.

The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate – at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s.

Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter and the global population began falling behind the forecasts – because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate.
We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13 “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on – prepping for the next doomsday scenario – it is worth asking what we can learn from this one.

For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal.

Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument.
To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity – that’s a good trick.Image 1: The Conversation

stories.title: Calgary water use remains in ‘green zone’ as Bearspaw feeder main work progresses
stories.summary: Calgary and neighbouring communities have now recorded five consecutive days in the 'green zone' with water use remaining below the city’s target of 500 million litres a day.
stories.author: Drew Stremick, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Calgarians continue to keep water consumption within the city’s target range as crews move ahead with work to connect the upgraded Bearspaw South Feeder Main.

Calgary and neighbouring communities have now recorded five consecutive days in the “green zone” with water use remaining below the city’s target of 500 million litres a day.

Water consumption was 482 million litres Friday, 483 million litres Saturday and 487 million litres Sunday.

The city says keeping demand below 500 million litres is important while the new feeder main is being connected, because there’s limits on how much water can be moved through the system during construction.

Lower consumption also ensures enough water is available for essential services and firefighting.

Crews spent the weekend preparing three sites along the feeder-main route, following work last week to safely shut down and drain the existing Bearspaw South Feeder Main.

The city said Monday that draining was on track to be completed that day and excavation had begun at some of the sites where the new pipe will be connected to the water system.

Starting Thursday, crews are expected to work around the clock at the 89th Street N.W. site to connect the new feeder main. That work is expected to take about two weeks. Excavation was also scheduled to begin Monday along Parkdale Boulevard as part of repairs to sections of a smaller feeder main.

The city is warning residents to expect traffic impacts and pathway detours around construction areas and to stay away from work sites where possible.

Water restrictions are expected to remain in place for at least another three-and-a-half weeks while the connection work is completed.

Michael Thompson, Calgary’s water chief operating officer, said the city will bring the original feeder main back online once the work is finished, allowing restrictions to be lifted while crews commission the new pipe.

“What will happen once we’re done this work is we will turn on the original Bearspaw South Feeder Main again, we’ll pull ourselves out of restrictions,” Thompson said.

“Use that pipe to flow water while we commission the new pipe, and then mid-December we’ll transition over to that new pipe.”

The Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant remains in operation during the restrictions, supplying about 20 per cent of Calgary’s daily water needs, while the Glenmore Water Treatment Plant handles the remaining 80 per cent.

While the city’s immediate focus is completing the feeder-main twinning project, Thompson said planning is already underway for the next stage.

The city is in the design phase for another section of pipe that would run from the Bearspaw Water Treatment Plant to the tie-in point in Bowness.

The city’s next construction update is expected Thursday, Nov. 12.

stories.title: Murder trial underway for man accused of setting best friend on fire
stories.summary: Disturbing details emerged on Monday at the start of a murder trial at the London Courthouse.
stories.author: Nick Paparella
stories.content:
Disturbing details emerged on Monday at the start of a murder trial at the London Courthouse.

In her opening address, Crown Attorney Sarah Dow told the court that Jonathan Graham, 29, and Bradley Joudrey, now 36, were like brothers growing up together from a young age.

However she said that friendship all ended on July 12, 2022 when Graham was doused with gasoline and set on fire.

She said the pair had an altercation and that Joudrey left to siphon gas into a pop bottle.

Later that night outside a convenience store near Trafalgar Street and Admiral Drive, “Joudrey poured gasoline on Jon while he was sitting in the driver’s seat of his car.”

“He (Joudrey) remained at the scene watching Jon in flames until a person stopped in his car,” she continued.

Before wrapping up the opening address the Crown said, “Joudrey committed the murder because he was angry with Jon for punching him earlier in the night.”

The court heard Graham died in the hospital days later from thermal injuries.

Joudrey would be arrested and has pled not guilty to first degree murder.

The first witness to testify in this case was the man who came upon the scene seconds after the flames erupted.

An emotional Philip Oskirko told the court he was driving to the house of a friend in the east end when, “I just noticed a fire and then I got out of my truck and noticed that fireball is a human...covered head to toe.”

“The guy started dropping and rolling and I grabbed my sweater and tried to help him. He had no clothes on,” said Oskirko.

He said he then saw a grey or silver Dodge SUV speed away, “It took off pretty quick.”

The witness called 911 and stayed with Graham, “You could see his health deteriorating and his speech deteriorating at a fast rate... and barely even conscious.”

Later, paramedic Michael Brock testified about responding to the scene, “We noticed he (Graham) was covered in very deep burns mostly front and back...full thickness burns.”

He went on, “I asked him what happened? And he responded, ‘I don’t want to talk about it.’” But eventually, “He said someone had doused him with gasoline and set him on fire.”

The trial is slated to last four weeks.

stories.title: Lambton opens new affordable housing building in Sarnia
stories.summary: A lengthy wait for affordable housing in Lambton County has just gotten a little shorter.
stories.author: Bryan Bicknell
stories.content:
A lengthy wait for affordable housing in Lambton County has just gotten a little shorter.

“Access to safe, affordable housing is fundamental to individual well being and strong communities. That is why county council has made affordable housing its top priority,” said Lambton County Warden Kevin Marriott.

He was joined by Sarnia and senior government representatives to open doors at the county’s newest affordable housing project.

The new building at 471 Kathleen Ave. in Sarnia includes 50 deeply supportive housing units, 14 of which are barrier free and will be operated by the March of Dimes, according to Lambton Manager of Housing Services Melisa Johnson.

The $30-million project was funded by the city and county, along with senior governments. Sarnia-Lambton-Bkejwanong MP Marilyn Gladu says more help is on the way, referencing last week’s federal budget announcement on homelessness in her remarks.

“I was also very encouraged the government putting forward a plan to end homelessness within ten years. And so, these are the kinds of things that we do to support one another and to build together,” said Gladu.

According to Lambton County Housing Services more than 1,100 households remain on the county’s housing waitlist. The wait to get into a new home is typically about four years.

In some of his last public remarks as mayor, Sarnia Mayor Mike Bradley urged the next county council to continue offering housing that includes wrap-around supports.

“Look at the March of Dimes, that’s supportive housing. Look at Community Living, that’s supportive housing. If you’re going to put someone into a new unit and give them a shot at a better life, then get them the supports they need to meet some of the challenges they have in their life. Because in the end, no-one wins unless everyone gets the win,” Bradley said.

The building has been named The Orchard, and its first tenants start moving in this Thursday.

stories.title: ‘There are 300 people in this neighbourhood really upset’: Quiet dead-end street planned for townhome access road

stories.author: Sean Irvine
stories.content:
Residents in a south London neighbourhood are up in arms over a development that could put a townhome entrance on their dead-end street. About a dozen homes dot Cowan Crescent in South London. The tree-lined street is calm despite its proximity to heavy traffic.

“You wouldn’t know that a stone’s throw away is Commissioners and Wellington,” said Nick McCallum, a resident since 2023. “We kind of pulled up to the house, and we were like, ‘I think this is it!’ before even stepping in.” But now McCallum and his neighbours worry their quiet life is about to be interrupted.

A small piece of land, at the end of the circle, is at the centre of their worries. Although a city planning sign disappeared within a day of being put up, a space between two homes is proposed as the entryway for a new townhouse development.

“I mean, you would just never assume something like that’s going to happen,” said 48-year resident Joe Svilpa, who lives just three doors away. Anger over the development extends beyond Cowan Crescent into the Lockwood Park neighbourhood.

Lawn signs are up, and a petition has already reached 200 signatures. “There are 300 people in this neighbourhood really upset about this!” exclaimed Svilpa. At the front of the lot to be redeveloped is a home on Commissioners Road.

The residents inside tell CTV News they sold to a London firm in 2023. As proposed, the new development will initially include 11 units. But over time, four more could be added once the home occupants decide to move on. For years, they’ve come and gone using Commissioners Road.

And that’s exactly what the residents on Cowan want to see continued if the townhouses go ahead. “I would prefer something like that as opposed to access from this circle,” said Svilpa. McCallum added, “I think just having the entrance off Commissioners is really the biggest thing that’s sticking right now.

You know, if you want to put that in, okay, but having access off Commissioners is really the biggest thing.” The residents state they are working with councillor Elisabeth Peloza, who represents the area. She did not respond to a message Monday from CTV News.

The residents have also retained their own planner who has prepared a 12-page report outlining reasons why the application should be modified or denied. Svilpa says many are obvious. “We don’t want more traffic, more people, parking problems.

It’s unfair to do this to people. I’m really amazed the city would even consider it.” A public meeting on the proposal slated for Dec. 1, was recently cancelled. A new date has not been announced.

stories.title: Ottawa extends tariff relief program for firms importing U.S. goods
stories.summary: Temporary remission program aims to reduce burden on Canadian firms caught in tariff crossfire
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
The federal government is extending its relief program for firms importing tariffed U.S. goods and is changing the mix of goods eligible for those remissions.

Since the early days of Canada’s retaliatory duties against the United States, Ottawa has offered what it calls a temporary remission program to reduce the burden on Canadian firms caught in the tariff crossfire.

The government has routinely extended that program and modified what’s eligible for remissions as it looks to give itself more time to help firms transition away from U.S. suppliers, particularly for steel.

The program’s expiration date will be extended by another year to June 30, 2028. Effective Monday, it will also expand to include non-steel goods used in mining, quarrying and oil and gas extraction.

Goods used by public education entities, including those mandated by Indigenous organizations, will be also be eligible for relief.

Certain goods integral to national security, public health and packaging in the agricultural and food and beverage sectors are also exempt.

Canada has maintained retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum imports for most of the trade dispute, but the federal government ramped up its response in September as a new wave of U.S. duties took effect.

The government now imposes counter-tariffs on a range of U.S. goods varying from 15 to 50 per cent.

Ottawa says it’s also planning to exclude goods from the remissions program that can reliably be sourced in Canada.

Certain trailers will be removed from the remissions program on Dec. 1, while aluminum wire and extrusions and paperboard products will be taken out on Feb. 1, 2027.

The federal government’s remissions program has been criticized in the past by the Canadian Steel Producers Association. The group said the relief program removes the pressure on firms to pivot to Canadian suppliers.

Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc argued in a media statement Monday that extending and adjusting these measures strikes the right balance.

“Extending these tariff relief measures gives Canadian companies the support they need today while encouraging greater use of Canadian-made goods and services,” LeBlanc said.

stories.title: Fanshawe’s main campus restaurant joins United Way’s burger battle fundraiser
stories.summary: Fanshawe College's campus restaurant is one of more than two dozen London eateries participating in the United...
stories.author: Callum Contursi
stories.content:
Fanshawe College’s campus restaurant is one of more than two dozen London eateries participating in the United Way’s Ultimate Burger Battle this year.

The Outback Shack will send two dollars from every burger sold to United Way Elgin Middlesex. Bragging rights go to the restaurant that raises the most donations.

“It’s been steady, maybe because this establishment is located inside a school,” said Ayla McLeod, manager of the Outback Shack.

The fundraiser began in 2025 with 18 restaurants across London in hopes of supporting local businesses. That number increased to 26 restaurants in this year’s event.

“The more we were able to continue with this fundraiser, the more interest we’re going to be able to grow from different restaurants.” Juan Marulanda, marketing and communications co-ordinator for United Way Elgin Middlesex.

Ultimate Burger Battle flyer shown at Fanshawe’s main campus on Monday, November. 9. (Photo: Callum Contursi)

“The two major awards that are given out are the People’s Choice Award (voted on by the public), and the Ultimate Burger, which is chosen by the ambassadors we have,” Marulanda, said.

After the Ultimate Burger Battle concludes, United Way Elgin Middlesex hosts a closing ceremony.

The fundraiser runs from November 1. to November 30. across 26 restaurants around London.

stories.title: Technical disruption at Canada Post affecting domestic shipping transactions
stories.summary: The problems began on Friday and are mainly affecting items being sent to or from postal codes in the Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal corridor.
stories.author: Dilshad Burman
stories.content:
With the busy holiday season on the horizon, Canada Post is experiencing technical difficulties which are disrupting domestic shipping transactions at retail post office locations.

Canada Post tells CityNews that the problems began on Friday and are mainly affecting items being sent to or from postal codes in the Toronto, Ottawa and Montreal corridor.

The issue does not impact shipments that are created online or any U.S. or international shipments.

“We are actively working to resolve the issue as soon as possible. In the meantime, prepaid products such as Canada Post Flat Rate Boxes, can be purchased for domestic shipments,” spokesperson Genevieve Joly told CityNews.

A timeline for when the issue is expected to be resolved was not provided.

stories.title: Cold outside, fitness inside: how Fanshawe students can stay fit on campus this winter
stories.summary: As colder weather approaches London, Ont., students May want to start moving outdoor fitness routines to indoo...
stories.author: Owen Schuller
stories.content:
As colder weather approaches London, Ont., students May want to start moving outdoor fitness routines to indoor workouts and programs.

But many students don’t know that they have access to a slew of free campus fitness activities, from dance classes to a golf simulator, as part of their student Fanshawe student card, said the school’s wellness director.

“We have a fitness centre with cardio equipment, free weights and machines, group fitness classes … yoga and spin. We have dance, a golf simulator and a rock wall,” said Tabitha Liston, fitness and wellness program director, describes the fitness opportunities available for students.

Lesson for golf simulator, rock wall and other activities are also available at no extra cost, she said.

stories.title: Canada Post says higher U.S., international mail costs will sustain company
stories.summary: Last week’s federal budget said the price of a single domestic stamp will go from $1.44 to $2 in 2027, with a seven per cent increase in cost each year after.
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler
stories.content:
A Canada Post spokesperson says the planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help the Crown corporation become self-sustaining after years of financial losses.

Last week’s federal budget said the price of a single domestic stamp will go from $1.44 to $2 in 2027, with a seven per cent increase in cost each year after.

Jon Hamilton, Canada Post’s vice-president of communications, says the price for U.S.-bound and international letter stamps will also go up but the amount has not yet been decided.

He says this move is an attempt to match the prices consumers are paying with the organization’s operating costs and help repay some of the assistance Ottawa has provided to keep Canada Post afloat.

The recent budget is providing another $1.2 billion over seven years to support Canada Post’s move to community mailboxes.

Canada Post’s annual report says the Crown corporation saw $1.57 billion in pre-tax losses in 2025, the highest amount on record.

stories.title: Stellantis signs deal with Roshel to sell idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant
stories.summary: Automaker Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with Canadian defence contractor Roshel to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta, Karen Bartko
stories.content:
Stellantis says it has signed an agreement to sell its idled Brampton, Ont., assembly plant to defence contractor Roshel.

Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and its associated equipment for an undisclosed amount.

In a joint release, the companies said they are also exploring opportunities to work together on vehicle technologies and related services for the defence industry.

The move comes as contract talks between Stellantis and the union representing more than 9,000 of its workers in Canada remain at an impasse.

The two sides have clashed over the future of the Brampton site as well as issues around job security. Last month, Stellantis workers in Canada voted to give their union a mandate to strike , with 97.3 per cent of members in favour of authorizing a potential job action.

“We’re currently not in a strike position and obviously lots of this to be worked out. Our goal here is to reach a resolution and to get to the bargaining table when we can, and we’ll do our best to get an agreement,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said at a press conference Monday evening.

“A strike is always a last resort and it remains a last resort here.”

She said the union will evaluate its next move and that it has a “four-party meeting” scheduled for later in the week with the company and government officials to discuss the future of the Brampton plant.

Payne said the sale of an auto assembly plant and loss of vehicle production capacity is devastating for Canada’s industry.

“Having sold an auto plant is a worst-case scenario, and that’s what we’re facing right now. Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to these workers,” she said.

“Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of our national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers from this U.S. trade war.”

Talks broke down in September when Stellantis signed a memorandum of understanding with Roshel , a Brampton-based manufacturer of armoured vehicles, for a potential sale of the facility.

More than 2,000 workers were laid off from the Brampton plant when it halted operations in 2023.

The facility had been slated to be retooled for Jeep production, a process that began early in 2024, before the company paused the plan in early 2025. It later announced it was moving production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois, leaving the plant idled indefinitely.

“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously. After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution,” said Stellantis CEO Antonio Filosa in the news release.

“With this announcement, we are driving forward our broader strategic goals, opening new opportunities for Stellantis in the defence industry, and creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”

Roshel founder and CEO Roman Shimonov said the company’s plan is to create a new centre of excellence for advanced manufacturing “which will allow Canadian companies to better serve customers at home and export into allied markets.”

“Aligned with Canada’s defence industrial strategy, it will strengthen our sovereign industrial capabilities, drive local economic growth and bring much-needed manufacturing space and jobs to the Toronto area,” Shimonov said in the release.

“We look forward to working collaboratively with government and the broader community to bring this vision to life.”

As the facility returns to operations, there will be opportunities for around 700 to 1,000 laid-off Stellantis employees to return to work under Roshel. The defence company also plans to lease around one-quarter of the site’s space back to Stellantis for automotive work.

The transaction is expected to close by the end of this year, subject to certain conditions, including government and regulatory requirements.

Brampton Mayor Patrick Brown said in a statement Monday that he welcomes the opportunity for a local company to bring manufacturing back to the site and strengthen Canadian defence production.

Brown called Roshel a “Brampton success story” and said members of Unifor Local 1285 and their families have lived with years of uncertainty.

“They deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis and a clear path to good-paying jobs,” he said.

Brown called on Stellantis to work with Unifor toward a resolution and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers.

He said Unifor members also deserve a fair resolution from Stellantis.

“I’m calling on Stellantis to work with Unifor to reach that resolution, and on Roshel to work directly with Local 1285 to identify hiring and training opportunities for laid-off Brampton autoworkers,” he said.

Brown said Stellantis also needs to repay taxpayers for the public funding it received to support automotive production in Brampton.

“I will continue pressing the federal government to recover that money and hold Stellantis accountable for the commitments it made to our workers and our city,” the statement reads.

Unifor has previously written to federal Industry Minister Mélanie Joly urging the government to block the potential sale and clarify whether Stellantis’ intentions to offload the plant breached its commitments to Ottawa.

Last year, Prime Minister Mark Carney expressed disappointment over Stellantis moving Jeep Compass production to the United States.

At the time, the prime minister said he reminded Stellantis of its commitments to the government under funding deals — such as keeping the Brampton plant — and warned there would be consequences if it failed to meet those obligations.

Joly has said the government would “get our money back” if the company doesn’t fulfil its obligations. She said Monday that Stellantis’ decision “does not erase the commitments they made to workers in Brampton.”

“They deserve answers, respect and above all, a secure future,” Joly said in a statement.

The minister urged all parties to return to the bargaining table and said she has reached out to the automaker, union, Ontario government and representatives of the Brampton plant to convene a meeting this week.

“I expect them to come to the table with a single focus: protecting good paying jobs in Brampton,” Joly said.

“For Brampton’s autoworkers, walking away is not an option.”

Stellantis said it acknowledges its obligations to employees under collective agreements and applicable laws and that it “remains prepared to engage with Unifor to negotiate a settlement to assist union represented employees.”

With files from Global News’ Rachel Morgan and The Canadian Press

stories.title: Stellantis finalizes sale of Brampton auto plant to defence contractor Roshel for undisclosed amount
stories.summary: Industry Minister calls on automaker to meet this week with government officials and union about protecting jobs in the Ontario city
stories.author: Eric Atkins
stories.content:
Automaker Stellantis NV Stla-N says it has finalized the sale of its idled factory in Brampton, Ont., to defence contractor Roshel Inc. for an undisclosed amount.

Stellantis closed the plant, which employed more than 3,000 people, for retooling in 2023, and moved planned production of the Jeep Compass to Illinois last year, after the U.S. imposed 25-per-cent tariffs on Canadian-made cars.

The deal is expected to close by the end of the year, subject to regulatory requirements, the companies said in a joint statement.

Roshel’s owner, Roman Shimanov, said the Brampton plant could employ “thousands” of people, paying taxes and producing civilian and armoured vehicles.

“Every Canadian should be happy because we’re talking about a substantial change to a plant that was idle for three years,” he said by phone.

Unifor, which represents the workers, said the sale was a breach of the collective agreement and commitments to the federal government, which provided hundreds of millions of dollars to Stellantis to refit the plant.

“Stellantis has betrayed our members with an underhanded deal to sell the plant and walk away from its commitments to our members,” Unifor national president Lana Payne said in a statement. “Allowing the sale to move forward is a critical failure of the national auto strategy and breaks the federal government’s promise to protect autoworkers in the U.S. trade war.”

Ms. Payne called the sale “a significant step backwards for Canada’s industrial economy,” citing the loss of good Stellantis jobs and thousands more at parts suppliers.

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said in a statement on X that she wants the automaker to meet with the Unifor union and provincial and federal officials this week to talk about “protecting good paying jobs in Brampton.”

“Stellantis’s decision does not erase the commitments they made to the workers of Brampton,” she said, adding that the government is focused on finding solutions for the more than 2,000 Stellantis workers who remain on layoff benefits.

“They deserve answers, respect and above all a secure future,” she said.

Ottawa has said Stellantis’s decision to shift production violated agreements the company made when it received taxpayer funding to retool the plant. Ms. Joly has said the government will get its money back.

Ottawa contributed as much as $529-million to Stellantis for work on plants in Brampton and Windsor.

A source familiar with the matter told The Globe and Mail that Stellantis will lease back 25-per-cent of the plant for possible vehicle assembly while Roshel will retain control over the rest.

The Globe and Mail is not identifying the person because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

The companies said in a statement that they will together pursue manufacturing opportunities for the massive factory northwest of Toronto.

Mr. Shimanov said it is too soon to talk about specific plans for the plant, but he has a letter of intent from a European carmaker that is interested in producing at the plant. That is in addition to the arrangement with Stellantis.

Roshel, which has plants in Mississauga, Brampton, Ohio, Mexico, France and Colombia, produced 1,500 armoured vehicles in 2025, he said. The company is among the bidders for the federal government’s light utility vehicle program, valued at about $5-billion.

“You cannot sign a contract before you have the ability to produce,” Mr. Shimanov said. “It doesn’t work like that. You have to first have the capacity infrastructure before you commit to your clients. And our plan is first to secure the infrastructure. And then based on having the infrastructure, to offer different solutions, and this plan can offer a lot of different capabilities that are unique.”

Stellantis chief executive officer Antonio Filosa said the sale creates new opportunities in the defence business, “creating a path to return the Brampton facility to productive industrial use.”

“Brampton employees have made lasting contributions to Stellantis, and we take our responsibilities to them and their families seriously,” he said. “After three years of paid layoff, we remain committed to working with Unifor on a fair resolution.”

Roshel is a Brampton-based maker of armoured vehicles for military and security industries.

Unifor has fought to reopen the plant, and walked away from collective bargaining talks with Stellantis in September when the employer confirmed it had a preliminary agreement to sell the facility, built in 1986. Before it closed in 2023, the plant made Dodge muscle cars.

The factory is 2.95 million square feet and sits on 269 acres.

Ottawa earlier rejected a Stellantis proposal to assemble Chinese car kits in the plant, dismissing it as a plan that would create few jobs and add little of value to the local supply chain.

Stellantis, maker of Fiat, Chrysler and several other global brands, has struggled to turn a profit and has excess capacity at its U.S. factories.

stories.title: Sirens sound throughout London as part of Labatt testing
stories.summary: During lunch time on Monday, you May have heard a loud siren screaming from downtown London. But there was no ...
stories.author: Ryan Baynton
stories.content:
During lunch time on Monday, you May have heard a loud siren screaming from downtown London.

But there was no need for alarm. The noise was part of Labatt Brewery’s planned siren and drill testing in partnership with the London Fire Department.

As the siren sounded, firefighters responded as if it were a real emergency dealing with hazardous materials.

“We are just training in the unlikely event of an emergency to make sure we’re prepared to handle that emergency,” said AJ Bratz, Hazardous Materials (Hazmat) team co-ordinator for the fire department.

“It’s something Labatt does every five years make sure that they are safe for the community. Some of the processes … use what would be considered hazardous materials.”

Although London Fire Department had notified the public about the drill ahead of time, some people in the area said they were startled by the siren.

stories.title: Canada Post says higher international and U.S. mail costs will sustain its operations
stories.summary: Ottawa - A Canada Post spokesperson says the planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help the Crown corporation become self-sustaining after years of financial losses.
stories.author: Alyssa Wheeler The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The planned increase in the price of stamps is meant to help Canada Post become self-sustaining after years of financial losses, the Crown corporation’s chief spokesperson said.

Last week’s federal budget announced the price of a single domestic stamp will go from $1.44 to $2 in 2027, with a seven per cent increase in cost each year after.

stories.title: What’s going on with the Russia Iihf World Juniors controversy?
stories.summary: The decision by the International Ice Hockey Federation to allow Russia back into the World Juniors Hockey Championship next month is continuing to stir backlash.
stories.author: Ariel Rabinovitch
stories.content:
The decision by the International Ice Hockey Federation to allow Russia back into the World Juniors Hockey Championship next month continued to stir backlash on Monday with Norway saying its team was being bumped to make room for Russia and Sweden vowing not to play against Russia .

In a statement to Global News on Monday, a spokesperson for the Prime Minister’s Office reiterated Ottawa’s stance saying, “athletes from Russia and Belarus will not be able to compete for their countries in Canada so long as the unjustified war against Ukraine continues. That position has not changed.”

It is not yet clear whether Russian and Belarussian players will be allowed to compete for a neutral team rather than for their national teams.

The first puck drops on Dec. 26., with the tournament taking place in Edmonton and Red Deer, Alta.

“For better or for worse, athletes that are participating and representing their country do get involved, whether they like it or not, in the political implications of international sports,” says Simon Darnell professor of kinesiology and Sport for Development & Peace at the University of Toronto.

“Allowing the Russians to play at the World Juniors, unfortunately, would be a tacit acceptance of the war in Ukraine, and I don’t think that’s what the international sports community should be doing.”

Here’s what to know about how this came to be and everything we know so far.

Russia has been waging an ongoing unprovoked war on Ukraine since early 2022, and various international sports groups banned Russia from participating in response, including the International Olympic Committee (IOC) and the International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf), which conducts the World Juniors Hockey Championship.

The Iihf ban on Russia’s participation was squashed last month after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Oct. 30 that the federation must allow Russia to compete in its sanctioned events, including the upcoming tournament.

Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the men’s under-20 tournament in Edmonton and Red Deer next month at Norway’s expense .

The Iihf has not formally announced the change, and its website still lists Norway among the 10 teams in the tournament.

Global News sent a request for comment to the Iihf on Monday asking if Russia has been added to the upcoming tournament and replaced Norway. A response was not received as of publication.

Shortly after the court ruling last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a ban on Russian athletes , in addition to those from Belarus, from participating in the tournament while in Canada because of the war with Ukraine.

“This is a decision we take on our own, which is we will deny, while Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal unjustified horrific war in Ukraine — as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney said last week.

That decision by Carney was also supported publicly by Wayne Gretzky.

Ukrainian Canadian leaders say the court ruling allowing Russia to participate was “unjustified, ridiculous and egregious.”

“The court decision to allow Russia back into international hockey is a disgrace and has brought shame onto that court,” says Orest Zakydalsky, senior policy advisor with the Ukrainian Canadian Congress.

“Norway and the Norwegian people have been strong supporters of Ukraine and continue to be. We are immensely grateful for all that they have done for Ukraine and I think that the Hockey Federation should take a look at the logic of this ruling and reverse it.”

Norway acknowledged that the Iihf has been handcuffed by the court’s ruling. As the 10th-ranked team entering the tournament, Norway said it was relegated to the 1A Division to open the spot for Russia.

“The situation is still unclear,” Norway’s ice hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said in a statement posted on the association’s website and translated from Norwegian to English. “This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.”

“We are aware of the status and the measures the Iihf feels compelled to take, and will await further information from the Iihf in the coming days,” Salsten said. “This also clearly shows all the practical challenges and immediate consequences for everyone involved when countries are reinstated immediately.”

The Russians haven’t competed in the tournament since a fourth-place finish in 2021, with their ban beginning after the nation invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

“I suspect that Norway’s probably trying to figure out how they’re going to deal with this situation and they know that they have allies,” says Darnell.

“It reminds us that sports and politics are always connected, and I think we can all agree that this is much more about politics than it is about sports at this point.”

Since the announcement from the Norwegian Hockey Association, the Swedish Ice Hockey Association says it will refuse to play Russia if the teams meet at the world juniors and stood in solidarity with Team Norway.

1:23 Canada intensifies sanctions on Russia amid ‘illegal and unjustifiable’ Ukraine war

What are the next steps for the controversy?

Adam van Koeverden, Secretary of State for Sport of Canada, spoke Monday and reaffirmed Ottawa’s stance on Russia’s involvement in the tournament, although few specifics were given regarding any exceptions.

“The prime minister was as clear as day last week. Russia will not be competing at the World Juniors in Alberta,” said van Koeverden to reporters when asked about Norway reportedly being bumped to allow Russia to participate.

He also suggested that Russian players could, in theory, participate in the tournament provided that they don’t represent Russia by wearing a neutral jersey.

“If they’re not competing with a neutral status as an AIN, that’s, en français, Athlètes Individuels Neutres, then they would not be permitted to compete, and that AIN designation has not been tested in a team format,” said van Koeverden.

“Working with Hockey Canada, working with the Iihf, with respect to Norway’s inclusion in this tournament. I spoke with the Minister of Sport from Norway last week and had a great conversation. We’re very, very aligned and we hope to see Norwegian athletes competing in Alberta December and January.”

When asked to clarify if he meant that Russian players could participate provided they wear a neutral jersey on the ice, van Koeverden said, “I want to be just as clear as the prime minister was last week. The Russians will not be represented at the World Juniors in Alberta.”

The Iihf ban on Russia’s participation was squashed last month after the Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Oct. 30 that the federation must allow Russia to compete in its sanctioned events, including the upcoming tournament.
Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the men’s under-20 tournament in Edmonton and Red Deer next month at Norway’s expense .
The Iihf has not formally announced the change, and its website still lists Norway among the 10 teams in the tournament.
Global News sent a request for comment to the Iihf on Monday asking if Russia has been added to the upcoming tournament and replaced Norway. A response was not received as of publication.

Shortly after the court ruling last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced a ban on Russian athletes , in addition to those from Belarus, from participating in the tournament while in Canada because of the war with Ukraine.

“This is a decision we take on our own, which is we will deny, while Russia and Belarus are supporting this illegal unjustified horrific war in Ukraine — as long as that’s going on, there will be none of those athletes competing for their countries in Canada,” Carney said last week.
That decision by Carney was also supported publicly by Wayne Gretzky.
Ukrainian Canadian leaders say the court ruling allowing Russia to participate was “unjustified, ridiculous and egregious.”

“The court decision to allow Russia back into international hockey is a disgrace and has brought shame onto that court,” says Orest Zakydalsky, senior policy advisor with the Ukrainian Canadian Congress.

“Norway and the Norwegian people have been strong supporters of Ukraine and continue to be. We are immensely grateful for all that they have done for Ukraine and I think that the Hockey Federation should take a look at the logic of this ruling and reverse it.”

Norway acknowledged that the Iihf has been handcuffed by the court’s ruling. As the 10th-ranked team entering the tournament, Norway said it was relegated to the 1A Division to open the spot for Russia.

“The situation is still unclear,” Norway’s ice hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said in a statement posted on the association’s website and translated from Norwegian to English. “This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.”

“We are aware of the status and the measures the Iihf feels compelled to take, and will await further information from the Iihf in the coming days,” Salsten said. “This also clearly shows all the practical challenges and immediate consequences for everyone involved when countries are reinstated immediately.”
The Russians haven’t competed in the tournament since a fourth-place finish in 2021, with their ban beginning after the nation invaded Ukraine in February 2022.
“I suspect that Norway’s probably trying to figure out how they’re going to deal with this situation and they know that they have allies,” says Darnell.
“It reminds us that sports and politics are always connected, and I think we can all agree that this is much more about politics than it is about sports at this point.”

Since the announcement from the Norwegian Hockey Association, the Swedish Ice Hockey Association says it will refuse to play Russia if the teams meet at the world juniors and stood in solidarity with Team Norway.
1:23 Canada intensifies sanctions on Russia amid ‘illegal and unjustifiable’ Ukraine war
What are the next steps for the controversy?

Adam van Koeverden, Secretary of State for Sport of Canada, spoke Monday and reaffirmed Ottawa’s stance on Russia’s involvement in the tournament, although few specifics were given regarding any exceptions.

“The prime minister was as clear as day last week. Russia will not be competing at the World Juniors in Alberta,” said van Koeverden to reporters when asked about Norway reportedly being bumped to allow Russia to participate.
He also suggested that Russian players could, in theory, participate in the tournament provided that they don’t represent Russia by wearing a neutral jersey.

“If they’re not competing with a neutral status as an AIN, that’s, en français, Athlètes Individuels Neutres, then they would not be permitted to compete, and that AIN designation has not been tested in a team format,” said van Koeverden.

“Working with Hockey Canada, working with the Iihf, with respect to Norway’s inclusion in this tournament. I spoke with the Minister of Sport from Norway last week and had a great conversation. We’re very, very aligned and we hope to see Norwegian athletes competing in Alberta December and January.”

When asked to clarify if he meant that Russian players could participate provided they wear a neutral jersey on the ice, van Koeverden said, “I want to be just as clear as the prime minister was last week. The Russians will not be represented at the World Juniors in Alberta.”

A Montreal Police canine unit works in front of Yeshiva Gedola school on Deacon St. in Côte-des-Neiges on Sunday, Nov. 12, 2023 after shots were fired at the school early in the morning. (John Kenney / Montreal Gazette)

November 9, 2026 at 4:17 p.m.

A Quebec Court judge called the man who pumped bullets into the door of a Jewish school in Côte-des-Neiges three years ago a coward while sentencing him to a 66-month sentence Monday afternoon.

In a decision delivered at the Montreal courthouse, Judge Pierre Labelle agreed with the joint recommendation made to him last week by the Crown and the defence in the case against 23-year-old Abdirazak Mahdi Ahmed.

On Nov. 12, 2023, Mahdi Ahmed and an accomplice pulled up to the Yeshiva Gedola school on Deacon St. around 5 a.m. in a stolen vehicle. Mahdi Ahmed used a 9 mm firearm to fire shots toward one of the school's doors before the pair drove away.

"A person who commits this kind of an attack on schools is, in the eyes of this court, a coward. I have nothing else to say (about Mahdi Ahmed)," Labelle said.

The judge noted how, last week, when the court gave Mahdi Ahmed a chance to say something before he was sentenced, he chose to stay silent.

"Unfortunately, the imposition of a sentence, whatever it is, cannot erase the consequences," the judge said.

With time served factored into the sentence, Mahdi Ahmed was left with a prison term of more than 21 months as of Monday. The prison term will be followed by three years of probation during which Mahdi Ahmed is not allowed to be within 200 metres of the school.

He is also not allowed to be in the presence of Feijhoo-Leito Joseph, 21, the man identified in court as the driver of the stolen vehicle that brought Mahdi Ahmed to and from the school.

Joseph was acquitted in the case brought against Mahdi Ahmed, but he is scheduled to plead guilty to a charge related to the stolen car in December.

While summarizing the evidence gathered in Mahdi Ahmed's case, Labelle said the impact from three bullets were found on the door of the school and four spent shell casings were found at a spot where Mahdi Ahmed is believed to have fired the shots.

Witnesses watched as Mahdi Ahmed jumped into a vehicle before it drove away, and some of what happened was recorded by surveillance cameras.

The police found the stolen vehicle the following morning. Nine-millimetre bullets were found inside it as well as a surgical mask and latex gloves. Mahdi Ahmed's DNA was found on the front and back door handles of the vehicle as well as on the mask and gloves.

During 2024, following Mahdi Ahmed's arrest, an undercover agent was placed inside his cell. Mahdi Ahmed made incriminating remarks to the agent that linked him to the shooting.

Data lifted from Mahdi Ahmed's phone showed its signal had pinged off of cellphone towers close to where the vehicle was stolen, where the shooting occurred on Deacon St. and where the stolen vehicle was found abandoned.

"It was a place consecrated to the education, the security and protection of children. The attack was perceived by the community, including the parents and the students and their families, as an attack on the Jewish community," Labelle said, noting the same school was attacked three days before the shooting.

"Acts of hate, attacks on schools or places of worship have a concrete and lasting effect on the whole of the Jewish community."

stories.title: Canada and China sign deal to deepen financial sector ties
stories.summary: Vancouver - Canada and China have struck an agreement to deepen collaboration across their financial systems as the two countries seek closer economic ties.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne and International Trade Minister Maninder Sidhu hosted He Lifeng, vice-premier of China, in Vancouver over the past two days.

After the meetings, Finance Canada released a joint statement saying the two sides agreed to “enhance financial sector co-operation.”

Article continues below

Meta’s methods of moderation

That includes granting greater market access for financial services and fostering engagement between Canadian and Chinese regulatory authorities.

The statement adds that both sides reaffirmed their support for multilateralism and “a transparent and predictable environment” for trade and investment.

The agreement to deepen financial ties comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney is set to visit China later next week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press
