stories.title: Journalist Raymond Heard asserted himself in newsrooms, boardrooms and political backrooms
stories.summary: After emigrating from South Africa during apartheid, he took on leadership roles at the Montreal Star and Global News, and later became a media adviser to Liberal leader John Turner and a speechwriter for bank executives
stories.author: Alan Freeman
stories.content:
It was late in the afternoon of Sept. 25, 1979, in the vast newsroom of the Montreal Star, the city’s long-dominant English-language daily. Raymond Heard, the newspaper’s brash managing editor, jumped up on a desk to make an announcement.

The Star was closing immediately, and the paper about to hit the streets would be its last, he told the stunned journalists. More than 1,000 newspaper employees would be left jobless.

“Nobody knew anything about it beforehand,” said David Yates, an overnight copy editor at the Star who later went on to a career at the Montreal Gazette, the Star’s historic rival, which became the city’s only English-language daily.

The Star’s demise was the result of a grueling eight-month strike by production workers which had ended several months earlier. The Star, arrogant after years of market superiority, had lost advertisers and subscribers during the dispute, never to recover.

Mr. Heard had been appointed the paper’s managing editor three years earlier, at the age of 39. The South African-born journalist had been a foreign correspondent in Washington and London, a restless man brimming with ideas and an avid skier, tennis player and surfer.

“I would wait for my shift to end at 8 a.m., when Ray Heard would barrel into the newsroom with his hair still glistening from the shower,” Mr. Yates recalled. “He would order remakes on the front page, much to the chagrin of the news editor and rim staff who had worked all night putting it together. Ray was hyper-energetic, a South African surfer dude.”

The closure of the Star would force reinvention for Mr. Heard, as he moved months later to Global Television News in Toronto. Mr. Heard, who died in Toronto on Oct. 17 at age 90 following a stroke, would take his legendary feistiness to become a media adviser to Liberal leader John Turner and a speechwriter to the top executives of Canada’s largest bank.

“Ray was a true original, always high energy,” said Matthew Fraser, former editor in chief of The National Post. “In media circles, his nickname was the ‘Road Runner.’ He charged at life with gusto and ebullience, his mind always spinning with brainwaves. He was also a great raconteur. Ray had entertaining gossip and stories about everything and everyone.

“He was a classic last-century print journalist,” said his lifelong friend Peter Kent, the former foreign correspondent and MP whom Mr. Heard urged to join Global News in 1992. “Ray was a creative force in newsrooms, control rooms, boardrooms and political backrooms.”

But that boundless energy and drive could irritate and exasperate others, which Mr. Heard himself seemed to acknowledge. When Peter C. Newman wrote a biography of media mogul Izzy Asper, he called Mr. Heard “the father” of Global News, a moniker which one former Global staffer said really belonged to former foreign correspondent Bill Cunningham. Mr. Heard responded that “while some people at Global May have seen me as the ‘father,’ others regarded me as an SOB.”

Raymond Elliott Heard was born on Dec. 18, 1935, in Johannesburg, South Africa, the elder of two sons of George and Vida Heard, both of them journalists. George, a crusading anti-fascist writer disappeared mysteriously in 1945 and was presumed dead, leaving Vida to raise their two young sons alone.

Raymond grew up in the city of Durban, where he learned to surf as a boy on its Indian Ocean beaches. He attended University of the Witwatersrand while working at night at the Rand Daily Mail, the legendary white-owned newspaper that opposed apartheid and closed in 1985. As a reporter, he covered the treason trial of Nelson Mandela and the Sharpeville Massacre, where police opened fire on a peaceful anti-apartheid protest in the township of Sharpeville, killing 69. He earned a BA in political science in 1960.

Mr. Heard was awarded a Frank Knox Fellowship, which allowed him to continue his studies at Harvard University. In an article for the student-run Harvard Crimson on contemporary South Africa, he described apartheid as “a combination of hatred, fear and ignorance.” Mr. Heard predicted that South Africa’s Black majority would eventually succeed in its struggle for emancipation. “It is merely a question of time now before the pot, which is blackened with much burning, will boil over.”

Mr. Heard had planned to return to South Africa to pursue his career but only did so briefly. With his wife pregnant, he decided that he didn’t want his child to grow up in a racist society, so he applied for jobs in North America, landing a position at the Montreal Star in 1962. But he remained deeply connected to his native country, where his brother, Anthony, was a leading anti-apartheid journalist and editor who became an adviser to the government after the transition to democracy. Raymond was later one of several prominent figures who lobbied successfully for the Canadian government to award honorary citizenship to Nelson Mandela, which it did in 2001.

Soon after he was hired by the Star, Mr. Heard was sent to Washington as a White House correspondent, where he also worked as a syndicated correspondent for the London Observer. He witnessed the assassination of Robert F. Kennedy at a Los Angeles hotel in 1968 and covered the civil rights movement and the Watergate scandal.

In 1973, he was appointed editor of the Observer News Service in London, staying for three years until returning to the Star as managing editor.

Mr. Heard moved to Toronto in 1979 and to the fledgling Global Television Network where he eventually became vice-president of news.

“He demanded excellence,” said John Dawe, who was hired as a business reporter when Mr. Heard was at Global. “He was in the newsroom all the time. His nickname was the Tasmanian devil. … He could inspire you but also challenge you.” Under Mr. Heard, the network improved ratings for its news shows and began a noon newscast.

But Mr. Heard clashed with the owners of Global and left in 1987. He moved into politics and was appointed communications director for John Turner, who was then opposition leader in Ottawa.

Eleanor McMahon was a young deputy press secretary who worked for Mr. Heard at Mr. Turner’s office. She will never forget his frantic work style. “He had a busy brain,” she said, though she praised him as a boss who was always generous with his time.

The job in Ottawa wasn’t an easy experience. There were miscues, including when a ship packed with 174 refugees landed in Nova Scotia in July 1987. Mr. Turner initially said that if he were prime minister, he would have turned the vessel away, only to reverse himself after realizing the action would contravene the Geneva Convention on the protection of refugees.

According to The Globe and Mail, Mr. Heard explained to reporters that his boss had neglected to put the issue “in its full context” and then added that “it was very windy that day” and that “Mr. Turner was walking down the street” as reasons why he was misunderstood. The Liberals lost the 1988 election and soon after, Mr. Heard ended his political interlude.

In the 1990s, Mr. Heard was hired by Royal Bank of Canada as a media consultant and speechwriter for the bank’s chief executive officer, first Allan Taylor and then his successor, John Cleghorn.

“He was an exciting guy to work with,” Mr. Cleghorn told The Globe, praising Mr. Heard for his ability to sense what the view of the man in the street was on important issues. “He had tremendous energy. It was a combination of the cerebral and the physical.”

In that role, Mr. Heard travelled to Vancouver in 1996 with a colleague to meet Bob Stall, a columnist with The Province newspaper and a dogged critic of Canada’s big banks. As Mr. Stall told it, Mr. Heard suggested they have lunch together at the Four Seasons Hotel. The bank paid.

The two men had known each other as journalists in Montreal many years earlier but now found themselves on opposing sides, with Mr. Heard whispering advice to big bankers and Mr. Stall writing columns about clients who are wronged by big institutions.

“I think we both feel the other has sunk pretty low,” Mr. Stall wrote.

Mr. Heard used his familiar skills in an attempt to charm Mr. Stall. “Heard, like an off-duty reporter, told gossipy, unverifiable stories about Peter Newman, Allan Fotheringham, John Turner and others I had better not mention.”

Mr. Stall ended the meal by trying and failing to find out Mr. Heard’s salary. The columnist’s sarcastic conclusion: “They seduced me with rich food and wine. … They scored all their points and I saw the light.”

After spending a decade with the Royal Bank, Mr. Heard retired but remained active as a media consultant, working with Gail Asper on the development of the Canadian Museum of Human Rights in Winnipeg and with Calgary real-estate developer Navjeet Singh (Bob) Dhillon.

After the death of the Montreal Star, Mr. Heard mused for a time about founding a replacement. In the mid-1980s, he held talks with the Toronto Sun about starting an English-language tabloid in Montreal and in 2010 he was part of a group of investors that proposed buying several newspapers from the insolvent Canwest chain. But none of these plans ever panned out.

His wife, Gillian Cosgrove, a journalist whom he married in 1977, said Mr. Heard was a left-leaning liberal whose views became more conservative over time. He was an inveterate writer of letters to the editor, which appeared in the National Post, The Globe and Mail and other newspapers, and his pen never lost its acerbic sting.

He called Margaret Atwood a “predictable, middling novelist” in one missive and in another letter, published in 2009, said that Michael Sabia, who had just been appointed as head of the Caisse de dépôt et placement du Québec, was “the biggest upwardly mobile failure in Canadian business history.” Mr. Sabia went on to become the CEO of Hydro-Quebec, federal deputy minister of finance and clerk of the Privy Council.

In a 2010 letter to the editor, he noted that it seemed as if successful candidates for governor-general had to have worked at CBC or Radio-Canada, pointing to Adrienne Clarkson and Michaëlle Jean. He suggested that, in the same spirit, the next holder of the vice-regal job should be Don Cherry or Rex Murphy. “Both would be excellent choices,” he wrote.

Commenting in the Toronto Star in 2015 on prime minister Stephen Harper’s proposed ban on the wearing of the niqab at Canadian citizenship ceremonies, Mr. Heard came to his defence. “Simple logic surely dictates that if a female Muslim can cover her entire face, except for her eyes, I, an agnostic, should be allowed to wear a ski mask when voting or attending other public proceedings.”

Mr. Heard leaves his wife, Ms. Cosgrove; his former wife, Susan Steyn (née Lewis); his daughter with Ms. Steyn, Josie Robson; and three grandchildren. Mr. Heard also experienced tragedy. In 2015, his daughter with Ms. Cosgrove, Jennifer Heard, died at age 28. His son from his first marriage, Antony Heard, died in 2024 at 59.

You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here .

He attended University of the Witwatersrand while working at night at the Rand Daily Mail, the legendary white-owned newspaper that opposed apartheid and closed in 1985. As a reporter, he covered the treason trial of Nelson Mandela and the Sharpeville Massacre, where police opened fire on a peaceful anti-apartheid protest in the township of Sharpeville, killing 69. He earned a BA in political science in 1960.

content_blocks.text: Mr. Heard was awarded a Frank Knox Fellowship, which allowed him to continue his studies at Harvard University. In an article for the student-run Harvard Crimson on contemporary South Africa, he described apartheid as “a combination of hatred, fear and ignorance.” Mr. Heard predicted that South Africa’s Black majority would eventually succeed in its struggle for emancipation. “It is merely a question of time now before the pot, which is blackened with much burning, will boil over.”

But he remained deeply connected to his native country, where his brother, Anthony, was a leading anti-apartheid journalist and editor who became an adviser to the government after the transition to democracy. Raymond was later one of several prominent figures who lobbied successfully for the Canadian government to award honorary citizenship to Nelson Mandela, which it did in 2001.

stories.title: Alberta First Nation claims B.C. hydroelectric projects violate treaty rights
stories.summary: Vancouver - The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation in Alberta is suing the British Columbia and federal governments and BC Hydro, alleging that provincial dam projects were built without regard for their rights, culture and way of life.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Vancouver - The Athabasca Chipewyan First Nation in Alberta is suing the British Columbia and federal governments and BC Hydro, alleging that provincial dam projects were built without regard for their rights, culture and way of life.

Chief Allan Adam filed a notice of civil claim on behalf of the First Nation in B.C. Supreme Court last week, claiming the projects have unlawfully interfered with the Athabasca Chipewyan’s treaty rights, dating from the 1960s when the W.A.C. Bennett Dam was built to the recent completion of the John Horgan Dam, formerly referred to as Site C.

stories.title: Supreme Court of Canada begins to hear arguments on feds firearms ban
stories.summary: The hearings will give opponents of the ban another chance to make their case after losing in the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill
stories.content:
The country’s top court began hearing legal arguments Monday about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.

The hearings, which continue Tuesday at the Supreme Court of Canada , will give opponents of the ban another chance to make their case after losing in the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal.

In May 2020, the government prohibited the use, sale and importation of 1,500 firearm models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14. The move was applauded by gun control advocates as a first step toward removing these firearms from circulation.

In October 2023, a Federal Court judge dismissed a request to strike down the ban as unlawful and beyond the scope of the powers delegated to the Governor in Council — effectively the federal cabinet.

A not-for-profit advocacy organization, firearm owners, businesses, hunters and recreational and sport shooters appealed the ruling.

In April 2025, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected that appeal, saying the Federal Court delivered “thorough and persuasive” reasons.

The list of guns banned by the Liberal government has grown to more than 2,500 varieties of what it calls assault-style firearms.

1:49 Ottawa’s gun buyback program falls drastically short of targets

Before the Supreme Court agreed to examine the matter, the government said the prohibited firearms would have to be disposed of or deactivated by the end of an amnesty period on Oct. 30 of this year.

That amnesty has been extended until 90 days after the Supreme Court delivers its decision, which is expected no later than next year.

On Monday, several judges put probing questions to counsel about the details of the federal measures.

A key question before the Federal Court of Appeal was whether the Governor in Council adhered to a provision of the law forbidding it from using regulations to outlaw a firearm if it considers the gun “reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes.”

Writing on behalf of a unanimous three-judge panel, Court of Appeal Chief Justice Yves de Montigny said he was not persuaded that the government erred in considering public safety when assessing whether the prohibited firearms were reasonable for use in Canada for such purposes.

“It May well be that, from the sole perspective of a sensible hunter or sportsman, it makes no sense to ban firearms that are well suited or even specifically designed for hunting or sport purposes,” he wrote.

The federal cabinet is the most senior policy-making body in government and, because of its role at the apex of the executive branch, is best situated to develop government policy and assess the public interest, de Montigny added.

“Surely, the inherent danger that some firearms pose to public safety because of their lethality and their ability to injure or kill a large number of people in a short period of time, the fact that they have been used in mass shootings in Canada and abroad, the fact that they are disproportionate for civilian use, and the increasing demand for measures to address gun violence are all valid considerations in determining whether their use is reasonable for hunting and sporting purposes,” he wrote.

In a written submission to the Supreme Court, federal lawyers say the Governor in Council’s exercise of its broad discretion was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms present.

The submission points to a regulatory impact analysis statement that supports the Governor in Council’s opinion. That statement said that while some hunters and sport shooters lawfully used some of these firearms in the past, these guns can increase the severity of mass shootings and have been used in such shootings in Canada and in other countries.

The firearms prohibited in 2020 were owned by a small minority of Canadian firearms owners, estimated at between three and five per cent of the total, the federal submission adds.

“Thousands of alternative firearms remain legally available for hunting and sporting use,” it says. “The Gic’s opinion, balancing public interest policy considerations, was reasonable.”

6:04 How impactful is the federal firearms ban on gun violence and crime?

A group of appellants that includes the Canadian Coalition for Firearm Rights says neither the Federal Court nor the Federal Court of Appeal considered whether the newly prohibited items were actually used for hunting or sport shooting.

“While recognizing that the misuse of firearms threatens public safety, Parliament chose to preserve hunting and sport shooting as legitimate, lawful, and socially accepted activities and uses of firearms,” they say in their submission to the Supreme Court.

For the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who lawfully owned and used the firearms prohibited by the 2020 regulations, this appeal is not an abstract debate about administrative law, the appellants add.

“It concerns the profound disruption of the lives of ordinary, law-abiding Canadians. Hunters, sport shooters, collectors and small businesses, individuals who complied with every requirement imposed by Parliament, found themselves overnight in possession of prohibited property, deprived of its lawful use and exposed to the prospect of criminal liability,” the submission says.

“They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters and neighbours in communities across Canada.”

Whether the Governor in Council acted within the limits Parliament imposed is not merely a question of statutory interpretation, the submission says.

“It determines whether the sweeping consequences imposed upon these Canadians were authorized by law.”

stories.title: 15 soldiers on ventilators, 9 critical after deadly CFB Wainwright fire
stories.summary: A senior Alberta government official provided Global News with a confidential briefing after nearly a week of unanswered questions to the Department of National Defence.
stories.author: Ashleigh Stewart
stories.content:
Fifteen Canadian soldiers remain on ventilators more than three weeks after the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright , according to information obtained by Global News.

A senior Alberta government official provided Global with a section of a confidential Alberta Health Services (AHS) briefing document after almost a week of unsuccessful attempts to get the Department of National Defence (DND) to disclose how many injured soldiers remained in critical condition.

The official referred Global to Acute Care Alberta (ACA) for further comment.

6:49 Mother of severely burned Wainwright soldier ‘identified him by his feet’

The document, dated Nov. 5, provides a detailed breakdown of the conditions of soldiers who remain hospitalized following the fire at CFB Wainwright on Oct. 17 that killed four soldiers and injured 39.

Global News sought clarification from AHS before publication to ensure the accuracy of the numbers.

The report showed that, as of Nov. 5, 21 soldiers remain hospitalized in Alberta.

Of that number, 10 were listed in critical condition, eight were stable in intensive care and three were stable in medical units.

By Nov. 9, the number of soldiers in critical condition had dropped to nine, while 12 were listed as stable across intensive care and medical units, an ACA spokeswoman confirmed.

Two weeks ago, 13 soldiers were in critical condition, according to officials.

Dr. Sayeh Zielke, interim CEO of Acute Care Alberta, told Global News that the hospitalized soldiers remained “gravely ill.”

She explained that some burn patients require prolonged ventilator assistance due to smoke inhalation or airway injuries, even when their condition is stable. Patients classified as critical typically require additional life-sustaining support, such as assistance with breathing or medications to maintain blood pressure.

1:31 Funeral held for Shaun Farrell, the Sask. soldier killed in CFB Wainwright fire

The briefing document also revealed the extent of the soldiers’ burns.

Four patients have burns covering 51 to 60 per cent of their bodies, three have burns covering 41 to 50 per cent, and seven have burns covering 30 to 40 per cent. The remaining patients have burns covering less than 30 per cent of their bodies.

Fourteen soldiers were being treated at the University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton and seven at the Foothills Medical Centre in Calgary, the report said. It also recorded three discharges and six repatriations, which can include transfers between provinces or within Alberta.

Global News repeatedly pressed DND for updated figures on injured soldiers after the department had not provided a public update on their condition since Oct. 22.

On Nov. 4, three days after Global submitted questions, DND issued a statement saying 25 soldiers remained hospitalized, 14 had been released and four had been transferred to hospitals in B.C. and Ontario. It did not provide updated critical condition figures.

After further unanswered inquiries, DND said on the evening of Nov. 6 that it would not comment further as patient status fell under the responsibility of provincial health authorities and attending clinicians, despite both Acute Care Alberta and the Prime Minister’s Office having directed questions to DND.

Zielke said going forward, she would work with the CAF to provide weekly updates on the injured soldiers.

DND has declined to answer numerous questions about the circumstances of the deadly fire, citing their Board of Inquiry investigation. The military says such investigations typically take nine to 12 months, although the timeline could be longer.

The medical update comes as Ottawa moves to provide additional nursing support for Alberta.

Federal Emergency Management Minister Eleanor Olszewski said on Saturday she had approved a request for federal assistance from the Alberta government and ACA to provide additional nursing support for injured soldiers.

An ACA spokeswoman said 15 CAF nurses will arrive on Nov. 9 and will remain until Jan. 15, 2027, providing additional capacity and relief for staff. The deployment replaces support previously provided by Ontario nurses, who have since returned home.

“This is not a sprint, this is a marathon. We expect to be providing care for these patients all the way through December, January, and going forward,” Zielke said.

Zielke praised Alberta hospitals’ response to the disaster, saying they “would have managed without that additional support,” but bringing in extra staff was “the right thing to do” to ease the burden on health-care workers.

She said Alberta’s health-care system had been able to manage the influx of patients, with 32 critical-care beds and 567 non-ICU beds available across the province as of Monday.

Zielke also rejected suggestions of coordination failures or shortages, saying necessary skin tissue, grafts and specialized equipment had been obtained.

“Anything that we’ve asked for, we have been provided,” she said.

The federal government on Nov. 5 also announced $25 million in the federal budget for the Canadian Forces Morale and Welfare Services to support CAF members, their families and local communities affected by the fire.

Another $3 million will be invested to support the Wainwright Military Family Resource Centre.

stories.title: Fact File: No permanent positions set up during Canadian-led Nato exercise in Latvia
stories.summary: A social media post last week claimed that a Canadian-led military exercise in Latvia was a prelude to war with Russia. The post included a map of Latvia showing where the brigade was purportedly establishing permanent defensive positions along the border with Russia. However, a spokesperson for the Canadian military dismissed the claim, saying the Nato exe…
stories.author: Timon Johnson The Canadian Press
stories.content:
A social media post last week claimed that a Canadian-led military exercise in Latvia was a prelude to war with Russia. The post included a map of Latvia showing where the brigade was purportedly establishing permanent defensive positions along the border with Russia. However, a spokesperson for the Canadian military dismissed the claim, saying the Nato exercise was intended to demonstrate the brigade’s ability to conduct operations in complex terrain, not to establish permanent positions.

The Nov. 3 post on the X platform claims Prime Minister Mark Carney sent about 2,000 Canadian troops and 1,000 troops from 14 Nato countries to establish permanent defensive positions along Latvia’s border with Russia, using a Nato military exercise as cover.

The user provided details — some of which appeared to be drawn from a Nov. 2 report by CTV journalists embedded with Canadian Forces — about the brigade involved in the exercise, its movements and its positions along the Russian border.

“He’s digging in on sending us to war,” the post said about Carney.

In a followup comment, the user questioned the official explanation given for the exercise: “‘It’s a temporary exercise’ like COVID was ‘2 weeks.’ They’re being sent to Build Permanent defensive structures. You think they will sit unmanned?” The user cited as evidence a comment from a Canadian officer in the CTV report that Canada’s military posture in eastern Latvia is “ready-to-defend.”

Asked about the claim, a spokesperson for the Canadian military said the training exercise “was not intended to establish a permanent defensive position near the Latvia-Russia border.”

Lt. Michaël Debled said in emailed comments that the goal of the Resolute Reforger exercise, which ended Sunday, was to demonstrate the brigade’s ability to operate in complex settings in eastern Latvia. It was “an opportunity to validate the brigade’s ability to move, sustain, and co-ordinate forces in realistic operational environments,” he said.

He noted that the brigade has maintained a “sustained and visible Nato presence in eastern Latvia” since April, but that is separate from the recent training exercise. “Through regular engagement with local communities, it contributes to deterrence, strengthens relationships with the population and demonstrates Nato’s commitment to collective defence,” he said.

Debled confirmed that the troop numbers contained in the claim were correct.

“Approximately 2,000 military personnel and hundreds of vehicles were transported by road and rail from the Adazi and Ceri military bases to various locations across eastern Latvia between Oct. 26 and Nov. 8,” he said.

The spokesperson said the exercise and the brigade’s presence are part of Operation Reassurance, a Canadian-led Nato mission aimed at deterring Russian aggression in eastern Europe.

According to the Canadian government’s website, the Canadian Armed Forces has gradually built up its presence and expanded its role in Latvia since June 19, 2017, as part of this operation.

Today, the Canadian Forces are based at Camp Adazi with around 2,000 soldiers. The Canadians lead a multinational brigade including about 1,000 personnel from over a dozen other Nato countries.

The operation is the Canadian Forces’ largest overseas mission, involving the deployment of land troops, ships and air support.

In the Nov. 2 CTV News report, the brigade’s commander, Lt.-Col. Simon Mailloux, said Canada’s military posture in the east has changed from “deterrence ” to “ready-to-defend.” However, the interview did not mention any plan for the brigade to establish permanent positions along the border.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

The post included a map of Latvia showing where the brigade was purportedly establishing permanent defensive positions along the border with Russia. However, a spokesperson for the Canadian military dismissed the claim, saying the Nato exercise was intended to demonstrate the brigade’s ability to conduct operations in complex terrain, not to establish permanent positions.

The Nov. 3 post on the X platform claims Prime Minister Mark Carney sent about 2,000 Canadian troops and 1,000 troops from 14 Nato countries to establish permanent defensive positions along Latvia’s border with Russia, using a Nato military exercise as cover.

The user provided details — some of which appeared to be drawn from a Nov. 2 report by CTV journalists embedded with Canadian Forces — about the brigade involved in the exercise, its movements and its positions along the Russian border.
“He’s digging in on sending us to war,” the post said about Carney.

In a followup comment, the user questioned the official explanation given for the exercise: “‘It’s a temporary exercise’ like COVID was ‘2 weeks.’ They’re being sent to Build Permanent defensive structures. You think they will sit unmanned?” The user cited as evidence a comment from a Canadian officer in the CTV report that Canada’s military posture in eastern Latvia is “ready-to-defend.”
Asked about the claim, a spokesperson for the Canadian military said the training exercise “was not intended to establish a permanent defensive position near the Latvia-Russia border.”

Lt. Michaël Debled said in emailed comments that the goal of the Resolute Reforger exercise, which ended Sunday, was to demonstrate the brigade’s ability to operate in complex settings in eastern Latvia. It was “an opportunity to validate the brigade’s ability to move, sustain, and co-ordinate forces in realistic operational environments,” he said.

He noted that the brigade has maintained a “sustained and visible Nato presence in eastern Latvia” since April, but that is separate from the recent training exercise. “Through regular engagement with local communities, it contributes to deterrence, strengthens relationships with the population and demonstrates Nato’s commitment to collective defence,” he said.
Debled confirmed that the troop numbers contained in the claim were correct.

“Approximately 2,000 military personnel and hundreds of vehicles were transported by road and rail from the Adazi and Ceri military bases to various locations across eastern Latvia between Oct. 26 and Nov. 8,” he said.
The spokesperson said the exercise and the brigade’s presence are part of Operation Reassurance, a Canadian-led Nato mission aimed at deterring Russian aggression in eastern Europe.
According to the Canadian government’s website, the Canadian Armed Forces has gradually built up its presence and expanded its role in Latvia since June 19, 2017, as part of this operation.

stories.title: World class equine event centre breaking ground near Milverton
stories.summary: A team of Clydesdales delivers dignitaries to the unveiling of the Waterfalls Agriplex, a privately funded equine event facility, soon to begin construction on the edge of Milverton.
stories.author: Scott Miller
stories.content:
“27 years ago this was a vision. And, it has taken that long to actually get the resources around it, and the community support that was required in order to pull this off,” said Ken Knox, spokesperson for the Waterfalls Agriplex.

“This is a huge, huge industry. Way bigger, I think, than all of us realize. The Royal Winter Fair, you know, it attracts thousands of people all over the world, from the States, from Canada, from different countries. So yes, this will attract all those people as well,” said former Municipality of Perth East Mayor Rhonda Ehgoetz.

Similar to Regional Equine and Agricultural Centre of Huron (R.E.A.C.H) in Clinton, but more than twice the size, the Waterfalls Agriplex plans to open with a bang hosting the 2029 World Clydesdale Show.

The show will feature more than 600 heavy horses, and thousands of visitors from around the world.

“We’ve committed to have this project up and operating to have a World Show of Clydesdale horses here in 2029. So, that’s the target, and we are going to meet that target in spades,” said Knox.

Unlike R.E.A.C.H Huron, which was largely funded with government dollars, the multi-million dollar Waterfalls Agriplex is entirely privately funded at the moment.

“That is a huge deal. Huge deal that it is privately funded, and the people are all behind what Eli wants to do. As Ken said, it’s a dream that he’s had, a vision and now it’s becoming a reality. And, for the people to all step up and help be part of it, that’s just wonderful,” said Ehgoetz.

“It is going to be developed in phases. The first phase is privately done. We need to encourage all levels of government to be more involved, though. We’ve got the local governments heavily involved now, and we need the province and the federal government involved as well in order to reach its full potential, because this will be an economic driver for livestock in Ontario and in Canada over the next half century.

It’s going to be able to house and host all sorts of livestock sales, livestock shows, educational opportunities, and it’s going to be able to showcase Ontario agriculture from the livestock perspective to the rest of the world,” said Knox.

stories.title: Chiefs question motive behind Indian Act talks after meeting with Carney, premiers
stories.summary: First Nations chiefs who attended a closed-door meeting with Mark Carney and premiers last month say their concerns were overshadowed by Wab Kinew’s call for the abolition of the Indian Act.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — First Nations chiefs who attended a closed-door meeting with Prime Minister Mark Carney and premiers last month say their concerns were overshadowed by Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew’s call for the abolition of the Indian Act.

One chief also criticized Carney’s tone as he responded to a comment about how the United States works with Indigenous people.

“We have to ask ourselves if this was a co-ordinated effort between Wab Kinew and the prime minister,” Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Mercredi said of the talk about abolishing the Indian Act.

Chief Sheila North of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in northern Manitoba said it’s beginning to appear that way to her.

“I hope that wasn’t the case because that would mean they were disingenuous in what they wanted the outcomes [of the meeting] to be,” North said. “It was a complete waste of time if that’s the only outcome that they were hoping for.”

Chiefs gathered with Carney and most premiers in Ottawa in late October for their first meeting since the 2005 Kelowna Accord talks. First Nations leaders prepared for the meeting for months and even enlisted the help of former Indigenous Services deputy minister Gina Wilson to tailor their messages to government.

Chiefs said they wanted to use the gathering to discuss the federal government’s controversial major projects legislation, health services, policing and public safety and the Natural Resources Transfer Acts.

Those resource agreements were negotiated with the Prairie Provinces at a time when First Nations were barred by the Indian Act from hiring their own lawyers. Chiefs have said those agreements should be abolished or changed to ensure resource development projects meaningfully benefit their communities.

But the main topic to come out of the closed-door meeting was Kinew’s sudden call to abolish the Indian Act — something he acknowledged he didn’t consult on with chiefs beforehand.

The law, which dates from 1876, gives Ottawa sweeping power over First Nations communities and people, including the authority to decide who qualifies for status and what reserves can and can’t do. While there is a widespread consensus that the law is outdated and restrictive, there’s little agreement on what could or should replace it.

In an audio recording of the closed-door meeting obtained by The Canadian Press, Kinew referred to his own First Nations status card and said he would keep it until he dies or the Indian Act is abolished.

“The idea that we have a race-based identification in our country in 2026 is inconsistent, at the very least, with Canada being a leader for human rights and democracy around the world,” Kinew, who is Anishinaabe, told Carney, chiefs and premiers.

“Typically, prime ministers are around for about a decade. And if we don’t put it on the agenda for this prime minister, that means we’ll be back here in 2036 and I’ll still have my laminated plastic card …

“And to the chiefs who May be like, ‘He didn’t consult with us before he’s saying this,’ I just wanted to say I think this is consistent with what you’re bringing forward here.”

Kinew made similar remarks to media following the session.

In a closing press conference after the meeting with chiefs, Carney said he was “very open” to the idea of abolishing the Indian Act. He said it’s important that the call came from community members and not the federal government.

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak told The Canadian Press Kinew and Carney were the only ones at the meeting who brought up eradicating the Indian Act.

North said members of the Liberal Indigenous caucus told chiefs shortly after the meeting wrapped they didn’t believe Carney fully understood the comments he made about the Indian Act and that they would speak to the prime minister about clarifying his stance.

“I think they were a little bit caught off-guard, based on some of the reaction we got from them afterwards,” North said.

Carney did clarify his stance the next day, saying the Indian Act could be reformed instead of abolished.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada did not say if the relevant ministers were told in advance the prime minister would be commenting on the Indian Act. The spokesperson said those ministers were in the meeting with chiefs when the Indian Act was raised.

North said it was inappropriate for Kinew to divert attention from the issues the chiefs wanted to talk about.

“He May be Anishinaabe, he May have a status card, but that was not his place as a sitting premier to be calling for that,” she said.

North said that when the controversial Natural Resources Transfer Acts were brought up during the meeting, Kinew left his seat and didn’t return until the subject had changed. The day prior, North said, Kinew told chiefs he wasn’t open to the idea of moving past those agreements.

The acts, known as NRTAs, signed in 1930, transferred control of Crown lands and the resources they hold to Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. First Nations did not have a say in the negotiations that led to the agreements, nor were they allowed to hire legal representation to challenge them.

Chiefs, including former national chief Matthew Coon Come, have called for negotiations to change those agreements to something that better reflects their rights.

The Canadian Press asked Kinew’s office if he is open to revisiting the NRTAs and if he discussed the Indian Act with Carney before the meeting, and requested his response to the chiefs’ criticisms. His office said it would not be commenting further on the matter

In a statement sent to The Canadian Press, the federal Crown-Indigenous Relations Department said Carney has made it clear First Nations must have a direct stake in Canada’s economic future, and the NRTAs do not prevent the negotiation of new resource revenue sharing agreements.

Mercredi said that while conversations about moving away from the Indian Act aren’t new, it seemed “a little bit offside” to bring the topic up at a meeting when chiefs really wanted to discuss the NRTAs.

Mercredi also questioned the format of the meeting, saying Carney only responded to a handful of chiefs “when he wanted to respond.”

“There was no real discussion around the issues that we’re facing,” Mercredi said. “There was really no positive outcome when it came to this meeting.”

Another chief in the meeting took issue with the way Carney responded to their concerns.

Chief Rodger Redman of Standing Buffalo Dakota Nation in Saskatchewan said he told Carney in the meeting he thinks Indigenous people in the United States have a better relationship with their governments, and that they are generally left alone to govern their nations.

In a video of the interaction posted online, Carney asked if Redman was “seriously making that point.”

“Just look around this table. Imagine, imagine this in the United States, under a Democratic administration, a Republican administration. It doesn’t even enter their thinking to have this discussion,” Carney said, interrupting Redman’s remarks.

“It kind of got under his skin a bit and he went sideways on me,” Redman told The Canadian Press.

Redman said he thought it was a valid point to bring up, since the push to accelerate major project development in Canada — a push that some chiefs say threatens First Nations rights — is largely being driven by pressures in the Canada-U.S. trade relationship.

“How can you say that you’re being equal sitting at the table?” Redman told The Canadian Press. “What happened in that circus in Ottawa was just there for the photo ops. We weren’t there for the photo ops.”

In remarks to chiefs shortly after responding to Kinew’s comments, Carney said he “can’t sit here and hear that there will be no progress” on the issues chiefs brought forward.

“Part of a respectful dialogue is recognizing facts and where those facts fall short, and where there’s gaps. And, very importantly, where there are programs that don’t work and why they don’t work,” he said in the audio recording.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026

Alessia Passafiume, The Canadian Press

North said members of the Liberal Indigenous caucus told chiefs shortly after the meeting wrapped they didn’t believe Carney fully understood the comments he made about the Indian Act and that they would speak to the prime minister about clarifying his stance.
“I think they were a little bit caught off-guard, based on some of the reaction we got from them afterwards,” North said.
Carney did clarify his stance the next day, saying the Indian Act could be reformed instead of abolished.

In an emailed statement, a spokesperson for Indigenous Services Canada did not say if the relevant ministers were told in advance the prime minister would be commenting on the Indian Act. The spokesperson said those ministers were in the meeting with chiefs when the Indian Act was raised.
North said it was inappropriate for Kinew to divert attention from the issues the chiefs wanted to talk about.
“He May be Anishinaabe, he May have a status card, but that was not his place as a sitting premier to be calling for that,” she said.

North said that when the controversial Natural Resources Transfer Acts were brought up during the meeting, Kinew left his seat and didn’t return until the subject had changed. The day prior, North said, Kinew told chiefs he wasn’t open to the idea of moving past those agreements.

Chiefs, including former national chief Matthew Coon Come, have called for negotiations to change those agreements to something that better reflects their rights.

“Just look around this table. Imagine, imagine this in the United States, under a Democratic administration, a Republican administration. It doesn’t even enter their thinking to have this discussion,” Carney said, interrupting Redman’s remarks.
“It kind of got under his skin a bit and he went sideways on me,” Redman told The Canadian Press.

Redman said he thought it was a valid point to bring up, since the push to accelerate major project development in Canada — a push that some chiefs say threatens First Nations rights — is largely being driven by pressures in the Canada-U.S. trade relationship.

“How can you say that you’re being equal sitting at the table?” Redman told The Canadian Press. “What happened in that circus in Ottawa was just there for the photo ops. We weren’t there for the photo ops.”
In remarks to chiefs shortly after responding to Kinew’s comments, Carney said he “can’t sit here and hear that there will be no progress” on the issues chiefs brought forward.

“Part of a respectful dialogue is recognizing facts and where those facts fall short, and where there’s gaps. And, very importantly, where there are programs that don’t work and why they don’t work,” he said in the audio recording.

One chief also criticized Carney’s tone as he responded to a comment about how the United States works with Indigenous people.
“We have to ask ourselves if this was a co-ordinated effort between Wab Kinew and the prime minister,” Treaty 8 First Nations Grand Chief Mercredi said of the talk about abolishing the Indian Act.
Chief Sheila North of Bunibonibee Cree Nation in northern Manitoba said it’s beginning to appear that way to her.

“I hope that wasn’t the case because that would mean they were disingenuous in what they wanted the outcomes [of the meeting] to be,” North said. “It was a complete waste of time if that’s the only outcome that they were hoping for.”

Chiefs gathered with Carney and most premiers in Ottawa in late October for their first meeting since the 2005 Kelowna Accord talks. stories.title: Many workers in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick earning below living wage
stories.summary: Two separate reports on the living wages in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia reveal big gaps between what people need to earn just to get by and what they're actually taking home.
stories.author: Rebecca Lau, Skye Bryden-Blom, Reeti Rohilla
stories.content:
Two separate reports taking a look at the living wages in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia reveal big gaps between what people need to earn to live and what they’re actually making.

A living wage is the minimum hourly pay a worker would need to cover a household’s basic needs, such as housing and food.

The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives report released Monday finds the average living wage increased in Nova Scotia this year by nearly four per cent. About half of workers in Nova Scotia earn less than the living wage, according to the report.

Halifax had the highest living wage rate at $30 an hour, up from $29.40 last year.

The sharpest increase was recorded in northern Nova Scotia, which jumped nearly 10 per cent to $28 an hour, mainly because of the rising cost of rent.

Nova Scotia’s actual minimum wage is $17 an hour, which came into effect on Oct. 1.

“If you are not earning this conservative estimate of what it takes, then really, truly, you’re struggling,” said Christine Saulnier, the think tank’s Atlantic director.

The report highlights that housing and transportation costs contributed to these increases.

The Nova Scotia Federation of Labour’s president, Melissa Marsman, says this comes as no surprise.

“We see the cost of fuel, housing, child care, groceries,” Marsman said.

“People just do not have enough money to survive nowadays.”

The goal, says Saulnier, is to have provincial governments not only raise minimum wages but also bring in more supports.

“We have some provincial income support programs (but) they phase out just at the poverty line. Living wage households are not getting access,” said Saulnier.

“Most working households are not getting to use those programs.”

Meanwhile, the Human Development Council has also released its report looking into the living wage in New Brunswick, which it pegged at $24.84 an hour.

This represents a nearly $9 gap between the living wage and the province’s minimum wage of $15.90 an hour.

The report found 40 per cent of workers in the province earned less than the living wage in 2025.

“We have found that 88 per cent were not students — so the majority — 74 per cent were working full-time and 89 per cent were over the age of 20,” said Liam Fisher, a data analyst and research coordinator with the council.

“As well, 53 per cent (worked) in firms that had 100 or more employees.”

Fredericton’s living wage tops the three major cities at $26.32, largely because of rent prices.

Fisher points out the living wage is just the basic necessities and doesn’t include other financial responsibilities.

“Any extra expense related to a disability is not included. There’s no retirement savings, there’s no savings for a down payment, there are no savings for children’s education,” he said.

2:33 New Brunswickers worry about the cost of living crisis ahead of provincial budget

According to a University of New Brunswick social work professor, the living wage is one of the best measures of poverty.

“It’s the bare minimum that somebody can make in order to keep themselves afloat. And I think that that’s a better definition of poverty than an arbitrary cut-off measure or an outdated basket of goods,” said Julia Woodhall-Melnik, the Canada Research Chair in Resilient Communities.

“We shouldn’t have the ability to pay people less for their work than it costs them to actually live.”

She says single-income households are especially vulnerable.

Chris Watson, president of the New Brunswick Federation of Labour, argues higher pay should be a priority for employers because it can boost local spending.

“Employers can actually start raising the wages and giving steady hours, making schedules that employees can plan their lives around,” said Watson.

He urges government, employers, and workers to collaborate on wage increases and support for small businesses.

While higher wages have the potential to raise business costs and prices for consumers, Woodhall-Melnik says she still believes the minimum wage should be brought in line with living costs, alongside more affordable housing and stronger rent protections.

“At the end of the day, if we’re not providing people with enough income to pay their rent, they won’t be affordably housed and they do risk homelessness,” she said.

stories.title: Ukrainian Canadians to protest Ovechkin's visit to Ottawa over Putin ties
stories.summary: Ottawa - Ukrainian Canadians plan to protest outside Ottawa's Canadian Tire Centre on Tuesday as Alex Ovechkin and the Washington Capitals visit the Senators.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The Ukrainian Canadian Congress is organizing the demonstration, called “No War Crimes in Hockey,” to protest the star Russian hockey player’s support for Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The group is also backing calls for Canada to impose sanctions on Ovechkin over his ties to the Russian leader.

Article continues below

Meta’s methods of moderation

Two House of Commons petitions, sponsored by Liberal MPs Yvan Baker and Bardish Chagger, have called for sanctions against Ovechkin that would bar him from entering Canada.

The NHL’s all-time leading goal scorer appeared in a campaign ad for Putin’s United Russia political party in September, standing behind Russian foreign minister Sergey Lavrov.

The Capitals said Ovechkin was asked to participate in the video while spending the summer in Russia, where he lives with his family during the off-season.

Ovechkin previously voiced support for Putin in 2017 when he launched a movement called “Putin Team.” At the time, he said he simply supported his country.

Following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Ovechkin called for an end to the war but defended his relationship with Putin, saying the Russian leader was his president and that he was an athlete, not a politician.

His visit comes amid a separate controversy over Russia’s possible return to international hockey.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled on Oct. 30 that the International Ice Hockey Federation must reinstate Russia, which has been barred from international competition since the invasion of Ukraine.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has said Russian players won’t be allowed to represent their country at next month’s world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

The dispute intensified after Norway said Sunday it had been informed by the Iihf that Russia would take its place at the men’s under-20 tournament.

Sweden and Finland have reiterated that they won’t face Russia while the war continues. The Iihf has not formally announced a change to the world junior lineup.

Tuesday’s game in Ottawa marks the 41-year-old Ovechkin’s first visit to Canada since announcing he’ll retire at the end of his 22nd NHL season.

With files from The Associated Press.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Victims of CFB Wainwright fire remembered as Grey Cup carried into Calgary
stories.summary: Calgary - The Grey Cup arrived in Calgary with traditional bagpipes and a Canadian Forces escort Monday as the dozens of soldiers involved in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base were honoured.
stories.author: Bill Graveland The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Calgary - The Grey Cup arrived in Calgary with traditional bagpipes and a Canadian Forces escort Monday as the dozens of soldiers involved in a deadly fire at an Alberta military base were honoured.

The Cup was transported to the Mewata Armoury in a horse-drawn wagon before it was marched inside.

Col. Kyle Clapperton, commander of 41 Canadian Brigade Group, choked up during the ceremony.

The Grey Cup arrived in Calgary with traditional bagpipes and a Canadian Forces escort as the dozens of soldiers involved in the deadly fire at an Alberta military base were honoured. Col. Kyle Clapperton, commander of 41 Canadian Brigade Group, says the arrival of the championship trophy is both the beginning of a celebration and a moment of reflection. (Nov. 9, 2026)

He said the arrival of the CFL’s championship trophy is both the beginning of a celebration and a moment of reflection.

“This year that reflection carries special significance,” Clapperton said of the four soldiers who died Oct. 17 during a training exercise at CFB Wainwright, southeast of Edmonton.

Dozens of others were injured after strong and sudden winds sent flames from a nearby grass fire racing toward a group of 84 soldiers from the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry.

The soldiers who died were: Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.; and Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton.

The funeral for 23-year old Pte. Aidan Goulding took place at the Seaforth Armoury in Vancouver. Goulding was one of four soldiers killed last month after a grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta overtook troops during a training exercise. (Nov. 8, 2026)

“We also keep the many injured soldiers, many of whom are reservists from 41 Brigade and serve in the Loyal Edmonton Regiment and the Calgary Highlanders, their families, their friends and their comrades in our thoughts as we wish them the best recovery possible,” Clapperton added.

Several members of the Armed Forces were on hand for the Cup’s arrival.

CFL commissioner Stewart Johnston said he realizes many in the Armed Forces community are carrying an enormous loss and the entire league is thinking about them.

“This is a kickoff to a weeklong celebration and it will be that, but we know for the Canadian Armed Forces’ community, and for so many people here in Alberta, you’re carrying an enormous loss after the tragedy at CFB Wainwright,” he said.

Johnston said that for more than a century, the Grey Cup has travelled through Canadian history and been celebrated in times of joy and carried by Canadians in times of sacrifice.

“There is something especially meaningful about having members of the Canadian Armed Forces help carry it to Calgary today,” he said. “This isn’t just a trophy arriving in a city, it’s more than a century of Canadian stories arriving with it.”

The Edmonton Elks play the Montreal Alouettes for the Cup at Calgary’s McMahon Stadium on Sunday.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa wrote off $4.5B in COVID benefit repayments last year: auditor general
stories.summary: The Office of the Auditor General of Canada says the federal government wrote off billions of dollars last year in COVID-19 benefits that it no longer expects to see repaid.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The Office of the Auditor General of Canada says the federal government wrote off billions of dollars last year in COVID-19 benefits that it no longer expects to see repaid.

The federal government is trying to recoup payments made to Canadians during the COVID-19 pandemic in cases where it determines someone was overpaid or was ineligible for the benefit.

But when the government expects not to be paid back, it writes off the debt and strikes it from its ledgers.

Audits of the government’s consolidated financial statements for the last fiscal year show Ottawa wrote off $4.5 billion tied to COVID-19 benefits -- up sharply from $26 million the previous year.

The government’s financial statements for 2025-26 were published on Friday -- a day after Ottawa tabled its 2026 federal budget -- as part of its annual public accounts.

Auditor General Karen Hogan’s office also released its commentary that day on the government’s previous fiscal year.

Hogan warned that Ottawa is also expecting a larger portion of business loans from the pandemic will not be repaid.

The government’s allowance for potential losses on loans through the Canada Emergency Business Account, or Ceba, increased to $5.6 billion in the last fiscal year, up from $5.4 billion previously. That’s out of a total of $7.2 billion in outstanding loans.

Businesses could get nearly a third of the value of their interest-free Ceba loans forgiven if they repaid before the applicable deadline, which the government extended twice. But if they hadn’t paid back the amount by then, the loans started to accrue interest.

The final due date for all Ceba loans is at the end of next month.

Hogan’s office flagged a number of other outstanding issues from the government’s last fiscal year.

The government failed to meet its promise to clear the backlog of pay issues related to the former Phoenix pay system that were more than a year old. While the number of outstanding issues has trended lower, there were still more than 110,000 transactions awaiting processing for more than a year as of March 31, 2026.

“These issues need to be addressed to support timely and accurate pay to employees as the government prepares to transition to a new pay and benefits system called Dayforce beginning in July 2027,” the audit read.

The auditor general also has been raising red flags for more than two decades about the ability of the Department of National Defence to keep track of its inventory. A promised bar code system to keep track of assets is still five years away, the office noted last week.

Errors in the quantities and valuations of the assets resulted in a $751 million understatement of the department’s deficit for the last fiscal year, the audit showed.

Other issues identified by the auditor general touch on Crown corporations, and a lack of risk management, board oversight and overall performance measurement and reporting.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Craig Lord, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Feds wrote off $4.5B in COVID benefit repayments in 2025: auditor general
stories.summary: The federal government is trying to recoup payments made to Canadians during the COVID-19 pandemic in cases where it determines someone was overpaid or was ineligible.
stories.author: Craig Lord
stories.content:
The Office of the Auditor General of Canada says the federal government wrote off billions of dollars last year in COVID-19 benefits that it no longer expects to see repaid.

The federal government is trying to recoup payments made to Canadians during the COVID-19 pandemic in cases where it determines someone was overpaid or was ineligible for the benefit.

But when the government expects not to be paid back, it writes off the debt and strikes it from its ledgers.

Audits of the government’s consolidated financial statements for the last fiscal year show Ottawa wrote off $4.5 billion tied to COVID-19 benefits — up sharply from $26 million the previous year.

The government’s financial statements for 2025-26 were published on Friday — a day after Ottawa tabled its 2026 federal budget — as part of its annual public accounts.

Auditor General Karen Hogan’s office also released its commentary that day on the government’s previous fiscal year.

Hogan warned that Ottawa is also expecting a larger portion of business loans from the pandemic will not be repaid.

The government’s allowance for potential losses on loans through the Canada Emergency Business Account, or Ceba, increased to $5.6 billion in the last fiscal year, up from $5.4 billion previously. That’s out of a total of $7.2 billion in outstanding loans.

Businesses could get nearly a third of the value of their interest-free Ceba loans forgiven if they repaid before the applicable deadline, which the government extended twice. But if they hadn’t paid back the amount by then, the loans started to accrue interest.

The final due date for all Ceba loans is at the end of next month.

stories.title: B.C. LifeLabs ordered to pay $46K in misgendering case after patients’ ‘dignity was harmed’
stories.summary: Provincial tribunal says lab misgendered and 'outed' three transgender and non-binary patients in 2019
stories.author: Chris Knight
stories.content:
Welcome to our new, improved site!

Read a note from our editor-in-chief

A B.C. health lab has been ordered to pay out more than $46,000 in damages, lost wages and other costs associated with three patients who the tribunal said were misgendered and “outed” by the health lab.

The decision was handed down by Theressa Etmanski of the British Columbia Human Rights Tribunal on Oct. 29 against LifeLabs and its subsidiary Excelleris Technologies clinics in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.

In the first instance, a non-binary patient arrived at the Vancouver lab with a doctor’s requisition for bloodwork that did not identify them as either male or female.

Staff repeatedly asked the patient to choose one of those two options, a discussion that took place in an area where other patients could potentially hear.

According to the complainant, the exchange went on for about an hour, with staff eventually saying they would not draw blood unless either male or female was marked on the form.

“Eventually, a staff member came to them with a piece of paper where they had written M and F and asked (the patient) to point to one,” the ruling reads. The patient says “they were so exhausted and upset by that point that they just pointed to a letter on the paper.”

A second complainant was a transgender, non-binary person who came to a Burnaby location of LifeLabs seeking to have their gender identity updated in the company’s records. They also requested different laboratory reference ranges for test results, explaining that their doctor had recommended this for medical reasons.

Four employees were involved in discussing the matter. The complainant “stated that this encounter occurred at the front counter, directly in front of the waiting area which was occupied with other people,” the ruling reads, adding that the complainant “said everyone in the waiting room could hear what he was saying, and that his requests had become a ‘huge thing.'”

The third complainant was a transgender man who visited the Vancouver lab, whose identification had reflected his male gender since 2011, and whose requisition from his doctor also said he was male.

B.C. doctor fined $28,000 for refusing to inject trans-identifying teen with puberty blocker

Federal government admits two trans inmates charged with sexual assault after transfer to women's prisons

However, when staff returned the requisition to him “the form now contained a circle around the M with the letters FTM handwritten slightly below.”

The ruling notes that the patient “understood these letters to mean ‘Female to Male,'” and added that the patient said “he had an emotional physiological reaction to seeing this writing, which he experienced as being ‘nauseatingly offensive.'” He scribbled the letters out on the form.

“The Complainants’ dignity was harmed by each of these interactions,” Etmanski wrote in her ruling.

“While these interactions had significant impacts on the Complainants,” she added, “I do not find the conduct of the LifeLabs staff members was malicious in nature; rather, it was informed by the Respondents’ policies and procedures … and lack of understanding or appreciation of the sensitivity of trans status information.”

The ruling noted that LifeLabs had argued that they were complying with provincial healthcare regulations and that their computer systems, designed for binary sex classifications, would be difficult to modify. However, these arguments were not accepted by the tribunal.

Etmanski ordered LifeLabs to pay $15,000 each to the first two complainants, and $2,000 to the third, “for injury to their dignity, feelings, and self-respect.”

She also awarded lost wages of between $491 and $1,921 to all three complainants, and an additional $11,100 for services rendered by Dr. Elizabeth Saewyc, whom the complainants called as an expert witness. Total costs came to $46,065.07.

The complainants asked that the tribunal order LifeLabs to make a $10,000 payment to an organization operated by trans people which supports transgender human rights or transgender healthcare as a “public interest remedy.” However, this was denied.

Etmanski ordered LifeLabs to correct the records of the complainants within 18 months; and to “take reasonable steps to ensure that transgender and non-binary patients have, and are made aware of, the option of a private space to discuss or answer questions relating to their sex or gender, that is not in close proximity to other patients,” within six months.

LifeLabs is also required, within a year of the ruling, to “develop training on trans and non-binary patients’ privacy considerations, and provide it to all staff and management in British Columbia.”

Chris Knight is a long-time reporter/critic/editor at National Post with a special interest in science, space and movies.

stories.title: Diab says immigration plan about predictability, doing the 'right thing'
stories.summary: Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the new immigration levels plan is meant to maintain predictability in the system while doing the “right thing” by clearing a severely backlogged humanitarian permanent residency stream.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — Immigration Minister Lena Diab says the new immigration levels plan is meant to make the system more predictable while doing the “right thing” by clearing a severely backlogged humanitarian permanent residency stream.

The levels plan, published Thursday, includes targets for 380,000 permanent residents and 370,000 new temporary residents annually through 2029, along with a pledge to make upwards of 200,000 longtime temporary residents permanent by the end of 2027.

Between the one-time plan to give 200,000 additional people permanent residency and a similar plan in last year’s immigration plan, the government looks to add more than 600,000 permanent residents next year. Many of those people are already in Canada and have been here for years, officials said.

Speaking at a press conference in Stellarton, N.S. Monday, Diab said half of that 200,000 target will be made up of workers already in Canada. She said they will be selected in collaboration with the provinces and territories.

“It’s the measure that builds our economy, it’s up to 100,000 people, mostly people that are already working in Canada. It is to collaborate and be in partnership exactly with those provinces and territories, who are jointly responsible for this wonderful and challenging file right now ... to make decisions directly on the up to 100,000, whether they want to use it or not,” Diab said.

The second half of the 200,000 target is focused on clearing the government’s backlog of humanitarian and compassionate permanent residency applications. Applicants to the humanitarian and compassionate permanent residency stream face wait times of more than a decade, both for specialty programs and family reunification.

Those in the backlog include about 50,000 former Hong Kong residents who came to Canada feeling Chinese political persecution and Ukrainians escaping Russia’s invasion.

“These are, for the most part, people that are already in Canada. They have housing, they have services, they’re paying taxes,” Diab said.

“We’re going to bring those in 2027 as permanent residents. Also spouses and children, you know, families. We don’t want families to be separated. That is the right thing to do for Canada economically, but it’s the right thing to do.”

In a video released Sunday, Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre called the government’s latest immigration plan “bonkers” and claimed it will bring in about 200,000 more permanent residents annually than the government did when Justin Trudeau was prime minister.

“This is insane. Population growth already outstripped housing, health care and jobs for a decade,” Poilievre said in his video.

The Conservative leader accused the government of pursuing an immigration plan to boost the population to 100 million by 2100 in order to “make corporate power brokers a lot richer.”

“They can lower wages with an endless supply of poor foreign workers who come in and accept less. And they can charge a lot more rent when the housing market gets overwhelmed with too many people. But that destroys the working class who pay more to get less,” Poilievre said.

Diab repeated the government’s assertion that immigration is back under control, with numbers of new international students and workers coming to Canada dropping significantly since their peaks in 2024.

Immigration has become a fraught political topic in recent years and polls suggest about half the population thinks too many immigrants have come to Canada. The government’s own study found that view tends to soften when people learn more about the plan beyond headline numbers.

Diab’s comments Monday were her first public statements about the new immigration levels plan since it was tabled last week.

She said she wanted to speak with “really important stakeholders” like provincial immigration ministers and permanent residency applicants from Ukraine and Hong Kong before speaking about the levels publicly.

The government’s stated policy goals are to maintain new permanent resident admissions at less than one per cent of the total population annually and to reduce the temporary resident population to less than five per cent of the total population by the end of 2027.

Statistics Canada estimates show that as of July 1, 6.7 per cent of Canada’s population was made up of non-permanent residents, down from the October 2024 peak of 7.4 per cent.

The Immigration Department’s annual report, tabled Thursday, says about 3.3 million people held temporary visas to enter or remain in Canada throughout 2025.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

David Baxter, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Canadian astronaut Kutryk having a blast in space
stories.summary: Kutryk is expected to be in space for six months as part of Nasa’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
It’s tough to sleep and brush your teeth in space and the food is mostly liquid, but Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk said Monday that he is nonetheless having a blast.

Kutryk beamed into a science centre in St. John’s, N.L., to answer a few questions from children and adults about his adventures aboard the International Space Station, where he has been living for more than a month.

“The work is challenging, sometimes it’s tedious, but it is a lot of fun being in microgravity,” he said. “It’s like when you were a child and you dreamt of flying. That’s your life up here.” He did a backflip to demonstrate his weightlessness, and the crowd on Earth in eastern Newfoundland applauded.

“I’m having the time of my life,” he said.

Kutryk and his fellow crew members took off for the space station on Oct. 1, as part of NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission. They are expected to be in space for six months.

The 44-year-old from Fort Saskatchewan, Alta., told the crowd of mostly schoolchildren that he prepared for space by learning to live and work with people in extreme conditions, including under water. The International Space Station is fairly comfortable, but it’s taken some time to get used to the food, he said.

“You end up, in many cases, almost drinking it out of a bag,” he said. “It’s hard to sometimes draw the same satisfaction out of the food as you might on Earth.”

In his spare time, he reads books on his Kindle or rides an exercise bike, just like he would at home. There’s even a treadmill the astronauts can chain themselves to, he added.

Kutryk conducted two spacewalks in which he exited the space station and performed maintenance work on the structure. As he worked, the Earth was a “giant globe of blue,” spinning 400 kilometres away, he said.

“Earth from space is just so stunningly beautiful,” Kutryk said. “All you can think of when you look at it is this desire, this interest in trying to take care of it better, to look after it more.”
