stories.title: Carly Rae Jepsen to host 2027 Juno Awards, Our Lady Peace to enter Hall of Fame
stories.summary: The Juno Awards are calling Carly Rae Jepsen, no maybes about it.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
The Juno Awards are calling Carly Rae Jepsen, no maybes about it.

The Canadian pop star is set to host the country’s biggest night in music.

The Canadian Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences says the “Call Me Maybe” singer will also perform at next year’s ceremony, set for April 4 at Winnipeg’s Canada Life Centre.

Jepsen, who hails from Mission, B.C., is a three-time Juno winner, having swept album of the year, pop album of the year and single of the year in 2013.

Also set to take the Junos stage are Quebec’s experimental rock sensations Angine de Poitrine. The masked duo are having a breakout year, winning the Polaris album and song prizes.

Meanwhile, Toronto alt-rock mainstays Our Lady Peace will be inducted into the Canadian Music Hall of Fame. The four-time Juno winners, known for hits including “Clumsy,” “Superman’s Dead” and “Somewhere Out There,” will also perform during the broadcast.

The band has sold more than five million albums and amassed more than 600 million streams over a three-decade career.

The 56th annual Juno Awards will air live on CBC and CBC Gem at 8 p.m. ET.

Tickets go on sale to the general public Nov. 13.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Alex Nino Gheciu, The Canadian Press

stories.title: B.C. Conservatives gain a seat in final election count
stories.summary: Victoria - The B.C. Conservatives have gained another seat after the final count of votes in the October provincial election.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Victoria - The B.C. Conservatives have gained another seat after the final count of votes in the October provincial election, but judicial recounts loom in two ridings due to the narrowness of their margins.

Conservative candidate David Xie reeled in NDP incumbent Paul Choi in Burnaby South-Metrotown, overcoming Choi’s 66-vote lead heading into the final count to win by 64 votes.

stories.title: Temporary foreign workers could be employed for longer under rule change
stories.summary: Ottawa is also proposing other changes that would exempt other professions from the six per cent rule and allow employers to hire more temporary foreign workers.
stories.author: David Baxter
stories.content:
The federal government is extending the period of time a business can employ a low-wage temporary foreign worker.

The change will mean a low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessment, the document an employer needs to hire a temporary foreign worker, will have a maximum duration of two years instead of one.

The government says restrictions on applications to hire temporary foreign workers in cities with more than six per cent unemployment will remain in place.

It is also adding early childhood educators to the list of professions exempted from those restrictions, a list which also includes health care, construction and food processing.

Ottawa is also proposing other changes that would exempt other professions from the six per cent rule and allow employers to hire more temporary foreign workers.

Those additional reforms are expected to take effect on March 1, 2027 if the provinces and territories endorse them.

stories.title: Van Koeverden casts doubt on Russia competing as neutrals at Alberta's world juniors
stories.summary: Canada's Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden has cast doubt on whether Russia can compete as a neutral team at the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta.
stories.author: Abdulhamid Ibrahim The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Canada’s Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden has cast doubt on whether Russia can compete as a neutral team at the upcoming world junior hockey championship in Alberta.

The development follows last month’s Court of Arbitration for Sport ruling that the International Ice Hockey Federation (Iihf) must reinstate Russia in international hockey, after Russia and Belarus were barred from international hockey competition in 2022 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said last week Russian and Belarusian athletes could not compete in Canada representing their countries while the war continues. The government’s Nov. 3 statement, however, allowed individual athletes to compete as neutrals but did not clarify whether that provision could extend to a Russian team at the men’s under-20 tournament, which opens Dec. 26.

However, Van Koeverden clarified Monday that the neutral athlete designation used for Russians at other events applied to individuals, not teams.

Van Koeverden’s comments come after Norway’s hockey federation said Sunday the Iihf had informed it that Russia would be added to the world juniors in Edmonton and Red Deer next month at Norway’s expense.

“This is a really quickly evolving situation with Norway,” van Koeverden said from a sports summit in Ottawa. “I’ve had conversations with ministers of sport from Finland, from Sweden, and from Norway and from Germany. Hoping to meet with the minister from Czechia this week as well as others to discuss this quickly evolving situation.

“The Prime Minister was extremely clear that sport will not be used for propaganda on Canadian soil, and the notion that there, you know, might be accommodations is one that the Prime Minister was extraordinarily clear about.

“So we’ll continue to move forward working with Hockey Canada. And, you note that the Iihf, their previous position was aligned with Canada’s, and we want to continue to ensure that great Canadian hockey, great international hockey is seen here on Canadian soil.”

Norway’s hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said the Iihf told Norway it was bound by the CAS ruling and had no choice but to reinstate Russia. The communication made no mention of Russia competing under a neutral designation, he added.

The Iihf has not formally announced any changes to the world junior participants, and its website still lists Norway among the 10 teams in the tournament.

The Swedish Ice Hockey Association said Monday it was also informed of the new development, while adding that it will maintain its stance of not competing against Russia.

The Swedish association told The Canadian Press on Monday it sympathized with Norway, which qualified for the tournament but now risks losing its place.

“I feel deeply for Norway’s national junior team, which qualified for the World Juniors but now risks losing its place in the tournament. It is difficult to see this as anything other than unfair,” said Siha Secretary General Tony Wiréhn.

The Finnish Ice Hockey Association also reiterated Monday that it would not play Russia as long as the war against Ukraine continues. It said it would not speculate further and would wait for the outcome.

Neither federation said whether it would play a Russian team competing under a neutral designation.

Norway said Sunday it still hoped to compete in the tournament.

“The situation is still unclear,” Norway’s hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said in a statement posted on the association’s website and translated from Norwegian. “This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.”

Hockey Canada referred The Canadian Press to the federal government’s Nov. 3 statement and said it had nothing to add.

The Iihf and Russian Hockey Federation did not immediately respond to requests for comment Monday.

Individual Russian athletes who have competed at the Olympics since the war began have done so as neutrals.

Russian and Belarusian professional tennis players have continued to compete as individuals under neutral status on the ATP and WTA tours, including at the National Bank Open events in Toronto and Montreal.

World Aquatics barred Russian and Belarusian athletes from its events in 2022, then allowed them to return as neutrals the following year. In April, it lifted restrictions on senior athletes, allowing them to compete under their national flags and with their anthems, subject to screening requirements.

— With files from Nick Murray in Ottawa.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Transferring money between accounts is about to get faster in Canada
stories.summary: Payments Canada on Monday announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system, allowing consumers and businesses to send and receive payments instantly.
stories.author: Uday Rana
stories.content:
Many Canadians will soon be able to move money between bank accounts faster and get paid more quickly with the launch of a new payment system for Canadian financial platforms.

Payments Canada on Monday announced the launch of Canada’s Real-Time Rail (RTR) payment system, allowing consumers and businesses to send and receive payments instantly.

From gig workers getting paid instantly to Canadians being able to transfer money between their accounts much faster, the new system could have impacts on how Canadians move their money.

RTR is “an important step in modernizing Canada’s payment infrastructure,” Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem said on Monday, as the central bank brought the new payment system under its formal oversight.

Typically, payments are processed in batches, which can take a long time. With RTR, payments can be cleared and settled within seconds, 24 hours a day and seven days a week, including on holidays and weekends.

Canada’s RTR system has been in development since 2021 and was built in collaboration with delivery partners CGI, Deloitte Canada, IBM Canada and Interac.

This makes Canada the last of the G7 nations to implement RTR, Payments Canada said in a press release, saying the move will come with a fraud reporting and intelligence platform, a “risk list or repository of fraud risks and indicators,” a fraud transaction “safety” score and confirmation of payee.

Lower processing costs, reduced use of cash and cheques, and reduced float (the period during which funds are temporarily unavailable to the recipient) would mean that Canada could save up to $14.5 in cost savings, the C.D. Howe institute estimates .

Canadians with accounts in different financial institutions can also transfer funds between their accounts in real time.

“Canada’s Real-Time Rail enables the secure sending and receiving of funds between accounts at different institutions in real time, offering instant me-to-me transfers to their customers,” Payments Canada said.

This money could be used for anything from paying off a credit card quickly or funding a brokerage account.

According to Payments Canada, this could change how employers pay their workers.

Typically, businesses must wait for the weekly or biweekly payday to process wages. With RTR, businesses can pay workers as soon as the work is completed. This will be especially helpful to gig workers, freelancers and contractors, Payments Canada said.

“It can help workers that are living paycheque-to-paycheque, helping them cover urgent bills or sudden expenses without relying on high-interest payday loans,” Payments Canada said.

The new payment system can also make payments to businesses much faster.

Landlords and property management companies can receive rent in real time with immediate confirmation of funds. Retailers, restaurants and other businesses can receive funds immediately from a customer purchase.

As of Monday, the intimal list of financial institutions participating in the new system is limited.

Wealthsimple

Questbank

Peoples Trust Company

Paramount Commerce

KOHO

DoBusiness.com

Digital Commerce Bank

Bank of America

“As an early adopter, Wealthsimple clients will be among the first Canadians to experience instant money movement between institutions through the RTR,” Wealthsimple said in a statement.

The company said it is “currently testing capabilities, with plans to roll out new instant payment features in 2027.”

However, many of Canada’s major banks are expected to join in as well. Royal Bank of Canada, for example, is expected to introduce RTR in the second quarter of 2027.

RTR “will expand to include many of our members across Canada,” said Anthony G. Ostler, president and CEO of the Canadian Bankers Association.

Royal Bank of Canada RY-T has signed a deal to buy Australian investment manager Yarra Capital Management Ltd.

RBC Global Asset Management CEO Damon Williams says Yarra’s investment and distribution capabilities are complementary to Rbc’s asset management business.

stories.title: Ottawa easing some temporary foreign worker rules, focus on early childhood educators
stories.summary: Ottawa - The federal government is extending the period of time a business can employ a low-wage temporary foreign worker.
stories.author: David Baxter The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa - The federal government is extending the period of time a business can employ a low-wage temporary foreign worker.

The change will lengthen the maximum duration of a low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessment — the document an employer needs in order to employ a temporary foreign worker — to two years instead of one.

The government said restrictions on hiring temporary foreign workers in cities with unemployment rates above six per cent will remain in place. But Ottawa is adding early childhood educators to the list of professions exempted from those restrictions — a list which also includes certain jobs in health care, construction and food processing.

Ottawa is also proposing a series of additional measures for low-wage Labour Market Impact Assessment applications that are set to take effect on March 1, 2027. The provinces and territories would need to opt-in to the changes in order for them to take effect.

These proposed measures include one that would allow the provinces and territories themselves to add or remove occupations from the list of jobs exempt from the six-per-cent rule.

The federal government is also proposing that provinces and territories have the power to allow employers to expand the share of their workforces made up of low-wage temporary foreign workers to 15 per cent — up from the current limit of 10 per cent.

Immigration Minister Lena Diab said Monday the government intends to work more closely with the provinces and territories on tailoring the temporary worker program to regional needs.

“I have heard also loud and clear from many people across the country, no matter who they are, that there is a need for that program,” Diab told a press conference in Stellarton, N.S.

Diab said while temporary workers’ share of the workforce might rise in some fields, the government maintains all jobs should be made available to Canadians first.

“But we do recognize that we also need the skilled trades and the skilled people that have different skills than what we have in Canada, but also there are regions in the country that do not have the Canadians applying,” Diab said.

“The percentages that you raise will be up to the provinces and territories to say yes or no. This is again working in partnership with the provinces in territories who will decide whether that is the right thing to do for their provinces, and if so, where in the regions.”

Diab was in Stellarton to announce that the Rural Community Immigration Pilot is being made into a permanent government program and a permanent residency pathway.

This program involved more than 1,950 vetted employers in 14 rural communities that faced labour shortages and couldn’t fill jobs solely with local workers. The government helped those employers connect with skilled foreign workers who would then be put on a path to permanent residency.

About 5,500 permanent residency slots are assigned to this program in the latest immigration levels plan and the government says it plans to open the program up to more communities in the future.

The government alluded to temporary foreign worker program reforms in Thursday’s budget. Government officials who briefed reporters on background Thursday said they did not have detailed information about the planned reforms — which were published the next day.

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre said Friday that the temporary foreign worker program should not be an option in communities where the unemployment rate is above 5.5. per cent.

The national unemployment rate was 6.7 per cent in October, according to Statistics Canada. The unemployment rate has fluctuated month-to-month between around 6.5 per cent and seven per cent for the last two years.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: PSP Investments to pay $1.6-billion for 50% stake in Brookfield’s Enercare
stories.summary: Deal adds to public-sector pension plan’s growing Canadian investment portfolio
stories.author: James Bradshaw
stories.content:
Public Sector Pension Investment Board is paying $1.6-billion to acquire a 50-per-cent stake in Ontario-based home services company Enercare Inc. from Brookfield Asset Management Ltd. BAM-T , betting on essential services as a hedge against a potential rise in inflation.

Brookfield took Enercare private in 2018 in a deal worth $4.3-billion including debt. Since then, PSP Investments has had a small, passive stake in the company as a co-investor with Brookfield, and is now taking over joint ownership with Brookfield.

Markham, Ont.-based Enercare rents and sells equipment such as water heaters, furnaces, air conditioners and water purifiers, as well as protection plans to cover them, to more than 1.4 million homes and businesses in Canada.

The company has a leading market share in Ontario. Since Brookfield took the company private, it has expanded its services into Quebec and is beginning to make a push into Western Canada.

“We just think it’s really a strong, long-term business for us,” said Andrew Alley, Psp’s global head of infrastructure investments, in an interview.

PSP declined to disclose Enercare’s current enterprise value, including any debt it carries. But the company’s “customer base has been growing, as has the product offering,” Mr. Alley said.

Enercare earns much of its revenue from rental contracts with customers, which provide a relatively stable and predictable stream of revenue. PSP is making its investment through a portfolio in its infrastructure arm that holds assets expected to perform well when inflation rises, which in turn helps protect the value of long-term pension liabilities.

“We look for things that provide stability over the long-term, so essential infrastructure assets,” Mr. Alley said. “We are looking to grow the portfolio. This is a helpful addition to that.

PSP and Brookfield plan to keep Enercare’s management team in place and add to its customer base, in part by introducing new products and services.

PSP manages $321-billion for pension plans in the federal public service, the Canadian Forces, Royal Canadian Mounted Police and military reserves.

The deal to buy half of Enercare adds to Psp’s $75-billion portfolio of investments in Canada, which the pension fund aims to increase to $100-billion in the next few years.

PSP chief executive Deborah Orida made the domestic investment pledge at the Canada Investment Summit in September, which was led by Prime Minister Mark Carney. Ms. Orida and Canada Pension Plan Investment Board CEO John Graham were summit co-organizers.

“We’re encouraged by the opportunity set in Canada,” Mr. Alley said. “Canada is stacking up very well on how it aligns with our areas of focus.”

PSP made more than $10-billion in investments in Canada last year.

Looking ahead, the pension fund is showing a keen interest in the federal government’s plan to open up the country’s four largest airports to private investment through long-term agreements. PSP already owns stakes in seven airports in cities such as Athens, Düsseldorf, Hamburg and Glasgow through its AviAlliance subsidiary, which manages operations.

Mr. Alley said digital services and energy are other priority areas for investment in Canada that align well with Psp’s strategy.

Brookfield, which is incorporated in Canada, also holds its Enercare stake in its infrastructure division. The asset manager has been looking for opportunities to sell assets and recycle capital, and outlined a plan to turn over more than US$2-billion of assets this year at a September investor presentation in Toronto.

BMO Capital Markets and TD Securities were financial advisers to PSP, and Cibc Capital Markets and Scotiabank advised Brookfield.

Blake, Cassels & Graydon LLP acted as Psp’s legal counsel, and McCarthy Tétrault represented Brookfield.

stories.title: 17 arrested, 55 charges laid in OPP child sexual exploitation investigation
stories.summary: Seventeen people are facing a total of 55 charges in connection to a “proactive” child sexual exploitation investigation across Ontario.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Seventeen people are facing a total of 55 charges in connection to a “proactive” child sexual exploitation investigation.

Ontario Provincial Police (OPP) said Monday that probe, dubbed Project Brace, involved 15 other police services. They were participating in the provincial strategy to protect children from sexual abuse and exploitation on the internet.

The OPP said investigators conducted online child exploitation investigations to identify and apprehend those who prey on children. Police targeted individuals making, possessing and distributing child sexual abuse material.

While the investigation did not directly identify any victims, police said the probe initiated 23 cases that remain active. Officers seized 424 electronic devices during Project Brace.

“Online offenders are increasingly leveraging digital technologies to access and exploit children and youth. Through social media, gaming platforms, messaging applications, and peer-to-peer networks, they use deceptive tactics to groom victims, distribute child sexual abuse material, and evade detection,” said OPP Det.-Staff Sgt. Tara Clark in a news release.

“Combating these crimes requires vigilance, education, and collective action from families, communities, industry partners, and law enforcement.”

Anyone with any information related to child sexual exploitation should contact their local police or report it to cybertip.CA.

stories.title: Favourite room: A galley kitchen with unexpected curves
stories.summary: In this Toronto home, a galley kitchen and former porch were combined to create one harmonious space
stories.author: Matthew Hague
stories.content:
When entrepreneurs Carmen Douville and Derek Hopfner bought their home in 2020, they knew it had what they affectionately call a “Toronto special.” The term refers to a rear addition that was likely built as a screened-in porch before being converted into a poorly insulated den. “It was probably 100 years old,” Hopfner says. “It didn’t have a foundation and was breaking away from the side of the house.”

The couple also knew exactly whom to call to fix it. Their long-time friend, architect Deborah Wang, was familiar with the home and its potential, having been over many times for dinner. Aware of how much Douville and Hopfner enjoy entertaining, she proposed incorporating the draughty den into the adjacent kitchen. “It was really about making a big, airy, livable and welcoming kitchen from two previous spaces that were less so,” she says.

The old kitchen was a narrow, stubby galley with counters on both sides. For the renovated, elongated space, Wang proposed an S-shaped floor plan, with two peninsulas extending from opposing walls. The peninsulas would frame a central cooking area and provide counter space for food prep and places for guests to gather. Most of the storage would run along one wall, with additional pantry cupboards beside the entryway.

At first, the couple was surprised by the design. “It was really dramatic,” says Douville. “We were not expecting the S-shaped plan. It both shocked and excited us.”

They trusted Wang to execute her vision, in part because Douville and Wang share a long history in design. They first met more than a decade ago, when Douville was co-owner of Loyal Loot, an Edmonton-based furniture company.

Douville showed her work at the Toronto Design Offsite Festival, which Wang co-founded in 2010. She later helped Wang program the festival, now called DesignTO , which runs every January. “I’ve known Deborah longer than I’ve known Derek,” she says.

Although Douville no longer works in design – she now co-runs a prebiotic beverage company called Geez Louise– she collaborated on several aspects of the kitchen. “The industrial designer me was very obsessed with the materiality,” she says. “I spent many hours at showrooms. I went into a deep, deep hole of research.”

“It was an interesting deep dive that I don’t often do with clients,” Wang says. “Not to say that people aren’t very specific with their choices. But we were really dialling in on the minutiae.” That meant finding the exact shade of terracotta for the floor, the right wood grain for the white oak cabinets and the right stone for the counters (which has rose, bone and matcha tones).

Douville and Hopfner are both thrilled with the results. The palette is warm, rich and harmonious, particularly when washed in the sunshine pouring through the floor-to-ceiling windows. “We also love the layout,” Hopfner says. “There are moments of pause around the peninsulas. Unlike a big open-concept space, you sort of have to slow down, wend your way, look out the windows.”

The couple has had Wang and her husband, architect Will Elsworthy, over for dinner many times since the renovation (Rosewood Estates in Niagara is a favourite wine and Douville usually picks up fresh produce from the nearby Trinity Bellwoods Farmers Market). “That kind of serpentine circulation gives space to move around, space to gather, hang out, watch your friends cook,” Wang says. “I think it works.”

As part of the renovation, Wang also took the opportunity to tweak other aspects of the house, enlarging an opening between the living and dining rooms, refinishing all the hardwood floors and painting the staircase banister a very vibrant, very specific shade of pink: Mexican Tile by Benjamin Moore.

Despite such a bold choice, the homeowners still consider the kitchen the home’s standout feature. “When we used to entertain, we would cook in the kitchen and eat in the dining room,” Douville says. “Now, depending on what’s going on, we might stay in the kitchen all night.”

The kitchen’s La Pietra Cromie Compact floor tiles look orange-y red, but are technically green. They are sustainably produced by reconstituting crushed construction waste, including offcuts of granite and porcelain.

Wang and the couple considered many shades of white for the walls before landing on Benjamin Moore’s Lambskin, a soft cream with warm, peach-y undertones.

The kitchen peninsulas are topped in Ceppo Antico, a natural stone that has a pebbled appearance similar to terrazzo. Prices vary but start around $70 per square foot.

The Ripple Sconces, from Brooklyn-based In Common With, have domed tops that reflect the other curves in the kitchen.

A minimalist kitchen can be tricky for homeowners that cook often, as it can be hard to conceal big, bulky appliances. For Douville and Hopfner, Wang specified the same Vent-a-Hood vent hood she has in her own home. It’s a go-to detail because it expertly sucks up steam but has a subtle aesthetic.

stories.title: Man killed in daytime Toronto shooting was 18 years old, police say
stories.summary: Mississauga resident Malik Abass was identified Sunday as the city’s 33rd homicide victim of the year following Saturday’s shooting.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
A man who was killed in a daytime shooting on the weekend was 18 years old, Toronto police say.

Mississauga resident Malik Abass was identified Sunday as the city’s 33 rd homicide victim of the year following Saturday’s shooting.

Police were called to Rathburn Road and The East Mall around 4:27 p.m. Nov. 7 and found a man with life-threatening injuries.

He was taken to hospital where he was later pronounced dead.

No suspect information was made available.

The investigation is ongoing.

Anyone with information is asked to contact police.

stories.title: Third storm heads for already drenched B.C. coast
stories.summary: The third in a series of storms is heading for B.C., after wild weather knocked out power to thousands, triggered evacuations and left one person dead over the weekend.
stories.author: Staff
stories.content:
The third in a series of storms is heading for British Columbia, after wild weather knocked out power to thousands, triggered evacuations and left one person dead over the weekend.

Environment Canada issued wind warnings and special statements predicting heavy rain across large swaths of the province over the next few days.

In Haida Gwaii and North Vancouver Island, heavy winds are expected into Monday afternoon with gusts up to 110 kilometres an hour and a second low-pressure system following with winds likely to reach warning criteria again.

A special weather statement covering most of B.C.’s coast and Vancouver Island says a “strong and potent” series of storms will approach the B.C. coast from Tuesday through Thursday, bringing heavy rain, particularly in upslope terrain and higher elevations.

It says the rain event follows several low-pressure systems that have already drenched the region in recent days, leaving thousands without electricity and triggering an evacuation order for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on the northwest coast of Vancouver Island.

In Surrey, B.C., a driver died Saturday after two vehicles became trapped under a fallen tree.

Environment Canada says there remains uncertainty about the exact amount of rain that’s coming and which regions will be affected the most, but some areas are expected to see gusty southerly winds.

It says high precipitation could lead to water pooling in areas with poor drainage, worsening localized flooding concerns, especially in communities already hit hard by significant rain.

stories.title: B.C. lab ordered to pay $32K for misgendering transgender, non-binary patients
stories.summary: British Columbia's human rights tribunal found LifeLabs and its subsidiary Excelleris Technologies misgendered and outed three patients at clinics in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.
stories.author: Aaron Sousa
stories.content:
British Columbia’s human rights tribunal has ruled that a private laboratory provider must pay $32,000 in damages, along with other costs, for discriminating against transgender and non-binary patients.

The tribunal found LifeLabs and its subsidiary Excelleris Technologies misgendered and outed three patients at clinics in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.

Its decision says a non-binary person was told they had to choose either male or female to receive lab services and was outed to other patients by being required to discuss their gender identity in a public space.

It also says one transgender patient was unable to update their gender marker on medical records, and another was misgendered on lab reports and opted out of necessary cancer screening to avoid being misgendered again.

The tribunal heard last year from one expert who said gender-diverse people face barriers in accessing health care, and that misgendering can be a “significant source of distress.”

Tribunal member Theressa Etmanski says LifeLabs must update its policies and staff training around gender identity, and make available to transgender and non-binary patients private spaces to discuss their identity.

“Information about a patient’s sex May be medically relevant in the provision of laboratory services. However, I wish to be clear that there is no evidence before me to support that the standard is medically necessary or justified,” Etmanski says in the decision issued Oct. 29, 2026.

stories.title: Late goal lifts Sting past Knights
stories.summary: Carter Chadwick scored the winner with 5:41 remaining as Sarnia broke a tie
stories.author: CTVNewsLondon.ca Staff
stories.content:
The London Knights suffered their first loss with Brian Cooke in goal this season, falling 4-2 to the Sarnia Sting despite outshooting their Highway 402 rivals 34-28.

Carter Chadwick scored the winner with 5:41 remaining as Sarnia broke a tie and handed Cooke his first defeat of the season. The Knights netminder stopped 24 of 27 shots.

Kale Osipenko turned aside 32 of 34 shots for the Sting, who improved to 8-11-1-0.

Cameron Aucoin, Alessandro Di Iorio and Chase Gaughan also scored for Sarnia.

Cohen Bidgood recorded two assists for London.

stories.title: Norway says it has been bumped for Russia to compete at world juniors in Canada
stories.summary: The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said Sunday it has been informed that it is being bumped by Russia from competing in the world junior championships in Canada.
stories.author: John Wawrow
stories.content:
The Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said Sunday it has been informed that it is being bumped by Russia from competing in the world junior championships in Canada, a decision creating further uncertainty involving the 10-nation tournament.

The switch, the Niha said, comes in the wake of the Court of Arbitration for Sport’s recent ruling reinstating Russian hockey teams to compete internationally, beginning with the world juniors set to open in Alberta on Dec. 26.

There remain complications in the decision, which has yet to be formally announced by the International Ice Hockey Federation. The Iihf’s website still includes Norway as a participant in a tournament featuring the top men’s players under age 20.

Russia, however, is not guaranteed of competing after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said he will bar the team from entering Canada, leaving open the possibility of Norway still being included.

“The situation is still unclear,” Norway’s ice hockey secretary general Peter Salsten said in a statement posted on the association’s website and translated from Norwegian to English. “This makes us hope that the last word has not been said about our participation in Canada.”

Other complicating factors involve six nations, including Norway, vowing to boycott games against Russia as long as the war in Ukraine is ongoing. Several long-time corporate sponsors also have said they will drop out if Russia competes.

Norway acknowledged that the Iihf has been handcuffed by the court’s ruling. As the 10th-ranked team entering the tournament, Norway said it was relegated to the 1A Division to open the spot for Russia.

The Russians haven’t competed in the tournament since a fourth-place finish in 2021, with their ban beginning after the nation invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

“We are aware of the status and the measures the Iihf feels compelled to take, and will await further information from the Iihf in the coming days,” Salsten said. “This also clearly shows all the practical challenges and immediate consequences for everyone involved when countries are reinstated immediately.”

stories.title: Osap pause May force dental college to close, school says
stories.summary: A spokesperson said evidence of systemic issues left the government with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to ensure the integrity of the system.
stories.author: Allison Jones
stories.content:
An Ontario career college that has trained dental hygienists and dental assistants for 22 years May have to close as early as next month, due to a provincewide pause on student financial aid in the sector.

Tuition at Southern Ontario Dental College in Hamilton is high, due to the technical programs students describe as rigorous and hands-on, and as a result most of the students rely on Ontario Student Assistance Program funding.

But Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn last month stopped Osap payments to all private post-secondary institution students due to what he calls serious concerns unearthed in the early stages of a sector-wide audit.

He has indicated the pause will continue into the new year, but Southern Ontario Dental College says it May not last until then without alternate funding.

“If we continue to go right now the way that we’re going without collecting any money from the students, we’ll have to close our doors probably in December,” said Alysse Estrabillo, the school’s chief operating officer.

For now, the students have set up a food bank in a room at the college to help each other out, she said.

Haylie Eady, a dental hygienist student and single mom, does not know how she could pay the tuition of nearly $52,000 for the two-year program, and she was also depending on an Osap loan to pay living expenses like child care, food and rent.

She quit her dental assistant job to go back to school and upgrade her skills, but is now taking odd jobs she finds through Facebook ads so she can provide for her children. Eady just recently received a notice of non-payment of rent, though she is hopeful that will be resolved.

“I want a career where I can make a difference, not only in the community but in my home, so that my kids never have to worry about a single thing,” Eady said.

“I feel like, in trying to make that step, I was put in a position to make them have to worry about when their next meal is going to be. … My kids have dreams too, and it leaves parents feeling like maybe they put their dreams ahead of their kids.”

Quinn has said the government is trying to secure third-party loans through financial institutions while the pause is ongoing, but he has not given any updates since making that announcement one month ago.

A spokesperson said evidence of systemic issues left the government with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to ensure the integrity of the system.

“We recognize the impact that this pause is having on students and are working to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to support students through this period of transition,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

Many other schools and students are left wondering why the government has not taken a more targeted approach to rooting out possible abuse in the system. Premier Doug Ford has said the Kpmg auditors have been asked to prioritize clearing low-risk schools first, but students like Eady wonder why their schools were cut off at all.

She and her fellow students had to meet certain criteria to apply, then do an interview and skills testing, she said.

“We all fought so unbelievably hard just to sit in a seat in that room,” Eady said.

Estrabillo said the school never imagined Osap would just suddenly one day stop.

“People come to our college and want to be educated, and they’re so excited to learn,” she said. “We’ve graduated so many classes in 22 years, and to think that would stop because of this just is unfathomable to me.”

With the college facing closure, the Osap pause is affecting even the students who never applied for the loans.

Diane Yu is one of those students, now in her second year of the dental hygiene program, and she worries that the Osap pause and potential school closure could derail her career path.

“It’s pretty devastating,” she said.

“This is my third term and I only have one left after this. I wanted to only focus on my board exam and the clinical hours. This is the most important time of this education and this is the worst timing to face this issue.”

Career Colleges Ontario said it couldn’t comment on specific cases, but a spokesperson said there is every reason to believe that more stories of schools facing closure will emerge.

“The ongoing Osap pause is creating significant uncertainty across the sector, with schools facing mounting pressure and no clear timeline for when students’ funding will resume,” Taylor Buck wrote in a statement.

“The longer this uncertainty continues, the harder decisions schools will be forced to make, and ultimately students will bear the consequences.”

“We recognize the impact that this pause is having on students and are working to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to support students through this period of transition,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.
The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

Many other schools and students are left wondering why the government has not taken a more targeted approach to rooting out possible abuse in the system. Premier Doug Ford has said the Kpmg auditors have been asked to prioritize clearing low-risk schools first, but students like Eady wonder why their schools were cut off at all.
She and her fellow students had to meet certain criteria to apply, then do an interview and skills testing, she said.
“We all fought so unbelievably hard just to sit in a seat in that room,” Eady said.
Estrabillo said the school never imagined Osap would just suddenly one day stop.

“People come to our college and want to be educated, and they’re so excited to learn,” she said. “We’ve graduated so many classes in 22 years, and to think that would stop because of this just is unfathomable to me.”
With the college facing closure, the Osap pause is affecting even the students who never applied for the loans.
Diane Yu is one of those students, now in her second year of the dental hygiene program, and she worries that the Osap pause and potential school closure could derail her career path.
“It’s pretty devastating,” she said.

“This is my third term and I only have one left after this. I wanted to only focus on my board exam and the clinical hours. This is the most important time of this education and this is the worst timing to face this issue.”
Career Colleges Ontario said it couldn’t comment on specific cases, but a spokesperson said there is every reason to believe that more stories of schools facing closure will emerge.

“The ongoing Osap pause is creating significant uncertainty across the sector, with schools facing mounting pressure and no clear timeline for when students’ funding will resume,” Taylor Buck wrote in a statement.
“The longer this uncertainty continues, the harder decisions schools will be forced to make, and ultimately students will bear the consequences.”

stories.title: Canada Child Benefit payments go out next week. Here's what you need to know
stories.summary: Nov. 20. Find out who qualifies, how much families can receive and when the next payment is scheduled.
stories.author: Matthew Daldalian
stories.content:
The next round of Canada Child Benefit (CCB) payments is scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20, with one more payment to follow before the end of the year.

The monthly benefit, administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), provides tax-free financial support to families raising children under 18. The amount varies depending on household income, the number of children and their ages.

Here’s what families should know ahead of November’s payment.

According to the CRA, the CCB is available to individuals who live with a child under 18 and take primary responsibility for their care.

Applicants must be Canadian residents for tax purposes. Either the applicant or their spouse or common-law partner must also meet one of several status requirements, including being a Canadian citizen, permanent resident, protected person, eligible temporary resident or someone registered or entitled to be registered under the Indian Act.

For temporary residents, eligibility generally begins after 18 consecutive months of living in Canada, provided they have a valid permit in the 19th month.

When parents share custody, the CRA generally divides the benefit between them. Each receives 50 per cent of the amount they would otherwise qualify for, based on their respective family incomes.

The amount a family receives is based on its adjusted net income, along with the number and ages of children in the household.

Payments for the current period, which runs from July 2026 to June 2027, are based on income reported on 2025 tax returns.

Families earning less than $38,237 in adjusted family net income qualify for the maximum payments.

That works out to $679.75 a month, or $8,157 a year, for each child younger than six. For children aged six to 17, the maximum is $573.58 a month, or $6,883 a year.

Families with higher incomes May still qualify, although payments begin to decrease above the $38,237 threshold. Additional reductions apply once adjusted family net income exceeds $82,847.

The maximum amounts were raised in July, increasing by $160 annually for children under six and $135 for those aged six to 17 compared with the previous benefit year.

For the current benefit year, families receiving the CCB for a child who qualifies for the disability tax credit could receive up to $290 more each month, or $3,480 annually.

The amount depends on family income. Eligible families do not need to submit a separate application for the child disability benefit, as the CRA calculates it automatically alongside their CCB.

Families should apply once they become eligible, whether that’s following the birth of a child, a change in custody or a child moving into their care.

In Ontario and most other provinces and territories, parents can request the benefit while registering their newborn’s birth through the Automated Benefits Application.

Applications can also be submitted through a CRA account or by mailing Form RC66, the Canada Child Benefits Application.

Those who apply online or by mail must provide proof of birth for any child the CRA hasn’t previously paid benefits for.

Families must also keep up with their annual tax filings to remain eligible. Both parents or partners, where applicable, need to file returns each year, even if they earned no income.

After the Nov. 20 payment, families have one more CCB payment scheduled for 2026.

According to the Cra’s payment calendar , the final payment of the year will be issued Friday, Dec. 11.

That’s earlier than the usual payment date of the 20th, which falls on a Sunday in December.

Although CCB payments are normally issued monthly, families whose total annual benefit is less than $240 receive their entitlement in a single payment in July instead.

Families can receive their benefits through direct deposit or by cheque in the mail.

The CRA encourages recipients to use direct deposit to get their money faster. Those already registered for direct deposit with the agency will generally have their CCB sent to the same bank account.

Payment details, including amounts and dates, can be viewed through a CRA account.

If a scheduled payment doesn’t arrive, recipients should check their account information and allow five business days after the payment date before contacting the CRA.

stories.title: York University investigating cybersecurity incident, data theft
stories.summary: York University is investigating a cybersecurity incident resulting in the theft of personal data which was discovered last month.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen
stories.content:
York University is investigating a cybersecurity incident resulting in the theft of personal data which was discovered last month.

The school said an unauthorized actor accessed information of individuals who completed online forms on select websites, such as residence applications and surveys, ranging from 2007 to October 2026.

The breach, discovered on Oct. 25, was limited to a specific list of websites and faculties posted on their website, the school said.

York University said a small number of directly affected individuals had their government identification or financial account information exposed.

The school said it immediately began an investigation into the breach alongside the help of external experts.

The university did not disclose when the incident took place or when it discovered the breach. The investigation found no evidence that the unauthorized actor moved beyond the affected websites or accessed other parts of the university.

“Affected individuals should remain alert for suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls, particularly communications asking for personal information or directing them to unfamiliar websites,” the school said in a news release.

It is also asking the affected individuals, who will be contacted directly, to monitor their financial accounts.

York University is offering two years of complimentary TransUnion credit monitoring and identity theft protection to the individuals who had their government or financial information exposed.

The incident was reported to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario and law enforcement.

“We recognize that this incident May be concerning to you,” the school said. “We take that seriously and regret these circumstances.”

stories.title: London resident charged after crash in Bruce County
stories.summary: Police, along with firefighters and paramedics, responded to a report of a vehicle in a ditch on Bruce Road 13, south of Pashwood Drive, at about 3:20 a.m. on Saturday.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A London woman is facing impaired driving and dangerous driving charges following a single-vehicle crash in South Bruce Peninsula.

Police, along with firefighters and paramedics, responded to a report of a vehicle in a ditch on Bruce Road 13, south of Pashwood Drive, at about 3:20 a.m. on Saturday.

According to police, the vehicle had left the roadway and entered the ditch. The driver, who was the lone occupant, was not injured.

A 54-year-old woman was arrested and charged with impaired operation and dangerous operation of a motor vehicle.

She was released from custody and is scheduled to appear in the Ontario Court of Justice in Walkerton on Dec. 17.

Police say the driver was also issued a 90-day driver’s licence suspension and had her vehicle impounded for seven days under provincial legislation.

The Grey Bruce OPP is reminding the public to report suspected impaired drivers by calling 911.

stories.title: B.C braces for more heavy rain and wind as third storm heads to the already drenched coast
stories.summary: Wild weather knocked out power to thousands, triggered evacuations and left one person dead over the weekend
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Forecasters are escalating rainfall warnings in southwest British Columbia, saying some areas could receive a deluge topping 250 millimetres in a new parade of storms that is set to drench the region.

Orange warnings have been raised for west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions, with Environment Canada warning of flooding and landslides after the “very robust” frontal system makes landfall Tuesday morning.

Wild weather has been pummelling B.C. since last week and May have claimed a second victim, after the death of a pedestrian who was hit by a car in Vancouver while she was crossing the road during a heavy downpour.

Police noted the weather conditions when they announced that the 78-year-old woman had died in hospital on Saturday, the day after the crash in an unmarked crosswalk at Dunbar Street and West 34th Avenue.

The storms had claimed their first known fatality on Saturday in Surrey, B.C., when a tree fell on two vehicles and killed one of the drivers, while a canoeist has been missing in stormy waters off northern Vancouver Island since Friday.

Environment Canada has issued about a dozen wind and rain warnings due to the new series of storms set to lash the southern and central coasts of B.C. until Thursday, after wild weekend weather that temporarily cut power to about 415,000 BC Hydro customers.

More than 250 millimetres of rain is forecast for parts of Vancouver Island, while Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky areas could get more than 160 millimetres, the agency said Monday. Metro Vancouver could get more than 120 millimetres near the mountains.

The province’s River Forecast Centre has also issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C.

The flood watch covers Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, parts of Metro Vancouver, most of Vancouver Island, the Central Coast and northern Fraser Valley.

“The heaviest rain is forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, with lingering rainfall continuing through the rest of the week,” the province’s River Forecast Centre said on Monday.

Residents are being asked to stay away from river banks of fast-moving water and to never cross flooded roads or bridges.

Communities have begun preparing for the incoming storms, with the City of Vancouver opening additional shelter spaces on Monday and Tuesday.

“This rainfall event comes on the heels of several low pressure systems that have moved through the region in recent days, already bringing substantial amounts of precipitation to parts of the coast,” Environment Canada said in a weather statement.

Low-pressure systems over the weekend drenched southwest B.C., triggering an evacuation order for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

Nearby, the Ma’amtagila Nation along the Central Coast says a man who went to sea on Friday in a canoe is missing in waters off northern Vancouver Island.

The nation says the vessel was found capsized, while Environment Canada says gusts reached 88 kilometres an hour in nearby waters that day.

“There are many beaches and forested areas that searchers have not been able to reach, and as the weather worsens, we desperately need the support of the trained personnel and equipment that exists for this exact situation,” the Ma’amtagila Tribe Society says in an open letter on Facebook pleading for federal search assistance.

“Our community will not stop looking, and we fear the danger they are in.”

Winds reached 116 kilometres an hour on Herbert Island off northern Vancouver Island on Sunday, with Victoria’s airport recording 96 kilometres an hour.
paragraphs: Forecasters are escalating rainfall warnings in southwest British Columbia, saying some areas could receive a deluge topping 250 millimetres in a new parade of storms that is set to drench the region.

Orange warnings have been raised for west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions, with Environment Canada warning of flooding and landslides after the “very robust” frontal system makes landfall Tuesday morning.

Wild weather has been pummelling B.C. since last week and May have claimed a second victim, after the death of a pedestrian who was hit by a car in Vancouver while she was crossing the road during a heavy downpour.

Police noted the weather conditions when they announced that the 78-year-old woman had died in hospital on Saturday, the day after the crash in an unmarked crosswalk at Dunbar Street and West 34th Avenue.

The storms had claimed their first known fatality on Saturday in Surrey, B.C., when a tree fell on two vehicles and killed one of the drivers, while a canoeist has been missing in stormy waters off northern Vancouver Island since Friday.

Environment Canada has issued about a dozen wind and rain warnings due to the new series of storms set to lash the southern and central coasts of B.C. until Thursday, after wild weekend weather that temporarily cut power to about 415,000 BC Hydro customers.

More than 250 millimetres of rain is forecast for parts of Vancouver Island, while Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky areas could get more than 160 millimetres, the agency said Monday. Metro Vancouver could get more than 120 millimetres near the mountains.
The province’s River Forecast Centre has also issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C.
The flood watch covers Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, parts of Metro Vancouver, most of Vancouver Island, the Central Coast and northern Fraser Valley.
“The heaviest rain is forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, with lingering rainfall continuing through the rest of the week,” the province’s River Forecast Centre said on Monday.
Residents are being asked to stay away from river banks of fast-moving water and to never cross flooded roads or bridges.
Communities have begun preparing for the incoming storms, with the City of Vancouver opening additional shelter spaces on Monday and Tuesday.

“This rainfall event comes on the heels of several low pressure systems that have moved through the region in recent days, already bringing substantial amounts of precipitation to parts of the coast,” Environment Canada said in a weather statement.
Low-pressure systems over the weekend drenched southwest B.C., triggering an evacuation order for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.
Nearby, the Ma’amtagila Nation along the Central Coast says a man who went to sea on Friday in a canoe is missing in waters off northern Vancouver Island.
The nation says the vessel was found capsized, while Environment Canada says gusts reached 88 kilometres an hour in nearby waters that day.

“There are many beaches and forested areas that searchers have not been able to reach, and as the weather worsens, we desperately need the support of the trained personnel and equipment that exists for this exact situation,” the Ma’amtagila Tribe Society says in an open letter on Facebook pleading for federal search assistance.
“Our community will not stop looking, and we fear the danger they are in.”
Winds reached 116 kilometres an hour on Herbert Island off northern Vancouver Island on Sunday, with Victoria’s airport recording 96 kilometres an hour.

stories.title: Can Canada afford Carney’s budget?
stories.summary: The Big Story discusses the message the government is trying to send with this federal budget, and how we're going to pay for it all.
stories.author: Patricia D'Cunha
stories.content:
“Masters of our Destiny” is the title of Mark Carney’s second federal budget since becoming Prime Minister. It outlines paths to build stronger Canadian sovereignty, including new spending to help at the grocery store, funding for local journalism, culture, and an ambitious goal to end homelessness — but it comes with a hefty price tag.

Host Maria Kestane speaks with Craig Lord, a reporter and editor specializing in economics at The Canadian Press , about the message the government is trying to send with this budget, and how we’re going to pay for it all.

stories.title: Navy Vets Recap - Nov 6th
stories.summary: The Woodstock Navy Vets suffered an 8-5 loss to the Strathroy Rockets on Friday.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 9 November 2026 at 06:57

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Woodstock Navy Vets suffered an 8-5 loss to the Strathroy Rockets on Friday.

Woodstock - It was a light weekend for the Woodstock Navy Vets in the Greater Ontario Hockey League.

They only had one game, where they suffered an 8-5 loss to the Strathroy Rockets at Southwood Arena on Friday. Jaxon Bagshaw scored twice for Woodstock while Robert Landry, Cole Shoup and Xander Zanier scored the other Vets goals.

The Vets will be back in action on Thursday when take on the Sarnia Legionnaires at Pat Stapleton Arena. Woodstock celebrated a 9-4 victory over Sarnia in their last matchup on Sunday, November 1st.

The Navy Vets are currently tied with the LaSalle Vipers for eighth place in the Western Conference standings with 14 points each. The London Nationals are in seventh place with 15 points, the Elmira Sugar Kings are in sixth place with 17 points, and the Stratford Warriors are tied with the Rockets for fifth place with 19 points each.

The Chatham Maroons are in fourth place with 24 points, one point behind the third place Listowel Cyclones with 25 points. The St. Thomas Stars are in second place with 29 points and the St. Mary's Lincolns top the standings with 34 points.

The Komoka Kings are in ninth place with 10 points and the Legionnaires are in last place with two points.

stories.title: More long-term beds aren’t a blanket solution to seniors’ care
stories.summary: An approach that aims to allow older Canadians to stay in their own homes is not only more humane – it’s also cheaper
stories.author: The Editorial Board
stories.content:
Ontario is facing a conundrum: the cost of long-term care keeps ballooning but the capacity to meet the needs of a rapidly aging population still isn’t there. The answer is to shift spending priorities from institutions such as nursing homes to more home and community-based care, an approach that is not only more cost-efficient but better aligns with the preference of Canadians.

The province’s 2026 budget projects $9.3-billion in long-term care spending, up from $8.3-billion just two years earlier. Yet further scrutiny suggests it will still fall short of meeting demand.

A recent report by the province’s Financial Accountability Office found that despite the government’s much-vaunted plan to build thousands more long-term care beds, the growth in the number of older adults will outpace the increase in beds. Meanwhile, last week’s fall economic update showed the deficit has grown by $3-billion above the $13.8-billion initially projected.

Long-term care beds come with high infrastructure, staffing and operations costs. The province could get more bang for its buck if it prioritized ways to support healthy aging in place, including preventive health care, home care, services such as Meals on Wheels and supports for unpaid caregivers.

Last week’s federal budget offered a step in the right direction, by allocating $845-million over four years to support low-income caregivers by making the Canada Caregiver Credit fully refundable. But more needs to be done.

A 2022 report from the National Institute on Ageing estimated Ontario could save an average of about $240,000 in infrastructure costs for every LTC bed it would no longer need to build or redevelop by delivering better home and community-based care. A recent report by Ontario community and senior care service providers found that alternate models of care such as cluster care, where older adults live independently but with access to round-the-clock supports, costs $110 a day per person, about half as much as for long-term care, at $201 a day.

The problem is not isolated to Ontario. Provinces and territories spend more on institutional care than home and community-based care compared with other Oecd countries, making Canada’s approach “both inefficient and unsustainable,” according to the NIA. A 2024 report from the National Seniors Council said all three levels of government should expand aging in place strategies.

Canada is now a “super-aged” country, with one in five Canadians aged 65 and older. Over the next two decades, the number of Canadians aged 85 and older – when chronic illnesses such as dementia often lead to more health care needs – could triple to nearly 2.5 million.

Dr. Samir Sinha, a geriatrician and director of health policy research at the NIA who is considered one of the country’s leading voices on care for older adults, points out that when Canada’s universal health care system was designed in the 1960s, it was not equipped for the realities of an older population the country now faces.

Add to that politicians’ penchant for tackling daunting long-term challenges with short- and medium-term infrastructure spends (and the ribbon cuttings that accompany them), plus a deeply ingrained bias toward institutional care, and you have a recipe for inertia. “I think we’re just paralyzed by trying to solve institutional problems with institutional solutions,” Dr. Sinha says.

He recently spoke to a meeting of health ministers in Winnipeg and urged them to think more creatively, and humanely, about how to care for their aging citizens. He offered Denmark as an example of a country that has a similarly aging population and decentralized health-care system like Canada, but which has taken a different approach. Rather than warehousing frail older adults, Dr. Sinha says, Denmark has managed to keep more of them living independently, with robust and well-co-ordinated supports, at home.

Policymakers would be wise to heed such advice, not only for the difference it will make to provincial budgets but also because it is what Canadians consistently say they prefer: to stay in their own homes and communities, with the right supports, for as long as possible.

It is time to look beyond the confines of institutionalized care as the default for Canada’s aging population, and open the door to a senior-friendly model – that also happens to be the more cost-efficient one.

stories.title: ‘Troubling’: Poll finds small minority of Canadians believe all Jews responsible for Israel’s actions
stories.summary: 'My concern is that collective blame can also provide a form of moral rationalization for antisemitic incidents,' says Jack Jedwab
stories.author: Courtney Greenberg
stories.content:
A new poll has found a strong majority of Canadians respect and trust their Jewish neighbours, but a small minority feels differently because they believe Jews have a collective responsibility for Israel’s actions.

Jack Jedwab, the president and CEO of the Association for Canadian Studies and the Metropolis Institute, who released the poll by Ekos, said the results are very disturbing in a time of rising antisemitism in Canada.

“My concern is that collective blame can also provide a form of moral rationalization for antisemitic incidents,” Jedwab told National Post.

“When Jews are treated as responsible for actions attributed to Israel, hostility, discrimination and even more extreme forms of antisemitism risk being presented as understandable or justified responses to events in the Middle East.”

The poll analyzed responses from 1,232 Canadians aged 18 and over between Oct. 9 and 15.

It was released today to mark International Day Against Fascism and Antisemitism. On the evening of Nov. 9, 1938, a series of antisemitic riots took place in Nazi Germany. Homes belonging to Jewish families, Jewish businesses and synagogues were targeted and vandalized. Jewish people were attacked. It became known as Kristallnacht, or Night of Broken Glass.

Berlin store windows smashed on ‘Kristallnacht’, the night of Nov. 9, 1938, in which Jewish businesses and synagogues throughout Germany were burned and looted by anti-Jewish mobs. INP/Bettmann-UPI

Canada has been battling a rise in antisemitism, notably since October 7, when Hamas terrorists murdered 1,200 people in Israel in 2023, sparking a war in the Middle East. An anti-Israel movement spread globally, affecting Canada and resulting in protests, boycotts, violence, and the targeting of Jewish and Israeli-owned businesses.

The poll sheds light on how Canadians feel about the Jewish community in the country. It found that 85 per cent of Canadians surveyed had “much or some” respect for Jewish Canadians.

Seventy-four per cent of Canadians said they trusted Jews and 70 per cent perceived that they shared values with them. Sixty per cent said they were in contact with Jews “often or sometimes.”

A small group of respondents reported little or no respect for Jews and provided explanations for how they felt. There were 100 responses.

Among those answers, the most common one (41 per cent) was that Jewish people had a collective responsibility for Israel’s actions.

Jedwab said he thought this kind of attitude was “most troubling.” Although, he noted, it was only a minority who felt this way — not Canadians as a whole.

One person who took part in the poll said they disrespected Jewish people because Jews “are participating in a genocide.”

It is repugnant to invoke the Holocaust to morally condemn Jews as a people

Jedwab said he found the statements that bordered on “Holocaust inversion” to be especially disturbing.

“Portraying Jews collectively as perpetrators of atrocities comparable to those historically committed against them turns the memory of Jewish suffering into an accusation against Jews themselves,” he said.

Other reasons given for not having respect for Jewish people included their religion, beliefs and cultural practices (16 per cent), stereotypes, conspiracies and perceived behaviour (also 16 per cent), insularity, exclusivity and lack of integration (10 per cent), and negative personal experiences (3 per cent.)

Fourteen per cent of reasons given were unclear.

“While the broader national findings are more reassuring as a majority of Canadians express much or some respect for Jews,” said Jedwab, “it remains critical to understand the nature of those expressing prejudice at a time when antisemitic incidents remain at troubling levels.”

All respondents were recruited by telephone randomly and were confirmed by live interviewers. The margin of error associated with the total sample is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20.

Courtney Greenberg is a Toronto-based journalist covering breaking news, with a focus on antisemitism in Canada. In 2026, she was a Postmedia Fellow with the Investigative Journalism Bureau, where she worked on in-depth investigations into women’s health and the justice system.

stories.title: Ltvca wins Canada Water Award
stories.summary: The Lower Thames Valley Conservation Authority (Ltvca) has been given the Canada Water Award.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The Lower Thames Valley Conservation Authority (Ltvca) has been given the Canada Water Award.

Water Canada, a magazine that focuses on management, research, stewardship, and trends on water in Canada, held its annual summit, recognizing projects and people across the country.

The Ltvca’s Precision Phosphorous Reduction Program (Pprp) won the Conservation Project Award.

“It brings me great pride to present this award to one of our fellow conservation authorities,” said Angela Coleman, general manager of Conservation Ontario.

“This initiative highlights the importance of working collaboratively with the local agricultural community to advance our shared mission of responsible management of Ontario’s water land and natural habitats now and into the future.”

Prpp started in 2024, with a four-year, $13 million commitment from the Canada Water Agency, through the Great Lakes Freshwater Ecosystem Initiative. It “adopts a precision conservation approach to reduce phosphorus loads from entering Lake Erie through priority sub-watersheds of the Lower Thames River to help prevent harmful algal blooms and areas of low oxygen.”

The program is in its third year and has worked with 626 participants, implementing 158,378 acres of agriculture best management practices. The program also supports water monitoring at 28 different sites throughout the watershed.

“The program would not be possible without the strong partnerships we’ve built with landowners, the financial support of our funders, and the dedication of our staff who work hard to bring these projects to life,” said Donna Small, agricultural and phosphorus reduction program coordinator.

“It’s through this shared commitment that we’re able to turn conservation goals into meaningful action.”

stories.title: Legal battle over federal firearms ban heads to Supreme Court of Canada
stories.summary: The country’s top court is set to hear legal arguments this week about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Ottawa — The country’s top court is set to hear legal arguments this week about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.

The hearings, slated for Monday and Tuesday at the Supreme Court of Canada, will give opponents of the ban another chance to make their case after losing in the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal.

In May 2020, the government prohibited the use, sale and importation of 1,500 firearm models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14. The move was applauded by gun control advocates as a first step toward removing these firearms from circulation.

In October 2023, a Federal Court judge dismissed a request to strike down the ban as unlawful and beyond the scope of the powers delegated to the Governor in Council — effectively the federal cabinet.

A not-for-profit advocacy organization, firearm owners, businesses, hunters and recreational and sport shooters appealed the ruling.

In April 2025, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected that appeal, saying the Federal Court delivered “thorough and persuasive” reasons.

The list of guns banned by the Liberal government has grown to more than 2,500 varieties of what it calls assault-style firearms.

Before the Supreme Court agreed to examine the matter, the government said the prohibited firearms would have to be disposed of or deactivated by the end of an amnesty period on Oct. 30 of this year.

stories.title: SIU stops investigation into injury of man in North Middlesex
stories.summary: The SIU has stopped its investigation into the serious injury of a man in August in North Middlesex.
stories.author: Kate Otterbein
stories.content:
The SIU has stopped its investigation into the serious injury of a man in August in North Middlesex.

On Aug. 23, a man was driving a vehicle westbound on Nairn Road and reportedly didn’t stop at a stop sign. As the driver entered the intersection, the SIU said the vehicle hit a marked OPP cruiser , headed north on Centre Road.

Both vehicles left the road, and both drivers were taken to hospital. The man sustained multiple fractures and other orthopedic injuries.

The SIU reviewed video that caught the incident in parts and Deputy Director Stacey O’Brien said the investigation should be discontinued.

“The available evidence indicated that the collision resulted from the man’s failure to stop at the stop sign before entering the intersection,” the SIU said.

There were no reasonable groups that shows the officer committed a criminal offence.
