stories.title: Automated insulin delivery systems help expectant mothers manage Type 1 diabetes
stories.summary: System called myLoop becomes the first to receive Health Canada clearance, company says
stories.author: Jennifer Yang
stories.content:
Like so many first-time expectant mothers before her, Alexandra Yeryomin heard a common refrain throughout her pregnancy: “You’re not going to sleep very much when that baby comes!”

She would laugh and respond that she was used to it. After all, she already had a “diabetes baby” that was waking her with its “cries,” sometimes three times in a single night.

“I have alarms in the night because of my Type 1 diabetes,” she says, referring to the beeping alerts triggered by her glucose monitoring device. “Your blood sugar is low and you have to do something about it — now.”

Ms. Yeryomin, a 26-year-old graduate student in Montreal, had only been living with her Type 1 diabetes diagnosis for nine months when she became pregnant in February.

Learning to manage a potentially life-threatening condition while navigating her first pregnancy was overwhelming, to say the least. But Ms. Yeryomin considers herself lucky because she had a critical resource: an automated insulin delivery system, or AID.

Over the last decade, AID systems have revolutionized diabetes care for patients who can access them. In Type 1 diabetes, a person’s pancreas can no longer make insulin, the hormone that helps glucose move into the body’s cells to be used for energy. But AID systems step in to act as a kind of artificial pancreas, combining three technologies to monitor glucose levels, calculate insulin needs and deliver insulin to the patient, sometimes in micro amounts.

For Ms. Yeryomin, these medical devices are a “game changer” during pregnancy, when both the risks and stress of Type 1 diabetes are amplified. But until recently, none of Canada’s four commercially available systems had been approved for use in pregnancy in North America.

This is finally changing. On Oct. 30, a system called myLoop became the first to receive Health Canada clearance for use in pregnancy for Type 1 diabetes, according to mylife Diabetes Care, the company behind the system.

(This means that all three components of the system, along with their integration, are now approved for use in pregnancy. On its website, mylife Diabetes Care said it’s targeting late 2026 or early 2027 for one component, the glucose monitor, to become commercially available. Health Canada was unable to respond to The Globe and Mail’s questions by deadline.)

A similar milestone was also recently met in the United States where, in April, a different system branded as Control-IQ+ became the first to receive Food and Drug Administration clearance for managing Type 1 diabetes in pregnancy.

While many Type 1 diabetes patients were already using the systems off-label in pregnancy, experts say regulatory approvals help improve access, enabling more health care providers to feel comfortable prescribing them and potentially expanding public funding or insurance coverage.

“We have come a very long way in how we manage glucose during pregnancy,” says Ilana Halperin , an endocrinologist with Sunnybrook Hospital and associate professor with the University of Toronto (Dr. Halperin does advisory work for diabetes technology companies, including mylife Diabetes Care).

“We’ve finally gotten to a place with our technology where we can make a really meaningful impact on a reduction in those diabetes complications. It’s remarkably changed the face of diabetes management.”

Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition affecting around 300,000 Canadians. In the pre-insulin era, pregnancy was often fatal for women with diabetes, according to Lois Donovan , an endocrinologist and clinical professor with the University of Calgary’s Cumming School of Medicine.

Nowadays, a safe and healthy pregnancy is not only possible, it’s a common outcome for women living with Type 1 diabetes, she says.

“I’m very excited about the advancements that AID have brought,” says Dr. Donovan, who co-led an international trial of an AID system using the Control-IQ technology . “I have lived through joys and tears with women over the years, and it’s just so exciting to be able to have more joys than tears these days.”

But Dr. Donovan never sugarcoats the situation with her patients; even with these new technologies, managing Type 1 diabetes in pregnancy is still incredibly hard work, she says.

Pregnancy is a particularly volatile time for blood sugars. The placenta releases hormones that increase insulin resistance, and many features of a typical pregnancy — like morning sickness, food cravings and disturbed sleep — can wreak havoc on blood sugar levels.

And pregnancy, already anxiety-inducing in the best of times, can be even more stressful with Type 1 diabetes in the mix. For the mother, pre-existing diabetes complications May worsen, and the risks of preeclampsia or miscarriage are heightened. For the baby, high blood sugars can lead to birth defects or babies born large for gestational age, which raises the risk of a difficult delivery or birth trauma.

“The sense of stress and failure and anxiety that I see in these women is insane,” Dr. Halperin says, adding that stressed and anxious expectant mothers are at high risk for postpartum depression. “Every time they see a high blood sugar, they have this kind of anxiety or panic feeling that they’re maybe harming their baby.”

AID systems go a long way toward relieving the stress and mental burdens of managing Type 1 diabetes, she says.

A growing body of research is also demonstrating the clear benefits of using AID systems in pregnancy. Studies have shown that continuous glucose monitoring, one of the components in AID systems, improves neonatal outcomes. Major trials of some AID systems have also demonstrated significant improvements in the amount of time patients spend within their target glucose range.

When Ms. Yeryomin was diagnosed with Type 1 diabetes in May, 2025, the first question she asked her endocrinologist was about whether she could safely deliver a healthy baby.

Today, she is enjoying her new life with a healthy baby boy, Justinian, who was born on Oct. 19 with no complications.

“I’m very grateful,” she says of her AID system. “Maybe it sounds a bit dramatic, but I just don’t know if I would be here talking about my baby right now otherwise.”

stories.title: In the burn-treatment world, Canada-U.S. camaraderie persists
stories.summary: After the Wainwright fire, U.S. doctors that specialize in treating severe burns have offered support to their Alberta counterparts
stories.author: Pippa Norman
stories.content:
When Jeffrey Carter heard about the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta, the New Orleans-based physician got to work putting together care packages for his Canadian comrades.

Louisiana delicacies such as pralines, socks that say “Actual Superhero,” and Yeti mugs were among the items that the director of trauma and burn services at University Medical Centre New Orleans and his staff sent to the burn centres in Calgary and Edmonton in boxes the size of small fridges.

But Dr. Carter’s parcels from Louisiana aren’t the only form of cross-border support that Canadian burn care specialists have received in recent weeks.

Spray-on skin technology and mineral oil used during surgery have been shipped from the United States to Canada under special emergency conditions in response to the Oct. 17 grass fire at Wainwright, which killed four soldiers and injured 39 military personnel, many of whom suffered serious burns.

The incident has revealed how unprepared the country’s fragmented health care system is for mass casualty events with high numbers of burn patients, and it has exposed Canada’s continued reliance on the U.S. for key supplies, even as political relations have deteriorated.

The burn-treatment communities in Canada and the U.S. are inextricably linked. Canadian burn centres and burn care professionals are listed as members of the American Burn Association alongside their U.S. colleagues. And the Canadian anthem is played before the American one at the association’s annual conference each year, said Dr. Carter, a past president of the organization. “We’ve always just worked together.”

Burn care is a particularly complex specialty . It’s time consuming and onerous, requiring regular painful dressing changes, temperature-controlled environments and often multiple surgeries.

Traditionally, major burns are healed using skin grafts either from the patient’s body or a donor. However, new and innovative technologies are becoming available to burn surgeons who choose to adopt them, such as a gel that helps regenerate tissue and a spray device that uses the patient’s own cells to regrow their skin.

That’s why, after the fire in Wainwright, Health Canada facilitated access to ReCell’s epidermal autograft system through its Medical Devices Special Access Program. The spray-on skin technology was invented in Australia. It uses an extremely small and thin piece of a patient’s skin to create a spray filled with their own cells to cover their wounds. It’s a particularly effective treatment for areas such as faces or fingers and toes, which can be hard to graft, said Dr. Carter, who was involved in some of its first trials in the U.S.

Although Health Canada expedited access to the product, the department said it does not currently have an application underway to otherwise authorize the sale of ReCell in the country.

When his Canadian colleagues received their shipment of the technology, Dr. Carter said he reached out to offer his support. He knows many of the specialists in Edmonton and Calgary personally, including Dr. Vincent Gabriel, who is both medical director at the Calgary Firefighters Burn Treatment Centre, where some of the Wainwright patients ended up, and treasurer for the American Burn Association.

“I offered to go up and help. They’re like, ‘We think we have it, but we’re going to bring in some of these new technologies. If you could be available by telehealth, we’ll be glad to ask questions,’ ” Dr. Carter said.

Light mineral oil has also been imported from the U.S. into Alberta under special circumstances to help treat the Wainwright patients, according to Health Canada. The product is used to reduce friction when surgeons harvest skin from a patient for a graft, Dr. Carter said.

“If you take your thumb and push it on the back of your hand, it crinkles up all the skin, makes it look like crepe paper. So, by creating a lubricant there, it allows the skin to slide into this very thin blade,” he said.

The Canadian-authorized version of this product has been in short supply since May 2026 owing to a manufacturing disruption that is estimated to end on Dec. 7. Last month, Health Canada accepted a proposal from Fresenius Kabi Canada Ltd. for the “exceptional importation and sale in Alberta of U.S.-authorized Muri-Lube (light mineral oil),” the department said in a written statement.

This co-ordination highlights the importance of maintaining national stockpiles in Canada and the U.S., as well as ensuring supply chain interoperability between the two countries, Colonel Jennifer Gurney, chief of the joint trauma system within the U.S. Department of Defence, said in a written statement.

Col. Gurney told The Globe and Mail that the U.S. Army offered support to Canada after the Wainwright fire in the form of military burn specialists, whose mandate is to assess, treat and evacuate critically ill burn patients around the world.

Alberta’s tissue banks in Edmonton and Calgary exhausted their inventories of skin within 13 days, according to Vanessa Gomez, senior communications adviser for Acute Care Alberta. She said hospitals were securing more skin from tissue banks in Manitoba and Quebec.

Ms. Gomez could not say whether grafts had been sourced from the U.S., though health care facilities in Canada often rely on skin from tissue banks in the United States.

AlloSource, a tissue bank based in Colorado that supplies donor skin to Canada, said it has been in touch with tissue banks in Alberta and Quebec to offer support via donated skin.

As of Nov. 2, AlloSource spokesperson Colleen Kilkenny said the company had not shipped tissue directly to Alberta in connection with the fire in Wainwright. Ms. Kilkenny added that AlloSource remains available to Héma-Québec, which co-ordinates that province’s tissue supplies, in case its inventory requires replenishing in connection with the tragedy.

Back in New Orleans, Dr. Carter said he plans to send more local food to the burn centres in Calgary and Edmonton in the weeks to come.

That’s when they really need it, he said. “That’s when they’re doing really long hours of wound care a day, hours and hours of wound care, hours and hours and hours of therapy a day.”

stories.title: EV drivers are making money charging their cars – and it’s not a scam
stories.summary: After plugging into Canada’s carbon-credit market, Neil Horner pocketed $300 from an aggregator network – with more payouts on the horizon
stories.author: Mark Richardson
stories.content:
Last December, I forwarded an e-mail to my EV-owning friend Neil Horner. It was from a Canadian charging company named Swtch and it described a program that would pay him to charge his electric vehicles. In fact, it would pay him more than his actual cost for the electricity.

“This is probably a scam,” I told him in my note. “It sounds too good to be true. Can you check it out and let me know what you think?”

Neil checked it out, ordered a Swtch charger for $300 plus $30 shipping and had it installed. After charging his two electric vehicles for a few months, Swtch paid him $300. He just received another $100. It’s not a scam.

In fact, Swtch is one of a number of companies that offer rebates to drivers who charge their EVs at home. They aggregate drivers’ charging histories and combine all those kilowatt-hours of clean energy to sell as compliance credits to fossil fuel companies, which must purchase them to meet federally mandated carbon emissions targets.

“The mechanism that generates this revenue is the Clean Fuel Regulations,” said Greg Overmonds, vice-president of marketing for Swtch Energy, during a recent interview. “It’s legislation that was put in years ago by the Liberal government that essentially says those that are generating dirtier, more carbon-intensive sources of fuel – which are oil and gas companies – need to buy credits from those who are generating cleaner sources of fuel.

“Those clean carbon credits are generated by people who are driving EVs, because an electric vehicle is basically displacing a dirty source of fuel, which is oil.”

In other words, when Neil drives somewhere in his EV, he’s choosing not to use any gasoline to power his vehicle. The company that supplies him the means to do so is rewarded with credits through the federal government’s Clean Fuel Regulations program, which can be resold. However, all of this must happen on an industrial scale: Neil’s use of electricity is too small to be useful on its own, but when it’s combined with thousands of other drivers, it’s worth something tangible.

“An individual homeowner generates about two to five credits a year, but major oil companies need to buy them by the tens of thousands to meet federal mandates. They aren’t going to sign 10,000 individual contracts with homeowners,” Overmonds wrote in a later e-mail.

Grizzl-E , for example, provides Canadian-made metal charge boxes and rebates of up to 16 cents per kilowatt-hour, but it’s a tiered system that pays more generously to heavier users. Swtch reimburses its members $300 once they use 1,500 kilowatt-hours and then pays every $100 after that, while ChargeLab lets its members use chargers from some other makers and pays every quarter with no minimum. Pion Power lets you schedule your unit to charge only in off-peak hours, while others must be scheduled through the car itself. There are many alternatives, few of which – if any – existed just 12 months ago.

“I think it was part of the initial legislation, but only recently, people realized that, hey, this means residential single-family homes are eligible,” Overmonds said. “So that’s when a year ago, all these programs, including Swtch, all spun up. I don’t know if someone got a memo, but we all realized, hey, single-family homes – as long as they’re aggregated and audited and tracked.”

But is this robbing Peter to pay Paul? Does this not encourage “dirty” companies to pollute more?

“The percentage of their costs that go to buy these credits is negligible,” said Overmonds. “The reality is the price of carbon isn’t that high that it will move the needle on their balance sheet for them to change their production levels. But on the other side, for the electrification movement, it’s huge, because it’s generating millions of dollars that’s going directly to homeowners and helping people make that change [to EVs]. The long game is that those new electric-vehicle owners are going to demand less oil, right?”

While every EV owner who subscribes to the Swtch program is paid the same, wherever they live in Canada, Overmonds said the carbon credits generated are sold provincially by Swtch to the oil companies; this accounts for the cleaner energy production used in provinces such as Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia. A carbon credit is worth more when it’s generated by electricity from sources such as hydro dams, solar, wind and nuclear rather than from the fossil-fuel energy production of oil wells and oil sands.

The oil-producing companies “are not getting much for a carbon credit in Alberta,” said Overmonds. “That’s the balancing mechanism that works to encourage and generate clean energy.”

The system is certainly working for my friend Neil. He charges his EVs overnight at his home near Brighton, Ont., and pays 3.9 cents per kilowatt-hour to do so. Swtch then pays him 11 cents per kilowatt-hour. He figures that by driving 20,000 kilometres a year and charging overnight at home more than 90 per cent of the time, he’ll earn about $400 annually.

“It’s been seamless so far,” he said. “Everything they said they’d do, they’ve done. It’s no scam.”

stories.title: Legal battle over federal firearms ban comes to Supreme Court of Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa — The country's top court began hearing legal arguments Monday about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
Ottawa — The country’s top court began hearing legal arguments Monday about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.

The hearings, which continue Tuesday at the Supreme Court of Canada, will give opponents of the ban another chance to make their case after losing in the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal.

In May 2020, the government prohibited the use, sale and importation of 1,500 firearm models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14. The move was applauded by gun control advocates as a first step toward removing these firearms from circulation.

In October 2023, a Federal Court judge dismissed a request to strike down the ban as unlawful and beyond the scope of the powers delegated to the Governor in Council — effectively the federal cabinet.

A not-for-profit advocacy organization, firearm owners, businesses, hunters and recreational and sport shooters appealed the ruling.

In April 2025, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected that appeal, saying the Federal Court delivered “thorough and persuasive” reasons.

The list of guns banned by the Liberal government has grown to more than 2,500 varieties of what it calls assault-style firearms.

Before the Supreme Court agreed to examine the matter, the government said the prohibited firearms would have to be disposed of or deactivated by the end of an amnesty period on Oct. 30 of this year.

That amnesty has been extended until 90 days after the Supreme Court delivers its decision, which is expected no later than next year.

On Monday, several judges put probing questions to counsel about the details of the federal measures.

A key question before the Federal Court of Appeal was whether the Governor in Council adhered to a provision of the law forbidding it from using regulations to outlaw a firearm if it considers the gun “reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes.”

Writing on behalf of a unanimous three-judge panel, Court of Appeal Chief Justice Yves de Montigny said he was not persuaded that the government erred in considering public safety when assessing whether the prohibited firearms were reasonable for use in Canada for such purposes.

“It May well be that, from the sole perspective of a sensible hunter or sportsman, it makes no sense to ban firearms that are well suited or even specifically designed for hunting or sport purposes,” he wrote.

The federal cabinet is the most senior policy-making body in government and, because of its role at the apex of the executive branch, is best situated to develop government policy and assess the public interest, de Montigny added.

“Surely, the inherent danger that some firearms pose to public safety because of their lethality and their ability to injure or kill a large number of people in a short period of time, the fact that they have been used in mass shootings in Canada and abroad, the fact that they are disproportionate for civilian use, and the increasing demand for measures to address gun violence are all valid considerations in determining whether their use is reasonable for hunting and sporting purposes,” he wrote.

In a written submission to the Supreme Court, federal lawyers say the Governor in Council’s exercise of its broad discretion was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms present.

The submission points to a regulatory impact analysis statement that supports the Governor in Council’s opinion. That statement said that while some hunters and sport shooters lawfully used some of these firearms in the past, these guns can increase the severity of mass shootings and have been used in such shootings in Canada and in other countries.

The firearms prohibited in 2020 were owned by a small minority of Canadian firearms owners, estimated at between three and five per cent of the total, the federal submission adds.

“Thousands of alternative firearms remain legally available for hunting and sporting use,” it says. “The Gic’s opinion, balancing public interest policy considerations, was reasonable.”

A group of appellants that includes the Canadian Coalition for Firearm Rights says neither the Federal Court nor the Federal Court of Appeal considered whether the newly prohibited items were actually used for hunting or sport shooting.

“While recognizing that the misuse of firearms threatens public safety, Parliament chose to preserve hunting and sport shooting as legitimate, lawful, and socially accepted activities and uses of firearms,” they say in their submission to the Supreme Court.

For the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who lawfully owned and used the firearms prohibited by the 2020 regulations, this appeal is not an abstract debate about administrative law, the appellants add.

“It concerns the profound disruption of the lives of ordinary, law-abiding Canadians. Hunters, sport shooters, collectors and small businesses, individuals who complied with every requirement imposed by Parliament, found themselves overnight in possession of prohibited property, deprived of its lawful use and exposed to the prospect of criminal liability,” the submission says.

“They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters and neighbours in communities across Canada.”

Whether the Governor in Council acted within the limits Parliament imposed is not merely a question of statutory interpretation, the submission says.

“It determines whether the sweeping consequences imposed upon these Canadians were authorized by law.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Jim Bronskill, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Why Indigenous stewards are bringing 'good fire' back to Canada's forests
stories.summary: Spring comes to Leona Antoine's field in patches. The snow retreats from the Nicola River valley, leaving islands of wet grass scattered across her family's land.
stories.author: Jordan Omstead The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Spring comes to Leona Antoine’s field in patches. The snow retreats from the Nicola River valley, leaving islands of wet grass scattered across her family’s land.

It’s an invitation to carry on a practice she first learned from her grandfather.

Antoine, who is Syilx and Nlaka’pamux, remembers her grandfather’s joy when he would drop a match and watch a low, patchy fire creep across the field. The fire would clear away dead brush, allowing sunlight to reach the ground. Nutrients would get recycled back to the soil. Within weeks, fresh green grass would shoot up alongside huckleberries and other traditional medicines, she said.

Antoine, a former forest firefighter and forestry consultant living in Merritt, B.C., calls it “good fire.”

Her grandfather came of age when Indigenous communities were largely outlawed from applying it. Now, decades of aggressive forest fire suppression and climate-fuelled extreme weather have left Canada’s forests primed to burn.

Her field, hemmed in by a highway and crossed by the Trans Mountain pipeline, is part of British Columbia’s increasingly flammable southern interior. Towns like Lytton and Summerland have become shorthand for recent megafires. Antoine says her grandson’s first home was a hotel room after his family was twice displaced by out-of-control blazes over the last five years, the most intense stretch of B.C. wildfire seasons on record.

“We keep reacting to these catastrophic fires,” Antoine said. “How can we restore our practices and our teachings and our culture into the future, where we’re actually restoring our ecosystems, where it’s sustainable?”

What Antoine is doing in the Nicola Valley is part of a movement among Indigenous fire practitioners and researchers to put strategic, controlled burns back on the land, outside peak wildfire season. Those low-intensity fires not only protect communities by clearing dead debris and depriving future out-of-control fires of fuel, practitioners say, but they cultivate healthier landscapes and put Indigenous people back at the centre of land stewardship.

“Mother Nature is already making up our minds for us,” said Antoine, chair of the Salish Firekeepers Society, a non-profit advocating for Indigenous cultural burns and land stewardship practices.

That movement appears to be gaining momentum. A recent Senate report on Canada’s “escalating wildfire crisis” highlighted cultural burning and recommended the federal government boost financial and logistical support for Indigenous-led fire management.

In Ontario, the province recently relaxed legislation making it so Indigenous communities no longer have to apply for a fire permit for cultural burns if the provincial ministry is notified in advance. Several provincial wildfire agencies, including B.C.‘s, publicly support the practice.

A recent study out of northern Australia linked a decline in the extent and severity of bush fires to Indigenous-led controlled burns. Another study out of Stanford University linked controlled burns to a roughly 16 per cent drop in fire intensity and a 14 per cent drop in smoke emissions.

Yet, fighting fire with fire is one of the most underused wildfire mitigation tools in Canada, lagging far behind in use compared to the United States.

Wildfire agencies in Canada set prescribed fires on about 110 square kilometres this past year, mostly in B.C., according to a report from the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre. While that was the highest annual total of the past decade, it still pales in comparison to the United States, where the federal Forest Service alone routinely oversees prescribed fires on thousands of square kilometres of land each year.

Amy Cardinal Christianson, a former research scientist with the Canadian Forest Service, attributes Canada’s hesitation partly to a risk-averse culture driven by liability fears and historical accidents where prescribed fires burned out of hand.

Canada directs far more resources to fighting wildfires than it does preventing them. But a “fire put out is just a fire deferred,” said Christianson, who is Cree-Metis from northern Alberta.

What if more money spent on fighting wildfires supported Indigenous fire guardians, people knowledgeable about their own culture and territories, with reliable funding and training to safely steward the land year-round?

“Those are the people that can make those decisions about where the fires need to happen that will be most impactful for their communities,” said Christianson, who left the forest service and pursued more direct advocacy for Indigenous fire stewardship.

“It’s so much more than just a tool because it’s so connected to who we are as people and that important relationship and responsibility we have just for land stewardship.”

The challenge to revive cultural burns

Daylan Chookomolin didn’t plan to work fighting forest fires. In 2018, he was working at a youth program in Weenusk First Nation when he noticed a smoke column rising above the community to the north. He followed it, “to be nosy,” and soon found himself running supply errands and working the hose line, he said.

Standing near a crown fire for the first time, seeing a wall of flames and listening to it roar like a jet engine, inspired fascination, not fear, he said.

Growing up, Chookomolin says he remembers how people in the community, just south of Hudson Bay in northern Ontario, would burn their lawns every spring before conditions “greened up.” He figured at the time it was just a bit of lawn care and only later recognized it as something more deeply rooted.

Reviving those cultural burns on a larger scale is an uphill battle for Chookomolin. Now, as the community’s fire management co-ordinator, he trains and manages a 15-person volunteer crew. When they’re not battling fires in and around their own community, they’re helping out on fires elsewhere, leaving little capacity for preparing large-scale burn plans, he said.

“We have capacity issues. We don’t have a very large staff, and our spring seasons are usually busy and then we only have a certain window when we can do these burns,” Chookomolin said in an August interview, during what was Ontario’s worst wildfire season on record.

At the same time, the community is “losing a lot of elders that have the knowledge” about how those burns were practised, he said. Climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, is rapidly warming the north, lengthening the fire season and drying out the peatlands, leaving Chookomolin with questions about how to safely carry out the burns on an altered landscape.

For help, he turned to Thunderbird Collective, a group bringing together Indigenous fire practitioners from across the country to strategize and share knowledge about cultural burns.

“I would like to see one day where, yes, we can suppress the bad fires we don’t want, but we can also be the reason for these good fires,” said Chookomolin, a member of the collective’s steering committee.

“We can be the ones controlling fire, starting these little burns to help the forest rejuvenate and to kind of help mitigate fire risk at the same time.”

Chookomolin’s experience mirrors several of the barriers identified by Christianson and facing Indigenous communities across the country. Cultural burning is still largely barred in most of Canada outside of Ontario and the approval of burn plans requires time and resources many Indigenous communities don’t have, said Christianson, now the director of fire stewardship at the Indigenous Leadership Initiative.

As fighting fire with fire gains more attention, Christianson says she worries governments will shift to mostly prescribed fires, keeping the power with wildfire agencies, and overlooking Indigenous-led cultural burns. Those burns, she says, are primarily about achieving community-driven “cultural objectives,” not only wildfire mitigation.

“We feel there’s a social justice issue as well,” she said.

Fire is integral to Canada’s forests. Charred wood recycles nutrients into soil, fresh grasslands provide for grazing elk and hunting badgers, and hollowed logs offer woodpeckers a place to nest. The cones of jack pine require fire’s extreme heat to melt its waxy coating and release its seeds.

Many Indigenous communities understood those relationships and sought to replace unpredictable fires with low-intensity controlled burns, Christianson said. Archeological evidence from one of the oldest Indigenous settlements on the continent, near Sturgeon Lake First Nation, points to controlled burns dating back 11,000 years.

As early as 1610 in Newfoundland, and later spreading across Canada, governments pursued a policy of near-total fire suppression and outlawed Indigenous burning practices. As fires receded, timber regions were filled in by thick stands of pine and spruce prized by foresters, pushing out more fire-resilient aspen and birch and swallowing up meadows and grasslands.

Parts of Canada’s forest are now in a fire deficit. Despite recent record-breaking seasons, many regions are burning far less than they did in the past, a peer-reviewed study co-authored last year by federal research scientists found. When a fire is lit, there’s more wood and debris to feed it. Add in climate-fuelled extreme weather and you have some of the key ingredients for a new era of severe, ecosystem-destroying megafires.

That risk is disproportionately shouldered by Indigenous communities. While Indigenous people make up about five per cent of the population, their communities account for 42 per cent of wildfire-related evacuations.

“Indigenous people are repeatedly kept out of decision-making about forest and fire management in their own territories, yet have to experience the effects over and over again,” Christianson said.

In the Nicola Valley, Antoine, the chair of the Salish Firekeepers, said she sees signs of change.

In an interview this summer, she said the province and industry had started to collaborate more meaningfully on land management, pointing to an Indigenous-led program to plant native species along the watershed. After B.C. relaxed fire legislation in 2023, the wildfire service has partnered with several First Nations on cultural burns.

Last spring, Antoine said she handed the torch to her 16-year-old daughter, the same age she was when she first started setting fires alongside her grandfather. Watching her daughter put fire to the field inspired in her a sense of pride and continuity, she said.

“I think our ancestors are smiling and I think that, you know, we’re starting to take our rightful place, and it feels good as a steward to be able to apply fire and be able to pass it on to the next generation,” she said.

“I think if we heal the land, the land will heal us.”

content_blocks.text: A recent study out of northern Australia linked a decline in the extent and severity of bush fires to Indigenous-led controlled burns. content_blocks.text: Wildfire agencies in Canada set prescribed fires on about 110 square kilometres this past year, mostly in B.C., according to a report from the Canadian Interagency Forest Fire Centre. While that was the highest annual total of the past decade, it still pales in comparison to the United States, where the federal Forest Service alone routinely oversees prescribed fires on thousands of square kilometres of land each year.

content_blocks.text: Daylan Chookomolin didn’t plan to work fighting forest fires. In 2018, he was working at a youth program in Weenusk First Nation when he noticed a smoke column rising above the community to the north. He followed it, “to be nosy,” and soon found himself running supply errands and working the hose line, he said.

content_blocks.text: Standing near a crown fire for the first time, seeing a wall of flames and listening to it roar like a jet engine, inspired fascination, not fear, he said.

content_blocks.text: Growing up, Chookomolin says he remembers how people in the community, just south of Hudson Bay in northern Ontario, would burn their lawns every spring before conditions “greened up.” He figured at the time it was just a bit of lawn care and only later recognized it as something more deeply rooted.

content_blocks.text: Reviving those cultural burns on a larger scale is an uphill battle for Chookomolin. Now, as the community’s fire management co-ordinator, he trains and manages a 15-person volunteer crew. When they’re not battling fires in and around their own community, they’re helping out on fires elsewhere, leaving little capacity for preparing large-scale burn plans, he said.

Charred wood recycles nutrients into soil, fresh grasslands provide for grazing elk and hunting badgers, and hollowed logs offer woodpeckers a place to nest. The cones of jack pine require fire’s extreme heat to melt its waxy coating and release its seeds.

stories.title: Temporary road closures on November 11, 2026, for London’s Remembrance Day Ceremony
stories.summary: Temporary road closures will be in place from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m.
stories.content:
Temporary road closures will be in place from 8 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday, November 11, for London’s Remembrance Day ceremony and parade.

8 a.m. – 12:30 p.m. closures

Dufferin Avenue from Clarence Street to Picton Street.

Wellington Street from Central Avenue to Queens Avenue.

Above: A map detailing the road closures on Dufferin and Wellington.

10 a.m. – 12:30 p.m. closures

Dundas Street from Wellington Street to Waterloo Street.

Waterloo Street from Dundas Street to Dufferin Avenue.

Dufferin Avenue from Waterloo Street to Clarence Street.

Above: A map detailing additional road closures on Dufferin, Waterloo, and Dundas.

Access to the public parking garage at City Hall will remain open before the parade arrives at 10:30 a.m. Employees and visitors May only access the garage by travelling west along Dufferin Avenue through the Waterloo Street intersection. Going in and out of the parking garage will not be possible during the parade and Ceremony. Access will be restored as soon as possible following the parade.

For information on the ceremony and parade, visit London.CA/RemembranceDay .

stories.title: Internet child exploitation (ice) unit investigation
stories.summary: London, ON (November 9, 2026) – A London man faces eleven charges in relation to an investigation by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 9, 2026) – A London man faces eleven charges in relation to an investigation by members of the London Police Service (LPS) Internet Child Exploitation (ICE) Unit.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) initiated an investigation between January and October 2025, into international child sex trafficking organizations who facilitate Livestream Child Sexual Abuse (Lcsa).

In October 2025, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation, Human Trafficking Division (NBI Htrad) carried out an operation that resulted in the rescue of five children. Following the operation, information pertaining to criminal offences was provided to RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (Ncecc) - Transnational Child Sex Offender Unit (Tcso), with the assistance of the Child Rescue Coalition (CRC), Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), and Fintrac.

During the RCMP Ncecc-led operation in Ottawa, in partnership with HSI, investigators were able to determine the identity of a London man sending money to a facilitator in the Philippines.

On June 9, 2026, the RCMP’s National Child Exploitation Crime Centre (Ncecc) notified LPS that the investigation involved a London man.

On Thursday, November 5, 2026, members of the LPS ICE Unit executed a search warrant at a residence in the area of Grosvenor Street and Gammage Street.

A male suspect was arrested, and electronic devices were seized. Evidence of Child Sexual Abuse and Exploitation Material (Csaem) was located.

As a result of the investigation, Timothy Ryan Shirk, 47, of London, has been charged with the following offences:

Three counts of telecommunication agreement to commit specific criminal offences with another under or believed under 16 years;

Two counts of telecommunication agreement to commit specific criminal offences with another under or believed under 18 years;

Print/publish/possess to publish child sexual abuse material;

Possess child sexual abuse and exploitation material

Sexual assault as party to offence with any other person;

Sexual assault;

Sexual interference with a person under 16 years of age; and,

Obtain sexual services for consideration from person under 18 years.

The accused appeared in London court November 5, 2026, in relation to the charges, and has since been released on the following court-imposed conditions:

Not to be within 20 meters of any public park, public swimming area, daycare centre, school grounds, playground or community centre;

Not to be alone with anyone under the age of 18; and,

Not to possess weapons.

A photograph of the accused is being released to assist in keeping the public informed given the nature of the charges and the conditions imposed upon the accused.

The accused is scheduled to re-appear in London court on January 28, 2027, in relation to the charges.

London Police Service is a member of the Provincial Strategy to Protect Children from Sexual Abuse and Exploitation on the Internet. The Strategy has been made possible by a grant from the Ministry of the Solicitor General.

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Missing Person – Reyah Wolfe
stories.summary: London, ON (November 9, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 14-year-old Reyah Wolfe, of London.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
London, ON (November 9, 2026) – The London Police Service is requesting the public’s assistance in locating 14-year-old Reyah Wolfe, of London.

The missing person is described as a female, White, approximately 5’4”, with long brown hair. She was last seen wearing a grey sweater, black pants, and Nike Jordan shoes with white, green, and blue on them.

The missing person was last seen on Friday, November 6, 2026, at approximately 8:30 p.m., in the area of Thompson Road and King Edward Avenue. She was reported missing on November 7, 2026.

stories.title: How new Ontario guidelines are changing students’ commemoration of Remembrance Day
stories.summary: Students at Central Toronto Academy created ceramic poppies as part of a project that’s a local fundraiser for the legion.
stories.author: Kristin Rushowy
stories.content:
But this year, they have more guidance on what to do, and teach, under new curriculum for all grades. It includes encouraging kids to wear poppies.

On Monday, students at Central Toronto Academy created ceramic poppies as part of a project that has become a neighbourhood hit and local fundraiser for the legion — a project that now fits right in with the province’s changes.

The school’s poppy project is “an important initiative that’s near and dear to my heart,” said art teacher Beckie Di Leo, who is behind the idea that involves her clay club, Grade 9 students studying Indigenous art and art students in older grades, as well as those in business classes who help market the pins.

“I believe that maintaining historical integrity is of the utmost importance in the education system, especially in today’s day and age (with social media). I’m finding new and exciting ways to compete with all the noise out there.”

Whenever she brings out the clay “you can hear a pin drop in the room,” she said, adding that students also research Indigenous veterans, whose stories are featured on cards that come with the poppies.

Beckie Di Leo, art teacher and creative director of Project Poppy at Central Toronto Academy.

The project first ran about six years ago, and raises about $1,000 yearly for the legion; Di Leo decided to revive it this fall after hearing from local business Red Pegasus that customers were asking for the poppies, which cost a minimum $10 donation.

While schools are required to mark Remembrance Day, practices have varied around the province.

The curriculum notes that school flags should be lowered to half-mast, and ceremonies include laying wreaths, a poetry reading of “In Flanders Fields” by Canadian Lt.-Col. John McCrae, playing of the “Last Post,” followed by two minutes of silence, followed by a playing of “Reveille” and singing the national anthem — things that most schools already do.

The new materials spell out some specific lessons and themes by grade, and urge schools to “focus on honouring those who have served and sacrificed their lives in military service for Canada and our allies, with a local perspective where possible.”

They should also “recognize the individual and collective accomplishments of the many Canadians who have served, including Indigenous Peoples, Black Canadians, women, French Canadians, immigrants and newcomers to Canada.”

It also notes that “all students should be encouraged to wear student-made or Royal Canadian Legion poppies throughout the day.”

Education Minister Paul Calandra said he’s visited a number of schools over the years and collected ideas about Remembrance Day ceremonies and activities, and consulted with teachers and the legion before providing a more consistent approach and easily available resources. Canada Company, a charity that works to build awareness about the Canadian Armed Forces, also weighed in, suggesting the curriculum emphasize not only the two world wars, but also peacekeeping missions.

Ceramic poppies from Project Poppy.

Calandra said he expects to further add to the curriculum in coming years, and maybe some of the resources of the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa.

Central Toronto Academy principal Lesley Wallace said her school’s Remembrance Day activities align with the new curriculum, with the laying of a wreath, a veteran as a keynote speaker, singing the national anthem and playing the “Last Post.”

While traditional, she said the school will also this year “bring it right up to modern day, and pay tribute to those who lost their lives in a fire at CFB Wainwright in Alberta last month.”

Calandra has said the changes are to “further deepen our shared understanding of the significance of Remembrance Day and ensure every student across the province receives a consistent education on our history.”

stories.title: Bring your future into focus: Fanshawe Open House is Saturday, November 7
stories.summary: Fanshawe College invites future students, families and career changers to explore every
stories.content:
Fanshawe College invites future students, families and career changers to explore everything Fanshawe has to offer at its Open House on Saturday, November 7, 2026, from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

Whether you’re planning your first step after high school, looking to upgrade your skills or considering a new career path, Open House offers a firsthand look at why Fanshawe is a leader in education, innovation and student success.

With more than 200 degree, diploma, and certificate programs, Fanshawe offers hands-on learning opportunities, industry connected experiences and strong partnerships with employers and community organizations. Attendees will gain valuable insight into how Fanshawe programs prepare graduates for meaningful careers in a rapidly evolving workforce.

AI and Machine Learning

Bachelor of Science – Nursing – Fanshawe’s new standalone degree

Commercial Flight and Aviation Leadership

Cyber Security (Co-op)

Green Vehicle Technician

On November 11, Fanshawe College will dedicate a new memorial that will stand as a symbol of remembrance for all those who have served in the Canadian Armed Forces.

The dedication will take place at the College's annual Remembrance Day service in what is now known as Valour Court. This courtyard, located outside the College's D Building, has been designated as a place of reflection to honour Canada's service members.

"As Canada's first Military-Connected College, Fanshawe is committed to ensuring that the stories and sacrifices of our veterans and those who continue to serve live on in the hearts and minds of future generations," said Peter Devlin, President of Fanshawe College. "Valour Court and our new memorial will serve as lasting tributes to the members of our armed forces."

Financial support for the memorial was provided by Fanshawe's Poppy Project and Veterans Affairs Canada's Commemoration Program.

As part of the College's Remembrance Day service, award-winning Canadian music artist, Terry Kelly, will perform his songs, A Pittance of Time and Safe Home. Kelly is past honorary colonel in the Royal Canadian Airforce and recipient of the Order of Canada.

Fanshawe College Remembrance Day Service

Date: Wednesday, November 11, 2026

Time:10:30 – 11:15 a.m. (program begins at approximately 10:40 a.m.)

Location: Valour Court (outside D Building, Green Zone [off Colvin Court]) Fanshawe College London Campus, 1001 Fanshawe College Blvd. A map of the campus is available on our website. This event will take place outdoors.

For any media inquiries, please reach out to mediainquiries@fanshawec.ca

stories.title: Second major storm hits B.C., leaving one dead, thousands without power
stories.summary: Another strong series of storms is expected mid-week, Environment Canada says
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The wind that blew outside Gerry Sullivan’s bedroom in the Village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island was enough to wake him up early Sunday morning.

“It was just howling, and we had thunder, we had lightning,” he said.

Sullivan and his wife Vicki said early Sunday that they hadn’t had power since Saturday afternoon as the second major storm to wallop parts of British Columbia over the last several days left thousands without electricity and one person dead when vehicles became trapped under a fallen tree.

The couple said they had two generators to keep the lights on and a wood stove for backup heat.

“I’m 72-years old and I’ve never ever experienced a wind like that,” Vicki Sullivan said, adding that she could hear trees falling outside their home Saturday.

On Sunday, the Village of Zeballos amended an evacuation order issued on Friday due to the risk of landslides, lifting the order on some of the initial 22 properties but adding others.

As of Sunday afternoon, an evacuation order was in place for 30 properties including both homes and vacant or unaddressed lots. An evacuation alert covered 19 properties.

The Strathcona Regional District said in a statement that a geotechnical assessment of the affected area had been received and recommendations are being implemented.

“Emergency officials continue to monitor conditions closely, particularly with additional storm systems and heavy rainfall forecast throughout the week. Conditions will be reassessed as weather systems move through the area,” the statement said.

Gerry Sullivan said the village of about 120 residents is located about 42 kilometres away from the main highway along a forest service road. He said he wasn’t sure whether the road was passable after the most recent storm.

At about 8 a.m. Sunday, he said the wind had died down but it was still raining in Zeballos.

Environment Canada issued a rainfall warning Sunday morning for the Fraser Canyon between Boston Bar and Lytton, with rainfall amounts of up to 50 millimetres expected.

A wind warning for north central B.C. cautioned gusts reaching up to 90km/h until early Sunday evening. Additional warnings covered parts of the Lower Mainland, the Sunshine Coast and Vancouver Island.

The weather agency said more bad weather is on the way.

A special weather statement for the north, central and south coasts and Vancouver Island, said a “strong and potent series of storms” will move through the region from Tuesday through Thursday.

It said “significant rainfall accumulations” are expected, with upslope terrain and higher elevations expected to bit hit the hardest.

Police in Surrey, B.C., said one person died after two vehicles became trapped under a fallen tree during the storm on Saturday evening.

Officers were called to a report of downed wires and a fallen tree across a highway and found the vehicles trapped under the tree, a statement said.

One of the drivers was pronounced dead at the scene and the other was treated for minor injuries.

BC Hydro said approximately 30,000 customers remained were without power Sunday afternoon after the windstorms caused nearly 415,000 to lose power since Friday.

The provincial Crown utility said parts of Central Interior, particularly east and north of Prince George are facing “the most significant challenge” with crews dealing with extensive damage across a large area, including downed wire, numerous broken poles and other damaged electrical equipment.

stories.title: Remembering an oft-forgotten unit of Canadians who took up arms in the fight against fascism in Spain
stories.summary: A small group dedicated to preserving the legacy of the Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion have made pilgrimages on Remembrance Day to known graves of those who fought in Spain
stories.author: Rod Mickleburgh
stories.content:
Bethany Whelan Jones remembers it to this day.

On a family trip to McDonald’s, sitting at an outside picnic table with her parents and sister, they noticed an old man with a scraggly beard, rummaging through a nearby garbage can.

Her mother went inside to buy him a meal. When she returned, she told them he reminded her of her father.

“Then, she looked at us kids in the eye, and said, ‘Remember that man? Somebody loves him. He has a family out there that cares for him still.’”

Ms. Whelan Jones’s mother, Melanie, who died in 2021, had a deeply personal reason for her compassion.

Her mother’s father was Jacob Okonski, one of an estimated 1,500 Canadians who journeyed across the Atlantic in 1937 to take up arms in support of the democratically elected Republican government of Spain against the invading fascist forces of Generalissimo Franco.

Amid thousands of volunteers from other countries, they formed a distinctly Canadian unit: Widely known as the Mac-Paps, the storied Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion was named after the leaders of the 1837 Rebellions in Upper and Lower Canada.

Hundreds died on the Spanish battlefield, never to see Canada again.

Mr. Okonski, a 25-year-old Polish-Ukrainian miner from Alberta, survived the savagery of the Spanish Civil War. But he was wounded twice, at the brutal Battle of Teruel and later, more severely, during the ill-fated Ebro Offensive in 1938, the Republic’s last-ditch, unsuccessful effort to halt Franco’s advancing armies.

Like a lot of Mac-Paps, he returned traumatized by what he saw and experienced in Spain.

Making matters worse was the reception accorded Mr. Okonski and his fellow combatants back in Canada. Rather than being lionized for their courage and willingness to put their lives on the line to confront fascism in a far-off country, the Mac-Paps were hounded and ostracized by Canadian authorities for defying a hastily passed ordinance making it illegal to enlist in a foreign war. Some had their passports confiscated. Others were threatened with arrest. Many were blacklisted for being communists, kept under regular surveillance by the RCMP.

Noting that just a year later, Canada, itself, was embroiled in all-out war against Germany and Italy, the same fascist countries whose military assistance had turned the tide in Spain, the Mac-Paps referred to themselves, sardonically, as “premature anti-fascists.”

Mr. Okonski was no longer the person who had left for Spain. He drifted from job to job, married and fathered two daughters but drifted away from those responsibilities, too. He became an alcoholic, eventually winding up on skid row in Vancouver, now known as the Downtown Eastside. He died in 1976 at the age of 64.

Ms. Whelan Jones’s mother did not know he had died until after she put a poignant personal ad in the Vancouver Sun, asking if anyone knew the whereabouts of her father. Someone referred her to his small death notice in the Sun. He was buried in an unmarked grave in the city’s Mountain View Cemetery.

But Mr. Okonski has not been entirely forgotten. In recent years, ON Remembrance Day, a small group of Canadians dedicated to preserving the legacy of the Mackenzie-Papineau Battalion have pinpointed and made pilgrimages to known graves of those who fought in Spain.

The initiative has been spearheaded by Raymond Hoff, a retired academic in Victoria, whose American father, Harold, also a volunteer in Spain, was taken in by the Mac-Paps during a hellish retreat from Italian warplanes and artillery. While researching and compiling biographies of as many Mac-Paps as the group could find, Mr. Hoff uncovered Mr. Okonski’s history and the location of his unmarked grave.

Last year, Ms. Whelan Jones came across a photo of two roses placed on her grandfather’s final resting place by the friends of the Mac-Paps. She was overcome.

“I saw the photo, and like, I cried, thinking of my mother. All these years, she thought that her dad didn’t matter to anybody because nobody contacted her when he passed.” Nobody contacted her mother’s sister. “They treated his death like he didn’t have a family.”

In a heartfelt message to the volunteers who gathered at his grave to pay tribute to her grandfather, she wrote: “Thank you for placing a rose on his grave and honouring his service. My mom carried a lot of sadness that her father ended up in an unmarked grave and felt that nobody cared about her dad or thought he was important.

“That is why seeing that photograph of a rose being placed on his grave meant so much to me. I wish my mom could have seen it. She would have known that all these years later, someone still remembered her dad.”

Like many Mac-Paps, Mr. Okonski had joined the Communist Party of Canada, persuaded by the economic hardships of the Depression that capitalism no longer worked. In 1935, he joined the famous On-to-Ottawa Trek by hundreds of unemployed, travelling by boxcar across the country to confront Prime Minister R. B. Bennett. The RCMP halted the protest in Regina with tear gas and billy clubs. Two years later, Mr. Okonski was in Spain.

Afterward, he worked intermittently as a butcher and was mostly missing from the lives of his two daughters. They remembered only brief visits when he would show up with a bunch of fruit, maybe do a special Ukrainian dance or teach them how to eat sausage. “You eat a piece of sausage and then you take a bite of bread,” her mother told Ms. Whelan Jones.

He had regular brushes with the law, usually brought on by his drinking. Ms. Whelan Jones believes he suffered from post-traumatic stress disorder. Her mom’s older sister remembered him waking in the night, running around the house and chasing his daughters outside, beset by a terrible flashback or night terror. He died alone, in his single room, of a weakened heart.

As she has learned more about her grandfather, Ms. Whelan Jones has become increasingly proud of him, despite his troubled life. “He had a lot of passionate ideals and fought for people’s rights,” she said.

Over the years, the renown of the Mac-Paps has been enhanced with monuments in Victoria, Toronto and Ottawa. Ms. Whelan Jones was moved to see a photograph of Mr. Okonski’s name on the Ottawa memorial, unveiled in 2001 by Governor-General Adrienne Clarkson.

Mac-Pap supporters, meanwhile, will be out again this Remembrance Day to pause and remember soldiers who have never been recognized as “official veterans” by government or the Canadian Legion.

“It’s sad that they’re not remembered at the traditional Remembrance Day ceremonies,” said Pamela Vincent, who co-ordinates the trek to the Mountain View Cemetery. Her great-uncle, Peter Johnson, was killed during an early bombing raid in Spain. “They saw the threat of fascism and did their part.”

As for Ms. Whelan Jones, she said she and her two siblings now hope to provide a proper headstone for their grandfather.

“My mother always thought he’d been buried in a mass grave with other uncollected ashes. Now that we know where he rests, we’re looking into having a beautiful grave marker placed there, so that he can be properly remembered,” she said.

“The marker will also identify him as a Mac-Pap veteran.”

stories.title: Budget 2026: Experts welcome Ottawa’s plan to eradicate homelessness, but call for more details, funding
stories.summary: Federal budget proposes nearly $30-billion in spending to end homelessness within a decade
stories.author: Patrick White
stories.content:
Save the date: Nov. 5, 2036.

That’s the deadline for ending homelessness in Canada laid out in last week’s federal budget , which proposes nearly $30-billion in spending to put a roof over every Canadian within a decade.

Governments here and abroad have tried – and mostly failed – to slap a best-before date on homelessness in the past, making Prime Minister Mark Carney’s pledge appear quixotic on its face. But housing researchers and advocates for the homeless say the latest plan is a worthy gamble, though one that will need more details, and more money, to be fully realized.

“What we see here is a substantial down payment, but I don’t think this by itself will be enough,” said Tim Richter, president and chief executive officer of the Canadian Alliance to End Homelessness (Caeh), of Ottawa’s recent financial commitment. “I expect this is an initial investment, and you’ll expect to see some provincial investment as part of the negotiations.”

The 2036 plan includes $10-billion in funding for 25,000 supportive and transitional homes through Build Canada Homes, Ottawa’s new housing agency. Another $12-billion will go to low-income rental assistance and the Reaching Home program, which funds community-based initiatives across the country.

The final plank focuses on health, with $5-billion to build facilities that address housing, health and other social-service needs under one roof, as well as $2-billion to construct and refurbish community mental-health and addictions treatment centres.

Ottawa has already identified its model city for the program, Winnipeg , where it has committed up to $800-million for 2,000 homes, plus another $200-million on a new mental-health and addictions centre. The housing will consist of both transitional units, which act as a temporary bridge for people moving away from the streets or shelters, and supportive units, which feature on-site assistance for health and well-being.

Provincial and municipal buy-in will be key, Mr. Carney said during a press conference last Friday in Winnipeg. Manitoba will operate the homes and pay for half the cost of the new mental-health centre.

The funding plan seems to mark an “important shift” in Ottawa’s housing strategy, said Abe Oudshoorn, associate professor in the school of nursing at Western University. A 2017 housing plan – the 10-year, $115-billion National Housing Strategy – yielded plenty of low-interest loans to for-profit developers building market rentals, but it did little to curb homelessness. Mr. Carney’s plan focuses on direct spending for people with the highest housing needs.

“I do think that’s important language and an important shift in what the feds might be doing on housing, and I do think that will work,” Dr. Oudshoorn said.

The 2017 strategy targeted a 50-per-cent reduction in chronic homelessness between 2016 and 2028. In 2023, the government doubled down on the timeline, vowing to eradicate chronic homelessness – typically referring to people who’ve been without stable housing for at least six months in the past year – by 2030.

Instead, homelessness has nearly doubled across Canada since 2018, to almost 65,000 people.

A 2024 from the Parliamentary Budget Officer found both goals were misaligned with actual funding, and said an extra $3.5-billion a year – a seven-fold budget increase – would be required to meet the 50-per-cent goal.

Few know the promise and peril of such timelines like federal Housing Minister Gregor Robertson, who, during his 2008 Vancouver mayoralty campaign, vowed to end street homelessness by 2015. Instead, the number of people living on the streets in the City of Vancouver has grown steadily, from around 1,400 in 2005 to 2,715 last year.

“We set the goal, but the federal and provincial governments were not co-ordinating, were not investing, at the scale that was needed to solve the challenge in Vancouver,” said Mr. Robertson at the Friday press conference.

Finland has targeted eradicating homelessness by 2027. Between 2012 and 2023, the country managed to reduce its homeless population by more than half with a housing-first policy that views a permanent home as a basic human right.

But a change of government brought cuts to social services and a subsequent surge in people without homes over the last two years.

In Britain, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has pledged to get rough sleepers off the streets by Christmas, drawing from his experience as Mayor of Greater Manchester, where a similar promise yielded mixed results.

Canada has a few basic problems to address first. For one, the country doesn’t keep close tabs on homeless numbers.

“It’s really hard to say we’re going to end homelessness when we still have no idea nationally how many people don’t have homes across Canada,” said Carolyn Whitzman, professor and researcher at the University of Toronto’s School of Cities.

Dr. Whitzman recently prepared a report for the Federal Housing Advocate, an independent, non-partisan watchdog, in which she estimated governments would need to create 50,000 low-cost supportive housing units a year to end homelessness by 2040.

The budget provides for far less than that. Still, Dr. Whitzman is optimistic.

“The federal government is a super-tanker, and now at least the super-tanker is headed in the right direction,” she said. “Now we just need the other levels of government to do the same.”

With a report from Jeff Gray

stories.title: Gun users battle Ottawa’s firearms ban at Supreme Court
stories.summary: Challengers against 2020 regulations banning assault-style weapons have lost twice in the lower courts
stories.author: David Ebner
stories.content:
The federal government will defend its 2020 ban on assault-style firearms at the Supreme Court of Canada on Monday, taking on an array of challengers that argue Ottawa exceeded its legal authority.

The case, to be heard Monday and Tuesday, is the biggest hearing at the top court this fall. It centres around legal questions about the reasonable extent of Ottawa’s power to ban weapons such the AR-15, Beretta Cx4 Storm and other firearms to protect public safety despite the use of the guns in some cases for sport shooting or hunting.

The federal Liberals enacted the ban under former prime minister Justin Trudeau. “Assault-style firearms designed for military use have no place in Canada,” he said at the time. Ottawa invoked its regulatory powers, rather than legislation, to ban more than 1,500 types of firearms in 2020, and increased the list of banned guns to more than 2,500 in late 2024 and early 2025.

The lower courts have twice ruled in Ottawa’s favour. The Supreme Court in March agreed to hear the appeals.

A continuing amnesty period for the possession of the prohibited weapons is in effect until 90 days after a judgment from the Supreme Court. Businesses and individuals can dispose of their guns or permanently deactivate them, and Ottawa is also buying them back. As of mid-2026, the federal government had paid businesses $96-million for about 74,000 guns – an average of $1,300 per weapon.

The firearms case involves four different challengers and, unusually, includes several self-represented litigants who will argue in front of the nine judges of the Supreme Court without a lawyer. Five other gun groups as well as the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario also oppose the ban.

The appellant Christine Generoux, from Ottawa and in her late 30s, has been dubbed “an unlikely heroine of Canadian gun culture” by a sport shooting group. She is set to argue her case herself on Monday morning, and in her legal filing said there was no justification to deem the guns unreasonable for use in recreational purposes. She also spoke of what she called the sentimental, life-sustaining and cultural nature of guns.

“Sport shooting is destroyed and hunting disrupted,” Ms. Generoux stated. She further argued the issue goes deeper than reasonableness – a key legal question of whether Ottawa stayed within the limits of its powers. “It strikes at the heart of Parliamentary democracy and Canadian identity.”

The Canadian Coalition for Firearms Rights, an appellant that does have legal counsel, argued the heart of the firearms case goes beyond the individual rights of gun owners. The group said Ottawa’s regulations were too vague to be within its powers and described this as legality succumbing to “ambiguous administrative will, leaving people to navigate a standardless whim.”

The group stated that mass shootings are rare in Canada, “claims of firearm use in homicides are exaggerated” and most high-profile shootings involve illegal guns.

The ban “concerns the profound disruption of the lives of ordinary, law-abiding Canadians,” it argued in its appeal. “They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters, and neighbours in communities across Canada.”

The federal government’s response began by listing a series of deadly mass shootings in Canada and around the world where the killers wielded assault-style firms, starting with Portapique, N.S., in 2020, Montreal’s L’École Polytechnique in 1989 and the Islamic Culture Centre in Quebec City in 2017.

Ottawa’s response then addressed the core of the legal case: whether the federal cabinet was allowed to use regulations based on a section in the Criminal Code to achieve its public-safety policy objectives rather than through the legislative powers of Parliament. The minority Liberal government tried and failed to codify the banned assault-style firearms in law in 2023.

The federal government is arguing that Parliament has long empowered cabinet with broad discretionary authority to prohibit firearms in the interest of public safety, and that the exercise of that political power “was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms pose.”

Ottawa has few allies at the top court. The Canadian Coalition for Gun Control, an intervener in the case, provides the only explicit backing, echoing the federal government’s position that the Criminal Code allows for the authority to pass regulations to ban the firearms. The group cited the overriding purpose of public safety and argued that the broad nature of the ban adheres with the rule of law.

The three provincial governments that intervened in the case are all conservative-led and are once more opposing the federal Liberals at the Supreme Court, as they had earlier this year in the landmark case on Quebec secularism and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

Alberta and Saskatchewan said Ottawa overstepped its powers in the firearms ban, while Ontario more plainly stated: “The regulations are unconstitutional.”

Alberta hired veteran lawyer Guy Pratte at Borden Ladner Gervais in Ottawa to helm its arguments. His father, Yves, was a Supreme Court judge in the late 1970s, and earlier this year Mr. Pratte argued on behalf of the federal government in the Quebec secularism case.

Alberta’s legal filing said Ottawa “at the stroke of a pen” criminalized firearms ownership for more than 100,000 Canadians licensed to own such guns for hunting and sport shooting “without any evidence that these firearms users pose a threat to public safety.”

The province also said hunting and participation in shooting sports are “matters of exclusive provincial jurisdiction” and that the Criminal Code only allows cabinet to ban guns by regulation if they are not reasonable to use for those purposes, rather than in pursuit of a policy of public safety.

The federal government is arguing that Parliament has long empowered cabinet with broad discretionary authority to prohibit firearms in the interest of public safety, and that the exercise of that political power “was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms pose.”

Ottawa has few allies at the top court. The Canadian Coalition for Gun Control, an intervener in the case, provides the only explicit backing, echoing the federal government’s position that the Criminal Code allows for the authority to pass regulations to ban the firearms. The group cited the overriding purpose of public safety and argued that the broad nature of the ban adheres with the rule of law.

The three provincial governments that intervened in the case are all conservative-led and are once more opposing the federal Liberals at the Supreme Court, as they had earlier this year in the landmark case on Quebec secularism and the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
Alberta and Saskatchewan said Ottawa overstepped its powers in the firearms ban, while Ontario more plainly stated: “The regulations are unconstitutional.”

Alberta hired veteran lawyer Guy Pratte at Borden Ladner Gervais in Ottawa to helm its arguments. His father, Yves, was a Supreme Court judge in the late 1970s, and earlier this year Mr. Pratte argued on behalf of the federal government in the Quebec secularism case.

Alberta’s legal filing said Ottawa “at the stroke of a pen” criminalized firearms ownership for more than 100,000 Canadians licensed to own such guns for hunting and sport shooting “without any evidence that these firearms users pose a threat to public safety.”

The province also said hunting and participation in shooting sports are “matters of exclusive provincial jurisdiction” and that the Criminal Code only allows cabinet to ban guns by regulation if they are not reasonable to use for those purposes, rather than in pursuit of a policy of public safety.

stories.title: Métis veteran reflects on Canada’s treatment of Indigenous veterans
stories.summary: For the Canadian Armed Forces veteran and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101 president, remembering that service is also an opportunity to honour his Métis heritage.
stories.author: Kamil Karamali
stories.content:
Toronto – Looking through photographs of his father and grandfather, Alan Roy traces a family history of military service through faded images and medals that predate his own time in uniform.

His father served in the Second World War. His grandfather, Roy says, served in both world wars.

“Third generation in the military,” Roy, 64, said, describing his own place in that family tradition.

For the Canadian Armed Forces veteran and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 101 president, remembering that service is also an opportunity to honour his Métis heritage.

“My pride in being Canadian is only increased by the fact that we can say we have Métis heritage,” Roy said, who describes his own military experience as one of belonging. “I never felt that I was being ostracized because of whatever my background was at that time.”

But he also acknowledges a broader history of discrimination against Indigenous veterans — one that recognition today cannot erase.

“It’ll never go away. It’s part of our history now,” he said. “Many of them have suffered for their heritage. I know from personal experience, many of these people are upset over the way things happened. There are a lot of horror stories out there.”

Service abroad, barriers at home

Veterans Affairs Canada acknowledges that many Indigenous veterans did not receive equal treatment when they returned from military service.

First Nations veterans faced unequal access to land and benefits. After the First World War, reserve land was transferred to non-Indigenous veterans, while most First Nations veterans applying for equivalent land grants received permission to use land already belonging to their communities rather than ownership.

Métis veterans faced different barriers. In a 2019 apology, Ottawa acknowledged that postwar benefits were poorly designed to meet their needs. Many lacked the prerequisites to access education and training programs, against a backdrop of prejudice, poverty and limited educational opportunities.

Veterans Affairs estimates that more than 12,000 First Nations, Métis and Inuit people served in the major conflicts of the 20th century. At least 500 lost their lives.

Rob Baskey, a senator with the Métis Nation of Ontario Veterans’ Council and an Eagle Staff carrier, says ensuring veterans receive the benefits they deserve is part of reconciliation.

“I think we can always be better,” he said. “If Indigenous Veterans are finally receiving those benefits that they should have been receiving... I think that’s a positive step forward towards reconciliation. But we can always do better.”

Making remembrance more visible

Dozens of people gathered Sunday at the Spirit Garden outside Toronto City Hall to mark Indigenous Veterans Day.

For Baskey, the public ceremony is one part of a year-round responsibility to remember those who served – saying that Indigenous Veterans Day needs to attract greater awareness and attendance.

“There’s a crowd here but it’s not on the scale that it should be. If people knew about this ceremony, it’s going to happen today... it would be more people,” he said.

In a joint statement Sunday, federal ministers said: “The Government of Canada remains committed to ensuring that all Indigenous Veterans receive the recognition and support they deserve.”

Roy sees progress in the recognition of Indigenous service and identity within the military, pointing to visible expressions of that heritage on uniforms.

“Every step is a good one,” he said.

As he looks through his family’s photographs, that history remains close at hand: three generations of service, preserved for another generation to remember.
