stories.title: Tale of two outbreaks: Canada stamps out measles while cases grow in the U.S.
stories.summary: Two infants among three deaths linked to the disease in the United States this week
stories.author: Alanna Smith
stories.content:
A string of measles deaths in the United States this week – two in states that haven’t reported deaths of this kind in more than three decades – is underscoring the divergent responses to the highly contagious virus in the U.S. and Canada and the resulting outcomes.

Both countries have faced widespread and deadly measles cases that have sickened thousands, fuelled by growing pockets of unvaccinated individuals, particularly in Mennonite communities. But Canada has managed to do what the U.S. hasn’t: Put an end to the outbreak.

Down south the situation is growing worse, with three deaths announced this week. On Thursday, health officials in Wisconsin reported an infant death, the first measles-related fatality in the state since 1990. It followed the deaths of a seven-month-old in New York – another first in 30 years – and a Pennsylvania resident.

Immunologist Dawn Bowdish, a professor of medicine at McMaster University in Hamilton, said it will take time and greater analysis to compare the response of the two countries, but Canada’s strong commitment to public health and emphasis on vaccination likely set it on a different path.

“In Canada, that’s been a very clear part of our control in these outbreaks, whereas in the U.S. we hear every day more and more misinformation about measles coming from the highest officials of the land.”

Dr. Bowdish said Canadian officials, regardless of their political stripe or the province they represent, have not questioned measles deaths or engaged in sustained vaccine misinformation efforts, unlike U.S. Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“People do make their decisions based on what they hear in the news and what they hear from public health officials,” she said. “There’s no doctor, public health official or chief medical officer who I can think of in Canada who’s ever criticized the value of vaccination in reducing the measles epidemic.”

Canada declared the years-long measles outbreak over in October, after more than two months without a new, linked case being reported. The outbreak began in October 2024 in New Brunswick before spreading across the country, infecting more than 6,400 people and killing two premature babies .

Cases in Canada greatly eclipsed the total count in the United States in 2025, even though the U.S. population is more than eight times larger.

The U.S. outbreak began in Texas that January and has resulted in around 7,000 confirmed cases, with the majority identified this year. The number of infections is likely much higher because of under-reporting. At least 10 deaths – a combination of children and adults – have been confirmed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments.

Many U.S. public health officials have blamed Mr. Kennedy for worsening the crisis. He has led a significant overhaul of federal health agencies – constraining the government’s ability to track and manage cases – advanced vaccine skepticism and disputed measles-related deaths.

The measles outbreak emerged as a prominent issue ahead of the recent midterms, which saw the Democrats take control of the House and Senate in a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump . Roughly a dozen doctors and nurses, many of whom made their opposition to Mr. Kennedy’s agenda a feature of their campaign, flipped Republican-held congressional seats.

There is now buzz that Democrats will work to strengthen public health and address a range of health issues, such as the price of prescription drugs and vaccine policies. This shift could help clamp down on the spread of measles, a once forgotten disease.

Annie Andrews, who became the first pediatrician to be elected to the U.S. Senate after she defeated Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina on Tuesday, has vowed to hold her “arch nemesis” Mr. Kennedy accountable for public health damage, also blaming him for the measles surge in her home state last spring.

Cross-border travel and shared religious and cultural communities mean the U.S. and Canada are intrinsically connected when it comes to measles transmission. While Canada was stripped of its measles elimination status last year, it is working hard to earn it back. Continued spread in the U.S. and elsewhere, however, pose a risk to these efforts.

Joss Reimer, Chief Public Health Officer, said last month that Canada had reached an “encouraging milestone” by ending its outbreak. But she warned that measles continues to circulate globally and said to expect travel-related cases to pop-up here.

“Vaccination remains our best defence against measles, and keeping routine vaccinations up-to-date is essential to preventing future outbreaks and protecting our communities,” Dr. Reimer said in a statement.

Achieving blanket immunity against measles requires 95 per cent of the population to be fully immunized with two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine or have had a previous infection. Both the U.S. and Canada are shy of the 95 per cent national threshold and, in certain regions, have rates far below.

Dr. Bowdish stressed that Canada cannot take its eye off the ball, considering measles is one of the world’s most contagious diseases.

“You can’t be lax with the rules we have in place. You can’t underfund public health and we have to work on trust,” she said. “You don’t get to relax with these sorts of things. You have to keep working on it, otherwise we’ll be in the same place again.”
paragraphs: A string of measles deaths in the United States this week – two in states that haven’t reported deaths of this kind in more than three decades – is underscoring the divergent responses to the highly contagious virus in the U.S. and Canada and the resulting outcomes.

Both countries have faced widespread and deadly measles cases that have sickened thousands, fuelled by growing pockets of unvaccinated individuals, particularly in Mennonite communities. But Canada has managed to do what the U.S. hasn’t: Put an end to the outbreak.

Down south the situation is growing worse, with three deaths announced this week. On Thursday, health officials in Wisconsin reported an infant death, the first measles-related fatality in the state since 1990. It followed the deaths of a seven-month-old in New York – another first in 30 years – and a Pennsylvania resident.

Immunologist Dawn Bowdish, a professor of medicine at McMaster University in Hamilton, said it will take time and greater analysis to compare the response of the two countries, but Canada’s strong commitment to public health and emphasis on vaccination likely set it on a different path.

“In Canada, that’s been a very clear part of our control in these outbreaks, whereas in the U.S. we hear every day more and more misinformation about measles coming from the highest officials of the land.”

Dr. Bowdish said Canadian officials, regardless of their political stripe or the province they represent, have not questioned measles deaths or engaged in sustained vaccine misinformation efforts, unlike U.S. Secretary of Health Robert F. Kennedy Jr.

“People do make their decisions based on what they hear in the news and what they hear from public health officials,” she said. “There’s no doctor, public health official or chief medical officer who I can think of in Canada who’s ever criticized the value of vaccination in reducing the measles epidemic.”

Canada declared the years-long measles outbreak over in October, after more than two months without a new, linked case being reported. The outbreak began in October 2024 in New Brunswick before spreading across the country, infecting more than 6,400 people and killing two premature babies .
Cases in Canada greatly eclipsed the total count in the United States in 2025, even though the U.S. population is more than eight times larger.

The U.S. outbreak began in Texas that January and has resulted in around 7,000 confirmed cases, with the majority identified this year. The number of infections is likely much higher because of under-reporting. At least 10 deaths – a combination of children and adults – have been confirmed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and state health departments.

Many U.S. public health officials have blamed Mr. Kennedy for worsening the crisis. He has led a significant overhaul of federal health agencies – constraining the government’s ability to track and manage cases – advanced vaccine skepticism and disputed measles-related deaths.

The measles outbreak emerged as a prominent issue ahead of the recent midterms, which saw the Democrats take control of the House and Senate in a stunning rebuke to U.S. President Donald Trump . Roughly a dozen doctors and nurses, many of whom made their opposition to Mr. Kennedy’s agenda a feature of their campaign, flipped Republican-held congressional seats.

There is now buzz that Democrats will work to strengthen public health and address a range of health issues, such as the price of prescription drugs and vaccine policies. This shift could help clamp down on the spread of measles, a once forgotten disease.

Annie Andrews, who became the first pediatrician to be elected to the U.S. Senate after she defeated Republican Darline Graham in South Carolina on Tuesday, has vowed to hold her “arch nemesis” Mr. Kennedy accountable for public health damage, also blaming him for the measles surge in her home state last spring.

Cross-border travel and shared religious and cultural communities mean the U.S. and Canada are intrinsically connected when it comes to measles transmission. While Canada was stripped of its measles elimination status last year, it is working hard to earn it back. Continued spread in the U.S. and elsewhere, however, pose a risk to these efforts.

Joss Reimer, Chief Public Health Officer, said last month that Canada had reached an “encouraging milestone” by ending its outbreak. But she warned that measles continues to circulate globally and said to expect travel-related cases to pop-up here.

“Vaccination remains our best defence against measles, and keeping routine vaccinations up-to-date is essential to preventing future outbreaks and protecting our communities,” Dr. Reimer said in a statement.

Achieving blanket immunity against measles requires 95 per cent of the population to be fully immunized with two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine or have had a previous infection. Both the U.S. and Canada are shy of the 95 per cent national threshold and, in certain regions, have rates far below.
Dr. Bowdish stressed that Canada cannot take its eye off the ball, considering measles is one of the world’s most contagious diseases.

“You can’t be lax with the rules we have in place. You can’t underfund public health and we have to work on trust,” she said. “You don’t get to relax with these sorts of things. You have to keep working on it, otherwise we’ll be in the same place again.”

stories.title: Seven officers fired, a force under scrutiny: Can Montreal police rebuild public trust?
stories.summary: Seven officers have been fired amid a sweeping misconduct scandal. Critics question if firings and transparency are enough for Montreal police to deliver accountability.
stories.author: Alessia Simona Maratta
stories.content:
Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher has put transparency at the centre of his public response to a months-long misconduct scandal that has rocked the force and raised broader questions about public trust and accountability, as the force investigates allegations of racism, discrimination, criminal misconduct and the mistreatment of vulnerable people.

He has appeared before reporters, ON television and in radio interviews while promising consequences for officers found to have committed wrongdoing. This week, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (Spvm) took its most significant action yet, announcing at once the unprecedented firing of seven officers .

But researchers and community advocates interviewed by Global News say the firings and Dagher’s public visibility raise fundamental questions about the force’s response. They argue that making misconduct public and punishing individual officers does not necessarily address the conditions that allowed it to occur, while some are also questioning how the Spvm is managing its message as the scandal unfolds.

“There’s transparency, which they’re great at as part of their PR, but then there’s also accountability, which I think they skirt around,” said Daniele-Jocelyne Otou, executive director of Montreal’s Black Healing Centre and co-founder of New Room.

Ricardo Lamour, a community worker, human rights advocate and former fellow of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights program in Geneva, was more pointed in his criticism.

“For me, it’s a push to control the narrative at all costs,” Lamour said.

He said the response should be viewed in the context of Dagher’s public image as a chief who has emphasized his proximity to Montreal communities.

“The proximity brand is cracking,” he said. He believes the chief and the mayor are now presenting what he described as a shared narrative of “a reforming chief against a resistant culture.”

The criticism comes after the Spvm announced Monday that seven officers had been fired over allegations involving racism, discrimination and the mistreatment of vulnerable people. Five were based at Station 39 in Montreal North and two were from Station 21 downtown.

Dagher called it an “unprecedented and historic” day, and said the seven officers, both men and women, had turned in their guns and badges.

“Some people say there are never any consequences at the Spvm. Today we are announcing exceptional measures,” he said. Dagher said the cases involve about one per cent of the force and praised the work of the other 99 per cent of officers. He also said the “culture of silence” within the Spvm had been broken.

Others have described the dismissals as a significant step.

Sonia Para Jordan of Action Plan Against Intimate Partner Violence called the firings a good start.

“This is a big step forward and sets a precedent of more definitive consequence to misconduct from police officers,” she said, adding she hopes criminal charges will be laid.

For Otou, however, the firings do not by themselves answer questions about whether broader problems within the force are being addressed.

“Announcing that seven officers have been fired is not in and of itself evidence that the underlying institutional conditions that allow the misconducts to occur in the first place have changed or are being dealt with,” she said.

The allegations involving Montreal police first surfaced earlier this year. Police began investigating a patrol team in Montreal North in March after receiving internal complaints about alleged racism and criminal misconduct. Those allegations included reports that officers cut the hair of racialized citizens and kept it as trophies. The team was later dismantled.

At Station 21 in downtown Montreal, separate allegations emerged involving the mistreatment of people experiencing homelessness, including one claim that an officer urinated on an unhoused person.

Police also announced last week that an officer could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a 2025 domestic violence case. Other allegations that have surfaced in recent months include an officer who allegedly posed for photographs mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions.

Dagher said Monday the cases have been submitted to the Crown prosecutor’s office. Prosecutors will determine whether criminal charges should be laid.

The way the Spvm has announced major developments has also drawn criticism.

Several news conferences throughout the scandal have been called on short notice, often late in the day and just before the weekend. The first, back in June, was announced just over an hour before it was held at 9 p.m. on a Friday.

Asked about the abrupt scheduling, the Spvm told Global News, “In certain situations that are exceptional in nature or of particular importance, the Montreal police service May call a media availability on short notice in order to quickly communicate information that is in the public interest.”

Ted Rutland, an associate professor at Concordia University whose research focuses on policing and public security in Canadian cities, said the immediacy makes it more difficult for journalists and others to prepare.

“It seems to me that the way that these press conferences are called late, that makes it very hard for journalists to prepare their questions and very hard to get responses from organizations,” he said.

Rutland said he believes it fits within “an overall public relations and communication strategy that seeks to control how we talk about the problems that we see with the police department.”

Otou raised a similar concern. “When an institution announces a press conference an hour before it happens, ON a Friday, it influences who has the opportunity to prepare and participate,” she said.

“It really dictates and controls the conditions of the conversation.”

Otou said the timing can affect whether journalists have time to independently investigate and verify information, challenge what is being presented and seek perspectives beyond the institution’s own framing.

Anne-Marie Livingstone, an assistant professor of sociology at McMaster University, whose research includes racism in policing, said she agrees with criticism of the Spvm’s response.

Livingstone said her research has found a lack of political will to address racism in policing across Canada and described police unions and rank-and-file officers as major opponents to change.

She characterized the Spvm leadership’s approach as a public relations and “damage control” strategy aimed at satisfying public concerns without alienating the union and rank-and-file officers.

The Montreal police union, La Fraternité des policiers et policières de Montréal (Fppm), also referred to as the Montreal Police Brotherhood, said this week it intends to challenge the seven dismissals.

Union president Yves Francoeur said in a message to members this week that the officers’ alleged actions, if substantiated, would profoundly violate police values.

But he said the administrative process used to fire them was unprecedented and raised “fundamental questions of law.”

“This is a method that’s entirely unprecedented in our history of labour relations, which has never been used and does not appear anywhere,” Francoeur wrote Tuesday. “This approach appears to us to be clearly non-compliant and could prove harmful in the future.”

Francoeur said the union “will defend the rule of law, and will take appropriate measures to do so.”

The police union did not respond to a request for additional comment.

Dagher said Monday that Montreal police consulted city lawyers before revoking the officers’ accreditation and security clearances through what he described as an administrative dismissal.

He acknowledged the officers could contest their dismissals and seek reinstatement. If they return, he said, the force would refer them to its disciplinary committee.

Dagher said immediate action was necessary to maintain public trust.

For Otou, however, rebuilding that trust requires more than managing how an institution presents itself publicly.

“If anything, it reinforces the lack of trust because the emphasis is placed on their image as opposed to addressing the actual root of the problem.”

Lamour said he believes the public also needs more information about police misconduct, including the names of the dismissed officers.

“There’s been a slow erosion of the information we need when it comes to police misconduct,” he said, referencing past documented incidents of racism in policing and cases of police brutality in Montreal.

He also called for outside oversight when public trust in local authorities has been seriously damaged.

“There should be some form of state oversight when there’s such a rupture of the trust that people have in regards to police,” Lamour said.

Alain Babineau, a McGill jurist, retired RCMP staff sergeant and Red Coalition racial profiling director, told Global News earlier this week that he welcomed Dagher’s efforts to address racist behaviour, but believes accountability should extend further up the ranks.

“I want to see more,” Babineau said. “I want to see some sergeants, some inspector, lieutenant, and if need be, some assistant commissioner or assistant director that takes the fall for this.”

Babineau also criticized Dagher for using part of Monday’s news conference to praise officers who were not implicated. “It was not the time to give the good cops flowers. It was a time to hit on the head of the bad cops and to also reassure the community,” he said.

Questions about accountability have also extended beyond the Spvm to Montreal City Hall.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said Monday the Spvm had taken “an unprecedented step to rebuild public trust.” “No one is above the rules,” she said. “This work is demanding and necessary, and it must continue.”

Rutland, however, said focusing primarily on Dagher risks overlooking the responsibility of the municipal government that oversees the police service.

“Fady Dagher is not a problematic police chief. The problem is not him.”

Rutland said he believes the problem is broader and includes successive municipal administrations that have relied on police to address public safety issues.

When Global News asked the mayor’s office to respond to Rutland’s criticism about the city’s accountability, it said it would not provide further comment.

Quebec’s newly minted internal security minister Guy Lapointe Jr. said the allegations against Montreal police officers are extremely troubling and unacceptable.

“This is not the kind of behaviour that can be tolerated under any circumstances by police officers, who must have the public’s trust,” said Lapointe. “The premier has given me a very clear mandate: to work on the public’s sense of security.”

For Otou, the question now is whether the consequences announced by the Spvm will be accompanied by changes that go beyond the seven officers who were fired.

“If they don’t have anybody who’s holding them accountable, then how are we supposed to trust that actual systemic change is being done internally?” she said.

Alain Babineau, a McGill jurist, retired RCMP staff sergeant and Red Coalition racial profiling director, told Global News earlier this week that he welcomed Dagher’s efforts to address racist behaviour, but believes accountability should extend further up the ranks.
“I want to see more,” Babineau said. “I want to see some sergeants, some inspector, lieutenant, and if need be, some assistant commissioner or assistant director that takes the fall for this.”

Babineau also criticized Dagher for using part of Monday’s news conference to praise officers who were not implicated. “It was not the time to give the good cops flowers. It was a time to hit on the head of the bad cops and to also reassure the community,” he said.
Questions about accountability have also extended beyond the Spvm to Montreal City Hall.

Montreal Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada said Monday the Spvm had taken “an unprecedented step to rebuild public trust.” “No one is above the rules,” she said. “This work is demanding and necessary, and it must continue.”
Rutland, however, said focusing primarily on Dagher risks overlooking the responsibility of the municipal government that oversees the police service.
“Fady Dagher is not a problematic police chief. The problem is not him.”
Rutland said he believes the problem is broader and includes successive municipal administrations that have relied on police to address public safety issues.

content_blocks.text: Montreal police Chief Fady Dagher has put transparency at the centre of his public response to a months-long misconduct scandal that has rocked the force and raised broader questions about public trust and accountability, as the force investigates allegations of racism, discrimination, criminal misconduct and the mistreatment of vulnerable people.

He has appeared before reporters, ON television and in radio interviews while promising consequences for officers found to have committed wrongdoing. This week, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (Spvm) took its most significant action yet, announcing at once the unprecedented firing of seven officers .
content_blocks.html: He has appeared before reporters, on television and in radio interviews while promising consequences for officers found to have committed wrongdoing. This week, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) took its most significant action yet, announcing at once the unprecedented firing of seven officers.

content_blocks.text: But researchers and community advocates interviewed by Global News say the firings and Dagher’s public visibility raise fundamental questions about the force’s response. They argue that making misconduct public and punishing individual officers does not necessarily address the conditions that allowed it to occur, while some are also questioning how the Spvm is managing its message as the scandal unfolds.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Montreal police fire 7 officers over misconduct allegations'

content_blocks.text: “There’s transparency, which they’re great at as part of their PR, but then there’s also accountability, which I think they skirt around,” said Daniele-Jocelyne Otou, executive director of Montreal’s Black Healing Centre and co-founder of New Room.

Ricardo Lamour, a community worker, human rights advocate and former fellow of the Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights program in Geneva, was more pointed in his criticism.
“For me, it’s a push to control the narrative at all costs,” Lamour said.
He said the response should be viewed in the context of Dagher’s public image as a chief who has emphasized his proximity to Montreal communities.
“The proximity brand is cracking,” he said. He believes the chief and the mayor are now presenting what he described as a shared narrative of “a reforming chief against a resistant culture.”

The criticism comes after the Spvm announced Monday that seven officers had been fired over allegations involving racism, discrimination and the mistreatment of vulnerable people. Five were based at Station 39 in Montreal North and two were from Station 21 downtown.
Dagher called it an “unprecedented and historic” day, and said the seven officers, both men and women, had turned in their guns and badges.

“Some people say there are never any consequences at the Spvm. Today we are announcing exceptional measures,” he said. Dagher said the cases involve about one per cent of the force and praised the work of the other 99 per cent of officers. He also said the “culture of silence” within the Spvm had been broken.
Others have described the dismissals as a significant step.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Montreal police chief promises to clean up force'

content_blocks.text: Sonia Para Jordan of Action Plan Against Intimate Partner Violence called the firings a good start.
“This is a big step forward and sets a precedent of more definitive consequence to misconduct from police officers,” she said, adding she hopes criminal charges will be laid.
For Otou, however, the firings do not by themselves answer questions about whether broader problems within the force are being addressed.

“Announcing that seven officers have been fired is not in and of itself evidence that the underlying institutional conditions that allow the misconducts to occur in the first place have changed or are being dealt with,” she said.

The allegations involving Montreal police first surfaced earlier this year. Police began investigating a patrol team in Montreal North in March after receiving internal complaints about alleged racism and criminal misconduct. Those allegations included reports that officers cut the hair of racialized citizens and kept it as trophies. The team was later dismantled.
At Station 21 in downtown Montreal, separate allegations emerged involving the mistreatment of people experiencing homelessness, including one claim that an officer urinated on an unhoused person.

Police also announced last week that an officer could face criminal charges after allegedly concealing evidence related to a 2025 domestic violence case. Other allegations that have surfaced in recent months include an officer who allegedly posed for photographs mocking suspects under arrest in humiliating positions.
Dagher said Monday the cases have been submitted to the Crown prosecutor’s office. Prosecutors will determine whether criminal charges should be laid.
‘Controlling the conditions of the conversation’
content_blocks.html: ‘Controlling the conditions of the conversation’

content_blocks.text: The way the Spvm has announced major developments has also drawn criticism.

Several news conferences throughout the scandal have been called on short notice, often late in the day and just before the weekend. The first, back in June, was announced just over an hour before it was held at 9 p.m. on a Friday.

Asked about the abrupt scheduling, the Spvm told Global News, “In certain situations that are exceptional in nature or of particular importance, the Montreal police service May call a media availability on short notice in order to quickly communicate information that is in the public interest.”

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Montreal police suspended over urination allegations'

content_blocks.text: Ted Rutland, an associate professor at Concordia University whose research focuses on policing and public security in Canadian cities, said the immediacy makes it more difficult for journalists and others to prepare.

“It seems to me that the way that these press conferences are called late, that makes it very hard for journalists to prepare their questions and very hard to get responses from organizations,” he said.
Rutland said he believes it fits within “an overall public relations and communication strategy that seeks to control how we talk about the problems that we see with the police department.”
Otou raised a similar concern. “When an institution announces a press conference an hour before it happens, ON a Friday, it influences who has the opportunity to prepare and participate,” she said.
“It really dictates and controls the conditions of the conversation.”

Otou said the timing can affect whether journalists have time to independently investigate and verify information, challenge what is being presented and seek perspectives beyond the institution’s own framing.
Anne-Marie Livingstone, an assistant professor of sociology at McMaster University, whose research includes racism in policing, said she agrees with criticism of the Spvm’s response.

content_blocks.alt: Click to play video: 'Montreal police chief addresses ‘catastrophic’ evidence yet to surface in officer misconduct case'

content_blocks.text: Livingstone said her research has found a lack of political will to address racism in policing across Canada and described police unions and rank-and-file officers as major opponents to change.
She characterized the Spvm leadership’s approach as a public relations and “damage control” strategy aimed at satisfying public concerns without alienating the union and rank-and-file officers.

stories.title: Aid sector calls out lack of any mention of foreign aid in federal budget
stories.summary: Ottawa — Canada's aid sector is expressing dismay over the first federal budget in more than 15 years to make no mention of foreign aid, and is calling on Ottawa to outline its vision in an upcoming foreign policy review.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
By Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

Posted November 7, 2026 6:00 am.

Last Updated November 7, 2026 7:50 am.

Ottawa — Canada’s aid sector is expressing dismay over the first federal budget in more than 15 years to make no mention of foreign aid, and is calling on Ottawa to outline its vision in an upcoming foreign policy review.

“The budget is largely silent on issues of international development co-operation and humanitarian action,” said Co-operation Canada head Kate Higgins, whose coalition includes most Canadian aid groups operating abroad.

She argued this is the wrong approach “at a time when the stakes around and the world are very high.”

The budget tabled Thursday by Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government makes no mention of international assistance, foreign aid or international development.

The Canadian Press reviewed all budgets tabled since 2010 and found references to those terms in each of those documents.

Thursday’s budget mentions Ukraine only in reference to drone production. It mentions aid workers only in passing, in a section on an existing permit program for aid organizations operating in areas under the control of groups Ottawa lists as terrorist entities.

Higgins said the sector assumes Ottawa will stick with its plan announced last year to cut $2.7 billion in foreign aid over four years.

She and other advocates said they were relieved the government did not announce further cuts. She also said Ottawa should acknowledge the important role development funding plays in addressing crises abroad, such as the humanitarian plight of Palestinians in Gaza and the spread of Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

“International development co-operation addresses the very challenges that the government is seeking to prioritize around defence, around stability, around diplomacy, around economic partnerships, around trade diversification, around a rules-based order that upholds democracy and human rights,” Higgins said.

She said she hopes Ottawa offers more details of its plans for “international development assistance and humanitarian action” in a foreign policy review expected later this month.

In a news conference Friday, Foreign Affairs Minister Anita Anand said the foreign policy update will come in “in a matter of weeks” and will include “our approach on development.”

“Rest assured, development assistance is a priority for Global Affairs Canada. It is the reason why we have come forth with humanitarian assistance for Cuba, for Lebanon, for Gaza, for Sudan, among others, this year alone,” she said on Parliament Hill.

The budget’s lack of any mention of foreign aid came just days after the United Nations’ global head of humanitarian issues, Tom Fletcher, praised Canada as a “humanitarian superpower” for the world’s most vulnerable.

“I really hope that Canada continues to hold the line,” he said four days before the budget.

Results Canada, an anti-poverty advocacy group, posted a photo Thursday of a deflated balloon on social media shortly after the budget’s release. The group’s policy director Lindsay Sheridan said her team searched the document in vain for terms relevant to her sector.

“International assistance, foreign aid, vaccines, tuberculosis — just seeing what was in it. And then continuously nothing came up. There was nothing on famines, either. And so, we were just surprised,” she told a video conference with supporters on Thursday.

“We thought that this might be the moment where we would get a little bit more context, a little more understanding of maybe the direction we would be going.”

Unicef Canada also expressed its disappointment in the budget. It said in a news release Ottawa should at least mention international development when it talks about its response to global threats and volatility.

“International assistance helps children survive and thrive while strengthening the health, education and protection systems on which peaceful, stable societies depend,” the group wrote.

The One Campaign, which advocates for African partnerships, says Ottawa should commit to spending $5.5 billion on development annually in the interest of “safeguarding global health and humanitarian investments that underpin long-term economic stability.”

The group also wrote in a news release that Ottawa should align its “development, trade and investment institutions to support co-ordinated, mutually beneficial partnerships with African countries.”

The House of Commons finance committee had urged Ottawa to use the budget to provide more transparency on where Canada’s aid dollars are going, and to focus funding on the world’s most vulnerable.

Critics have argued the Carney government should outline clearer priorities in aid spending, and spearhead initiatives with peer countries.

Sheridan cited the Harper government’s focus on maternal health and the Trudeau government’s work on providing education to children in conflict zones. Canada led both initiatives with support from G7 peers and global financing institutions.

“It seems like a missed opportunity to make a really well-rounded, robust strategy,” she said. “It seems confusing. Not even a mention.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 2026

Dylan Robertson, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Crisis in Cuba sending Canadian travellers to pricier sun destinations: travel agents
stories.summary: As the winter holiday season approaches, one of the most popular sunny destinations for Canadian travellers remains out of reach.
stories.author: Sharif Hassan The Canadian Press
stories.content:
As the winter holiday season approaches, one of the most popular sunny destinations for Canadian travellers remains out of reach.

The United States’ oil blockade against Cuba triggered severe fuel shortages in the country and prompted Canadian airlines to indefinitely suspend flights to the island destination earlier this year.

Travel agents say Canadians looking to escape the cold weather this year will have to pay more than what they’re used to for affordable all-inclusive packages in Cuba.

One of the most popular sunny destinations for Canadian travellers remains out of reach as bookings ramp up for the winter holiday season. The United States’ oil blockade against Cuba triggered severe fuel shortages in the country and prompted Canadian airlines to indefinitely suspend flights to the island destination earlier this year. (Nov. 7, 2026)

Ashley Harold, a travel agent at Flight Centre Canada, said Mexico, Dominican Republic and several other Caribbean countries and territories such as Aruba, Barbados and Jamaica seem to be getting most of the diversions.

“There isn’t one new Cuba, if you will. Canadians, they’re really spreading their winter travel across a much wider mix of destinations and trip types,” she said in a recent interview.

“We’re also seeing some travellers consider Caribbean cruises or tours to still-warm places like Costa Rica or Peru.”

Domestic tourism is also gaining traction as some Canadians are choosing to visit “fantastic” winter destinations, from Alberta to the West Coast, she said.

“Folks, now more than ever, are wanting to explore their own backyard and keep their dollar within Canada,” she said.

Even though advance bookings have become a new normal after COVID-19, the lack of Cuban vacations has led Canadians to make reservations in other destinations much earlier for best pricing and choice, Harold said.

Cuba welcomed more than a million Canadians annually before the pandemic but that number has been steadily declining in recent years, with visits dropping to around 700,000 in 2025, according to Statistics Canada. The agency recorded 127,000 Canadian visits to Cuba in the first quarter of this year.

Those numbers dropped significantly after U.S. President Donald Trump imposed the oil blockade on Cuba early this year, and the Canadian government subsequently issued a travel advisory due to the shortage of medicine, food and fuel in the country. It still advises Canadians to avoid all non-essential travel to Cuba.

After airlines suspended flights and major hotel chains pulled out of Cuba, the country’s tourism industry and the local economy that heavily depended on it were further devastated. The country of around 11 million people is facing a humanitarian crisis caused by the latest sanctions and the decades-long U.S. trade embargo.

Cuba’s tourism market was dominated by Canadians who relished its affordable winter vacation options. Now, they need to spend hundreds of dollars more to explore other destinations or cut down the number of trips they are making each year, travel agents say.

John Wood, president of Durham Travel east of Toronto, said Cuba visitors are “value conscious” and want to travel as often as they can within their budgets.

Some of Durham Travel’s clients used to go to Cuba “three, four or five times a year … because they could go for a very reasonable price, get away and enjoy the sun and beautiful beaches,” he said in a recent interview.

“And now they can’t do that anymore.”

Wood said his travel agency’s sales to Cuba dropped from more than $389,000 last year to just $24,000 so far into 2026.

Meanwhile, travel sales for the Dominican Republic increased from about $1 million in 2025 to nearly 1.3 million so far this year, he said.

“The Dominican Republic appears to have absorbed most of the difference from Cuba,” he said, noting travellers’ concerns about crime and large seaweed blooms in Mexico.

At Flight Centre Canada, however, Mexico remains the top destination — even if it’s pricier, Harold said.

A seven-day package at a four-star resort in Varadero, Cuba with a flight from Toronto cost under $1,400 per person around the last holiday season, she said. Comparable trips to Mexico, Dominican Republic and Jamaica cost around $1,800 this year, according to Flight Centre data.

“So, for travellers that are used to Cuba pricing, there may need to be a reset in expectations before they start shopping,” Harold said.

But that means tourists can “get creative” with their vacation plans this holiday season, she said.

“I think this is a great opportunity for Canadians to branch out a little bit more with their travels and experience something new.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 2026.

stories.title: N.L. ferry backups are starting to sting the bottom line, and next summer is looking busier
stories.summary: With sales already ahead of last summer’s pace, advocates in Newfoundland and Labrador say it’s time to beef up the province’s link with Canada.
stories.author: Garrett Barry
stories.content:
ST. John’s - On the heels of a busy tourism season — one that saw the Marine Atlantic break records on the North Sydney to Argentia route — a lobby group in Newfoundland and Labrador is calling on the federal government to prepare to meet surging ferry traffic.

With bookings for next summer already ahead of pace, the NL Gulf Ferry Coalition wants the federal government to keep the MV Leif Ericson, Marine Atlantic’s soon-to-retire ferry, in service for as long as it possibly can.

“It’s already approved for two years more sailing, you know, it would be beneficial to use that,” said Chris Howlett, the owner of Akita Equipment near St. John’s. His trucking company — like others — relies on access to the Newfoundland-Nova Scotia ferry routes to keep goods moving on and off the province.

“To me it’s a no brainer … it’s like if your parents gave you a car that was already paid for and you’re a teenager.”

A spokesperson for Marine Atlantic told CTV News that no decision has yet been made as to when the Ericson will leave service, although its replacement vessel arrived last month.

The Ericson is one of four vessels that Marine Atlantic, the federal ferry operator, has used in 2026 between Newfoundland and Nova Scotia. It’s the oldest of the four, built in 1991.

Marine Atlantic sails two routes, a Port aux Basques to North Sydney route, and a summertime Argentia to North Sydney route.

More than 51,000 crossings have already been booked for 2027, according to spokesperson Darrell Mercer. That advance booking number is up about 32 per cent from what it was at a similar point in 2025, for 2026 travel.

“People want to travel. It’s just not for tourism. It’s for a lifeline to Newfoundland and Labrador, for health care, for retail, for trucking, everything else,” said John Devereaux, the chair of Hospitality Newfoundland and Labrador’s board.

Devereaux and Howlett — both part of the NL Gulf Ferry Coalition — met with Transportation Minister Steve MacKinnon in Ottawa last week.

Howlett said long lineups at ferry terminals this summer have started eating into his company’s bottom line, whether he’s paying his drivers to simply wait to get on a vessel, or deciding to have them drop cargo at the dock and come back and pick it up later.

“There’s times that it would take us up to 20, 24 hours to get across just with the amount of people that’s there,” Howlett said. “There’s times we’ll come back to St. John’s and go back out. When your fuel is $2.70 a litre…it’s pretty costly.”

A rate cut to Marine Atlantic ferries that took effect last year — part of Prime Minister Mark Carney’s election campaign in 2025 — further juiced demand. Howlett says now the federal government needs to make a plan for how it will catch up.

“It’s like selling half-priced tickets to a sold-out concert, is what one of my friends explained it as.”

“It’s like having a Blue Rodeo concert, and you’re sold out,. And you say ‘OK, you get half your ticket back,’” added Deveraux. “No, you don’t. You put on an extra Blue Rodeo concert.”

stories.title: How a 60th birthday turned into a mission for 100 blood donations
stories.summary: A Prince Edward Island woman had one wish for her 60th birthday: a blood donation for every candle on her cake, and then some.
stories.author: Maria Sarrouh
stories.content:
Charlottetown – A Prince Edward Island woman had one wish for her 60th birthday: a blood donation for every candle on her cake, and then some.

“It’s hard turning 60, to be honest,” O’Hanley said with a laugh. “So, I wanted to make it something positive.”

She’d spent months rallying people to take part. Among them was Stuart Wight, whose blood was flowing a little slower than usual. He and his colleagues at O’Hanley’s brokerage usually race to see who finishes first.

“So many people need it, and you never know when it could be you or a loved one,” Wight said.

Pam Foy knows that reality firsthand. In 2015, she was diagnosed with breast cancer and needed blood transfusions during her treatment.

“Once I was eligible and in full remission, I decided that I would give back to Canadian Blood Services because they helped me when I needed it most,” Foy said.

She has joined O’Hanley’s campaign, with three donations planned this year.

Canadian Blood Services is on a mission of its own, to recruit one million new donors by 2030. But for some, getting past the fear of that first appointment is no small feat.

“I think there’s still some lack of understanding of what a donation event looks like, what it’s going to feel like,” said Stephen Empringham, the organization’s regional development manager for Atlantic Canada. He added that staff truly care about making the experience enjoyable.

“It’s a very seamless and easy process when you walk in the donation centre.”

About a dozen of O’Hanley’s recruits this week are facing the needle together as first-time donors. Darlene Balderston remembers finding strength in numbers.

“I always wanted to donate and was terrified of needles my whole life. Absolutely terrified,” Balderston said. “I thought, okay, perfect opportunity. I’m going as a group. These are safe people. I’ll be good. And I did it. And it was, honestly, it was the most amazing day ever.”

O’Hanley, whose O-negative blood type makes her a universal red blood cell donor, hopes her birthday campaign will have a similarly lasting impact.

She’s drawn support from all corners of her life, including her 18-year-old son, who recently became eligible to donate, an old high school friend she hadn’t seen in about two decades.

Now, she’s setting her sights on 100 donations by the end of the year - or as many as she can get.

“You can literally save a life by coming here and spending less than an hour and donating blood,” O’Hanley said.

stories.title: Art Toronto Opening Night fundraises for the McMichael, Soulpepper’s the Bootleggers Ball supports training and education programs
stories.summary: Portion of art fair’s proceeds support acquisition of new works from event, while Jazz Age Europe theme a tip to theatre’s coming production
stories.author: Nolan Bryant
stories.content:
More than 100 national and international galleries brought their best for the latest edition of Art Toronto, Canada’s most important annual art fair, held over the last weekend of October. The evening saw art collectors and enthusiasts from across the city gather for an opening night preview, which once again served as a fundraiser for the McMichael Canadian Art Collection.

In addition to supporting the gallery, which is currently closed for a major renovation , a portion of the proceeds went toward the acquisition of a handful of new works from the fair, now destined to join the permanent collection. Elaine Stocki’s Flock from Blouin Division, Peter Campbell’s Belle Coté Harbor from Corkin Gallery and a piece by Lee Henderson from Zalucky Contemporary are among those scooped up by the museum. Other institutions at the fair included the Power Plant Contemporary Art Gallery, the National Gallery in Ottawa, the Banff Centre for Arts and Creativity and the Yellowknife Artist Run Community Centre.

A number of large-scale installations were on offer, including Kathy Slade’s enormous tapestry Sinking in the West, presented by Mónica Reyes Gallery. Also showcased were works by Lynn Donoghue, Abraham Anghik Ruben and Douglas Scholes.

Among those out for opening night: Calgary Contemporary CEO David Leinster and Calgary-based gallerist Shannon Norberg of Norberg Hall; Sarah Milroy, the Frances and Tim Price executive director and chief curator of the McMichael; arts professional Michelle Koerner; AGO photography curator Sophie Hackett and photographers Edward Burtynsky and Christopher Sherman; artists June Clark and Natalka Husar; philanthropic duo Don Tapscott and Ana Lopes; architect Alexander Josephson; fashion designers Andrea Lenczner and Christie Smythe of the label Smythe; and Art Toronto director Emily-Jean Alexander.

On Oct. 28, Soulpepper Theatre hosted the third edition of the Bootleggers Ball, this year with the theme of Jazz Age Europe, a hat tip to the company’s coming production of Parfumerie . Guests entered the party through an alleyway at the side of the building, providing a behind-the-scenes look at the inner-workings of the theatre, which has been housed in Toronto’s historic Distillery District for more than 20 years. It was a winding path through backstage spaces, racks of costumes and set pieces; in one area, performers Divine Brown and Beau Dixon warmed up for the night’s festivities. Guests emerged stage left, and there to greet supporters was the company’s new artistic director, Paolo Santalucia.

Next stop was the lobby, which was abuzz with craps and poker tables (the house always won, and the funds went to the theatre), while offshoot studio spaces hosted a cabaret in full swing and a Prohibition-themed bar. The more casual set-up was a hit, with a handful of guests noting that the typical gala dinner tables were not missed. Later, attendees gathered in the Baillie Theatre for a teaser of Soulpepper’s coming works. Among those on stage were five Soulpepper Academy members and several past participants including Akosua Amo-Adem and Peter Fernandes (who presented a preview of Parfumerie ), and Hailey Gillis who alongside Frank Cox-O’Connell performed a piece from their recent work Tiger Bride .

The night raised a record $440,000 that will support the company’s education and training programs, among other initiatives. Attendees included theatre advocate and producer Elly Barlin-Daniels and senior vice-president of Power Corporation of Canada Paul Genest, who served as co-chairs; fashion designer Kirk Pickersgill; philanthropic duo Stephen Smith and Diane Blake; Soulpepper board chair Dana Lafarga; and actors Damien Atkins and Nancy Palk.

stories.title: As Canada looks to grow its skilled workforce, an Alberta school is starting young
stories.summary: As Canada looks to train more skilled tradespeople to support its ambitious infrastructure and housing plans, a new Alberta charter school is taking a different approach to education by putting hands-on training at the centre of its curriculum, beginning as early as Grade 7.
stories.author: Kathy Le
stories.content:
Grande Prairie, Alta. - As Canada looks to train more skilled tradespeople to support its ambitious infrastructure and housing plans, a new Alberta charter school is taking a different approach to education by putting hands-on training at the centre of its curriculum, beginning as early as Grade 7.

“I was actually very surprising on how much we were actually doing hands on,” said Landen Zacharias, a 15-year-old Grade 10 student at Grande Prairie Technical Institute, known as GP Tech. “I was comparing some of it to my friends in other schools, and they were very jealous.”

The publicly funded school opened in September, offering students opportunities to explore construction, automotive technology and culinary arts alongside traditional academic subjects.

But the school’s opening has not been without challenges. Some programs and facilities remain under development, and board chair Noshaba Harji acknowledges the school is still finding its footing.

“We are in the initial stages. We’ve only been open for a few months, but we do want to build an institution that delivers on what the community needs,” she said.

Harji said administrators had just 10 weeks to prepare the building before welcoming students, describing the process as a major hurdle.

Despite the challenges, students are already taking part in practical projects.

Ryzdyn Shaw, a Grade 9 student who hopes to become a licensed automotive mechanic, developed an interest in the trade when he was young.

“I’ve been working with my dad in our driveway and in our garage since I was, like eight,” he said.

He is currently studying construction at GP Tech and will begin automotive training next semester.

What is a charter school?

Alberta is the only province in Canada with a public charter school system.

Charter schools are publicly funded and independently operated by non-profit organizations rather than traditional school boards. They must follow Alberta’s curriculum but can offer specialized educational approaches, including programs focused on science, technology, arts and alternative learning methods.

There are 36 charter school authorities in Alberta, with dozens of school sites across the province. Most are concentrated in larger urban centres, particularly Calgary and Edmonton.

Unlike private schools, public charter schools do not charge tuition.

Traditional public schools already offer trades-related courses, including construction, mechanics and culinary arts, raising questions about the need for a separate charter school.

Harji says the difference lies in how GP Tech incorporates those skills into everyday learning.

“We are not just focusing on the core subjects as well as the options for skills and trades. We’re looking at it from a completely different lens.”

Harji said students spend about 70 per cent of their time in workshops, developing foundational skills alongside their academic studies.

Recruiting young workforce

The school’s approach comes amid growing concerns about a shortage of skilled trades workers in Canada, with federal officials warning that the country needs to attract more people into the sector.

According to the federal government, Canada will need more than 1.4 million new skilled trades workers by 2033, with an estimated 21 per cent of the existing workforce expected to retire.

Harji believes exposing students to the trades earlier could help address future workforce needs, particularly as more experienced workers approach retirement.

“This way we are able to fill that gap earlier on, and we’re able to meet that need and be ready for it, rather than waiting for it to come up,” she said.

But while schools like GP Tech aim to introduce more young people to the trades, economist Jim Stanford cautions that demand for those workers can fluctuate significantly.

“Employers often pull their hair out and complain about a shortage of skilled trades, but there is a real boom and bust aspect to this career path, unfortunately,” said Stanford, director of the Centre for Future Work.

He pointed to downturns in home construction and broader economic uncertainty, including U.S. tariffs, as factors affecting employment.

Still, Stanford said Canada’s plans for major investments in housing, mining and resources, and manufacturing could create significant demand for skilled workers.

“If all of those plans came to fruition, then there’s no doubt that the existing need for skilled trades training in Canada, which is already there, would get that much more intense,” he said.

Regardless of how demand evolves, education experts say introducing students to different trades at a younger age can help them explore potential career paths.

Bonnie Watt, a University of Alberta faculty of education professor, says combining practical training with traditional academic subjects can also make learning more meaningful.

“When we can actually have the object or the three-dimensional piece that we’re working with and bring in the physics and the science and the English and the social,” she said, students can better understand how those subjects apply to the work they’re doing.

Watt believes Grade 7 is an opportunity for students to discover what interests them — and what doesn’t — before making decisions about their futures.

“If I can make a decision in grade seven that I don’t like that particular skill set, and I have no attraction to it, but I can move on to another one . , I don’t have to be 20 years old, try it and then decide that I’m not doing it,” she said.

GP Tech has established partnerships with Northwestern Polytechnic in Grande Prairie and Sait in Calgary, offering potential pathways to further training.

But the school’s ambitions extend beyond the classroom.

“The vision for it is to be a community hub, creating it with community partnerships,” Harji said.

Longer-term plans include a student-run café and free automotive services, such as oil changes and tire changes, for community members.

The school also plans to expand its programming.

“We will be offering aviation in the near future,” Harji said.

For Zacharias, who hopes to one day own a construction business, introducing young people to the trades could help meet Canada’s future workforce needs.

“We’ll just have a higher demand more and more. So it’s good that we have schools like this to make kids want to do this more and be more engaged with it,” he said.

And as his father often reminds him, skilled trades workers will always have a role to play.

“My dad always said even a lawyer or a doctor need a roof to live under,” he said.

“We are in the initial stages. We’ve only been open for a few months, but we do want to build an institution that delivers on what the community needs,” she said.
Harji said administrators had just 10 weeks to prepare the building before welcoming students, describing the process as a major hurdle.
Despite the challenges, students are already taking part in practical projects.
Ryzdyn Shaw, a Grade 9 student who hopes to become a licensed automotive mechanic, developed an interest in the trade when he was young.
“I’ve been working with my dad in our driveway and in our garage since I was, like eight,” he said.
He is currently studying construction at GP Tech and will begin automotive training next semester.
What is a charter school?
Alberta is the only province in Canada with a public charter school system.

Charter schools are publicly funded and independently operated by non-profit organizations rather than traditional school boards. They must follow Alberta’s curriculum but can offer specialized educational approaches, including programs focused on science, technology, arts and alternative learning methods.
There are 36 charter school authorities in Alberta, with dozens of school sites across the province. Most are concentrated in larger urban centres, particularly Calgary and Edmonton.
Unlike private schools, public charter schools do not charge tuition.
Traditional public schools already offer trades-related courses, including construction, mechanics and culinary arts, raising questions about the need for a separate charter school.
Harji says the difference lies in how GP Tech incorporates those skills into everyday learning.
“We are not just focusing on the core subjects as well as the options for skills and trades. We’re looking at it from a completely different lens.”
Harji said students spend about 70 per cent of their time in workshops, developing foundational skills alongside their academic studies.
Recruiting young workforce
The school’s approach comes amid growing concerns about a shortage of skilled trades workers in Canada, with federal officials warning that the country needs to attract more people into the sector.
According to the federal government, Canada will need more than 1.4 million new skilled trades workers by 2033, with an estimated 21 per cent of the existing workforce expected to retire.
Harji believes exposing students to the trades earlier could help address future workforce needs, particularly as more experienced workers approach retirement.
“This way we are able to fill that gap earlier on, and we’re able to meet that need and be ready for it, rather than waiting for it to come up,” she said.
But while schools like GP Tech aim to introduce more young people to the trades, economist Jim Stanford cautions that demand for those workers can fluctuate significantly.

“Employers often pull their hair out and complain about a shortage of skilled trades, but there is a real boom and bust aspect to this career path, unfortunately,” said Stanford, director of the Centre for Future Work.
He pointed to downturns in home construction and broader economic uncertainty, including U.S. tariffs, as factors affecting employment.
Still, Stanford said Canada’s plans for major investments in housing, mining and resources, and manufacturing could create significant demand for skilled workers.
“If all of those plans came to fruition, then there’s no doubt that the existing need for skilled trades training in Canada, which is already there, would get that much more intense,” he said.
Regardless of how demand evolves, education experts say introducing students to different trades at a younger age can help them explore potential career paths.
Bonnie Watt, a University of Alberta faculty of education professor, says combining practical training with traditional academic subjects can also make learning more meaningful.

“When we can actually have the object or the three-dimensional piece that we’re working with and bring in the physics and the science and the English and the social,” she said, students can better understand how those subjects apply to the work they’re doing.
Watt believes Grade 7 is an opportunity for students to discover what interests them — and what doesn’t — before making decisions about their futures.

“If I can make a decision in grade seven that I don’t like that particular skill set, and I have no attraction to it, but I can move on to another one . , I don’t have to be 20 years old, try it and then decide that I’m not doing it,” she said.
GP Tech has established partnerships with Northwestern Polytechnic in Grande Prairie and Sait in Calgary, offering potential pathways to further training.
But the school’s ambitions extend beyond the classroom.
“The vision for it is to be a community hub, creating it with community partnerships,” Harji said.
Longer-term plans include a student-run café and free automotive services, such as oil changes and tire changes, for community members.
The school also plans to expand its programming.
“We will be offering aviation in the near future,” Harji said.
For Zacharias, who hopes to one day own a construction business, introducing young people to the trades could help meet Canada’s future workforce needs.
“We’ll just have a higher demand more and more. So it’s good that we have schools like this to make kids want to do this more and be more engaged with it,” he said.
And as his father often reminds him, skilled trades workers will always have a role to play.
“My dad always said even a lawyer or a doctor need a roof to live under,” he said.

stories.title: Photographer's new book tells the stories behind Canada's war graves and monuments
stories.summary: Halifax - Nova Scotia author and photographer Len Wagg was on his day off 30 years ago when he discovered how powerful and poignant a war cemetery could be.
stories.author: Devin Stevens The Canadian Press
stories.content:
Halifax - Nova Scotia author and photographer Len Wagg was on his day off 30 years ago when he discovered how powerful and poignant a war cemetery could be.

Wagg was on assignment for the Halifax Chronicle Herald in Italy when he accepted an invitation to visit the small Sicilian town of Agira.

A few hours later, he was walking through the Agira Canadian War Cemetery, an oasis of immaculately manicured lawns and pine trees, looking at row after row of headstones inscribed with the names of Canadians who served during the Second World War.

Len Wagg has spent the last five years travelling across Canada and Europe photographing war graves, monuments and the people who maintain them. While the book visits well-known sites such as Vimy Ridge and Juno Beach, it also tells the stories of people setting up new monuments and those helping to identify Canadian soldiers whose unmarked graves are still being found today. (Nov. 7, 2026)

He wrote a story for the paper, and said the response to it stayed with him for years.

“I got calls from Nova Scotia and from the United States,” Wagg said in a recent interview at the Last Steps memorial in Halifax, where more than 350,000 First World War service members boarded ships to Europe, many never to return.

“People had said they knew their father had died overseas but they didn’t know where it was. And this picture of the headstone was the first time that they had seen where it was.”

For the past five years, Wagg has travelled across Canada and Europe photographing war graves, monuments and other sites for his new book, “At Home and Beyond: Honouring Canada’s War Dead.”

The book captures images of well-known sites such as Vimy Ridge, Juno Beach and the grave of poet John McCrae, who wrote “In Flanders Fields.” But it also tells the stories of the people who care for those monuments or make other contributions to honour Canada’s war dead.

More than 110,000 Canadians are buried overseas at more than 5,800 sites. Another 27,000 have no known graves, having gone into battle and disappeared.

Wagg said he’s not a historian, and didn’t want the book to focus only on war monuments. Instead, he focused on the people.

The book includes chapters dedicated to Canadian war nurses, the organizers behind relatively new memorials like the Last Steps, and the stories of individual soldiers like Pte. George Lawrence Price of Port Williams, N.S., the last Commonwealth soldier to die in the First World War. He was killed by a German sniper at 10:58 a.m. on Nov. 11, 1918 — two minutes before the armistice went into effect.

By coincidence, Price’s grave in Belgium is metres away from that of Pte. John Parr, a 17-year-old British soldier who became the first Commonwealth serviceman killed during the First World War, which had been declared less than a month earlier.

Wagg profiles Sarah Lockyer and her team at the Department of National Defence’s casualty identification unit in Ottawa. The group of historians and anthropologists use various tools, including DNA analysis, to identify Canadians whose unmarked graves are still being found in Europe. Once identified, those service members are given full military funerals in France.

“One of the quotes from (Lockyer) was, ‘They gave their lives for the country. It’s the least we can do to give them back their names.’ And that was something I found very powerful,” said Wagg.

The book’s foreword is written by Warren (Whitey) Bernard, the 91-year-old Tofino, B.C., resident who was the subject of a famous photo known as “Wait for Me Daddy,” taken in 1940.

The image, which has inspired a bronze statue, souvenir coins and a stamp, appeared on the front page of the Vancouver Province. It features a young Bernard breaking away from his mother to reach for his father’s hand as he marches off to war in New Westminster, B.C. Wagg said the photo once hung in every school in British Columbia.

Wagg said he wondered what happened to the little boy in the photo and set out to find him, calling his meeting with Bernard one of the high points of his career.

Bernard said he’s been interviewed many times over the years but was impressed by Wagg’s passion for the project.

“I appreciated the way he was taking this on,” Bernard said in an interview. “When guys like Len come along, they’re not trying to get the story for a five-minute or a two-minute shot.… They’re interested in the story. I was really impressed.”

Wagg said the way many people see Canada as a country today is a ripple of what the country did in the First and Second World Wars, especially in Europe, where graveyards are actively maintained and host various ceremonies every year.

Wagg said that from the beaches of Normandy to the buglers playing the Last Post every night at the Menin Gate memorial in Ypres, Belgium, he’s heard the same message from the young people involved in caring for war monuments.

“It’s a generational gratitude,” he said. “The reason why young people in their 30s and 40s are doing this is because of the stories they heard around the kitchen table from their parents and grandparents. It’s important for us to understand (that) part of who we are as Canadians comes from the ripples of their sacrifice.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 7, 2026.
