stories.title: An Ontario teen lived in this shed while under the watch of Children’s Aid. ‘Everybody knew, nobody cared’
stories.summary: The story of a teen who lived in a shed for months at a time while under the watch of Children’s Aid is a stark illustration of how Ontario’s health and child welfare systems are failing youth with complex needs, leaving agencies and families to rely on makeshift, unlicensed arrangements when appropriate treatment and housing can’t be found.
stories.author: Amy Dempsey Raven; Megan Ogilvie
stories.content:
James was 15 when he first moved into the shed in his parents’ driveway in Woodstock, Ont. It was a small, weathered building meant to store tools and camping gear. It had no window, no bathroom. Just a futon and a desk, his PlayStation, some fishing rods, and a few hockey posters taped to the plywood walls.

The teen lived in the shed for months at a time, through summer heatwaves and winter storms, all while under the watch of an Ontario children’s aid society.

James — that’s his middle name — has a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes behaviours his parents could no longer safely manage at home. Over two stretches since 2024, he spent a total of 15 months in the shed.

The Children’s Aid Society of Oxford County approved the placement, according to James’s parents, and emails reviewed by the Star show staff at the ministry responsible for children and youth were also aware of the living arrangement.

“Everybody knew,” said his mother, Ruth. “Nobody cared.”

Between stints in the shed, James bounced around. He lived in a minivan in a Walmart parking lot. In a roadside motel, where police conducted a drug raid in a nearby room. In a group foster home that didn’t have the resources to meet his complex needs.

“This is not OK on any level,” his mother said. “This is not how we treat vulnerable people.”

‘I don’t know why I’m like this’

James has fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, a condition that causes lifelong cognitive and behavioural challenges, including aggression. Fasd is best treated with early intervention but James didn’t get that. His parents, who adopted him from the children’s aid society when he was an infant, say it took 14 years just to get James diagnosed. Throughout his life, they tried every therapy, every service, every program they could find, but nothing met his intense needs.

At home, when James got angry, he punched holes in the walls, smashed mirrors, broke doors off hinges, his parents said. He set a fire on the front porch and threw bricks at the house, cracking the siding. He threatened to kill his parents.

“It is only a matter of time before he hurts one of us,” his mother warned child welfare workers in an email in 2023. The Star is using middle names for James and his family because Ontario law says kids involved in child protection proceedings cannot be identified.

James’s parents believe that early support and more consistent care through his childhood and early teen years could have minimized some of his more challenging behaviours and helped stabilize their family life.

James has a good heart, his mother said. Growing up, he was protective of his older sister. He loved the children’s book The Invisible String, about an unbreakable bond that connects people who love each other when they can’t be together.

After his rages, James would sob and tell his parents, “I don’t know why I’m like this.”

In December 2023, Ruth and Thomas asked the children’s aid society to find supportive housing for him. They said they couldn’t care for James at home anymore because his violent outbursts put them in danger.

The Oxford CAS, the same agency they had adopted James from years earlier, initially said they couldn’t help because it wasn’t a child protection matter; James was not in danger. But our family is in danger, Ruth thought.

“If I was being abused by my husband, I could go to a women’s shelter,” Ruth said. “But there’s no agency for parents who are living like this. We’re just supposed to take it and deal with it because we’re parents.”

Ruth and Thomas said the Oxford CAS told them they should call the police if they feared for their safety. But the parents worried that if they called the police, their son would end up in jail, and if they kicked him out, he’d end up on the streets, or dead.

The shed was meant to be a hangout space for James, a place where he could play video games and be as loud as he wanted. His father insulated the building and installed heating, air conditioning and a fire alarm.

But the shed became James’s home after a family crisis.

After one incident in March 2024, the parents felt unsafe and refused to let their son back into the house. He stayed in the shed that night, and the next. Ruth and Thomas couldn’t believe what their life had come to: their son was living in the shed.

Weeks later, a health-care provider who had seen James called Ruth, sounding curt, and said: Your son tells us he’s living in a shed?

“Yes,” Ruth said. “He is.”

Ruth said the hospital worker reported them to CAS. She and Thomas were relieved. Now, they thought, CAS would be forced to find a place for James to live. But that’s not what happened.

Ruth and Thomas said a child protection worker came to the house to examine the shed. He took a look, shook his head sadly and said he’d talk to his manager. Soon after, Ruth heard back: the shed was approved, so long as the family installed a carbon monoxide detector. The CAS worker dropped one off.

A public reckoning

We need better options for kids like my son.

Experts say these children need early intervention but too few programs exist, especially outside major cities, so many are left in the cold. Desperate parents like James’s who can’t get appropriate health services for their kids end up in crisis and are increasingly forced to turn to a child welfare state that is also unequipped to handle them.

Ontario children’s aid societies share the same challenges accessing treatment and services, and have fewer foster families willing to take in kids who have been violent or use drugs. Left without options, some agencies — particularly in southwestern Ontario — have been housing kids in unlicensed settings such as motels and office buildings.

Two years after the province announced an audit of children’s aid societies and the Ontario ombudsman launched an investigation into kids being housed in these unlicensed placements, little has changed.

Advocates, front-line workers and families say the situation has only gotten worse for children and youth with “complex needs,” an umbrella term used to describe overlapping mental health diagnoses, developmental disorders and severe behavioural challenges. The solutions cobbled together by the agencies — including budget motels where teens have fallen prey to traffickers and drug dealers — often compound the crisis and deepen the trauma they are meant to resolve.

Tina Diamond, the CEO of the Oxford CAS, said she couldn’t comment on an individual case due to privacy legislation, but emphasized the agency would “not endorse a plan that involves a young person living in an unsafe or unsuitable environment.”

“Decisions regarding the safety and well-being of young persons are based on individual circumstances, needs, risks, proximity to community and available supports,” Diamond said, adding that a safe heat source, access to running water and bathroom facilities are “markers of safety” the agency considers.

She said consent is required for teens in state care under a voluntary youth service agreement, or Vysa, a contract between a child welfare agency and a youth who can’t live at home.

“Adolescents May decline available placement or housing options, even when concerns exist about their current living situation,” she said. “Under provincial legislation, [a CAS] cannot compel a young person to attend a placement because it believes it is the safer, more appropriate choice.”

From the shed to a minivan

James’s first stint living in the shed, from March to November 2024, ended when he was charged with assaulting his mother and a court order forced him to stay away from the family home, his parents said. James had just turned 16. The parents say CAS told them they had no place for him.

For weeks, Ruth and Thomas left the family minivan in a Walmart parking lot for their son to sleep in. Thomas brought him food and checked on him daily. The Office of the Children’s Lawyer, a provincial agency that advocates for the rights of children under 18 in legal proceedings, eventually intervened and insisted the Oxford CAS find a place for him, his mother said.

James signed a voluntary youth service agreement. The CAS placed James in a budget motel in Woodstock, a rundown place where a drug raid occurred while he was living there. He fell into a depression.

Fed up with placements that made things worse for her son, Ruth filed a complaint with the provincial ombudsman’s office, but said the office told her to file an internal complaint with CAS.

Ruth said complaining to CAS wouldn’t get her anywhere because they didn’t have a better option for James. “The bigger issue here,” Ruth wrote to the ombudsman, “is that there are no appropriate agencies or living spaces to help kids with complex needs and families like ours.”

The motel placement ended when police arrested James for uttering threats. The CAS moved him into a group foster home, but that didn’t go well either, Ruth said. Staff at the home didn’t have Fasd training. James hated the place and said he felt abandoned. James said he texted his CAS workers and his parents, asking them to get him out of there, but they didn’t reply. His hurt turned into rage and he “trashed the place,” he said. He was kicked out after five days for causing property damage.

“They think that group homes, shelters, all this is gonna help a person?” James said. “It actually makes it worse.”

CAS workers eventually told his parents they had only one placement option left for him: a youth homeless shelter 40 minutes away in Kitchener.

His parents were outraged. A homeless shelter? Fasd was a brain injury. Their son was vulnerable. How could a homeless shelter be a viable option?

A parole officer from the ministry’s youth justice department intervened and told the Oxford CAS that “an offer to call a shelter is not an appropriate response.” But James refused to live in a group home, and CAS said there was nothing else. So he moved back into the shed.

Ruth believes most of the people involved in James’s care have wanted to help him. And she acknowledges that James sometimes refuses treatment and rejects housing options. Ruth herself has even advocated for James to remain in the shed at times, when CAS offered alternatives that seemed worse.

Ruth said the province needs to figure out how to treat and support kids with Fasd, which is estimated to be twice as prevalent as autism but receives far fewer resources, because the status quo is making them worse. Things would have been different if her family had gotten more help sooner, she said, and it would have avoided the need for a years-long crisis response.

“We need better options for kids like my son,” she said.

The Ministry of Children, Community and Social Services said in a statement that it was “unable to comment on specific cases,” instead highlighting its nearly $2 billion annual investment in child welfare, including $315 million earmarked for young people transitioning out of CAS care.

“While the province provides funding to Children’s Aid Societies, they are independent entities responsible for making decisions based on the individual needs, circumstances and best interests of each child and youth, including decisions related to services and placements.”

Nowhere else to go

From September until May this year, James lived in the shed again. Ruth filed another complaint with the ombudsman, urging the office to push the provincial government to create and fund better treatment and interventions for kids with Fasd.

The ombudsman’s office was already in the middle of an investigation into the practice of child welfare agencies housing children in inappropriate settings — a probe that was announced in September 2024 but still isn’t finished. James was still living in the shed when someone from the ombudsman’s office interviewed him, he and his mother said. A spokesperson for the office said they couldn’t comment on individual investigations.

In May, James was arrested after breaking into his parents’ house in the night. Now he is again prohibited by a court order from returning to his family home.

He turned 18 last month and remains in CAS care under a transition program for young adults. He said the CAS has him on a waiting list for housing.

In the meantime, James has been moving from one temporary living arrangement to another, renting a room in a house, staying with friends. Then, a few weeks ago, he moved into another shed. A smaller one, at the home of a family friend.

James wants to get his life sorted out, but said that without a place to live it feels impossible.

“It’s going on two years that I’m homeless,” he said. “You get lonely. You’re on your own. You’ve gotta grow up real quick.”
paragraphs: James was 15 when he first moved into the shed in his parents’ driveway in Woodstock, Ont. It was a small, weathered building meant to store tools and camping gear. It had no window, no bathroom. Just a futon and a desk, his PlayStation, some fishing rods, and a few hockey posters taped to the plywood walls.
The teen lived in the shed for months at a time, through summer heatwaves and winter storms, all while under the watch of an Ontario children’s aid society.

James — that’s his middle name — has a neurodevelopmental disorder that causes behaviours his parents could no longer safely manage at home. Over two stretches since 2024, he spent a total of 15 months in the shed.

The Children’s Aid Society of Oxford County approved the placement, according to James’s parents, and emails reviewed by the Star show staff at the ministry responsible for children and youth were also aware of the living arrangement.
“Everybody knew,” said his mother, Ruth. “Nobody cared.”

Between stints in the shed, James bounced around. He lived in a minivan in a Walmart parking lot. In a roadside motel, where police conducted a drug raid in a nearby room. In a group foster home that didn’t have the resources to meet his complex needs.
“This is not OK on any level,” his mother said. “This is not how we treat vulnerable people.”
‘I don’t know why I’m like this’

James has fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, a condition that causes lifelong cognitive and behavioural challenges, including aggression. Fasd is best treated with early intervention but James didn’t get that. His parents, who adopted him from the children’s aid society when he was an infant, say it took 14 years just to get James diagnosed. Throughout his life, they tried every therapy, every service, every program they could find, but nothing met his intense needs.

At home, when James got angry, he punched holes in the walls, smashed mirrors, broke doors off hinges, his parents said. He set a fire on the front porch and threw bricks at the house, cracking the siding. He threatened to kill his parents.

“It is only a matter of time before he hurts one of us,” his mother warned child welfare workers in an email in 2023. The Star is using middle names for James and his family because Ontario law says kids involved in child protection proceedings cannot be identified.

James’s parents believe that early support and more consistent care through his childhood and early teen years could have minimized some of his more challenging behaviours and helped stabilize their family life.

James has a good heart, his mother said. Growing up, he was protective of his older sister. He loved the children’s book The Invisible String, about an unbreakable bond that connects people who love each other when they can’t be together.
After his rages, James would sob and tell his parents, “I don’t know why I’m like this.”

In December 2023, Ruth and Thomas asked the children’s aid society to find supportive housing for him. They said they couldn’t care for James at home anymore because his violent outbursts put them in danger.

Ruth and Thomas said the Oxford CAS told them they should call the police if they feared for their safety. But the parents worried that if they called the police, their son would end up in jail, and if they kicked him out, he’d end up on the streets, or dead.

The shed was meant to be a hangout space for James, a place where he could play video games and be as loud as he wanted. His father insulated the building and installed heating, air conditioning and a fire alarm.
But the shed became James’s home after a family crisis.

“Yes,” Ruth said. “He is.”

stories.title: How Carney government's changes will affect different groups of immigrants
stories.summary: Carney government’s updated immigration plan will create a pathway to permanent residence for some temporary residents.
stories.author: Ghada Alsharif
stories.content:
The Carney government’s updated immigration plan will create a pathway to permanent residence for some temporary residents who have spent years trying to secure status, while leaving many others with few options to stay in Canada.

The new plan, released by the Immigration Department on Thursday, includes a one-time initiative to help as many as 200,000 people already living in Canada transition to permanent residence in 2027, benefiting select workers and humanitarian applicants already in the country. But critics say the measure will do little for the millions of other temporary residents who do not qualify.

The government says its 2027-29 immigration levels plan will admit 380,000 permanent residents and 370,000 temporary residents each year. New temporary resident targets are split between 220,000 workers and 150,000 students for each year of the plan.

The goal is for more than 64 per cent of new permanent resident admissions to be economic immigrants, according to a document provided by the department .

Here’s how the changes will affect different groups of immigrants, including who stands to benefit and who May be left without a pathway to stay.

Ottawa will work with provinces to decide how to divvy up the extra 100,000 permanent resident spots set aside in 2027 for temporary foreign w…

The federal government is introducing a one-time measure to grant permanent residency to as many as 200,000 temporary residents already in Canada, split into two cohorts of 100,000 people each.

The workers’ cohort will prioritize people who have already applied for permanent residence through specific immigration programs, including the Home Care Worker pilot, Start-Up Visa and Agri-Food Pilot programs, as well as workers eligible for the Provincial Nominee Program. The government suspended several of these immigration pathways in late 2025 because of processing backlogs.

The second, humanitarian cohort will focus on clearing remaining applications under permanent residence pathways for Hong Kong residents and the Ukraine family reunification pathway. It will also process applications for spouses, common-law partners and children of Canadians and permanent residents who are awaiting a final decision.

“Those who are currently inside Canada are the ones who stand the most to benefit from this,” said Ottawa-based immigration lawyer Cédric Marin.

The immigration plan emphasizes Canada’s need to “address the diverse labour market and regional needs of our provinces, territories and communities.” It highlights workers eligible for the Provincial Nominee Program to give the provinces and territories greater ability to nominate people for permanent residency based on local labour needs.

“Provinces have more say in terms of who gets to immigrate to Canada and who gets to stay here,” Marin said.

Shamira Madhany, managing director of World Education Services Canada, said this focus suggests Ottawa will work closely with provinces to identify and address regional labour shortages, particularly in sectors such as health care and in rural communities .

“The government is now very focused on where the actual needs are and where people can contribute,” Madhany said.

Shamira Madhany, managing director of World Education Services Canada.

The current levels plan marks “a significant shift away from the federal economic selection program in favour of the provincial nominee programs,” said Queen’s University immigration law professor Sharry Aiken.

She warned the shift May address immediate regional labour needs by allowing provinces to select immigrants to fill local shortages but questioned whether a more regionally focused approach would deliver the same long-term benefits, given that permanent residents are free to move elsewhere in Canada.

That mobility is reflected in a 2024 Auditor General report , which found that nearly 5,000 individuals migrated to Ontario from another provincial nominee program over the five-year period ending in 2021. Of those, 63 per cent settled in the GTA.

“There is that empirical question in terms of the long-term benefits of recruiting immigrants that fit the needs of one particular region,” Aiken said.

The new plan will continue to boost the levels of French-speaking permanent residents settling outside Quebec, from 31,825 in 2027 to 40,200 in 2029. The increase May seem small but will ultimately bring up the percentage of newcomers proficient in French from 9.5 per cent to 12 per cent of the annual permanent resident intake.

This move is not without controversy as French-speaking immigrants face challenges in accessing services and finding jobs settling in English-dominant provinces and territories. Under the skilled immigration selection system, proficiency in French itself has given francophone candidates an advantage over other skilled candidates.

“It’s going to be really important for the federal government and provinces to make sure that they’re actually leveraging the bilingual language skills of the individuals that are coming here,” Madhany said. “People come here who can speak French but find then can’t find jobs and end up in English-speaking jobs.”

Ottawa will continue to limit the number of new international student permits to 150,000 from a previous target of 305,900 in 2025. Admissions had climbed to more than 700,000 earlier in the decade, as Canada promoted itself to newcomers as a place to “study, work and stay.”

The government imposed a cap on the number of international students in 2024 and initially proposed it as a two-year measure, but the reductions, which have caused financial headaches at colleges and universities, are now projected to continue.

Aiken warned that the sharp decline in international student numbers is having a dramatic impact on the post-secondary sector , reducing revenue and forcing institutions to cut programs that Canadian students want and need. She said the cuts are also making Canada less attractive to international talent at a time when the country has said it needs to attract skilled workers .

“The message is going out there that Canada’s not necessarily a destination country anymore for international students at the very time that all of our universities and colleges are seeking to internationalize,” Aiken said.

The government has maintained its annual refugee and protected persons admissions target at 49,300.

“Since 2023 Canada’s refugee resettlement levels have been cut by 43 per cent, more than twice the 18 per cent cut to immigration overall,” the Canadian Council for Refugees said in a statement Friday.

“The people with the fewest options are losing the most, and refugees are bearing a disproportionate share of these cuts.”

Overall, cuts in targets for refugees, humanitarian applications and Family Class reflect the government’s objective of increasing the economic share of immigration to 64 per cent, the council said.

“An overly economic focus on the levels distorts the role that immigration plays in building our society and telling the story of who we are,” said Gauri Sreenivasan, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees.

The federal budget said the government plans to reform the Temporary Foreign Worker (TFW) Program to ensure it lines up with regional labour market needs, improve processing times and strengthen employer compliance.

Details of the program review are scarce, although the budget sets aside $151.5 million to implement the reforms.

The TFW program is intended as a “last resort for employers to fill jobs for which qualified Canadians are not available,” according to Employment and Social Development Canada. But critics say jobs across all sectors — including agriculture, health care, food-service and construction — are being occupied by a precarious and vulnerable workforce simply to keep wages low.

With files from The Canadian Press

stories.title: Sexual assault
stories.summary: London, ON (November 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying a suspect in relation to a sexual assault and break and enter that took place earlier this week.
stories.author: London Police Service
stories.content:
LONDON, ON (November 7, 2026) – Members of the London Police Service Sexual Assault and Child Abuse Section are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying a suspect in relation to a sexual assault and break and enter that took place earlier this week.

On Thursday, November 5, 2026, at approximately 3 p.m., police responded to a residence in the 900-block of Blythwood Road after receiving a report of a residential break and enter.

Additional information was received that a suspect entered a residence and sexually assaulted a woman inside the home. Another resident heard the woman and attended the main floor, at which point the suspect fled from the home.

The suspect male was last seen travelling westbound on Blythwood Road on a black push scooter.

Multiple officers, including members of the LPS Canine Unit, searched the area but did not locate the suspect.

The victim did not sustain any physical injuries.

The suspect was described as male, Brown, approximately 25 years of age, 5’8, with short black hair and dark eyes. He was clean shaven, and wearing a white t-shirt and dark pants. He was observed riding a black push scooter. He was also described as speaking English with an accent.

Investigators are asking anyone who may have been in the area at the time of the incident, or who may have dashcam, residential or business video surveillance that could assist with the investigation, to contact police.

If you or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, support is available. Confidential assistance can be accessed at any time. For more information and links to local support agencies, please visit https://www.londonpolice.ca/crime-prevention/sexual-assaults-faqs/ .

Anyone with information in relation to this incident is asked to call the London Police Service at (519) 661-5670.

stories.title: Amherstburg contractor charged in alleged $155K renovation fraud
stories.summary: Joel Charron and his wife took out a $200,000 loan to pay for a renovation and expansion of their Amherstburg home plus a new garage. They trusted a friend of the family to do the job.
stories.author: Bob Bellacicco
stories.content:
Joel Charron and his wife took out a $200,000 loan to pay for a renovation and expansion of their Amherstburg home plus a new garage. They trusted a friend of the family to do the job.

“It weighs on me. It weighs on me every day,” Charron said. “It’s tough looking myself in the mirror knowing that I failed my family this bad. I failed my family in the most tragic of ways by trusting someone that couldn’t do this job.”

Charron’s wife filed a report with the Amherstburg detachment of Windsor Police.

“Within 24 hours we got a call from the officer saying her intuition was right.”

Earlier this week Jessie Flaricee of MBS Home Solutions turned himself in after police issued a warrant for his arrest.

He is facing fraud and forgery related charges. Police say his company was dissolved in 2024 for non-compliance.

“You want to make sure that that person has insurance. If that person doesn’t have insurance the likelihood of you getting restitution for everything you went through is highly unlikely,” Constable Bianca Jackson warned.

Police are reminding residents research is vital when looking for a contractor. “Look at those google reviews. Get references and also look at the person’s work.”

Charron says the family is out $155-thousand dollars and spent the bulk of the remaining cash to undo the work already done.

Loose wires, improperly installed drywall, and a deficient foundation were some of the problems others pointed out to Charron.

The family asked the town to inspect the work, and the home did not pass.

The family now has a lawyer but not their home. They are staying with family.

Charron says a new contractor is scheduled to begin tackling the problem starting Monday. There is no timeline on when the family can move back in.

“I can’t wait for that day to come.”

A GoFundMe page has been set up to help the family through.

stories.title: One of Okanagan’s most colourful characters dies at 96
stories.summary: Eddy Haymour died Wednesday at the age of 96, leaving behind a remarkable story of ambition, controversy and a dream that never quite came to fruition.
stories.author: Klaudia Van Emmerik
stories.content:
For decades, a distinctive castle overlooking Highway 97 in Peachland has served as a reminder of one of the Okanagan’s most colourful characters.

Eddy Haymour died Wednesday at the age of 96, leaving behind a remarkable story of ambition, controversy and a dream that never quite came to fruition.

For many locals, his name is synonymous with both the castle and Rattlesnake Island.

“Rattlesnake island and a bit of trouble, a lot of trouble,” said Okanagan resident Don Scramstad.

It was the island that captured Haymour’s imagination and ultimately became the focus of a decades-long dispute with the provincial government.

A Lebanese immigrant, Haymour purchased Rattlesnake Island in 1971 with plans to transform the five-acre property into a Middle Eastern-themed amusement park. His ambitious vision caught the attention of filmmaker Greg Crompton, who produced the 2019 documentary “Eddy’s Kingdom.” “As a filmmaker, when we were you know kicking around ideas, this one just seemed like such a compelling story to tell,” Crompton said. “So I was quite motivated personally but also as a filmmaker, I want to tell interesting stories. This is a very interesting story.”

But Haymour’s pursuit of his dream took an extraordinary turn.

His dispute with the province escalated dramatically in 1974, when he and his relatives took hostages at the Canadian embassy in Beirut.

For Crompton, it was Haymour’s unusual way of thinking that made him such a fascinating subject. “He did all these like wild things but his rationale for it for me was maybe the most interesting part of him… was this character study of saying, “What? So, so you were wronged by the government but then you were going to get some grenades and chuck it into the legislature and and cause mayhem,” Crompton said. “Like it just, his thought process for me was maybe the most compelling.”

At the Peachland Museum, Haymour remains a prominent figure in the community’s history.

“He was zealously committed to his dream. That would be what I would say succinctly. It didn’t matter what obstacle was in his way; he pursued it to the end,” said Jeff Green, the museum’s assistant curator.

Although Haymour eventually won his legal battle with the province, his dream of developing the island never materialized.

He did, however, build his distinctive castle in Peachland, and beside it, a statue of himself pointing across the lake toward the island he had big dreams for.

“He was a visionary. He was impassioned about what he was doing,” said Tracy Janes, a customer service agent at the museum. “Just everything about the man was larger than life.”

“He was a visionary. He was impassioned about what he was doing,” said Tracy Janes, a customer service agent at the museum. “Just everything about the man was larger than life.”

stories.title: Being obsessed with Angine de Poitrine is my microtonal math-rock midlife crisis
stories.summary: The Quebecois duo – now trio? – has a certain appeal to middle aged dads like myself
stories.author: J. Kelly Nestruck
stories.content:
The sold-out crowd at History gasped and pulled out their phones: There’s a third one now!

Angine de Poitrine, the intergalactic microtonal math-rock duo based in Saguenay, Que., introduced a new band member on stage in Toronto on Thursday night.

She – he? they? – was smaller than Khn, the two-piece’s guitar-bassist with the polka-dotted pope hat and priapic proboscis, and Klek, the flaccid-nosed bucket-headed drummer. The shy box-headed musician with antennae for ears played, fittingly, the triangle – which, shape-wise, is the symbol of the band.

I thought Khn and Klek were alone among their kind on our planet – and was unexpectedly moved to learn that they have started a family together. Or maybe they have a little sister who has joined the band? (“Unfortunately, we will not be providing any clarification on the subject!” a publicist for the band said by e-mail, in French.)

But a big part of the pleasure of being a fan of Angine de Poitrine is learning that we are not alone – in the universe, or on our planet. Indeed, there more and more of us stanning the ridiculous, virtuosic duo out every day.

I joined the band’s fanbase in April on the day I turned 45.

My initial conversion came, counterintuitively as their songs are unsingable, in a karaoke room I had rented for my birthday.

My oldest friend showed up first and as we were waiting for others, he popped on the famous video of Angine de Poitrine that was uploaded to YouTube by Seattle’s Kexp in February and made them go viral. I was entranced – but a little skeptical.

Then my fellow middle-aged friends arrived and we all sang the old familiar songs from the 1990s and 2000s; there was, naturally, a sing-along of Cornershop’s Brimful of Asha (On the 45) .

But the next morning, all I could hear in my head was Angine de Poitrine. I played the Kexp video a couple more times, then downloaded the band’s two albums Vol I and Vol II .

I’d fallen out practice of searching for new music and the algorithms kept feeding me the tried and true. But these angular, looping tunes became the soundtrack to the summer and I slowly discovered how many of my male friends had become similarly snapped out of old listening ways.

During a summer camping trip with fellow dads, there was a day where we floated down a lazy river in canoes and communicated primarily by trying to imitating the first squawky, herky-jerky notes of the band’s unlikely hit single Fabienk .

Watching Angine de Poitrine on stage for the first time on Thursday was the first time I’d been to a concert that wasn’t a reunion tour or anniversary revisit of a classic album since the pandemic.

Seeing the band in person, I realized exactly what their alien costuming does – and how it’s not a gimmick at all. It’s part and parcel of what helps the band appeal to many demographics, perhaps particularly mine.

For one thing, the alien conceit – the band speaks in their own squeak-grunt language – creates the conditions for the band to not have to make political statements on stage. And also, crucially, for them not have to make statements about not making political statements.

I’m all for artists who want to say something to the crowd – but it changes the energy of a room and, to someone of my generation, can come across as branding or second-hand clicktivism at best.

Even more annoying, however, are musical artists who come on stage to lecture you about how they’re not lecturing you. Metallica frontman James Hetfield went viral last month in that manner, saying he wasn’t playing a concert “like some other entertainers, to influence you.” Great, man, then just play Enter Sandman , already.

Angine de Poitrine’s body-covering costumes conjure a listening space where we can forget about all kinds of hang-ups and divides, including old Canadian ones around language or nationalism.

There’s definitely something quintessentially Quebecois about Angine de Poitrine, from its unapologetic embrace of prog to its polka-dot painted toes.

Folks usually reference Cirque du Soleil, which is fair, but the shape-oriented costumes also summon old memories of the hosts on the old children’s show Passe-Partout for me. I’m reminded too of the funny aliens in Le facteur de l’espac e, a popular series of Quebec graphic novels about an intergalactic postman that my son reads.

As a francophile ex-Montrealer, however, I didn’t realize how fun it was to engage with a group of artists from my home province without having to think about my own complicated relationship to Quebec culture – or that dated old idea of the two solitudes.

Instead, I could just immerse myself in a room full of solid dudes who know to dim their phone screen if they’re going to take a picture and to keep videos short. (There were lots of women at History, too; please forgive the pun.)

I enjoyed my night among them, combatting the male loneliness epidemic and worshipping a triangle symbol without having to join the Freemasons.

I ran into an old pal at History who told me he doesn’t go to gigs as much as he used to – but was seeing Angine de Poitrine for the second time. He, in turn, ran into another friend who was on his third Angine concert.

The music is addictive. There’s something obsessive about it – the repetition in the music itself, the rhythms that keep you off balance – that appeals to brains that might otherwise go down wormholes online wondering what the purpose of life exactly was again.

As far as male midlife crises go, you could do worse than to be become obsessed with Khn and Klek. △

stories.title: Nearly 3,000 Parks Canada employees face potential job cuts
stories.summary: Work force adjustment expected to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments
stories.author: Andrea Woo
stories.content:
Thousands of Parks Canada employees have received notice that their jobs May be cut as the federal agency moves to shrink its work force and reduce services in line with the government’s cost-cutting measures.

Parks Canada has sent letters to 2,917 employees across the country to inform them their jobs are “impacted by workforce adjustment,” spokesperson Meaghan Bradley said in an e-mail. Not every one of those employees will lose their job, but decisions will be made in the coming weeks, she said.

The cuts are expected to eliminate about 500 full-time-equivalent positions, close 13 park-warden detachments and scale back visitor program, outreach and camping services. As well, the search-and-rescue dog program at Banff National Park – the only such program in Canada – has been discontinued.

“Over the coming months, Parks Canada will implement organizational changes to align with available funding, modernize operations, strengthen field-based decision-making and ensure it remains well positioned to deliver on our mandate into the future,” Ms. Bradley said.

The Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, an environmental charity, said it is “deeply concerned” by the planned reductions, which it said could put ecosystems, visitor safety and local economies at risk. It also argued the move makes little economic sense: Parks Canada had a budget of about $1.3-billion in 2025-26, while visitors spent $6.5-billion in or near its sites, according to the federal agency.

Kecia Kerr, executive director of the society’s northern Alberta chapter, said the province’s national parks are already struggling to manage tourism and its effects on wildlife and visitor safety.

In Elk Island National Park, which is slated to lose its park-warden detachment, Ms. Kerr said speeding drivers have resulted in at least 11 bison deaths that she is aware of. There have also been issues with poaching at both Elk Island and Jasper National Park.

“Human-wildlife conflict, and a need for additional education for visitors on how to behave around wildlife, are already issues and these cuts will make those issues much worse,” she said.

She added that the federal cuts compound provincial decisions that have reduced protections for ecological reserves and removed portions of provincial parks for resort development, putting more pressure on Alberta’s protected areas.

A recent employment equity annual report stated that as of March 2025, Parks Canada had a total work force of about 6,000 employees, of which 48.5 per cent were seasonal. The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, meanwhile, recorded 4,773 active Parks Canada employees this year.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada said 2,671 of its members at Parks Canada received the notices. To date, the employer has not explained which specific programs or services will be affected, the union said.

Jamey Mills, Psac regional executive vice-president for B.C., said 217 Parks Canada staff across seven sites in the province received the letters, including “entire workforces” at some sites. The park-warden detachment in B.C.’s Gulf Islands National Park Reserve will also close.

He said the cuts are particularly concerning in a province with geographically diverse parks that require workers with specialized training.

“It is important that there are on-the-ground staff with the ability to respond to potential emergencies, maintain critical infrastructure, meet visitor needs, and protect sensitive ecosystems,” Mr. Mills said in a statement.

Jean-Michel Lavergne, president of the Union of National Employees, a component of Psac, said in an e-mail that ending the search-and-rescue dog program in Banff raises concerns about avalanche searches, missing-person rescues and replacement response capacity. He added that park-warden detachment closures could mean longer response times and less backup for officers.

Other detachments set to close include those in Kluane National Park and Reserve in Yukon, Point Pelee National Park in Ontario, Kejimkujik National Park in Nova Scotia, Fundy National Park in New Brunswick and Nahanni National Park Reserve in the Northwest Territories.

Ms. Bradley said Parks Canada will maintain law-enforcement coverage through a regionalized model, with wardens redistributed according to need and risk.

Janet Sumner, executive director of the conservation organization Wildlands League, said the cuts undermine a plan announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney to protect 30 per cent of the country’s land and waters by the end of the decade.

“How do you do that while at the same time cutting the very agency that’s going to be responsible for managing some of that?” she said.

Reducing the agency’s work force could also have implications for national urban parks, which are particularly important because of the biodiversity they contain, she said.

The agency reductions are part of the Carney government’s comprehensive expenditure review. The review is expected to cut federal spending by $9-billion in 2026-27, $10-billion in 2027-28 and $13-billion in 2028-29, according to the government.

Parks Canada’s share of those cuts totals about $145-million: $24.6-million in 2026-27, $45.3-million in 2027-28 and $75-million in 2028-29.

The 2026 federal budget , released Thursday, commits $3.6-billion over 10 years to Parks Canada to maintain capital assets, as well as $282.7-million over 11 years, and $18-million annually, to establish and operate two new national marine conservation areas. The funding is separate from the planned spending reductions, which target the agency’s operating costs, staffing and existing services.

The budget also allocates $76-million to renewing the popular Canada Strong Pass program, which was first introduced in summer 2025 and offered free or discounted admission to Parks Canada sites, participating museums and galleries, as well as discounted rail travel. Visits to Parks Canada sites increased by 13 per cent because of the pass, the budget document said.

However, Psac said in its October statement on the work force cuts that there was no additional staffing to handle the increased tourism.

“This announcement is an insult after our members did more with less all summer long,” the union said.

The Canadian Parks and Wilderness Society, an environmental charity, said it is “deeply concerned” by the planned reductions, which it said could put ecosystems, visitor safety and local economies at risk. It also argued the move makes little economic sense: Parks Canada had a budget of about $1.3-billion in 2025-26, while visitors spent $6.5-billion in or near its sites, according to the federal agency.
Kecia Kerr, executive director of the society’s northern Alberta chapter, said the province’s national parks are already struggling to manage tourism and its effects on wildlife and visitor safety.

In Elk Island National Park, which is slated to lose its park-warden detachment, Ms. Kerr said speeding drivers have resulted in at least 11 bison deaths that she is aware of. There have also been issues with poaching at both Elk Island and Jasper National Park.
“Human-wildlife conflict, and a need for additional education for visitors on how to behave around wildlife, are already issues and these cuts will make those issues much worse,” she said.

She added that the federal cuts compound provincial decisions that have reduced protections for ecological reserves and removed portions of provincial parks for resort development, putting more pressure on Alberta’s protected areas.

A recent employment equity annual report stated that as of March 2025, Parks Canada had a total work force of about 6,000 employees, of which 48.5 per cent were seasonal. The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat, meanwhile, recorded 4,773 active Parks Canada employees this year.

The Public Service Alliance of Canada said 2,671 of its members at Parks Canada received the notices. To date, the employer has not explained which specific programs or services will be affected, the union said.

Jamey Mills, Psac regional executive vice-president for B.C., said 217 Parks Canada staff across seven sites in the province received the letters, including “entire workforces” at some sites. The park-warden detachment in B.C.’s Gulf Islands National Park Reserve will also close.
He said the cuts are particularly concerning in a province with geographically diverse parks that require workers with specialized training.

“It is important that there are on-the-ground staff with the ability to respond to potential emergencies, maintain critical infrastructure, meet visitor needs, and protect sensitive ecosystems,” Mr. Mills said in a statement.

Jean-Michel Lavergne, president of the Union of National Employees, a component of Psac, said in an e-mail that ending the search-and-rescue dog program in Banff raises concerns about avalanche searches, missing-person rescues and replacement response capacity. He added that park-warden detachment closures could mean longer response times and less backup for officers.

Other detachments set to close include those in Kluane National Park and Reserve in Yukon, Point Pelee National Park in Ontario, Kejimkujik National Park in Nova Scotia, Fundy National Park in New Brunswick and Nahanni National Park Reserve in the Northwest Territories.
Ms. Bradley said Parks Canada will maintain law-enforcement coverage through a regionalized model, with wardens redistributed according to need and risk.

Janet Sumner, executive director of the conservation organization Wildlands League, said the cuts undermine a plan announced by Prime Minister Mark Carney to protect 30 per cent of the country’s land and waters by the end of the decade.
“How do you do that while at the same time cutting the very agency that’s going to be responsible for managing some of that?” she said.
Reducing the agency’s work force could also have implications for national urban parks, which are particularly important because of the biodiversity they contain, she said.

The agency reductions are part of the Carney government’s comprehensive expenditure review. The review is expected to cut federal spending by $9-billion in 2026-27, $10-billion in 2027-28 and $13-billion in 2028-29, according to the government.
Parks Canada’s share of those cuts totals about $145-million: $24.6-million in 2026-27, $45.3-million in 2027-28 and $75-million in 2028-29.

The 2026 federal budget , released Thursday, commits $3.6-billion over 10 years to Parks Canada to maintain capital assets, as well as $282.7-million over 11 years, and $18-million annually, to establish and operate two new national marine conservation areas. The funding is separate from the planned spending reductions, which target the agency’s operating costs, staffing and existing services.

The budget also allocates $76-million to renewing the popular Canada Strong Pass program, which was first introduced in summer 2025 and offered free or discounted admission to Parks Canada sites, participating museums and galleries, as well as discounted rail travel. Visits to Parks Canada sites increased by 13 per cent because of the pass, the budget document said.
However, Psac said in its October statement on the work force cuts that there was no additional staffing to handle the increased tourism.
“This announcement is an insult after our members did more with less all summer long,” the union said.

stories.title: Dangerous bacteria found in tests of 11K vials of seized peptides: Health Canada
stories.summary: Health Canada says it found dangerous bacteria in tests done on more than 11,000 vials of unauthorized peptides seized from online retailers.
stories.author: John Marchesan
stories.content:
Health Canada says it found dangerous bacteria in tests done on more than 11,000 vials of unauthorized peptides seized from online retailers.

The federal health agency says injectable peptides from Shanghai ERP Peptide Biotechnology Co. Ltd. – a Chinese-based wholesaler of peptide products – were sold by two Canadian retailers, truenorthbiolabs.CA and bcaxiompeptide.com. Tests conducted on more than 11,400 vials seized found bacteria capable of causing serious infections.

“While unauthorized peptides are often promoted for weight loss, muscle growth, anti-aging, or wellness, they May expose you to significant and unpredictable health risks,” Health Canada said in a statement.

“Injecting contaminated products can cause serious infections, hospitalization, and in severe cases, life-threatening sepsis. The risk of infection is higher in people with a compromised immune system.”

Health Canada says if you have used an unauthorized injectable peptide drug and develop symptoms such as redness, swelling, pain at the injection site, fever, chills or you feel unwell, seek medical attention immediately, as these May be signs of a serious infection.

Health Canada says as a result of compliance and enforcement action, the two websites have been shut down. They have requested ERP Peptide to immediately stop selling illegal peptides into Canada while directing the Canada Border Services Agency to stop unauthorized shipments from entering the country.

Authorized prescription drugs in Canada have an eight-digit Drug Identification Number (DIN) on the label. You can also check whether a drug has been authorized for sale by searching Health Canada’s Drug Product Database .

stories.title: Farm truck caught going 92 km/h in 40 km/h zone: OPP
stories.summary: Ontario Provincial Police say a 49-year-old driver is charged with careless driving after a farm truck was caught going 92 km/h in a 40 km/h zone.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Ontario Provincial Police say a 49-year-old driver has been charged with careless driving after a farm truck was caught going 92 km/h in a 40 km/h zone.

The OPP said the incident occurred around 2:15 p.m. on Nov. 11 in Mapleton Township, which is roughly 50 kilometres west of Orangeville, Ont.

Officers pulled over a truck hauling farm equipment after catching it on radar.

“The piece of farm equipment was also observed to be occupying almost both lanes of traffic, posing as a traffic hazard,” the OPP told Global News in an email.

The driver was charged, and the OPP said the tires on the truck had a safety rating only designed to be driving at 40 km/h.

The OPP said Friday in a post on X the speed is more than double the maximum allowed speed for certain types of farm equipment operating on Ontario roads.

stories.title: Four arrested, 220 charges laid in Cape Breton organized crime probe
stories.summary: The Cape Breton police probe began in July 2025 when police were called to find a stolen vehicle that was tracked to a property in Florence, N.S.
stories.author: Aaron D'Andrea
stories.content:
Four people are facing 220 charges after Cape Breton police disrupted an organized crime group.

Cape Breton Regional Police said the investigation unfolded over 16 months and involved the possession, trafficking, dismantling and resale of more than $10 million in stolen vehicles and related property across several provinces.

The probe began in July 2025 when police were called to find a stolen vehicle that was tracked to a property in Florence, N.S.

There, police said officers discovered more stolen vehicles. Five properties were searched and police seized several vehicles, parts, commercial equipment, machinery and firearms.

“The investigation determined that vehicles were being acquired from Ontario, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Newfoundland and Manitoba, and then being altered through the replacement or manipulation of vehicle identification numbers for resale, or dismantled for their components to be sold through an online retailer,” police said in a Facebook post Thursday.

The charges laid against the four people include participating in activities of a criminal organization, laundering proceeds of crime, possession and trafficking property obtained by crime and tampering with a vehicle identification number.

stories.title: Ontario career college forced into layoffs as student funding stalls
stories.summary: A school that says it plays by the rules warns that continuing to withhold student funding hurts Ontario’s workforce and could put good actors out of business.
stories.author: Olivia Bowden
stories.content:
As the Ford government cracks down on private career colleges over alleged student loan fraud, a school that says it plays by the rules warns that continuing to withhold student funding hurts Ontario’s workforce and could put good actors out of business.

“Our revenues and income completely stopped all of a sudden, which resulted in layoffs. After 35 years, we did layoffs for the first time Monday,” said Muraly Srinarayanathas, the chairman of Computek College, a private career college with locations in Toronto, Ajax and Marhkam.

“We’ve requested the ministry to be first in terms of the inspections so that we can get back to what we do best, which is serving our students,” he said.

Computek mainly offers training for those entering healthcare, business and technology.

It’s one of hundreds of private career colleges where thousands of students have had their promised student loans cut as the province said it’s investigating “serious concerns” about alleged Ontario Student Assistance Program (Osap) fraud.

But the blanket ban has been “confusing,” said Srinarayanathas, as Computek is audited each year and is visited by inspectors annually, indicating a clean record.

It’s now not only upended the lives of students, but the Osap ban has also put the college on shaky financial ground, he said.

In July, the Ford government first disqualified students at five private career colleges from Osap loans due to concerns about enrollment practices and unusually high concentration of student loan applications.

By October, the government extended the Osap ban to all 242 private career colleges as the province investigated “serious concerns” raised by the federal government, advocacy groups and internal audits and inspections.

On Thursday, College and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that legislation will be introduced Monday with the intent to increase oversight and accountability. He said the significant concerns around Osap usage in the sector are far more widespread than first suspected.

stories.title: Toronto orthodox priest criticized for accepting medal from Putin
stories.summary: The Ukrainian Canadian Congress said it was disgraceful that Father Vladimir Malchenko shook hands with Putin two days after Russia bombed a school in Ukraine, killing 55.
stories.author: Stewart Bell
stories.content:
A Toronto priest is facing criticism for accepting a medal from Vladimir Putin last week as the Russian president is waging a war on Ukraine that has killed thousands of civilians.

At a ceremony at the Kremlin on Nov. 4, Putin presented the Order of Friendship to Father Vladimir Malchenko, head priest at Toronto’s Holy Trinity Russian Orthodox Church.

A video of the event obtained by Global News shows Malchenko striding onto a stage to greet Putin, who shakes the priest’s hand and pins the Russian state honour onto his frock.

Putin commended Malchenko for helping Canadian “parishioners maintain their connection with their historical homeland.” Malchenko’s acceptance speech lauded the “Fatherland.”

The awards ceremony took place on Russia’s National Unity Day. In his remarks praising Malchenko, Putin also celebrated Russian troops he said were “bravely” fighting in Ukraine.

Reached by phone this week, Malchenko said he had no regrets about being honoured by Putin, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes for the abduction of Ukrainian children.

“I don’t look at it as a political act. It’s an act of recognition of our pastoral duties here in Canada,” Malchenko told Global News after returning to Toronto from Moscow.

“And our community is very grateful that there’s been a certain amount of recognition of our work here to comfort people’s lives in Canada,” said Malchenko.

But the Ukrainian Canadian Congress said it was “disgraceful” that the Canadian priest had accepted a medal from the Russian leader as he continues to attack his neighbours.

Two days before Malchenko exchanged pleasantries with Putin, Russia bombed a school in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region that was used as a humanitarian hub, killing more than 50 people.

“This is a textbook case of moral hypocrisy unbecoming of an individual who purports to promote Christian teaching,” said Danylo Korbabicz, CEO of the Canadian Ukrainian group.

The Order of Friendship is awarded for “outstanding contributions to strengthening friendship” and “fostering peace and friendly relations among countries.”

Past recipients include pro-Russia actor Steven Seagal and former prime minister Jean Chretien, but that was before Putin sent his troops into Ukraine in 2014.

Following Russia’s 2022 assault on Kyiv, Canada placed Putin on its Russia sanctions list, citing his “grave breach of international peace and security.”

Also sanction was Kirill, the patriarch of the Russian Orthodox church and a cheerleader of Putin’s attack on Ukraine, which he has deemed a “holy war.”

In his comments to Global News, Malchenko said his Toronto church was “above politics,” did not support any wars and was “greatly” concerned about the human suffering caused by armed conflicts.

But he said he didn’t raise the war in Ukraine with Putin at the medal ceremony. “No, it really wasn’t time for a conversation,” he explained.

He characterized his award as recognition for “fulfilling our Christian duties in Canada,” and said the church was apolitical. “We never talk about the war,” he said.

However, the church’s website links to Russian online platforms that parrot the claim that Ukraine is an “imaginary country” and Ukrainians are “imaginary” people.

The links, which also claim there is “no such thing” as Ukraine, are in line with Russian propaganda that aims to justify Putin’s military campaign.

Malchenko’s church is a registered charity that receives government tax breaks. In 2012, the Conservative government awarded him the Queen’s Diamond Jubilee Medal .

In his brief acceptance speech, Malchenko said that Russians lived “in all cities, in all countries of this world. But we have one Fatherland. Russia, Holy Rus.”

“And May the Lord God bless our beloved Fatherland. May He bless it with prosperity and well-being forever.”

Putin’s speech harkened back to past wars that he said “drove invaders” out of what he called Russia’s “native lands.”

“Today our fighters are just as bravely defending Russia’s interests and our statehood as part of the special military operation,” he said , using his term for the Ukraine war.

Malchenko’s visit to the Kremlin came at a time of some of the worst atrocities of Putin’s attempt to use his military might to turn Ukraine into a vassal of Moscow.

The night before Russia’s deadly attack on a school in Zaporizhzhia, a hospital complex was struck, injuring at least 73, while the bombing of a hospice in Dnipro forced the evacuation of dozens of terminally ill and elderly patients.

On Wednesday, Canada joined its G7 allies in condemning Putin’s attacks on “residential buildings, civilian infrastructure, and cultural heritage.”

Global Affairs Canada did not respond to requests for comment about the matter.

Stewart.Bell@globalnews.CA

stories.title: Blue Jays apologize to Muslim community and fans in wake of Santander’s posts
stories.summary: The Blue Jays are the only MLB team in Canada, with a population of over 1.78 million Muslims, per 2021 census data from Statistics Canada.
stories.author: Lucas Casaletto
stories.content:
By Gregory Strong, The Canadian Press

Posted November 13, 2026 8:25 am.

The Toronto Blue Jays apologized Thursday to the Muslim community and the team’s fans for the “pain and harm” caused by outfielder Anthony Santander’s social media posts .

Santander shared anti-Muslim posts last week and deleted them two days later.

“We met with leaders in Toronto’s Muslim communities today, who shared the harm caused by Anthony Santander’s Islamophobic social media posts,” team president and chief executive officer Mark Shapiro said in a statement. “The opportunity to listen and learn was important and reaffirms our beliefs and values as an organization. We condemn Islamophobia and all forms of hate.

“The Blue Jays are deeply sorry to the Muslim community and our fans for the pain and harm these Islamophobic posts have caused. We will work with leaders in Muslim communities to fight against all forms of hate. The Blue Jays will continue to ensure our organization reflects the inclusive community we are proud to call home.”

Blue Jays general manager Ross Atkins, speaking Tuesday at Major League Baseball’s GM meetings in Las Vegas, said he recently spoke with Santander and asked him to publicly address the controversy.

However, Santander has yet to publicly comment or apologize. The 32-year-old Venezuelan and the sports management agency that represents him have not responded to multiple messages.

“There really aren’t words to express my level of disappointment,” Atkins told reporters.

Santander shared posts in the aftermath of the U.S. midterm elections last week.

The videos included a Christian preacher saying, “There is no such thing as kind Muslims,” with another suggesting Sharia law would be imposed on the U.S. after Abdul El-Sayed was elected to the Senate in Michigan.

Santander didn’t play at the big-league level last season due to injuries. He signed a five-year, US$92.5-million deal with Toronto in January 2025.

The Blue Jays are the only MLB team in Canada, which has a population of over 1.78 million Muslims, per 2021 census data from Statistics Canada. About 10 per cent of Toronto’s 2.8 million residents identify as Muslim, the agency said.

Steven Zhou, the media and communications lead for the National Council of Canadian Muslims, said several community advocates were on hand for the meeting, which lasted about an hour.

“This is an initial meeting and we considered it a positive step in the right direction,” he said Thursday night. “Because there is a commitment to putting this player through training, and also there was a public statement apologizing for what happened from the CEO and from the organization itself, these are all very positive signs.

“The next step, of course, we would like to see an apology from the player himself and an expression from him about why this is wrong, and an expression also about trying to build a positive way forward.”

In an interview earlier in the week , Zhou said Santander’s posts had a significant impact on the community.

“I think some people might be surprised at just how many Muslims are fans of baseball and the Blue Jays, and Toronto is a massive sports city,” Zhou said. “The kind of response I’ve gotten from our community members from different circles, from various people, has been unbelievable. People are very, very upset.”

It remains unclear whether the Blue Jays will discipline Santander. There are also unanswered questions remaining about how potential social media policy and morality clause contract violations might be handled.

Messages left with the team, and club owner Rogers Communications Inc., ON those subjects were not immediately returned.

Santander hit 44 homers for the Baltimore Orioles in 2024 but hit just .175 with six homers over 54 games in an injury-plagued 2025 season with Toronto.

He’s expected to be healthy for the 2027 season and become an everyday player again.

Spring training is scheduled to begin in February but there is a strong possibility an MLB lockout will begin next month when the current collective bargaining agreement expires.

stories.title: Fatality reported after October collision in Morris-Turnberry
stories.summary: The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.
stories.author: Kristylee Varley
stories.content:
A 68-year-old Huron-Kinloss Township man has died from injuries sustained in a two-vehicle collision last month in Morris-Turnberry, provincial police say.

Huron County OPP, Huron County Paramedic Services and the North Huron Fire Department responded to the crash on Amberley Road between Currie Line and Helena Street on Oct. 14.

Police said the collision involved a passenger vehicle and a van.

The lone occupant of the passenger vehicle suffered serious injuries and was airlifted to a London hospital for treatment.

OPP said the 68-year-old driver died on Nov. 10 as a result of injuries sustained in the collision.

No further details were released.

stories.title: Ontario to cap Osap growth at career colleges following massive increases
stories.summary: Toronto - Career colleges in Ontario could soon be subject to limits on the growth of students funded by financial aid, following explosive increases in the sector that prompted the government to call in the police.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
TORONTO - Career colleges in Ontario could soon be subject to limits on the growth of students funded by financial aid, following explosive increases in the sector that prompted the government to call in the police.

Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn announced that legislation will be introduced on Monday, saying the significant concerns around Ontario Student Assistance Program usage in the sector are far more widespread than first suspected and the bill is intended to increase oversight and accountability.

“What we have found here are not minor administrative concerns, but rather co-ordinated, sophisticated efforts to take advantage of students and taxpayers for personal gain,” he said Thursday at a press conference.

Career Colleges Ontario, which processes OSAP applications for the schools, has removed 24 more campuses from their membership, with an additional 13 under review, Quinn said. The association has also identified concerns about backdating applications at 33 additional campuses, he said.

“This behaviour is despicable, and it must be stopped,” Quinn said.

The legislation is set to include the as-yet undefined cap, limit OSAP funding to in-person and hybrid programs at those institutions and require them to have a physical location, and prohibit them from operating unrelated businesses on campus.

Quinn has said that concerns about career colleges being co-located with immigration and recruitment firms are among issues raised by an ongoing KPMG audit of the sector. As well, the legislation would allow the province to more easily recover OSAP funding from career colleges by holding them liable for students’ loans.

Critics say the problem is one of the government’s own making, allowing online-only programs to qualify for OSAP in the first place during the COVID-19 pandemic and not watching closely enough as growth skyrocketed.

“If the minister is indicating that this is so systemic, how come they let it get this bad?” Liberal critic Tyler Watt said.

NDP critic Peggy Sattler said oversight measures proposed in the bill are important, but it never should have come to this.

“This bill is a classic case of closing the barn door after the horses are gone,” she said.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

While the KPMG audit is ongoing, Quinn has paused OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institutions, causing some students to drop out and some colleges to consider closing their doors.

Quinn has said the government is working on securing low-interest loans for students through banks until the pause is lifted in the new year, but he has so far not indicated a timeline for that.

Colleges and students are calling on the government to weed out any bad actors in a way that doesn’t also penalize institutions and students who follow the rules. Premier Doug Ford has said KPMG auditors have been tasked with clearing low-risk schools first.

Career Colleges Ontario said it will review the details of the legislation once it is actually introduced, but in the meantime the announcement does nothing for the compliant institutions affected by the broad pause.

“Innocent students continue to bear the consequences of the sector-wide pause, and we continue to call on the government to reinstate OSAP for students attending compliant institutions,” the association wrote in a statement.

Interim Liberal leader John Fraser said the government is holding innocent students hostage with the OSAP pause.

“The rent doesn’t wait,” he said. “The grocery bill doesn’t wait. The kids’ clothes don’t wait, and this government’s saying, ‘wait,’” Fraser said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

stories.title: Impacts from B.C. drenching mount as water levels rise
stories.summary: Vancouver - The impacts of the drenching on British Columbia's south coast have been increasing as heavy rain triggers evacuation orders and alerts, flood warnings and the shutdown of a water treatment plant.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Peter Spitzer is among residents of Paradise Valley Road who are sheltering in place north of Squamish, B.C., after their homes were cut off by river waters swollen by drenching rains and a dam discharge that followed.

He’s been at his property near the confluence of the Cheakamus River and Culliton Creek for nearly 40 years and has seen floodwaters break their banks before.

Spitzer and his neighbours in the flood zone about 16 kilometres from Squamish know the drill.

“We all stay put and help the neighbours out if somebody needs anything. We usually have food and water for quite a few days before we run out,” he said Thursday.

A procession of storms has drenched parts of southwest British Columbia with more than 300 millimetres of rain in 48 hours leading to multiple evacuation orders and alerts, as well as the shelter-in-place decree that was issued by the District of Squamish on Thursday morning.

The entire village of Pemberton, population 3,400, is under an evacuation alert “out of an abundance of caution.”.

But rains have eased for most of the province, including Metro Vancouver.

Environment Canada had lowered most rainfall warnings by Thursday, although yellow warnings were still active for west and inland Vancouver Island, where heavy rains were forecast to last into Friday afternoon.

But the impacts of the deluge continue. Spitzer said parts of Paradise Valley Road were flooded and water under the now-closed Bailey Bridge out of the community is “very close to the top.”

“At the moment there’s no way out of the valley,” he said.

Spitzer said the water hadn’t reached his home but others were surrounded or their basements were flooded.

Video posted online shows trucks driving down roads covered in fast-flowing water. Another shows a resident standing at the front door of his home, which is under several feet of water, while a friend on the opposite bank calls across the water to make sure he is OK.

The District of Squamish said in a statement Thursday that the spill level from the Cheakamus Dam at Daisy Lake peaked at approximately 5 a.m. and was expected to decrease slowly throughout the day.

The district said that would create room in the reservoir for more rain, and eventually allow for roads to be reopened, adding that river levels were also expected to peak Thursday.

The flooding came after the rate of water flowing into the dam’s reservoir more than tripled expectations, due to back-to-back storms.

Whitney Deane, a spokesperson for B.C. Hydro, said forecasters were originally expecting the rate of water flowing into the reservoir to peak at a manageable 235 cubic metres per second by midday Thursday.

But at 11 p.m. on Wednesday, the hydro company issued a flood warning and about an hour later, flows into the reservoir peaked at 735 cubic metres per second, she said.

“That’s roughly three times the forecast coming at a much shorter window,” she said.

The string of weather systems that slammed southwestern B.C. since last week brought 306 millimetres of rain to Port Mellon in the Howe Sound region since Tuesday, while 261 millimetres fell at Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island.

The rain forced evacuation orders for parts of Vancouver Island, the Lil’wat First Nation in the central Interior, and parts Pemberton, about 150 kilometres north of Vancouver.

Pemberton’s evacuation order covers properties on Airport Road, including the community’s airport, wastewater treatment facility, wildland fire management base and a public golf course. The B.C. Ministry of Transportation’s DriveBC website says Highway 99 east of Pemberton has been shut in both directions.

The Lilʼwat Nation has expanded an evacuation order and alert for the area from Kwetsa7 along the Lillooet River corridor to Lillooet Lake.

Elsewhere, the Strathcona Regional District issued a water conservation notice for the village of Sayward on the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, as high flows in Newcastle Creek led to extra sediment in the water, and an evacuation order due to flooding and landslide risks remains in place for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

“A strong frontal system over the area will weaken today. Rain will continue to ease as the front weakens,” Environment Canada said Thursday.

Environment Canada said several locations reported more than 100 millimetres of rain in the last 48 hours, including Kennedy Lake on Vancouver Island (248 mm), Port Alberni (123 mm), Porteau Cove on the Sea to Sky Highway (140 mm), Whistler (138 mm), and Squamish (134 mm).

The storms have been associated with a spike in temperatures which saw daily records fall in more than 30 locations on Wednesday, including Abbotsford, where the mercury reached 20.1 Celsius, smashing a 45-year-old record by three degrees.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

Note to readers:This is a corrected story. An earlier version misidentified data provided by B.C. Hydro as being the rate of discharge from the dam. In fact, those numbers represent inflow.
