stories.title: Canadians gather for Remembrance Day ceremonies across the country
stories.summary: Ottawa - Canadians across the country are gathering today to reflect on the legacy of war and remember the men and women who served and died defending this country.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - Guns boomed, bagpipes wailed and CF-18 Hornets thundered overhead as Canadians paused at the National War Memorial in Ottawa on Wednesday to remember those who served and died defending this country.

This Remembrance Day comes just weeks after a deadly training accident at Canadian Forces Wainwright left four dead and dozens of other soldiers with burn injuries.

Sgt. Morgan Wong of Edmonton, Pte. Shaun Farrell of Prince Albert, Sask., Pte. Aidan Goulding of North Vancouver and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark of Langley, B.C., were killed at the Alberta training base last month.

They died and dozens of others were injured when strong winds suddenly swept up a grass fire that was burning on the automatic grenade launcher range and carried it across the training area.

“We mourn their loss, stand with those recovering from their injuries, and hold their families and fellow service members in our thoughts,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a media statement.

Gov. Gen. Louise Arbour said Canadians’ thoughts “remain with the soldiers we lost, those who were wounded, as well as the families, friends, comrades and all others affected by this tragic event.”

National Defence has said that, as of Nov. 4, 14 of the 39 injured had been released from hospital while another 25 remained in hospital.

Thoughts for Wainwright victims poured out from people across the country.

A prayer for the victims was read at the ceremony in Place du Canada in Montreal, as cannon fire rang in the air. In Toronto, Mayor Olivia Chow said she wished the injured “strength and healing.”

Hundreds gathered at an arena in Wainwright, Alta. for the local ceremony. They included Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, whose riding includes the training facility.

South of the border, Rear-Admiral Kristjan Monaghan spoke at the Canadian Embassy on Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington, D.C., about those who died in Alberta last month.

“The loss experienced there has been felt across the Canadian Forces family, across the nation and beyond,” Monaghan said.

“It reminds us that sacrifice is not defined solely by geography. Service members accept risks, not only when deployed overseas but also while preparing themselves to serve their country.”

Canadians are also marking a quarter-century this year since the Afghanistan war began. The war — the longest in Canadian history — stretched on for more than 12 years and involved some 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members.

Veterans Affairs Canada said 158 Canadian Armed Forces members and seven Canadian civilians — a diplomat, four aid workers, a government contractor and a journalist — lost their lives in Afghanistan.

Ian Moffat, a retired Royal Canadian Navy commander who served for 41 years, said Wednesday he was thinking about a soldier who died in Afghanistan.

“When I was in Afghanistan, there was a young armoured soldier in her very early 20s who was killed by an [improvised explosive device],” he told The Canadian Press at the ceremony in Ottawa.

“If you saw her picture, you’d swear she wasn’t any older than 17. I was at the ramp ceremony when she was loaded on board and I’ve never forgotten that.”

Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch as his son marched in his first Remembrance Day parade after joining the military last year.

McGill said his job during the Afghanistan war was to notify next of kin when soldiers were killed.

“It’s a pretty powerful day and gives us an opportunity to come out and pay tribute to those who can’t be here today,” he said. “Those guys gave their todays for our tomorrows.”

Kyle Scott, a Canadian Army veteran of the Afghanistan war who travelled to Ottawa from Alberta, said he was thinking about the comrades he served with who never made it home — and those who died after their return.

“I think of my own family and the troubles they faced when they returned from the First and Second World Wars,” he added.

“Life after service is often harder than when you are serving, so today has a lot of meaning.”

Marcel Huot, a Second World War veteran wounded twice in Normandy, was one of several veterans of that war who came out to the national ceremony.

He said he remembers a heavy barrage of artillery fire, “sand everywhere” and live fire directed at him. He recalled dropping to the ground to avoid the shelling before being hit in the back by a piece of shrapnel.

Huot said his thoughts are of his wife, who enjoyed coming out to the national remembrance ceremony.

“She died of Alzheimer’s. I’m lonely sometimes,” he said.

Veterans Affairs estimates the population of living Canadian veterans from the Second World War and the Korean War has dropped to approximately 4,306 people.

This year also marks the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Royal Canadian Legion — created in 1926 to serve as the main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits — and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.

Hundreds of cadets came out to celebrate RMC’s anniversary.

“The cadets here and across Canada have grown considerably. There’s almost 70,000 cadets in the organization now across Canada,” said Dave Edwards, who works with the Connaught Cadet Training Centre in Ottawa. “It’s a great thing to see.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

“It reminds us that sacrifice is not defined solely by geography. Service members accept risks, not only when deployed overseas but also while preparing themselves to serve their country.”

Canadians are also marking a quarter-century this year since the Afghanistan war began. The war — the longest in Canadian history — stretched on for more than 12 years and involved some 40,000 Canadian Armed Forces members.
Veterans Affairs Canada said 158 Canadian Armed Forces members and seven Canadian civilians — a diplomat, four aid workers, a government contractor and a journalist — lost their lives in Afghanistan.
Ian Moffat, a retired Royal Canadian Navy commander who served for 41 years, said Wednesday he was thinking about a soldier who died in Afghanistan.
“When I was in Afghanistan, there was a young armoured soldier in her very early 20s who was killed by an [improvised explosive device],” he told The Canadian Press at the ceremony in Ottawa.
“If you saw her picture, you’d swear she wasn’t any older than 17. I was at the ramp ceremony when she was loaded on board and I’ve never forgotten that.”
Ray McGill of Courtice, Ont. came to Ottawa so he could proudly watch as his son marched in his first Remembrance Day parade after joining the military last year.
McGill said his job during the Afghanistan war was to notify next of kin when soldiers were killed.
“It’s a pretty powerful day and gives us an opportunity to come out and pay tribute to those who can’t be here today,” he said. “Those guys gave their todays for our tomorrows.”

Kyle Scott, a Canadian Army veteran of the Afghanistan war who travelled to Ottawa from Alberta, said he was thinking about the comrades he served with who never made it home — and those who died after their return.
“I think of my own family and the troubles they faced when they returned from the First and Second World Wars,” he added.
“Life after service is often harder than when you are serving, so today has a lot of meaning.”
Marcel Huot, a Second World War veteran wounded twice in Normandy, was one of several veterans of that war who came out to the national ceremony.

He said he remembers a heavy barrage of artillery fire, “sand everywhere” and live fire directed at him. He recalled dropping to the ground to avoid the shelling before being hit in the back by a piece of shrapnel.
Huot said his thoughts are of his wife, who enjoyed coming out to the national remembrance ceremony.
“She died of Alzheimer’s. I’m lonely sometimes,” he said.
Veterans Affairs estimates the population of living Canadian veterans from the Second World War and the Korean War has dropped to approximately 4,306 people.

This year also marks the 100th anniversary of the founding of the Royal Canadian Legion — created in 1926 to serve as the main advocacy group for veterans’ benefits — and the 150th anniversary of the Royal Military College.
Hundreds of cadets came out to celebrate RMC’s anniversary.

“The cadets here and across Canada have grown considerably. There’s almost 70,000 cadets in the organization now across Canada,” said Dave Edwards, who works with the Connaught Cadet Training Centre in Ottawa. “It’s a great thing to see.”
This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.
— With files from Nick Murray, Alyssa Wheeler and David Baxter in Ottawa, Charlotte Glorieux in Montreal, Jordan Omstead in Toronto, Kelly Malone in Washington and Bill Graveland in Wainwright

stories.title: Ontario student accused of working for Chinese official pleads not guilty in U.S.
stories.summary: An Ontario student accused of working for someone he believed to be a Chinese government official has pleaded not guilty in the United States to making false statements.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
An Ontario student accused of working for someone he believed to be a Chinese government official has pleaded not guilty in a United States court to making false statements.

Documents from a Michigan court show Weiheng Zeng entered his plea at his arraignment on Monday.

Zeng, a Chinese citizen who was studying at the University of Waterloo, was arrested after allegedly taking photos of Toronto’s Pearson airport and Chicago’s O’Hare airport at the request of a mysterious Chinese contact he’d met on an online forum.

In an affidavit filed earlier this year, an FBI agent said Zeng was first flagged by authorities in connection with an incident at O’Hare in April, when a man was seen taking photos, climbing a forklift and trying to open locked trailers at a FedEx facility.

The affidavit said Zeng, who had driven into the United States about 10 days before the incident, was later linked to a minivan seen at the site.

When Zeng tried to drive into the country with the same vehicle in August, he was pulled aside for several interviews, during which he allegedly gave conflicting statements, it said.

The allegations have not yet been tested in court.

Zeng initially said he took photos of planes during his trip to Chicago, but when border agents went through his phone, they found photos of aircraft and military planes as well as some of Zeng and others in tactical clothes holding firearms, the document said.

He told the agents he took photos of model aircraft for a flight radar website and denied having any kind of military training, it said.

In a second interview with border agents, Zeng said he took photos of planes landing at O’Hare from a public parking lot, but later said he took pictures from a forklift at a FedEx facility, the affidavit said. He also said he’d previously trespassed at a FedEx facility at Pearson airport but had been caught, the document said.

Zeng first mentioned a Chinese contact in his third interview, and his story continued to change as he gave more details, the document said.

At first, he said the contact reached out through a website for aviation spotters and asked him to take photos of specific planes for research, the affidavit said.

Then he admitted that was a cover story provided by the contact, who actually wanted information on transportation logistics and wanted photos of particular locations around airports, the agent alleged.

Zeng also said the contact sent him a photo of a badge and videos of scenes only security officials could access, and that he suspected the contact was connected to the Chinese Communist Party, the document said.

His trial is set to begin in January, according to a schedule filed with the court.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: 'Things will never be the same': Wainwright prepares for Remembrance Day after fire
stories.summary: Edmonton - The Alberta town of Wainwright is gearing up for what could be the most solemn Remembrance Day in its recent history, says Mayor Bruce Pugh.
stories.author: Fakiha Baig The Canadian Press
stories.content:
EDMONTON - The Alberta town of Wainwright is gearing up for what could be the most solemn Remembrance Day in its recent history, says Mayor Bruce Pugh.

A fire on Oct. 17 at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright killed four soldiers and injured 39. Officials said last week that 25 were still in various hospitals.

“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” said Pugh.

“Wainwright is a military community and it’s a big family.

“I get a sense that things will never be the same.”

Hundreds of military personnel, residents and dignitaries are set to fill the local ice rink on Wednesday for the town’s annual Remembrance Day ceremony.

A memorial is laid at the entrance of CFB Wainwright for four Canadian Armed Forces members — from left, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, Pte. Shaun Farrell and Sgt. Morgan Wong — who died in a fire during a training exercise at the base in Wainwright, Alta., on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.

Flowers and wreaths are also to be placed at the town’s clock tower, said Pugh. The fieldstone tower, which commemorates Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars, has been standing in the middle of a downtown roundabout for about a century.

Remembrance Day has been significant in Wainwright for many years.

The town of about 7,000 people, located 210 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is home to one of the busiest Canadian Forces bases in the country, and its members are deeply intertwined in local life.

The children of Armed Forces members go to school and play hockey in town. And residents are accustomed to hearing artillery blasts and feeling their windows shake during training exercises.

“We’re worried about our CAF friends,” Pugh said.

“I know they have tremendous support and strength, but how can you go through an event like that and not have a scar?”

Mayor Bruce Pugh of Wainwright, Alta, is photographed in his home on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.

Roughly 84 soldiers with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in a field exercise at the base, when strong and sudden winds whipped a grass fire into their path.

Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

The four killed were: Sgt. Morgan Wong, 26, of Edmonton; Pte. Shaun Farrell, 23, of Prince Albert, Sask.; Pte. Aidan Goulding, 23, of North Vancouver, B.C.; and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, 19, of Langley, B.C.

The brother of Shaun Farrell and a friend of Morgan Wong, two of four who died on Saturday, shared memories of the soldiers.

Among the injured is Sean Hiatt, a 24-year-old corporal with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, who also worked as a railway track maintenance supervisor with CN Rail.

The railway said it plans to station locomotives outside the Wainwright arena on Wednesday.

“We recognize that this year’s Remembrance Day comes at a particularly difficult time following the recent tragedy at CFB Wainwright,” the railway said in a statement.

Jennifer Ford, an archivist with the Wainwright and District Museum and Visitor Information Center, said the mood in Wainwright has been serious since the fire.

“I went to school with people whose families served in the military and they were just involved in community,” she said.

“It’s a very close-knit community.”

Seventh grade students of the Blessed Sacrament Catholic School place messages at a memorial dedicated to military personnel involved in a training accident that killed four soldiers at CFB Wainwright earlier this week, in Wainwright, Alta., on Thursday, Oct. 22, 2026.

paragraphs: EDMONTON - The Alberta town of Wainwright is gearing up for what could be the most solemn Remembrance Day in its recent history, says Mayor Bruce Pugh.
A fire on Oct. 17 at the nearby Canadian Forces Base Wainwright killed four soldiers and injured 39. Officials said last week that 25 were still in various hospitals.
“It will be different this year just with the weight of what happened,” said Pugh.
“Wainwright is a military community and it’s a big family.
“I get a sense that things will never be the same.”
Hundreds of military personnel, residents and dignitaries are set to fill the local ice rink on Wednesday for the town’s annual Remembrance Day ceremony.

A memorial is laid at the entrance of CFB Wainwright for four Canadian Armed Forces members — from left, Pte. Aidan Goulding, Pte. Hayden Lykkemark, Pte. Shaun Farrell and Sgt. Morgan Wong — who died in a fire during a training exercise at the base in Wainwright, Alta., on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.

Flowers and wreaths are also to be placed at the town’s clock tower, said Pugh. The fieldstone tower, which commemorates Canadians who died in the First and Second World Wars, has been standing in the middle of a downtown roundabout for about a century.
Remembrance Day has been significant in Wainwright for many years.
The town of about 7,000 people, located 210 kilometres southeast of Edmonton, is home to one of the busiest Canadian Forces bases in the country, and its members are deeply intertwined in local life.
The children of Armed Forces members go to school and play hockey in town. And residents are accustomed to hearing artillery blasts and feeling their windows shake during training exercises.
“We’re worried about our CAF friends,” Pugh said.
“I know they have tremendous support and strength, but how can you go through an event like that and not have a scar?”
Mayor Bruce Pugh of Wainwright, Alta, is photographed in his home on Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026.
Roughly 84 soldiers with the Princess Patricia’s Canadian Light Infantry were taking part in a field exercise at the base, when strong and sudden winds whipped a grass fire into their path.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has called it one of the worst tragedies for the Armed Forces on Canadian soil during peacetime. Three investigations are looking into what happened.

The brother of Shaun Farrell and a friend of Morgan Wong, two of four who died on Saturday, shared memories of the soldiers.
Among the injured is Sean Hiatt, a 24-year-old corporal with the Loyal Edmonton Regiment, who also worked as a railway track maintenance supervisor with CN Rail.
The railway said it plans to station locomotives outside the Wainwright arena on Wednesday.

stories.title: B.C. deluge could bring 250 mm of rain as forecasters predict flooding, landslides
stories.summary: A deluge hitting Vancouver Island and other parts of southwest British Columbia could bring more than 250 millimetres of rain in some places, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Wild weather that is slamming into the south coast of British Columbia has forced the suspension of search-and-rescue efforts for a missing canoeist off Vancouver Island, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides triggered by drenching rains.

A series of atmospheric rivers has been hitting southwest B.C. since last week, with the latest storms forecast to bring up to 250 millimetres of rain in some places.

The storms had already turned deadly, with the deaths of a driver in Surrey, B.C., whose car was crushed by a falling tree on Saturday, and a Vancouver pedestrian who was hit by a car during what police called a heavy rainstorm last Friday.

A deluge hitting Vancouver Island and other parts of southwest British Columbia could bring more than 250 millimetres of rain in some places, as forecasters warn of floods and landslides. (Nov. 10, 2026)

RCMP in Sayward, B.C., said worsening weather had made it unsafe for water and shoreline searches for 35-year old Dakota Smith, who was reported missing last Friday after going fishing.

Smith’s capsized canoe had been found in waters off the northeast coast of Vancouver Island, but police said the chances of his survival had been “drastically reduced” by “high unpredictable winds, heavy rainfalls and the frigid water temperature.”

The Ma’amtagila Nation community indicated members were continuing to look for Smith despite the end of the official search.

Environment Canada recorded high winds the day Smith went missing, and the province was being struck by storm systems that are continuing.

Environment Canada meteorologist Michael Gismondi said in an interview Tuesday that the drenching from the atmospheric river storms is “fairly typical for this time of year.”

“Typically we get a few every year, so it’s not unusual for this to happen.”

Gismondi said he does not expect “catastrophic” impacts, but flooding was possible as the rain continued across the region for a day or more.

“It kind of taps into some warm tropical air from the lower latitudes and it brings it right up to the B.C. coast,” he said of the atmospheric river. “So we’ll expect heavy rain, mild conditions, high freezing levels and then there’s another system coming in that will sort of re-intensify that front as we go into Wednesday.”

Environment Canada has raised orange rainfall warnings in west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea-to-Sky regions, meaning the “severe” storms were likely to cause significant damage and disruption.

The agency said parts of Vancouver Island could see more than 250 millimetres of rain, while Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions could see upwards of 160 millimetres.

Parts of Metro Vancouver could receive 160 millimetres, while Haida Gwaii and north Vancouver Island could get wind gusts of up to 110 kilometres an hour.

Grouse Mountain Regional Park in North Vancouver closed early on Tuesday due to inclement weather, and the mountain’s website says both the Grouse Grind and BCMC trail will be closed on Wednesday due to heavy rains.

The mountain’s website said park staff will assess conditions over the coming days to determine when it can safely reopen.

The forecaster also issued orange warnings for potentially “damaging winds” in central B.C., on Tuesday. It said the southeasterly wind would increase into Wednesday, with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour expected in some regions before easing Wednesday evening.

British Columbia’s River Forecast Centre issued ongoing flood watches on Monday for much of Vancouver Island and the South Coast, with the worst weather expected to last into Wednesday before tapering off Thursday.

The agency issued high streamflow advisories for southern Vancouver Island, the Fraser Valley and Fraser Canyon on Tuesday.

BC Hydro said in a news release Tuesday that its crews were working to restore power to customers “following a series of damaging storms that affected approximately 415,000 customers across the province since Friday.”

It noted some of the most extensive storm damage happened in the northern and central Interior, adding that about 2,300 properties remained without power as of Tuesday.

Gismondi said the precipitation along B.C.‘s coastal regions is expected to slow early Wednesday before the next system is forecast to pass through the region. That, he said, is expected to continue until Friday, when another short break is expected.

“It kind of looks like another system coming for the weekend — so probably back into some rain for the weekend,” he said.

B.C.‘s Transportation Ministry issued a news release late Tuesday, advising drivers travelling along the south coast to monitor conditions and prepare for heavy rain, wind and possible flooding through the rest of the week.

“Ministry contractors are actively preparing by clearing debris from roadways and drainage infrastructure,” the statement said. “They will continue monitoring corridors throughout the storm and be ready to respond immediately to issues.”

Gismondi suggested people take steps to try to mitigate flooding, including making sure their storm drains are clear and to ensure loose objects are put away as heavy winds are also expected in the region.

“If you’re driving, watch for water pooling on the roads, try not to drive through any deep water,” he warned.

“Be aware of possible hydroplaning, keep your headlights on, keep a safe distance and slow down. Just try and be careful out there, and stay safe.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

stories.title: Ottawa says 4,306 Canadian veterans of Second World War, Korea still alive today
stories.summary: Ottawa — The number of living Canadian veterans of the Second World War and the Korean War has fallen sharply since Remembrance Day last year.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
OTTAWA — The number of living Canadian veterans of the Second World War and the Korean War has fallen sharply since Remembrance Day last year.

Veterans Affairs Canada said the estimated population of living Canadian veterans from those two wars has dropped to approximately 4,306.

Last year, the federal government department estimated their number at 5,649.

Veterans Affairs said it did not have a specific breakdown this year for the separate conflicts, or of the numbers of men and women who served.

In 2025, the department said it believed there were 3,691 surviving Second World War veterans and another 1,909 from the Korean War.

Michael Petrou, a historian at the Canadian War Museum in Ottawa, said the country is losing its “last living bridge” to the Second World War.

“We’re living in a society that was made or certainly impacted by the Second World War, so to lose that direct personal connection to those events is something very, very sad for us as citizens and especially, speaking from a personal perspective, for us as historians,” he told The Canadian Press.

Petrou recently edited the book “Ripples of War: The Canadian Veteran Experience.” The book, published Nov. 2, is a wide-ranging collection of academic essays and personal reflections from veterans.

The book examines personal experiences of war across a range of conflicts and social groups, including francophones, Indigenous peoples and merchant navy mariners who were long denied veteran status.

The book grew out of an oral history project at the museum called “In their own voices,” which included interviews with Second World War veterans.

“I had that opportunity,” said Petrou. “I feel very lucky for it but I’m also keenly aware that I will likely never have it again, and very soon no one else will.”

He said learning about the veteran experience and how it transcends generations and different conflicts, eras and wars reveals a unique sense of comradeship, purpose and grief that is “uncommon in the civilian world.”

Most veterans from the Second World War are at least in their late 90s now, while those who served in the Korean War are in their early to mid-90s.

The 2021 Census made a rare count of Canadians who served in the military and reported 461,240 Canadian Armed Forces vets living in Canada with an average age of 61.

More than 1.1 million Canadians and Newfoundlanders served during the Second World War. More than 45,000 of them died in the conflict.

Upwards of 26,000 Canadians served during the Korean War, which claimed the lives of 516 Canadian soldiers.

Three veterans of the Second World War were scheduled to attend Wednesday’s national Remembrance Day ceremony in Ottawa, each of them a centenarian.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

Kyle Duggan, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Some common forensics techniques aren't as reliable as courts presume: professor
stories.summary: A police dog sniffs out narcotics concealed in the depths of a nondescript car. An officer links a bullet found at a crime scene to a specific gun — and a specific suspect. An expert details the sequence of an attack based on the pattern of bloodstains in the area.
stories.author: Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press
stories.content:
flag wire: true flag sponsored: false article_type: pubinfo.section: cms.site.custom.site_domain : thestar.com sWebsitePrimaryPublication : publications/toronto_star bHasMigratedAvatar : false firstAuthor.avatar :

By Paola Loriggio The Canadian Press

A police dog sniffs out narcotics concealed in the depths of a nondescript car. An officer links a bullet found at a crime scene to a specific gun — and a specific suspect. An expert details the sequence of an attack based on the pattern of bloodstains in the area.

Such scenarios have been mainstays in crime shows and court cases for years, but new research suggests these forensic and investigative techniques are far less reliable than many presume.

Sara Gordon, an associate professor of law at the University of British Columbia, examined how Canadian courts deal with evidence related to sniffer dogs, ballistics analysis and blood spatter patterns in a series of papers, one recently issued and two slated for publication.

“With all three of them I saw this sort of tendency of courts and attorneys generally to just sort of assume that all of these different techniques are reliable,” Gordon said in a recent interview.

“We’ve all seen ‘CSI.’ People just sort of automatically believe that if a police officer is testifying that a bullet was fired from a particular gun, they must be correct. And that’s just not the case with all of these different techniques.”

While they have the “veneer of science,” the vast majority of forensic techniques weren’t developed in a lab or university but in police departments, Gordon said.

It’s only in the last 10 to 20 years or so that their validity has been put to the test empirically, and “for many of them, the evidence isn’t supportive of the types of conclusions examiners tend to reach,” she said.

For one thing, each of these techniques is vulnerable to some form of bias, she noted.

“If the police officer is pretty sure that a person has narcotics, they might unintentionally signal that to the dog. They can do that, just something as simple as kind of slowing down when they walk past the person and that can, unconsciously on the human’s part ... cue the dog to alert maybe even if there’s not drugs present,” Gordon said.

In ballistics and bloodstain pattern analyses, there’s a risk of contextual bias, since the majority of examiners are police officers, she said.

“By virtue of their position, they have access to information about the crime scene that can be biasing,” she said.

“For instance, if a bloodstain examiner has information about the crime scene, you know, maybe who was involved, the relationship between the victim and the accused ... they might go into that crime scene with a preconceived expectation about what they might find, and that can bias their interpretation of what they see there at the crime scene.”

A couple of major reports in the United States flagged the lack of scientific support for several forensics techniques used throughout North America about a decade ago, setting off a flurry of research, Gordon said.

Courts, however, have largely not caught up to the science, said Gordon, adding she aims to provide that information with her papers so that judges and attorneys can make informed decisions about the admissibility of evidence.

The Supreme Court of Canada last looked at the constitutionality of sniffer dog searches in 2013, finding that police could conduct such searches with less cause than for others because they are minimally intrusive and accurate.

Since then, a number of studies across jurisdictions have shown sniffer dogs to be far less reliable than believed, Gordon said.

Successful dog alerts, meaning those that lead to the discovery of illicit drugs, “are often no better than chance,” according to her paper in the Alberta Law Review. An ombudsman’s review out of New South Wales in Australia examined more than 10,000 alerts by 17 drug detection dogs and found that dogs falsely alerted to the presence of narcotics 74 per cent of the time, the paper said.

“There are no national standards for the training, testing, and deployment of police sniffer dogs in Canada, nor any meaningful transparency about how these functions are carried out by the dozens of canine units around the country,” Gordon wrote in the paper.

Dog searches are also far from minimally intrusive, she said.

“It can be embarrassing, it can be humiliating, and it can really scary for people. And that’s especially the case for racialized people or people who are sort of often subject to enhanced police scrutiny,” she said in the interview.

As such, the same standard of reasonable and probable grounds should be applied to sniffer dog searches to make sure they comply with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, she wrote in the paper.

Canadian courts have admitted ballistics evidence for nearly a century based primarily on examiners’ testimony that it’s reliable, “without subjecting those claims to meaningful scrutiny or limiting examiner conclusions to those that are empirically supported,” according to Gordon’s upcoming paper in the Dalhousie Law Journal.

While courts in the United States have started to push back, Gordon said she could only find one case in Canada where a judge refused to admit forensic firearms testimony due to concerns over the scientific validity of the technique.

The case, heard in Ontario five years ago, included testimony from a firearms examiner with the province’s Centre of Forensic Sciences, who said shell casings found at the scene were fired from a handgun found at the home of one of the accused, she wrote in the forthcoming paper.

Under cross-examination, the examiner said there was no specific number of “agreements,” or tiny corresponding markings on the two cartridge cases, required to conclude there was a match, the paper said.

That was one of the concerns raised by the judge in rejecting her testimony, the paper said. The judge also noted the examiner had not undergone proficiency testing, and that she had acknowledged the absence of a discipline-wide error rate for ballistics examiners, it said. He pointed to a landmark 2016 report in the United States that found no scientific support for the validity or reliability of firearms analysis.

Gordon’s paper said the validation studies ballistics examiners typically invoke to back up their expertise “suffer from significant methodological flaws,” including unrepresentative samples, testing conditions that don’t align with actual working conditions and the categorization of inconclusive results as correct. Meanwhile, examiners routinely present their conclusions in “highly certain terms” without disclosing the limitations of the technique, it said.

Ballistics examiners “will regularly testify in court that the error rate for that forensic technique is one per cent, one-and-a-half per cent,” the researcher said in the interview.

“It is absolutely not true that the error rates are that low. And forensic examiners just shouldn’t be permitted to testify to that.”

Recent studies on bloodstain pattern analysis have also shown very high levels of error, up to 32 per cent, Gordon wrote in another upcoming paper, this one for the Canadian Bar Review.

The technique does not appear to have received the scrutiny courts are required to apply to novel or contested scientific evidence, the paper said. Rather, courts have focused on the training and experience of the examiners in deciding whether to admit the evidence, “taking it for granted that the field is sufficiently reliable,” the paper said.

The principle underlying blood spatter analysis is said to be fluid dynamics, an “incredibly complicated” physics principle, Gordon said in the interview. While police officers receive training, some courses are as short as a weekend, and the vast majority of officers just don’t have the scientific training to apply those physics principles, she said.

“It’s a scientific language that dresses up this forensic technique, which is largely just the examiner ... looking at a particular pattern and saying, oh, that matches up with this other pattern that I’ve read about or that I studied,” she said.

“The problem is that they often try to go far beyond that and recreate crime scenes in really extreme detail,” she said. The science doesn’t support those kinds of conclusions, which are also particularly vulnerable to contextual bias, she said.

As a result, crime scene reconstruction based on bloodstain pattern analysis should generally be inadmissible, she wrote in the paper.

“A forensic technique with error rates exceeding 30 per cent should not be relied upon to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt,” the paper said.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

“There are no national standards for the training, testing, and deployment of police sniffer dogs in Canada, nor any meaningful transparency about how these functions are carried out by the dozens of canine units around the country,” Gordon wrote in the paper.
Dog searches are also far from minimally intrusive, she said.

“It can be embarrassing, it can be humiliating, and it can really scary for people. And that’s especially the case for racialized people or people who are sort of often subject to enhanced police scrutiny,” she said in the interview.
As such, the same standard of reasonable and probable grounds should be applied to sniffer dog searches to make sure they comply with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, she wrote in the paper.

Canadian courts have admitted ballistics evidence for nearly a century based primarily on examiners’ testimony that it’s reliable, “without subjecting those claims to meaningful scrutiny or limiting examiner conclusions to those that are empirically supported,” according to Gordon’s upcoming paper in the Dalhousie Law Journal.

While courts in the United States have started to push back, Gordon said she could only find one case in Canada where a judge refused to admit forensic firearms testimony due to concerns over the scientific validity of the technique.

The case, heard in Ontario five years ago, included testimony from a firearms examiner with the province’s Centre of Forensic Sciences, who said shell casings found at the scene were fired from a handgun found at the home of one of the accused, she wrote in the forthcoming paper.

Under cross-examination, the examiner said there was no specific number of “agreements,” or tiny corresponding markings on the two cartridge cases, required to conclude there was a match, the paper said.

That was one of the concerns raised by the judge in rejecting her testimony, the paper said. The judge also noted the examiner had not undergone proficiency testing, and that she had acknowledged the absence of a discipline-wide error rate for ballistics examiners, it said. He pointed to a landmark 2016 report in the United States that found no scientific support for the validity or reliability of firearms analysis.

Gordon’s paper said the validation studies ballistics examiners typically invoke to back up their expertise “suffer from significant methodological flaws,” including unrepresentative samples, testing conditions that don’t align with actual working conditions and the categorization of inconclusive results as correct. Meanwhile, examiners routinely present their conclusions in “highly certain terms” without disclosing the limitations of the technique, it said.
Ballistics examiners “will regularly testify in court that the error rate for that forensic technique is one per cent, one-and-a-half per cent,” the researcher said in the interview.
“It is absolutely not true that the error rates are that low. And forensic examiners just shouldn’t be permitted to testify to that.”
Recent studies on bloodstain pattern analysis have also shown very high levels of error, up to 32 per cent, Gordon wrote in another upcoming paper, this one for the Canadian Bar Review.

The technique does not appear to have received the scrutiny courts are required to apply to novel or contested scientific evidence, the paper said. Rather, courts have focused on the training and experience of the examiners in deciding whether to admit the evidence, “taking it for granted that the field is sufficiently reliable,” the paper said.

The principle underlying blood spatter analysis is said to be fluid dynamics, an “incredibly complicated” physics principle, Gordon said in the interview. While police officers receive training, some courses are as short as a weekend, and the vast majority of officers just don’t have the scientific training to apply those physics principles, she said.

“It’s a scientific language that dresses up this forensic technique, which is largely just the examiner ... looking at a particular pattern and saying, oh, that matches up with this other pattern that I’ve read about or that I studied,” she said.

“The problem is that they often try to go far beyond that and recreate crime scenes in really extreme detail,” she said. The science doesn’t support those kinds of conclusions, which are also particularly vulnerable to contextual bias, she said.
As a result, crime scene reconstruction based on bloodstain pattern analysis should generally be inadmissible, she wrote in the paper.
“A forensic technique with error rates exceeding 30 per cent should not be relied upon to establish guilt beyond a reasonable doubt,” the paper said.

stories.title: Legal battle over federal firearms ban heads to Supreme Court of Canada
stories.summary: Ottawa - The country's top court is set to hear legal arguments this week about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.
stories.author: Jim Bronskill The Canadian Press
stories.content:
OTTAWA - The country’s top court began hearing legal arguments Monday about the validity of a federal ban on hundreds of types of firearms the government says are fit only for the battlefield.

The hearings, which continue Tuesday at the Supreme Court of Canada, will give opponents of the ban another chance to make their case after losing in the Federal Court and Federal Court of Appeal.

In May 2020, the government prohibited the use, sale and importation of 1,500 firearm models and variants, including the AR-15 and Ruger Mini-14. The move was applauded by gun control advocates as a first step toward removing these firearms from circulation.

In October 2023, a Federal Court judge dismissed a request to strike down the ban as unlawful and beyond the scope of the powers delegated to the Governor in Council — effectively the federal cabinet.

A not-for-profit advocacy organization, firearm owners, businesses, hunters and recreational and sport shooters appealed the ruling.

In April 2025, the Federal Court of Appeal rejected that appeal, saying the Federal Court delivered “thorough and persuasive” reasons.

The list of guns banned by the Liberal government has grown to more than 2,500 varieties of what it calls assault-style firearms.

Before the Supreme Court agreed to examine the matter, the government said the prohibited firearms would have to be disposed of or deactivated by the end of an amnesty period on Oct. 30 of this year.

That amnesty has been extended until 90 days after the Supreme Court delivers its decision, which is expected no later than next year.

On Monday, several judges put probing questions to counsel about the details of the federal measures.

A key question before the Federal Court of Appeal was whether the Governor in Council adhered to a provision of the law forbidding it from using regulations to outlaw a firearm if it considers the gun “reasonable for use in Canada for hunting or sporting purposes.”

Writing on behalf of a unanimous three-judge panel, Court of Appeal Chief Justice Yves de Montigny said he was not persuaded that the government erred in considering public safety when assessing whether the prohibited firearms were reasonable for use in Canada for such purposes.

“It may well be that, from the sole perspective of a sensible hunter or sportsman, it makes no sense to ban firearms that are well suited or even specifically designed for hunting or sport purposes,” he wrote.

The federal cabinet is the most senior policy-making body in government and, because of its role at the apex of the executive branch, is best situated to develop government policy and assess the public interest, de Montigny added.

“Surely, the inherent danger that some firearms pose to public safety because of their lethality and their ability to injure or kill a large number of people in a short period of time, the fact that they have been used in mass shootings in Canada and abroad, the fact that they are disproportionate for civilian use, and the increasing demand for measures to address gun violence are all valid considerations in determining whether their use is reasonable for hunting and sporting purposes,” he wrote.

In a written submission to the Supreme Court, federal lawyers say the Governor in Council’s exercise of its broad discretion was reasonable and justified by the serious public safety concerns these firearms present.

The submission points to a regulatory impact analysis statement that supports the Governor in Council’s opinion. That statement said that while some hunters and sport shooters lawfully used some of these firearms in the past, these guns can increase the severity of mass shootings and have been used in such shootings in Canada and in other countries.

The firearms prohibited in 2020 were owned by a small minority of Canadian firearms owners, estimated at between three and five per cent of the total, the federal submission adds.

“Thousands of alternative firearms remain legally available for hunting and sporting use,” it says. “The GIC’s opinion, balancing public interest policy considerations, was reasonable.”

A group of appellants that includes the Canadian Coalition for Firearm Rights says neither the Federal Court nor the Federal Court of Appeal considered whether the newly prohibited items were actually used for hunting or sport shooting.

“While recognizing that the misuse of firearms threatens public safety, Parliament chose to preserve hunting and sport shooting as legitimate, lawful, and socially accepted activities and uses of firearms,” they say in their submission to the Supreme Court.

For the hundreds of thousands of Canadians who lawfully owned and used the firearms prohibited by the 2020 regulations, this appeal is not an abstract debate about administrative law, the appellants add.

“It concerns the profound disruption of the lives of ordinary, law-abiding Canadians. Hunters, sport shooters, collectors and small businesses, individuals who complied with every requirement imposed by Parliament, found themselves overnight in possession of prohibited property, deprived of its lawful use and exposed to the prospect of criminal liability,” the submission says.

“They are not extremists; they are farmers, veterans, competitive athletes, Indigenous harvesters and neighbours in communities across Canada.”

Whether the Governor in Council acted within the limits Parliament imposed is not merely a question of statutory interpretation, the submission says.

“It determines whether the sweeping consequences imposed upon these Canadians were authorized by law.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: Third storm heads for already drenched B.C. coast
stories.summary: Vancouver - The third in a series of storms is heading for British Columbia, after wild weather knocked out power to thousands, triggered evacuations and left one person dead over the weekend.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
VANCOUVER - Forecasters are escalating rainfall warnings in southwest British Columbia, saying some areas could receive a deluge topping 250 millimetres in a new parade of storms that is set to drench the region.

Orange warnings have been raised for west and central Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky regions, with Environment Canada warning of flooding and landslides after the “very robust” frontal system makes landfall Tuesday morning.

Wild weather has been pummelling B.C. since last week and may have claimed a second victim, after the death of a pedestrian who was hit by a car in Vancouver while she was crossing the road during a heavy downpour.

Police noted the weather conditions when they announced that the 78-year-old woman had died in hospital on Saturday, the day after the crash in an unmarked crosswalk at Dunbar Street and West 34th Avenue.

The storms had claimed their first known fatality on Saturday in Surrey, B.C., when a tree fell on two vehicles and killed one of the drivers, while a canoeist has been missing in stormy waters off northern Vancouver Island since Friday.

Environment Canada has issued about a dozen wind and rain warnings due to the new series of storms set to lash the southern and central coasts of B.C. until Thursday, after wild weekend weather that temporarily cut power to about 415,000 BC Hydro customers.

More than 250 millimetres of rain is forecast for parts of Vancouver Island, while Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky areas could get more than 160 millimetres, the agency said Monday. Metro Vancouver could get more than 120 millimetres near the mountains.

The province’s River Forecast Centre has also issued a flood watch for much of southwest B.C.

The flood watch covers Howe Sound and the Sea to Sky, parts of Metro Vancouver, most of Vancouver Island, the Central Coast and northern Fraser Valley.

“The heaviest rain is forecast for Tuesday and Wednesday, with lingering rainfall continuing through the rest of the week,” the province’s River Forecast Centre said on Monday.

Residents are being asked to stay away from river banks of fast-moving water and to never cross flooded roads or bridges.

Communities have begun preparing for the incoming storms, with the City of Vancouver opening additional shelter spaces on Monday and Tuesday.

“This rainfall event comes on the heels of several low pressure systems that have moved through the region in recent days, already bringing substantial amounts of precipitation to parts of the coast,” Environment Canada said in a weather statement.

Low-pressure systems over the weekend drenched southwest B.C., triggering an evacuation order for about 30 properties in the village of Zeballos on northwest Vancouver Island.

Nearby, the Ma’amtagila Nation along the Central Coast says a man who went to sea on Friday in a canoe is missing in waters off northern Vancouver Island.

The nation says the vessel was found capsized, while Environment Canada says gusts reached 88 kilometres per hour in nearby waters that day.

“There are many beaches and forested areas that searchers have not been able to reach, and as the weather worsens, we desperately need the support of the trained personnel and equipment that exists for this exact situation,” the Ma’amtagila Tribe Society says in an open letter on Facebook pleading for federal search assistance.

“Our community will not stop looking, and we fear the danger they are in.”

Winds reached 116 kilometres an hour on Herbert Island off northern Vancouver Island on Sunday, with Victoria’s airport recording 96 kilometres an hour.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

stories.title: B.C. lab ordered to pay $32K for misgendering transgender, non-binary patients
stories.summary: British Columbia's human rights tribunal has ruled that a private laboratory provider must pay $32,000 in damages, along with other costs, for discriminating against transgender and non-binary patients.
stories.author: News Staff
stories.content:
British Columbia’s human rights tribunal has ruled that a private laboratory provider must pay $32,000 in damages, along with other costs, for discriminating against transgender and non-binary patients.

The tribunal found LifeLabs and its subsidiary Excelleris Technologies misgendered and outed three patients at clinics in Vancouver and Burnaby in 2019.

Its decision says a non-binary person was told they had to choose either male or female to receive lab services and was outed to other patients by being required to discuss their gender identity in a public space.

It also says one transgender patient was unable to update their gender marker on medical records, and another was misgendered on lab reports and opted out of necessary cancer screening to avoid being misgendered again.

The tribunal heard last year from one expert who said gender-diverse people face barriers in accessing health care, and that misgendering can be a “significant source of distress.”

Tribunal member Theressa Etmanski says LifeLabs must update its policies and staff training around gender identity, and make available to transgender and non-binary patients private spaces to discuss their identity.

“Information about a patient’s sex may be medically relevant in the provision of laboratory services. However, I wish to be clear that there is no evidence before me to support that the standard is medically necessary or justified,” Etmanski says in the decision issued Oct. 29, 2026.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 8, 2026.

Aaron Sousa, The Canadian Press

stories.title: Pjhl Recap - Nov 6th to Nov 8th
stories.summary: The Braves had a winning weekend while the Merchants and the Trojans had mixed results.
stories.author: Marcie Culbert
stories.content:
News Home

Monday, 9 November 2026 at 07:23

By Marcie Culbert X @marcieculbert

Share on Facebook

Share on Messenger

Share on Messenger

The Braves had a winning weekend while the Merchants and the Trojans had mixed results.

PJHL - The Tavistock Braves have cemented their place at the top of the PJHL Doherty Division standings.

They suffered three wins over the weekend, starting with a 6-0 shutout win over the Dorchester Dolphins on Friday. They also slipped past the Paris Mounties 3-2 in overtime on Saturday and narrowly beat the Hespeler Shamrocks 4-3 in overtime yesterday.

The Norwich Merchants suffered a 6-1 loss to the Wellesley Applejacks on Friday and doubled the Dolphins 6-3 on Saturday.

stories.title: Osap pause May force dental college to close, school says
stories.summary: An Ontario career college that has trained dental hygienists and dental assistants for 22 years May have to close as early as next month, due to a provincewide pause on student financial aid in the sector.
stories.author: The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario career college that has trained dental hygienists and dental assistants for 22 years May have to close as early as next month, due to a provincewide pause on student financial aid in the sector.

Tuition at Southern Ontario Dental College in Hamilton is high, due to the technical programs students describe as rigorous and hands-on, and as a result most of the students rely on Ontario Student Assistance Program funding.

But Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn last month stopped Osap payments to all private post-secondary institution students due to what he calls serious concerns unearthed in the early stages of a sector-wide audit.

He has indicated the pause will continue into the new year, but Southern Ontario Dental College says it May not last until then without alternate funding.

“If we continue to go right now the way that we’re going without collecting any money from the students, we’ll have to close our doors probably in December,” said Alysse Estrabillo, the school’s chief operating officer.

For now, the students have set up a food bank in a room at the college to help each other out, she said.

Haylie Eady, a dental hygienist student and single mom, does not know how she could pay the tuition of nearly $52,000 for the two-year program, and she was also depending on an Osap loan to pay living expenses like child care, food and rent.

She quit her dental assistant job to go back to school and upgrade her skills, but is now taking odd jobs she finds through Facebook ads so she can provide for her children. Eady just recently received a notice of non-payment of rent, though she is hopeful that will be resolved.

“I want a career where I can make a difference, not only in the community but in my home, so that my kids never have to worry about a single thing,” Eady said.

“I feel like, in trying to make that step, I was put in a position to make them have to worry about when their next meal is going to be. ... My kids have dreams too, and it leaves parents feeling like maybe they put their dreams ahead of their kids.”

Quinn has said the government is trying to secure third-party loans through financial institutions while the pause is ongoing, but he has not given any updates since making that announcement one month ago.

A spokesperson said evidence of systemic issues left the government with no choice but to pause Osap payments to all private institutions to ensure the integrity of the system.

“We recognize the impact that this pause is having on students and are working to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to support students through this period of transition,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial Osap grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

Many other schools and students are left wondering why the government has not taken a more targeted approach to rooting out possible abuse in the system. Premier Doug Ford has said the Kpmg auditors have been asked to prioritize clearing low-risk schools first, but students like Eady wonder why their schools were cut off at all.

She and her fellow students had to meet certain criteria to apply, then do an interview and skills testing, she said.

“We all fought so unbelievably hard just to sit in a seat in that room,” Eady said.

Estrabillo said the school never imagined Osap would just suddenly one day stop.

“People come to our college and want to be educated, and they’re so excited to learn,” she said. “We’ve graduated so many classes in 22 years, and to think that would stop because of this just is unfathomable to me.”

With the college facing closure, the Osap pause is affecting even the students who never applied for the loans.

Diane Yu is one of those students, now in her second year of the dental hygiene program, and she worries that the Osap pause and potential school closure could derail her career path.

“It’s pretty devastating,” she said.

“This is my third term and I only have one left after this. I wanted to only focus on my board exam and the clinical hours. This is the most important time of this education and this is the worst timing to face this issue.”

Career Colleges Ontario said it couldn’t comment on specific cases, but a spokesperson said there is every reason to believe that more stories of schools facing closure will emerge.

“The ongoing Osap pause is creating significant uncertainty across the sector, with schools facing mounting pressure and no clear timeline for when students’ funding will resume,” Taylor Buck wrote in a statement.

“The longer this uncertainty continues, the harder decisions schools will be forced to make, and ultimately students will bear the consequences.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.

Allison Jones, The Canadian Press

stories.title: York University investigating cybersecurity incident, data theft
stories.summary: Toronto - York University is investigating a cybersecurity incident resulting in the theft of personal data which was discovered last month.
stories.author: Sadeen Mohsen The Canadian Press
stories.content:
The school said an unauthorized actor accessed information of individuals who completed online forms on select websites, such as residence applications and surveys, ranging from 2007 to October 2026.

The breach, discovered on Oct. 25, was limited to a specific list of websites and faculties posted on their website, the school said.

Meta’s methods of moderation

Image 10Image 11

York University said a small number of directly affected individuals had their government identification or financial account information exposed.

The school said it immediately began an investigation into the breach alongside the help of external experts.

The university did not disclose when the incident took place or when it discovered the breach. The investigation found no evidence that the unauthorized actor moved beyond the affected websites or accessed other parts of the university.

“Affected individuals should remain alert for suspicious emails, text messages and telephone calls, particularly communications asking for personal information or directing them to unfamiliar websites,” the school said in a news release.

It is also asking the affected individuals, who will be contacted directly, to monitor their financial accounts.

York University is offering two years of complimentary TransUnion credit monitoring and identity theft protection to the individuals who had their government or financial information exposed.

The incident was reported to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario and law enforcement.

“We recognize that this incident may be concerning to you,” the school said. “We take that seriously and regret these circumstances.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 8, 2026.

The Canadian Press

stories.title: Osap pause May force dental college to close, school says
stories.summary: An Ontario career college that has trained dental hygienists and dental assistants for 22 years May have to close as early as next month, due to a provincewide pause on student financial aid in the sector.
stories.author: Allison Jones The Canadian Press
stories.content:
An Ontario career college that has trained dental hygienists and dental assistants for 22 years may have to close as early as next month, due to a provincewide pause on student financial aid in the sector.

Tuition at Southern Ontario Dental College in Hamilton is high, due to the technical programs students describe as rigorous and hands-on, and as a result most of the students rely on Ontario Student Assistance Program funding.

But Colleges and Universities Minister Nolan Quinn last month stopped OSAP payments to all private post-secondary institution students due to what he calls serious concerns unearthed in the early stages of a sector-wide audit.

He has indicated the pause will continue into the new year, but Southern Ontario Dental College says it may not last until then without alternate funding.

“If we continue to go right now the way that we’re going without collecting any money from the students, we’ll have to close our doors probably in December,” said Alysse Estrabillo, the school’s chief operating officer.

How students in different situations are coping with the sudden loss of access to student aid.

For now, the students have set up a food bank in a room at the college to help each other out, she said.

Haylie Eady, a dental hygienist student and single mom, does not know how she could pay the tuition of nearly $52,000 for the two-year program, and she was also depending on an OSAP loan to pay living expenses like child care, food and rent.

She quit her dental assistant job to go back to school and upgrade her skills, but is now taking odd jobs she finds through Facebook ads so she can provide for her children. Eady just recently received a notice of non-payment of rent, though she is hopeful that will be resolved.

“I want a career where I can make a difference, not only in the community but in my home, so that my kids never have to worry about a single thing,” Eady said.

“I feel like, in trying to make that step, I was put in a position to make them have to worry about when their next meal is going to be. ... My kids have dreams too, and it leaves parents feeling like maybe they put their dreams ahead of their kids.”

Quinn has said the government is trying to secure third-party loans through financial institutions while the pause is ongoing, but he has not given any updates since making that announcement one month ago.

A spokesperson said evidence of systemic issues left the government with no choice but to pause OSAP payments to all private institutions to ensure the integrity of the system.

All Ontario private colleges have been caught up in a ban on access to student aid during the third-party audit.

“We recognize the impact that this pause is having on students and are working to develop options for low-interest, third-party loans facilitated by financial institutions to support students through this period of transition,” Bianca Giacoboni wrote in a statement.

Between 2023-24 and 2024-25, the amount of provincial OSAP grants to career colleges nearly doubled, to about $1 billion in the latter year. That was largely due to activity at a small number of career colleges, according to data obtained by The Canadian Press through a freedom-of-information request.

The ministry alleges that some of those schools were unable to verify students were attending class or completing their own coursework, allegations the schools deny.

Many other schools and students are left wondering why the government has not taken a more targeted approach to rooting out possible abuse in the system. Premier Doug Ford has said the KPMG auditors have been asked to prioritize clearing low-risk schools first, but students like Eady wonder why their schools were cut off at all.

She and her fellow students had to meet certain criteria to apply, then do an interview and skills testing, she said.

“We all fought so unbelievably hard just to sit in a seat in that room,” Eady said.

Estrabillo said the school never imagined OSAP would just suddenly one day stop.

“People come to our college and want to be educated, and they’re so excited to learn,” she said. “We’ve graduated so many classes in 22 years, and to think that would stop because of this just is unfathomable to me.”

With the college facing closure, the OSAP pause is affecting even the students who never applied for the loans.

Diane Yu is one of those students, now in her second year of the dental hygiene program, and she worries that the OSAP pause and potential school closure could derail her career path.

“It’s pretty devastating,” she said.

“This is my third term and I only have one left after this. I wanted to only focus on my board exam and the clinical hours. This is the most important time of this education and this is the worst timing to face this issue.”

Career Colleges Ontario said it couldn’t comment on specific cases, but a spokesperson said there is every reason to believe that more stories of schools facing closure will emerge.

“The ongoing OSAP pause is creating significant uncertainty across the sector, with schools facing mounting pressure and no clear timeline for when students’ funding will resume,” Taylor Buck wrote in a statement.

“The longer this uncertainty continues, the harder decisions schools will be forced to make, and ultimately students will bear the consequences.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 9, 2026.
